items.text: משנת הפתיחה: דיני חלוקת טלית בשבועה
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Two holding a garment
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents two cases: both claimants say 'I found it' and 'it is all mine', so they swear and divide; one says 'all mine' and the other 'half mine', so they swear and take three-quarters and one-quarter respectively. It also covers two riders on an animal, and notes that if they admit or have witnesses, they divide without an oath.
items.desc: המשנה פותחת במקרה של שניים האוחזים בטלית, כל אחד טוען שמצאה כולה שלו. הדין הוא שכל אחד נשבע שאין לו בה פחות מחציה, והם חולקים. המשנה מביאה גם מקרה שבו אחד טוען כולה שלו והשני חציה, ואז חלוקת החלקים היא לפי שבועות שונות. כמו כן מובא דין דומה לגבי בהמה, וסייג לחלוקה ללא שבועה כשהם מודים או יש עדים.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of two claimants holding a garment, each claiming full ownership, and prescribes an oath and division.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בדין שניים האוחזים בטלית וכל אחד טוען שמצאה כולה שלו, והדין שישבעו ויחלוקו.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the second case where one claims all and the other claims half, with proportional oaths and division.
sub.desc: המשנה מביאה מקרה נוסף שבו אחד טוען כולה שלו והשני חציה, והדין הוא חלוקה לפי שבועות שונות.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah extends the rule to two riders on an animal, applying the same oath and division.
sub.desc: המשנה מביאה דין דומה לגבי בהמה, ששניים רוכבים או אחד רוכב ואחד מנהיג, והדין שישבעו ויחלוקו.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah concludes that if the parties admit or have witnesses, they divide without an oath.
sub.desc: המשנה מסכמת שכאשר הם מודים או יש עדים, חולקים ללא שבועה.

items.text: Gemara's first question: Why both phrases?
items.text_en: Gemara's first question: Why both phrases?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah includes both 'I found it' and 'it is all mine' – it could have taught only one. It suggests that the Mishnah is actually one statement: 'I found it and it is all mine'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah includes both 'I found it' and 'it is all mine' – it could have taught only one. It suggests that the Mishnah is actually one statement: 'I found it and it is all mine'.

items.text: Answer: To exclude acquisition by sight
items.text_en: Answer: To exclude acquisition by sight
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that if only 'I found it' were taught, one might think mere sight (ראיה) acquires ownership. Therefore the Mishnah adds 'it is all mine' to show that sight does not acquire.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that if only 'I found it' were taught, one might think mere sight (ראיה) acquires ownership, so the Mishnah adds 'it is all mine' to show that sight does not acquire.

items.text: Objection and resolution: 'Found' implies possession
items.text_en: Objection and resolution: 'Found' implies possession
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the word 'found' (מצאתיה) implies coming into one's hand, as per the verse 'ומצאתה'. It resolves that the Mishnah uses common language, where one says 'I found' even upon mere sight, but the addition of 'it is all mine' teaches that sight does not acquire.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the word 'מצאתיה' (I found it) must imply physical possession, citing the verse 'ומצאתה' which indicates coming into one's hand.

The Gemara resolves that the verse indeed implies possession, but the Mishnah uses common language where one says 'I found' upon mere sight; the addition 'it is all mine' teaches that sight alone does not acquire.

items.text: Alternative question: Why not just 'it is all mine'?
items.text_en: Alternative question: Why not just 'it is all mine'?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah did not teach only 'it is all mine' without 'I found it'. It answers that if only 'it is all mine' were taught, one might think that 'found' in the Mishnah means sight acquires; therefore the Mishnah teaches both to show that sight does not acquire.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah did not teach only 'it is all mine' without the phrase 'I found it'.
The Gemara answers that if only 'it is all mine' were taught, one might think that 'found' in the Mishnah means sight acquires; therefore the Mishnah teaches both to show that sight does not acquire.

items.text: Objection: The Mishnah's wording implies two cases
items.text_en: Objection: The Mishnah's wording implies two cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's repeated 'this one says... and this one says...' indicates two separate statements, not one combined statement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's wording 'this one says... and this one says...' indicates two separate statements, not one combined statement.

items.text: Resolution: Two distinct cases – found object and purchase
items.text_en: Resolution: Two distinct cases – found object and purchase
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa (or Rav Shimi bar Ashi) resolves that the first part of the Mishnah deals with a found object (מציאה) and the latter part with a purchase (מקח וממכר). The Gemara adds that both cases are necessary.

sub.text: Rav Pappa (or Rav Shimi bar Ashi)
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa (or Rav Shimi bar Ashi)
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa (or Rav Shimi bar Ashi) resolves that the first part of the Mishnah deals with a found object (מציאה) and the latter part with a purchase (מקח וממכר).
The Gemara adds that both cases are necessary.

items.text: Why both cases are necessary
items.text_en: Why both cases are necessary
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that if only the case of a found object were taught, one might think the oath applies only there because the finder loses nothing, but not in a purchase where both parties pay. Conversely, if only purchase were taught, one might think the oath applies only there because each claims to have paid, but not in a found object. Therefore both are needed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara argues that if only the case of a found object were taught, one might think the oath applies only there because the finder loses nothing, but not in a purchase where both parties pay.
The Gemara concludes that both cases are necessary, because if only purchase were taught, one might think the oath applies only there, but not in a found object.

items.text: Question about identifying the payer
items.text_en: Question about identifying the payer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: In a purchase, why not examine the coins to see from whom they came? It answers that the case is where each party holds one coin, one willingly and one under duress, and we don't know which is which.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: In a purchase case, why not examine the coins to see from whom they came?
The Gemara answers: The case is where each party holds one coin, one willingly and one under duress, and we don't know which is which.

items.text: Challenge from Ben Nannas and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from Ben Nannas and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the Mishnah might not align with Ben Nannas, who says that when both claimants swear, it leads to a vain oath. It responds that even Ben Nannas would agree here, since there is no vain oath if both lifted the garment together.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah might not align with Ben Nannas, who holds that when both claimants swear, it leads to a vain oath (שבועת שוא).
The Gemara resolves that even Ben Nannas would agree here, since there is no vain oath if both lifted the garment together (אגבוהי).

items.text: Challenge from Sumkhos and multiple resolutions
items.text_en: Challenge from Sumkhos and multiple resolutions
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the Mishnah might not align with Sumkhos, who says disputed money is divided without oath. It defends the Mishnah by distinguishing: Sumkhos only applies to uncertain claims (שמא ושמא), not certain ones (ברי וברי). Even according to Rabbah bar Rav Huna who extends Sumkhos, it applies only where there is a monetary loss (דררא דממונא), which is absent here.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah does not align with Sumkhos, who rules that disputed money is divided without an oath.
The Gemara objects that if the Mishnah follows the Rabbis, they would require the burden of proof on the claimant, which is not the case here.
The Gemara resolves that the Rabbis distinguish between cases where neither party holds the object (requiring proof) and where both hold it (dividing with an oath).
The Gemara objects that according to Sumkhos, if disputed money is divided without oath even when neither holds it, then when both hold it, it should certainly be divided without oath.
The Gemara resolves that Sumkhos only applies to uncertain claims (שמא ושמא), not to certain ones (ברי וברי), which is the case here.
The Gemara asks what can be said according to Rabbah bar Rav Huna, who extends Sumkhos even to certain claims (ברי וברי).
The Gemara resolves that even according to Rabbah bar Rav Huna, Sumkhos only applies where there is a monetary loss (דררא דממונא), which is absent here.
The Gemara objects with a קל וחומר (a fortiori) argument: if Sumkhos applies where there is a monetary loss for one party, it should certainly apply where both parties have a monetary loss.

items.text: Sumchos' principle and the Gemara's defense
items.text_en: Sumchos' principle and the Gemara's defense
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers Sumchos' view that disputed money is divided without oath, and argues that here, where both might own it, an oath is rabbinic to prevent theft, per Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question from Sumchos' principle that disputed money is divided without oath, arguing that here, where both might own it, the case is even stronger.
The Gemara answers that even according to Sumchos, this oath is a rabbinic enactment per Rabbi Yochanan, to prevent each person from seizing another's garment.

items.text: Attempt to identify the Mishnah as not Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Attempt to identify the Mishnah as not Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the Mishnah might not follow Rabbi Yosei, who would leave the money until Elijah comes to penalize a liar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah does not follow Rabbi Yosei, who would leave the money until Elijah comes to penalize a liar.

items.text: Rejection: The Rabbis would also leave it
items.text_en: Rejection: The Rabbis would also leave it
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that even the Rabbis would leave the money until Elijah in a certain case, but here they divide with an oath because both might own it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that since the Rabbis rule 'the remainder shall be left until Elijah comes' in a case of doubt, here too the money is doubtful and should be left.
The Gemara resolves that the Rabbis distinguish: there, one party definitely owns the money, so it is left; here, both might own it, so they divide with an oath.

items.text: Reconsideration: It could be Rabbi Yosei after all
items.text_en: Reconsideration: It could be Rabbi Yosei after all
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that even Rabbi Yosei would not penalize here because there is no certain liar, unlike the case of a deposit where one is definitely lying.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara argues that if the mishna follows Rabbi Yosei, then the case of a found garment should certainly require the money to be set aside until Elijah comes, since even in a case of definite ownership Rabbi Yosei requires that.
The Gemara answers that even according to Rabbi Yosei, here there is no certain liar because both may have lifted the garment together, so the penalty of setting aside the money does not apply.
Alternatively, the Gemara explains that Rabbi Yosei only penalizes a definite liar to force him to admit the truth, but here there is no loss to the claimant that would motivate a false denial.

items.text: Transition to the storekeeper and laborer case
items.text_en: Transition to the storekeeper and laborer case
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's ruling for a found object is settled, but questions the case of a purchase and sale, then resolves it as previously taught.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: the case of a found object is settled, but what can be said about the case of a purchase and sale?
The Gemara resolves: it is clarified as we originally taught.

items.text: Comparison with the storekeeper and laborer
items.text_en: Comparison with the storekeeper and laborer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why in the storekeeper and laborer case they swear and take from the homeowner, rather than leaving the money until Elijah, and explains that each party blames the homeowner for trusting the other.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that in the storekeeper and laborer case, both parties swear and take from the homeowner, regardless of whether the ruling follows the Rabbis or Rabbi Yosei.
The Gemara asks why in this case the money is not left until Elijah comes, since there is certainly a liar involved.
The Gemara explains that each party blames the homeowner for trusting the other, so both swear and take from the homeowner rather than leaving the money pending.

items.text: Baraita of Rabbi Chiyya and the kal vachomer
items.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Chiyya and the kal vachomer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya teaches that if witnesses testify to part of a claim, the defendant pays that part and swears on the rest, derived from a kal vachomer that testimony is stronger than admission. The Gemara explains the logic using Rabba's principle about a partial admitter.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya teaches a baraita: if a claimant says 'you owe me a maneh' and the defendant denies entirely, but witnesses testify that he owes fifty zuz, the defendant pays fifty and swears on the remainder.
The baraita justifies the ruling with a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument): verbal admission should not be stronger than witness testimony.

The Gemara objects: in the Mishnah of two holding a garment, each is physically holding part, yet the Mishnah requires an oath — contradicting the baraita's implication that physical possession eliminates the need for an oath.

sub.text: Gemara's question about the kal vachomer
sub.text_en: Gemara's question about the kal vachomer
sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what exactly is the קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) meant to teach?

The Gemara answers by citing Rabba's principle: the Torah imposes an oath on a partial admitter because a person is not brazen enough to deny entirely in front of his creditor, so partial admission reveals truthfulness.

items.text: Gemara's explanation of the Mishnah's logic
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the Mishnah's logic
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's ruling that witnesses impose an oath is derived from a kal vachomer from the defendant's own admission. The admission case involves a defendant who admits partially to avoid full payment, so an oath is imposed to compel full admission; witnesses, who cannot be avoided, might not seem to require an oath, but the kal vachomer teaches otherwise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the defendant who partially admits intends to avoid full payment, so the Torah imposes an oath to compel full admission; but witnesses, who cannot be avoided, might not require an oath.
The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah teaches the ruling through a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument).

items.text: The kal vachomer argument
items.text_en: The kal vachomer argument
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents the kal vachomer: if a person's own admission, which does not obligate him to pay money, obligates him to take an oath, then witnesses, who do obligate him to pay money, should certainly obligate him to take an oath.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the kal vachomer argument is.

The kal vachomer argues: if a person's own admission, which does not obligate him to pay money, obligates him to take an oath, then witnesses, who do obligate him to pay money, should certainly obligate him to take an oath.

items.text: Objection: admission does obligate payment
items.text_en: Objection: admission does obligate payment
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the premise is false: a person's admission does obligate him to pay money, as the principle 'admission of a litigant is like a hundred witnesses' applies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to the premise that a person's admission does not obligate him to pay money, citing the principle that admission of a litigant is like a hundred witnesses.

items.text: Refinement: 'money' refers to a fine
items.text_en: Refinement: 'money' refers to a fine
items.desc_en: The Gemara refines the kal vachomer: 'money' in the argument refers specifically to a fine (kenas). Admission does not obligate a fine, but witnesses do, so the kal vachomer stands.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the objection by reinterpreting 'money' in the kal vachomer as a fine (קנס), which admission does not obligate but witnesses do, thereby preserving the argument.

items.text: Objection: admission obligates a sacrifice
items.text_en: Objection: admission obligates a sacrifice
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the kal vachomer is flawed because admission has a unique stringency: it obligates a sacrifice (for an oath of testimony), which witnesses do not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the kal vachomer is flawed because admission (פיו) has a unique stringency: it obligates a sacrifice (קרבן) for an oath of testimony, which witnesses do not.

items.text: Defense: Rabbi Chiya follows Rabbi Meir's view
items.text_en: Defense: Rabbi Chiya follows Rabbi Meir's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara defends the kal vachomer by noting that Rabbi Chiya holds like Rabbi Meir, who rules that witnesses do obligate a sacrifice via a kal vachomer. The Mishnah in Keritot is cited where Rabbi Meir argues that if witnesses can bring a person to a severe death penalty, they can certainly bring him to a light sacrifice; the Sages object that one could claim intent to exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the objection by stating that Rabbi Chiya holds like Rabbi Meir, who rules that witnesses obligate a sacrifice via a kal vachomer.
The Gemara cites a Mishnah in Keritot where Rabbi Meir obligates a sacrifice based on witnesses' testimony, while the Sages exempt.
Rabbi Meir argues via kal vachomer that if witnesses can bring a person to severe death, they can certainly bring him to a light sacrifice.
The Sages object that one could claim intent to exempt, undermining the kal vachomer.

items.text: Alternative objection: admission obligates an asham or chomesh
items.text_en: Alternative objection: admission obligates an asham or chomesh
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers other unique aspects of admission: it obligates an asham (a type of sacrifice) or a chomesh (fifth). It concludes that Rabbi Chiya, following Rabbi Meir, would also derive these via kal vachomer, so the objection is not decisive.

sub.desc_en: The objection raises that admission (פיו) obligates an asham sacrifice, which is a type of korban, and this unique aspect cannot be derived by kal vachomer for witnesses.
The objection shifts to argue that admission obligates a chomesh (fifth), another unique aspect not applicable to witnesses.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Chiya follows Rabbi Meir, who derives both korban and chomesh from witnesses via kal vachomer, so the objection is not decisive.

items.text: Objection: admission cannot be contradicted or disqualified
items.text_en: Objection: admission cannot be contradicted or disqualified
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that admission is unique because it cannot be contradicted or disqualified (hach'chashah and hazamah), unlike witnesses. This undermines the kal vachomer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the kal vachomer from admission to witnesses fails because admission cannot be contradicted or disqualified (הכחשה והזמה), unlike witnesses.

items.text: Alternative derivation from a single witness
items.text_en: Alternative derivation from a single witness
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a different kal vachomer from a single witness: if one witness, who does not obligate payment, obligates an oath, then two witnesses, who do obligate payment, should certainly obligate an oath. The Gemara then notes an objection: a single witness is unique because he himself takes an oath on his testimony.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a new kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) from a single witness: if one witness, who does not obligate payment, obligates an oath, then two witnesses, who do obligate payment, should certainly obligate an oath.
The Gemara objects that a single witness is unique because he himself takes an oath on his testimony, a feature not shared by two witnesses.

items.text: Attempt to derive from the principle of גלגול שבועה
items.text_en: Attempt to derive from the principle of גלגול שבועה
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa proposes deriving the liability of witnesses to swear from the principle of גלגול שבועה (rolling oath) of a single witness. The Gemara rejects this because a single witness's oath is unique in that it is a 'rolling' oath, whereas witnesses impose a monetary liability. The Gemara then attempts to compare witnesses to the defendant's own admission (פיו) and to a single witness, but each comparison is refuted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that in the case of two witnesses, the defendant swears about what he denies, not about what they testify.
Rav Pappa proposes deriving the liability from the principle of גלגול שבועה (rolling oath) of a single witness.
The Gemara rejects this because a single witness's oath is unique in that one oath leads to another, whereas witnesses impose monetary liability.

The Gemara attempts to compare witnesses to the defendant's own admission (פיו), but notes that admission is not subject to contradiction, whereas a single witness is subject to contradiction and still obligates an oath.

The Gemara rejects the comparison to a single witness because a single witness's oath is about what he testifies, whereas witnesses' oath is about what the defendant denies; admission (פיו) can prove this difference irrelevant.

items.text: The common denominator argument (הצד השוה)
items.text_en: The common denominator argument (הצד השוה)
items.desc_en: The Gemara constructs a formal argument from the common denominator (הצד השוה) of the cases of a single witness and the defendant's own admission. Both involve a claim and denial, and the defendant swears. Therefore, witnesses, who also come through a claim and denial, should also cause the defendant to swear.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara constructs a formal argument from the common denominator (הצד השוה) of the cases of a single witness and the defendant's own admission: both involve a claim and denial, and the defendant swears; therefore, witnesses, who also come through a claim and denial, should also cause the defendant to swear.

items.text: Refutation of the common denominator and resolution
items.text_en: Refutation of the common denominator and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara refutes the common denominator argument by noting that the common denominator cases do not involve a person who has been established as a confirmed liar (מוחזק כפרן), whereas witnesses do. This is challenged by Rav Idi bar Avin citing Rav Chisda that a borrower who denies a loan is still fit for testimony, but one who denies a deposit is disqualified. The Gemara then offers a different refutation: the common denominator cases are not subject to the law of conspiracy (הזמה), whereas witnesses are. The Gemara notes that Rabbi Chiyya did not raise the issue of conspiracy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to the common denominator argument: the common denominator cases do not involve a person established as a confirmed liar (מוחזק כפרן), whereas witnesses do.
The Gemara challenges the refutation by citing Rav Idi bar Avin quoting Rav Chisda: a borrower who denies a loan is still fit for testimony, but one who denies a deposit is disqualified.
The Gemara offers a different refutation: the common denominator cases are not subject to the law of conspiracy (הזמה), whereas witnesses are.
The Gemara notes that Rabbi Chiyya did not raise the issue of conspiracy, so the second refutation does not challenge his position.

items.text: Challenge from the Mishnah of 'two are holding a garment'
items.text_en: Challenge from the Mishnah of 'two are holding a garment'
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Chiyya's position by citing the Mishnah of two people holding a garment (שנים אוחזין בטלית). In that case, since each is holding the garment, we are witnesses that what he holds is his, yet the Mishnah requires an oath. This contradicts Rabbi Chiyya's logic that witnesses cannot impose an oath.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Chiyya's position by citing the Mishnah of two people holding a garment (שנים אוחזין בטלית), where each is holding the garment and we are witnesses that what he holds is his, yet the Mishnah requires an oath, contradicting Rabbi Chiyya's logic that witnesses cannot impose an oath.

items.text: Reassignment of the challenge to Rabbi Chiyya's other statement
items.text_en: Reassignment of the challenge to Rabbi Chiyya's other statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the challenge from the Mishnah was actually directed at a different statement of Rabbi Chiyya. Rabbi Chiyya ruled that if someone says 'I have a maneh of yours' and the other responds 'You only have fifty zuz, and here it is (הֵילָךְ)', he is liable to swear. The Gemara explains the reasoning: saying 'הֵילָךְ' is considered a partial admission.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the challenge from the Mishnah was actually directed at a different statement of Rabbi Chiyya.

Rabbi Chiyya rules that if someone says 'I have a maneh of yours' and the other responds 'You only have fifty zuz, and here it is (הֵילָךְ)', he is liable to swear, because saying 'הֵילָךְ' is considered a partial admission.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's dispute and resolution of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's dispute and resolution of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara now cites the Mishnah of two holding a garment as a challenge to Rav Sheshet, who holds that 'הֵילָךְ' exempts from an oath. Rav Sheshet answers that the Mishnah's oath is a rabbinic enactment. The Gemara questions why the rabbis would enact an oath if the Torah exempts, and Rav Sheshet's position is left with a difficulty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah of two holding a garment, where each swears and divides, to challenge Rav Sheshet's view that 'הֵילָךְ' (take it) exempts from an oath.

The Gemara points out that in the Mishnah, since each claimant holds the garment, we witness that what he holds is effectively 'הֵילָךְ' (taken by him), yet the Mishnah requires an oath, contradicting Rav Sheshet's position.

Rav Sheshet explains his position: 'הֵילָךְ' (take it) exempts because the money he admits to is as if already held by the creditor, so there is no partial admission (הודאת מקצת הטענה) to trigger a Torah oath.
Rav Sheshet resolves the contradiction by asserting that the Mishnah's oath is a rabbinic enactment (תקנת חכמים), not a Torah obligation.

The Gemara objects: if 'הֵילָךְ' is exempt by Torah law, why would the rabbis enact an oath that has no parallel in Torah law, whereas if it were Torah-obligated, the rabbinic oath would be a natural extension.

items.text: Introduction of a new challenge (מיתיבי)
items.text_en: Introduction of a new challenge (מיתיבי)
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a new challenge with the term 'מיתיבי' (an objection is raised), setting up the next section of the argument.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a new challenge with the term 'מֵיתִיבִי' (an objection is raised), signaling a forthcoming refutation.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where a lender claims five silver coins and the borrower admits to three. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says he must swear because he admitted to part of the claim, while Rabbi Akiva says he is exempt as if returning a lost item.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where a lender claims five silver coins and the borrower admits to three, with Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar requiring an oath and Rabbi Akiva exempting him as if returning a lost item.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar rules that the borrower must swear because he admitted to part of the claim.
Rabbi Akiva rules that the borrower is exempt as if returning a lost item.

items.text: Gemara's initial inference from Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
items.text_en: Gemara's initial inference from Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's statement that if the borrower admitted to two (not three), he would be exempt, implying that a document supporting the claim is like 'here you are' and exempts from an oath.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's statement that if the borrower admitted to two (not three), he would be exempt, implying that a document supporting the claim is like 'here you are' and exempts from an oath.

items.text: First rejection: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's case is to exclude Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: First rejection: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's case is to exclude Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the inference, arguing that even admitting to two would obligate an oath; the case of three is taught only to counter Rabbi Akiva's view that it is returning a lost item, showing it is a partial admission.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the inference from Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's case, arguing that even admitting to two would obligate an oath, and the case of three is taught only to counter Rabbi Akiva's view that it is returning a lost item, showing it is a partial admission.

items.text: Objection: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar should have said 'also this one shall swear'
items.text_en: Objection: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar should have said 'also this one shall swear'
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the case is to exclude Rabbi Akiva, Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar should have said 'also this one shall swear' to emphasize the obligation, not just 'shall swear'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the case is to exclude Rabbi Akiva, Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar should have said 'also this one shall swear' to emphasize the obligation, not just 'shall swear'.

items.text: Resolution: Two is exempt, but here the document supports the claim
items.text_en: Resolution: Two is exempt, but here the document supports the claim
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that admitting to two is indeed exempt, and the document is like 'here you are' and exempts, but in this case the document supports the lender, or alternatively because the document is a lien on land and there is no oath for denying a land lien.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that admitting to two is exempt, but here the document supports the lender's claim, distinguishing the case.
The Gemara offers an alternative resolution: the document is a lien on land, and there is no oath for denying a land lien.

items.text: Alternative inference from Rabbi Akiva's statement
items.text_en: Alternative inference from Rabbi Akiva's statement
items.desc_en: Some raise an objection from the end of the Mishnah: Rabbi Akiva exempts only when three are admitted, implying that admitting to two would obligate an oath, showing that 'here you are' is obligated.

sub.desc_en: Some raise an objection from the end of the Mishnah: Rabbi Akiva exempts only when three are admitted, implying that admitting to two would obligate an oath, showing that 'here you are' is obligated.

items.text: Rejection of the alternative inference and support for exemption
items.text_en: Rejection of the alternative inference and support for exemption
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the inference, arguing that even two would be exempt; the case of three is taught to exclude Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's view that it is a partial admission. This is supported by logic: if two obligated an oath, the borrower could evade by claiming three, so both must be exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the inference, stating that even admitting to two dinars would be exempt; the case of three is taught to exclude Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's view that it is a partial admission, and to teach that it is like returning a lost item and exempt.
The Gemara provides logical support: if admitting to two obligated an oath, the borrower could evade by claiming three, so both must be exempt.

items.text: Difficulty for Rabbi Chiyya and resolution
items.text_en: Difficulty for Rabbi Chiyya and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a difficulty for Rabbi Chiyya's position but resolves it by distinguishing that here the document supports the lender, or because the document is a lien on land and there is no oath for denying a land lien.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty for Rabbi Chiyya's position that one who says 'הרי שלך לפניך (here you are)' is obligated to take an oath, given the exemption for admitting two dinars.
The Gemara answers that the case is different because the promissory note supports the debtor, indicating he owes only two dinars.
Alternatively, the Gemara answers that a promissory note creates a lien on land, and one does not take an oath for denying a lien on land.

items.text: Objection from Mar Zutra's baraita
items.text_en: Objection from Mar Zutra's baraita
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra bar Rav Nachman cites a baraita: if one claims vessels and land, and admits to vessels but denies land, or vice versa, he is exempt; admitting to part of land is exempt, but to part of vessels is obligated. The Gemara infers that if the claim were vessels and vessels (like 'here you are'), it would be obligated, proving 'here you are' is obligated.

sub.text: Mar Zutra bar Rav Nachman's objection
sub.text_en: Mar Zutra bar Rav Nachman's objection
sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra bar Rav Nachman cites a baraita: if one claims vessels and land, admitting to vessels and denying land or vice versa is exempt; admitting to part of land is exempt, but to part of vessels is obligated.
The Gemara infers that if the claim were vessels and vessels (like 'here you are'), it would be obligated, proving that 'here you are' is obligated.

items.text: Rejection of Mar Zutra's inference and clarification
items.text_en: Rejection of Mar Zutra's inference and clarification
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the inference, arguing that even vessels and vessels would be exempt; the baraita teaches that admitting to part of vessels obligates an oath even regarding the land. This is not novel, as it is already taught that property without liability can obligate property with liability for an oath, but here it is the primary teaching, while there it was incidental.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects Mar Zutra's inference, arguing that even a case of vessels and vessels would be exempt, and the baraita teaches that admitting to part of vessels obligates an oath even regarding the land.

The Gemara questions what novelty the baraita teaches, since the principle of זוֹקְקִין (linking property without liability to property with liability for an oath) is already known from a previous mishnah.
The Gemara resolves that here the principle is the primary teaching (עִיקָּר), while there it was mentioned incidentally (אַגַּב גְּרָרָא).

items.text: Question on the need for a verse to exclude land from oath
items.text_en: Question on the need for a verse to exclude land from oath
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to the opinion that 'here you are' (הילך) exempts one from an oath, why would a verse be needed to exclude land from the oath? After all, land is always considered 'here you are' (since it cannot be stolen). The Gemara answers that the verse is needed for cases where one dug pits in the land, or where one was claimed for both movables and land and admitted to the movables but denied the land.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to the opinion that 'here you are' (הילך) exempts one from an oath, why would a verse be needed to exclude land from the oath, since all land is inherently 'here you are' (cannot be stolen)?
The Gemara answers that the verse is needed for cases where one dug pits in the land, or where one was claimed for both movables and land and admitted to the movables but denied the land.

items.text: Baraita of the four watchmen requiring partial admission
items.text_en: Baraita of the four watchmen requiring partial admission
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita from Rami bar Chama: the four types of watchmen (unpaid bailee, borrower, paid bailee, and renter) require a partial admission and partial denial to be liable for an oath. The Gemara initially assumes this refers to a case of 'here you are' (הילך), but then rejects this: it refers to a case where the bailee claimed that some animals never existed, some died by accident, and some died through negligence, which is not a 'here you are' case.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Rami bar Chama's baraita
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Rami bar Chama's baraita
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita from Rami bar Chama stating that all four types of watchmen require partial admission and partial denial to be liable for an oath.
The Gemara initially assumes the baraita refers to a case of 'הילך' (here you are), where the bailee admits the deposit exists but denies part of it.

The Gemara rejects the assumption, explaining that the baraita refers to a case where the bailee claims some animals never existed, some died by accident, and some died through negligence — which is not a 'הילך' case.

items.text: Baraita of Avuh de-Rabbi Aftoriki: partial admission with witnesses
items.text_en: Baraita of Avuh de-Rabbi Aftoriki: partial admission with witnesses
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites another baraita: if one claims 'you have a maneh of mine' and the other denies entirely, but witnesses testify that he has fifty zuz, one might think he must swear about the remainder. The verse 'על כל אבדה אשר יאמר כי הוא זה' teaches that liability is only for admission by his own mouth, not for testimony of witnesses.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that if one denies a claim entirely but witnesses testify to part, the verse 'על כל אבדה אשר יאמר כי הוא זה' exempts him from an oath, because liability is only for admission by his own mouth, not for testimony of witnesses.

items.text: Reconciliation of the baraita with Rabbi Chiyya's opinion
items.text_en: Reconciliation of the baraita with Rabbi Chiyya's opinion
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: this baraita contradicts Rabbi Chiyya's earlier teaching? It answers that Rabbi Chiyya is a Tanna and can argue. The Gemara then explains that the verse 'הוא זה' is used differently: one opinion uses it for partial admission, another for admission by witnesses (exempting), and a third for admission of a different type of item. The latter opinion follows Rabban Gamliel who holds one liable for admitting to barley when claimed for wheat.

items.text: Case of the shepherd and Rabbi Zeira's ruling
items.text_en: Case of the shepherd and Rabbi Zeira's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case: a shepherd was given animals daily with witnesses, but one day without witnesses. He later denied everything. Witnesses testified he ate two of them. Rabbi Zeira said: if Rabbi Chiyya's earlier ruling exists, he would swear about the remainder. Abaye objected: he is a robber (and cannot swear). Rabbi Zeira clarified: he meant the claimant (the owner) would swear and collect.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case: a shepherd was given animals daily with witnesses, but one day without witnesses; he later denied everything, and witnesses testified he ate two of them.
Rabbi Zeira rules that if Rabbi Chiyya's earlier ruling exists, the shepherd would swear about the remainder.
Abaye objects: the shepherd is a robber (גזלן) and cannot swear.
Rabbi Zeira clarifies that he meant the claimant (the owner) would swear and collect, not the shepherd.

items.text: Application of Rav Nachman's institution of the oath of inducement
items.text_en: Application of Rav Nachman's institution of the oath of inducement
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests: even without Rabbi Chiyya's ruling, we could obligate him based on Rav Nachman's ruling. The Mishnah states that if one claims 'you have a maneh of mine' and the other says 'I have nothing of yours', he is exempt. Rav Nachman said: we administer an oath of inducement (שבועת היסת) to him. The Gemara notes that Rav Nachman's oath is a rabbinic institution.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that even without Rabbi Chiyya's ruling, we could obligate the shepherd based on Rav Nachman's institution of the oath of inducement (שבועת היסת).

sub.text: Supporting Mishnah and Rav Nachman's statement
sub.text_en: Supporting Mishnah and Rav Nachman's statement
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah where one claims 'you have a maneh of mine' and the other denies, and Rav Nachman's ruling that we administer an oath of inducement (שבועת היסת) to him.
The Gemara notes that Rav Nachman's oath is a rabbinic institution (תקנתא), not a Torah obligation.

items.text: The shepherd's credibility and the principle of 'ein adam choteh v'lo lo'
items.text_en: The shepherd's credibility and the principle of 'ein adam choteh v'lo lo'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a shepherd is not considered a valid witness, given that he is suspected of stealing. It resolves that a shepherd who tends his own flock is suspect, but one who tends others' flocks is not, based on the principle that a person does not sin for another's benefit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that we do not institute one remedy that leads to another remedy.
The Gemara questions why the shepherd is not considered a disqualified witness, citing Rav Yehuda's rule that a shepherd is presumptively invalid.
The Gemara resolves that a shepherd tending his own flock is suspect, but one tending others' flocks is not, based on the principle that a person does not sin for another's benefit.

items.text: The formulation of the oath for the claimant
items.text_en: The formulation of the oath for the claimant
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines the wording of the oath in the Mishnah: 'I swear that I have no less than half of it.' It questions why the claimant does not simply swear that the entire garment is his, and why he does not swear that half is his. The Gemara explains that the oath is a compromise between the two claims.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the oath in the Mishnah is about what the claimant has or about what he does not have.
Rav Huna explains that the oath is formulated as 'I swear that I have in it and I have no less than half of it.'
The Gemara objects: why not simply swear that the entire garment is his, since the court would not give him the whole garment anyway?
The Gemara further objects: why not swear that half is his, noting that this would weaken his claim.
The Gemara resolves that even the current formulation weakens his claim, as he says 'the whole is mine' but then swears only that he has no less than half.

items.text: The purpose of the oath: a rabbinic enactment
items.text_en: The purpose of the oath: a rabbinic enactment
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that the oath is a rabbinic enactment to prevent people from seizing each other's garments and claiming them as their own. The oath serves as a deterrent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: since both parties are already holding the garment, why is an oath needed?
Rabbi Yochanan answers that the oath is a rabbinic enactment to deter people from seizing each other's garments and claiming them as their own.

items.text: The principle of 'miggo' and the distinction between monetary and oath suspicion
items.text_en: The principle of 'miggo' and the distinction between monetary and oath suspicion
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why one who is suspected of dishonesty regarding money is not also suspected regarding oaths. It answers that in cases of partial admission, the debtor may be trying to delay payment, as per Rabbah's principle, and is not necessarily a liar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: since one who is suspected of dishonesty regarding money is also suspected regarding oaths, why does the Mishnah require an oath from such a person?
The Gemara rejects the premise: we do not apply the principle that one suspected regarding money is suspected regarding oaths.
The Gemara supports its rejection: if the principle applied, then the Torah's requirement that a partial admitter swear would be undermined, since he too would be suspected.
The Gemara resolves: in the case of partial admission, the debtor is merely trying to delay payment (אישתמוטי), as per Rabbah's principle, and is not a liar regarding money.

items.text: The distinction between a loan and a deposit regarding credibility
items.text_en: The distinction between a loan and a deposit regarding credibility
items.desc_en: Rav Idi bar Avin quotes Rav Chisda: one who denies a loan is still fit for testimony, but one who denies a deposit is disqualified. The Gemara explains that in a deposit, the denial is not due to delay, but if witnesses testify that the deposit was in his possession, he is considered a liar.

sub.text: Rav Idi bar Avin citing Rav Chisda
sub.text_en: Rav Idi bar Avin citing Rav Chisda
sub.desc_en: Rav Idi bar Avin cites Rav Chisda's ruling: one who denies a loan is still fit for testimony, but one who denies a deposit is disqualified.

The Gemara objects: Rami bar Chama taught that four types of guardians require partial denial and partial admission, yet they swear — why not apply the principle that one suspected of monetary dishonesty is also suspected regarding oaths?
The Gemara answers: there too the guardian is merely stalling, hoping to find the thief or recover the item from the marsh.
The Gemara objects: if so, why is one who denies a deposit disqualified from testimony? He too could be stalling until he searches and finds it.
The Gemara resolves: the disqualification applies only when witnesses testify that the deposit was in his possession at the time and he knew it, or if he was actually holding it in his hand.

items.text: The oath that the deposit is not in his possession and the prohibition of coveting
items.text_en: The oath that the deposit is not in his possession and the prohibition of coveting
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why one who swears that a deposit is not in his possession is not suspected of lying, given the 'miggo' principle. It answers that he may think he is paying its value. Rav Acha from Difti objects that this violates the prohibition of coveting, but the Gemara explains that 'lo tachmod' applies only to taking without payment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why, regarding Rav Huna's ruling that one swears the deposit is not in his possession, we do not apply the 'miggo' principle that one suspected of monetary dishonesty is also suspected of false oaths.
The Gemara answers that there, the depositary considers himself permitted, reasoning that he will pay its value.
Rav Acha from Difti objects to Ravina that the depositary thereby violates the negative commandment 'לֹא תַחְמֹד' (You shall not covet).
Ravina resolves that 'לֹא תַחְמֹד' (You shall not covet) applies only to taking without payment, not when one intends to pay.

items.text: Rejection of the inference from monetary dishonesty to oath dishonesty
items.text_en: Rejection of the inference from monetary dishonesty to oath dishonesty
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises three cases where oaths are administered despite potential monetary dishonesty, challenging the assumption that one who is dishonest about money is also dishonest about oaths. It concludes that we do not make such an inference.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle that one who is dishonest about money is dishonest about oaths, citing Rav Nachman's case of imposing a שבועת היסת (oath of inducement) on a defendant who denies the claim entirely.
The Gemara adds a second challenge from Rabbi Chiyya's baraita, where both claimants swear and collect from the homeowner, implying an oath is administered despite potential monetary dishonesty.
The Gemara raises a third challenge from Rav Sheshet's case of three oaths imposed on a bailee, questioning why oaths are administered if monetary dishonesty implies oath dishonesty.
The Gemara resolves that we do not infer from monetary dishonesty to oath dishonesty, rejecting the proposed inference.

items.text: Abaye's explanation and Rav Sheshet's resolution
items.text_en: Abaye's explanation and Rav Sheshet's resolution
items.desc_en: Abaye suggests the oath is due to concern for an old loan, but the Gemara objects that this would allow taking without oath. Abaye revises to a possible old loan, and the Gemara questions why we don't seize money on uncertainty. Rav Sheshet answers that people refrain from uncertain oaths but not uncertain money, because money can be returned.

sub.desc_en: Abaye answers that the oath is required because we suspect the claimant may have an old loan against the defendant.
The Gemara objects that if there is a definite old loan, the claimant should take the money without an oath.
Abaye revises his answer, saying we suspect only a possible (ספק) old loan, not a definite one.
The Gemara questions why we do not apply the same logic to seizing money on uncertainty, requiring an oath on uncertainty as well.

sub.text: Rav Sheshet the son of Rav Idi's resolution
sub.text_en: Rav Sheshet the son of Rav Idi's resolution
sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet the son of Rav Idi resolves that people refrain from a doubtful oath because an oath cannot be undone, but they do not refrain from doubtful money because money can be returned.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's inquiry about seizure in front of us
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's inquiry about seizure in front of us
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks: if one party seizes the object in front of us, what is the law? The Gemara clarifies the scenario: the party was initially silent and then cried out, raising the question of whether silence constitutes admission.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks: if one party seizes the object in front of us (the court), what is the law?
The Gemara clarifies the scenario: if the party was silent, that constitutes admission; if he cried out, what could he have done?

The Gemara refines the case: the party was initially silent and then cried out — does the initial silence constitute admission, or does the later outcry reveal that he was relying on the court's presence?

items.text: Rav Nachman's proof and alternative interpretations
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's proof and alternative interpretations
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman brings a baraita about a garment emerging from one party's hand, suggesting it refers to seizure in front of us. The Gemara rejects this, explaining the case as one where they came to court holding it together, then one seized it later. An alternative explanation involves one party merely attaching a claim to the garment, which even Sumchus would not consider significant.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman cites a baraita about a garment emerging from one party's hand, suggesting it refers to a case where one party seized it in front of witnesses.

The Gemara rejects Rav Nachman's proof, explaining the baraita as a case where the parties came to court holding the garment together, then one later seized it, and the other's silence is not an admission.

An alternative explanation is presented: the baraita describes a case where one party merely attaches a claim (סירכא) to the garment, which even Sumchus would not consider significant enough to require division without oath.

items.text: Consequences of seizure for consecration
items.text_en: Consequences of seizure for consecration
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether if one seizes the object in front of us, we remove it from him, and whether his consecration of it is valid. It compares the case to one who consecrates without seizure, debating whether his statement to Heaven is like delivery to a commoner, or whether the object is not in his domain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara poses two conditional questions: if we rule that we remove the seized object, then consecration is invalid; if we do not remove it, what is the status of consecration without seizure?
The Gemara suggests that since the principle 'speaking to Heaven is like delivery to a commoner' applies, the consecrator is considered as if he seized the object.
The Gemara objects that currently he has not seized it, and the verse 'when a man consecrates his house' implies the object must be in his domain, excluding this case.

items.text: Beginning of a new proof
items.text_en: Beginning of a new proof
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to bring a proof from a specific incident, but the text cuts off.

sub.text: Gemara's attempt to bring a proof
sub.text_en: Gemara's attempt to bring a proof
sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins to introduce a proof from a specific incident, but the text cuts off.

items.text: The case of the disputed animal and the question to Rav Chisda
items.text_en: The case of the disputed animal and the question to Rav Chisda
items.desc_en: Two people argue over a donkey; one consecrates it. Rav Oshaya tells Rava to ask Rav Chisda about the halacha.

sub.desc_en: The gemara sets the scene: two people argue over a donkey, and one consecrates it.
Rav Oshaya tells Rava to ask Rav Chisda about the halacha when he goes to Kafri.

items.text: Rav Hamnuna's citation of the Mishnah on safek bechorot
items.text_en: Rav Hamnuna's citation of the Mishnah on safek bechorot
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna cites the Mishnah that safek bechorot require the claimant to bring proof, and the Tosefta adds that they are forbidden in shearing and work. He argues that if the kohen seized it, we do not take it from him, and if not, it is forbidden in use.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna cites the Mishnah that for ספק בכורות (doubtful firstborns), the claimant must bring proof.
Rav Hamnuna adds the Tosefta that these doubtful firstborns are forbidden in shearing and work.
Rav Hamnuna infers that if the kohen seized it, we do not take it from him, and if not, it is forbidden in use.

items.text: Rava's distinction: bechor sanctity is different
items.text_en: Rava's distinction: bechor sanctity is different
items.desc_en: Rava argues that even if the kohen seized it and we take it from him, the animal is still forbidden in shearing and work because its sanctity came automatically.

sub.desc_en: Rava responds that the case of bechor sanctity is different because the sanctity comes automatically, so even if the kohen seized it and we take it from him, the animal remains forbidden in shearing and work.

items.text: Rav Chananya's support from a baraisa on safek bechorot entering the pen
items.text_en: Rav Chananya's support from a baraisa on safek bechorot entering the pen
items.desc_en: Rav Chananya cites a baraisa that safek bechorot enter the pen to be tithed. He argues that if the kohen could keep it after seizure, the owner would be exempting his own animal through the kohen's property.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chananya cites a baraisa that safek bechorot enter the pen to be tithed, supporting Rava's position.
Rav Chananya argues that if the kohen could keep the animal after seizure, the owner would be exempting his own animal through the kohen's property, which is impossible.

items.text: Abaye's first answer: the case is where the owner has only nine animals
items.text_en: Abaye's first answer: the case is where the owner has only nine animals
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that the baraisa refers to a case where the owner has only nine animals, so tithing the safek bechor is harmless: if it is obligated, it is properly tithed; if not, nine animals are not subject to tithing.

sub.desc_en: Abaye rejects the support for Rabbah by explaining that the baraisa refers to a case where the owner has only nine animals, so tithing the safek bechor is harmless: if it is obligated, it is properly tithed; if not, nine animals are not subject to tithing.

items.text: Abaye's retraction and Rava's principle of minyan haraui
items.text_en: Abaye's retraction and Rava's principle of minyan haraui
items.desc_en: Abaye retracts, citing a Mishnah that if one of the counted animals jumps in, all are exempt, proving that a safek is not subject to tithing. Rava's principle that minyan haraui (a count that could have been valid) exempts is invoked.

sub.desc_en: Abaye retracts his earlier position, citing a Mishnah that if one of the counted animals jumps into the pen, all are exempt, proving that a safek (doubtful animal) is not subject to tithing.
Abaye argues that if a safek required tithing, one could tithe from it regardless, and the exemption would be due to the principle of minyan haraui (a count that could have been valid).
Rava's principle that minyan haraui (a count that could have been valid) exempts from tithing is invoked to support the conclusion.

items.text: Application of the principle to the Mishnah
items.text_en: Application of the principle to the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara applies the principle that the Torah commands a definite tithe, not a doubtful one, to the Mishnah's case of uncertain ownership, arguing that the same logic applies here.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara applies the principle that the Torah commands a definite tithe, not a doubtful one, to the Mishnah's case of uncertain ownership, arguing that the same logic applies here.

items.text: Clarifying the uncertainties: firstborn and donkey redemption
items.text_en: Clarifying the uncertainties: firstborn and donkey redemption
items.desc_en: Rav Acha from Difti asks Ravina what uncertainties are meant, excluding firstborn animals because they are already sanctified, and explaining that it refers to the uncertainty of redeeming a firstborn donkey, as per Rav Nachman's ruling.

sub.text: Rav Acha from Difti's question to Ravina
sub.text_en: Rav Acha from Difti's question to Ravina
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha from Difti asks Ravina what uncertainties are meant, rejecting the possibility of firstborn animals because they are already sanctified.

Ravina explains that the uncertainties refer to the redemption of a firstborn donkey, citing Rav Nachman's ruling that one separates ten sheep for ten uncertain firstborn donkeys and tithes them, keeping them for himself.

items.text: Resolving the uncertainty with Rav Nachman's principle
items.text_en: Resolving the uncertainty with Rav Nachman's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks to resolve the uncertainty by citing a case from Rav Chisda and Rav Huna, and Rav Nachman's principle that money which cannot be recovered through court is not sanctified, but if it can be, it is sanctified even if not yet recovered. The Gemara distinguishes between movable and real property.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how to resolve the uncertainty regarding the case of the cloak (מסותא).
Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin brings a case from Rav Chisda and Rav Huna, citing Rav Nachman's principle that money which cannot be recovered through court is not sanctified.

The Gemara resolves the difficulty by distinguishing movable property from real property: in the case of the cloak (מסותא), which is real property, once it can be recovered through court it is considered in the owner's domain.

items.text: Baraita on two holding a garment
items.text_en: Baraita on two holding a garment
items.desc_en: Rav Tachlifa bar Ma'arava teaches a baraita before Rabbi Avahu: two people holding a garment each take what they can reach, and the rest is divided equally. Rabbi Avahu adds that this is done under oath.

sub.desc_en: Rav Tachlifa bar Ma'arava teaches a baraita before Rabbi Avahu: two people holding a garment each take what they can reach, and the rest is divided equally.
Rabbi Avahu adds that the division is done under oath.

items.text: Reconciling the Mishnah with the baraita
items.text_en: Reconciling the Mishnah with the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the Mishnah, which says they divide without specifying reaching, can be reconciled. Rav Pappa explains it refers to a case where they are holding it by a fringe. Rav Mesharshiya derives that a garment held by a three-by-three handbreadth piece is considered in the holder's possession for the law of 'giving to his fellow'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the Mishnah, which states they divide without specifying reaching, can be reconciled with the baraita.
Rav Pappa answers that the Mishnah refers to a case where they are holding the garment by a fringe (כרכשתא), so neither can reach the other's part.
Rav Mesharshiya derives from this that a garment held by a three-by-three handbreadth piece is considered in the holder's possession for the law of 'giving to his fellow' (ונתן לרעהו).

items.text: Distinguishing from Rav Chisda's ruling on a get
items.text_en: Distinguishing from Rav Chisda's ruling on a get
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why this case differs from Rav Chisda's ruling about a get where if the husband can pull it back, she is not divorced. The answer is that divorce requires severance, which is lacking, while here acquisition requires giving, which is present.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why this case differs from Rav Chisda's ruling about a get (bill of divorce) where if the husband can pull it back, she is not divorced.
The Gemara answers that divorce requires severance (כריתות), which is lacking here, while acquisition requires giving (נתינה), which is present.

items.text: Rava's ruling on a gold-embroidered garment
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on a gold-embroidered garment
items.desc_en: Rava rules that if the garment is gold-embroidered, they divide it equally. The Gemara clarifies that this is necessary even if the gold is in the middle or closer to one side, to prevent one from claiming a specific division.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that if the garment is gold-embroidered, they divide it equally.
The Gemara questions why this ruling is necessary, as it seems obvious.
The Gemara explains that the ruling is needed even when the gold is in the middle or closer to one side.
The Gemara objects that even this case seems obvious.
The Gemara resolves that the ruling is needed to prevent one party from demanding a specific division; instead, each can demand the other to divide differently.

items.text: Dispute over a promissory note
items.text_en: Dispute over a promissory note
items.desc_en: The Tannaim teach a case of two holding a promissory note: the lender says it is his and fell from him, the borrower says it is his and he paid. Rabbi says the note must be validated by its signatures, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says they divide. The Gemara explains the dispute hinges on whether one who admits to writing a note must validate it.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents a case of two holding a promissory note; Rabbi rules that the note must be ratified by its signatories.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel states that the litigants divide the debt.
The baraita adds that if the note fell into a judge's hands, it is not removed; Rabbi Yosei says it retains its presumptive validity.
The Gemara questions Rabbi's ruling: if the note is ratified, does the creditor collect the whole debt, contradicting the mishna's principle of dividing?
Rava citing Rav Nachman explains that when the note is ratified, all agree they divide; the dispute is only when it is not ratified.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi holds a debtor who admits writing the note must still ratify it; otherwise it is worthless because the debtor claims repayment.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds a debtor who admits writing the note need not ratify it, so they divide even without ratification.
The Gemara cites the baraita's final ruling that a note in a judge's hands is never removed.

items.text: Gemara's question and Rava's explanation of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rava's explanation of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies 'fell into the hands of a judge' and explains that it refers to a document with a court endorsement. Even with such endorsement, one should not return it due to concern that it was paid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies 'fell into the hands of a judge'.
Rava explains that the Mishnah refers to a document with a court endorsement, and even then one should not return it due to concern that it was paid.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei's position and a challenge from a baraita
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei's position and a challenge from a baraita
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei says the document is in its presumptive status and we do not suspect payment. The Gemara challenges this from a baraita about finding a ketubah, where Rabbi Yosei distinguishes between a wife still with her husband and one who is widowed or divorced.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei states that the document retains its presumptive status and we do not suspect payment.
The Gemara challenges: Does Rabbi Yosei not suspect payment at all?
The Gemara cites a baraita about finding a ketubah, where the Tanna Kamma distinguishes based on the husband's admission.
Rabbi Yosei distinguishes: if the wife is still married, return the ketubah; if widowed or divorced, do not return it.

items.text: Attempt to reverse the Mishnah's attributions
items.text_en: Attempt to reverse the Mishnah's attributions
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests reversing the Mishnah: Rabbi Yosei says not to return, and the Sages say it is in its presumptive status.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests reversing the attributions in the baraita: Rabbi Yosei says the document may never be removed, and the Sages say it retains its presumptive status.

items.text: Contradiction among the Sages and resolution by emendation
items.text_en: Contradiction among the Sages and resolution by emendation
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between the Sages' positions. It resolves by emending the baraita: the entire baraita is Rabbi Yosei's view, and the Sages' position is omitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the Sages' position in the reversed baraita (segments 5) contradicts their position in the original baraita (segments 3-4).

The Gemara resolves by emending the baraita: the entire baraita about the ketubah is Rabbi Yosei's view, and the Sages' position is omitted; the baraita is actually a single statement by Rabbi Yosei distinguishing between a widow/divorcée and a woman still married.

items.text: Rav Pappa's alternative: no reversal, Rabbi Yosei speaks to the Rabbis
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's alternative: no reversal, Rabbi Yosei speaks to the Rabbis
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa says not to reverse; Rabbi Yosei is speaking to the Rabbis according to their reasoning. He concedes that while the wife is with her husband, return it, but for a widow or divorcee, he still does not suspect payment.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asserts that the mishnah should not be reversed; Rabbi Yosei is speaking to the Rabbis according to their own reasoning.

sub.text: Rav Pappa's explanation of Rabbi Yosei's position
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa's explanation of Rabbi Yosei's position
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa elaborates that Rabbi Yosei himself does not suspect payment even for a widow or divorcee, but he concedes to the Rabbis that while the wife is with her husband, the document should be returned because she is not capable of having paid the ketubah.

The Rabbis object to Rav Pappa's explanation, arguing that even while with her husband, the wife might have given the document as a pledge (צררי) to secure a loan, so return is not automatically safe.

items.text: Ravina's explanation: reversal stands, Sages suspect two ketubot
items.text_en: Ravina's explanation: reversal stands, Sages suspect two ketubot
items.desc_en: Ravina says the original reversal stands; the Sages here suspect two ketubot, while Rabbi Yosei does not.

sub.desc_en: Ravina resolves the contradiction by asserting the original reversal stands, explaining that the Sages here suspect two ketubot (כתובות) while Rabbi Yosei does not.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yochanan on dividing a garment
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yochanan on dividing a garment
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar says the dispute about dividing a garment applies only when both hold the same part; if one holds the top and the other the bottom, each takes their part. Rabbi Yochanan says they always divide. The Gemara clarifies a case where the middle is between them.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that the dispute about dividing a garment applies only when both hold the same part (the top or the bottom), but if one holds the top and the other the bottom, each takes their respective part.
Rabbi Yochanan counters that in all cases, including when each holds a different part, they divide the garment equally.
The Gemara objects to Rabbi Yochanan's position by citing a baraita that says each takes up to where their hand reaches, implying no equal division.
The Gemara resolves that the case is where the bottom part lies between them, so neither holds it exclusively, justifying equal division.
The Gemara questions why the baraita's ruling is necessary if the case is obvious.
The Gemara explains that the case is where the bottom is closer to one party, and the baraita teaches that even then they divide equally, rejecting a claim that the closer party should take it all.

items.text: Rav Acha's question and the value-based resolution
items.text_en: Rav Acha's question and the value-based resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Acha asks why Rabbi Elazar's ruling is needed, since one needs the whole garment. The Gemara explains it is for monetary value: a document with a date is worth more. The principle of dividing applies to value, not the physical item.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha asks Ravina why Rabbi Elazar's ruling that one takes the top copy and the other takes the bottom copy is needed, since each person only needs the part they are holding.
Ravina answers that the ruling is about monetary value, not physical possession.
The Gemara explains that a document with a date is worth more because it allows collection from liened property, so the division is based on the difference in value between the two parts.
The Gemara resolves that the principle of dividing (ויחלוקו) in the Mishnah also refers to value, not the physical garment, otherwise two people holding a tallit would destroy it by dividing.

items.text: Gemara's initial objection and resolution regarding the Mishnah's case of two holding a garment
items.text_en: Gemara's initial objection and resolution regarding the Mishnah's case of two holding a garment
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Mishnah can say they divide a garment if it is ruined by cutting, and resolves that it is fit for small children or, in Rava's case of a gold-embroidered garment, for princes. Similarly, the case of two riding an animal is resolved by saying they divide the value.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that cutting the garment in the Mishnah would ruin it, questioning how they can divide it.
The Gemara answers that the garment is fit for small children, so cutting does not ruin it.
The Gemara objects that Rava's case of a gold-embroidered garment (טלית מוזהבת) would also be ruined by cutting.
The Gemara answers that a gold-embroidered garment is fit for princes, so cutting does not ruin it.

sub.text: Gemara's question on the animal case
sub.text_en: Gemara's question on the animal case
sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how two riders dividing an animal would work, since cutting the animal would ruin it.

sub.text: Gemara's answer for the animal case
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer for the animal case
sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that a kosher animal can be divided for its meat, and a non-kosher animal is divided by its monetary value (לדמי).

items.text: Rami bar Chama's inference: one who lifts a found object for another acquires it for him
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's inference: one who lifts a found object for another acquires it for him
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama argues from the Mishnah that if one lifts a found object for another, the other acquires it; otherwise, neither would acquire it, which is absurd.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama states that the Mishnah implies that one who lifts a found object for another acquires it for him.
Rami bar Chama argues that if one did not acquire for another, neither would acquire the item, which is absurd; therefore the other must acquire.

items.text: Rava's counter: the principle of 'miggo' (since he acquires for himself, he acquires for his friend)
items.text_en: Rava's counter: the principle of 'miggo' (since he acquires for himself, he acquires for his friend)
items.desc_en: Rava rejects Rami bar Chama's inference, explaining that the Mishnah's ruling is due to the principle that since each rider acquires the animal for himself, he also acquires it for his friend. He supports this with the analogy of a thief's agent and partners who steal.

sub.desc_en: Rava rejects Rami bar Chama's inference, explaining that the Mishnah's ruling is due to the principle that since each rider acquires the animal for himself, he also acquires it for his friend.
Rava supports his principle with the analogy of a thief's agent and partners who steal, concluding that the principle is correct.

items.text: Rava's attempted application of 'miggo' to a deaf-mute and a hearing person, and its refutation
items.text_en: Rava's attempted application of 'miggo' to a deaf-mute and a hearing person, and its refutation
items.desc_en: Rava tries to apply the 'miggo' principle to a case where a deaf-mute and a hearing person lift a found object, but the Gemara shows that the hearing person does not acquire, and therefore the deaf-mute also does not acquire, because the deaf-mute cannot acquire for the hearing person.

sub.desc_en: Rava proposes that since we apply the 'miggo' principle, when a deaf-mute and a hearing person lift a found object, the hearing person acquires through the deaf-mute's acquisition.
The Gemara objects: the deaf-mute acquires because a person of sound mind lifts for him, but how does the hearing person acquire?
The Gemara revises: the deaf-mute acquires, the hearing person does not; the 'miggo' is that just as two deaf-mutes acquire, so too this deaf-mute acquires.

The Gemara objects further: even if one who lifts a found object for another acquires for him, here the deaf-mute lifts for himself, not for the hearing person; if he does not acquire for himself, can he acquire for others?
The Gemara concludes: since the hearing person does not acquire, the deaf-mute also does not acquire.
The Gemara explains the difference from two deaf-mutes: there the Sages instituted acquisition to prevent conflict, but here the hearing person says 'since I do not acquire, will I acquire?'

items.text: Rav Acha's challenge to Rami bar Chama's proof from the Mishnah, and the Gemara's analysis
items.text_en: Rav Acha's challenge to Rami bar Chama's proof from the Mishnah, and the Gemara's analysis
items.desc_en: Rav Acha questions the source of Rami bar Chama's proof, examining various parts of the Mishnah. The Gemara concludes that the proof is from the extra Mishnah clauses, but Rava consistently explains it via the 'miggo' principle.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Adda to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Adda to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha asks Rav Ashi from which part of the Mishnah Rami bar Chama derived his proof, and rejects the first possibility (the opening clause) because both claimants there claim full ownership and lifting.
Rav Ashi suggests the proof is from the extra Mishnah clause 'this one says it's all mine' — the redundancy implies the principle that one who lifts a found object for another acquires it for him.
The Gemara objects that the first clause was already established as dealing with a found object, while the latter clause deals with a purchase, so the redundancy may not apply to found objects.
Rav Ashi then suggests the proof is from the later clause 'this one says it's all mine, this one says half is mine' — the redundancy again implies the principle.
The Gemara objects that this clause might also refer to a purchase, not a found object.

The Gemara resolves that if it were a purchase, the clause would be unnecessary, but it teaches that the partial claimant is not considered a 'returner of a lost object' exempt from oath, but rather a schemer.

items.text: Introduction to the next Mishnah case: two riding an animal
items.text_en: Introduction to the next Mishnah case: two riding an animal
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to discuss the case of two people riding an animal, citing a tradition from Rav Yosef in the name of Rav Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the Mishnah case of two people riding an animal as a potential source for the principle that one who lifts a found object for another acquires it for him.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the Mishnah merely teaches that a rider also acquires the found object, not the broader principle.
The Gemara cites the latter clause of the Mishnah where the riders divide without an oath when they admit or have witnesses, proving the principle that one who lifts for another acquires for him.
Rava resolves the proof by explaining that the rider acquires for his fellow because he acquires for himself (מגו דזכי לנפשיה).
Rav Yosef introduces a tradition from Rav Yehuda regarding the case of two riders.

items.text: Gemara's question about riding vs. leading
items.text_en: Gemara's question about riding vs. leading
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from Mar Shmuel that riding and leading are two distinct modes of acquisition—one acquires and one does not—but it is unclear which is which. It then clarifies the possible scenarios: if riding alone and leading alone are compared, leading certainly acquires; the doubt is whether riding alone acquires. Alternatively, the question is about riding in place of leading: which is superior?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from Mar Shmuel that riding and leading are two distinct modes of acquisition—one acquires and one does not—but it is unclear which is which.
The Gemara clarifies the possible scenarios: if riding alone and leading alone are compared, leading certainly acquires; the doubt is whether riding alone acquires.
The Gemara poses the alternative question: when riding is compared to leading, which mode is superior—riding because the rider holds the animal, or leading because the animal moves on its own?

items.text: Rav Yosef's proof from the Mishnah of the driver and passenger
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's proof from the Mishnah of the driver and passenger
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef cites a Mishnah where a driver (מנהיג) receives lashes, and a passenger (יושב בקרון) also receives lashes, but Rabbi Meir exempts the passenger. Shmuel reversed the tradition to say that the Sages exempt the passenger. From this, the Gemara concludes that riding alone does not acquire, and certainly riding in place of leading does not acquire.
