items.text: Shmuel's ruling and Rava's support
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling and Rava's support
items.desc_en: Shmuel rules that a creditor collects the appreciation. Rava supports this by citing the standard deed where the seller guarantees the land and its improvements. Rav Chiyya bar Avin questions whether a gift without such a deed would not collect appreciation, and Rava confirms this, noting that a gift's power is indeed greater.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that a creditor collects the appreciation (שבח) of the land.
Rava supports Shmuel by citing the standard deed where the seller guarantees the land and its improvements.
Rav Chiyya bar Avin questions whether a gift without such a deed would not collect appreciation.
Rava confirms that a gift without such a deed indeed does not collect appreciation.

sub.text: Rav Chiyya bar Avin's further question
sub.text_en: Rav Chiyya bar Avin's further question
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Avin questions whether a gift's power is greater than a sale.
Rava affirms that a gift's power is indeed greater than a sale.

items.text: Supporting baraitot and resolution of contradictions
items.text_en: Supporting baraitot and resolution of contradictions
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman cites a baraita supporting Shmuel, but Huna the colleague interprets it as referring to a purchaser from a robber. Another baraita discusses a creditor collecting appreciation, and the Gemara resolves the contradiction by suggesting either the case of a purchaser from a robber with land or a creditor, distinguishing between different types of appreciation.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman cites a baraita that supports Shmuel's position, but notes that Huna the colleague interprets it differently.
The baraita states that when a sold field is repossessed, the creditor collects the principal from liened property but the appreciation from unencumbered property.
Huna the colleague interprets the baraita as referring to a purchaser from a robber, not a creditor.
Another baraita discusses a creditor collecting appreciation when a sold field was improved, with rules for dividing the appreciation and expenses.
The Gemara asks how Shmuel would interpret this second baraita, given his positions that a purchaser from a robber has no appreciation and a creditor collects appreciation.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by suggesting either the case of a purchaser from a robber with land or a formal acquisition, or the case of a creditor, distinguishing between different types of appreciation.

items.text: Resolving the contradiction about Shmuel's practice
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction about Shmuel's practice
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a contradiction between the mishnah and Shmuel's practice. It distinguishes between cases where the debtor owes the full value of land and improvement versus only the land value.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Shmuel's practice of collecting even for improvement that reaches the shoulders aligns with the Mishnah's distinction.
The Gemara resolves by distinguishing between cases where the debt equals the land and improvement versus only the land.

items.text: Challenge based on the dispute about the buyer's right to redeem
items.text_en: Challenge based on the dispute about the buyer's right to redeem
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the resolution based on the dispute between those who say the buyer can redeem and those who say he cannot. It then explains that the case is where the debtor made the land an apotiki (collateral).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the resolution based on the dispute about whether a buyer can redeem the land if he has money.
The Gemara concludes that the case involves an apotiki, where the creditor's claim is limited to that land.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel: money and improvement
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel: money and improvement
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel argue about a buyer who knew the land was not the seller's. Rav says he gets his money back but not the improvement; Shmuel says he gets neither. Their reasoning is explained: Rav says the buyer intended a deposit, Shmuel says a gift.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the dispute: Rav holds that the buyer gets his money back but not the improvement, while Shmuel says he gets nothing.
The Gemara asks what is the basis of their dispute.
Rav holds that the buyer knows the land is not his and gives the money as a deposit, but cannot say so explicitly because the seller would not accept it.
Shmuel holds that the buyer knows the land is not his and gives the money as a gift, but cannot say so explicitly because he would be embarrassed.

items.text: Comparison with the dispute about betrothing one's sister
items.text_en: Comparison with the dispute about betrothing one's sister
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rav and Shmuel had a similar dispute regarding a man who betrothed his sister. It explains why both disputes are necessary: each case has a unique factor that might have led one to concede to the other.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rav and Shmuel had a similar dispute regarding one who betroths his sister.

sub.text: Rav's reasoning in the sister case
sub.text_en: Rav's reasoning in the sister case
sub.desc_en: Rav applies the same reasoning: the man knows betrothal does not take effect with his sister, so he gives the money as a deposit, but cannot say so because she would not accept it.

sub.text: Shmuel's reasoning in the sister case
sub.text_en: Shmuel's reasoning in the sister case
sub.desc_en: Shmuel applies the same reasoning: the man knows betrothal does not take effect, so he gives the money as a gift, but cannot say so because she would be embarrassed.
The Gemara explains why both disputes are necessary, as each case has unique features that might lead one to concede to the other.

items.text: How the buyer justifies entering the land and eating produce
items.text_en: How the buyer justifies entering the land and eating produce
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to both Rav and Shmuel, the buyer enters the land and eats produce with the intention that when the true owner comes, the money will be treated as a deposit or gift accordingly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the buyer enters the land and consumes produce according to both Rav and Shmuel.
The Gemara explains that the buyer intends to work the land and consume produce, treating the money as a deposit or gift accordingly, to repay the owner when he comes.

items.text: Rava's ruling
items.text_en: Rava's ruling
items.desc_en: Rava rules that in a standard sale, the buyer gets both money and improvement, but if he knew the land was not the seller's, he gets money but not improvement.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that if the seller explicitly promised improvement, the buyer gets both money and improvement; if the buyer knew the land was not the seller's, he gets only money.

items.text: Achrayut is a scribal error; Shmuel's question about repurchase
items.text_en: Achrayut is a scribal error; Shmuel's question about repurchase
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that a clause of 'achrayut' (liability) is a scribal error in both loan and sale documents. Shmuel asks Rav: if the seller later repurchased the land from the original owners, what is the law? Rav says all rights pass to the buyer. Two reasons are given, and a difference between them is noted.

items.text: Distinction between the two rationales when the robber dies
items.text_en: Distinction between the two rationales when the robber dies
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the practical difference between the two opinions: one who cares about being called a robber is satisfied when the robber dies, while one who cares about maintaining his credibility still wants the sale upheld even after the robber's death.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the practical difference between the two opinions when the robber dies.

items.text: Objection: the buyer's children are called 'robbers' children'
items.text_en: Objection: the buyer's children are called 'robbers' children'
items.desc_en: An objection is raised: even if the robber dies, the buyer's children will be called 'children of a robber,' which undermines the first rationale.

sub.desc_en: The gemara objects that even if the robber dies, the buyer's children will be called 'children of a robber,' undermining the first rationale.

items.text: Refined distinction: the robber's death vs. the buyer's children
items.text_en: Refined distinction: the robber's death vs. the buyer's children
items.desc_en: The Gemara refines the distinction: the first opinion cares about the buyer himself not being called a robber, so the robber's death suffices; the second opinion cares about the buyer's credibility, which persists even after the robber's death.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the dispute: the difference between the two opinions is the case where the robber died; one opinion cares about the buyer not being called a robber, so the robber's death suffices, while the other cares about the buyer's credibility, which persists even after the robber's death.

items.text: Further objection: the buyer's children are called 'children of a robber'
items.text_en: Further objection: the buyer's children are called 'children of a robber'
items.desc_en: Another objection: even if the robber dies, the buyer's children will be called 'children of a robber,' which still bothers the first opinion.

sub.desc_en: The gemara raises an objection: even if the robber dies, the buyer's children will be called 'children of a robber,' which still bothers the first opinion.

items.text: Distinction when the land is given as a gift
items.text_en: Distinction when the land is given as a gift
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces another distinction: if the robber gives the land as a gift, the one who cares about credibility is satisfied, but the one who cares about being called a robber says, 'What did he rob from you?' since the buyer did not pay.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a new distinction between the two opinions: when the robber gives the land as a gift, the one who cares about credibility is satisfied.
The second opinion holds that the one who cares about not being called a robber says, 'What did he rob from you?' since the buyer did not pay.

items.text: Cases where the buyer does not seek to uphold the sale
items.text_en: Cases where the buyer does not seek to uphold the sale
items.desc_en: The Gemara lists cases where the buyer does not intend to enforce the sale: if the robber sold, inherited, or gave the land as a gift, or if the buyer collected it as a debt (if he has other land). In these cases, the buyer does not rely on the seller's credibility.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states it is obvious that if the robber sold, inherited, or gave the land as a gift, the buyer does not seek to uphold the sale.
The Gemara explains that inheritance comes automatically, so the buyer did not exert effort to acquire it.
The Gemara analyzes the case of debt collection: if the buyer has other land and specifically wants this land, he seeks to uphold the sale; otherwise, he only wants repayment.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Acha and Ravina about a gift
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Acha and Ravina about a gift
items.desc_en: Rav Acha and Ravina dispute whether a gift is like an inheritance (automatic, so the buyer does not rely on the seller) or like a sale (the seller worked to ingratiate himself, so the buyer relies on his credibility).

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a dispute between Rav Acha and Ravina regarding a gift given by the seller to the buyer.
One opinion (Rav Acha) holds that a gift is like an inheritance, automatic, so the buyer does not rely on the seller's credibility.
The other opinion (Ravina) holds that a gift is like a sale, because the seller worked to ingratiate himself, so the buyer relies on his credibility.

items.text: Time limit for the seller's willingness to uphold the sale
items.text_en: Time limit for the seller's willingness to uphold the sale
items.desc_en: Rav Huna, Chiyya bar Rav, and Rav Papa debate until when the seller is willing to uphold the sale: until the time of standing in court, until the writ of execution reaches his hand, or until the days of the proclamation begin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks until when the seller is willing to uphold the sale.
Rav Huna answers that the seller is willing until the time of standing in court.
Chiyya bar Rav answers that the seller is willing until the writ of execution reaches his hand.
Rav Papa answers that the seller is willing until the days of the proclamation begin.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's challenge and Rava's answer
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's challenge and Rava's answer
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama challenges: how can the buyer acquire the land through the document, which is worthless? Rava answers: the buyer relies on the seller's credibility because the seller worked to bring the document, and thus the seller transfers the land through the benefit of the buyer's trust.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama challenges: how can the buyer acquire the land through this document, which is merely worthless clay?
Rava answers: the buyer relies on the seller's credibility, and because the seller worked to bring the document and the buyer trusts him, the seller transfers the land.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's objection and Rava's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's objection and Rava's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet objects from a mishna: selling 'what I will inherit' or 'what my net will catch' is invalid unless specified 'today.' Rava distinguishes: here the buyer relies on the seller because the seller worked to avoid being called a robber; there the buyer does not rely.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet objects from a mishna: selling 'what I will inherit' or 'what my net will catch' is invalid unless specified 'today.'
Rami bar Chama declares that this is a decisive refutation of Rava's position.
Rava distinguishes: in the case of the robber, the buyer relies on the seller because the seller worked to avoid being called a robber; in the inheritance case, the buyer does not rely.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Abba bar Zavda and Rava, and between Rav Yosef and Abaye
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Abba bar Zavda and Rava, and between Rav Yosef and Abaye
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda says the mishna's case does not require 'lifnim' (inner reasoning), while Rava says it does. Similarly, Rav Yosef says it does not require 'lifanim,' but Abaye says it does, both applying the distinction of reliance.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda rules that the case of selling an inheritance not yet received does not require the inner reasoning (לִפְנִים) of the seller's reliance.
Rava objects, asserting that this case does require the inner reasoning (לִפְנִים) and even deeper reasoning (לִפְנַי לִפְנִים).
The gemara resolves the dispute by explaining the distinction of reliance (סָמְכָא דַּעְתֵּיהּ): in one case the seller relies on the buyer's trust, in the other he does not.
Rav Yosef, in a parallel incident in Pumbedita, rules that the case does not require the inner reasoning (לְפָנִים).
Abaye objects to Rav Yosef, asserting that the case does require the inner reasoning (לִפְנִים) and even deeper reasoning (לִפְנַי לִפְנִים).
The gemara again resolves the dispute by applying the same distinction of reliance (סָמְכָא דַּעְתֵּיהּ) as in the previous dispute.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's explanation of the mishna's distinction
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's explanation of the mishna's distinction
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains why the mishna distinguishes between the first clause (invalid) and the second clause (valid when 'today' is specified): the second clause is due to the honor of his father, and similarly for the net.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what distinguishes the first clause (invalid) from the second clause (valid).
Rabbi Yochanan answers that the second clause is valid because specifying 'today' invokes the honor of his father, and similarly for the net catch.

items.text: Opening context from previous daf
items.text_en: Opening context from previous daf
items.desc_en: The Gemara continues from the previous discussion, referencing the concept of 'for the sake of his livelihood' (משום כדי חייו).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara continues from the previous discussion, referencing the concept of 'for the sake of his livelihood' (משום כדי חייו).

items.text: Rav's ruling on conditional acquisition and Rava's qualification
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on conditional acquisition and Rava's qualification
items.desc_en: Rav Huna quotes Rav that one who says 'any field I buy is yours from now' acquires it. Rava limits this to an unspecified field, but the Gemara objects that Rav follows Rabbi Meir who allows acquiring a future object even for a specific field, as shown by a baraita about betrothal after conversion.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna reports Rav's ruling that one who says 'any field I buy is yours from now' acquires it.
Rava limits Rav's ruling to an unspecified field, but not a specific field, since the seller might not sell it.
The Gemara objects that Rav follows Rabbi Meir, who allows acquiring a future object even for a specific field.
A baraita is cited showing that Rabbi Meir rules a woman is betrothed even when the condition depends on a future event, analogous to a specific field.
The Gemara concludes that since a woman is like a specific field and Rabbi Meir rules she is betrothed, Rav's ruling applies even to a specific field.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on returning found acquisition deeds
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on returning found acquisition deeds
items.desc_en: Shmuel rules that one who finds an acquisition deed (שטר הקנאה) in the market should return it, because the debtor has already obligated himself, and we do not fear repayment since he would have torn it. Rav Nachman confirms this was the practice in Shmuel's court.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that one who finds an acquisition deed (שטר הקנאה) in the market should return it, because the debtor obligated himself and we do not fear repayment since he would have torn the document.
Rav Nachman testifies that in Shmuel's academy, they used to announce that found acquisition deeds should be returned to their owners.

items.text: Rav Amram's support and Rava's distinction regarding repayment
items.text_en: Rav Amram's support and Rava's distinction regarding repayment
items.desc_en: Rav Amram cites a mishna about returning court documents, but Rabbi Zeira limits it to חליטתא ואדרכתא (documents not subject to repayment). Rava objects that even those can be redeemed, but concludes the reason is that the creditor harmed himself by not tearing the document, and the return is only due to 'doing what is right and good' (ועשית הישר והטוב).

sub.desc_en: Rav Amram cites a mishna that all court documents found are returned, arguing that we do not suspect repayment.
Rabbi Zeira objects that the mishna refers only to חליטתא ואדרכתא (documents not subject to repayment).
Rava objects that even these documents can be redeemed, citing the Nehardeans and Ameimar that a court sale can be redeemed.
Rava resolves that the creditor harmed himself by not tearing the document upon repayment, and the return is only due to 'doing what is right and good' (ועשית הישר והטוב).

items.text: Distinction for debt documents
items.text_en: Distinction for debt documents
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about a debt document (שטר חוב): there we fear repayment because the debtor might stall or the scribe might have inflated the amount, so we do not return it.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks what reason there is to fear returning a debt document (שטר חוב), given that if it were paid the debtor should have torn it, proposing that the debtor might stall or the scribe might have inflated the amount.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling and Rava's resolution
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling and Rava's resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu quotes Rabbi Yochanan that even a debt document with הנפק (validation) should not be returned due to fear of repayment. Rabbi Yirmeya objects with the mishna about court documents, but Rava resolves that the mishna refers to חליטתא ואדרכתא as per Rabbi Zeira.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu quotes Rabbi Yochanan that one who finds a debt document in the market, even if it has הנפק (validation), should not return it.
The gemara clarifies that Rabbi Yochanan's ruling applies even with validation, because we fear the debt was already repaid.
Rabbi Yirmeya objects from the mishna that all court documents are returned, and Rabbi Avahu's son Yirmeya answers that the mishna refers only to a confirmed denier.
Rava rejects the answer about a confirmed denier and resolves that the mishna refers to חליטתא ואדרכתא (court seizure and execution documents), as per Rabbi Zeira.

items.text: Discussion of a confirmed denier (כפרן)
items.text_en: Discussion of a confirmed denier (כפרן)
items.desc_en: The Gemara briefly discusses the case of a confirmed denier (כפרן) who has been established as a liar, citing Rav Yosef bar Minyomi quoting Rav Nachman about a court order to pay.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the topic of a confirmed denier (כפרן) and states that since the case has come before us, we should discuss it.

sub.text: Rav Yosef bar Minyomi quoting Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef bar Minyomi quoting Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Minyomi quotes Rav Nachman that the court tells the confirmed denier 'Go out and pay him'.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Distinction between 'צא תן לו' and 'חייב אתה ליתן לו'
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Distinction between 'צא תן לו' and 'חייב אתה ליתן לו'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the court said 'צא תן לו' and the debtor claims 'פרעתי', he is believed; if the court said 'חייב אתה ליתן לו' and he claims 'פרעתי', he is not believed. This establishes a basic distinction based on the type of court order.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that when the court says 'צא תן לו' and the debtor claims 'פרעתי', he is believed, and the court does not write an authorization for the creditor.
The Mishnah rules that when the court says 'חייב אתה ליתן לו' and the debtor claims 'פרעתי', he is not believed, and the court writes an authorization for the creditor.

items.text: Rav Zevid's challenge and resolution: All cases are believed, with exception for witnesses
items.text_en: Rav Zevid's challenge and resolution: All cases are believed, with exception for witnesses
items.desc_en: Rav Zevid in the name of Rav Nachman argues that in both cases the debtor is believed. He then distinguishes: if witnesses testify he did not pay, and he later claims he paid, he is established as a denier (הוּחְזַק כַּפְרָן) only in the 'צא תן לו' case, because in the 'חייב אתה ליתן לו' case he may be stalling for a court hearing.

sub.text: Rav Zevid in the name of Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rav Zevid in the name of Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid states that in both court formulations ('צא תן לו' and 'חייב אתה ליתן לו'), the debtor who claims repayment is believed, so no authorization is written for the creditor.
Rav Zevid distinguishes: if witnesses testify the debtor did not pay and he later repeats his claim, he becomes a confirmed denier (הוּחְזַק כַּפְרָן) only in the 'צא תן לו' case.
In the 'חייב אתה ליתן לו' case, even with witnesses and repeated claim, the debtor is not established as a denier.
The Gemara explains the reason: in the 'חייב אתה ליתן לו' case, the debtor is merely stalling (משתמיט) until the court investigates his case, so he is not a confirmed liar.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling: Denial of debt followed by claim of payment
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling: Denial of debt followed by claim of payment
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that if one says 'מנה לי בידך' and the other denies, then witnesses testify he owes, and he later claims 'פרעתי', he is established as a denier. A story about Shabtai bar Rabbi Marinus illustrates this: he wrote a cloak in his daughter-in-law's ketubah, later denied it, and when witnesses confirmed, he claimed he paid, and Rabbi Chiyya declared him a denier.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that if one denies a debt and then claims payment after witnesses testify, he is established as a denier (כַּפְרָן).

sub.text: Supporting story about Shabtai bar Rabbi Marinus
sub.text_en: Supporting story about Shabtai bar Rabbi Marinus
sub.desc_en: A story illustrates the ruling: Shabtai bar Rabbi Marinus denied writing a cloak in his daughter-in-law's ketubah, witnesses confirmed it, he later claimed payment, and Rabbi Chiyya declared him a denier.

items.text: Rabbi Avin's ruling: Oath denial and the distinction of court-imposed oath
items.text_en: Rabbi Avin's ruling: Oath denial and the distinction of court-imposed oath
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avin in the name of Rabbi Yochanan rules that if one was obligated to take an oath and claims 'נשבעתי', but witnesses testify he did not, and he repeats the claim, he is established as a denier for that oath. Rabbi Avahu clarifies this applies only when the oath was imposed by a court, not when he voluntarily obligated himself. Rabbi Avin confirms he meant in court.

sub.text: Rabbi Avin citing Rabbi Ila'a citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Avin citing Rabbi Ila'a citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: רבי אבין (Rabbi Avin) in the name of רבי אלעא (Rabbi Ila'a) citing רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) rules that if one was obligated to take an oath and claims 'נשבעתי' (I swore), but witnesses testify he did not, and he repeats the claim, he is established as a denier for that oath.

רבי אבהו (Rabbi Avahu) clarifies that the ruling applies only when the oath was imposed by a court, but if one voluntarily obligated himself, he is deemed credible because a person may say he will take an oath and then change his mind.
רבי אבין (Rabbi Avin) confirms that he too meant the case where the oath was imposed by a court.
The Gemara cites an explicit version of the statement that includes 'בבית דין' (in court), confirming Rabbi Avahu's interpretation.

items.text: Rabbi Asi's ruling: Found promissory note with 'הנפק' and same-day date
items.text_en: Rabbi Asi's ruling: Found promissory note with 'הנפק' and same-day date
items.desc_en: Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan rules that if one finds a promissory note in the market with a receipt (הנפק) and the date is the same day, it should be returned to the owner. The Gemara explains: since it has a receipt, it wasn't written without a loan; and we do not suspect same-day repayment. Rabbi Zeira objects based on another ruling that a repaid note cannot be reused because its lien is void. The Gemara resolves that people do sometimes repay on the same day, but it is uncommon.

sub.text: Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan rules that a found promissory note with a ratification and same-day date should be returned to the owner.
The Gemara explains the ruling: the ratification eliminates concern that the note was written without a loan, and same-day repayment is not suspected.
Rabbi Zeira objects, citing Rabbi Yochanan's own ruling that a repaid note cannot be reused because its lien is void, implying same-day repayment is possible.
The Gemara analyzes Rabbi Zeira's objection: if the second loan was the next day, the note would be invalid as antedated, not because the lien was forgiven.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yochanan's ruling must refer to a same-day second loan, proving that people do repay on the same day.
Rabbi Asi clarifies that he did not deny same-day repayment entirely, but said it is uncommon, so the found note is still returned.

items.text: Rav Kahana's explanation and comparison to found debt documents
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's explanation and comparison to found debt documents
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana explains the case is when the debtor admits the debt. The Gemara questions why this is stated, and explains it teaches that the debtor would not risk the lender's reputation by using the note again. The Gemara compares this to a Mishnah about found debt documents with property lien, where we suspect the debtor wrote a backdated note. The distinction is that there the debtor gains by seizing property from buyers, so he remains silent; here there is no gain since the lien is already void.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana states that the case of the found debt document is when the debtor admits the debt, and the Gemara questions why this needs to be stated.
The Gemara asks: if the debtor admits, what novel point is being taught?

The Gemara explains that without the ruling, one might think the debtor's denial is due to a plan to borrow again using the same document, but the ruling teaches that the lender himself would not risk the rabbis' suspicion.
The Gemara asks: what is the difference between this case and the Mishnah about found debt documents with property lien, where we do not return them even when the debtor admits?
The Gemara explains that in the Mishnah, the debtor admits but we suspect he wrote a backdated note to seize property from buyers unlawfully.
The Gemara objects: there too, why don't we say the lender would not risk the rabbis' suspicion?

The Gemara resolves: there, the debtor gains by seizing property from buyers, so he stays silent; here, since the lien is already void, there is no gain and the lender would not risk the rabbis' suspicion.

items.text: Introduction to the next topic: Claiming after a court ruling
items.text_en: Introduction to the next topic: Claiming after a court ruling
items.desc_en: The daf begins a new discussion introduced by Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan about one who makes a claim after a court ruling (מעשה בית דין). This sets up the next section of the Gemara.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan begins a new statement about one who makes a claim after a court ruling.

items.text: Gemara's principle: court document is like holding a deed
items.text_en: Gemara's principle: court document is like holding a deed
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that a court document is considered as if the holder has the deed in hand, explaining why one who says 'I paid' after a court judgment says nothing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that one who says 'I paid' after a court judgment says nothing, because a court document is considered as if the holder has the deed in hand.

items.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba's question and Rabbi Yochanan's response
items.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba's question and Rabbi Yochanan's response
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba asks Rabbi Yochanan if this principle is not already taught in the Mishnah about a woman who produces a get without a ketubah. Rabbi Yochanan replies that if not for him raising a potsherd, he would not find a pearl beneath it.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba asks Rabbi Yochanan whether the principle that a woman who produces a גט (bill of divorce) without a כתובה (marriage contract) collects her כתובה is not already taught in the Mishnah.
Rabbi Yochanan replies that without Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba raising a potsherd (i.e., raising the Mishnah), he would not find the pearl beneath it (i.e., the deeper insight).

items.text: Abaye's first interpretation of the pearl
items.text_en: Abaye's first interpretation of the pearl
items.desc_en: Abaye explains the pearl: the Mishnah deals with a place where they do not write a ketubah, so the get itself serves as the ketubah. But where they write a ketubah, she needs the actual document to collect.

sub.desc_en: Abaye explains that the Mishnah's pearl refers to a place where they do not write a ketubah (כתובה), so the get (גט) itself serves as the ketubah; but where they write a ketubah, she needs the actual document to collect.

items.text: Abaye retracts: problem of the widow from betrothal
items.text_en: Abaye retracts: problem of the widow from betrothal
items.desc_en: Abaye retracts his statement, arguing that if the Mishnah only applies where no ketubah is written, then how does a widow from betrothal collect her ketubah? She would need witnesses of the husband's death, but then the husband could claim he paid. This would undermine the Sages' enactment.

sub.desc_en: Abaye retracts his earlier statement, arguing that if the Mishnah only applies where no ketubah is written, then a widow from betrothal would need witnesses of the husband's death to collect, but the husband could claim he paid.
Abaye asks how a widow from betrothal would collect her ketubah if she needs witnesses of the husband's death, since the husband could claim he already paid.
Abaye objects that if the husband could claim payment, then the Sages' enactment for the widow's protection would be undermined.

items.text: Mar Kashisha's question: source for widow from betrothal having a ketubah
items.text_en: Mar Kashisha's question: source for widow from betrothal having a ketubah
items.desc_en: Mar Kashisha, son of Rav Chisda, asks Rav Ashi: from where do we know that a widow from betrothal has a ketubah at all?

sub.text: Mar Kashisha's question to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Mar Kashisha's question to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Mar Kashisha asks Rav Ashi: from where do we derive that a widow from betrothal (אלמנה מן האירוסין) is entitled to a ketubah (כתובה) at all?

items.text: Rav Ashi's answer and proof from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's answer and proof from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi suggests the source is a Mishnah where a widow or divorcee from betrothal collects everything. He considers that this might be where he wrote her a ketubah, and explains that the Mishnah is needed to exclude Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's view. The Gemara then notes that the language 'collects everything' supports the idea that a ketubah was written.

sub.text: Mar Kashisha's question to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Mar Kashisha's question to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Mar Kashisha asks Rav Ashi: from where do we derive that a widow from betrothal has a ketubah?
Rav Ashi suggests the source is the Mishnah where a widow or divorcee from betrothal collects everything.
The Gemara objects: perhaps the Mishnah refers to a case where he wrote her a ketubah.
Rav Ashi explains that the Mishnah is needed to exclude Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's view that the ketubah was written only on condition of marriage.
The Gemara notes that the language 'collects everything' supports the idea that a ketubah was written, as otherwise the phrase would be problematic.

items.text: Clarification of 'goveh et hakol'
items.text_en: Clarification of 'goveh et hakol'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'goveh et hakol' means, explaining that it refers to the maneh and two hundred zuz that she has.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'goveh et hakol' means, and answers that it refers to the maneh and two hundred zuz that she has.

items.text: Challenge from Rav Chiyya bar Ami's baraita
items.text_en: Challenge from Rav Chiyya bar Ami's baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Chiyya bar Ami's baraita about an arusah who does not mourn or become impure for her husband, and who does not inherit but collects her ketubah. It then suggests that the baraita refers to a case where he wrote her a ketubah, but questions why it needed to state that he does not inherit her.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Rav Chiyya bar Ami's baraita
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Rav Chiyya bar Ami's baraita
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Chiyya bar Ami's baraita about an arusah who does not mourn or become impure for her husband, and who does not inherit but collects her ketubah.
The Gemara questions whether the baraita refers to a case where he wrote her a ketubah, and if so, why it needed to state that he does not inherit her.

items.text: Abaye's retraction and the logic of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Abaye's retraction and the logic of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Abaye retracts his earlier position based on the Mishnah itself: if the Mishnah deals with a place where they do not write a ketubah, the get itself is the ketubah, but a get does not specify the amount. The Gemara then considers and rejects several possible defenses: that the get is considered as if written, that one could claim payment, that the woman would want to remarry with it, and that one could tear it and write a note. The final objection is that not everyone collects in court.

sub.desc_en: Abaye retracts his position based on the Mishnah itself: if the Mishnah deals with a place where they do not write a ketubah, the get itself is the ketubah, but a get does not specify the amount of 100 or 200 zuz.
The Gemara objects: one might say that since the rabbis instituted that she collects with it as if the amount were written in it, the husband could claim 'I already paid'.
The Gemara objects further: one might say we tell the husband 'if you paid, you should have torn it', but the woman could respond 'I wanted to remarry with it'.
The Gemara objects: one might say we tell the husband 'you should have torn it and written a note on the back', but the final objection is that not everyone who collects does so in court.

items.text: Mishnah: Found documents not returned
items.text_en: Mishnah: Found documents not returned
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one finds gittin, shichrurei avadim, deeds of gift, or receipts, they should not be returned, because one might have written them and then changed their mind about giving them.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that found documents of divorce, emancipation, gifts, and receipts are not returned, due to suspicion that the writer changed his mind.

items.text: Gemara's inference from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's inference from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers that if the person said 'give it,' then we do return it, even after a long time.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's language that if the person said 'give it,' we return the document even after a long time.

items.text: Contradiction from the baraita about a lost get
items.text_en: Contradiction from the baraita about a lost get
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita: if one brings a get and it is lost, if found immediately it is valid, otherwise it is invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita: if one brings a get and it is lost, if found immediately it is valid, otherwise it is invalid.

items.text: Rabbah's resolution and the case of two Yosef ben Shimon
items.text_en: Rabbah's resolution and the case of two Yosef ben Shimon
items.desc_en: Rabbah resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a place where caravans are common and where they are not. Even where caravans are common, it must be established that there are two Yosef ben Shimon in the city. This is supported by a case in Rav Huna's court where a get was found and Rav Huna ruled accordingly.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a place where caravans (שיירות) are common and where they are not.
The Gemara adds that even where caravans are common, it must be established that there are two Yosef ben Shimon in the city.

sub.text: Supporting case from Rav Huna's court
sub.text_en: Supporting case from Rav Huna's court
sub.desc_en: The Gemara supports the refinement by citing a case in Rav Huna's court where a get was found and Rav Huna ruled accordingly, otherwise Rabbah's own position would be contradictory.

items.text: Rabbah's inference from the Mishnah about court documents
items.text_en: Rabbah's inference from the Mishnah about court documents
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda tells Rabbah to examine a case because Rav Huna will ask about it later. Rabbah finds a Mishnah stating that any court document must be returned, and infers that this applies only when two Yosef ben Shimon are known to exist in that town.

sub.desc_en: The gemara opens by stating that we are concerned for two Shviri (a town name), and Rav Chisda tells Rabbah to examine the matter because Rav Huna will ask about it later.
Rabbah goes out, examines, and finds a Mishnah stating that any court document is returned, and infers that this applies only when two Yosef ben Shimon are known to exist in that town.

items.text: Two versions of Rabbah's ruling about a get found in a flax bundle
items.text_en: Two versions of Rabbah's ruling about a get found in a flax bundle
items.desc_en: Rabbah ruled practically regarding a get found in a flax bundle in Pumbedita according to his own reasoning. Two alternative versions of the ruling are presented: one where flax is sold and there are no known duplicates, and another where flax is processed even if duplicates are known, because caravans are not common.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah issued a practical ruling regarding a get found in a flax bundle in Pumbedita, consistent with his own reasoning.
One version states the ruling applies where flax is sold and no duplicate names are known, even though caravans are common.
Another version states the ruling applies where flax is processed, even if duplicate names are known, because caravans are not common.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's contradiction between Mishnah and Baraita
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's contradiction between Mishnah and Baraita
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira raises a contradiction: a Mishnah says a get found immediately is valid, otherwise invalid, but a Baraita says if the husband admits, it is returned even after a long time. He resolves that the Mishnah refers to a place where caravans are not common, while the Baraita refers to a place where they are common.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira raises a contradiction: the Mishnah rules that a get found immediately is valid, otherwise invalid, while a Baraita says that if the husband admits, it is returned even after a long time.
The Gemara cites the Baraita that distinguishes between cases where the husband admits (returned) and where he does not (not returned).
The Gemara objects that the Baraita explicitly allows return even after a long time when the husband admits.
Rabbi Zeira resolves the contradiction: the Mishnah refers to a place where caravans are not common, while the Baraita refers to a place where they are common.

items.text: Two interpretations of Rabbi Zeira's position
items.text_en: Two interpretations of Rabbi Zeira's position
items.desc_en: Two versions are given: one says Rabbi Zeira requires known duplicates to invalidate return (agreeing with Rabbah), the other says even without known duplicates the get is not returned, disagreeing with Rabbah.

sub.desc_en: The first version states that Rabbi Zeira requires known duplicates (הוחזקו) to invalidate return, aligning with Rabbah's position.
The second version holds that even without known duplicates the get is not returned, disagreeing with Rabbah.

items.text: Why Rabbah and Rabbi Zeira disagree
items.text_en: Why Rabbah and Rabbi Zeira disagree
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbah does not follow Rabbi Zeira because he finds the Mishnah difficult to question. Rabbi Zeira does not follow Rabbah because the Mishnah only says 'if he said 'give it' they give it', but not necessarily even after a long time; it might only be immediately.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbah does not follow Rabbi Zeira's position, and answers that the Mishnah is too strong for him to question.
The Gemara asks why Rabbi Zeira does not follow Rabbah's position.
Rabbi Zeira explains that the Mishnah only says 'if he said give it, they give it' but does not specify even after a long time; it might only be immediately (לאלתר).

items.text: The core dispute between Rabbah and Rabbi Zeira
items.text_en: The core dispute between Rabbah and Rabbi Zeira
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies their disagreement: Rabbah holds that the Mishnah 'all court documents are returned' refers to documents found in court, which is like a place with caravans, and only if duplicates are known it is not returned. Rabbi Zeira argues the Mishnah does not specify 'found in court', so it applies even outside, and the location determines the ruling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to the version that attributes to Rabbi Zeira the view that even without established duplicates the document is not returned, on what do Rabbah and Rabbi Zeira disagree?
Rabbah holds that the Mishnah 'all court documents are returned' deals with documents found in court, which is like a place with caravans, and only if duplicates are known it is not returned.
Rabbi Zeira argues that the Mishnah does not specify 'found in court', so it applies even outside, and the location determines the ruling.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya and Rav Ashi's solutions using simanim
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya and Rav Ashi's solutions using simanim
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya suggests the case is where witnesses say they only signed one get for Yosef ben Shimon. Rav Ashi suggests the finder identifies a specific hole next to a certain letter. The Gemara notes that Rav Ashi is uncertain whether simanim are biblical or rabbinic.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya proposes that the case involves witnesses who testify they only ever signed one get for Yosef ben Shimon, providing a unique identifying feature.
The Gemara questions what novel point Rabbi Yirmeya's proposal adds, since the witnesses' testimony seems obvious.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yirmeya's statement is needed to counter a possible concern that the names might coincidentally match, teaching that such testimony is sufficient.
Rav Ashi proposes that the finder identifies the get by a specific hole next to a particular letter, serving as a unique siman (identifying mark).

sub.text: Gemara's clarification of Rav Ashi's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's clarification of Rav Ashi's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara specifies that Rav Ashi requires the hole to be next to a specific letter, not just any hole, to serve as a valid siman.

sub.text: Gemara's note on Rav Ashi's uncertainty
sub.text_en: Gemara's note on Rav Ashi's uncertainty
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rav Ashi is uncertain whether the validity of simanim (identifying marks) is biblical (דאורייתא) or rabbinic (דרבנן).

items.text: Rav Ashi's uncertainty about simanim and the end of the daf
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's uncertainty about simanim and the end of the daf
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi is uncertain whether simanim are biblical or rabbinic. The daf ends with the name Rabbah bar bar Chanah, likely the beginning of the next sugya.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi is uncertain whether the validity of simanim (identifying marks) for returning lost objects is biblical (דאורייתא) or rabbinic (דרבנן).
The daf ends with the name Rabbah bar bar Chanah, likely marking the beginning of the next sugya (Talmudic discussion).

items.text: Opening story: Rava's lost get in the study hall
items.text_en: Opening story: Rava's lost get in the study hall
items.desc_en: Rava lost a get in the study hall. He said he had a sign (siman) or recognition (tevi'ut ayin) in it. They returned it to him. He then questioned whether they returned it due to siman (which is Torah law) or due to tevi'ut ayin (which only a scholar can rely on).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Rava lost a get in the study hall, identified it by a siman (sign) or tevi'ut ayin (visual recognition), and then questioned whether the return was based on siman (Torah law) or tevi'ut ayin (only reliable for a scholar).

items.text: Mishnah: Found get with husband admitting
items.text_en: Mishnah: Found get with husband admitting
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states: If one finds a woman's get in the market, when the husband admits (it is his), return it to the woman. If the husband does not admit, do not return it to either.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule for finding a get: if the husband admits, return it to the woman; if not, return it to neither.

items.text: Gemara's question: Concern for retroactive land seizure
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Concern for retroactive land seizure
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Why return the get when the husband admits? We should worry that the husband wrote the get in Nisan but did not give it until Tishrei, and he sold produce in the interim. The wife could then use the get (dated Nisan) to seize purchasers' land improperly. The Gemara answers: When she comes to seize, we tell her to bring proof of when the get reached her hand.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the get is returned when the husband admits, raising the concern that the husband may have written the get in Nisan but not given it until Tishrei, and the wife could use the backdated get to seize land from purchasers improperly.

The Gemara notes that the concern is resolved for the opinion that once the husband sets his eyes on divorce he has no rights to produce, but objects: for the opinion that the husband retains produce rights until the moment of delivery, what can be said?
The Gemara resolves: when the wife comes to seize, we tell her to bring proof of when the get actually reached her hand.

items.text: Comparison to found promissory notes (shtarot chov)
items.text_en: Comparison to found promissory notes (shtarot chov)
items.desc_en: The Gemara compares to found promissory notes: if the debtor admits, we do not return them due to similar concerns. Why not apply the same solution (bring proof of when the note reached you)? The Gemara explains: In the case of a get, the purchaser will come and demand the wife prove when she received it, so she will not seize improperly. In the case of a promissory note, the purchaser will not come to demand proof, assuming the court returned it for collection, so the creditor could seize improperly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the case of a found get is different from found promissory notes (שטרי חוב), where even when the debtor admits, we do not return them due to concern the creditor wrote the note early and collected improperly.
The Gemara objects that in the promissory note case too, the court could return the document and demand proof of when it reached the creditor.
The Gemara answers that in the case of a get, the purchaser will come and demand proof from the wife, knowing the court returned it only to prevent her from being an agunah (עגונה).
The Gemara explains that in the promissory note case, the purchaser will not demand proof, assuming the court returned it for collection, so the creditor could seize improperly.

items.text: Found document of manumission (shichrur avadim)
items.text_en: Found document of manumission (shichrur avadim)
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: If one finds a document of manumission, when the master admits, return it to the slave. The Gemara questions: We should worry that the master wrote it in Nisan but did not give it until Tishrei, and the slave acquired property in the interim, then the master sold it, and the slave could seize purchasers improperly. The answer: When he comes to seize, we tell him to bring proof of when the manumission reached his hand.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: If one finds a document of manumission (שִׁחְרוּר עֲבָדִים), when the master admits, return it to the slave; otherwise, do not return it to either party.

The Gemara questions: Why return it? We should worry that the master wrote it in Nisan but did not give it until Tishrei, and the slave acquired property in the interim, then the master sold it, and the slave could seize purchasers improperly.

The Gemara notes: This works for the opinion that freedom is a benefit (זְכוּת) for the slave, as per Abaye's principle that witnesses' signatures acquire for him; but for the opinion that freedom is a detriment (חוֹב), what can be said?
The Gemara resolves: When the slave comes to seize property, we tell him to bring proof of when the manumission document reached his hand.

items.text: Found diyathiki/matana and the contradiction
items.text_en: Found diyathiki/matana and the contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara defines diyathiki (a will) and matana (a gift). It then raises a contradiction: a baraita says that if one finds such documents, even if both parties admit, do not return them. Rabbi Abba bar Memel resolves the contradiction.

sub.desc_en: The baraita defines דיָיתֵיקֵי (a will) as a document stating that if the testator dies, his property goes to a named recipient, and a מַתָּנָה (gift) as one written with the phrase 'from today and after death'.
The Gemara infers from the baraita that only a document with the phrase 'from today and after death' effects acquisition; otherwise it does not, raising a difficulty.

Abaye explains that the baraita refers to a healthy person's gift that is like a dying person's gift, which only takes effect after death, and the phrase 'from today and after death' is the defining condition.
The Gemara infers that if the document includes the instruction 'give' (תְּנוּ), the finder should return it, implying a distinction from the case without that instruction.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that says if one finds wills or gifts, even if both parties admit, do not return them.
Rabbi Abba bar Memel begins to resolve the contradiction, stating that it is not difficult.

items.text: Initial resolution of the contradiction
items.text_en: Initial resolution of the contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the Mishnah (which says 'if he said 'give' we give') refers to a deathly ill person, who can retract, while the baraita (which says we do not return) refers to a healthy person, who cannot retract.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a healthy person (בריא) and a deathly ill person (שכיב מרע).

items.text: Explanation of the Mishnah's ruling for a deathly ill person
items.text_en: Explanation of the Mishnah's ruling for a deathly ill person
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that for a deathly ill person, we give the deed because there is no loss: if he gave to another later, the later recipient acquires, as he retracted from the first.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the Mishnah's ruling
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the Mishnah's ruling
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's case (where 'give' is said and we give) applies to a deathly ill person who can retract, and even if he gave to another later, the later recipient acquires because the first gift was retracted.
The Gemara explains the concern: perhaps the sick person wrote a deed for one recipient, reconsidered, and gave it to another, and now retracts from the second.
The Gemara resolves that for a gift of a healthy person (מתנת בריא), there is no loss because the later recipient acquires, as the giver retracted from the first.
The Gemara similarly resolves that for a gift of a deathly ill person (מתנת שכיב מרע), there is no loss because the later recipient acquires, as the giver retracted from the first.

items.text: Explanation of the baraita's ruling for a healthy person
items.text_en: Explanation of the baraita's ruling for a healthy person
items.desc_en: For a healthy person, we do not return the deed because he might have written to one, changed his mind, and given to another; now he claims he gave to the first to retrieve the deed and let the first collect, but we suspect he is retracting from the later recipient.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the baraita's ruling
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the baraita's ruling
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the baraita's case (where we do not return the document) applies to a healthy person who cannot retract, and we suspect he may have written the document but not given it, then given it to another, so we tell him to write a new document now.
The Gemara raises the suspicion that the healthy person wrote a deed to one recipient, changed his mind, and gave it to another, and now claims he gave it to the first to retrieve the deed.
The Gemara resolves that we tell the claimant: we will not return this deed; if you truly gave it to the first, write a new deed now, and if you gave it to another, the later recipient prevails.

items.text: Rav Zevid's objection and alternative resolution
items.text_en: Rav Zevid's objection and alternative resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Zevid objects that both the Mishnah and baraita deal with deathbed gifts (דייתיקאות), and resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the ill person himself and his son.

sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid objects that both the Mishnah and the baraita deal with deathbed gifts (דייתיקי), so the distinction between healthy and deathly ill is invalid, and he proposes a new resolution: the Mishnah refers to the dying person himself, the baraita to his son.
Rav Zevid resolves the contradiction by explaining that both cases involve a deathly ill person, but the Mishnah refers to the ill person himself, while the baraita refers to his son.

items.text: Explanation of the Mishnah regarding the ill person himself
items.text_en: Explanation of the Mishnah regarding the ill person himself
items.desc_en: When the ill person says 'give', we give to him because he can retract; if he gave to another later, the later recipient acquires.

sub.text: Rav Zevid's explanation of the Mishnah's ruling
sub.text_en: Rav Zevid's explanation of the Mishnah's ruling
sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid explains that when the dying person says 'give', we give because he can retract, and even if he gave to another later, the later recipient acquires since the first gift was retracted.

items.text: Explanation of the baraita regarding the ill person's son
items.text_en: Explanation of the baraita regarding the ill person's son
items.desc_en: When the son says 'give', we do not return the deed because the father might have written to one and not given, and the son later gave to another; now the son claims the father gave to the first to retrieve the deed and collect, but we suspect he is retracting from the later recipient.

sub.text: Rav Zevid's explanation of the baraita's ruling
sub.text_en: Rav Zevid's explanation of the baraita's ruling
sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid explains that the baraita's case (where we do not return the document) applies to the son of the dying person, who cannot retract, and we suspect the son may have written a document after his father's failed gift, so we tell him to write a new document now.

The Gemara raises the suspicion that the father wrote the deed to one person but did not give it, then the son later gave it to another, and now the son is retracting from the later recipient by claiming the father gave it to the first.
The Gemara resolves that we tell the son we will not return the deed, because the father may have written but not given, and the son may have given it to another and is now retracting.
The Gemara proposes an alternative: if the son's claim is true, he should write a new deed now, since if he had given to another, the first recipient prevails.

items.text: Baraita about finding a receipt for a ketubah
items.text_en: Baraita about finding a receipt for a ketubah
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches: if one finds a receipt (שובר), when the wife admits she received her ketubah, we return it to the husband; if she does not admit, we do not return it. The Gemara raises a concern that she might have written the receipt in Nisan but sold her ketubah's benefit from Nisan to Tishrei, and then produce the receipt to collect from buyers improperly.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: if one finds a receipt (שובר), when the wife admits she received payment, we return it to the husband; otherwise we do not, and the Gemara raises a concern that the wife might have sold her ketubah rights and then use the receipt to wrongfully collect from buyers.

The Gemara objects that even when the wife admits, returning the receipt is problematic because she might have written it in Nisan but sold the benefit of her ketubah from Nisan to Tishrei, then produce the receipt to improperly collect from buyers.

items.text: Rava's statement (beginning of next discussion)
items.text_en: Rava's statement (beginning of next discussion)
items.desc_en: Rava begins to address the concern about the receipt, but the argument is cut off at the end of the amud.

sub.desc_en: Rava begins his response to the concern raised about the baraita.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the found deed of gift
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the found deed of gift
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah's ruling supports Shmuel's view that a seller who forgives a debt renders the document void. Abaye counters that the case involves a ketubah that was found, and Rava objects that two ketubot are a concern. Abaye defends his position, citing his principle that witnesses' signatures grant rights.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah's ruling supports Shmuel's view that a seller who forgives a debt renders the document void, even if the forgiver is an heir.
Abaye objects that even without Shmuel's principle, the case involves a found ketubah (marriage contract), which is different.
Rava objects that if it is a ketubah, we must worry about two ketubot (the woman might have two marriage contracts).
Abaye defends his position, stating that we do not worry about two ketubot, and he cites his principle that witnesses' signatures grant rights to the document holder.

items.text: Mishnah: Documents that must be returned
items.text_en: Mishnah: Documents that must be returned
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists documents that must be returned when found, including court records, documents found in a bundle, and a case where a document is found among one's own papers. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds a rule about returning to the borrower or lender based on the number of parties.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing specific documents that must be returned when found: court assessment records, sustenance records, חליצה (release from levirate marriage) and מיאונין (refusal of marriage) documents, arbitration records, and all court actions.

The Mishnah continues with rules for finding documents in a bundle or tied together, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds a distinction: if one borrower borrowed from three lenders, return to the borrower; if three borrowers borrowed from one lender, return to the lender.

The Mishnah concludes with a case where one finds a document among one's own papers and does not know its nature: it must be left until Elijah comes, but if there are supporting documents (סימפונות), one acts according to them.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying 'shtarot berurin' and a case
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying 'shtarot berurin' and a case
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that 'shtarot berurin' are arbitration documents, with Rabbi Yirmeya specifying that each party selects one arbitrator. It then recounts a case where a get was found in Rav Huna's court, and Rav Huna comments on its validity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'שטרי ברורין' (arbitration documents) are.
The local sages in the West (ארץ ישראל) explain that they are documents of claims (שטרי טענתא).
Rabbi Yirmeya explains that each litigant selects one arbitrator, and together they choose a third.

sub.text: Supporting case from Rav Huna's court
sub.text_en: Supporting case from Rav Huna's court
sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts a case where a get (bill of divorce) was found in Rav Huna's court, written with the location 'בשוירי מתא דעל רכיס נהרא' (in Shviri, a town on the Rakhis River).
Rav Huna begins to comment on the validity of the found get, setting up the continuation of the sugya.

items.text: Rav Chisda's challenge and Rav Amram's objection
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's challenge and Rav Amram's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda tells Rabba to go check a matter for Rav Huna, and Rabba finds a Mishnah that all court documents are returned. Rav Amram objects that Rabba is deriving a prohibition from a monetary law, but Rabba responds that the Mishnah explicitly mentions 'divorce and refusal documents'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a concern about two signatures.
Rav Chisda tells Rabba to go investigate a matter that Rav Huna will ask him about later.
Rabba goes out, examines, and finds a Mishnah stating that all court documents are returned.
Rav Amram objects that Rabba is deriving a prohibition from a monetary law.
Rabba dismisses the objection, noting that the Mishnah explicitly mentions 'divorce and refusal documents'.

items.text: Dispute about the cedar beam
items.text_en: Dispute about the cedar beam
items.desc_en: A cedar beam in Rav's house split, and two sages each claim it was due to their own study pressure.

sub.desc_en: The narrator reports that a cedar beam in Rav's house split.
One Mar claims the beam split due to his own study pressure.
The other Mar claims the beam split due to his own study pressure.

items.text: Definitions of ḥafisa and deluskema
items.text_en: Definitions of ḥafisa and deluskema
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the terms from the Mishnah: ḥafisa is a small leather bag, and deluskema is an old man's cloak.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the definitions of the terms 'חפיסה' and 'דלוסקמא' from the Mishnah.
Rabba bar bar Chana defines 'חפיסה' as a small leather bag (חמת קטנה).
Rabba bar Shmuel defines 'דלוסקמא' as an old man's cloak (טליקא דסבי).

items.text: Definition of a bundle and the announcement
items.text_en: Definition of a bundle and the announcement
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses a bundle of documents. The Gemara defines a bundle as three documents tied together, and infers that a knot is a sign. It then questions what is announced: the count? Why specifically three? Ravina explains that the finder announces 'documents'.

sub.desc_en: The baraita defines a bundle (תכריך) as three documents rolled together and a tied bundle (אגודה) as three tied together.
The Gemara infers from the baraita that a knot is a valid identifying sign (סימן) for returning lost documents.
Rabbi Chiyya's baraita is cited, which also states the definition of a bundle as three documents rolled together.
The Gemara distinguishes between a bundle (תכריך) where each document is rolled at the head of the other, and a tied bundle (אגודה) where they are placed together and rolled.
The Gemara asks: what does the finder announce — the count of documents?
The Gemara objects: why specifically three documents? Even two would be a valid bundle.
Ravina resolves: just as the finder of coins announces 'coins', here the finder announces 'documents' (שטרי), not the count.

items.text: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling: one borrower from three lenders
items.text_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling: one borrower from three lenders
items.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says that if one borrowed from three, the document is returned to the borrower. The Gemara questions why the lenders would have their documents together, and suggests they might have gone for validation, but that is unlikely. Similarly, for three who borrowed from one, the document is returned to the lender, as the borrowers would not have their documents together.

sub.text: Mishnah citation: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
sub.text_en: Mishnah citation: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling that if one borrowed from three lenders, the document is returned to the borrower.
The Gemara questions why the lenders would have their documents together if they are lenders.
The Gemara suggests that the lenders might have gone together for validation of their documents.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the documents fell from the scribe's hand, but then notes that no one leaves their validation in the scribe's hand.

sub.text: Mishnah continuation: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
sub.text_en: Mishnah continuation: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites the second part of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling: if three borrowed from one, the document is returned to the lender.
The Gemara questions why the borrowers would have their documents together if they are borrowers.
The Gemara suggests that the borrowers might have gone together to have their documents written by three different scribes.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the borrowers went for validation, but then notes that the lender validates his document, not the borrower.

items.text: Simpon found among documents: Rav's ruling
items.text_en: Simpon found among documents: Rav's ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba quotes Rav that a simpon (promissory note) found in the lender's possession is invalid, even if written in his own hand, as it is considered a game. The Gemara explains that the lender might have written it to ensure payment. The Mishnah's ruling that one acts according to the simpon is explained by Rav Safra as referring to one found among torn documents.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if simponot (promissory notes) are found with other documents, one acts according to the simpon.

sub.text: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba quoting Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba quoting Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav rules that a simpon found in the lender's possession is invalid, even if written in his own hand, as it is considered a game.
The Gemara explains that the lender might have written the simpon himself to ensure payment if he happened to come at twilight.
Rav Safra resolves the contradiction by explaining that the Mishnah's ruling applies only when the simpon was found among torn documents.

items.text: Further proofs about simpon and found documents
items.text_en: Further proofs about simpon and found documents
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings additional sources: a document found among one's own documents stating another's debt is paid, and a simpon with witnesses. Rav Safra consistently explains that these cases refer to documents found among torn documents. The final source suggests a simpon with witnesses must be validated by its signatures.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita: if one found among his documents a document stating that Yosef ben Shimon's debt is paid, both documents are considered paid.
Rav Safra explains that this case also refers to a document found among torn documents.
The Gemara brings another source: heirs swear that they did not find among their father's documents a statement that a particular document is paid.
Rav Safra again explains that this case refers to a document found among torn documents.
The Gemara brings a final source: a simpon (receipt) that has witnesses must be validated by its signatures.
The Gemara resolves: read the baraita as 'it must be validated from its signatures' (i.e., the simpon itself must be validated, not that it validates other documents).

items.text: דין סימפון היוצא מידי שליש או לאחר חיתום שטרות
items.text_en: Conclusion of the simpōn discussion
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the witnesses mentioned in the mishnah about a simpōn are witnesses to its validation (עֵדֵי קִיּוּם), not witnesses to the loan. It then cites the baraita that a simpōn with witnesses is valid, and explains why a document emerging from a third party or after sealing is valid.
items.desc: הגמרא דנה בסימפון (שטר זיכרון) שעליו עדים, ומבארת שהמדובר בעדי קיום. אם הסימפון יוצא מידי שליש או לאחר חיתום השטר, הוא כשר, משום שהמלוה האמין לשליש או שלא היה מריע לשטרו אילו נפרע החוב.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the witnesses in the simpōn are asked about repayment.
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת בהסבר כיצד מבררים אם שטר נפרע על ידי שאלת העדים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that a simpōn with witnesses is valid, and interprets the witnesses as witnesses to its validation (עֵדֵי קִיּוּם).
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא על סימפון שיש עליו עדים ומקשה, ומתרצת שמדובר בעדי קיום.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara confirms this interpretation by analyzing the baraita's continuation: if the simpōn has no witnesses at all, it is invalid, so the witnesses must be witnesses to validation.
sub.desc: הגמרא מוכיחה מדקדוק לשון הברייתא שאכן מדובר בעדי קיום.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita's full text: a simpōn with witnesses is validated by its signatures; without witnesses, if it emerges from a third party or after sealing, it is valid.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה את גוף הברייתא המפרשת את דיני הסימפון: כשר אם יוצא מידי שליש או לאחר חיתום שטרות.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains why a document emerging from a third party or after sealing is valid: the lender trusted the third party, and if the debt were paid, the lender would not have damaged his own document.
sub.desc: הגמרא מבארת את טעמי הכשרות: האמינות של השליש, והעובדה שהמלוה לא היה מריע לשטרו אילו נפרע החוב.

items.text: סיום הפרק הקודם
items.text_en: Transition to new chapter
items.desc_en: The phrase 'הֲדַרַן עֲלָךְ' marks the end of the previous chapter and the beginning of the new one.
items.desc: מילת מעבר המסמנת את סיום הפרק הקודם ('הדרן עלך שנים אוחזין').

sub.desc_en: The stam marks the end of the previous chapter and the beginning of the new one with the formula 'הדרן עלך' (we return to you).
sub.desc: מילת מעבר המסמנת את סיום הפרק הקודם.

items.text: משנת אלו מציאות שלו
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: items that are the finder's vs. those requiring announcement
items.desc_en: The mishnah lists items that a finder may keep (e.g., scattered fruits, coins, round cakes of pressed figs) and those that require an announcement. Rabbi Yehuda adds that anything with a distinctive mark must be announced, and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says that all vessels of anpurya (a type of market) do not require announcement.
items.desc: המשנה מפרטת אילו מציאות שייכות למוצא (ללא הכרזה) ואילו חייבות בהכרזה. רבי מאיר מונה פריטים ללא סימן, רבי יהודה מחייב הכרזה כשיש שינוי, ורבי שמעון בן אלעזר פוטר כלי אנפוריה.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens by listing items that are the finder's to keep, including scattered fruits, coins, round cakes of pressed figs, and others, according to Rabbi Meir.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בהבחנה בין מציאות שהמוצא זכאי להן לבין אלו שחייב להכריז, ורבי מאיר מונה רשימת פריטים שהמוצא זכאי להם.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda adds that anything with a distinctive change (שינוי) must be announced, giving examples like a fig cake with a potsherd inside or a loaf with coins inside.
sub.desc: רבי יהודה חולק וקובע שכל מציאה שיש בה שינוי מחייבת הכרזה, ומביא דוגמאות לעיגול ובו חרס או כיכר ובו מעות.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar states that all vessels of anpurya (a type of market) do not require announcement.
sub.desc: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר פוטר כלי אנפוריה מהכרזה, משום שאין להם סימן.

items.text: Gemara: measure of scattered produce that indicates abandonment
items.text_en: Gemara: measure of scattered produce that indicates abandonment
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how much scattered produce is considered ownerless. Rabbi Yitzchak says a kav in four amot. Rav Ukva bar Chama explains that this applies to a pile of produce that fell from a harvester's bundle; if the effort to gather it is great (a kav in four amot), the owner abandons it; if less, he will return for it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: how much scattered produce constitutes the finder's own property (indicating owner abandonment)?
Rabbi Yitzchak answers: a kav (a measure of volume) within four amot (cubits) is the threshold.
The Gemara objects: if the produce fell accidentally, even a large amount is ownerless; if it was placed intentionally, even less than a kav in four amot is not abandoned.
Rav Ukva bar Chama resolves: we deal with a pile that fell from a harvester's bundle; a kav in four amot involves great effort, so the owner abandons it; less than that, he will return for it.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's unresolved queries about varying measures and types
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's unresolved queries about varying measures and types
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya raises several unresolved questions (תֵּיקוּ): whether half a kav in two amot, two kav in eight amot, a kav of sesame seeds in four amot, or a kav of dates or pomegranates in four amot are considered abandoned. The Gemara leaves these questions unanswered.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya raises an unresolved query: whether half a kav in two amot is considered abandoned, analyzing the two possible rationales (effort vs. value).
Rabbi Yirmeya raises a second unresolved query: whether two kav in eight amot are considered abandoned, again weighing the two rationales.
Rabbi Yirmeya raises a third unresolved query: whether a kav of sesame seeds in four amot is considered abandoned, given their higher value but greater effort to gather.
Rabbi Yirmeya raises a fourth unresolved query: whether a kav of dates or pomegranates in four amot is considered abandoned, and the Gemara concludes all queries remain unresolved (תֵּיקוּ).

items.text: פתיחת סוגיה חדשה
items.text_en: Transition to next sugya
items.desc_en: The phrase 'אִיתְּמַר' signals the beginning of a new discussion, likely about scattered coins.
items.desc: מילת מעבר 'איתמר' המציינת תחילת סוגיה חדשה (המשך הדיון יופיע בעמוד הבא).

sub.desc_en: The stam signals a transition to a new sugya, likely about scattered coins.
sub.desc: מילת מעבר המציינת תחילת סוגיה חדשה, שהמשך הדיון יופיע בעמוד הבא.

items.text: Abaye and Rava's dispute on יאוש שלא מדעת
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava's dispute on יאוש שלא מדעת
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava argue whether יאוש שלא מדעת is valid. They agree that for an item with a siman, it is not יאוש even if the owner later despairs, because he relies on the siman. For an item without a siman, Abaye says it is not יאוש since the owner does not know, while Rava says it is יאוש because when he finds out he will despair immediately.

sub.desc_en: The Stam opens by stating the dispute between Abaye and Rava on whether יאוש שלא מדעת (despair without knowledge) constitutes valid despair.
The Gemara explains that for an item with a סימן (identifying mark), all agree it is not יאוש because the owner relies on the siman and will not despair even upon learning of the loss.
The Gemara notes an exception: for items lost in the sea's undertow or river's current, even with a siman, the Torah permits them, as will be explained later.

The Gemara explains that the dispute is only over an item without a siman: Abaye says it is not יאוש because the owner does not know, while Rava says it is יאוש because when he finds out he will despair immediately.

items.text: Siman for the sugya
items.text_en: Siman for the sugya
items.desc_en: A mnemonic sign (סימן) is provided to help remember the sequence of proofs that follow.

sub.desc_en: A mnemonic sign (סימן) is provided to help remember the sequence of proofs that follow.

items.text: First attempted proof: scattered fruits
items.text_en: First attempted proof: scattered fruits
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about scattered fruits being permitted, implying the owner despairs even without knowledge. It is rejected because the case involves a storage area where the loss is known.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about scattered fruits being permitted, implying the owner despairs even without knowledge.
Rav Ukva bar Chama rejects the proof, explaining the case involves a storage area where the loss is known (אבידה מדעת).
