items.text: Second attempted proof: scattered coins
items.text_en: Second attempted proof: scattered coins
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about scattered coins being the finder's, implying יאוש שלא מדעת. It is rejected because people constantly feel their purse, so the loss is known immediately, per Rabbi Yitzchak.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove that יאוש שלא מדעת (unconscious despair) is effective by citing a baraita that scattered coins belong to the finder, questioning how this could be if the owner does not know of the loss.

The Gemara rejects the proof by invoking Rabbi Yitzchak's principle that a person constantly feels his purse, so the loss is immediately known, making the case one of conscious despair rather than unconscious despair.

items.text: Third attempted proof: cakes of dried figs and baker's loaves
items.text_en: Third attempted proof: cakes of dried figs and baker's loaves
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about cakes of dried figs and baker's loaves being the finder's. It is rejected because these items are heavy and their loss is known.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita stating that cakes of dried figs and baker's loaves belong to the finder, and asks why this is so, since the owner does not know they fell.
The Gemara answers that because these items are heavy, the owner knows of the loss, so the finder may keep them.

items.text: Fourth attempted proof: tongues of scarlet wool
items.text_en: Fourth attempted proof: tongues of scarlet wool
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about tongues of scarlet wool being the finder's. It is rejected because these are valuable and people feel them, like Rabbi Yitzchak's principle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that tongues of scarlet wool found are the finder's, implying that the owner despairs even without knowing, challenging Abaye's position.
The Gemara objects: why should the finder keep them? The owner does not know they fell, so there is no יאוש (despair) at the time of finding.
The Gemara answers that since the tongues are valuable, the owner constantly feels for them, so he knows immediately when they fall, consistent with Rabbi Yitzchak's principle.

items.text: Fifth attempted proof: money found in synagogues
items.text_en: Fifth attempted proof: money found in synagogues
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about money found in synagogues being the finder's because the owners despair. It is rejected because people constantly feel their purse, per Rabbi Yitzchak.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about finding money in synagogues and study halls, which states the finder keeps it because the owners despair, and questions how this is possible if the owner does not know of the loss.
Rabbi Yitzchak answers that a person constantly feels his purse, so he immediately knows of the loss and despairs, explaining why the finder may keep the money.

items.text: Sixth attempted proof: gleanings and the time of permission
items.text_en: Sixth attempted proof: gleanings and the time of permission
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about when the poor may take gleanings, implying יאוש. The Gemara questions why the poor in other places would despair, and answers that since there are poor here, the others despair from the outset, assuming the local poor will take them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about when gleanings become permitted to all, with explanations by Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish, as an attempted proof regarding יאוש (despair) without knowledge.
The Gemara questions why the poor in other places would despair, since they do not know about the gleanings.
The Gemara answers that since there are poor people in this location, the poor elsewhere despair from the outset, assuming the local poor will take the gleanings.

items.text: Seventh attempted proof: figs and olives by the road
items.text_en: Seventh attempted proof: figs and olives by the road
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about figs under a tree being permitted but olives and carobs forbidden. The Gemara explains that for Abaye, the first clause is not difficult because figs are known to fall. For Rava, the second clause is difficult; Rabbi Avahu answers that olives are different because their appearance proves ownership, and Rav Papa adds that figs become repulsive upon falling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about figs under a tree being permitted but olives and carobs forbidden, as a seventh attempted proof regarding יאוש שלא מדעת (unconscious despair).
The Gemara explains that for Abaye, the first clause about figs is not difficult because figs are known to fall and the owner checks them.
The Gemara raises a difficulty for Rava from the second clause that olives and carobs are forbidden, and Rabbi Avahu answers that olives are different because their appearance proves ownership.
The Gemara objects that if appearance proves ownership, then even the first clause about figs should be forbidden.
Rav Papa resolves the objection by explaining that figs become repulsive upon falling, so the owner despairs of them.

items.text: Eighth attempted proof: thief who stole and gave to another
items.text_en: Eighth attempted proof: thief who stole and gave to another
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to cite a baraita about a thief or robber who takes from one and gives to another, but the segment ends before the proof is completed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita about a thief or robber who takes from one and gives to another, as an attempted proof for the dispute about יאוש שלא מדעת (unconscious despair).

items.text: Gemara's question about the thief and despair
items.text_en: Gemara's question about the thief and despair
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that a thief acquires the stolen object through יאוש, asking how the owner can despair if he does not know who stole it. Rav Papa resolves this by explaining the case involves an armed robber, which is a type of robber, not a thief.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the Jordan River, which takes from one and gives to another, the taker acquires and the giver loses.
The Gemara asks: regarding a robber and the Jordan River, the owner sees them and despairs, but regarding a thief, does the owner see him to despair?
Rav Papa explains the Mishnah refers to an armed robber, and the Gemara objects that this is still a robber, to which Rav Papa responds that there are two types of robber.

items.text: Proof from the river flood case
items.text_en: Proof from the river flood case
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a river that swept away wood and deposited it in another's field, which belongs to the finder because the owners despaired. The Gemara infers that without explicit despair, it would not belong to the finder. It then distinguishes between cases where the owner can or cannot rescue the property, and further refines this with the possibility of rescue under duress.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a river that swept away wood and deposited it in another's field, which belongs to the finder because the owners despaired.
The Gemara infers that without explicit despair, the finder would not acquire the property.
The Gemara answers that the baraita deals with a case where the owner can rescue the property.
The Gemara objects that if the owner can rescue, why does the baraita specify that they are chasing? Even without chasing, they would not despair.
The Gemara resolves that the case is where the owner can rescue only with difficulty; chasing indicates no despair, while not chasing implies despair.

items.text: Baraita on terumah taken without permission
items.text_en: Baraita on terumah taken without permission
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about one who enters another's field and separates terumah without permission. If the owner would be concerned about theft, the terumah is invalid; otherwise it is valid. The baraita then discusses a case where the owner finds him and says 'go to the nicer ones,' which validates the terumah if nicer ones are found, and also a case where the owners themselves add to the pile.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that establishes the rule for one who separates תרומה (terumah) from another's field without permission: if the owner is concerned about theft the terumah is invalid, otherwise it is valid.
The baraita provides a test for the owner's concern: if the owner arrives and tells him 'go to the nicer ones,' and nicer ones are found, the terumah is valid; otherwise it is not.
The baraita adds that if the owners themselves collect and add to the pile, the terumah is valid regardless of whether nicer ones were found.

items.text: Rava's explanation of the terumah case
items.text_en: Rava's explanation of the terumah case
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the owner's statement 'go to the nicer ones' can validate the terumah retroactively, since at the time of separation the owner did not know. Rava explains, according to Abaye, that the owner had appointed the person as his agent. The Gemara supports this with a derivation from the verse 'you' and 'also you' to include agents, and then elaborates the scenario: the owner said 'go separate terumah' without specifying from which produce, and the agent took from nicer ones; the owner's later statement confirms the agency.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the terumah can be valid retroactively when the owner did not know at the time of separation.
Rava explains, according to Abaye, that the owner had appointed the person as his agent.
The Gemara supports Rava's explanation by citing the derivation from 'אַתֶּם' and 'גַּם אַתֶּם' that agents act with the owner's knowledge.

The Gemara elaborates the scenario: the owner appointed an agent without specifying from which produce, the agent took from nicer ones, and the owner's later statement 'go to the nicer ones' confirms the agency retroactively.

items.text: Story of Amemar, Mar Zutra, and Rav Ashi
items.text_en: Story of Amemar, Mar Zutra, and Rav Ashi
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates a story where Amemar and Rav Ashi ate fruit brought by a tenant, but Mar Zutra refrained. When the owner arrived and asked why they were not given better fruit, Amemar and Rav Ashi argued that this is like the case of 'go to the nicer ones' which validates the terumah. Mar Zutra responded that Rava limited that principle to terumah, where the owner is pleased due to the mitzvah, but here the owner's statement was only out of embarrassment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara relates that Amemar, Mar Zutra, and Rav Ashi visited the orchard of Mari bar Isak; the tenant brought inferior fruit, Amemar and Rav Ashi ate, Mar Zutra did not, and when the owner arrived he asked why better fruit was not served.

sub.text: Amemar and Rav Ashi to Mar Zutra
sub.text_en: Amemar and Rav Ashi to Mar Zutra
sub.desc_en: Amemar and Rav Ashi ask Mar Zutra why he does not eat, citing the baraita that if nicer fruit is found, the terumah is valid.
Mar Zutra answers that Rava limited the principle of 'go to the nicer ones' to terumah, where the owner is pleased due to the mitzvah, but here the owner's statement was only out of embarrassment.

items.text: Beginning of a new baraita about dew and joy
items.text_en: Beginning of a new baraita about dew and joy
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita about a case where dew is still on produce and the owner is happy, which is considered 'ki yutan' (susceptible to impurity). The baraita continues with a contrasting case where the dew has dried.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita stating that when dew is still on produce and the owner is happy, it is considered susceptible to impurity (כי יותן).
The baraita continues with a contrasting case: if the dew has dried, even if the owner is happy, the produce is not susceptible to impurity.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's principle of 'ki yitun'
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's principle of 'ki yitun'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's ruling that water cannot become susceptible to impurity (כי יותן) implies that we apply retroactive consent. It distinguishes based on the verse 'כי יתן' requiring intent, and resolves via Rav Pappa's teaching that 'כי יותן' must parallel 'כי יתן' in requiring the owner's consent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's ruling that water cannot become susceptible to impurity (כי יותן) implies that we apply retroactive consent (כיון דאיגלאי מילתא דהשתא ניחא ליה מעיקרא נמי ניחא ליה).
The Gemara distinguishes the case based on the verse 'כי יתן' (when he gives), which requires the owner's active intent at the time of giving.

The Gemara objects that if intent is required, the same logic should apply to the first clause of the Mishnah, and then cites Rav Pappa's difficulty: the verse is written 'כי יתן' but read as 'כי יותן'.
Rav Pappa resolves that 'כי יותן' must parallel 'כי יתן': just as 'יתן' requires the owner's intent (לדעת), so too 'כי יותן' requires the owner's intent.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's proof for lost property swept away by a river
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's proof for lost property swept away by a river
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan cites a verse to permit a lost item swept away by a river, as it is lost to the owner and not accessible to others. The Gemara then draws an analogy to forbidden items (איסורא), concluding that just as permitted items are allowed regardless of simanim, so too forbidden items are prohibited regardless of simanim, which refutes Rava's position.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Yishmael ben Yehotzadak
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Yishmael ben Yehotzadak
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan cites a verse to prove that a lost item swept away by a river is permitted, because it is lost to the owner and not accessible to others.

The Gemara draws an analogy from permitted to forbidden items, concluding that just as permitted items are allowed regardless of simanim, so forbidden items are prohibited regardless of simanim, which refutes Rava's position.

items.text: Halakha follows Abaye in the case of ya'al kagam, and the case of dates in a bundle
items.text_en: Halakha follows Abaye in the case of ya'al kagam, and the case of dates in a bundle
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the halakha follows Abaye in the case of ya'al kagam. Rav Acha bar Rava asks Rav Ashi how we can eat dates from a bundle (זיקא) if Rava was refuted; Rav Ashi answers that since vermin eat them, the owner despairs from the outset.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rules that the halakha follows Abaye in the case of ya'al kagam.
Rav Acha bar Rava asks Rav Ashi how we can eat dates from a bundle (זיקא) if Rava was refuted.
Rav Ashi answers that since vermin eat the dates, the owner despairs from the outset.

items.text: Orphans and the status of a mound or basket
items.text_en: Orphans and the status of a mound or basket
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about orphans who cannot grant forgiveness, and about a mound (באגא) on orphans' land, which is not presumed to be theirs. It also asks about a basket (כרכתא) that is standing and accessible, and rules that such items are forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the status of a mound (באגא) on orphans' land, who cannot grant forgiveness, and rules that such a mound is not presumed to belong to them.
The Gemara asks about a basket (כרכתא) that is standing and accessible, and Rav Ashi answers that such items are forbidden.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbah and Rava on siman ha'asui l'darres
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbah and Rava on siman ha'asui l'darres
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that bundles (כריכות) in the public domain belong to the finder. Rabbah says this applies even if they have a siman, because a siman that is likely to be trampled (סימן העשוי לידרס) is not a valid siman. Rava disagrees, saying only if there is no siman, but if there is a siman, one must announce. An alternative version presents the dispute independently.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that bundles (כריכות) found in the public domain belong to the finder.
Rabbah rules that even if the bundles have a distinguishing mark (סימן), they belong to the finder, because a mark likely to be trampled (סימן העשוי לידרס) is not a valid siman.
Rava disagrees, holding that the Mishnah's leniency applies only when there is no siman; if there is a siman, one must announce, because a siman likely to be trampled is still a valid siman.
An alternative version presents the dispute independently, without reference to the Mishnah: Rabbah says a siman likely to be trampled is not a valid siman, and Rava says it is.

items.text: Refutation of Rava from the Mishnah and Rava's defense
items.text_en: Refutation of Rava from the Mishnah and Rava's defense
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava from the Mishnah: if bundles have a siman, why in the public domain are they the finder's? This implies siman ha'asui l'darres is not a siman, refuting Rava. Rava responds that the case is without a siman, and the announcement is about location (מקום). Rabbah holds that location is not a siman, while Rava holds it is.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava from the Mishnah: if bundles have a siman (identifying mark), why in the public domain are they the finder's? This implies that a siman ha'asui l'darres (a mark prone to being trampled) is not a valid siman, refuting Rava.
Rava responds that the Mishnah's case is without a siman, and the announcement is about location (מקום), which he holds is a valid siman, while Rabbah holds it is not.

items.text: Reconciliation of the Mishnah with both opinions
items.text_en: Reconciliation of the Mishnah with both opinions
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings another Mishnah about bundles (כריכות) and sheaves (אלומות) to test Rabbah and Rava. Rabbah explains the distinction based on siman, while Rava explains it based on location. The Gemara begins to elaborate Rabbah's explanation, stating that bundles in the public domain belong to the finder because...

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a Mishnah about bundles (כריכות) and sheaves (אלומות) to challenge Rabbah and Rava, asking how each would reconcile it with their positions.
Rabbah explains the Mishnah according to his view, distinguishing bundles from sheaves based on the presence of a סימן (identifying mark).

items.text: Rava's resolution of the baraita about bundles and sheaves
items.text_en: Rava's resolution of the baraita about bundles and sheaves
items.desc_en: Rava explains the baraita: in a public domain, bundles are the finder's because they are trampled; in a private domain, one must announce because they are not trampled. Sheaves always require announcement because they are too heavy to be trampled.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the baraita by explaining that bundles in a public domain are trampled and thus the finder keeps them, while in a private domain they are not trampled and require announcement; sheaves are always announced because they are too heavy to be trampled.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbah from the baker's loaves baraita
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbah from the baker's loaves baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbah's view that a siman ha'asui lidadres is not a valid siman. The baraita states that a baker's loaves are the finder's, but a homeowner's loaves require announcement because they have a siman (the bread is recognizable). This implies that even a siman likely to be trampled is valid, contradicting Rabbah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about baker's loaves to challenge Rabbah's view that a סימן העשוי לידרס (a sign likely to be trampled) is not a valid sign.
The Gemara concludes that the baraita implies a סימן העשוי לידרס is a valid sign, presenting a refutation (תיוובתא) of Rabbah's position.

items.text: Rabbah's defense: concern for food and Gentiles
items.text_en: Rabbah's defense: concern for food and Gentiles
items.desc_en: Rabbah deflects the challenge by arguing that the reason the homeowner's loaves must be announced is not because of a siman, but because one may not step over food. Gentiles are afraid of sorcery and won't take them, and in a place without animals, the food remains undisturbed.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah deflects the challenge by arguing that the reason the homeowner's loaves must be announced is not because of a siman, but because one may not step over food.
The Gemara objects that Gentiles might take the loaves, but Rabbah counters that Gentiles fear sorcery.
The Gemara objects that animals might trample the loaves, but Rabbah answers that this applies only in a place without animals and dogs.

items.text: First attempt to resolve the Tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: First attempt to resolve the Tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Tanna Kamma about whether a change in the object requires announcement. The Gemara initially assumes both agree that a siman ha'ba me'eilav is valid and that one may step over food, and that they disagree about siman ha'asui lidadres.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes to resolve the dispute by citing a Tannaitic source where Rabbi Yehuda requires announcement for an object with a change, implying the Tanna Kamma disagrees.
The Gemara assumes both sides agree on siman ha'ba me'eilav and stepping over food, and asks whether they dispute siman ha'asui lidadres.

items.text: Rav Zevid's first resolution and Rabbah's alternative
items.text_en: Rav Zevid's first resolution and Rabbah's alternative
items.desc_en: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava rejects the initial assumption, arguing that the Tanna Kamma must hold siman ha'asui lidadres is valid, otherwise the baraita about homeowner's loaves would be problematic. He reinterprets the dispute as being about siman ha'ba me'eilav. Rabbah offers a different resolution: both agree siman ha'asui lidadres is invalid and one may not step over food, and they dispute siman ha'ba me'eilav.

sub.text: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava objects to the initial assumption: if the Tanna Kamma held that a distinguishing mark prone to trampling is invalid and that one passes over food, why would the baraita require proclamation for homeowner's loaves in a public area?

sub.text: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava resolves: everyone agrees that a distinguishing mark prone to trampling is valid and that one passes over food; the dispute is about a distinguishing mark that comes on its own, with the Tanna Kamma rejecting it and Rabbi Yehuda accepting it.

Rabbah offers an alternative resolution: everyone agrees that a distinguishing mark prone to trampling is invalid and that one does not pass over food; the dispute is about a distinguishing mark that comes on its own, with the Tanna Kamma rejecting it and Rabbi Yehuda accepting it.

items.text: Alternative version of the dispute resolution
items.text_en: Alternative version of the dispute resolution
items.desc_en: An alternative version of the Gemara's initial assumption: both agree siman ha'ba me'eilav is valid and siman ha'asui lidadres is invalid, and they dispute whether one may step over food. Rav Zevid again rejects this, and both Rava and Rabbah offer the same resolutions as before, now applied to this version.

sub.text: Alternative version of the Gemara's assumption
sub.text_en: Alternative version of the Gemara's assumption
sub.desc_en: An alternative version of the Gemara's initial assumption: everyone agrees that a distinguishing mark that could come on its own is valid and a distinguishing mark prone to trampling is invalid, and they dispute whether one passes by food without picking it up.

sub.text: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava objects: if the first tanna held that a distinguishing mark prone to trampling is invalid and that one passes by food, why would he require proclamation for homeowner's loaves in a public area?

sub.text: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava resolves: everyone agrees that a distinguishing mark prone to trampling is valid and one passes by food; the dispute is over a distinguishing mark that could come on its own, with the first tanna invalidating it and Rabbi Yehuda validating it.

Rabbah's alternative position: everyone agrees that a distinguishing mark prone to trampling is invalid and one does not pass by food; the dispute is over a distinguishing mark that could come on its own, with the first tanna invalidating it and Rabbi Yehuda validating it.

items.text: Rav Zevid's halakhic rulings
items.text_en: Rav Zevid's halakhic rulings
items.desc_en: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava states two halakhic principles: one who says 'woe is me for the loss of money' has already despaired of the lost object; and the practical ruling for bundles: in a public domain they are the finder's, in a private domain if fallen they are his, if placed he must announce. For items with a siman, one must always announce.

sub.text: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava states a general principle of lost property: once the owner says 'ווי לה לחסרון כיס' (woe is me for the monetary loss), he has despaired of recovering it.

sub.text: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava gives the halakhic ruling: bundles in a public domain belong to the finder; in a private domain, if fallen they are his, if placed he must announce; for items with a siman (distinguishing mark), one must always announce regardless of domain or manner of finding.

items.text: Question on fish strings and quantity as a sign
items.text_en: Question on fish strings and quantity as a sign
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah lists fish strings among items that are returned without announcement; perhaps the knot or the count of fish could serve as a sign. It answers that fishermen all tie the same knot and the count is uniform.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why fish strings are returned without announcement, given that the knot or the count could serve as a sign.
The Gemara answers that all fishermen tie the same knot and the fish count is uniform, so neither is a distinguishing sign.

items.text: Rav Sheshet rules that quantity is a sign
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet rules that quantity is a sign
items.desc_en: The Gemara inquires whether quantity is a valid sign. Rav Sheshet cites a baraita: one who finds metal vessels must return them only if the finder provides a mark or matches the weight, proving that weight is a sign, and by extension, measure and quantity are also signs.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks Rav Sheshet whether quantity (מנין) is a valid identifying sign.
Rav Sheshet answers by citing a baraita about metal vessels, proving that weight is a sign, and by extension, measure and quantity are also signs.

items.text: Meat pieces and the case of a bitten fish
items.text_en: Meat pieces and the case of a bitten fish
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah lists meat pieces as the finder's own; perhaps weight or the piece itself could be a sign. It cites a baraita that found fish pieces and a bitten fish require announcement. The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah deals with pieces that have a sign in the cut, like Rabbah bar Rav Huna's practice of cutting on three corners, and the baraita's mention of a bitten fish supports this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why meat pieces are the finder's own, suggesting weight or the piece itself could be a sign.
The Gemara cites a baraita that found fish pieces and a bitten fish require announcement, implying that pieces can have a sign.

The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah deals with pieces that have a sign in the cut, like Rabbah bar Rav Huna's practice of cutting on three corners, and the baraita's mention of a bitten fish supports this.

items.text: Barrels: sealed vs. open, and the resolution by Abaye
items.text_en: Barrels: sealed vs. open, and the resolution by Abaye
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the baraita says barrels of wine, oil, etc. are the finder's own, but a Mishnah requires announcement for such barrels. Rav Zeira says the Mishnah refers to sealed barrels, while the baraita refers to open ones. Rav Hoshaya explains the baraita deals with floating barrels. Abaye resolves that both are sealed, but the baraita is before the storehouses were opened (when the owner despairs) and the Mishnah after they were opened; a story with Rav Yaakov bar Abba supports this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points out a contradiction: the baraita says barrels of wine, oil, etc. are the finder's own, but a Mishnah requires announcement for such barrels.
Rav Zeira answers that the Mishnah refers to sealed barrels, implying the baraita refers to open ones.
The Gemara objects that if the baraita deals with open barrels, the finder would know the owner has despaired, making it an intentional loss that need not be returned.
Rav Hoshaya answers that the baraita deals with floating barrels, which are not considered an intentional loss.
Abaye resolves that both sources refer to sealed barrels, but the baraita is before the storehouses were opened (when the owner despairs) and the Mishnah after they were opened.

sub.text: Supporting story with Rav Yaakov bar Abba
sub.text_en: Supporting story with Rav Yaakov bar Abba
sub.desc_en: A story is cited where Rav Yaakov bar Abba found a barrel of wine after the storehouses were opened, and Abaye told him to take it for himself, supporting the resolution.

items.text: Is location a sign? The case of riverbanks
items.text_en: Is location a sign? The case of riverbanks
items.desc_en: Rav Bibi asks Rav Nachman whether location is a sign. Rav Nachman cites the baraita that barrels are the finder's own, implying location is not a sign; otherwise, one could announce the location. Rav Zevid explains the case involves a riverbank, where many people pass. Rav Mari explains that a riverbank is not a sign because one can say that another person also found it there.

sub.text: Rav Bibi's question to Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rav Bibi's question to Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rav Bibi asks Rav Nachman whether location (מקום) is considered a valid identifying sign (סימן) for returning a lost object.

sub.text: Rav Nachman's answer citing a baraita
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman's answer citing a baraita
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman answers by citing the baraita that one who finds barrels of wine, oil, etc. keeps them, implying location is not a sign.
The gemara objects that if location were a sign, the finder could announce the location, but the baraita does not require that.
Rav Zevid resolves that the case involves a riverbank (רקתא דנהרא), where many people pass, so location is not unique.
Rav Mari explains that a riverbank is not a sign because one can say that another person also found it there.

items.text: A story with Rav: location and despair
items.text_en: A story with Rav: location and despair
items.desc_en: A man found a basket in a press-house and Rav told him to take it. Seeing the man hesitate, Rav told him to share with his son Chiya. The Gemara wonders if Rav holds location is not a sign. Rabbi Abba explains that the owner had despaired because willows had grown through the basket, indicating it was long abandoned.

sub.desc_en: A man found a basket in a press-house and came before Rav, who told him to take it for himself.
Seeing the man hesitate, Rav told him to share the basket with his son Chiya.
The Gemara questions whether Rav's ruling implies that location is not a valid identifying sign (סימן).
Rabbi Abba explains that the case involves despair of the owners (יאוש), because willows had grown through the basket, indicating it was long abandoned.

items.text: Definition of 'anpurya' and returning to a scholar by sight
items.text_en: Definition of 'anpurya' and returning to a scholar by sight
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's term 'anpurya' as new vessels not yet familiar to the eye. It asks: if they have a sign, why does familiarity matter? If no sign, why does unfamiliarity matter? It answers that the case is without a sign, and the ruling applies to returning to a Torah scholar based on visual recognition: if the vessels are familiar, we return them; if not, we do not, citing a principle that rabbis change their speech in three matters.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the meaning of the term 'anpurya' used by Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel defines 'anpurya' as new vessels that the eye has not yet become familiar with.
The Gemara challenges: if the vessels have a distinguishing sign, why does familiarity matter? If they have no sign, why does unfamiliarity matter?
The Gemara resolves: the case involves vessels without a sign, and the distinction applies to returning lost items to a Torah scholar (צורבא מרבנן) based on visual recognition (טביעות עינא).

Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel cites a principle that rabbis change their speech in three matters: tractate (מסכת), bed (פוריא), and hospitality (אושפיזא), supporting the idea that visual recognition is reliable for a scholar.

items.text: Mar Zutra's ruling and story about the hostel
items.text_en: Mar Zutra's ruling and story about the hostel
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra explains the practical difference of the hostel case: if the guest only stays at three specific hostels, we return the lost object by recognition; if he stays elsewhere, we do not. He then recounts how he caught a thief who stole his silver cup by observing his disregard for another's property.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference arises from the case of the hostel.
Mar Zutra explains that the difference is whether to return a lost object by recognition: if the guest only stays at three specific hostels, we return it; if he stays elsewhere, we do not.
Mar Zutra the Pious recounts how he caught a thief who stole his silver cup by observing his disregard for another's property.

items.text: Baraita: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar on new vessels
items.text_en: Baraita: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar on new vessels
items.desc_en: A baraita states that Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar agrees that for new vessels that are distinctive (satiate the eye), one must announce; for common items like needle cases, awls, and axe chains, one need not announce. If found in pairs, one must announce.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar agrees that for new vessels that are distinctive (satiate the eye), one must announce, and lists common items for which one need not announce.
The baraita adds a condition: if found singly they are permitted, but if found in pairs one must announce.

items.text: Explanation of 'badei'
items.text_en: Explanation of 'badei'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that 'badei' means 'sokhei' (weaver's rods), and it is called 'bad' because things are hung on it, as in the Mishnah about a leaf on a branch.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the term 'badei' means.
The Gemara answers that 'badei' means weaver's rods (שוכי).
The Gemara asks why these rods are called 'badei'.
The Gemara explains that it is called 'bad' because things are hung on it, citing a Mishnah about a leaf on a branch.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's ruling on items found in public places
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's ruling on items found in public places
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar rules that one who rescues from a lion, bear, leopard, bardelas, sea serpent, or river current, or finds in a main road or large plaza where many people are found, the finder keeps it because the owners despair.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar rules that one who rescues from dangerous animals or finds in public places keeps the item because the owners despair.

items.text: Series of inquiries about Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's opinion
items.text_en: Series of inquiries about Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's opinion
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a series of conditional questions: whether Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's ruling applies only when the majority are Gentiles or even when the majority are Jews; whether the Rabbis disagree with him; and whether the halakha follows him in each case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises the first inquiry: whether Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's ruling applies only when the majority are Gentiles or even when the majority are Jews.
The Gemara raises the second inquiry: assuming the ruling applies even among a Jewish majority, whether the Rabbis disagree with Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar.
The Gemara raises the third inquiry: assuming the Rabbis disagree, whether their disagreement applies only to a Jewish majority or also to a Gentile majority.
The Gemara raises the fourth inquiry: assuming the Rabbis disagree even regarding a Gentile majority, whether the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar.
The Gemara raises the fifth inquiry: assuming the הלכה follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, whether that applies only to a Gentile majority or even to a Jewish majority.

items.text: First attempted resolution: money in synagogues
items.text_en: First attempted resolution: money in synagogues
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to resolve from a baraita about finding money in synagogues and study halls: since it follows the majority, and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar is the one who follows the majority, this implies he applies even to a Jewish majority. The Gemara deflects by saying the coins are scattered (so no identification) or that the synagogues are of Gentiles or that Gentiles sit in them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about finding money in synagogues and study halls, where the finder keeps it because the owners despair, implying the ruling follows the majority.
The Gemara infers that since Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar follows the majority, this baraita must reflect his view even when the majority is Jewish.

The Gemara deflects by suggesting the coins are scattered (מפוזרין), so the ruling is not about majority but about lack of identification, but then objects that this would apply even where the public is not present.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita refers to synagogues of Gentiles, or Jewish study halls where Gentiles sit, so the majority is non-Jewish and the proof is deflected.

items.text: Second attempted resolution: lost object in a city
items.text_en: Second attempted resolution: lost object in a city
items.desc_en: Another baraita states: if the majority are Jews, one must announce; if Gentiles, not. The Gemara infers that Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar only applies his ruling to a Gentile majority. It then suggests the baraita is the Rabbis' view, showing they agree with him regarding a Gentile majority.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about finding a lost object in a city: if the majority are Jews, one must announce; if Gentiles, not.
The Gemara infers that the baraita follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, and that he only applies his ruling to a Gentile majority, not a Jewish majority.

items.text: Final resolution: hidden items in a trash heap
items.text_en: Final resolution: hidden items in a trash heap
items.desc_en: The Gemara reinterprets the baraita as Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar even for a Jewish majority, but the case is of a hidden item in a trash heap that was not meant to be cleared but later reconsidered, following Rav Pappa's explanation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the baraita is indeed Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar even for a Jewish majority, but the case involves a hidden item in a trash heap.
The Gemara objects: if the item is hidden, why would the finder have any claim to it, citing the Mishnah that a covered item in a trash heap is not to be touched.
Rav Pappa explains that the case is a trash heap not originally designated for clearing, but the owner later reconsidered and decided to clear it, so the item is now considered abandoned.

items.text: Alternative resolution of the earlier dispute
items.text_en: Alternative resolution of the earlier dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: the Mishnah does not say 'they are his' but rather 'he is not obligated to announce', allowing a Jew to provide a sign and take the item even in a Jewish majority area.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative resolution: the Mishnah does not say 'they are his' but rather 'he is not obligated to announce', allowing a Jew to provide a sign and take the item even in a Jewish majority area.

items.text: Rav Asi's ruling on a wine barrel in a non-Jewish majority city
items.text_en: Rav Asi's ruling on a wine barrel in a non-Jewish majority city
items.desc_en: Rav Asi rules that a found barrel of wine in a city with a non-Jewish majority is permitted as a find but forbidden for benefit; if a Jew provides a sign, it becomes permitted for drinking. The Gemara analyzes this as consistent with Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's view only in a non-Jewish majority, but Rav Asi may hold like him in one respect and disagree in another. Rav Ashi explains the practical relevance: the barrel itself is permitted.

sub.desc_en: Rav Asi rules that a wine barrel found in a non-Jewish majority city is permitted as a find but forbidden for benefit; if a Jew provides a sign, it becomes permitted for drinking.
The Gemara asks whose view Rav Asi follows, suggesting it aligns with Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar only in a non-Jewish majority.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar holds even in a Jewish majority, but Rav Asi agrees with him in one respect and disagrees in another.
The Gemara asks: since the barrel is forbidden for benefit, what practical relevance does its being permitted as a find have?
Rav Ashi answers that the practical relevance is the barrel itself (the container), which is permitted for use.

items.text: Case of four zuzim tied in a cloth in the Beiran River
items.text_en: Case of four zuzim tied in a cloth in the Beiran River
items.desc_en: A man found four zuzim tied in a cloth thrown into the Beiran River. Rav Yehuda ruled he must announce it, despite the river being like the sea (where owners despair) and the majority being non-Jews. The Gemara explains that since Jews dammed and dug the river, it is presumed to be from a Jew and the owner does not despair.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a case where a man found four zuzim tied in a cloth thrown into the Beiran River and brought it before Rav Yehuda.
Rav Yehuda rules that the finder must announce the find, implying the owner has not despaired.
The Gemara objects that the river is like the sea (זוטו של ים), where owners typically despair of recovery.
The Gemara answers that the Beiran River is different because it is dammed and dug by Jews, so the owner does not despair.
The Gemara objects that the majority of people in the area are non-Jews, so the find should be permitted without announcement according to Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar.
The Gemara answers that the Beiran River is different because Jews dammed and dug it, so it is presumed to be from a Jew and the owner does not despair.

items.text: Rav Yehuda and Shmuel on finding a purse in a non-Jewish market
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda and Shmuel on finding a purse in a non-Jewish market
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda asked Shmuel about finding a purse in a non-Jewish market; Shmuel initially said it belongs to the finder, but when asked about a Jew providing a sign, he said it must be returned. Rav Yehuda noted the contradiction, and Shmuel explained it is beyond the letter of the law, citing his father's precedent of returning donkeys after a year.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda, walking behind Shmuel in the non-Jewish market of Bei Daisa, asks what the law is if one finds a purse there.
Shmuel answers that the purse belongs to the finder.
Rav Yehuda then asks what the law is if a Jew provides a identifying sign for the purse.
Shmuel answers that the finder is obligated to return the purse to the Jew who provides a sign.
Rav Yehuda objects that Shmuel's two answers contradict each other.
Shmuel resolves the contradiction by explaining that the requirement to return the purse is beyond the letter of the law (לפנים משורת הדין).

The gemara supports Shmuel's explanation by citing the precedent of Shmuel's father, who found donkeys in the desert and returned them to their owners after twelve months, acting beyond the letter of the law.

items.text: Rava and Rav Nachman on finding a purse in a non-Jewish market
items.text_en: Rava and Rav Nachman on finding a purse in a non-Jewish market
items.desc_en: Rava asked Rav Nachman about finding a purse in a non-Jewish market; Rav Nachman ruled it belongs to the finder even if a Jew provides a sign, comparing the owner's cries to someone crying over a collapsed house or sunken ship, indicating despair.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman about finding a purse in a non-Jewish market, and whether returning it is required if a Jew provides a identifying mark.
Rav Nachman rules that the purse belongs to the finder even if a Jew provides a sign, comparing the owner's cries to someone crying over a collapsed house or sunken ship, indicating despair.

items.text: Case of meat thrown in a corner in a Jewish majority area
items.text_en: Case of meat thrown in a corner in a Jewish majority area
items.desc_en: A man found meat thrown in a corner in a Jewish majority area; Abaye ruled he may take it for himself. The Gemara infers this follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar even in a Jewish majority, but distinguishes because the meat is like something lost at sea. It also addresses Rav's concern about meat that has disappeared from sight, noting the finder was watching it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a case where a man took meat in the market and threw it in a corner of Bar Marion's house.
The finder came before Abaye, who ruled that he may take the meat for himself.
The Gemara objects: since the majority in the area is Jewish, this ruling seems to follow Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar even in a Jewish majority.
The Gemara distinguishes: the case of a butcher (דַּיּוֹ) is different because the meat is like something lost at sea (זוֹטוֹ שֶׁל יָם), where the owner despairs.
The Gemara objects further: Rav ruled that meat that has disappeared from sight (נִתְעַלֵּם מִן הָעַיִן) is forbidden, so how could Abaye permit it?
The Gemara resolves that the case is different because the finder was standing and watching the meat (עוֹמֵד וְרוֹאֵהוּ), so it never truly disappeared from sight.

items.text: Rabbi Chanina's found goat and the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Chananya
items.text_en: Rabbi Chanina's found goat and the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Chananya
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina found a slaughtered goat between Tiberias and Tzipori, and the Sages permitted it. Rabbi Ami explains it was permitted as a find per Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and as slaughtered per Rabbi Chananya ben Yosei HaGlili. The Gemara infers this supports Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar even in a Jewish majority, but Rava limits it to a majority of non-Jews or Jewish butchers.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina found a slaughtered goat between Tiberias and Tzipori, and the Sages permitted it to him.
Rabbi Ami explains that the permission was based on two leniencies: as a find per Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, and as slaughtered per Rabbi Chananya ben Yosei HaGlili.
A baraita is cited: if one's goats or chickens were lost and found slaughtered, Rabbi Yehuda forbids and Rabbi Chananya ben Yosei HaGlili permits.
Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi) reconciles the dispute: Rabbi Yehuda's prohibition applies when found in a garbage heap, Rabbi Chananya's permission when found in the house.
The Gemara infers from the permission that the majority must be Jewish, implying Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar applies even in a Jewish majority.
Rava rejects the inference, explaining that the majority there was of non-Jews or Jewish butchers, not a general Jewish majority.

items.text: Additional cases of found slaughtered animals
items.text_en: Additional cases of found slaughtered animals
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami found slaughtered chickens and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha found a bundle of arrows; both were told by the academy to take them for themselves, consistent with the previous rulings.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ami found slaughtered chickens between Tiberias and Tzippori, and the academy (or Rabbi Asi / Rabbi Yochanan) told him to take them for himself.

sub.text: Stam (narrative of Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha's case)
sub.text_en: Stam (narrative of Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha's case)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha found a bundle of arrows in the arrow-makers' quarter, and Rabbi Yochanan (or the academy) told him to take them for himself.

items.text: Mishnah: Items that require an announcement
items.text_en: Mishnah: Items that require an announcement
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items that must be announced: fruits in a vessel, a vessel as is, money in a purse, a purse as is, piles of fruits, piles of money.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items that require an announcement: fruits in a vessel, a vessel as is, money in a purse, a purse as is, piles of fruits, piles of money.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items that must be announced: three coins stacked, bundles in a private domain, homeowner's loaves, and wool purchased from a craftsman.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items that must be announced: three coins stacked, bundles in a private domain, homeowner's loaves, and wool purchased from a craftsman.

items.text: Gemara's initial inference and supporting baraita
items.text_en: Gemara's initial inference and supporting baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that if one finds fruit in a vessel or coins in a pouch, they must be announced, but if the vessel is next to fruit or the pouch next to coins, they belong to the finder. A baraita supports this and adds that if some are in the vessel and some on the ground, they must be announced.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that finding fruit in a vessel or coins in a pouch requires announcement, but a vessel next to fruit or a pouch next to coins belongs to the finder.
A baraita supports the inference and adds that if some fruit or coins are in the vessel and some on the ground, they must be announced.

items.text: Contradiction from another baraita
items.text_en: Contradiction from another baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: another baraita states that if one finds an item without a siman next to an item with a siman, he must announce, and the owner of the siman takes his item and the finder keeps the unsimaned item.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that says if one finds an item without a siman next to an item with a siman, he must announce, and the owner of the siman takes his item and the finder keeps the unsimaned item.

items.text: Three resolutions of the contradiction
items.text_en: Three resolutions of the contradiction
items.desc_en: Rav Zevid resolves by distinguishing between a basket with flax (where the flax is a siman) and a basket with fruit (where the fruit is not). Rav Pappa distinguishes whether something remains in the basket. A third resolution distinguishes whether the basket faces the fruit.

sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a basket with flax (where the flax is a siman) and a basket with fruit (where the fruit is not).
Rav Pappa resolves the contradiction by distinguishing whether something remains in the basket.
A third resolution distinguishes whether the basket faces the fruit.
A fourth resolution distinguishes whether the basket has handles.

items.text: Implication about simanim
items.text_en: Implication about simanim
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's phrase 'piles of fruit' that both quantity and location are simanim.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's phrase 'piles of fruit' that quantity (מנין) is a valid siman (identifying mark).
The Gemara cites a baraita that uses the singular 'pile of fruit' to prove that location (מקום) is also a siman.

items.text: Definition of 'like towers' and resolution of a contradiction
items.text_en: Definition of 'like towers' and resolution of a contradiction
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak Magdela'ah explains that the coins must be arranged like towers. A baraita is cited, and the Gemara resolves an internal contradiction in the baraita by clarifying that any arrangement not like towers is considered scattered.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak Magdela'ah explains that the Mishnah's case of three coins stacked applies only when they are arranged like towers, and a baraita confirms this.

The Gemara raises a contradiction within the baraita: the first clause implies scattered coins are the finder's, but the second clause implies that coins arranged in a pile (not like towers) are also the finder's, creating a logical inconsistency.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by clarifying that the baraita's term 'scattered' includes any arrangement that is not like towers, so the two clauses are consistent.

items.text: Distinction by coins' kings
items.text_en: Distinction by coins' kings
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina initially says the law applies only to coins of three different kings, but the Gemara challenges this and rephrases: the law applies to coins of one king that appear like three different kings (stacked in a tower), but if they are identical, they belong to the finder.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina states that the Mishnah's obligation to announce applies only to coins of three different kings, but coins of one king do not require announcement.
The Gemara objects: if the coins are stacked like towers, even one king's coins should require announcement; if not stacked, even three kings' coins should not require announcement.

The Gemara rephrases Rabbi Chanina's statement: the law applies to coins of one king that appear like three different kings (stacked in a tower), but if they are identical, they belong to the finder, as they likely fell together.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's opinion and Ravina's explanation
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's opinion and Ravina's explanation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan holds that even coins of one king must be announced, and the announcement is about the number of coins. Ravina clarifies that the announcement is about the type of coin.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that even coins of one king require an announcement, and the announcement is about the number of coins.
The Gemara questions why the Mishnah specifies three coins, implying even two should suffice.
Ravina clarifies that the announcement is about the type of coin, not the number.

items.text: Questions about other arrangements and a partial answer
items.text_en: Questions about other arrangements and a partial answer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks about arrangements like a row, a line, a row of bricks, or a ladder. Rav Nachman quotes a principle: if one could insert a stick between them and lift them all at once, they must be announced.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks about the status of coins arranged in a row, a line, a row of bricks, or a ladder.

sub.text: Rav Nachman quoting Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman quoting Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman cites a principle from Rabbah bar Avuha: if one could insert a stick between the coins and lift them all at once, the finder must announce them.

items.text: Rav Ashi's unresolved question
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's unresolved question
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi raises a question that is left unresolved, ending the daf.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi raises an unresolved question, which concludes the daf without an answer.

items.text: Question about stones of Beit Kulis and the baraita's answer
items.text_en: Question about stones of Beit Kulis and the baraita's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the status of stones arranged like those of Beit Kulis. A baraita is cited: scattered coins are the finder's, but stones of Beit Kulis require an announcement. The baraita defines these stones as one on each side and one on top.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the status of stones arranged like those of Beit Kulis.
A baraita is cited: scattered coins are the finder's, but stones of Beit Kulis require an announcement, defined as one on each side and one on top.

items.text: Baraita on finding a coin with identifying claims
items.text_en: Baraita on finding a coin with identifying claims
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches: if one finds a coin and another claims it with specific descriptions (new, Neronian, of a certain king), the claim is invalid. Even if the claimant's name is written on it, it is not accepted, because coins have no distinguishing siman, as the coin may have been spent by someone else.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that a coin found in the market cannot be claimed by a description (new, Neronian, of a certain king) or even by a name written on it, because coins have no distinguishing siman (סימן) and may have been spent by another person.

items.text: Mishnah: finding tied birds or a covered vessel
items.text_en: Mishnah: finding tied birds or a covered vessel
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states: if one finds tied fledglings behind a fence or in field paths, he should not touch them. If he finds a vessel in a garbage heap, if covered he should not touch it; if uncovered, he takes it and announces.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that tied fledglings found in hidden places must not be touched, and a covered vessel in a garbage heap must not be touched, but an uncovered one is taken and announced.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's first case: tied birds
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's first case: tied birds
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the reason: the birds were hidden by someone, and if taken, the owner would have no siman. It questions why the knot is not a siman; Rabbi Abba bar Zavda answers that they are tied by their wings, which is common. It then questions why the location is not a siman; Rav Ukva bar Chama says they are wandering birds. The Gemara concludes it is a case of uncertainty (safeik hinuch), and Rabbi Abba bar Zavda rules: initially one should not take, but if taken, not return.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Mishnah's first case: the tied birds were hidden by someone, so the owner has no siman (identifying mark), and one should leave them until the owner comes.
The Gemara asks: why is the knot not a siman (identifying mark) for the owner?

sub.text: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda answers that the birds are tied by their wings, which is a common practice, so the knot is not distinctive.
The Gemara asks: why is the location not a siman (identifying mark)?
Rav Ukva bar Chama answers that the birds are wandering (מִדַּדִּין), so their location is not fixed.
The Gemara objects: if the birds are wandering, they came from elsewhere and should be permitted (i.e., the finder may take them).

sub.text: Gemara's resolution citing Rabbi Abba bar Zavda citing Rav
sub.text_en: Gemara's resolution citing Rabbi Abba bar Zavda citing Rav
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves: there is a doubt (ספק הינוח) whether they came from elsewhere or were hidden, so Rabbi Abba bar Zavda rules that לכתחילה (the ideal standard) one should not take, but if taken, one does not return them.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's second case: vessel in garbage heap
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's second case: vessel in garbage heap
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the Mishnah says a covered vessel should not be touched, but another baraita says one takes and announces because garbage heaps are cleared. Rav Zevid resolves: the Mishnah refers to cups and bowls (valuable, likely hidden), the baraita to knives and necklaces (small, likely discarded). Rav Papa resolves: both refer to cups and bowls, but the Mishnah is for a heap not designated for clearing, the baraita for one designated for clearing. The Gemara questions the latter, concluding the baraita refers to a heap not designated but later decided to clear. It then explains the baraita's phrase 'since the way of a garbage heap is to be cleared' according to each Amora.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a covered vessel found in a garbage heap should not be touched, but an uncovered one is taken and announced.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that says a vessel hidden in a garbage heap is taken and announced because garbage heaps are cleared.
Rav Zevid resolves: the Mishnah refers to cups and bowls (valuable, likely hidden), the baraita to knives and necklaces (small, likely discarded).
Rav Papa resolves: both refer to cups and bowls, but the Mishnah is for a heap not designated for clearing, the baraita for one designated for clearing.
The Gemara objects that a heap designated for clearing is an intentional abandonment, and concludes the baraita refers to a heap not designated but later decided to clear.

sub.text: Gemara's analysis of the baraita's phrase
sub.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the baraita's phrase
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the baraita's phrase 'since the way of a garbage heap is to be cleared' according to each Amora: for Rav Papa it means the heap is cleared, for Rav Zevid it means small vessels are discarded there.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on finding items in a wall
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on finding items in a wall
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states: if one finds items in a pile or old wall, they are his. In a new wall, from halfway outward they are his, inward they belong to the homeowner. If the house was rented, even inside they are his. The Gemara cites a Tanna: because the owner can say they are from the Amorites. It questions whether only Amorites hide items, and answers that the case is not needed.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule that items found in a pile or old wall belong to the finder.
The Mishnah distinguishes a new wall: items from halfway outward belong to the finder, inward to the homeowner.
The Mishnah adds that if the house was rented, even items found inside belong to the renter.
A Tanna explains the Mishnah's rule: the homeowner can claim the items are from the Amorites (ancient Canaanites), so the finder keeps them.
The Gemara objects: do only Amorites hide items, and not Israelites?
The Gemara resolves that the Tanna's statement is not needed for its literal meaning, but rather to clarify the Mishnah's reasoning.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Found objects in a wall
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Found objects in a wall
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if a coin is found in a new wall, from the midpoint outward it belongs to the finder, and from the midpoint inward it belongs to the homeowner. This sets the basic principle for the discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that in a new wall, a coin found from the midpoint outward belongs to the finder, and from the midpoint inward belongs to the homeowner.

items.text: Rav Ashi's principle and the Gemara's challenge
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's principle and the Gemara's challenge
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi states that the handle of a knife and the opening of a purse indicate the direction of the owner. The Gemara questions the Mishnah: why not look at the handle or opening to determine ownership? It answers that the Mishnah deals with a case where the object is embedded in the wall without a clear orientation.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi states that the orientation of a knife follows its handle and a purse follows its opening.
The Gemara challenges the Mishnah: why not simply look at the handle or opening to determine ownership?
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah deals with a case where the object is embedded in a wall niche or plastered over, so its orientation is not discernible.

items.text: Tosefta: A wall filled with coins
items.text_en: Tosefta: A wall filled with coins
items.desc_en: A Tosefta teaches that if a wall is filled with coins, the finder and homeowner divide them. The Gemara clarifies this is necessary only when the coins protrude on one side, lest one think they all fell from that side.

sub.desc_en: A Tosefta is cited: if a wall is filled with coins, the finder and homeowner divide them.
The Gemara objects that the Tosefta's ruling is obvious.
The Gemara explains the Tosefta is necessary only when the coins protrude on one side, lest one think they all fell from that side; the Tosefta teaches that they still divide.

items.text: Found in a rented house: presumption of ownership
items.text_en: Found in a rented house: presumption of ownership
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a house is rented to others, even if found inside the house, the finder keeps it. The Gemara challenges this: why not follow the last tenant? It brings a parallel from coins found in Jerusalem during festivals, where the principle is that earlier people took them, and these are from later ones. So here too, the earlier tenant likely lost it and despaired.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a house was rented to others, even if found inside the house, the finder keeps it.
The Gemara questions why the finder keeps it, arguing that the presumption should follow the last tenant.
The Gemara cites a baraita about coins found in Jerusalem during festivals, where the principle is that earlier people took them and these are from later ones.

Rav Shmaya bar Zeira explains that in Jerusalem the markets are swept daily, so earlier coins are gone and these are from later people; similarly, the earlier tenant likely lost the item and despaired, so the finder keeps it.

items.text: Resh Lakish's answer: A lodging house for three Jews
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's answer: A lodging house for three Jews
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish in the name of Bar Kappara explains that the case is where the house was made a lodging house for three Jews, so the finder keeps it because the owner despairs when multiple people have access.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish in the name of Bar Kappara answers that the case is where the house was made a lodging house (פונדק) for three Jews, so the finder keeps the item because the owner despairs when multiple people have access.

items.text: Inference: Halakha follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar even with a Jewish majority
items.text_en: Inference: Halakha follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar even with a Jewish majority
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from Resh Lakish's statement that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar even when the majority are Jews, implying that the finder keeps the object.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from Resh Lakish's statement that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar even when the majority are Jews, implying the finder keeps the object.

items.text: Rav Menashya's alternative: A lodging house for three gentiles
items.text_en: Rav Menashya's alternative: A lodging house for three gentiles
items.desc_en: Rav Menashya bar Yaakov says the case is where the house was made a lodging house for three gentiles, so the finder keeps it because gentiles do not return lost items, leading to despair.

sub.desc_en: Rav Menashya bar Yaakov proposes that the case is where the house was made a lodging house for three gentiles, so the finder keeps the item because gentiles do not return lost items, leading to the owner's despair.

items.text: Rav Nachman's explanation: Despair due to multiple tenants
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's explanation: Despair due to multiple tenants
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rabbah bar Avuha explains that even with three Jews, the finder keeps it because the owner despairs, reasoning that since the others did not return it, they intend to steal it. This aligns with Rav Nachman's earlier ruling about a found coin.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman explains that even with three Jewish tenants, the owner despairs because he assumes the others intend to steal the item, so the finder keeps it.
The gemara notes that this ruling aligns with Rav Nachman's earlier position regarding a found coin.

items.text: Mishnah: Lost object with two or three people
items.text_en: Mishnah: Lost object with two or three people
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a coin falls from two people, the finder must return it because the loser does not despair. If it falls from three, the finder does not need to return it because the loser despairs, assuming one of the others took it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a coin falling from two people must be returned because the loser does not despair, but from three it need not be returned because the loser despairs.

items.text: Rava's qualification: value per person
items.text_en: Rava's qualification: value per person
items.desc_en: Rava qualifies the Mishnah's ruling: the exemption for three applies only if the coin is not worth a perutah for each. If it is worth a perutah each, the finder must return it, as they may be partners and have not despaired. An alternative version states that even if it is worth two perutot total, the finder must return it, as one partner may have relinquished his share to the other.

sub.desc_en: Rava qualifies the Mishnah's ruling: the exemption for three applies only if the coin is not worth a perutah for each; if it is, the finder must return it, as they may be partners and have not despaired.
An alternative version states that even if the coin is worth only two perutot total, the finder must return it, as one partner may have relinquished his share to the other.

items.text: Rava: Intent at time of taking
items.text_en: Rava: Intent at time of taking
items.desc_en: Rava discusses cases based on the finder's intent. If one takes a coin before despair intending to steal, he violates multiple prohibitions. If he intends to return but later decides to steal, he violates only 'return you shall return'. If he waits until after despair to take it, he violates only 'you cannot hide yourself'.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that if one takes a coin before יאוש (despair) intending to steal, he violates multiple prohibitions, and even returning it after יאוש does not undo the violation.
Rava rules that if one takes the coin before יאוש intending to return it but later decides to steal, he violates only the positive command of השב תשיבם (return you shall return).
Rava rules that if one waits until after יאוש (despair) to take the coin, he violates only the prohibition of לא תוכל להתעלם (you cannot hide yourself).

items.text: Rava: Coins found in a bathhouse
items.text_en: Rava: Coins found in a bathhouse
items.desc_en: Rava rules that if one sees coins fall from his friend in a bathhouse and finds them, he need not return them because the loser despairs. Even if the loser brings a sieve and sifts, he assumes the coins fell from someone else.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that one who sees coins fall from his friend in a bathhouse and finds them is not obligated to return them, because the loser despairs, even if the loser brings a sieve and sifts.

items.text: Mishnah: Found in a store or by a money changer
items.text_en: Mishnah: Found in a store or by a money changer
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one finds money in a store, it is his. Between the counter and the storekeeper, it belongs to the storekeeper. Similarly, before a money changer, it is the finder's; between the chair and the money changer, it belongs to the money changer. If one buys produce and finds money inside, it is his unless it is tied, in which case he must announce.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule for finding money in a store or by a money changer: if found in the public area it belongs to the finder, but if found between the counter and the storekeeper or between the chair and the money changer it belongs to the proprietor.
The Mishnah adds that if one buys produce and finds money inside, it is his unless the money is tied, in which case he must announce the find.

items.text: Gemara: Rabbi Elazar's extension and Rava's proof
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabbi Elazar's extension and Rava's proof
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar says that even if coins are placed on the table, they belong to the finder. The Gemara questions this from the Mishnah, but Rava resolves it by noting that the Mishnah's phrasing implies that even on the table, they are the finder's.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that even if coins are placed on the money-changer's table, they belong to the finder.

The Gemara objects from the Mishnah: the Mishnah says 'before the money-changer' are the finder's, implying that on the table they belong to the money-changer, and the second clause also fails to prove otherwise.

Rava resolves the objection: Rabbi Elazar deduced his ruling from the Mishnah's phrasing — why did the Mishnah specify 'between the chair and the money-changer' rather than simply 'on the table'? This implies that even on the table, the coins belong to the finder.

items.text: Resh Lakish's qualification on produce
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's qualification on produce
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yannai begins to qualify the Mishnah's ruling about finding money in produce, but the text cuts off.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yannai begins to qualify the Mishnah's ruling about finding money in produce, but the text cuts off.

items.text: Distinction between buyer from a storekeeper and from a householder
items.text_en: Distinction between buyer from a storekeeper and from a householder
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah's leniency (no need to return) applies only when buying from a storekeeper, but from a householder one must return. Rav Nachman questions the source, and the Tanna explains it applies when the householder's Canaanite slaves threshed the grain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the Mishnah's leniency applies only when buying from a storekeeper, but from a householder one must return the item.
A Tanna recites a baraita before Rav Nachman that explicitly states the same distinction between storekeeper and householder.
Rav Nachman questions the baraita, asking whether the householder himself threshes the grain (implying the distinction is unrealistic).
The Tanna clarifies that the Mishnah applies when the householder's Canaanite slaves threshed the grain, so the householder does not personally handle the produce.

items.text: Mishnah: The garment as a paradigm for items with simanim
items.text_en: Mishnah: The garment as a paradigm for items with simanim
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the garment was included in the general category of lost items, but was singled out to teach that only items with identifying marks (simanim) and claimants must be proclaimed.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the garment was included in the general category of lost items, but was singled out to teach that only items with identifying marks (simanim) and claimants must be proclaimed.

items.text: Gemara: What is 'included in all these'?
items.text_en: Gemara: What is 'included in all these'?
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the garment was included in the general phrase 'all lost items of your brother'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means by 'included in all these'.
Rava explains that the garment was included in the general phrase 'all lost items of your brother'.

items.text: Rava's analysis of the Torah's enumeration of lost items
items.text_en: Rava's analysis of the Torah's enumeration of lost items
items.desc_en: Rava questions why the Torah specified ox, donkey, sheep, and garment. He initially suggests each teaches a unique law: garment for its own simanim, donkey for saddle simanim, ox for its tail wool, sheep for its fleece. He then refines this, noting that the sheep verse is problematic for simanim, and concludes that the sheep teaches that simanim are Torah law.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks why the Torah enumerated the specific lost items: ox, donkey, sheep, and garment.
Rava explains that each item is needed: garment teaches about its own simanim, donkey teaches about saddle simanim.
Rava questions why both ox and sheep are needed, suggesting ox teaches about tail wool and sheep about fleece, but then objects that sheep would be redundant.
Rava refines: the donkey verse is needed for Rabbi Yehuda's bee case, but the sheep verse remains problematic for everyone.
Rava rejects the possibility that the sheep verse teaches about dung (which is ownerless) and concludes it teaches that simanim are Torah law.

items.text: Proof that sheep does not come for simanim
items.text_en: Proof that sheep does not come for simanim
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that since the Mishnah derives the requirement for simanim from the garment, the sheep verse must come for something else, not for simanim.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara argues that since the Mishnah derives the requirement for simanim from the garment, the sheep verse must come for something else, not for simanim.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages on the minimum value of a lost object
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages on the minimum value of a lost object
items.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma derives from 'asher tovad' that a lost object must be worth at least a perutah, while Rabbi Yehuda derives it from 'umetzatah'. Abaye explains the difference is in the exegetical method. The Gemara then explores the uses of the other verse: one for Ravnai's teaching that the object must come into one's hand, and one for Rabbi Yochanan's teaching that a river-swept object is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yehuda, each deriving from different verses that a lost object must be worth at least a perutah.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two positions.
Abaye answers that the difference is merely exegetical: each sage derives the same law from a different verse.
The Gemara asks what the Tanna Kamma does with the verse 'וּמְצָאתָהּ' (and you find it).
The Gemara answers that the Tanna Kamma uses 'וּמְצָאתָהּ' for Ravnai's teaching that the object must come into one's hand.
The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yehuda does with the verse 'אֲשֶׁר תֹּאבַד' (which is lost).
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yehuda uses 'אֲשֶׁר תֹּאבַד' for Rabbi Yochanan's teaching that a river-swept object is permitted.
The Gemara asks how Rabbi Yehuda derives Ravnai's teaching.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yehuda derives Ravnai's teaching from 'וּמְצָאתָהּ' (and you find it).
The Gemara asks how the Tanna Kamma derives Rabbi Yochanan's teaching.
The Gemara answers that the Tanna Kamma derives Rabbi Yochanan's teaching from the word 'מִמֶּנּוּ' (from him).
The Gemara asks how Rabbi Yehuda derives the same teaching.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yehuda does not derive anything from 'מִמֶּנּוּ' (from him).

items.text: Rava's alternative explanation of the dispute
items.text_en: Rava's alternative explanation of the dispute
