items.desc_en: Rava suggests the difference is whether a perutah that depreciated or appreciated is considered valid. After rejecting several possibilities, the Gemara concludes the difference is a perutah that appreciated and then depreciated and then appreciated again.

sub.desc_en: Rava proposes that the dispute between the two Tanna'im is about a perutah (small coin) that depreciated in value: the one who derives from 'אֲשֶׁר תֹּאבַד' requires value at the time of loss, so a depreciated coin is excluded, while the one who derives from 'וּמְצָאתָהּ' requires value at the time of finding, so it is included.

The Gemara objects: for the one who derives from 'אֲשֶׁר תֹּאבַד', we still require 'וּמְצָאתָהּ' (finding), and if the coin depreciated, it is not worth a perutah at the time of finding, so it should be excluded for him as well.

Rava revises his proposal: the dispute is about a perutah that appreciated in value; the one who derives from 'וּמְצָאתָהּ' requires value at the time of finding, so an appreciated coin is included, while the one who derives from 'אֲשֶׁר תֹּאבַד' requires value at the time of loss, so it is excluded.

The Gemara objects: for the one who derives from 'וּמְצָאתָהּ', we still require 'אֲשֶׁר תֹּאבַד' (loss), and if the coin appreciated, it was not worth a perutah at the time of loss, so it should be excluded for him as well.

The Gemara resolves: the dispute is about a perutah that appreciated, then depreciated, and then appreciated again; the one who derives from 'אֲשֶׁר תֹּאבַד' requires value at the time of loss (when it was worth a perutah), while the one who derives from 'וּמְצָאתָהּ' requires value continuously from the time of loss until the time of finding, which is not the case here.

items.text: Question: Are simanim Torah law or rabbinic?
items.text_en: Question: Are simanim Torah law or rabbinic?
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises the question whether the requirement for simanim is Torah law or rabbinic, setting up the next discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the requirement for simanim (identifying marks) is Torah law or rabbinic, and inquires about the practical difference.

items.text: Opening question: Torah or rabbinic status of simanim for returning a get
items.text_en: Opening question: Torah or rabbinic status of simanim for returning a get
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises the question of whether returning a lost object based on simanim is Torah law or rabbinic. It suggests that if it is rabbinic, the rabbis enacted it for monetary matters but not for prohibitions like a get.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether returning a get (bill of divorce) based on simanim (identifying marks) is Torah law or rabbinic, suggesting that if rabbinic, the rabbis enacted it for monetary matters but not for prohibitions.

items.text: First proof: the Mishnah's derivation from the garment
items.text_en: First proof: the Mishnah's derivation from the garment
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a Mishnah that derives from the word 'simlah' that only items with simanim and claimants require proclamation. The Tanna notes that simanim alone are sufficient for return.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah that derives from the word 'simlah' that only items with simanim (identifying marks) and claimants require proclamation.
The Tanna notes that claimants are necessary, but simanim alone are sufficient for return.

items.text: Second proof: donkey returned by saddle marks
items.text_en: Second proof: donkey returned by saddle marks
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a case where a donkey is returned by the simanim of its saddle, but suggests it might be returned by witnesses of the saddle instead.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where a donkey is returned by the simanim (identifying marks) of its saddle (אוכף), as a proof that simanim are de-oraita (Torah-level).
The Gemara rejects the proof by suggesting the baraita might mean the donkey is returned by witnesses (עדים) of the saddle, not by its marks.

items.text: Third proof: the verse 'until your brother inquires'
items.text_en: Third proof: the verse 'until your brother inquires'
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse that requires inquiry about the finder's honesty. It asks whether this inquiry is by simanim, but concludes it is by witnesses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse 'until your brother inquires' and explains that it requires investigating whether the claimant is a deceiver.
The Gemara asks whether this inquiry is conducted by means of סימנין (identifying marks).
The Gemara rejects the suggestion and concludes that the inquiry is by witnesses (עדים), not by marks.

items.text: Fourth proof: testimony requires face and nose, not simanim
items.text_en: Fourth proof: testimony requires face and nose, not simanim
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that testimony is only given on facial features, not on simanim of the body or clothing. This suggests simanim are not Torah law. The Gemara deflects: body simanim are general (tall/short), and clothing simanim are suspect due to borrowing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that testimony is only given on facial features (פרצוף הפנים עם החוטם), not on simanim of the body or clothing.
The Gemara infers from the baraita that simanim are not Torah law (דרבנן).
The Gemara deflects: body simanim are general (tall/short), and clothing simanim are suspect due to borrowing (שאלה).

items.text: Objection and resolution: borrowing concern for saddle and clothing
items.text_en: Objection and resolution: borrowing concern for saddle and clothing
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if we suspect borrowing for clothing, how can we return a donkey by saddle simanim? It answers that people do not borrow saddles because they damage the donkey. Alternatively, clothing simanim refer to color (white/red), which are not borrowed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if we suspect borrowing for clothing, how can we return a donkey by saddle simanim? It answers that people do not borrow saddles because they damage the donkey.
The Gemara offers an alternative answer: clothing simanim refer to color (white/red), which are not borrowed.

items.text: Further objection: found tied in a bag or ring
items.text_en: Further objection: found tied in a bag or ring
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that a get found tied in a bag or ring is valid even after a long time, implying no borrowing concern. It answers that bags, purses, and rings are not borrowed because they are distinctive or easily forged.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that a get found tied in a bag or ring is valid even after a long time, implying no concern for borrowing, and asks why we do not suspect borrowing.
The Gemara answers that bags, purses, and rings are not borrowed because bags and purses are distinctive (מסמני) and rings are easily forged (מזייף).

items.text: Debate among Tanna'im: simanim as Torah or rabbinic
items.text_en: Debate among Tanna'im: simanim as Torah or rabbinic
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute between the first Tanna and Elazar ben Mahavai about testifying on a mole (שומא). Rava offers three alternative explanations: the dispute is about whether a mole is common among peers, whether simanim change after death, or whether a mole is a distinctive sign. In each, the underlying status of simanim is assumed differently.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the Tannaic dispute about testifying on a mole (שומא) reflects a disagreement over whether simanim are Torah law or rabbinic.
Rava explains that all agree simanim are Torah law; the dispute is whether a mole is common among peers (בן גילו).
Rava offers an alternative: all agree the mole is not common among peers; the dispute is whether simanim change after death.
Rava offers a third explanation: all agree simanim are rabbinic and the mole does not change after death; the dispute is whether a mole is a distinctive sign (סימן מובהק).

items.text: Rava's hypothetical: if simanim are rabbinic, why return by them?
items.text_en: Rava's hypothetical: if simanim are rabbinic, why return by them?
items.desc_en: Rava asks: if simanim are rabbinic, why would the finder return the object? He answers that the finder benefits from the system, as he hopes others will return his lost items. Rav Safra objects that one cannot do good with another's money. The Gemara revises: the owner prefers to give simanim because he has no witnesses, and he trusts that only he knows the distinctive marks.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks: if simanim are only rabbinic, how can we return lost objects by them? He answers that the finder benefits from the system, hoping others will return his own lost items.
Rav Safra objects: can one do a favor for himself with money that is not his own?
The Gemara revises: the owner prefers to give simanim because he has no witnesses and trusts that only he knows the distinctive marks.

items.text: Final objection: the case of three borrowers and one lender
items.text_en: Final objection: the case of three borrowers and one lender
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel about returning a loan document. It asks why the borrower would want to return it to the lender. Rava answers that it is logical: the borrower is more likely to be found with the lender, and the lender with the borrower, so the document is returned to the party where it is more likely to have been lost.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel about returning a loan document and asks why the borrower would want to return it to the lender.
Rava answers that it is logical: the document is returned to the party where it is more likely to have been lost.

items.text: Proof that simanim are Torah law
items.text_en: Proof that simanim are Torah law
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the mishnah's rule about returning a bundle of documents relies on the finder's convenience, then Rava proves from the verse 'until your brother seeks it' that simanim are Torah law, as the verse implies one must investigate the claimant's honesty through simanim.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the mishnah's rule about returning a bundle of documents is also explained by the finder's convenience.
Rava asserts that סימנים (identifying marks) are a Torah law, deriving it from the verse 'until your brother seeks it', which implies investigation through simanim.

items.text: Rava's hypothetical about simanim
items.text_en: Rava's hypothetical about simanim
items.desc_en: Rava begins with 'if you find it possible to say simanim are Torah law', but the Gemara objects that this is already proven; the Gemara explains that Rava's phrasing is due to a possible alternative interpretation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rava's formulation 'if you might say', since he had already proven that simanim are Torah law.
The Gemara explains that the conditional language is because of a possible alternative interpretation (like the earlier preference for the finder's convenience).
The Gemara answers that Rava's conditional phrasing is because there might be an alternative interpretation of the proof, as we have already explained.

items.text: Priority rules for conflicting simanim and witnesses
items.text_en: Priority rules for conflicting simanim and witnesses
items.desc_en: The Gemara lists cases where multiple claimants offer different types of simanim or witnesses: when both offer simanim, the item is left; when one has simanim and the other has witnesses, it goes to the one with witnesses; when one has simanim and a single witness, the witness is disregarded; witnesses of weaving take precedence over witnesses of falling; length measurement takes precedence over width; weight takes precedence over length and width; and in a case of a get or a string, specific simanim like a hole near a letter or length are decisive, while a claim about a box is given to the husband.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the first rule: when both claimants offer simanim, the item is left in place.
The Gemara rules that witnesses of falling take precedence over witnesses of weaving, because the finder may have bought it from someone else.
The Gemara rules that length measurement takes precedence over width, because width can be estimated when the garment is folded, but length cannot.
The Gemara rules that when one claimant gives length and width and another gives the number of loops, the item goes to the one with length and width.
The Gemara rules that weight takes precedence over both length and width.

The Gemara asks about a case where both husband and wife claim simanim of the get: it is given to her, and explains that the decisive siman is a hole near a specific letter, not mere length and width.
The Gemara asks about a case where both claim simanim of the string: it is given to her, and explains that the decisive siman is length, not color.
The Gemara rules that when both claim the box, it is given to the husband, because the wife knows that everything he has is placed in the box.

items.text: Mishnah on announcement duration and Gemara's clarification
items.text_en: Mishnah on announcement duration and Gemara's clarification
items.desc_en: The mishnah states Rabbi Meir says the finder must announce until neighbors know, and Rabbi Yehuda says three festivals plus seven days. The Gemara clarifies that 'neighbors' refers to neighbors of the place where the item was found, not the owner's neighbors.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah presents the dispute: Rabbi Meir says the finder must announce until neighbors know, and Rabbi Yehuda says three festivals plus seven days after the last festival.
The Gemara asks: what does 'neighbors of the lost item' mean? If it means the owner's neighbors, why not just return it directly?
The Gemara resolves: it means neighbors of the place where the item was found, not the owner's neighbors.

items.text: Debate on the reason for Rabbi Yehuda's seven days
items.text_en: Debate on the reason for Rabbi Yehuda's seven days
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between Rabbi Yehuda's seven days and a baraita about asking for rain, which requires 15 days for the last traveler to reach the Euphrates. Rav Yosef resolves by distinguishing between the First Temple period (many Jews, need more time) and the Second Temple period (fewer Jews, need less time). Abaye objects with a verse showing Jews lived in cities, and reverses the reasoning. Rava concludes that the rabbis did not impose excessive burden on finders, regardless of the period.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Rabbi Yehuda's opinion that the finder must announce the lost object for three festivals and then seven days after the last festival.

The Gemara raises a contradiction: a baraita about asking for rain requires fifteen days after the festival for the last traveler to reach the Euphrates, implying a longer travel time than Rabbi Yehuda's seven days.
Rav Yosef resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the First Temple period (many Jews, requiring more time) and the Second Temple period (fewer Jews, requiring less time).

Abaye objects by citing a verse showing that Jews lived in cities even in the Second Temple period, and reverses the reasoning: in the First Temple period, with many Jews and frequent caravans, less time was needed; in the Second Temple period, with fewer Jews and fewer caravans, more time was needed.
Rava concludes that regardless of the period, the rabbis did not impose an excessive burden on finders, so the seven-day period is sufficient.

items.text: What is announced: the garment or 'lost item'?
items.text_en: What is announced: the garment or 'lost item'?
items.desc_en: Ravina deduces from the seven-day period that the finder announces the specific garment (e.g., 'a cloak'), because if he announced 'a lost item', the claimant would need an extra day to examine his clothes. Rava counters that even if 'lost item' is announced, the rabbis did not impose excessive burden.

sub.desc_en: Ravina deduces from the seven-day period that the finder announces the specific garment (e.g., 'a cloak'), because if he announced 'a lost item', the claimant would need an extra day to examine his clothes.
Rava counters that even if 'lost item' is announced, the rabbis did not impose excessive burden.

items.text: The formula for announcements on each festival
items.text_en: The formula for announcements on each festival
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that on the first festival the announcer says 'first festival', on the second 'second festival', and on the third he says it without specification. The Gemara questions why not say 'third festival', and explains it is to avoid confusion with the second.

sub.desc_en: A baraita: on the first festival one announces 'first festival', on the second 'second festival', on the third one announces vaguely.
The Gemara questions why the announcer does not simply say 'third festival' for the third festival.
The Gemara answers that saying 'third festival' is avoided because it might be confused with the second festival, since the second is also a 'second' in a different sense.

items.text: Transition from previous daf: concern about exchanging lost items
items.text_en: Transition from previous daf: concern about exchanging lost items
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern that if a finder announces a lost object, it might be exchanged with another lost object found earlier. It notes that a third festival would come to prevent this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern that announcing a lost object might lead to exchanging it with a previously found one, and notes that a third festival would prevent this.

items.text: Tannaic source: historical practice of announcing lost objects
items.text_en: Tannaic source: historical practice of announcing lost objects
items.desc_en: A baraita describes the original practice of announcing lost objects for three festivals, then after the Temple's destruction, announcements were made in synagogues and study halls. When oppressors increased, they instituted informing neighbors and acquaintances only.

sub.desc_en: A baraita recounts the historical progression of announcing lost objects: originally for three festivals, then in synagogues and study halls after the Temple's destruction, and finally only to neighbors and acquaintances when oppressors increased.

items.text: Explanation of 'oppressors' and a story with Rabbi Ami
items.text_en: Explanation of 'oppressors' and a story with Rabbi Ami
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that 'oppressors' refers to those who claim lost property belongs to the king. It relates a story where Rabbi Ami found a purse of dinars and told a Roman who was afraid to take it, saying they are not Persians who claim lost property for the king.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is meant by 'when oppressors increased' in the baraita.
The Gemara answers that oppressors are those who claim lost property belongs to the king.
The Gemara relates a story where Rabbi Ami found a purse of dinars and told a frightened Roman that they are not Persians who claim lost property for the king.

items.text: The 'Even HaTo'in' in Jerusalem
items.text_en: The 'Even HaTo'in' in Jerusalem
items.desc_en: A baraita describes a stone in Jerusalem called the 'Even HaTo'in' where people who lost or found objects would go. The finder would announce, and the claimant would give signs and take it. This is the source of the Mishnah's phrase about the stone being worn away.

sub.desc_en: A baraita describes the 'Even HaTo'in' stone in Jerusalem where finders and losers would gather, and the finder would announce the lost object while the claimant provided identifying signs to retrieve it, concluding that this is the source of the Mishnah's phrase about the stone being worn away.

items.text: Mishnah: claimant must give signs; concern for fraudsters
items.text_en: Mishnah: claimant must give signs; concern for fraudsters
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a claimant says 'I lost an object' but does not give its signs, the finder should not return it. Even if a known fraudster gives signs, it should not be returned, based on the verse 'until you search out your brother' to determine if he is a fraudster.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a claimant who does not provide signs for the lost object does not receive it, and even a known fraudster who gives signs is denied, based on the verse 'עַד דְּרֹשׁ אָחִיךָ אֹתוֹ' (until you search out your brother) to determine if he is a fraudster.

items.text: Gemara: dispute between Rav Yehuda and Rav Nachman on what to announce
items.text_en: Gemara: dispute between Rav Yehuda and Rav Nachman on what to announce
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says the finder announces 'avedta' (lost object) to avoid fraudsters, while Rav Nachman says 'gelima' (cloak) because otherwise there is no end. The Gemara supports Rav Yehuda from the Mishnah, but Rav Safra explains that even if 'gelima' is announced, the Mishnah refers to not giving precise signs.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute: Rav Yehuda says the finder announces 'avedta' (lost object), while Rav Nachman says 'gelima' (cloak).
Rav Yehuda explains his position: announcing 'avedta' avoids giving fraudsters a clue to fabricate a claim.
Rav Nachman explains his position: announcing 'gelima' is necessary, otherwise there is no end to the process (since every claimant could say 'I lost a cloak').

The Gemara challenges Rav Nachman: if the finder announces 'gelima', then a claimant who also says 'gelima' without precise signs would obviously not get the object, so the Mishnah's ruling would be redundant.
Rav Safra resolves the objection: even with 'gelima', the Mishnah refers to a case where the claimant gave only general signs (not precise ones), so the ruling is not redundant.

items.text: Baraita on fraudsters and a story with Rav Pappa's father
items.text_en: Baraita on fraudsters and a story with Rav Pappa's father
items.desc_en: A baraita states that originally claimants gave signs and took the object, but when fraudsters increased, they instituted requiring witnesses that the claimant is not a fraudster. A story illustrates this: Rav Pappa's father brought witnesses who said he is not a fraudster, but the court suspected they might be lying; Rav Huna concluded that a person does not bring harm upon himself.

sub.desc_en: A baraita reports that originally claimants gave signs and took the object, but when fraudsters increased, the court instituted requiring witnesses that the claimant is not a fraudster.

sub.text: Story about Rav Pappa's father and Rabbah bar Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Story about Rav Pappa's father and Rabbah bar Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: A story illustrates the baraita: Rav Pappa's father brought witnesses who said he is not a fraudster, but the court suspected they might be lying; Rabbah bar Rav Huna concluded that a person does not bring harm upon himself.

items.text: Mishnah: finder's responsibility for maintenance and sale of lost property
items.text_en: Mishnah: finder's responsibility for maintenance and sale of lost property
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if a lost animal works and eats, the finder should work it and feed it; if not, it should be sold. The proceeds are disputed: Rabbi Tarfon says the finder may use them but is liable if lost; Rabbi Akiva says he may not use them and is not liable.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule that a lost animal that works and eats should be worked and fed by the finder, while one that does not should be sold, based on the verse 'והשבותו לו' (and you shall return it to him).
The Mishnah asks what should be done with the proceeds from the sale of the lost property.
Rabbi Tarfon rules that the finder may use the proceeds, but is liable for their loss.
Rabbi Akiva rules that the finder may not use the proceeds, and is not liable for their loss.

items.text: Gemara: time limits for tending lost animals and resolving contradictions
items.text_en: Gemara: time limits for tending lost animals and resolving contradictions
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel sets a 12-month limit for tending animals that work and eat. Baraitot provide different time limits for calves, foals, geese, and chickens. The Gemara resolves contradictions: for calves/foals, one baraita refers to grazing animals (3 months), the other to fattened ones (30 days); for geese/chickens, one refers to large birds (30 days), the other to small ones (3 days).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the finder tends the animal indefinitely, and Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel answers with a 12-month limit, supported by a baraita.
A baraita is cited that provides specific time limits for tending different types of lost animals: 12 months for large working animals, 3 months for calves and foals, 30 days for geese and chickens.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak rules that a hen is treated like large cattle (12 months), and a second baraita is cited with different time limits: 30 days for calves/foals, 3 days for geese/chickens.
The Gemara raises a contradiction between the two baraitot regarding the time limits for calves/foals and geese/chickens.

The Gemara resolves the contradictions: for calves/foals, one baraita refers to grazing animals (3 months) and the other to fattened ones (30 days); for geese/chickens, one refers to large birds (30 days) and the other to small ones (3 days).

items.text: Baraita on not feeding young animals and the dispute on proceeds
items.text_en: Baraita on not feeding young animals and the dispute on proceeds
items.desc_en: A baraita derives from the verse that the finder should not feed a calf to calves, etc. The Gemara then notes that the dispute between Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva about the proceeds continues, and the daf ends mid-discussion.

sub.desc_en: A baraita derives from the verse 'וַהֲשֵׁבוֹתוֹ לוֹ' (and you shall return it to him) that the finder must not feed a calf to calves, a foal to foals, a goose to geese, or a rooster to roosters.
The Gemara notes that the dispute between Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva about the proceeds continues, and the daf ends mid-discussion.

items.text: Opening Mishnah excerpt
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah excerpt
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a finder used the found object, he is liable; if he did not use it and it was lost, he is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: a finder who used the object is liable for its loss, but if he did not use it and it was lost, he is exempt.

items.text: Gemara's challenge to Rav Yosef
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge to Rav Yosef
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah's ruling poses a difficulty for Rav Yosef, who holds that a finder is like a paid bailee, because the Mishnah exempts the finder when he did not use the object.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a challenge: does this Mishnah refute Rav Yosef, who holds that a finder of a lost object is like a paid bailee (שומר שכר)?

items.text: Rav Yosef's defense
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's defense
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef explains that the dispute between Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva is not about theft or loss, but about accidents of a borrower. Rabbi Tarfon holds that the finder may use the object, making him a borrower liable for accidents; Rabbi Akiva holds he may not, so he is not a borrower.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef responds: all agree that a finder is liable for theft and loss (גניבה ואבידה); the dispute between Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva is only about אונסין (unavoidable accidents) of a borrower (שואל), where Rabbi Tarfon permits use and thus makes the finder a borrower, while Rabbi Akiva forbids use and thus exempts him from borrower-level liability.

items.text: First analysis of Rabbi Akiva's 'therefore'
items.text_en: First analysis of Rabbi Akiva's 'therefore'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabbi Akiva's statement includes 'therefore' if the dispute is about theft and loss. It suggests that without 'therefore', one might think the finder is a paid bailee liable for theft and loss, so 'therefore' teaches he is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the dispute is only about אונסין, why does Rabbi Akiva need the word 'לְפִיכָךְ' (therefore)? It explains that without it, one might think the finder is a paid bailee (שומר שכר) and liable for theft and loss; 'לְפִיכָךְ' teaches that since use is forbidden, he is not a paid bailee and not liable for theft and loss.
The Gemara explains that without 'לְפִיכָךְ', one might think the finder is a paid bailee (שומר שכר) liable for theft and loss, so the word teaches he is exempt.
The Gemara concludes that since Rabbi Akiva prohibits use, the finder is not a paid bailee and is exempt from theft and loss.

items.text: Second analysis: difficulty with Rav Yosef's explanation
items.text_en: Second analysis: difficulty with Rav Yosef's explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that if the dispute is only about accidents, Rabbi Akiva's 'therefore' is superfluous, since it is obvious that if he may not use it, he is not a borrower and not liable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects further: if all agree on liability for theft and loss, and the dispute is only about אונסין, then Rabbi Akiva's 'לְפִיכָךְ' is superfluous, since the logic is obvious: if use is forbidden, he is not a borrower and not liable for אונסין.

items.text: Answer: 'therefore' refers to Rabbi Tarfon
items.text_en: Answer: 'therefore' refers to Rabbi Tarfon
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that Rabbi Akiva's 'therefore' is needed because of Rabbi Tarfon's 'therefore'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers: Rabbi Akiva's 'לְפִיכָךְ' is needed because of Rabbi Tarfon's 'לְפִיכָךְ' (to balance the formulation).

items.text: Explanation of Rabbi Tarfon's 'therefore'
items.text_en: Explanation of Rabbi Tarfon's 'therefore'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Tarfon's 'therefore' teaches that since the Sages permitted him to use the object, he is considered as if he used it and is liable for its loss.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is the purpose of Rabbi Tarfon's 'לְפִיכָךְ'? It explains that it teaches: since the Sages permitted use, the finder is considered as if he used it and is liable for its loss.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Tarfon's 'therefore' teaches that since the Sages permitted him to use the object, he is considered as if he used it and is liable for its loss.

items.text: Final objection: the Mishnah says 'lost'
items.text_en: Final objection: the Mishnah says 'lost'
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah explicitly says 'if they were lost', implying the case is about loss, not accidents, contradicting Rav Yosef's explanation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: but the Mishnah says 'אָבְדוּ' (they were lost), not 'אָבְדוּ בְּאוֹנֶס' (lost through unavoidable accident), implying liability even for ordinary loss, which contradicts the explanation that the dispute is only about אונסין.

items.text: Clarification of R' Tarfon's ruling and its application to orphans' money
items.text_en: Clarification of R' Tarfon's ruling and its application to orphans' money
items.desc_en: The Gemara first cites Rava's definition of 'stolen' and 'lost'. Then Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel that the halakha follows R' Tarfon. Rav Yosef permits using orphans' money based on this, but Abaye objects citing Rav Huna's limitation that the ruling applies only to lost items where the finder exerted effort, not to money. Rav Yosef concedes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbah's definitions of 'stolen' (by armed bandits) and 'lost' (shipwreck at sea) to clarify the terms in the Mishnah.
Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Tarfon's ruling.
Rachbah, who had orphans' money, asks Rav Yosef whether he may use it.
Rav Yosef permits using the money, citing the same ruling that the הלכה follows Rabbi Tarfon.
Abaye objects, citing Rav Huna's limitation that Rabbi Tarfon's ruling applies only to lost items where the finder exerted effort, not to money, and the orphans' money is like lost money.
Rav Yosef concedes to Abaye's objection, telling Rachbah to go because they did not leave him room to permit it.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of found books, garments, and vessels
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of found books, garments, and vessels
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents rules for a finder: found books may be read once every thirty days; if illiterate, one may roll them. One may not learn from them initially or read with another. Found garments may be shaken and spread for their own preservation, not for honor. Silver and copper vessels may be used for their preservation, but not to wear them out; gold and glass vessels may not be touched until Elijah comes. A sack or basket that is not normally taken is not to be taken.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule for found books: one may read them once every thirty days, or roll them if illiterate, but may not learn from them initially or read with another.
The Mishnah states that found garments may be shaken and spread for their own preservation, not for the finder's honor.
The Mishnah rules that silver and copper vessels may be used for preservation, but gold and glass vessels may not be touched until Elijah comes.
The Mishnah concludes that a sack or basket not normally taken should not be taken by the finder.

items.text: Gemara on found tefillin and the distinction from books
items.text_en: Gemara on found tefillin and the distinction from books
items.desc_en: Shmuel rules that one who finds tefillin in the market may appraise their value and immediately deposit them. Ravina challenges this from the Mishnah which says found books may be read but not appraised and deposited. Abaye resolves that tefillin are commonly found in bundles, unlike books.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that one who finds tefillin in the market appraises their value and deposits them immediately.
Ravina challenges Shmuel from the Mishnah, which permits reading found books but not appraising and depositing them.
Abaye resolves that tefillin are commonly found in bundles, unlike books, so the Mishnah's restriction does not apply.

items.text: Baraita on borrowing and depositing a Torah scroll, and disputes about rolling frequency
items.text_en: Baraita on borrowing and depositing a Torah scroll, and disputes about rolling frequency
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that a borrower of a Torah scroll may not lend it to another, but may open and read it, provided he does not learn from it initially or read with another. A depositary may roll it every twelve months, opening it for that purpose; if he opens it for his own study, it is forbidden. Sumchos and R' Eliezer ben Yaakov dispute the rolling interval for new vs. old scrolls. The Gemara clarifies that R' Eliezer ben Yaakov actually says thirty days for both.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the rule that a borrower of a Torah scroll may not lend it to another, but may open and read it, provided he does not learn from it initially or read with another.
The baraita continues with the rule for a depositary: he may roll the scroll every twelve months, opening it for that purpose, but if he opens it for his own study it is forbidden.
Sumchos disputes the rolling interval: for a new scroll thirty days, for an old one twelve months.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov rules that both new and old scrolls require a twelve-month rolling interval.
The Gemara questions why the baraita specifically mentions a Torah scroll, implying the rule might apply to all borrowed items.
The Gemara answers that the rule applies to all items, citing Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish's principle that a borrower may not lend and a hirer may not re-hire.

The Gemara explains that the Torah scroll was specifically needed because one might think the owner is pleased to have a מצוה (commandment) performed with his property, so the baraita teaches that even so, the borrower may not lend it.
The Gemara questions why the baraita states the obvious that the borrower may open and read the scroll.
The Gemara answers that the latter clause was necessary: the restriction that he may not learn from it initially.
The Gemara questions why the depositary would open and read the scroll at all, given that he is not the owner.
The Gemara further questions the apparent contradiction: the baraita says he may open and read, yet also says if he opens for his own sake it is forbidden.
The Gemara resolves: the baraita means that if while rolling he opens and reads, it is permitted; but if he opens solely for his own study, it is forbidden.
The Gemara notes that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's ruling (twelve months for both) is identical to the first Tanna's position.
The Gemara emends the text: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov actually says both new and old require thirty days.

items.text: Contradiction regarding reading with another and its resolution
items.text_en: Contradiction regarding reading with another and its resolution
items.desc_en: The Mishnah forbids reading with another, but a baraita permits two people to read from the same scroll. Abaye resolves that the Mishnah refers to the same topic, while the baraita refers to different topics.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the Mishnah forbids reading with another, but a baraita permits two people to read from the same scroll.
Abaye resolves the contradiction: the Mishnah refers to reading the same topic, while the baraita refers to different topics.

items.text: Contradiction regarding shaking garments and its resolutions
items.text_en: Contradiction regarding shaking garments and its resolutions
items.desc_en: The Mishnah says shaking a garment once every thirty days is beneficial, but R' Yochanan says one with a skilled weaver at home should shake it daily. The Gemara offers three resolutions: daily shaking harms, monthly helps; or the distinction is between one garment and two; or between shaking by hand and with a stick; or between wool and linen.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's ruling that shaking a garment once every thirty days is beneficial implies that shaking is always beneficial.
The Gemara objects by citing Rabbi Yochanan's statement that one with a skilled weaver at home should shake his garment daily, contradicting the Mishnah's monthly schedule.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing that daily shaking harms the garment, while monthly shaking is beneficial.
An alternative resolution distinguishes between shaking one garment (monthly) and two garments (daily).
Another resolution distinguishes between shaking by hand (daily) and shaking with a stick (monthly).
A final resolution distinguishes between wool garments (monthly shaking) and linen garments (daily shaking).

items.text: R' Yochanan's statements on vessels and advice for wasting money
items.text_en: R' Yochanan's statements on vessels and advice for wasting money
items.desc_en: R' Yochanan distinguishes between a cup of hot water and a cup of lukewarm water for metal vessels, with exceptions for cracked or lined vessels. He also advises one who wishes to waste his father's money to wear linen garments, use glass vessels, and hire workers without sitting with them, with explanations for each.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that a cup of hot water is preferable to a cup of lukewarm water for metal vessels.
Rabbi Yochanan qualifies that the rule applies only to metal vessels, not earthenware ones.
Rabbi Yochanan further qualifies that the rule applies only to uncracked metal vessels, not cracked ones.
Rabbi Yochanan finally qualifies that the rule applies only to vessels not lined with pitch, not to lined ones.
Rabbi Yochanan advises one who wishes to waste his father's money to wear linen garments, use glass vessels, and hire workers without sitting with them.

The Gemara explains each piece of advice: linen garments mean expensive Roman linen, glass vessels mean white glassware, and hiring workers without sitting with them means paying them without supervising their work.

items.text: Opening statement on items with high loss
items.text_en: Opening statement on items with high loss
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins with a brief statement about items whose loss is common, setting the context for the discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a statement about items whose loss is common, setting the context for the discussion.

items.text: Question on using for both owner and finder
items.text_en: Question on using for both owner and finder
items.desc_en: A dilemma is raised: may one spread a garment for both his own need and the owner's? The Gemara attempts to resolve it from the Mishnah, but finds contradictory implications from the first and second clauses, concluding no proof.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: may one spread a garment for both his own need and the owner's?

sub.text: Gemara's attempted proof from first clause
sub.text_en: Gemara's attempted proof from first clause
sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove from the first clause that only for the owner's need is permitted, but not for both.
The Gemara counters from the second clause that for both needs it is fine, contradicting the first clause's implication.
The Gemara concludes that no proof can be derived from this Mishnah due to the contradiction between clauses.

items.text: Second attempt: Baraita on spreading
items.text_en: Second attempt: Baraita on spreading
items.desc_en: A Baraita is cited: one may spread a garment for the owner's need but not for his own; if guests arrive, he may not spread it at all. The Gemara deflects this proof, distinguishing the case due to concern for the evil eye or thieves.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: one may spread a garment for the owner's need but not for his own; if guests arrive, he may not spread it at all.
The Gemara deflects the proof, distinguishing the case due to concern for the evil eye or thieves.

items.text: Third attempt: Heifer whose neck is broken
items.text_en: Third attempt: Heifer whose neck is broken
items.desc_en: A Mishnah about a heifer that was used for both the owner's and the finder's benefit is cited, which rules it invalid. The Gemara deflects this by citing a unique verse that disqualifies any use.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about a heifer used for both the owner's and the finder's benefit, which rules it invalid, to prove that mixed-use is forbidden.
The Gemara deflects the proof by noting that the heifer's disqualification stems from a unique verse that prohibits any use whatsoever, not from a general rule about mixed-use.

items.text: Clarification of the verse and Rav Pappa's principle
items.text_en: Clarification of the verse and Rav Pappa's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the first case of the heifer is valid, and resolves it with Rav Pappa's explanation: the verse is read as 'עוּבַּד' but written as 'עָבַד', requiring that the work be beneficial to the owner, which excludes mere nursing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the verse excludes any work, even the first case of the heifer nursing should be invalid.
The Gemara distinguishes the case by citing a baraita about a bird perching versus an animal mounting, and asks for the reason.
Rav Pappa explains that if the verse were written and read as 'עוּבַּד', it would include even unintentional work; if written and read as 'עָבַד', it would require direct human action.
Rav Pappa resolves that since the verse is written as 'עָבַד' but read as 'עוּבַּד', we require the work to be beneficial to the owner, like direct human work.

items.text: Baraita on using found vessels and deposit
items.text_en: Baraita on using found vessels and deposit
items.desc_en: A Baraita details how one may use different types of found vessels to prevent decay, and extends these rules to a deposit when the owner is abroad, as stated by Rav Adda bar Hamah quoting Rav Sheshet.

sub.desc_en: A baraita details how one may use different types of found vessels (wood, copper, silver, iron, gold, glass) to prevent decay, with restrictions based on material.
The Gemara asks: what relevance does a deposit (פיקדון) have in the context of found objects, since the finder is not the owner?

sub.text: Rav Adda bar Hamah quoting Rav Sheshet
sub.text_en: Rav Adda bar Hamah quoting Rav Sheshet
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Hamah quoting Rav Sheshet answers: the baraita refers to a deposit whose owners have gone overseas, so the bailee may use the vessels to prevent decay.

items.text: When one may refrain from returning a lost item
items.text_en: When one may refrain from returning a lost item
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses cases where one is exempt from returning a lost item, such as a priest in a cemetery or when his own work exceeds the loss, derived from the verse 'וְהִתְעַלַּמְתָּ'. It questions the need for the verse for the priest case, and concludes it is needed for the case of one's own work being greater, citing Rav Yehuda quoting Rav.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the biblical source of the Mishnah's ruling that one may not take an item whose nature is not to be picked up.

A baraita is cited, deriving from the verse 'וְהִתְעַלַּמְתָּ' that there are times when one may refrain from returning a lost item, such as a priest in a cemetery, an elder whose dignity is compromised, or when one's own work exceeds the loss.
The Gemara objects that the verse seems unnecessary for the case of a priest in a cemetery, since a positive commandment does not override both a negative and a positive commandment.
The Gemara further rejects the priest case as a source, noting that we do not push aside a prohibition for the sake of monetary loss.
The Gemara concludes that the verse is needed for the case where one's own work exceeds the loss, citing Rav Yehuda quoting Rav.

items.text: Opening principle: priority and exemption for the elderly
items.text_en: Opening principle: priority and exemption for the elderly
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse 'there shall be no needy among you' to establish that one's own property takes precedence over another's. It then introduces the case of an elder for whom returning a lost item is beneath his dignity, exempting him from the obligation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse 'לֹא יִהְיֶה בְּךָ אֶבְיוֹן' (there shall be no needy among you) to establish that one's own property takes precedence over another's, and then introduces the case of an elder for whom returning a lost item is beneath his dignity, exempting him from the obligation.

items.text: Rabbah's ruling and Abaye's test
items.text_en: Rabbah's ruling and Abaye's test
items.desc_en: Rabbah rules that if one causes an animal to flee, he is liable for it. Abaye tests this by startling goats and Rabbah confirms his liability, instructing him to return them.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah rules that if one startles an animal and causes it to flee, he is liable for it.
Abaye, sitting before Rabbah, sees goats and startles them to test the ruling.
Rabbah confirms that Abaye is liable for the startled goats and instructs him to return them.

items.text: Unresolved query: field vs. city
items.text_en: Unresolved query: field vs. city
items.desc_en: A question is raised: if one finds an animal in a field where returning is natural, but then it goes to the city where returning is not his way, is he still obligated? The Gemara leaves this unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an unresolved query (תיקו) about whether finding an animal in a field obligates returning it even after it moves to a city where returning is not the finder's usual practice.

items.text: Rava's principle: what one does for himself, he does for others
items.text_en: Rava's principle: what one does for himself, he does for others
items.desc_en: Rava states that whatever one would return for himself, he must also return for his fellow; similarly, whatever he would load or unload for himself, he must do for his fellow.

sub.desc_en: Rava establishes the principle that whatever one would return, load, or unload for himself, he must also do for his fellow.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Yishmael and the bread carrier
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Yishmael and the bread carrier
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei encounters a man carrying baked bread who is exhausted. He asks the price, pays half a zuz, and declares the bread ownerless. When the man tries to reclaim it, Rabbi Yishmael says he declared it ownerless for everyone except him.

sub.desc_en: The narrator describes Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei meeting a man carrying baked bread, paying half a zuz, and declaring the bread ownerless.
When the man tries to reclaim the bread, Rabbi Yishmael declares he made it ownerless for everyone except him.

items.text: Challenge and resolution: validity of partial ownerless declaration
items.text_en: Challenge and resolution: validity of partial ownerless declaration
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether such a conditional ownerless declaration is valid, citing a dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel. It resolves that Rabbi Yishmael actually declared it ownerless for everyone, but merely told the man that to prevent him from taking it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a conditional ownerless declaration (הפקר) that excludes a specific person is valid.

The Gemara cites a baraita where Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel dispute whether a partial ownerless declaration (הפקר) is valid, with Beit Hillel requiring it to be ownerless for all, like the Sabbatical year.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei actually declared the bread ownerless for everyone, and his statement to the man was merely a verbal deterrent to prevent him from taking it.

items.text: Justification: acting beyond the letter of the law
items.text_en: Justification: acting beyond the letter of the law
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yishmael was an elder for whom returning was beneath his dignity, yet he acted beyond the letter of the law (lifnim mishurat hadin).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei was an elder for whom returning the lost item was beneath his dignity, yet he did so.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yishmael acted beyond the letter of the law (לפנים משורת הדין), which is praiseworthy even for an elder.

items.text: Exegesis of the verse: derech eretz and lifnim mishurat hadin
items.text_en: Exegesis of the verse: derech eretz and lifnim mishurat hadin
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef expounds a verse to include various acts of kindness: visiting the sick, burial, and acting beyond the letter of the law. The Gemara clarifies that visiting the sick applies even to a peer, burial applies even to an elder whose dignity is compromised, and acting beyond the letter of the law is illustrated by Rabbi Yochanan's statement that Jerusalem was destroyed because they judged strictly by Torah law without going beyond it.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef's baraita expounds the verse 'וְהוֹדַעְתָּ לָהֶם' (and you shall make known to them) to include: their house of life (בית חייהם), the way (דרך) as acts of kindness (גמילות חסדים), 'which they shall walk' (אשר ילכו) as visiting the sick (ביקור חולים), 'in it' (בה) as burial (קבורה), 'the deed' (המעשה) as the law (הדין), and 'which they shall do' (אשר יעשון) as acting beyond the letter of the law (לפנים משורת הדין).
The Gemara questions why visiting the sick is listed separately from acts of kindness, since it is a subset of גמילות חסדים (acts of kindness).
The Gemara answers that the separate mention is necessary to teach that one must visit even a peer (בן גילו), who takes one-sixtieth of his illness, and even so one is obligated to visit him.
The Gemara similarly questions why burial is listed separately from acts of kindness.
The Gemara answers that the separate mention is necessary to teach that one must bury even an elder whose dignity is compromised (זקן ואינה לפי כבודו).

Rabbi Yochanan states that Jerusalem was destroyed only because they judged strictly by Torah law (דין תורה) without acting beyond the letter of the law (לפנים משורת הדין), and the Gemara clarifies that this does not mean they judged wrongly, but that they did not go beyond the strict law.

items.text: Mishnah: definition of a lost object and return obligations
items.text_en: Mishnah: definition of a lost object and return obligations
items.desc_en: The Mishnah defines what constitutes a lost object: animals grazing normally are not lost, but overturned donkeys or cows running among vineyards are. One must return even multiple times. If one loses wages, he is paid as a worker; if a court is available, he stipulates; otherwise, his own property takes precedence.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by defining what constitutes a lost object: animals grazing normally are not lost, but overturned donkeys or cows running among vineyards are.
The Mishnah states that one must return even multiple times, and if one loses wages, he is paid as a worker; if a court is available, he stipulates; otherwise, his own property takes precedence.

items.text: Gemara: clarification of the Mishnah and time limit
items.text_en: Gemara: clarification of the Mishnah and time limit
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's wording. Rav Yehuda explains it means: which type of lost object is one obligated to return? He then cites Rav that the obligation applies only up to three days. The Gemara clarifies that this refers to an animal seen at morning and evening; within three days it may have wandered, but after that it is certainly lost.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's wording: are all the cases listed not really lost objects?
Rav Yehuda explains that the Mishnah means: which type of lost object is one obligated to return? — distinguishing between objects that are clearly lost and those that are not.
The Gemara asks: is the obligation to return the animal unlimited in time?
Rav Yehuda cites Rav that the obligation to return applies only up to three days.
The Gemara questions the three-day rule: if the animal is seen only at night or only during the day, the time limit seems illogical.
The Gemara clarifies that the case is an animal seen both at morning and evening; within three days it may have wandered, but after that it is certainly lost.

items.text: Supporting baraita
items.text_en: Supporting baraita
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited in support of the previous ruling, mentioning the case of finding a cloak or an axe.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited in support of the previous ruling, mentioning the case of finding a cloak or an axe.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Signs of Lost Property
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Signs of Lost Property
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases where an animal or object is considered lost (e.g., a donkey running among vineyards) and cases where it is not (e.g., a cow grazing among vineyards). It also mentions that water flooding is considered lost and requires damming.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases of lost property: a donkey running among vineyards is lost, a cow grazing among vineyards is not, and flooding water requires damming.

items.text: Rava's Derivation and Rav Chananya's Support
items.text_en: Rava's Derivation and Rav Chananya's Support
items.desc_en: Rava derives from the verse 'for every lost thing of your brother' that land can be considered lost property. Rav Chananya cites the Mishnah's case of flooding water as support, but Rava deflects by explaining the case involves sheaves that need the land, so it is not a pure land-loss case.

sub.desc_en: Rava derives from the verse that lost land is included in the obligation to return lost property, and Rabbi Chananya cites a supporting baraita about flooding water.
Rava rejects the support, explaining the baraita deals with sheaves needing the land, not land itself.
Rava deflects the support by explaining the baraita deals with sheaves that need the land, so it is not a pure land-loss case.

items.text: Contradiction in the Mishnah's Cases
items.text_en: Contradiction in the Mishnah's Cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara points out an internal contradiction in the Mishnah: the first clause implies that a cow running among vineyards is lost, but the second clause implies that a cow running on the road is not lost. Abaye resolves this by saying each clause teaches the more lenient case, and the stricter case is implied.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points out an internal contradiction in the Mishnah: the first clause implies running is lost, the second implies running in vineyards is lost but grazing is not.
Abaye resolves the contradiction by saying the Mishnah uses a 'tell its friend' style: each clause teaches its own case and the other is implied by a kal vachomer.

items.text: Rava's Rejection and Alternative Resolution
items.text_en: Rava's Rejection and Alternative Resolution
items.desc_en: Rava rejects Abaye's resolution, arguing that the Mishnah should have taught the stricter cases explicitly. Instead, Rava resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between cases: when the animal faces the wilderness (lost) vs. the town (not lost), and between loss of the animal itself vs. loss of land.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects to Abaye's resolution, arguing that if the Mishnah used the principle of יגיד עליו רעו (it tells about its fellow), it should have taught the lighter case and all the more so the stricter case, but it did not.
Rava resolves the contradiction regarding 'running' by distinguishing whether the animal faces the wilderness (lost) or the town (not lost).
Rava resolves the contradiction regarding 'grazing' by distinguishing between loss of the animal itself (אבידת גופה) and loss of land (אבידת קרקע).

Rava synthesizes the Mishnah's rulings: grazing on the road is not lost regarding the animal itself, but grazing among vineyards is lost regarding land; running among vineyards is lost regarding the animal itself, but grazing among vineyards is not lost regarding the animal itself because it is not likely to be taken.

items.text: Further Questions on the Cow Grazing Among Vineyards
items.text_en: Further Questions on the Cow Grazing Among Vineyards
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a cow grazing among vineyards is not considered lost due to land damage or danger to the animal. It answers that the case involves a gentile owner (so no land-loss obligation) and a place where they warn before killing, so the animal is not in danger.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Even if the cow grazing among vineyards is not considered lost due to danger to its body, why is it not considered lost due to potential damage to the land (אבידת קרקע)?
The Gemara answers that the case involves a gentile owner, so there is no obligation to prevent land damage (אבידת קרקע) to a gentile's property.
The Gemara further asks: Even so, why is the cow not considered lost due to danger to its body (אבידת גופה), as people might kill it?
The Gemara answers that this is in a place where they issue a warning before killing, so the animal is not in immediate danger.
The Gemara asks: But what if they did warn about the cow and it was not heeded?
The Gemara resolves: If they warned about the cow and the owner did not take care of it, then it is certainly a deliberate loss (אבידה מדעת), and there is no obligation to return it.

items.text: Derivation from 'Hashev Teshivem' for Returning Lost Property
items.text_en: Derivation from 'Hashev Teshivem' for Returning Lost Property
items.desc_en: A certain rabbi suggests that the doubled verb 'hashev teshivem' teaches that one must return the animal even if it runs away multiple times. Rava explains that 'hashev' implies even a hundred times, and 'teshivem' teaches that one must return it to any place (house, garden, ruin). The Gemara concludes that this applies even without the owner's knowledge, as per Rabbi Elazar.

sub.desc_en: A certain rabbi asks Rava why the verse uses both 'hashav' and 'teshivem' to teach multiple returns.
Rava explains that 'hashav' implies even a hundred times, and 'teshivem' teaches returning to any place, but the Gemara questions the case of a guarded courtyard.
The Gemara resolves that even in a guarded courtyard, the verse teaches that returning lost property does not require the owner's knowledge, as per Rabbi Elazar's principle.

The Gemara resolves that the place is guarded, and the verse teaches that returning lost property does not require the owner's knowledge, as per Rabbi Elazar's principle that the Torah multiplied returns.

items.text: Derivation from 'Shaleach Teshallach' for Sending Away the Mother Bird
items.text_en: Derivation from 'Shaleach Teshallach' for Sending Away the Mother Bird
items.desc_en: A similar question is asked about the doubled verb 'shaleach teshallach' for sending away the mother bird. Rava explains that 'shaleach' implies even a hundred times, and 'teshallach' teaches that one must send away even for a mitzvah purpose.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse uses both 'shaleach' and 'teshalach' for sending away the mother bird.
Rava explains that 'shaleach' implies even a hundred times, and 'teshalach' teaches that the mitzvah applies even for a mitzvah purpose.

items.text: Derivation from 'Hocheach Tochiach' for Rebuke
items.text_en: Derivation from 'Hocheach Tochiach' for Rebuke
items.desc_en: The same rabbi asks about the doubled verb 'hocheach tochiach' for rebuke. Rava explains that 'hocheach' implies even a hundred times, and 'tochiach' teaches that even a student may rebuke a teacher.

sub.desc_en: A certain rabbi asks Rava why the verse uses both 'hocheach' and 'tochi'ach' for rebuke.
Rava explains that 'hocheach' implies even a hundred times, and 'tochi'ach' teaches that rebuke applies even from a student to a rabbi.

items.text: Derivations from 'Azov Ta'azov' and 'Hakem Takim'
items.text_en: Derivations from 'Azov Ta'azov' and 'Hakem Takim'
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the doubled verbs 'azov ta'azov' (unloading) and 'hakem takim' (loading) that the obligation applies even when the owner is not present.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from the verse 'azov ta'azov imo' we only know the obligation when the owner is present; where do we derive it when the owner is absent?
The Gemara answers: the doubled verb 'azov ta'azov' teaches that the obligation applies in all cases.
The Gemara asks: from the verse 'hakem takim imo' we only know the obligation when the owner is present; where do we derive it when the owner is absent?
The Gemara answers: the doubled verb 'hakem takim' teaches that the obligation applies in all cases.

items.text: Why Both Unloading and Loading Are Written, and Why Lost Property Is Added
items.text_en: Why Both Unloading and Loading Are Written, and Why Lost Property Is Added
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Torah wrote both unloading (free) and loading (paid), and why lost property is a separate category. Each teaches a unique aspect: unloading involves animal suffering and financial loss, loading involves payment, and lost property involves the owner's distress but no animal suffering. The Gemara notes that for Rabbi Shimon, who says loading is also free, the verses are not concluded.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah wrote both the commandment of unloading (פריקה) and loading (טעינה), since they seem redundant.

The Gemara explains that both are necessary: unloading teaches about animal suffering (צער בעלי חיים) and financial loss, while loading teaches about paid service, and each alone would not imply the other.
The Gemara objects that according to Rabbi Shimon, who says loading is also free, the distinction between the two verses collapses, and the verses are not concluded.
The Gemara asks why the Torah also wrote the category of lost property (אבידה) separately, and answers that it teaches a case where the owner's distress exists but the animal's suffering does not.

items.text: Introduction: The principle of doubled verbs
items.text_en: Introduction: The principle of doubled verbs
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the general principle that doubled verbs in the Torah (e.g., 'השב תשיב', 'חבל תחבול') teach that the action applies even in cases not explicitly stated. It provides examples from the verses about murder, striking, returning a pledge, and taking a pledge.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the need to explain why two doubled verbs are necessary, stating that they are indeed needed.
The baraita cites the doubled verb 'מות יומת' (he shall surely be put to death) to teach that if the prescribed death penalty cannot be applied, any death penalty may be used.
The baraita cites the doubled verb 'הכה תכה' (you shall surely strike) to teach that if the prescribed striking cannot be done, any striking may be used.
The baraita cites the doubled verb 'השב תשיב' (you shall surely return) to teach that the obligation to return a pledge applies even when the pledge was taken without court authorization.
The baraita cites the doubled verb 'חבל תחבול' (you shall surely take a pledge) to teach that the prohibition applies even when the pledge is taken without court authorization.

items.text: Clarification: Two verses for day and night garments
items.text_en: Clarification: Two verses for day and night garments
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why two verses (one for 'חבל תחבול' and one for 'השב תשיב') are needed, and answers that one teaches about taking a garment used during the day and the other about a garment used at night.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why two verses (חבל תחבול and השב תשיב) are needed.
The Gemara answers that one verse teaches about taking a garment used during the day and the other about a garment used at night.

items.text: Additional examples of the principle
items.text_en: Additional examples of the principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara continues with more examples of doubled verbs: 'פתח תפתח' teaches giving to the poor of another city, 'נתון תתן' teaches a small gift, and 'הענק תעניק' teaches granting a gift even if the house was not blessed because of the servant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the doubled verb 'פתח תפתח' to teach that the obligation to open one's hand extends to the poor of another city.
The Gemara cites the doubled verb 'נתון תתן' to teach that the obligation to give applies even to a small gift.
The Gemara cites the doubled verb 'הענק תעניק' to teach that the grant is given even if the house was not blessed because of the servant.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's view on 'הענק תעניק'
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's view on 'הענק תעניק'
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that according to Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, who holds that the gift is only given if the house was blessed because of the servant, the doubled verb 'תעניק' is superfluous and is explained as the Torah speaking in human language.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks that according to Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, who holds that the gift is given only if the house was blessed because of the servant, what is the purpose of the doubled verb 'תעניק'.
The Gemara answers that the doubled verb is simply the Torah speaking in human language, with no additional halachic implication.

items.text: The verse 'העביט תעביטנו' and Rabbi Shimon's view
items.text_en: The verse 'העביט תעביטנו' and Rabbi Shimon's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the doubled verb 'העביט תעביטנו' teaches that even if a person has money but does not want to support himself, we give him a loan. According to Rabbi Shimon, who says we do not get involved in such a case, the doubled verb is explained as the Torah speaking in human language.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the doubled verb 'העביט תעביטנו' to teach that even if a person has money but does not want to support himself, we give him a loan.
Rabbi Shimon objects that if a person has money but does not want to support himself, we do not get involved, and explains the doubled verb as the Torah speaking in human language.

items.text: The law of a worker who was idle: 'פועל בטל'
items.text_en: The law of a worker who was idle: 'פועל בטל'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a worker was idle from a sela's worth of work, he is paid as a 'פועל בטל'. Abaye explains that this means he is paid like a worker who is idle from that specific type of work.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a worker was idle from a sela's worth of work, he is not paid a full sela but rather as a פועל בטל (idle worker).
The gemara cites the Mishnah's formulation that he is paid as a פועל בטל (idle worker).
The gemara asks: what exactly is meant by 'as a פועל בטל (idle worker)'?
Abaye explains: he is paid like a worker who is idle from that specific type of work (i.e., the wage he would accept to sit idle rather than do that particular job).

items.text: Conditioning before a court and the case of Issur and Rav Safra
items.text_en: Conditioning before a court and the case of Issur and Rav Safra
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses that if there is a court, one can stipulate before them. It then recounts a story where Rav Safra divided profits with Issur without Issur's knowledge in front of two witnesses, and Rabba bar Rav Huna instructed him to bring three witnesses before whom he divided.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that if a court is present, one can stipulate before them.

sub.text: Story about Issur and Rav Safra
sub.text_en: Story about Issur and Rav Safra
sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Issur and Rav Safra were business partners, and Rav Safra divided profits with Issur without his knowledge in front of two witnesses.
Rabba bar Rav Huna instructs Rav Safra to bring three witnesses before whom he divided, implying that two witnesses are insufficient for this purpose.

items.text: Gemara's discussion on witnesses for returning a lost animal
items.text_en: Gemara's discussion on witnesses for returning a lost animal
items.desc_en: The Gemara debates whether two witnesses are sufficient or if three are needed when the owner claims the animal in front of a court. Abaye challenges the proof from the Mishnah about a widow selling property, citing Rav Nachman's distinction between expert and lay courts.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether two witnesses suffice or three are needed when the owner claims the animal before a court.
The Gemara answers by citing a Mishnah about a widow selling property, which requires a court for monetary transfer.
The Gemara objects that the cases are different: the widow case involves transferring money, while here it is merely clarifying ownership, which two witnesses suffice.
Abaye rejects the objection by citing Rav Nachman's distinction: a widow needs a court of laymen (הדיוטות), not experts (מומחין), so the proof from the Mishnah is inconclusive.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of finding an animal and the mitzvah of unloading
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of finding an animal and the mitzvah of unloading
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one finds an animal in a stable, he is not obligated to return it; in the public domain, he is. It also discusses the obligation to unload a burden multiple times, exemptions when the owner is present, and disputes between Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili about loading and excessive loads.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the law of finding an animal in a stable (פטור) versus the public domain (חייב), and the case of a cemetery where one must not become impure, overriding parental commands.
The Mishnah states that one must unload and reload even multiple times, citing the verse 'עָזֹב תַּעֲזֹב'.
The Mishnah exempts one if the owner sits and says 'since the mitzvah is upon you, unload if you wish', but obligates if the owner is elderly or sick.
The Tanna Kamma states that the Torah mitzvah is to unload but not to load; Rabbi Shimon says even to load.
Rabbi Yosei HaGelili exempts one from an excessive load beyond what the animal can bear, based on the verse 'תַּחַת מַשָּׂאוֹ'.

items.text: Gemara: Rava's explanation of 'refet'
items.text_en: Gemara: Rava's explanation of 'refet'
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the Mishnah's term 'refet' (stable) implies it is neither misleading nor protective. If it were protective, one would be obligated to return the animal even if found inside, but the Mishnah exempts, proving it is not protective.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens by stating that the Mishnah's 'refet' (stable) is neither misleading nor protective.
Rava argues that if the refet were protective, finding the animal inside would obligate return, but the Mishnah exempts, proving it is not protective.

items.text: Gemara: Rabbi Yitzchak's qualification about the stable and public domain
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabbi Yitzchak's qualification about the stable and public domain
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak qualifies the Mishnah: the exemption for a stable applies only if the animal is within the techum (Sabbath boundary), implying that in the public domain, even within the techum, one is obligated. An alternative version applies this to the public domain, stating that the obligation applies only if the animal is outside the techum.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak qualifies the Mishnah's exemption for a stable: it applies only if the animal is within the techum (Sabbath boundary), implying that in the public domain, even within the techum, one is obligated.

sub.text: Alternative version of Rabbi Yitzchak's statement
sub.text_en: Alternative version of Rabbi Yitzchak's statement
sub.desc_en: An alternative version applies Rabbi Yitzchak's qualification to the public domain: the obligation applies only if the animal is outside the techum, implying that in a stable, even outside the techum, one is exempt.

items.text: Gemara: Source for not obeying a father who says to become impure or not return an animal
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for not obeying a father who says to become impure or not return an animal
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'I am the Lord' that one must not obey a father if it conflicts with God's commandments. It explains that without the verse, one might think the positive commandment of honoring parents overrides the negative and positive commandments of returning a lost animal, so the verse teaches otherwise.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verse 'איש אמו ואביו תיראו ואת שבתותי תשמרו אני ה (a person shall fear his mother and father and keep My Sabbaths; I am the Lord)' to derive that one must not obey a father who commands to become impure or not return a lost animal, because all are obligated in God's honor.

The Gemara questions why the verse is needed: without it, one might think the positive commandment of honoring parents overrides the negative and positive commandments of returning a lost animal, but a positive commandment cannot override a negative and positive commandment.

The Gemara resolves that the verse is necessary because one might have thought that honoring parents is equated to honoring God through a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) from the word 'כבוד (honor)', so the verse teaches that one must not obey the father.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute between the Sages and Rabbi Shimon on unloading and loading for free or for pay
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute between the Sages and Rabbi Shimon on unloading and loading for free or for pay
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah's statement 'a mitzvah to unload but not to load' means unloading is free, loading is for pay. It explains the Sages' reasoning: if loading were free, the Torah would have written only about loading, and unloading would be inferred a fortiori. Rabbi Shimon argues that the verses do not conclude the matter, and the Gemara discusses the interpretation of the verses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means by 'but not to load' — if it means no loading at all, why is loading different from unloading, since both have biblical verses?
The Gemara clarifies: unloading is a mitzvah to be done for free, but loading is only for pay; it cites the baraita where the Sages and Rabbi Shimon dispute this.

The Sages reason: if loading were free, the Torah would have written only about loading, and unloading would be inferred a fortiori; thus the verse for unloading teaches it is free, while loading is for pay.
Rabbi Shimon argues that the verses do not conclude the matter (i.e., the verses are not decisive).

The Gemara objects: why do the Sages not agree that the verses are inconclusive? It explains that the Sages interpret the verses differently — one verse implies the animal is lying under its load, the other implies the men and their loads are fallen on the road.

items.text: Gemara: Rava's statement (unfinished)
items.text_en: Gemara: Rava's statement (unfinished)
items.desc_en: The daf ends with Rava beginning a statement, which is cut off, likely continuing the discussion on the previous topic.

sub.desc_en: Rava begins a statement that is cut off at the end of the daf, likely continuing the discussion on the previous topic.

items.text: Initial proof that צער בעלי חיים is Torah law
items.text_en: Initial proof that צער בעלי חיים is Torah law
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that from the words of both Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon, we learn that צער בעלי חיים is Torah law. Even Rabbi Shimon only disagreed because the verses are not complete, but if they were complete, we would derive a kal vachomer—and why? Because of צער בעלי חיים. The Gemara then suggests an alternative: perhaps it is due to financial loss.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara argues that from the positions of both Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon, we learn that צער בעלי חיים (animal suffering) is a Torah law, as even Rabbi Shimon would derive a kal vachomer if the verses were complete, presumably due to animal suffering.
The Gemara suggests an alternative: perhaps the kal vachomer is not due to animal suffering but because of financial loss (חסרון כיס), as loading has no financial loss while unloading does.

items.text: Challenge to the financial loss explanation
items.text_en: Challenge to the financial loss explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the idea that loading has no financial loss, noting that during the delay the animal's owner loses market time or risks theft.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that loading does involve financial loss, because the owner loses market time or risks theft during the delay.

items.text: Second proof from the Mishnah's end
items.text_en: Second proof from the Mishnah's end
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove that צער בעלי חיים is Torah law from the Mishnah's end, where Rabbi Yose HaGelili limits the obligation to a load the animal can bear, implying the first Tanna requires unloading even an excessive load—presumably due to צער בעלי חיים. The Gemara deflects: perhaps they dispute the interpretation of 'under its load.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove that צער בעלי חיים (animal suffering) is a Torah law from the end of the Mishnah, where Rabbi Yose HaGelili limits the obligation to a load the animal can bear, implying the first Tanna requires unloading even an excessive load due to animal suffering.
The Gemara deflects: perhaps the dispute is about the interpretation of the verse 'תחת משאו' (under its load), not about animal suffering.

items.text: Counterproof from the Mishnah's beginning
items.text_en: Counterproof from the Mishnah's beginning
