items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a counterproof: the Mishnah's beginning says if the owner sits and says 'since the mitzvah is upon you, unload,' the passerby is exempt, implying that when the owner is absent the obligation is stronger. If צער בעלי חיים were Torah law, why would the owner's presence matter?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if צער בעלי חיים (animal suffering) were a Torah law, the owner's presence should not affect the obligation, yet the Mishnah's beginning exempts the passerby when the owner sits and says 'since the mitzvah is upon you, unload.'

items.text: Resolution: exemption is only from free service
items.text_en: Resolution: exemption is only from free service
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves: the exemption is only from free service, but the passerby is still obligated for pay. Thus, the Torah says: when the owner is present, do it for free; when absent, do it for pay. So צער בעלי חיים remains Torah law.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that צער בעלי חיים (animal suffering) is indeed Torah law, and the exemption in the Mishnah applies only to free service, not to paid service.

items.text: Siman for the following sugyot
items.text_en: Siman for the following sugyot
items.desc_en: A mnemonic sign listing the topics: בהמת, בהמת, אוהב, שונא, רבצן.

sub.desc_en: The gemara provides a mnemonic sign (סימן) listing the topics of the following sugyot: בהמת, בהמת, אוהב, שונא, רבצן.

items.text: Proof from a gentile's animal
items.text_en: Proof from a gentile's animal
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove that צער בעלי חיים is Torah law from the rule that one must tend to a gentile's animal like a Jew's. If it were not Torah law, why would one tend to it? The Gemara deflects: it is due to enmity. A supporting proof is brought from the case of wine used for idolatry, where one is not obligated to load it, implying the obligation is not Torah law.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove that צער בעלי חיים (animal suffering) is Torah law from the rule that one must tend to a gentile's animal like a Jew's, arguing that if it were not Torah law, there would be no reason to tend to it.
The Gemara deflects that the obligation to tend to a gentile's animal is due to enmity (איבה), not because of a Torah law regarding animal suffering.
A supporting baraita is cited: if the animal is loaded with wine used for idolatry (יין נסך), one is not obligated to tend to it, implying that the obligation is not Torah law.

The Gemara resolves that the baraita means one is not obligated to load the animal with wine used for idolatry, but the obligation to unload still applies, preserving the possibility that the obligation is Torah law.

items.text: Proof from the verses 'וחדלת' and 'עזב תעזב'
items.text_en: Proof from the verses 'וחדלת' and 'עזב תעזב'
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita: for a gentile's animal with a Jew's load, the verse says 'וחדלת' (you shall refrain), but if צער בעלי חיים were Torah law, it should say 'עזב תעזב' (you shall surely unload). The Gemara answers that this refers to loading, not unloading. The Gemara then challenges that the same verses are written about unloading. Rav answers that the baraita follows Rabbi Yose HaGelili, who holds that צער בעלי חיים is not Torah law.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita: for a gentile's animal with a Jew's load, the verse says 'וחדלת' (you shall refrain), but if צער בעלי חיים (animal suffering) were Torah law, it should say 'עזב תעזב' (you shall surely unload).
The Gemara answers that the baraita refers to loading, not unloading, so the verse 'וחדלת' is appropriate.
The Gemara objects: the same verses are written about unloading, so the answer is inconsistent.
The Gemara answers that the first case involves a gentile donkey driver and the second a Jewish donkey driver, so the distinction is based on who accompanies the animal.
The Gemara objects that both verses 'וחדלת' and 'עזב תעזב' are written about unloading, not loading.
Rav answers that the baraita follows Rabbi Yose HaGelili, who holds that צער בעלי חיים (animal suffering) is not Torah law.

items.text: Proof from the preference for a friend to unload and an enemy to load
items.text_en: Proof from the preference for a friend to unload and an enemy to load
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a Mishnah: if a friend needs to unload and an enemy needs to load, the mitzvah is with the enemy to subdue his evil inclination. If צער בעלי חיים were Torah law, wouldn't unloading (which relieves pain) be more important? The Gemara answers: even so, subduing the evil inclination takes precedence.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah: if a friend needs to unload and an enemy needs to load, the mitzvah is with the enemy to subdue his evil inclination. If צער בעלי חיים (animal suffering) were Torah law, wouldn't unloading (which relieves pain) be more important?
The Gemara answers: even so, subduing the evil inclination takes precedence over relieving animal suffering.

items.text: Proof from the definition of 'enemy'
items.text_en: Proof from the definition of 'enemy'
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita: the 'enemy' mentioned is a Jewish enemy, not a gentile enemy. If צער בעלי חיים were Torah law, why would it matter whether the enemy is Jewish or gentile? The Gemara answers: the baraita refers to the enemy in the Mishnah, not the verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita that the 'enemy' mentioned is a Jewish enemy, not a gentile one, and argues: if צער בעלי חיים (animal suffering) were Torah law, why would the enemy's identity matter?
The Gemara answers: the baraita refers to the enemy in the Mishnah, not the verse, so it does not challenge the Torah status of animal suffering.

items.text: Introduction of a new proof
items.text_en: Introduction of a new proof
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces another attempt to prove the matter, beginning with 'תא שמע'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a new attempt to prove the matter by saying 'תא שמע' (come and hear).

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's exclusions regarding the lost animal
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's exclusions regarding the lost animal
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah specifies 'lying down' and not 'sitting' or 'standing', and suggests that this supports the view that the prohibition of causing pain to animals is rabbinic. It then identifies the Mishnah as following Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, who holds that view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah specifies 'רֹבֵץ' (lying down) and excludes 'רַבְצָן' (a habitual lier) and 'עוֹמֵד' (standing), arguing that if the prohibition of causing pain to animals were biblical, all cases should be included.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, who holds that the prohibition of causing pain to animals is rabbinic (דְּרַבָּנַן), not biblical.
The Gemara provides supporting evidence that the Mishnah is Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's, because only he holds the view that the animal's load must be one it can stand under.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding the Mishnah's attribution
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding the Mishnah's attribution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's later clause about 'not unloaded' seems to follow the Rabbis, not Rabbi Yosei HaGelili. It resolves that the Mishnah is indeed Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, but he agrees with the Rabbis regarding the matter of loading.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's ruling about 'not unloaded' (לֹא מְפוֹרָק) follows the Rabbis, not Rabbi Yosei HaGelili.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah is indeed Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, but he agrees with the Rabbis regarding the matter of loading (טעינה).

items.text: Baraita on the distance for the mitzvah of unloading and Rabba bar bar Chana's addition
items.text_en: Baraita on the distance for the mitzvah of unloading and Rabba bar bar Chana's addition
items.desc_en: A baraita derives from the verses that the obligation to help with a fallen animal applies only within a certain distance, which the Sages set at one-seventh and a half of a mil (a ris). A Tanna adds that one walks with the animal up to a parasang, and Rabba bar bar Chana says one receives payment for this.

sub.desc_en: The baraita derives from the verses that the obligation to help with a fallen animal applies only within a specific distance, which the Sages set at one-seventh and a half of a mil (a ris).
A Tanna adds that one walks with the animal up to a parasang.
Rabba bar bar Chana adds that one receives payment for walking with the animal.

items.text: Mishnah: Priority of returning lost objects and redeeming captives
items.text_en: Mishnah: Priority of returning lost objects and redeeming captives
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that one's own lost object takes precedence over that of one's father or teacher. The lost object of one's teacher takes precedence over that of one's father, unless the father is a scholar. Similar rules apply when both are carrying a load or are in captivity.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one's own lost object takes precedence over that of one's father or teacher.
The Mishnah rules that the lost object of one's teacher takes precedence over that of one's father, unless the father is a scholar.
The Mishnah extends the priority rule to cases of carrying a load or captivity, with the teacher taking precedence unless the father is a scholar.

items.text: Gemara's source for the priority of one's own lost object
items.text_en: Gemara's source for the priority of one's own lost object
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav derives from the verse 'אֶפֶס כִּי לֹא יִהְיֶה בְּךָ אֶבְיוֹן' that one's own needs take precedence over others'. He adds that one who consistently prioritizes himself will eventually come to poverty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where are these matters (the priority of one's own lost object) derived?

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav cites the verse 'אֶפֶס כִּי לֹא יִהְיֶה בְּךָ אֶבְיוֹן' (only if there will be no poor among you) to teach that your own needs take precedence over everyone else's.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav adds a warning: one who consistently prioritizes himself will eventually come to poverty.

items.text: Baraita defining 'teacher' and related discussions
items.text_en: Baraita defining 'teacher' and related discussions
items.desc_en: A baraita presents three opinions on who is considered a teacher for the purpose of precedence over one's father: Rabbi Meir says one who taught him wisdom (Talmud), Rabbi Yehuda says one from whom he learned most of his wisdom, and Rabbi Yosei says even one who illuminated his eyes in a single Mishnah. Rava and Shmuel give examples, and Ulla adds that Babylonian sages honor each other but for lost objects, only a primary teacher (רב מובהק) takes precedence over the father.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by defining 'teacher' as one who taught wisdom, not just Scripture or Mishnah, with three opinions: Rabbi Meir (wisdom), Rabbi Yehuda (most of his wisdom), Rabbi Yosei (even one Mishnah).
Rava and Shmuel give concrete examples of teachers who illuminated their eyes in a single teaching, illustrating Rabbi Yosei's definition.
Ulla rules that Babylonian sages honor each other, but for lost objects in the presence of the father, only a primary teacher (רב מובהק) takes precedence.

items.text: Story of Rav Chisda and Rav Huna regarding a student who needs his teacher
items.text_en: Story of Rav Chisda and Rav Huna regarding a student who needs his teacher
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda asked Rav Huna about a student who needs his teacher. Rav Huna responded dismissively, leading to a rift where each fasted forty fasts due to the slight and suspicion.

sub.text: Rav Chisda's question to Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda's question to Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda asks Rav Huna about the status of a student who still needs his teacher.
Rav Huna dismisses Rav Chisda, saying he does not need Rav Chisda but Rav Chisda needs him for forty years.
Both became offended and avoided each other, each fasting forty fasts — Rav Chisda for slighting Rav Huna's dignity, and Rav Huna for suspecting Rav Chisda.

items.text: Ruling on the halakha regarding the definition of a teacher
items.text_en: Ruling on the halakha regarding the definition of a teacher
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rav Sheshet rule on the dispute: Rabbi Yochanan holds like Rabbi Yehuda, but the Gemara questions this because Rabbi Yochanan generally rules like a stam Mishnah, which defines a teacher as one who taught him wisdom, which is interpreted as most of his wisdom.

sub.text: Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yehuda's definition of a teacher.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Huna citing Rav Sheshet
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Huna citing Rav Sheshet
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Huna reports in the name of Rav Sheshet that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yosei's definition of a teacher.

The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yochanan could really rule like Rabbi Yehuda, given that Rabbi Yochanan generally rules like a stam Mishnah, and the stam Mishnah defines a teacher as one who taught him wisdom.
The Gemara resolves the difficulty by interpreting the Mishnah's term 'חׇכְמָה (wisdom)' to mean 'רוֹב חׇכְמָתוֹ (most of his wisdom)', thereby aligning the stam Mishnah with Rabbi Yehuda's position.

items.text: Baraita on the value of studying Scripture, Mishnah, and Talmud
items.text_en: Baraita on the value of studying Scripture, Mishnah, and Talmud
items.desc_en: A baraita states that studying Scripture is a minor virtue, Mishnah is a virtue with reward, and Talmud is the greatest. It then paradoxically says to always run to Mishnah more than Talmud. The Gemara notes the contradiction and begins to resolve it with Rabbi Yochanan's statement.

sub.desc_en: A baraita ranks the study of Scripture, Mishnah, and Talmud, declaring Talmud the greatest.
The same baraita paradoxically instructs one to always run to Mishnah more than Talmud.
The Gemara points out the internal contradiction in the baraita: it first says Talmud is the greatest, then says to run to Mishnah more.
Rabbi Yochanan begins to resolve the contradiction, though his full statement is cut off at the section boundary.

items.text: Story of Rabbi's ruling on Mishnah vs. Talmud and related homilies
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi's ruling on Mishnah vs. Talmud and related homilies
items.desc_en: The section recounts that in Rabbi's days, everyone abandoned Mishnah for Talmud, so Rabbi taught to always run to Mishnah more than Talmud. It then cites Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai's homilies on verses about scholars and ignoramuses, and concludes with the return to the chapter.

sub.desc_en: The gemara recounts that in Rabbi's days, everyone abandoned Mishnah for Talmud, so Rabbi taught to always run to Mishnah more than Talmud.
The gemara asks what homily Rabbi taught to support his ruling.

The gemara cites Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai's homily on the verse 'הַגֵּד לְעַמִּי פִּשְׁעָם' (declare to my people their transgression), interpreting it as referring to Torah scholars whose unintentional sins are considered intentional, and the Mishnah of Rabbi Yehuda about being careful with Talmud.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai's second homily
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai's second homily
sub.desc_en: The gemara cites another homily by Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai on the verse 'שִׁמְעוּ דְּבַר ה׳ הַחֲרֵדִים אֶל דְּבָרוֹ' (hear the word of the Lord, you who tremble at His word), identifying four groups and concluding that Israel will rejoice while the nations are ashamed.

items.text: Return to the chapter
items.text_en: Return to the chapter
items.desc_en: A brief statement marking the return to the chapter 'These are the found items'.

sub.desc_en: The gemara marks the return to the chapter 'These are the found items'.

items.text: Mishnah: Bailee who paid and thief found
items.text_en: Mishnah: Bailee who paid and thief found
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where a bailee paid for lost or stolen items without swearing, and later the thief is found. If the bailee paid, the thief pays double or four/five to the bailee; if the bailee swore and didn't pay, the thief pays to the owner.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of a bailee who paid compensation without swearing, and the thief is caught — the thief pays double payment to the bailee; if the bailee swore and refused to pay, the thief pays double to the owner.
The Mishnah rules that if the thief is found, he pays double or four/five to the bailee who holds the deposit.
The Mishnah presents the alternative case: if the bailee swore and did not pay, the thief pays the penalties to the original owner.

items.text: Gemara: Why both 'animal' and 'vessels'?
items.text_en: Gemara: Why both 'animal' and 'vessels'?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah mentions both 'animal' and 'vessels', and explains that each is necessary: for animal, one might think the bailee acquires the double because of its high maintenance, but for vessels not; for vessels, one might think the bailee acquires the double because their double is small, but for animal with four/five payment, not.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks why the Mishnah mentions both 'animal' and 'vessels'.

The gemara explains that both are necessary: if only 'animal' were taught, one might think the bailee acquires the double payment only because of the animal's greater effort, but not for vessels; if only 'vessels' were taught, one might think the bailee acquires the double payment only because the double payment is small, but not for an animal where the penalty can be four or five times the value.
The Gemara explains that for vessels, one might think the bailee acquires the double because their double is small, but for animal with four/five payment, not.

items.text: Rami bar Hama's objection: acquiring something not yet in the world
items.text_en: Rami bar Hama's objection: acquiring something not yet in the world
items.desc_en: Rami bar Hama objects that one cannot acquire something not yet in the world, and even according to Rabbi Meir who allows it, that applies only to things that will certainly come, like dates of a palm tree, but not here.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama objects that a person cannot transfer ownership of something that has not yet come into the world, and even according to Rabbi Meir who allows it, that applies only to future produce of a palm tree that will certainly come.
Rami bar Chama argues that here, the double payment is not certain to come, so the bailee cannot acquire it.

items.text: Rava and Rabbi Zeira on the transfer of ownership upon declaration
items.text_en: Rava and Rabbi Zeira on the transfer of ownership upon declaration
items.desc_en: Rava suggests that when a bailee says 'when it is stolen and you wish to pay me, my cow is yours from now,' it transfers ownership. Rabbi Zeira objects that this would include shearings and offspring, which the Mishnah excludes, so he amends: the transfer excludes shearings and offspring. The Gemara explains the rationale: one would transfer external appreciation but not intrinsic appreciation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the feasibility of a bailee's conditional transfer, noting the uncertainty of theft, discovery of the thief, and the bailee's payment.
Rava proposes that the bailee's statement is treated as if he said, 'When it is stolen and you wish to pay me, my cow is yours from now,' effecting a retroactive transfer.
Rabbi Zeira objects that Rava's proposal would include shearings and offspring, which the Mishnah explicitly excludes, so he amends the statement to exclude them.
The Gemara explains the rationale: one would transfer external appreciation (שבחא דאתי מעלמא) but not intrinsic appreciation (שבחא דמגופה).

items.text: Alternative version of Rava's statement and the difference between versions
items.text_en: Alternative version of Rava's statement and the difference between versions
items.desc_en: An alternative version has Rava saying the transfer occurs 'close to its theft.' The difference between the two versions lies in Rabbi Zeira's objection and the case where the animal is in a marsh.

sub.desc_en: Presents an alternative version of Rava's statement, where the transfer occurs 'close to its theft' (סמוך לגניבתה).
Asks what practical difference exists between the two versions of Rava's statement.
Answers that the difference lies in Rabbi Zeira's objection and the case where the animal is standing in a marsh (אגם).

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's interpretation of 'shileim' in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's interpretation of 'shileim' in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that 'shileim' in the Mishnah does not mean actual payment but merely saying 'I will pay.' The Gemara questions this from the Mishnah's wording, but concludes that no proof can be derived from it.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan interprets 'שִׁילֵּם' in the Mishnah not as actual payment but as merely saying 'I will pay.'
The Gemara objects from the Mishnah's wording 'שִׁילֵּם' that it implies actual payment, not mere speech.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's wording is inconclusive, as the parallel clause 'נִשְׁבַּע' shows that 'שִׁילֵּם' may not be literal.

items.text: Supporting baraita for Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Supporting baraita for Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: A baraita supports Rabbi Yochanan: a renter who says 'I will pay and not swear' and then the thief is found, the renter receives the double payment.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Rabbi Yochanan's position: a renter who says 'I will pay and not swear' and then the thief is found, the renter receives the double payment.

items.text: Rav Pappa's distinction between different types of bailees
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's distinction between different types of bailees
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa rules that an unpaid bailee who admits negligence transfers the double payment, as he could have exempted himself by claiming theft. A paid bailee who says 'it was stolen' transfers it, as he could have exempted himself by claiming breakage or death. A borrower who says 'I will pay' does not transfer it, as he has no common exemption (death due to work is uncommon).

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa rules that an unpaid bailee who admits negligence transfers the double payment, as he could have exempted himself by claiming theft; a paid bailee who says 'it was stolen' transfers it, as he could have exempted himself by claiming breakage or death.
Rav Pappa adds that a borrower who says 'I will pay' does not transfer the double payment, since death due to work is uncommon and thus not a standard exemption.

items.text: Alternative version: Rav Pappa includes the borrower, and Rav Zevid's objection
items.text_en: Alternative version: Rav Pappa includes the borrower, and Rav Zevid's objection
items.desc_en: An alternative version has Rav Pappa including the borrower, since he could exempt himself by claiming death due to work. Rav Zevid cites Abaye that a borrower only transfers ownership upon actual payment, because all benefit is his and mere speech does not transfer the double payment.

sub.desc_en: The alternative version introduces Rav Pappa's statement that the borrower also transfers the double payment upon saying 'I will pay', because he could exempt himself by claiming death due to work.
Rav Zevid objects by citing Abaye that a borrower only transfers ownership of the double payment upon actual payment, not by mere speech, because all benefit is his.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rav Zevid and resolution of the contradiction
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rav Zevid and resolution of the contradiction
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a borrower who paid first receives the double payment, supporting Rav Zevid. The Gemara questions whether this refutes the first version of Rav Pappa. Rav Pappa responds that the baraita can be interpreted as 'he said first,' similar to the Mishnah. The Gemara questions the precise wording, but a query to the Tannaim of Rabbi Chiya and Rabbi Oshaya reveals that the cases were taught together, resolving the issue.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rav Zevid's position: a borrower who paid first receives the double payment.
The Gemara asks whether this baraita constitutes a refutation of the second version of Rav Pappa's statement.
Rav Pappa responds that the baraita is no stronger than the Mishnah, which uses the term 'שילם' (paid) and was interpreted as 'he said,' so here too it can be interpreted as 'he said.'
The Gemara objects that the cases are not comparable: the Mishnah does not use the term 'קידם' (preceded), while the baraita does, so it might mean actual payment.
The Gemara questions whether the baraita's different wording for borrower ('קידם') versus renter ('אמר') indicates a precise distinction, and asks if the cases were taught together.
The Gemara resolves the issue by querying the Tannaim of Rabbi Chiya and Rabbi Oshaya, who confirm that the cases were taught together, so the wording is not precise.

items.text: Clarification: retracting a refusal to pay
items.text_en: Clarification: retracting a refusal to pay
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that if one first said 'I will not pay' and then said 'I will pay,' it is considered as saying 'I will pay.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the obvious: if one first said 'I will not pay' and then said 'I will pay,' it is considered as saying 'I will pay,' so the question is elsewhere.

items.text: Series of unresolved questions (תיקו) about retraction and partial payment
items.text_en: Series of unresolved questions (תיקו) about retraction and partial payment
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises multiple scenarios where a borrower or his heirs retract a promise to pay for a lost deposit, or where payment is made to or by heirs, or where only partial payment is made. Each case is left unresolved with תיקו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a borrower who retracts his promise to pay for a lost deposit is considered to have fully withdrawn or merely stalling.
The Gemara asks whether heirs who retract their father's promise to pay are considered to have withdrawn or are merely stalling.
The Gemara asks whether heirs who actually pay can be told that the double payment was only promised for the father's peace of mind, not theirs.
The Gemara asks whether payment made to heirs is valid, and whether heirs paying other heirs is valid.
The Gemara raises multiple unresolved questions about partial payment, borrowing from partners, and women borrowing, all left as תיקו.

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling: the borrower must take an oath that the deposit is not in his possession
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling: the borrower must take an oath that the deposit is not in his possession
items.desc_en: Rav Huna states that a borrower who claims the deposited item was lost must take an oath that it is not in his possession, because we suspect he may have cast his eye on it (i.e., intends to keep it).

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that the borrower must take an oath that the deposit is not in his possession.
The Gemara explains the reason: we suspect the borrower cast his eye on the deposit (i.e., intends to keep it).

items.text: Objection from a baraita about conflicting claims over a pledge
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita about conflicting claims over a pledge
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita detailing cases where a lender and borrower dispute the value of a lost pledge. The baraita concludes that the oath is administered to the one in whose possession the deposit is (the borrower). The Gemara questions which case this refers to, and Shmuel explains it applies to the latter part of the first case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a lender and borrower disputing the value of a lost pledge, presenting the first case where the borrower is exempt.
The baraita presents the second case where the borrower is liable.
The baraita presents the third case where the borrower is exempt.
The baraita presents the fourth case where the borrower is liable.
The baraita rules that the oath is administered to the one in whose possession the deposit is (the borrower), with the rationale that otherwise the lender might swear and then produce the pledge.
The Gemara questions which case of the baraita this ruling refers to, rejecting the possibility that it applies to the latter cases because there the lender admits part of the claim.
Shmuel explains that the baraita's ruling applies to the first part of the first case (the second clause of the first case).

items.text: Shmuel's clarification: the oath is imposed on the lender in the latter part of the first case
items.text_en: Shmuel's clarification: the oath is imposed on the lender in the latter part of the first case
items.desc_en: Shmuel specifies that the baraita's ruling about the oath being taken by the one holding the deposit refers to the latter part of the first case, where the borrower admits partial liability. The rabbis instituted that the lender should swear, lest the borrower swear and then the lender produce the deposit.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel specifies that the baraita's question 'on which part?' refers to the latter part of the first case, where the lender claims a sela loan and the borrower admits the collateral was worth a shekel.

Shmuel explains that although the oath would normally be taken by the borrower (who admits partial liability), the rabbis instituted that the lender swear instead, lest the borrower swear and then the lender produce the deposit.

items.text: Incomplete segment (continuation cut off)
items.text_en: Incomplete segment (continuation cut off)
items.desc_en: The text breaks off mid-sentence with 'וְאִם', indicating the daf continues to the next page.

sub.desc_en: The text breaks off mid-sentence with 'וְאִם' (and if), indicating the daf continues to the next page.

items.text: Gemara's question on Rav Huna's statement
items.text_en: Gemara's question on Rav Huna's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rav Huna's ruling that the borrower swears the collateral is not in his possession, asking how he can then produce it. Rava suggests there are witnesses it was burned, Rav Yosef suggests witnesses it was stolen, and the Gemara objects that the borrower could also produce it. The Gemara resolves that the borrower knows who enters his house, unlike the lender.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rav Huna's ruling: if the borrower swears the collateral is not in his possession, how can he later produce it?
Rava answers that the borrower can produce it if there are witnesses it was burned.
The Gemara objects: if there are witnesses it was burned, from where can the borrower produce it?
Rav Yosef answers that the borrower can produce it if there are witnesses it was stolen.
The Gemara objects again: ultimately, from where can he produce it? The answer is that he can trouble himself and bring it.
The Gemara objects: if so, when the lender swears, let the borrower also trouble himself and bring it.
The Gemara resolves: the lender knows who enters his house, but the borrower does not know who enters the lender's house.

items.text: Abaye and Rav Ashi's explanations
items.text_en: Abaye and Rav Ashi's explanations
items.desc_en: Abaye explains the oath is a decree lest the borrower claim he found the collateral after the oath. Rav Ashi explains that both swear: the borrower that it is not in his possession, and the lender as to its value, and the lender swears first lest the borrower swear and then produce the deposit.

sub.desc_en: Abaye explains that the oath is a decree (גזירה) lest the borrower claim he found the deposit after swearing.

Rav Ashi explains that both swear: the borrower that the deposit is not in his possession, and the lender as to its value, and the lender swears first lest the borrower swear and then produce the deposit.

items.text: Rav Huna bar Tachlifa's challenge to Rav Huna
items.text_en: Rav Huna bar Tachlifa's challenge to Rav Huna
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Tachlifa in the name of Rava challenges Rav Huna from a mishna: if the borrower says 'You lent me a sela on it, it was worth two' and the lender says 'I lent you a sela on it, it was worth a sela', the borrower is exempt. If Rav Huna were correct, the lender should swear by extension about its value.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Tachlifa in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Tachlifa in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Tachlifa challenges Rav Huna from a mishna: if the borrower says 'You lent me a sela on it, it was worth two' and the lender says 'I lent you a sela on it, it was worth a sela', the borrower is exempt; if Rav Huna were correct, the lender should swear by extension about its value.

items.text: Rav Ashi's resolution and the principle of trust
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's resolution and the principle of trust
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi reports that Rav Kahana said the borrower trusts the lender regarding the value, but the lender does not trust the borrower. The Gemara explains that the borrower trusts the lender because of the verse 'The integrity of the upright guides them', while the lender does not trust the borrower because of 'the perverseness of the treacherous destroys them'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi reports that he presented the teaching before Rav Kahana, who said the borrower trusts the lender regarding the value.
The Gemara asks why the borrower should not also trust the lender regarding the value.
The Gemara answers that the borrower does not have intimate knowledge of the lender's property to know its value.
The Gemara asks why the lender should not trust the borrower, who does have intimate knowledge of the value.
The Gemara answers that the lender does not trust the borrower.
The Gemara asks what distinguishes the borrower who trusts the lender from the lender who does not trust the borrower.

The Gemara resolves that the borrower trusts the lender due to the verse 'The integrity of the upright guides them', while the lender does not trust the borrower due to 'the perverseness of the treacherous destroys them'.

items.text: Story of the cloak and Rav Nachman's ruling
items.text_en: Story of the cloak and Rav Nachman's ruling
items.desc_en: A man deposited cloaks with a friend who claimed not to know where he put them. Rav Nachman ruled this is negligence and ordered payment. When the man didn't pay, Rav Nachman seized his estate. Later the cloaks were found and appreciated. Rav Nachman returned the cloaks to their owner and the estate to its owner. Rava questioned this, and Rav Nachman explained that in the first case the borrower didn't trouble the court, but here he did.

sub.desc_en: A man deposited cloaks with a friend, and when he asked for them back, the friend claimed not to know where he put them.
Rav Nachman ruled that not knowing where the deposit was placed is negligence and ordered the bailee to pay.
When the bailee did not pay, Rav Nachman seized his estate; later the cloaks were found and appreciated, and Rav Nachman returned both the cloaks and the estate to their original owners.
Rava questioned Rav Nachman's ruling, noting that in a previous case where the bailee paid but did not want to swear, Rav Nachman did not return the property.
Rav Nachman explained that in the earlier case the bailee did not trouble the court, but here the bailee troubled the court, justifying the different outcome.

items.text: Discussion on whether a court seizure can be reversed
items.text_en: Discussion on whether a court seizure can be reversed
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rav Nachman holds that a court seizure can be reversed, and answers that this case is different because the seizure was based on an error (the cloaks existed from the start). The Nehardeans say a seizure can be reversed within twelve months, while Amemar says it can be reversed forever, and the halakha follows that it can be reversed forever due to the verse 'do what is right and good'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rav Nachman's ruling implies that a court seizure (שומא) can be reversed.
The Gemara answers that this case is different because the seizure was based on an error, as the cloaks existed from the start.
The Nehardeans state that a court seizure can be reversed within twelve months.
Amemar says that a court seizure can be reversed forever.
The halakha is that a court seizure can be reversed forever, based on the verse 'do what is right and good'.

items.text: Cases where seizure is not reversed
items.text_en: Cases where seizure is not reversed
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses cases where a seizure is not reversed: if the creditor seized and then his own creditor seized from him, we say you are no better than the one you came from; if the debtor sold, inherited, or gave the property as a gift, the buyer acquired it with the intention of land, not money. Also, if a woman's property was seized and she married, or if property was seized from a woman and she married and died, the husband is a buyer and does not return it, based on a takanah from Usha.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states obvious cases where seizure is not reversed: if the creditor seized and his own creditor seized from him, we say you are no better than the one you came from; if the debtor sold, inherited, or gave the property as a gift, the buyer acquired it with the intention of land, not money.
The Gemara adds another case: if a woman's property was seized and she married, or if property was seized from a woman and she married and died, the husband is a buyer and does not return it.
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina cites a takanah from Usha: a woman who sold her melog property during her husband's lifetime and died, the husband takes it from the buyers.

items.text: Dispute over the validity of the sale
items.text_en: Dispute over the validity of the sale
items.desc_en: Rav Acha and Ravina argue whether a debtor who voluntarily sells his land to pay a debt can later reclaim it. One holds it is a valid sale and cannot be reclaimed; the other holds it is not a valid sale because the debtor acted out of embarrassment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the case of a debtor who voluntarily sells his land to pay a debt, and introduces the dispute between Rav Acha and Ravina over whether the sale can be reclaimed.
The one who says the sale cannot be reclaimed (Rav Acha) holds it is a valid sale because the debtor acted willingly.
The one who says the sale can be reclaimed (Ravina) holds it is not a valid sale because the debtor acted out of embarrassment.

items.text: When does the buyer acquire the produce?
items.text_en: When does the buyer acquire the produce?
items.desc_en: Rabbah, Abaye, and Rava debate the point from which the buyer of the land may consume its produce. Rabbah says from when the deed reaches his hand; Abaye says from the date of the deed; Rava says from the end of the proclamation period.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From what point does the buyer of land become entitled to consume its produce?
Rabbah rules: the buyer may eat produce only from when the deed (adrakhta) reaches his hand.
Abaye holds that the buyer acquires the produce immediately from the date of the deed, because the witnesses' signatures effect acquisition.
Rava rules: the buyer may eat produce only after the proclamation period for the land sale is completed.

items.text: Mishnah: Renting and borrowing an animal
items.text_en: Mishnah: Renting and borrowing an animal
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where one rents a cow and then lends it to another, and it dies naturally. The renter swears it died naturally, and the borrower pays the renter. Rabbi Yosei objects, saying the cow should go back to the owner.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where one rents a cow and then lends it to another, and it dies naturally. The renter swears it died naturally, and the borrower pays the renter. Rabbi Yosei objects, saying the cow should go back to the owner.

items.text: Gemara: The renter's acquisition and the oath
items.text_en: Gemara: The renter's acquisition and the oath
items.desc_en: Rav Idi bar Avin asks Abaye: How does the renter acquire the cow? Through the oath. Could the owner bypass the renter and sue the borrower directly? Abaye responds that the renter acquires the cow from the moment of death, and the oath is only to appease the owner.

sub.desc_en: Rav Idi bar Avin asks Abaye: Since the renter acquires the cow only through the oath, why can't the owner bypass the renter and sue the borrower directly?
Abaye responds: the renter acquires the cow at the moment of death, not through the oath; the oath is only to appease the owner.
The Gemara elaborates the objection: the owner could tell the renter 'forget your oath and I will sue the borrower directly'.
Abaye responds: the renter acquires the cow from the moment of death, not through the oath; the oath is merely to appease the owner.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira: Multiple payments for multiple loans
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira: Multiple payments for multiple loans
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira states that sometimes the owner must pay the renter multiple cows, e.g., if the renter repeatedly rents and borrows the same cow, and it dies during a loan period, the borrower must pay a cow for each loan period.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira observes that the owners might have to pay multiple cows to the renter if the same cow was repeatedly rented and lent, and dies during one of the loan periods.

items.text: Objection and resolution: How many cows?
items.text_en: Objection and resolution: How many cows?
items.desc_en: Rav Acha from Difti objects to Ravina: Since it is the same cow, how can multiple payments be required? Ravina responds that the cow is not present to argue. Mar bar Rav Ashi rules that only two cows are paid: one for the loan and one for the rental, because each type of bailment has a single status.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha from Difti objects to Ravina: since it is the same cow repeatedly moved between rental and borrowing, how can multiple payments be required?
Ravina responds that the cow is not present to argue, so the objection is irrelevant.
Mar bar Rav Ashi rules that only two cows are paid: one for the loan and one for the rental, because each type of bailment has a single status.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya: Both liable for a sin-offering
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya: Both liable for a sin-offering
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya begins a statement that sometimes both parties are liable for a sin-offering, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya adds that sometimes both parties are liable to bring a sin-offering, but the segment is cut off.

items.text: Mishnah: Four cases of false oaths by bailees
items.text_en: Mishnah: Four cases of false oaths by bailees
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents four scenarios where a renter and a borrower swear falsely about the animal's death or theft, classifying each oath as either an asham (for monetary denial) or a hattat (for verbal falsehood). It details the combinations based on the actual event and the claim made.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that there are times when both the renter and the borrower bring an asham (guilt offering) and times when each brings a different offering.
The Mishnah asks 'How so?' and answers that denial of money (כְּפִירַת מָמוֹן) brings an asham, while a verbal falsehood (בִּטּוּי שְׂפָתַיִם) brings a hattat (sin offering).
The Mishnah gives the first example: when the animal died naturally and they claimed it was stolen, both bring a hattat because the renter is exempt anyway and the borrower is liable regardless.

items.text: Gemara: What does the Mishnah teach?
items.text_en: Gemara: What does the Mishnah teach?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what novel point the Mishnah conveys, answering that it rejects Rabbi Ami's view that court-administered oaths are exempt from the law of sh'vuat bitui (oath of utterance). The Mishnah implies that such oaths are indeed subject to that law.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what novel point the Mishnah teaches.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah comes to exclude Rabbi Ami's view, teaching that court-administered oaths are subject to the law of שְׁבוּעַת בִּיטּוּי (oath of utterance).

items.text: Dispute: Bailee who entrusts to another bailee
items.text_en: Dispute: Bailee who entrusts to another bailee
items.desc_en: A dispute is cited: Rav says a bailee who passes the deposit to another bailee is exempt, while Rabbi Yochanan says he is liable. Abaye explains each position: Rav exempts even if the second bailee is less reliable, because the bailee entrusted it to a competent person; Rabbi Yochanan holds liable even if the second bailee is more reliable, because the owner can object to his deposit being in another's hands.

sub.desc_en: The gemara cites a dispute: Rav says a bailee who entrusts the deposit to another bailee is exempt, while Rabbi Yochanan says he is liable.
Abaye explains Rav's reasoning: even if the second bailee is less reliable, the first bailee is exempt because he entrusted it to a competent person (בן דעת).

sub.text: Abaye's explanation of Rabbi Yochanan's position
sub.text_en: Abaye's explanation of Rabbi Yochanan's position
sub.desc_en: Abaye explains Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning: even if the second bailee is more reliable, the first bailee is liable because the owner can object that he does not want his deposit in another's hands.

items.text: Rav's ruling derived from a story
items.text_en: Rav's ruling derived from a story
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda reports that Rav's ruling was not stated explicitly but inferred from a case: gardeners who regularly deposited tools with an old woman, but one day one gardener deposited them with another, who left them with the old woman and they were stolen. Rav exempted the gardener, but not because of the general rule of a bailee entrusting to another; rather, because the owners themselves usually deposited with that old woman.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda reports that Rav's ruling was not stated explicitly but inferred from a case: gardeners deposited tools with an old woman, one gardener deposited with another who left them with the old woman, and the tools were stolen.
Rav Chisda explains that Rav exempted the gardener not because of the general rule of a bailee entrusting to another, but because the owners themselves usually deposited with that old woman.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita about a renter who lends
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita about a renter who lends
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami taught the principle that a bailee is liable for entrusting to another. Rabbi Abba bar Memel challenged him with a baraita: a renter who lent the cow to another and it died naturally—the renter swears and the borrower pays the renter. If the renter could object, why doesn't he? Rabbi Ami answers that the owners gave permission to lend. The Gemara then questions: if so, the borrower should pay the owners directly, but the baraita says he pays the renter; the answer is that the owners said to act according to your own understanding.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ami sits and teaches the principle that a bailee who entrusts to another is liable.
Rabbi Abba bar Memel objects with a baraita: a renter who lent the cow to another and it died naturally—the renter swears and the borrower pays the renter, implying the renter is not liable.
The Gemara asks: if Rabbi Ami is correct, why can't the owner object that he does not want his deposit in another's hands?
Rabbi Ami answers that the case is where the owners gave the renter permission to lend the cow.
The Gemara asks: if so, the borrower should pay the owners directly, not the renter.
The Gemara resolves that the owners told the renter to act according to his own understanding, so the borrower pays the renter.

items.text: Challenge from a mishnah about depositing with minors
items.text_en: Challenge from a mishnah about depositing with minors
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama challenges Rabbi Ami's position from a mishnah: one who deposits money and gives it to his minor children is liable, implying that if given to adults he is exempt. Why? Shouldn't the owner object? Rava answers that any depositor implicitly agrees to the bailee's standard practice, which may include entrusting to adults.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama challenges Rabbi Ami by citing a mishnah: one who deposits money and gives it to his minor children is liable, implying that if given to adults he is exempt.
Rami bar Chama infers that giving to adults would exempt the bailee, and objects: why shouldn't the owner say 'I do not want my deposit in another's hands'?
Rava answers that any depositor implicitly agrees to the bailee's standard practice, which may include entrusting to adults.

items.text: Proof from the Mishnah regarding delegation to family members
items.text_en: Proof from the Mishnah regarding delegation to family members
items.desc_en: The Nehardeans infer from the Mishnah's mention of 'minor sons and daughters' that only delegation to minors renders the bailee liable, while delegation to adults is exempt. By implication, delegation to strangers is always liable, regardless of age, otherwise the Mishnah would have stated 'minors' in general terms.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a bailee deposits on the basis of his wife and children.
The Nehardeans infer from the Mishnah's mention of 'minor sons and daughters' that delegation to adults is exempt, while delegation to strangers is always liable regardless of age.

items.text: Rava's ruling on a bailee who delegates to another bailee
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on a bailee who delegates to another bailee
items.desc_en: Rava rules that a bailee who hands over the deposit to another bailee is liable, even if the second bailee is more stringent. The reason is that the bailee can argue: 'You (the first bailee) are credible to me via oath, but this other bailee is not credible to me via oath.'

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that a bailee who delegates to another bailee is liable, even if the second bailee is more stringent.
The Gemara asks for the reason behind Rava's ruling.
Rava explains that the first bailee is liable because the owner can say: 'You are credible to me via oath, but this other bailee is not credible to me via oath.'

items.text: Dispute between Abaye and Rava on negligence followed by accident
items.text_en: Dispute between Abaye and Rava on negligence followed by accident
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava debate a case where the bailee was negligent (the animal went to a marsh) and then died naturally. Abaye, citing Rabbah, holds the bailee liable because the marsh fumes killed it. Rava, citing Rabbah, holds him exempt because the angel of death would have killed it anywhere. Each concedes exceptions: Abaye exempts if the animal returned home and died, Rava imposes liability if a thief stole it from the marsh.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a dispute between Abaye and Rava regarding a case where the bailee was negligent (the animal went to a marsh) and then died naturally.
Abaye, citing Rabbah, holds the bailee liable, while Rava, citing Rabbah, holds him exempt.
Abaye explains that even according to the view that negligence followed by accident exempts, here the marsh fumes killed the animal, so the bailee is liable.
Rava explains that even according to the view that negligence followed by accident imposes liability, here the angel of death would have killed the animal anywhere, so the bailee is exempt.
Abaye concedes that if the animal returned home and died, the bailee is exempt; Rava concedes that if a thief stole it from the marsh and it died naturally, the bailee is liable.

items.text: Dialogue between Abaye and Rava on the angel of death argument
items.text_en: Dialogue between Abaye and Rava on the angel of death argument
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rava's principle that the angel of death would have killed the animal anywhere, citing a case where Rabbi Abba bar Memel questioned Rabbi Ammi and distinguished by permission to lend. Rava responds that his own principle (trustworthiness via oath) is unaffected by that proof.

sub.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rava's principle that the angel of death would have killed the animal anywhere, citing a case where Rabbi Abba bar Memel questioned Rabbi Ammi and distinguished by permission to lend, asking why Rava's principle was not invoked there.

Rava responds that his own principle (trustworthiness via oath) is unaffected by that proof, whereas Abaye's position (based on 'I do not want my deposit in another's hand') is vulnerable to that objection.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's objection from the Mishnah of leading to cliffs
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's objection from the Mishnah of leading to cliffs
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama cites a Mishnah where if one led an animal to cliff tops and it fell, it is not an accident, but if it died naturally it is an accident. He questions why the bailee cannot argue that the mountain air or mist killed it, challenging the ruling.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama cites a Mishnah where leading an animal to cliff tops and falling is not an accident, but natural death is an accident, and questions why the bailee cannot argue that the mountain air or mist killed it.

items.text: Resolution of the objection regarding mountain air
items.text_en: Resolution of the objection regarding mountain air
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the case involves a rich pasture, where the bailee could have held the animal back. If the animal dragged him up, the bailee is not liable for the fall, but the ruling that natural death is an accident stands only when the animal dragged him both up and down.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the objection by specifying that the case involves a rich pasture, where the bailee could have held the animal back, and his failure to do so makes him liable for the fall.
The Gemara clarifies that the ruling of natural death as an accident applies only when the animal dragged the bailee both up and down, so he could not have prevented the fall.

items.text: Citation of Rabbi Yosei and the halakhic resolution
items.text_en: Citation of Rabbi Yosei and the halakhic resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei's statement about not trading with the cow is cited, and Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel that the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei. The daf ends with a question about whether Rabbi Yosei disputed a related point.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei opens with a rhetorical question criticizing the depositor for trading with the cow.
Rav Yehuda reports that Shmuel ruled the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yosei.
Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda asks Rav Yehuda whether Shmuel also said that Rabbi Yosei disputed a related point.

items.text: Dispute about Rabbi Yosei's position in the first case
items.text_en: Dispute about Rabbi Yosei's position in the first case
items.desc_en: The Gemara records a dispute between Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yochanan: Rabbi Elazar says Rabbi Yosei disagreed even in the first case and the law follows him, while Rabbi Yochanan says Rabbi Yosei conceded in the first case that he had already paid. The Gemara clarifies that 'already paid' means he had said 'I will pay,' not actual payment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the law follows Rabbi Yosei even in the first case of the Mishnah.
Rabbi Elazar states that Rabbi Yosei disagreed even in the first case and the law follows him.
Rabbi Yochanan says that Rabbi Yosei conceded in the first case that he had already paid.
The Gemara objects: does 'paid' mean only actual payment, not a mere promise?

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba clarifies that 'paid' means he had said 'I will pay,' not actual payment, resolving the objection.

items.text: Mishnah: Cases of uncertain theft and deposit
items.text_en: Mishnah: Cases of uncertain theft and deposit
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases: one who says 'I robbed one of you of a maneh' or 'one of your fathers deposited a maneh with me' gives a maneh to each. For two depositors, one with a maneh and one with two hundred, each claiming the larger amount, the depositary gives each a maneh and leaves the rest until Elijah. Rabbi Yosei objects that this rewards the liar, so all should be left until Elijah. The same applies to two vessels of different values.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of a robber or depositary who admits uncertainty between two claimants, ruling that he must pay a maneh to each because he admitted on his own.

The Mishnah presents a second case: two depositors, one with a maneh and one with two hundred, each claiming the larger amount; the depositary gives each a maneh and leaves the remainder until Elijah.
Rabbi Yosei objects that the Tanna Kamma's ruling rewards the liar, and argues that all the money should be left until Elijah.

items.text: Gemara's question: Why does the Mishnah remove money from uncertainty?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why does the Mishnah remove money from uncertainty?
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's ruling that the robber gives a maneh to each seems to remove money from its owner's presumptive status (חזקת מרא). It raises a contradiction from a baraita about two depositors where the depositary gives each a maneh and leaves the rest. The answer distinguishes robbery (where a prohibition was violated, so the Sages penalized) from deposit (where no prohibition was violated, so no penalty).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah removes money from its owner's presumptive status (חזקת מרא) in the case of robbery.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita about two depositors where the depositary gives each a maneh and leaves the rest, which seems to follow the same principle.
The Gemara answers that robbery (גזל) involves a prohibition, so the Sages penalized the robber, while deposit (פיקדון) involves no prohibition, so no penalty applies.

items.text: Contradiction within deposit cases and Rava's resolution
items.text_en: Contradiction within deposit cases and Rava's resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between two deposit cases in the Mishnah itself: the first case (father's deposit) gives a maneh to each, while the second case (two depositors) gives only a maneh each and leaves the rest. Rava resolves: the first case is like two separate bundles (the depositary should have been careful), the second is like one bundle (deposited together, so he couldn't distinguish).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between two deposit cases in the Mishnah: the first case (father's deposit) gives a maneh to each, while the second case (two depositors) gives only a maneh each and leaves the rest.
Rava resolves the contradiction: the first case is like two separate bundles (the depositary should have been careful), the second is like one bundle (deposited together, so he couldn't distinguish).

items.text: Contradiction within robbery cases and resolution
items.text_en: Contradiction within robbery cases and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between the Mishnah's robbery case (gives a maneh to each) and a baraita of Rabbi Tarfon (where one who robbed one of five leaves the item and walks away). It suggests the Mishnah is Rabbi Tarfon's view, but then distinguishes: there the claimants demand payment, here the robber comes to fulfill his heavenly obligation, as indicated by 'he admitted of his own accord.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between the Mishnah's robbery case (giving a maneh to each) and a baraita of Rabbi Tarfon (where one who robbed one of five leaves the item and walks away).
The Gemara cites the baraita of Rabbi Tarfon, where the robber leaves the stolen item among the claimants and walks away, indicating that money is not extracted from a ספק (doubt).
The Gemara asks how we know that the Mishnah here follows Rabbi Tarfon's view, and cites that Rabbi Tarfon himself admits in the case of 'one who says to two' that he gives a maneh to each.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction: there (in Rabbi Tarfon's baraita) the claimants demand payment, but here (in the Mishnah) the robber comes to fulfill his heavenly obligation, as indicated by 'he admitted of his own accord.'

items.text: Clarification: What does the claimant claim?
items.text_en: Clarification: What does the claimant claim?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the claimant claims in the case where the robber comes to fulfill his heavenly obligation. Rav Yehudah says Rav ruled that the claimant is silent. Rav Mattanah says Rav ruled that the claimant claims. The text breaks off mid-sentence.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the claimant claims in the case where the robber comes to fulfill his heavenly obligation.
Rav Yehudah reports that Rav ruled the claimant is silent.
Rav Mattanah reports that Rav ruled the claimant claims, but the text breaks off mid-sentence.

items.text: Debate on silence as admission
items.text_en: Debate on silence as admission
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses two views: one holds that silence is like admission, while the other argues that silence here is not admission because the defendant can claim he was silent for each claimant, thinking perhaps this is the one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the first opinion that silence is like admission.
The second opinion argues that silence here is not admission because the defendant can claim he was silent for each claimant, thinking perhaps this is the one.

items.text: Objection from Rav's ruling on uncertain deposit
items.text_en: Objection from Rav's ruling on uncertain deposit
items.desc_en: Mar's statement that the robber places the stolen object between them and withdraws is questioned: if all claimants take it, this contradicts Rav's rule that in a case of uncertain deposit one should not initially take it, but if taken, not return it. Rav Safra answers: let him place it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Mar's ruling that the robber places the stolen object between them and withdraws, and all claimants take it, contradicts Rav's rule that in a case of uncertain deposit (ספק הינוח) one should not initially take it, but if taken, not return it.
Rav Safra answers: let him place it (i.e., the robber places the object, but does not actively give it to them; they take it themselves, so the rule about not initially taking does not apply).

items.text: Abaye's challenge from Rabbi Akiva's ruling
items.text_en: Abaye's challenge from Rabbi Akiva's ruling
items.desc_en: Abaye asks Rava: Does Rabbi Akiva really require paying each claimant, implying we extract money from uncertainty, not applying 'establish property in its owner's possession'? He then cites a contradiction from a case where a house fell on a son and mother, where Rabbi Akiva says the property remains in its presumptive owner's hands.

sub.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rava: Does Rabbi Akiva really require paying each claimant, implying we extract money from uncertainty and do not apply the principle of 'establish property in its owner's possession'?

sub.text: Abaye's citation of a contradictory baraita
sub.text_en: Abaye's citation of a contradictory baraita
sub.desc_en: Abaye cites a baraita about a house falling on a son and mother, where Rabbi Akiva rules that the property remains in its presumptive owner's hands, contradicting the earlier implication.

items.text: Rava's distinction: certain vs. uncertain claims
items.text_en: Rava's distinction: certain vs. uncertain claims
items.desc_en: Rava answers: There, both claims are uncertain (שמא ושמא); here, the robber's claim is certain (ברי) and the victim's is uncertain (שמא). He then challenges this from the Mishnah where one says to two 'I robbed one of you a maneh' – which is uncertain-uncertain – yet the ruling is to give each a maneh.

sub.desc_en: Rava answers Abaye's objection by distinguishing the case of uncertain-uncertain (שמא ושמא) from the case of certain-uncertain (ברי ושמא).
Rava challenges his own distinction by citing the Mishnah where one says 'I robbed one of you a maneh' — which is uncertain-uncertain.
Rava cites the Mishnah's ruling that in the uncertain-uncertain case, the robber gives each claimant a maneh.

items.text: Proof that the Mishnah is Rabbi Akiva's and is uncertain-uncertain
items.text_en: Proof that the Mishnah is Rabbi Akiva's and is uncertain-uncertain
items.desc_en: The Gemara proves the Mishnah is Rabbi Akiva's because it cites Rabbi Tarfon's admission to him. It then proves it is uncertain-uncertain because the claimants do not sue, and Rabbi Chiya taught that each says 'I don't know'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from what source do we know that the Mishnah is Rabbi Akiva's opinion?
The Gemara answers: because the Mishnah cites Rabbi Tarfon's admission to Rabbi Akiva, his disputant.
The Gemara asks: from what source do we know that the case is uncertain-uncertain (both claimants are uncertain)?
The Gemara answers: first, the Mishnah does not state that the claimants sue him; second, Rabbi Chiya taught that each says 'I don't know'.

items.text: Resolution: the Mishnah is about one seeking to fulfill Heaven's will
items.text_en: Resolution: the Mishnah is about one seeking to fulfill Heaven's will
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves: we already established that the Mishnah deals with one who comes to fulfill his obligation to Heaven, not a legal obligation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the difficulty by stating that the Mishnah was already established as dealing with one who seeks to fulfill his obligation to Heaven (יְדֵי שָׁמַיִם), not a legal obligation.

items.text: Ravina's challenge from the shepherd case
items.text_en: Ravina's challenge from the shepherd case
items.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi: Did Rava really require precision in two bundles? He cites Rava (or Rav Pappa) that all agree in the case of two who deposited with a shepherd, the shepherd places the animal between them and withdraws. Rav Ashi answers: That case is when they deposited in the shepherd's flock without his knowledge.

sub.desc_en: Ravina challenges Rav Ashi by citing Rava's (or Rav Pappa's) ruling that in a case of two depositors with a shepherd, the shepherd places the animal between them and withdraws, implying no need for precision in two bundles.
Rav Ashi distinguishes the shepherd case: the deposit was made in the shepherd's flock without his knowledge, so the shepherd is not liable for precision.

items.text: Need for both cases: two vessels and the earlier case
items.text_en: Need for both cases: two vessels and the earlier case
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why both cases (the earlier one and the case of two vessels, one worth a maneh and one a thousand zuz) are necessary: to show that the Rabbis and Rabbi Yosei each rule only in their specific context, and the rulings are not automatically transferable.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah introduces the case of two vessels, one worth a maneh and one a thousand zuz, where the robber claims he stole one but doesn't know which.
The Gemara states that both cases (the earlier one and this one) are necessary.

The Gemara explains that if only the earlier case were taught, one might think the Rabbis rule there only because there is no loss, but here where there is a loss of the larger vessel, they might concede to Rabbi Yosei.
The Gemara explains that if only this case were taught, one might think Rabbi Yosei rules here only because of the loss, but in the earlier case he might concede to the Rabbis.
The Gemara concludes that both cases are indeed necessary to prevent erroneous inferences.

items.text: Transition from previous daf
items.text_en: Transition from previous daf
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a contradiction between two earlier explanations for Rabbi Yosi's position, concluding that both are needed and the Mishnah teaches both cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that both explanations for Rabbi Yosi's position are necessary, and the Mishnah teaches both cases using the 'not only this but also that' structure.

items.text: Mishnah: Depositor may not touch deteriorating produce
items.text_en: Mishnah: Depositor may not touch deteriorating produce
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who deposits produce with another may not touch them even if they are spoiling. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permits selling them in court because it is like returning a lost object.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule that a depositor may not touch deteriorating produce.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permits selling the produce in court, comparing it to returning a lost object.

items.text: Gemara: Two reasons for the prohibition
items.text_en: Gemara: Two reasons for the prohibition
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana explains the prohibition because a person prefers his own small measure over nine measures of his friend's. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says we fear the depositor may have already designated the produce as terumah and ma'aser elsewhere.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the reason behind the Mishnah's prohibition.
Rav Kahana explains that a person prefers his own small measure (a קַב) over nine measures of his friend's.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says the prohibition is because we fear the depositor may have already designated the produce as תרומה ומעשר (priestly portion and tithe) elsewhere.

items.text: Support for Rav Kahana from the Mishnah's wording
items.text_en: Support for Rav Kahana from the Mishnah's wording
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that says 'therefore' the owner may designate the produce as terumah elsewhere. This fits Rav Kahana's reason but challenges Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak. The Gemara explains that Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak interprets 'therefore' as: since the Sages said not to sell due to concern, the owner may designate.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that says 'therefore' the owner may designate the produce as תרומה ומעשר (teruma and tithe) elsewhere, which fits Rav Kahana's reason but challenges Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak.

The Gemara explains that according to Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, 'therefore' means that since the Sages said not to sell due to concern, the owner may designate the produce as תרומה ומעשר (teruma and tithe) elsewhere.

items.text: Dispute limited to normal spoilage; beyond that all agree
items.text_en: Dispute limited to normal spoilage; beyond that all agree
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah says in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the dispute is only when the produce has not yet lost more than its normal shrinkage. Beyond that, all agree it may be sold in court. The Gemara clarifies that Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak certainly disputes this, while Rav Kahana's statement about preferring his own measure is hyperbole.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah says in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the dispute in the mishna is limited to normal spoilage (בכדי חסרונן), but if the loss exceeds that, all agree the bailee sells it in court.

The Gemara notes that Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak certainly disputes Rabbi Yochanan's limitation, and asks whether Rav Kahana also disputes it, answering that Rav Kahana spoke only about normal spoilage.
The Gemara objects that Rav Kahana's statement about preferring one kav of his own to nine of another's seems to apply even beyond normal spoilage, and answers that it is merely hyperbole.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding terumah concern
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding terumah concern
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the owner may designate terumah elsewhere, what if the produce had more than normal shrinkage and was sold? The answer: such cases are uncommon. If they occur, they are sold to priests at terumah prices. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak holds that such cases are common, so selling is prohibited lest the owner unknowingly eat tevel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the owner may designate תרומה ומעשר (terumah and tithe) elsewhere, what if the produce had more than normal shrinkage and was sold, causing the owner to eat טבלים (untithed produce)?
The Gemara answers that deterioration greater than the standard rate is uncommon, so no decree is needed.
The Gemara asks: if such a case does occur, should we sell it, and what about the concern that the owner already designated תרומה ומעשר (terumah and tithe) elsewhere?
The Gemara answers that even when sold, it is sold to priests at the price of תרומה (terumah), so there is no concern.
The Gemara asks: according to רב נחמן בר יצחק (Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak) as well, why not sell to priests at terumah prices?

Rabbah bar bar Chanah holds that greater-than-normal shrinkage is uncommon and occurs only from now on, so if the owner designated תרומה (terumah) it was before; therefore, sell to priests at terumah prices.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak holds that greater-than-normal shrinkage is common and immediate, so selling early could lead the owner to unknowingly eat טבלים (untithed produce).

items.text: Baraita about spoiled produce and its analysis
items.text_en: Baraita about spoiled produce and its analysis
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses cases where produce rots, wine sours, etc. Rabbi Meir prohibits touching them; the Sages permit selling in court. The Gemara questions whether this applies beyond normal shrinkage, and distinguishes: for produce that rots it is within normal shrinkage, but for wine that sours it is beyond; however, once such items spoil they are completely ruined and will not recover.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Meir rules that a bailee may not touch deposited produce that rotted, wine that soured, oil that putrefied, or honey that spoiled.
The Sages respond: the bailee may effect a remedy and sell them in court, but must sell to others, not to himself.
A parallel case is cited: charity collectors and food collectors may exchange or sell to others but not to themselves.
The Gemara asks whether the baraita applies even to deterioration beyond the standard rate, and notes that wine, oil, and honey cases seem to be beyond the standard rate.
The Gemara rejects: the baraita refers only to standard deterioration; wine, oil, and honey are different because once they spoil they are completely ruined and will not deteriorate further.
The Gemara repeats the cases of oil and honey as a brief concluding note.

items.text: Dispute over selling spoiled wine and oil
items.text_en: Dispute over selling spoiled wine and oil
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if wine and oil become spoiled, the Sages say one should make a remedy and sell them through court. Rav Ashi explains the remedy is to sell the containers. The dispute between the first Tanna and the Sages is about whether they were concerned for a large loss or even a small loss.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the spoiled wine and oil are still fit for, answering that oil is fit for plasterers and honey for camel fodder.
Rav Ashi explains that the remedy the Sages prescribe is to sell the containers (קנקנים) themselves.
The Gemara resolves the dispute between the first Tanna and the Sages: the first Tanna was concerned only for a large loss, while the Sages were concerned even for a small loss.

items.text: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling and the halachic dispute
items.text_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling and the halachic dispute
items.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says to sell them through court because it is like returning a lost object. Rabbi Abba bar Yaakov said Rabbi Yochanan ruled the halacha follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, while Rava said Rav Nachman ruled the halacha follows the Sages.

sub.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules that the court sells the deposited goods, because this is like returning a lost object to its owner.

sub.text: Rabbi Abba bar Rabbi Yaakov citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba bar Rabbi Yaakov citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Rabbi Yaakov reports that Rabbi Yochanan ruled the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
Rava reports that Rav Nachman ruled the הלכה (binding law) follows the Sages, contradicting Rabbi Yochanan's position.

items.text: Reconciling Rabbi Yochanan's statements
items.text_en: Reconciling Rabbi Yochanan's statements
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabbi Yochanan needed to state the halacha here, since he already said a general rule that wherever Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel teaches in the Mishnah, the halacha follows him except for three cases. The answer is that these are different Amoraim reporting Rabbi Yochanan's opinion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabbi Yochanan needed to state the halacha here, since he already said a general rule that wherever Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel teaches in the Mishnah, the halacha follows him except for three cases.
The Gemara answers that these are different Amoraim reporting Rabbi Yochanan's opinion, so the general rule and the specific ruling come from different transmitters.

items.text: Inferring the rule for property of a captive
items.text_en: Inferring the rule for property of a captive
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to infer from the dispute whether a relative may descend to manage the property of a captive. It suggests that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel would allow it and the Sages would not, but then rejects this inference, arguing that the reasons may be different. The Gemara concludes that the two issues have separate rationales, citing Rav Yehuda and Shmuel, and Rava and Rav Nachman.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the dispute that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel would allow a relative to manage a captive's property, while the Sages would not.
The Gemara rejects the inference, arguing that the positions in the Mishnah may be based on different rationales than the captive property case.

The Gemara questions whether the two issues have separate rationales, citing Rav Yehuda and Shmuel who rule like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and also allow a relative to manage a captive's property, but concludes they are separate.
The Gemara confirms the conclusion by noting that Rava and Rav Nachman rule like the Sages yet also allow a relative to manage a captive's property, proving the two issues have separate rationales.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on property of a captive
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on property of a captive
items.desc_en: The Gemara states the explicit dispute: Rav says one does not allow a relative to descend to the property of a captive, while Shmuel says one does. They agree that if they heard he died, one does allow it. The dispute is when they did not hear he died: Rav fears the relative will cause loss, while Shmuel says since we appoint him as a sharecropper, he won't cause loss.
