sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the explicit dispute: Rav says one does not allow a relative to descend to the property of a captive, while Shmuel says one does.
The Gemara clarifies that both agree when they heard he died, one does allow the relative to descend.
The Gemara explains the dispute is when they did not hear he died: Rav fears the relative will cause loss, while Shmuel says since we appoint him as a sharecropper, he won't cause loss.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the dispute from a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer says that the verse teaches that wives are not allowed to remarry and children are not allowed to descend to their father's property. Rava explains that the baraita refers to descending to sell, not to manage. A story in Nehardea where Rav Sheshet ruled from this baraita is recounted, and Rav Amram questions whether it refers to descending to sell, but Rav Sheshet dismisses him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the dispute by citing a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer derives from a verse that wives may not remarry and children may not inherit.
Rava explains that the baraita refers to descending to sell the property, not to manage it.
A story is recounted where Rav Sheshet ruled from this baraita, and when Rav Amram questioned whether it refers to descending to sell, Rav Sheshet dismissed him with a sharp retort.

items.text: Tannaitic sources on property of captives, abandoned, and fugitives
items.text_en: Tannaitic sources on property of captives, abandoned, and fugitives
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that distinguishes between property of a captive (shavuy), where one who descends is not removed, and property of an abandoned person (natush), where he is removed. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says abandoned are like captives. It also defines property of a fugitive (ratush) and asks about the terminology.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces the rule for property of a captive (shavuy): a relative who descends to manage the property is not removed, and even if he hears they are coming and harvests early, he is considered diligent and rewarded.
The baraita states that for property of an abandoned person (natush), the relative is removed, but Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules that abandoned are like captives and the relative is not removed.
The baraita defines property of a fugitive (ratush): a relative who descends is removed, and the fugitive is one who was present but disappeared without known destination.
The Gemara asks why the baraita uses different terms — 'נטושים' (abandoned) for those who left without news of death, and 'רטושים' (fugitives) for those who disappeared locally.

items.text: Definition of נטושים and רטושים
items.text_en: Definition of נטושים and רטושים
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the terms 'נטושים' (abandoned against their will) and 'רטושים' (abandoned willingly) by citing biblical verses. 'נטושים' refers to those forced to leave, as in the Sabbatical year, while 'רטושים' refers to those who leave willingly, as in the verse about a mother bird.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara defines 'נטושים' as those abandoned against their will, citing the Sabbatical year verse, and 'רטושים' as those who leave willingly, citing the verse about a mother bird.

items.text: Clarifying the ruling of שמין להם כאיסר
items.text_en: Clarifying the ruling of שמין להם כאיסר
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions which category the ruling 'שמין להם כאיסר' applies to. It rejects the possibility of captives (since they are entitled to all profits) and those who left willingly (since they are removed from property). It concludes it applies to נטושים, and then specifies that it follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view, who considers נטושים like captives but not identical: they are not removed from property, but are assessed as a tenant farmer.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna states that for all these categories, the court assesses the caretaker's compensation like a tenant farmer (אריס).
The Gemara asks: to which category does this ruling apply?
The Gemara rejects the possibility that it applies to captives, since a captive's caretaker is diligent and hired, and thus entitled to all profits.
The Gemara rejects the possibility that it applies to those who left willingly (רטושים), since the Mishnah explicitly says they are removed from the property.
The Gemara concludes that the ruling applies to נטושים (those forced to abandon their property).
The Gemara asks: according to which authority does this apply?
The Gemara rejects the possibility that it follows the Rabbis, since they hold that the caretaker is removed from the property.
The Gemara rejects the possibility that it follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, since he equates נטושים with captives, who are entitled to all profits.

The Gemara resolves that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel considers נטושים like captives but not identical: they are not removed from property, but are assessed as a tenant farmer (אריס) rather than receiving all profits.

items.text: Comparison with mishnayot about husband's expenses on wife's property
items.text_en: Comparison with mishnayot about husband's expenses on wife's property
items.desc_en: The Gemara compares the ruling to two mishnayot: one about a husband who spends on his wife's property (where he only gets credit for what he spent minus what he consumed), and another about a minor wife's property (where he is treated like any other spender). The latter case is analogous because the husband does not rely on the property, so the Sages instituted a rule to prevent loss, just as here.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the ruling for נטושים (abandoned captives) differs from the mishnah about a husband who spends on his wife's property, where he only recovers what he spent minus what he consumed.

The Gemara answers that the case is analogous to a husband who spends on his minor wife's property, where the Sages instituted a rule to prevent loss because the husband does not rely on the property, and similarly here they instituted a rule to prevent loss.

items.text: Inclusion of Rav Nachman's ruling about a captive and a fugitive
items.text_en: Inclusion of Rav Nachman's ruling about a captive and a fugitive
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what additional cases are included by the phrase 'וכולן'. It answers that it includes the ruling of Rav Nachman citing Shmuel: for a captive, a relative is appointed to manage his property, but for one who left willingly, no relative is appointed. Rav Nachman himself adds that a fugitive (from danger) is like a captive. The Gemara clarifies that a fugitive from taxes is considered willing, but a fugitive from persecution is like a captive.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what additional cases are included by the phrase 'וכולן' (and all of them) in the Mishnah's ruling that they are assessed like a sharecropper.

The Gemara answers that it includes the ruling of Rav Nachman citing Shmuel: for a captive, a relative is appointed to manage his property, but for one who left willingly, no relative is appointed; Rav Nachman adds that a fugitive from persecution is like a captive, while a fugitive from taxes is considered willing.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's ruling about a captive with ripening crops
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's ruling about a captive with ripening crops
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel rules that if a captive left standing crops ready for harvest, the court appoints a temporary guardian to harvest them, and only afterward appoints a relative. The Gemara questions why a permanent guardian is not appointed, and answers that we do not appoint guardians for adults.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel rules that for a captive who left standing crops, the court appoints a temporary guardian to harvest them and only afterward appoints a relative.
The Gemara questions why a permanent guardian is not appointed instead of a temporary one.
The Gemara answers that we do not appoint guardians for adults (bearded men).

items.text: Rav Huna's three prohibitions regarding minors and captives
items.text_en: Rav Huna's three prohibitions regarding minors and captives
items.desc_en: Rav Huna states three rules: a minor is not appointed over a captive's property (lest he cause loss), a relative (e.g., a maternal brother) is not appointed over a minor's property (lest he claim ownership), and a relative is not appointed over a minor's property because he might establish a hazakah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna states three prohibitions: not appointing a minor over a captive's property, not appointing a relative over a minor's property, and not appointing a relative via a relative over a minor's property.

The gemara explains each prohibition: a minor might cause loss, a maternal brother might claim ownership, and a relative might establish a hazakah (presumption of ownership) since the minor cannot protest.

items.text: Rava's inference about hazakah on a minor's property
items.text_en: Rava's inference about hazakah on a minor's property
items.desc_en: Rava infers from Rav Huna's ruling that one cannot establish a hazakah (prescriptive ownership) on a minor's property, because if a relative is not appointed for fear of hazakah, then certainly a stranger cannot acquire through hazakah.

sub.desc_en: Rava infers from Rav Huna's ruling that one cannot establish a hazakah (prescriptive ownership) on a minor's property.

items.text: Distinction between paternal and maternal relatives, and between land and houses
items.text_en: Distinction between paternal and maternal relatives, and between land and houses
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially distinguishes between paternal and maternal relatives regarding the rule of not appointing a guardian, and between land and houses. It then rejects all these distinctions, concluding that in all cases we do not appoint a guardian.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that even after the orphan has grown up, we do not appoint a guardian.
The Gemara proposes a series of distinctions: the rule applies only to paternal relatives, only to land, and only to land that does not produce a known yield.
The Gemara rejects all distinctions, concluding that in all cases we do not appoint a guardian.

items.text: Abaye's dilemma regarding the property of a captive grandmother
items.text_en: Abaye's dilemma regarding the property of a captive grandmother
items.desc_en: Abaye presents a case of a grandmother and one daughter who were captured, leaving two other daughters, one of whom died leaving a minor. He questions whether to give the property to the surviving daughter or to the minor, due to the principle that we do not appoint a guardian for the property of a captive or for a minor.

sub.desc_en: Abaye presents a case of a captive grandmother and daughter, with two other daughters, one deceased leaving a minor, and questions whether to give the property to the surviving daughter or the minor due to the principle that we do not appoint a guardian for the property of a captive or a minor.

items.text: Abaye and Rava's first solution: appoint a guardian for half
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava's first solution: appoint a guardian for half
items.desc_en: Abaye proposes giving half the property to the surviving daughter and appointing a guardian for the minor's half. Rava argues that since we appoint a guardian for half, we should also appoint a guardian for the other half, implying the daughter also gets a guardian.

sub.desc_en: Abaye proposes giving half the property to the sister and appointing a guardian for the minor's half.
Rava objects that since a guardian is appointed for half, a guardian should also be appointed for the other half, implying the sister also gets a guardian.

items.text: Abaye and Rava's second solution after hearing the grandmother died
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava's second solution after hearing the grandmother died
items.desc_en: Upon hearing the grandmother died, Abaye revises his plan: give a third to the daughter, a third to the minor, and the remaining third is split into two halves—one for the daughter and one for the minor with a guardian. Rava again argues that since we appoint a guardian for one half, we should for the other.

sub.desc_en: The narrative reports that they eventually heard the grandmother had died.
Abaye proposes a new division: a third to the sister, a third to the minor, and the remaining third is split into two halves—one for the sister and one for the minor with a guardian.
Rava objects that since we appoint a guardian for one half of the remaining third, we should also appoint a guardian for the other half, effectively giving the entire remaining third to the minor.

items.text: The case of Mari bar Isak and his brother from Bei Hozae
items.text_en: The case of Mari bar Isak and his brother from Bei Hozae
items.desc_en: A brother from Bei Hozae claims his share from Mari bar Isak, who denies knowing him. Rav Chisda rules that the claimant must bring witnesses, and even suggests the defendant bring witnesses to prove the claimant is not his brother, despite the principle that the burden of proof is on the claimant. Rav Chisda justifies this for powerful defendants.

sub.desc_en: A brother from Bei Hozae comes to Mari bar Isak and demands his share; Mari denies knowing him.
Rav Chisda supports Mari's denial, citing the verse about Joseph's unrecognizability after growing a beard.
Rav Chisda tells the claimant to bring witnesses, but the claimant fears them because Mari is a powerful man.
Rav Chisda tells Mari to bring witnesses that the claimant is not his brother, despite the usual burden of proof on the claimant.
The claimant objects that the burden of proof should be on him, not on the defendant.
Rav Chisda justifies his ruling, stating that he judges this way for all powerful defendants, and notes that witnesses will not commit two wrongs (refusing to testify and lying).

items.text: Ruling on improvements made by heirs
items.text_en: Ruling on improvements made by heirs
items.desc_en: After witnesses confirm the brother's identity, he also claims a share in orchards planted by Mari bar Isak. Rav Chisda rules that the brother is entitled to a share, citing the Mishnah that if adult heirs improve the estate, the improvement is for the common benefit.

sub.desc_en: The brother from Bei Hozae demands a share of the orchards and gardens that Mari bar Isak planted.
Rav Chisda rules in favor of the brother, citing the Mishnah that when adult heirs improve the estate, the improvement is for the common benefit.

items.text: Conclusion of the dispute about the guardian's improvement
items.text_en: Conclusion of the dispute about the guardian's improvement
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rabbah's ruling that improvements are split equally, arguing that in the earlier case the adults knowingly waived rights, unlike here. The case is brought before Rabbi Ami, who initially rules in favor of the guardian, but Rav Chisda objects because the guardian entered without permission and the owner is a minor. Rabbi Ami then retracts, noting he was not informed of the minority.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah rules that improvements made by a guardian are split equally between the guardian and the orphan.
Abaye challenges Rabbah by distinguishing the earlier case where adults knowingly waived rights, unlike here where the guardian entered without knowledge of the owner's minority.
Rabbi Ami initially rules in favor of the guardian, reasoning that if a larger allowance is given to a sharecropper, certainly the guardian should receive compensation.
Rav Chisda objects because the guardian entered without permission and the owner is a minor, and one may not appoint a relative over a minor's property.
Rabbi Ami retracts his ruling, noting that he was not informed of the owner's minority.

items.text: Mishnah: Deductions for storage losses
items.text_en: Mishnah: Deductions for storage losses
items.desc_en: The Mishnah specifies the standard deductions a bailee may claim for storage losses of various produce: for wheat and rice, nine half-kav per kor; for barley and millet, nine kav per kor; for spelt and flax seed, three se'ah per kor. Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri argues that mice eat regardless of quantity, so the deduction should be only for one kor. Rabbi Yehuda says if the measure is large, no deduction is made because the produce increases.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the standard deductions for storage losses of various produce: for wheat and rice, nine half-kav per kor; for barley and millet, nine kav per kor; for spelt and flax seed, three se'ah per kor, all according to measure and time.
Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri objects that mice eat regardless of quantity, so the deduction should be only for one kor.
Rabbi Yehuda says if the measure is large, no deduction is made because the produce increases.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying the Mishnah's rates
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying the Mishnah's rates
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the high loss rate for rice, and Rabbi Yochanan explains it refers to peeled rice. For flax seed, Rabbi Yochanan says it refers to flax in stalks. A baraita supports these interpretations. The phrase 'all according to the measure and all according to the time' is explained to mean for each kor and each year.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah's loss rate for rice is so high, given that rice is not typically subject to such loss.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah reports that Rabbi Yochanan explained the Mishnah refers to peeled rice (אורז קלוף), which loses more volume.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Chiyya
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Chiyya
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan further explains, citing Rabbi Chiyya, that the Mishnah's rate for flax seed applies to flax in stalks (בגבעולין), which have greater shrinkage.
A baraita supports these interpretations, stating that the rates for rice and flax seed apply only to unpeeled rice and flax in stalks.
The Tanna explains that the Mishnah's phrase 'all according to the measure and all according to the time' means the loss rate applies to each kor and each year.

items.text: Gemara: Discussion of Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's view and conditions for deduction
items.text_en: Gemara: Discussion of Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's view and conditions for deduction
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where the Sages respond to Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri that many produce items are lost or scattered. A baraita then states that the Mishnah's deduction applies only when the bailee mixed the deposit with his own produce; if he set aside a separate corner, he can say 'yours is before you.' The Gemara questions how to know the loss if mixed, and explains it is when the bailee is uncertain how much he consumed from the deposit.

sub.desc_en: A baraita reports that the Sages responded to Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri that many produce items are lost or scattered.
A Tanna states that the Mishnah's deduction applies only when the bailee mixed the deposit with his own produce; if he set aside a separate corner, he can say 'yours is before you.'
The Gemara asks: if the bailee mixed the deposit with his own produce, why can't he simply see how much of his own produce remains to calculate the loss?
The Gemara answers: the case is where the bailee is uncertain how much he consumed from the deposit.
The Gemara asks further: why can't the bailee determine how much he consumed?
The Gemara answers: because the bailee does not know how much he consumed.

items.text: Gemara: Rabbi Yehuda's view and further conditions
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabbi Yehuda's view and further conditions
items.desc_en: The Gemara defines 'large measure' as ten korim, citing a baraita. A baraita before Rav Nachman adds that the deduction applies only if the bailee measured from his threshing floor and returned from his threshing floor; if he returned from his house, no deduction because the produce increases. Rav Nachman corrects this to refer to seasons: if measured and returned during the threshing season, deduction applies; if returned during the rainy season, no deduction because the produce swells. Rav Pappa questions Abaye about a jar bursting, and an incident is cited where a jar did burst; alternatively, it is attributed to pressure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how large a 'large measure' must be for Rabbi Yehuda's ruling.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah cites Rabbi Yochanan that a large measure is ten korim.
A baraita is cited that also defines a large measure as ten korim.

A Tanna before Rav Nachman teaches that the deduction applies only if the bailee measured from his threshing floor and returned from his threshing floor; if he returned from his house, no deduction because the produce increases.
Rav Nachman objects that the Tanna's distinction between threshing floor and house is irrelevant, suggesting it refers to seasons instead.
Rav Nachman corrects that the deduction applies only if measured and returned during the threshing season; if returned during the rainy season, no deduction because the produce swells.
Rav Pappa asks Abaye that if produce swells in the rainy season, a jar would burst.
An incident is cited where a jar did burst, supporting the concern.
Alternatively, the bursting is attributed to pressure rather than swelling.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara: Deductions for wine and oil
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara: Deductions for wine and oil
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that for wine, the bailee deducts one-sixth; Rabbi Yehuda says one-fifth. For oil, he deducts three log per hundred: one and a half for sediment and one and a half for absorption. If the oil is refined, no sediment deduction; if the containers are old, no absorption deduction. Rabbi Yehuda adds that a seller of refined oil throughout the year accepts one and a half log sediment per hundred. The Gemara explains that the dispute about wine depends on local practice: where they seal with clay, less absorption; where with pitch, more. Alternatively, it depends on the type of grape. The Gemara then discusses local measures and prices.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the deductions for wine and oil: one-sixth for wine (Rabbi Yehuda says one-fifth), and for oil three log per hundred (one and a half for sediment, one and a half for absorption), with exceptions for refined oil and old containers, and Rabbi Yehuda adds that a seller of refined oil accepts one and a half log sediment per hundred.

The Gemara explains that the dispute between the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yehuda is not a fundamental disagreement but depends on local practice: in places where they seal wine jars with clay (קירָא) there is less absorption, while where they seal with pitch (כוּפְרָא) there is more absorption; alternatively, it depends on the type of grape (גַּרְגִּישְׁתָּא) — some absorb more and some less.

The Gemara digresses to describe the local measures in Rav Yehuda's place: forty-eight jugs (כּוּזֵי) per barrel (דַּנָּא), with a barrel costing six zuz, and Rav Yehuda would divide the wine into sixths per zuz.

items.text: Gemara's calculation and Shmuel's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's calculation and Shmuel's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara calculates that if one deducts a sixth from a sixth, the remainder is a sixth, but Shmuel said a bailee should not profit more than a sixth. The Gemara resolves this by accounting for the value of the dregs and sediment, as well as the labor and cost of the jars.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara calculates that deducting a sixth from a sixth leaves a sixth, and then deducting eighths leaves four.
The Gemara objects that Shmuel ruled a bailee should not profit more than a sixth.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by accounting for the value of dregs and sediment, and the labor and cost of the jars.

items.text: Clarifying the Mishnah's allowance for refined oil
items.text_en: Clarifying the Mishnah's allowance for refined oil
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the oil was refined, the seller does not give sediment. The Gemara objects that some absorption is inevitable. Rav Nachman answers that the Mishnah refers to sealed barrels, while Abaye says even unsealed barrels, once the oil is absorbed, it is considered absorbed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that even with refined oil, some absorption into the barrel is inevitable, so the seller should still deduct for sediment.
Rav Nachman answers that the Mishnah's ruling applies only to sealed (pitched) barrels, which prevent absorption.
Abaye counters that even with unsealed barrels, once the oil is absorbed into the barrel, it is considered the buyer's loss and the seller is not liable.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's statement and Abaye's summary
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's statement and Abaye's summary
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda says that one who sells refined oil throughout the year accepts upon himself a log and a half of sediment per hundred. Abaye summarizes that according to Rabbi Yehuda it is permitted to mix sediments, while according to the Sages it is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda states that one who sells refined oil throughout the year accepts upon himself a log and a half of sediment per hundred.
Abaye summarizes that according to Rabbi Yehuda it is permitted to mix sediments, while according to the Sages it is forbidden.

items.text: Explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning
items.text_en: Explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to Rabbi Yehuda, the seller accepts the sediment because he could have mixed it in anyway. The buyer cannot claim that the sediment would have sold separately, since we are dealing with a homeowner who prefers the shade (i.e., the oil is for personal use). The buyer also cannot claim that the seller waived his rights, because Rabbi Yehuda does not recognize waiver.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to Rabbi Yehuda, since the seller could have mixed the sediment into the oil, the buyer must accept it now.
The buyer could object that if the seller had mixed the sediment, it would have been sold with the oil, but now the sediment alone is unsellable.
The Gemara answers that the case involves a homeowner who uses the oil for personal use (preferring the shade), so the sediment would not have been sold separately anyway.
The buyer could further claim that by not mixing the sediment, the seller waived his right to demand acceptance of the sediment.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yehuda holds his consistent position that waiver (מחילה) is not recognized, so the buyer's claim of waiver fails.

items.text: Support for Rabbi Yehuda's view from a Mishnah
items.text_en: Support for Rabbi Yehuda's view from a Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda says that the price indicates what was sold, implying he does not accept waiver. The Sages disagree, saying the price is not evidence.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that Rabbi Yehuda's position in the Mishnah follows his own consistent reasoning, that he does not accept the concept of waiver (מחילה).
The Gemara cites a Mishnah where selling a yoke does not include the cattle, establishing the baseline rule.
Rabbi Yehuda argues that the price indicates what was sold, so if someone pays 200 zuz for a yoke, it must include the cattle, as a yoke alone is not worth that much.
The Sages disagree, asserting that the price is not evidence of what was sold.

items.text: Explanation of the Sages' reasoning and Rav Pappa's objection
items.text_en: Explanation of the Sages' reasoning and Rav Pappa's objection
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to the Sages, the seller does not accept sediment because the buyer could have mixed it. Rav Pappa objects and reverses the reasoning: according to the Sages it is permitted to mix, and the seller refuses because the buyer waived his right; according to Rabbi Yehuda it is forbidden to mix, and the seller accepts because the buyer could not have mixed it himself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to the Sages, mixing sediment is forbidden, so the seller refuses to accept it back, arguing the buyer could not have mixed it.

Rav Pappa objects to Abaye, reversing the reasoning: according to the Sages mixing is permitted, so the seller refuses because the buyer waived his right; according to Rabbi Yehuda mixing is forbidden, so the seller accepts because the buyer could not have mixed.

items.text: Discussion of the Tanna's statement about buyer and depositor regarding sediment
items.text_en: Discussion of the Tanna's statement about buyer and depositor regarding sediment
items.desc_en: A Tanna states that both a buyer and a depositor receive sediment. The Gemara initially thinks this means neither receives sediment, but then concludes that both receive sediment. It questions whether a buyer really receives sediment, citing a baraita that says a buyer only receives a log and a half of sediment without sediment. The Gemara resolves this by distinguishing between paying in Tishrei and taking in Nisan (using the Tishrei measure) and paying and taking in Nisan (using the Nisan measure).

sub.desc_en: A Tanna states that both a buyer and a depositor receive sediment (פקטים).
The Gemara asks what 'לפקטים' means.
The Gemara initially suggests that 'לפקטים' means neither receives sediment, but objects that the depositor could then refuse to accept sediment.
The Gemara concludes that 'לפקטים' means both receive sediment.
The Gemara questions whether a buyer really receives sediment.
A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yehuda states that a buyer only receives a log and a half of sediment without sediment (פקטים).

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between paying in Tishrei and taking in Nisan (using the Tishrei measure, which includes sediment) versus paying and taking in Nisan (using the Nisan measure, which does not).

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on a deposited barrel
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on a deposited barrel
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses a deposited barrel that was moved and broken, distinguishing between cases where the owner designated a place and where they did not. The Gemara identifies the Mishnah as following Rabbi Yishmael, who holds that the owner's knowledge is not required, citing a baraita about a thief returning a lamb to the flock.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of a deposited barrel that was moved and broken, distinguishing liability based on whether the owner designated a place and whether the movement was for the bailee's or the barrel's needs.
The Gemara asks which Tanna's view underlies the Mishnah, identifying it as Rabbi Yishmael.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yishmael holds that a thief returns the stolen item to the place of theft without requiring the owner's knowledge, while Rabbi Akiva disagrees.

items.text: Opening Mishnah clause
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah clause
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a borrower who moves a barrel without the owner's knowledge is liable, but if the owner designated a place for it, the borrower is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a borrower who moves a barrel without the owner's knowledge is liable, but if the owner designated a place for it, the borrower is exempt.

items.text: Gemara's question on the first clause
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the first clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies 'did not designate' if even designating a place should require da'at ba'alim according to Rabbi Yishmael. It answers that the Mishnah is stating a fortiori: even without designation, no da'at ba'alim is needed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies 'did not designate' if even designating a place should require da'at ba'alim according to Rabbi Yishmael.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah is stating a fortiori: even without designation, no da'at ba'alim is needed.

items.text: Gemara's question on the second clause
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the second clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the second clause, which distinguishes between the borrower's benefit and the barrel's benefit, aligns with Rabbi Akiva who requires da'at ba'alim. It asks why it specifies 'designated' if even without designation it would require da'at ba'alim, and answers that it is a fortiori: even with designation, da'at ba'alim is needed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the second clause aligns with Rabbi Akiva, who requires דעת בעלים (the owner's awareness), and asks why the clause specifies 'designated' if even without designation it would require such awareness.
The Gemara objects: if the clause follows Rabbi Akiva, why mention 'designated' at all? Even without designation, the owner's awareness would be required.

The Gemara answers that the clause uses a fortiori (לא מיבעיא) formulation: even with designation, where the barrel is in its designated place, the owner's awareness is required; all the more so without designation.

items.text: Reconciliation of the two clauses
items.text_en: Reconciliation of the two clauses
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the first clause follows Rabbi Yishmael and the second follows Rabbi Akiva, citing Rabbi Yochanan's statement that he would follow anyone who can explain the entire Mishnah according to a single Tanna.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the first clause follows Rabbi Yishmael and the second follows Rabbi Akiva.
The Gemara affirms the split, citing Rabbi Yochanan's statement.
Rabbi Yochanan declares that he would follow anyone who can explain the entire Mishnah according to a single Tanna.

items.text: Two interpretations of the Mishnah's case
items.text_en: Two interpretations of the Mishnah's case
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Abba and Rabbi Natan bar Abba offer different interpretations before Rav: one says the borrower took the barrel with intent to steal it (legazlah), the other with intent to misappropriate it (lishlo'ach yad). The Gemara explains they dispute whether shelichut yad requires a diminution (chesron).

sub.text: Rabbi Yaakov bar Abba's interpretation before Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Abba's interpretation before Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Abba interprets the Mishnah's case before Rav as one where the borrower took the barrel with intent to steal it (legazlah).

sub.text: Rabbi Natan bar Abba's interpretation before Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbi Natan bar Abba's interpretation before Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Natan bar Abba interprets the Mishnah's case before Rav as one where the borrower took the barrel with intent to misappropriate it (lishlo'ach yad).

The Gemara explains that the two interpretations dispute whether shelichut yad (misappropriation) requires a diminution (chesron) of the deposit: the one who says 'to steal it' holds it requires a diminution, while the one who says 'to misappropriate' holds it does not.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's objection and alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's objection and alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet objects that the Mishnah says 'tilte'lah' (moved), not 'netalah' (took). He explains the case is where the borrower moved the barrel to bring pigeons onto it, and holds that a borrower without permission is a thief. The entire Mishnah follows Rabbi Yishmael, and the second clause refers to leaving it in a place that is not its designated place. Rabbi Yochanan argues that 'hinichah' implies leaving it in its designated place.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet objects that the Mishnah uses the word 'טילטלה' (moved), not 'נטלה' (took), challenging the earlier interpretations.

Rav Sheshet explains that the case involves moving the barrel to bring pigeons onto it, and holds that a borrower without permission is a thief; the entire Mishnah follows Rabbi Yishmael, and the second clause refers to leaving it in a non-designated place.
Rabbi Yochanan argues that the Mishnah's term 'הניחה' (left it) implies leaving it in its designated place, contradicting Rav Sheshet's interpretation.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Levi on shelichut yad
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Levi on shelichut yad
items.desc_en: The Gemara reports a dispute between Rav and Levi: one says shelichut yad requires chesron, the other says it does not. It attempts to prove that Rav holds it does not require chesron from a baraita about a shepherd who left his staff and bag on an animal and is liable, even though he did not diminish it. Rav Sheshet's explanation that the staff was still on the animal is rejected, and Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's explanation that he struck the animal with a stick and it ran is accepted, proving that shelichut yad does not require chesron.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports a dispute between Rav and Levi: one holds that shelichut yad (misappropriation by a bailee) requires chesron (a diminution of the deposit), the other holds it does not.

sub.text: Gemara's attempt to prove Rav's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's attempt to prove Rav's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a shepherd who left his staff and bag on an animal and is liable, to prove that Rav holds shelichut yad does not require chesron.
The Gemara objects: why is the shepherd liable if he removed the staff and bag from the animal?

sub.text: Rav Nachman quoting Rabbah bar Avuha quoting Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman quoting Rabbah bar Avuha quoting Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rav explains that the baraita refers to a case where the staff and bag were still on the animal.
The Gemara objects: even if the items are still on the animal, the shepherd has not diminished the deposit.

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak quoting Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak quoting Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak in the name of Rav explains that the shepherd struck the animal with a stick, causing it to run, and the Gemara concludes that this proves Rav holds shelichut yad does not require chesron.

items.text: Conclusion and Levi's reasoning
items.text_en: Conclusion and Levi's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that Rav holds shelichut yad requires chesron, while Levi holds it does not. It explains Levi's reasoning via Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Yosei ben Nehorai: the shelichut yad mentioned regarding a paid guardian is different from that mentioned regarding an unpaid guardian.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that Rav holds shelichut yad requires chesron, while Levi holds it does not.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Yosei ben Nehorai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Yosei ben Nehorai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains Levi's reasoning by citing Rabbi Yosei ben Nehorai: the shelichut yad mentioned regarding a paid guardian is different from that mentioned regarding an unpaid guardian.

items.text: Opening statement: 'I say it is not different'
items.text_en: Opening statement: 'I say it is not different'
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins with a statement that the law of shlichut yad is not different for a paid bailee compared to an unpaid bailee, implying it applies equally.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by asserting that the law of שליחות יד (unauthorized use) is not different for a paid bailee compared to an unpaid bailee, implying it applies equally.

items.text: Explanation: Derivation from unpaid bailee
items.text_en: Explanation: Derivation from unpaid bailee
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that shlichut yad for a paid bailee is derived from an unpaid bailee via a kal vachomer argument: if an unpaid bailee, who is exempt for theft and loss, becomes liable when he misappropriates, then a paid bailee, who is liable for theft and loss, certainly should be liable. The Torah wrote this to teach that shlichut yad does not require a reduction in value.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is meant by 'different' and proposes that shlichut yad for a paid bailee is not written separately but derived from an unpaid bailee.

The Gemara presents a kal vachomer argument: if an unpaid bailee, exempt for theft and loss, becomes liable for shlichut yad, then a paid bailee, liable for theft and loss, certainly should be liable; the Torah wrote it to teach that shlichut yad does not require a reduction in value.

items.text: Alternative view: Like Rabbi Elazar
items.text_en: Alternative view: Like Rabbi Elazar
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents an alternative view that the law is not different, following Rabbi Elazar who says both bailees are the same. However, a refutation is raised: the kal vachomer from an unpaid bailee is flawed because an unpaid bailee pays double when falsely claiming theft, which a paid bailee does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents an alternative view that the law is not different, aligning with Rabbi Elazar who holds both bailees are the same.
The Gemara raises a refutation: the kal vachomer from an unpaid bailee is flawed because an unpaid bailee pays double when falsely claiming theft, which a paid bailee does not.

items.text: Resolution of the refutation
items.text_en: Resolution of the refutation
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the one who does not raise this refutation holds that a principal without an oath is superior to double payment with an oath, thus the kal vachomer stands.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the refutation by stating that the one who does not raise it holds that a principal without an oath (קרנא בלא שבועה) is superior to double payment with an oath (כפילא בשבועה), so the kal vachomer (קל וחומר) stands.

items.text: Rava's derivation from a borrower
items.text_en: Rava's derivation from a borrower
items.desc_en: Rava says that shlichut yad is not derived from an unpaid or paid bailee but from a borrower: just as a borrower, who acts with the owner's permission, is liable when he misappropriates, so too an unpaid and paid bailee are certainly liable. The two verses teach that shlichut yad does not require a reduction, and that the kal vachomer is limited by the principle that the derived law cannot be more stringent than the source (so bailees are exempt when the owner is with them).

sub.desc_en: Rava opens by rejecting the derivation of shlichut yad from unpaid or paid bailees, instead deriving it from a borrower via a kal vachomer.

The Gemara explains that the two verses of shlichut yad serve two purposes: one teaches that shlichut yad does not require a reduction, and the other limits the kal vachomer by the principle that the derived law cannot be more stringent than the source, so bailees are exempt when the owner is with them.

items.text: For one who requires reduction: one verse suffices
items.text_en: For one who requires reduction: one verse suffices
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: for the one who holds that shlichut yad requires a reduction, why do we need two verses? One verse is needed to teach that the derived law cannot be more stringent than the source.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: for the one who holds that shlichut yad requires a reduction, why are two verses needed?
The Gemara answers: one verse is needed to teach that the derived law cannot be more stringent than the source (דיו לבא מן הדין להיות כנדון).

items.text: The other verse: for the oath
items.text_en: The other verse: for the oath
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the other verse is used for the teaching of a baraita: the verse 'and the master of the house shall approach God' refers to an oath, not a judgment, derived from a verbal analogy of shlichut yad.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the other verse is used for the teaching of a baraita: the verse 'וְנִקְרַב בַּעַל הַבַּיִת אֶל הָאֱלֹהִים' refers to an oath, not a judgment, derived from a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) of שליחות יד (misappropriation).

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases where a bailee is liable for failing to safeguard deposited money properly, and states that if he guards it properly he is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a bailee who deposits money improperly is liable, but if he guards it properly he is exempt.

items.text: Gemara's question and Rabbi Yitzchak's teachings
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rabbi Yitzchak's teachings
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's first case, asking what else the bailee could have done. Rava quotes Rabbi Yitzchak who derives from a verse that money should be kept in hand. Rabbi Yitzchak then gives three additional teachings: one should keep money accessible, divide assets into three parts, and that blessing is found only in what is hidden from the eye.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's first case, asking what else the bailee could have done with the money to avoid liability.
Rava quotes Rabbi Yitzchak who derives from the verse 'וְצַרְתָּ הַכֶּסֶף בְּיָדְךָ' that even when money is tied up, it should be kept in hand.
Rabbi Yitzchak teaches that a person's money should always be kept accessible in hand, citing the same verse.
Rabbi Yitzchak teaches that a person should divide his money into three parts: one-third in land, one-third in business, and one-third kept in hand.
Rabbi Yitzchak teaches that blessing is found only in what is hidden from the eye, citing the verse 'יְצַו ה׳ אִתְּךָ אֶת הַבְּרָכָה בַּאֲסָמֶיךָ'.
The Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael adds that blessing is found only in what the eye does not control, citing the same verse.

items.text: Baraita on blessing and measurement
items.text_en: Baraita on blessing and measurement
items.desc_en: A Baraita teaches that one prays for blessing before measuring his grain, but blessing is not found in measured, weighed, or counted items, only in what is hidden from the eye.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one going to measure his granary should pray for blessing before measuring.
If one begins measuring, he says a blessing over the pile, but blessing after measuring is a vain prayer.
The baraita explains that blessing is not found in weighed, measured, or counted items, but only in what is hidden from the eye.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on safeguarding coins and later additions
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on safeguarding coins and later additions
items.desc_en: Shmuel rules that coins can only be safeguarded by burying them in the ground. Rava adds exceptions for Friday twilight and for a Torah scholar who might need coins for Havdalah. The Gemara then discusses contemporary concerns: informers, Persians, and thieves, requiring hiding in ceilings, between beams, or within a handbreadth of the floor or ceiling.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that coins can only be safeguarded by burying them in the ground.
Rava adds exceptions to Shmuel's rule: Friday twilight when the Sages did not impose the burden, and a Torah scholar who might need coins for Havdalah.
The Gemara discusses contemporary concerns: informers require hiding in the ceiling, Persians require between beams, and thieves require within a handbreadth of the floor or ceiling.

items.text: Inquiry about required depth for hiding coins
items.text_en: Inquiry about required depth for hiding coins
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yosef asks Rav Ashi whether the three handbreadths required for hiding leaven (so a dog cannot find it) are also needed for hiding coins. Rav Ashi distinguishes: leaven requires three handbreadths due to smell, but coins only need one handbreadth for concealment from sight.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Yosef's question to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Yosef's question to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yosef asks Rav Ashi whether the three handbreadths required for hiding leaven (so a dog cannot find it) are also required for hiding coins.
Rav Ashi distinguishes: leaven requires three handbreadths due to smell, but coins only need concealment from sight, not three handbreadths.
Rafram from Sikra rules that one handbreadth (טפח) suffices for hiding coins from sight.

items.text: Case of coins placed in a reed hut and stolen
items.text_en: Case of coins placed in a reed hut and stolen
items.desc_en: A man deposited coins with a friend who placed them in a reed hut; they were stolen. Rav Yosef rules that since the placement was negligent regarding fire but secure regarding thieves, it is a case of initial negligence followed by unavoidable loss, and the bailee is liable. An alternative version says he is exempt, but the halakha follows that he is liable.

sub.desc_en: A man deposited coins with a friend who placed them in a reed hut, and they were stolen.
Rav Yosef rules that although the location was safe from thieves, it was negligent regarding fire, so the bailee is liable for beginning with negligence.
An alternative opinion holds that since it was safe from thieves, the bailee is exempt despite negligence regarding fire.
The halacha concludes that if the bailee began with negligence, he is liable even if the loss was ultimately due to an unavoidable accident.

items.text: Case of bailee who forgot where he placed the coins
items.text_en: Case of bailee who forgot where he placed the coins
items.desc_en: A bailee who says 'I don't know where I put them' is deemed negligent and must pay, as Rava rules.

sub.desc_en: A man deposited coins with a friend who later claimed he did not know where he placed them.
Rava rules that any claim of 'I don't know' is negligence, and the bailee must pay.

items.text: Case of coins given to the bailee's mother and stolen
items.text_en: Case of coins given to the bailee's mother and stolen
items.desc_en: A bailee gave deposited coins to his mother, who placed them in a basket, and they were stolen. Rava questions how to judge this case, beginning to consider whether to hold the bailee liable.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a case: a man deposited coins with his friend, who gave them to his mother, who placed them in a basket, and they were stolen.
Rava asks how the judges should adjudicate this case, beginning to consider whether to hold the bailee liable.
The gemara begins to articulate a possible ruling: should we tell the bailee himself to go and pay, and then he says...

items.text: First case: deposit with wife and children
items.text_en: First case: deposit with wife and children
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers a case where a depositor entrusts money to a bailee, who gives it to his mother for safekeeping. The mother claims she thought it was her son's money and buried it, and the bailee argues he didn't correct her to ensure better care. The discussion explores the liability of each party.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with the principle that a depositor entrusts money with the understanding that the bailee may involve his wife and children.
The Gemara asks: why not tell the mother to pay, since she claims she buried the money thinking it was her son's?
The bailee responds that by claiming the money was his own, he ensured greater care from his mother.

items.text: Rava's ruling on the first case
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on the first case
items.desc_en: Rava rules that the bailee swears he gave the money to his mother, and the mother swears she placed it in a basket and it was stolen, and both are exempt from liability.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the case by ruling that the bailee swears he gave the money to his mother, the mother swears she placed it in a basket and it was stolen, and both are exempt from liability.

items.text: Second case: guardian buys a cow for orphans
items.text_en: Second case: guardian buys a cow for orphans
items.desc_en: A guardian buys a cow for orphans and entrusts it to a herdsman. The cow dies because it cannot eat. Rami bar Chama asks how to judge. The herdsman is a paid guardian and should have checked for loss, but here there was no loss because the cow's owner was found and paid. The dispute is between the cow's owner and the guardian.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case: a guardian bought a cow for orphans and entrusted it to a herdsman; the cow died because it could not eat.
Rami bar Chama asks how the judges should adjudicate this case.
The guardian argues that he should not pay because he entrusted the cow to the herdsman.
The herdsman argues that he placed the cow with other cattle and provided food, so he did not know it was not eating.
The Gemara resolves that the herdsman, as a paid guardian (שומר שכר), should have checked for loss, but here there was no loss to the orphans because the cow's owner was found and compensated them.

items.text: Resolution of the second case
items.text_en: Resolution of the second case
items.desc_en: The cow's owner claims the guardian should have informed him. The guardian argues it was a mistaken transaction, but since the guardian bought from a middleman, the owner swears he didn't know, and the herdsman pays the cheap meat price.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the plaintiff in this case, and answers that it is the cow's owner.
The Gemara objects that the guardian should have informed the owner, but then notes that the owner already knows it was a mistaken transaction.
The Gemara resolves that since the guardian bought from a middleman, the owner swears he didn't know, and the herdsman pays the cheap meat price.

items.text: Third case: deposit of wine with a friend
items.text_en: Third case: deposit of wine with a friend
items.desc_en: A man deposits wine with a friend who also has his own wine. He tells the servant to pour from his own wine, but the servant pours from the other. Rav Amram asks how to judge. The owner says he instructed correctly, and the servant says he wasn't told not to pour from the other.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a case: a man deposited wine (כשותא) with a friend who also had his own wine; he instructed the servant to pour from his own, but the servant poured from the other.
Rav Amram asks how the judges should rule in this case.
The owner argues that he instructed the servant correctly, so he is not liable.
The servant argues that he was not explicitly told not to pour from the other wine, so he is not liable.

items.text: Discussion on liability and loss
items.text_en: Discussion on liability and loss
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether the servant's delay in bringing wine indicates consent, and whether there is any loss since the wine takes root. Rav Sama bar Rava says the wine was vinegar, and Rav Ashi says it was in bags, implying a loss.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the servant's delay in bringing wine indicates consent to the substitution, implying no loss.
The Gemara clarifies that the case is where the servant did not delay, so there is no indication of consent.
The Gemara asks what loss there is, since the wine takes root in the ground and thus benefits the owner.
Rav Sama bar Rava answers that the wine was vinegar (חַלָּא), which is a loss because vinegar does not improve with rooting.
Rav Ashi answers that the wine was in bags (כִּיסֵי), which do not take root, so there is a loss.

items.text: Transition from previous Mishnah
items.text_en: Transition from previous Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the previous Mishnah's discussion about a bailee who uses a money pouch, stating that he pays the value of the pouch.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the previous discussion by stating that the bailee pays the value of the pouch.

items.text: Mishnah: Depositing money with a money-changer or homeowner
items.text_en: Mishnah: Depositing money with a money-changer or homeowner
items.desc_en: The Mishnah distinguishes between a money-changer and a homeowner regarding the use of deposited money. If the money is tied (and sealed), the bailee may not use it and is not liable for loss; if loose, he may use it and is liable. A storekeeper is like a homeowner according to Rabbi Meir, but like a money-changer according to Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the laws of depositing money with a money-changer or a householder, distinguishing between bound and loose coins, and records the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda regarding the status of a storekeeper.
The Mishnah states that with a homeowner, whether tied or loose, the bailee may not use the money and is not liable for loss.
Rabbi Meir rules that a storekeeper is like a homeowner.
Rabbi Yehuda rules that a storekeeper is like a money-changer.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying 'tied' money
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying 'tied' money
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions what 'tied' means. Rav Asi quoting Rav Yehuda says it means tied and sealed. Rav Mari says it means a distinctive knot. Some say Rav Mari asked about a distinctive knot, and the answer is unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's implication that mere binding prevents use.
Rav Asi in the name of Rav Yehuda explains that the Mishnah refers to coins that are both bound and sealed.
Rav Mari offers an alternative explanation: the coins are tied with an unusual knot.
Some transmit that Rav Mari raised a question: what is the definition of an unusual knot?
The Gemara leaves the question unresolved with 'תֵּיקוּ' (let it stand).

items.text: Rav Huna: Liability even for unavoidable loss
items.text_en: Rav Huna: Liability even for unavoidable loss
items.desc_en: Rav Huna says that if the bailee uses the money, he is liable even for unavoidable loss (ones). The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah's term 'lost' includes cases like a ship sinking at sea, as per Rabbah's distinction between theft and loss.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna states that the bailee is liable even for unavoidable accidents (אונסין).
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah only mentions 'lost' (אבוד), not 'forced' (אונס).
Rabbah explains that 'lost' (אבוד) in the Mishnah includes cases of unavoidable accident, such as a ship sinking at sea.

items.text: Rav Nachman: No liability for ones, but is a paid bailee
items.text_en: Rav Nachman: No liability for ones, but is a paid bailee
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman disagrees, saying he is not liable for ones. Rava challenges him: if he is not a borrower, he is not even a paid bailee. Rav Nachman concedes that since he benefits from the money (e.g., using it for profitable opportunities), he becomes a paid bailee.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman disagrees, stating that the bailee is not liable for unavoidable accidents.
Rava challenges Rav Nachman: if he is not a borrower (שואל), he is not even a paid bailee (שומר שכר), so why is he liable at all?
Rav Nachman concedes that because the bailee benefits from the potential profit opportunity, he becomes a paid bailee (שומר שכר).

items.text: Rav Nachman's objection to Rav Huna from a baraita
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's objection to Rav Huna from a baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman cites a baraita about Temple funds: if a money-changer uses loose money, the treasurer is liable for misuse (me'ilah) only if he actually spent it. This implies that without spending, there is no liability, contradicting Rav Huna. Rav Huna deflects, saying the baraita's case is the same even without spending, but it mentions 'spent' to parallel the first clause.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman cites a baraita about Temple funds: if a money-changer uses loose money, the treasurer is liable for misuse (מעילה) only if he actually spent it, implying that without spending there is no liability.

Rav Nachman challenges Rav Huna: if you say the depositor is liable even for unavoidable loss (אונסין), why does the baraita specifically mention 'spent' — even without spending there would be liability.
Rav Huna deflects, saying the baraita's case is the same even without spending, but it mentions 'spent' to parallel the first clause.

items.text: Mishnah: One who misappropriates a deposit
items.text_en: Mishnah: One who misappropriates a deposit
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses a bailee who uses a deposit. Beit Shammai say he pays according to the time of the depreciation or appreciation; Beit Hillel say according to the time of the court's ruling; Rabbi Akiva says according to the time of the claim.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute regarding a bailee who misappropriates a deposit: Beit Shammai, Beit Hillel, and Rabbi Akiva differ on the valuation time.
Beit Hillel rule that the payment is assessed according to the time the deposit is taken out of the world (i.e., when it is lost or consumed).
Rabbi Akiva rules that the payment is assessed according to the time the owner makes the claim in court.

items.text: Gemara: Rabbah's case of a stolen barrel of wine
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabbah's case of a stolen barrel of wine
items.desc_en: Rabbah illustrates the principle: if one steals a barrel of wine worth one zuz and later it is worth four, if he breaks or drinks it, he pays four (the value at the time of the act). If it breaks on its own, he pays one (the value at the time of the theft), because he did nothing to it.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah states the law: if one steals a barrel of wine worth one zuz that later appreciates to four, if he breaks or drinks it he pays four, but if it breaks on its own he pays one.

The Gemara explains the reasoning: since the barrel could be returned intact, the act of breaking or drinking constitutes a new גזילה (theft) at the current value, while if it breaks on its own, the thief is liable only for the value at the time of the original theft.

items.text: Gemara: Interpreting Beit Hillel's 'at the time of removal'
items.text_en: Gemara: Interpreting Beit Hillel's 'at the time of removal'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Beit Hillel means by 'at the time of removal' – if from the world (death), then in a case of depreciation, who would disagree? The Mishnah already says all robbers pay at the time of the robbery. And if it means appreciation, that is Beit Shammai's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah and asks what Beit Hillel means by 'at the time of removal'.
The Gemara proposes that 'removal' might mean removal from the world, i.e., death.
The Gemara objects: if it refers to depreciation, who would disagree, since the Mishnah already rules that all robbers pay at the time of the robbery.
The Gemara objects further: if it refers to appreciation, that is already Beit Shammai's position.

items.text: Rabbah's position aligned with Beit Shammai?
items.text_en: Rabbah's position aligned with Beit Shammai?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbah's view that shelichut yad is judged at the time of removal from the owner's domain aligns with Beit Shammai. It explains that all agree on a case of excess (yater), and the dispute is only about deficiency (chaser). Beit Shammai holds that shelichut yad does not require a deficiency, while Beit Hillel holds that it does.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbah's view that shelichut yad is judged at the time of removal aligns with Beit Shammai.
Rabbah responds that all agree on a case of excess (yater), and the dispute is only about deficiency (chaser).

sub.text: Stam's explanation of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
sub.text_en: Stam's explanation of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Beit Shammai holds shelichut yad does not require a deficiency, while Beit Hillel holds it does.

items.text: Rava's position on shelichut yad without deficiency
items.text_en: Rava's position on shelichut yad without deficiency
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rava's statement that shelichut yad does not require a deficiency, suggesting it aligns with Beit Shammai. It reinterprets the dispute as being about a borrower without knowledge (sho'el shelo mida'at): Beit Shammai considers such a borrower a robber, while Beit Hillel considers him a borrower, affecting liability for deficiencies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rava's statement that shelichut yad does not require a deficiency aligns him with Beit Shammai.
The Gemara reinterprets the dispute as being about a sho'el shelo mida'at (a borrower without knowledge), not about the requirement of deficiency.
The Gemara explains that Beit Shammai considers a sho'el shelo mida'at a robber, while Beit Hillel considers him a borrower, affecting liability for deficiencies.

items.text: Rava's view on the robber's status and the dispute over improvement
items.text_en: Rava's view on the robber's status and the dispute over improvement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rava's statement that a borrower without knowledge is considered a robber according to the Rabbis, suggesting it aligns with Beit Shammai. It explains that the dispute is actually about the improvement (shevach) of stolen property: Beit Shammai holds that the improvement belongs to the victim, while Beit Hillel holds it belongs to the robber.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Rava's statement that an unauthorized borrower is a robber according to the Rabbis — does this mean Rava holds like Beit Shammai?

The Gemara resolves: the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel here is actually about the improvement (שבח) of stolen property — Beit Shammai says it belongs to the victim, Beit Hillel says it belongs to the robber.

items.text: Support from a Tannaitic dispute and the Mishnah
items.text_en: Support from a Tannaitic dispute and the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehudah dispute the law of a robber who shears or gives birth to a stolen ewe, paralleling the dispute over improvement. It then notes that the Mishnah's phrasing (Beit Shammai says 'yilkeh b'chaser u'vyater') supports the interpretation that the dispute is about deficiency and excess.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehudah dispute the law of a robber who shears or gives birth to a stolen ewe, paralleling the dispute over improvement.
The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's phrasing (Beit Shammai says 'יִלְקֶה בְּחָסֵר וּבְיָתֵר') supports the interpretation that the dispute is about deficiency and excess.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's view on valuation at the time of claim
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's view on valuation at the time of claim
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva holds that valuation is at the time of the claim (k'sha'at hatevi'ah). Rav Yehudah citing Shmuel rules the halakhah follows Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Akiva concedes that if there are witnesses, the valuation is at the time of the oath, based on the verse 'la'asher hu lo yitnenu b'yom ashmato'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva states that the valuation of the stolen object is at the time of the claim (כִּשְׁעַת הַתְּבִיעָה).
Rav Yehudah reports in the name of Shmuel that the binding law (הֲלָכָה) follows Rabbi Akiva's position.

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Akiva concedes that when there are witnesses, the valuation is at the time of the oath, based on the verse 'לַאֲשֶׁר הוּא לוֹ יִתְּנֶנּוּ בְּיוֹם אַשְׁמָתוֹ' (to whom it belongs he shall give it on the day of his guilt), since from that moment he becomes liable for the guilt-offering.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's dispute: Rabbi Akiva disagreed even with witnesses
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's dispute: Rabbi Akiva disagreed even with witnesses
items.desc_en: Rav Oshaya challenges Rav Yehudah, citing Rabbi Asi quoting Rabbi Yochanan that Rabbi Akiva disagreed even when there are witnesses, because the court imposes liability at the time of judgment, not at the time of the oath.

sub.text: Rav Oshaya's challenge to Rav Yehudah
sub.text_en: Rav Oshaya's challenge to Rav Yehudah
sub.desc_en: Rav Oshaya challenges Rav Yehudah's position that Rabbi Akiva conceded when there are witnesses.

sub.text: Rav Oshaya citing Rabbi Asi citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Oshaya citing Rabbi Asi citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rav Oshaya reports that Rabbi Yochanan said Rabbi Akiva disagreed even when there are witnesses.

sub.text: Rav Oshaya's explanation of the reasoning
sub.text_en: Rav Oshaya's explanation of the reasoning
sub.desc_en: Rav Oshaya explains that Rabbi Akiva derives from the verse that the court imposes liability at the time of judgment, not at the time of the oath.

items.text: Clarification of Rabbi Yochanan's ruling: halakhah always follows Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Clarification of Rabbi Yochanan's ruling: halakhah always follows Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira instructs Rabbi Abba bar Pappa to ask Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi whether Rabbi Yochanan ruled the halakhah follows Rabbi Akiva. The response is that Rabbi Yochanan said the halakhah follows Rabbi Akiva always (le'olam). Rav Ashi explains that 'le'olam' excludes the possibility that the ruling applies only when there are no witnesses.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira's instruction to Rabbi Abba bar Pappa
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's instruction to Rabbi Abba bar Pappa
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira instructs Rabbi Abba bar Pappa to go to Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi and ask whether Rabbi Yochanan ruled the halakhah follows Rabbi Akiva.

sub.text: Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi's response quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi's response quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi responds that Rabbi Yochanan said the halakhah follows Rabbi Akiva always (לעולם).
Rav Ashi explains that 'לעולם' excludes the possibility that the ruling applies only when there are no witnesses, but not when there are witnesses.

items.text: Additional clarification and Rava's ruling
items.text_en: Additional clarification and Rava's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara adds that the ruling also excludes the case where the deposit was returned to its place and then broken, to counter Rabbi Yishmael's view that da'at ba'alim (knowledge of the owner) is not required. It concludes that da'at ba'alim is required. Rava rules that the halakhah follows Beit Hillel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara adds that the ruling also excludes the case where the deposit was returned to its place and then broken, to counter Rabbi Yishmael's view that da'at ba'alim (knowledge of the owner) is not required, and concludes that da'at ba'alim is required.
Rava rules that the halakhah follows Beit Hillel.

items.text: Mishnah: The law of one who intends to misappropriate a deposit
items.text_en: Mishnah: The law of one who intends to misappropriate a deposit
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding one who merely intends to misappropriate a deposit: Beit Shammai holds him liable, Beit Hillel holds he is not liable until he actually acts. It then gives cases of tilting a barrel versus lifting it to determine liability.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding one who merely intends to misappropriate a deposit, citing the verse.
The Mishnah presents the case of tilting a barrel and taking a quarter-log: the bailee pays only for the quarter-log.
The Mishnah presents the case of lifting the barrel and taking a quarter-log: the bailee pays for the entire barrel.

items.text: Source for liability in a deposit
items.text_en: Source for liability in a deposit
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the law that a watchman is liable for theft. It cites a dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding the verse 'על כל דבר פשע', with Beit Shammai holding that intent alone makes one liable, and Beit Hillel requiring an actual act of taking. The Gemara then explains that the verse also includes liability for one's agent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the law that a watchman is liable for theft.

The baraita cites the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding the verse 'על כל דבר פשע', with Beit Shammai holding that intent alone makes one liable, and Beit Hillel requiring an actual act of taking.
The Gemara explains that the verse 'על כל דבר פשע' also includes liability for one's agent.

items.text: Rabbah's ruling on a tilted barrel
items.text_en: Rabbah's ruling on a tilted barrel
items.desc_en: Rabbah comments on the Mishnah's case of tilting a barrel: if it broke, the watchman pays only the difference, but if it soured, he pays the full value, because his action directly caused the damage.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah rules that the Mishnah's case of tilting a barrel applies only if it broke; if it soured, the watchman pays the full value because his action directly caused the damage.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on lifting for taking
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on lifting for taking
items.desc_en: Shmuel explains that in the Mishnah's case of lifting a barrel to take from it, the watchman is liable even if he did not actually take, because the lifting itself constitutes an act of acquisition. The Gemara questions whether this implies that Shmuel holds that an act of taking does not require a reduction in the deposit, and answers that here it is different because the watchman wants the entire barrel to serve as a base for the quarter-log he intends to take.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that lifting the barrel to take from it constitutes an act of taking (שליחות יד) even without actual removal.
The Gemara questions whether Shmuel holds that שליחות יד (misappropriation) does not require a reduction in the deposit.
The Gemara answers that here it is different because the watchman wants the entire barrel to serve as a base for the quarter-log he intends to take.

items.text: Rav Ashi's query about lifting a purse
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's query about lifting a purse
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi raises a question: if one lifted a purse to take a dinar from it, is he liable? The doubt is whether the purse is protected only by virtue of the wine (as in the barrel case) or whether the protection of the purse differs from that of the dinar. The Gemara concludes with 'תיקו' (let it stand).

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks whether lifting a purse to take a dinar from it constitutes a liable act of shlichut yad (sending a hand), given the doubt about the purse's protection compared to the barrel case.
The Gemara leaves the question unresolved with 'תיקו' (let it stand).

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter
items.desc_en: The Gemara marks the end of the chapter with the phrase 'הדרן עלך המפקיד' (we return to you, the chapter of 'המפקיד').

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the chapter with the standard formula 'הדרן עלך המפקיד' (we return to you, the chapter of 'המפקיד').

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of acquisition by money and movables
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of acquisition by money and movables
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that gold acquires silver (i.e., when one pays with gold for silver, the transaction is complete upon taking the gold), but silver does not acquire gold. Similarly, copper acquires silver, bad coins acquire good coins, and uncoined metal (אסימון) acquires a coin. Movables acquire coins, but coins do not acquire movables. The general rule is that movables acquire each other through meshikha (pulling). Rabbi Shimon says that the one holding the money has the upper hand.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that gold acquires silver, but silver does not acquire gold.
The Mishnah continues: copper acquires silver, bad coins acquire good coins, but not vice versa.
The Mishnah states that uncoined metal (אסימון) acquires a coin, and movables acquire coins, but coins do not acquire movables.
The Mishnah gives the general rule: movables acquire each other through meshikha (pulling), and a buyer who pays without pulling can retract.
The Mishnah adds a moral warning: God will exact punishment from those who renege on their word.
Rabbi Shimon states that the one holding the money has the upper hand.

items.text: Gemara: Rabbi's contradictory teachings
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabbi's contradictory teachings
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Rabbi taught his son Rabbi Shimon that gold acquires silver, but his son objected that in his youth Rabbi had taught the opposite. The Gemara explains the reasoning: in his youth, Rabbi considered gold, being more valuable, as currency (טיבעא) and silver as a commodity (פירא), so the commodity acquires the currency. In his old age, he reversed his view, considering silver as currency and gold as a commodity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Rabbi taught his son Rabbi Shimon that gold acquires silver.
Rabbi Shimon objects that in his youth Rabbi had taught the opposite rule, that silver acquires gold.
The Gemara explains that in his youth Rabbi considered gold, being more valuable, as currency (טיבעא) and silver as a commodity (פירא), so the commodity acquires the currency.
The Gemara explains that in his old age Rabbi reversed his view, considering silver as currency and gold as a commodity.

items.text: Opening principle: gold as currency vs. commodity
items.text_en: Opening principle: gold as currency vs. commodity
items.desc_en: The Gemara states a general rule: sharp (non-minted) gold is currency, while non-sharp gold is commodity, and the commodity is acquired by the currency.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the general principle: sharp (minted) gold is currency (טִבְעָא), non-sharp gold is commodity (פֵּירָא), and the commodity is acquired by the currency.

items.text: Rav Ashi's proof from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's proof from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi argues that the Mishnah's statement 'copper acquires silver' implies silver is commodity relative to gold, because if silver were currency relative to gold, the Mishnah would be redundant. The Gemara adds that the Mishnah was necessary to counter a potential assumption that local sharp coins are currency.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi opens by arguing that the Mishnah's statement 'copper acquires silver' proves that silver is commodity relative to gold, because if silver were currency relative to gold, the Mishnah would be redundant.
The Gemara objects: if silver were currency relative to gold, then it would obviously be currency relative to copper, making the Mishnah's statement unnecessary.

The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah was necessary to counter a potential assumption that local sharp coins are currency, teaching that since there is a place where they do not circulate, they are commodity.

items.text: Rabbi Chiyya's ruling supports gold as currency
items.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya's ruling supports gold as currency
items.desc_en: A story about Rav borrowing dinars from Rabbi Chiyya's daughter shows that Rabbi Chiyya considered gold currency, as he required repayment in 'good and heavy' coins, which would be forbidden if gold were a commodity subject to interest.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asserts that Rabbi Chiyya also holds the view that gold is currency (טִבְעָא).

The Gemara recounts that Rav borrowed dinars from Rabbi Chiyya's daughter, and when the value of dinars increased, Rabbi Chiyya instructed Rav to repay her with 'good and heavy' coins, which would be forbidden as interest if gold were a commodity.
The Gemara resolves that Rav had dinars at the time of the loan, so the repayment was considered a request for an extension of time, not interest.

items.text: Rava's proof from a Tannaitic source
items.text_en: Rava's proof from a Tannaitic source
items.desc_en: Rava cites a baraita that defines a prutah as 1/8 of an Italian issar, an issar as 1/24 of a silver dinar, and a silver dinar as 1/25 of a gold dinar.
