The Gemara argues that if gold were a commodity, its fluctuating value would make the fixed ratio impossible; thus gold must be currency.

sub.desc_en: Rava introduces a baraita that defines a prutah as 1/8 of an Italian issar and an issar as 1/24 of a silver dinar, and states that the Tanna holds gold is currency.
The baraita further states that a silver dinar is 1/25 of a gold dinar, used for פדיון הבן (redemption of the firstborn).
The Gemara argues that if gold were a commodity (פֵּירָא), its fluctuating value would make the fixed ratio impossible; therefore, gold must be currency (טִבְעָא).

items.text: Dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on exchanging coins
items.text_en: Dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on exchanging coins
items.desc_en: The Mishnah records a dispute: Beit Shammai prohibits exchanging silver coins for gold dinars, while Beit Hillel permits it. Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish debate whether the dispute applies only to silver coins for gold dinars or also to produce for gold dinars. The Gemara explains the reasoning behind each opinion.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited: Beit Shammai prohibits exchanging silver coins (סלעים) for gold dinars, and Beit Hillel permits it.

The Gemara presents the first opinion: Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish disagree about the scope of the dispute; one says the dispute is only about silver coins for gold dinars, but all agree that produce for gold dinars is permitted.

The Gemara explains the reasoning of the first opinion: for Beit Hillel, silver is considered currency (טִבְעָא) relative to produce, and for Beit Shammai, gold is considered currency relative to produce.
The Gemara presents the second opinion: the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel extends even to exchanging produce for gold dinars.
The Gemara objects: according to the second opinion, why did the Mishnah specify the case of silver coins for gold dinars rather than the more novel case of produce for gold dinars?

The Gemara resolves: the Mishnah teaches the case of silver coins to preempt a potential error — one might think Beit Hillel concedes to Beit Shammai regarding silver coins, so the Mishnah shows they dispute even there.

items.text: Conclusion: Rabbi Yochanan's position
items.text_en: Conclusion: Rabbi Yochanan's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yochanan is the one who holds that one may not redeem (second tithe) with gold, citing his statement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yochanan is the one who holds that one may not redeem (second tithe) with gold, citing his statement.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that it is forbidden to lend a dinar for a dinar, implying a prohibition against interest in kind.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the prohibition against lending a dinar for a dinar, implying a ban on interest in kind.

items.text: Gemara's question and initial analysis
items.text_en: Gemara's question and initial analysis
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions which type of dinar is meant, suggesting it must be a gold dinar, and that the prohibition aligns with Beit Shammai's view that gold is not considered currency for redemption, implying Rabbi Yochanan holds that one may not redeem second tithe with gold.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which type of dinar is forbidden, rejecting the possibility of a silver dinar because all agree it is currency, and concluding it must be a gold dinar.

The Gemara asks whose view this prohibition reflects, ruling out Beit Hillel who consider gold currency, and concluding it must be Beit Shammai, implying Rabbi Yochanan holds that one may not redeem second tithe with gold.

items.text: Rejection: distinction between loan and redemption
items.text_en: Rejection: distinction between loan and redemption
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the inference, arguing that Rabbi Yochanan actually permits redemption with gold, but loans are different because the Sages treated gold as a commodity for loans, as its value fluctuates.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the inference, arguing that Rabbi Yochanan actually permits redemption with gold, but loans are different because the Sages treated gold as a commodity for loans, as its value fluctuates.

items.text: Support from Ravin's report
items.text_en: Support from Ravin's report
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Ravin's report that Rabbi Yochanan explicitly said that while lending a dinar for a dinar is forbidden, one may redeem second tithe with a gold dinar, confirming the distinction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that Ravin's report supports the distinction: Rabbi Yochanan explicitly stated that while lending a dinar for a dinar is forbidden, one may redeem second tithe with a gold dinar.

items.text: First challenge from the baraita on changing a selah
items.text_en: First challenge from the baraita on changing a selah
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita where Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel dispute changing a selah into smaller coins for second tithe, and questions whether this implies that Beit Shammai permits redeeming with gold, but the Gemara deflects by noting that small coins are considered currency in places where they circulate.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yochanan's position by citing a baraita where Beit Shammai permits changing a selah into small coins for second tithe, implying they permit redeeming with gold, which contradicts the earlier assumption.
The Gemara deflects the challenge by noting that small coins (פריטי) are considered currency in places where they circulate, so the case is not comparable to gold.

items.text: Alternative version: dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish
items.text_en: Alternative version: dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents an alternative version where Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish dispute the scope of the disagreement between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel: one says it is only about silver coins for gold dinars, while the other says it extends to produce for gold dinars. The Gemara then questions and resolves the logic of the first opinion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an alternative version of the dispute, now between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish.

sub.text: First opinion (Rabbi Yochanan or Resh Lakish)
sub.text_en: First opinion (Rabbi Yochanan or Resh Lakish)
sub.desc_en: One sage states that the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel is limited to silver coins (סלעים) exchanged for gold dinars, with Beit Shammai restricting redemption to 'first silver' and Beit Hillel expanding it to 'second silver'.

sub.text: Second opinion (Resh Lakish or Rabbi Yochanan)
sub.text_en: Second opinion (Resh Lakish or Rabbi Yochanan)
sub.desc_en: The other sage argues that the dispute extends even to produce exchanged for gold dinars.
The Gemara objects: according to the opinion that limits the dispute to silver coins for gold dinars, why not also dispute silver coins for silver coins?

The Gemara resolves: if the dispute were about silver for silver, one might think Beit Hillel concedes to Beit Shammai regarding gold as produce; therefore the dispute is specifically about silver for gold to teach otherwise.

items.text: Second challenge: baraita about Jerusalem
items.text_en: Second challenge: baraita about Jerusalem
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings another baraita about changing a selah in Jerusalem, which seems to show that even silver can be redeemed with small coins, implying that gold should also be redeemable. This challenges the view that gold is not considered currency.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about changing a selah of second tithe in Jerusalem, where Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel dispute how much small change one may receive.

The Gemara infers that since silver can be redeemed for small coins (פריטי) without invoking the rule of 'first silver and not second silver', surely gold, which is more valuable, should also be redeemable, challenging the view that gold is not currency.

items.text: Rava's distinction: Jerusalem is different
items.text_en: Rava's distinction: Jerusalem is different
items.desc_en: Rava responds that Jerusalem is different because the verse explicitly allows purchasing any food with the money, so the rules of redemption are more lenient there.

sub.desc_en: Rava rejects the challenge by distinguishing Jerusalem, where the verse explicitly permits purchasing any food with the money, thus allowing more lenient redemption rules.

items.text: Final resolution and conclusion
items.text_en: Final resolution and conclusion
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings the baraita again and concludes that all agree that the verse 'the silver' includes even second silver, and the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish is about whether the prohibition of lending a dinar for a dinar applies to gold, with one opinion holding that we decree a prohibition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about redeeming a sela of second tithe with smaller coins, citing the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel.

The Gemara concludes that all agree the verse 'הכסף' includes even second silver, and the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish is about whether we decree a prohibition for lending a gold dinar for a gold dinar.

items.text: Beit Hillel's reasoning on delaying ascent
items.text_en: Beit Hillel's reasoning on delaying ascent
items.desc_en: Beit Hillel holds that we do not decree a delay in ascending because even if the coins are not full, one can still ascend. However, all agree that produce for dinars is redeemed because it will not be delayed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises the concern that one might delay ascending to Jerusalem because the coins are not full in the dinar.
Beit Hillel holds that we do not decree a delay because even if the coins are not full, one can still ascend.
All agree that produce for dinars is redeemed because it will not be delayed.

items.text: Alternative version on produce for dinars
items.text_en: Alternative version on produce for dinars
items.desc_en: One Amora states that even regarding produce for dinars there is a dispute, contrary to the previous unanimous ruling.

sub.desc_en: An anonymous Amora states an alternative version: even regarding produce for dinars there is a dispute, contrary to the previous unanimous ruling.

items.text: Gemara's question on the two versions
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the two versions
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the version that says the dispute is biblical, because then the Mishnah should use 'mechallel' and 'lo mechallel' rather than 'ya'aseh' and 'lo ya'aseh'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the version that says the dispute is biblical, because then the Mishnah should use 'מחללינן' and 'לא מחללינן' rather than 'יעשה' and 'לא יעשה'.

items.text: Rav and Levi dispute whether coin becomes halipin
items.text_en: Rav and Levi dispute whether coin becomes halipin
items.desc_en: Rav and Levi argue: one says coin can be used for halipin, the other says not. Rav Pappa explains the latter's reasoning: one's mind is on the form, which is liable to be nullified.

sub.desc_en: The gemara reports a dispute between Rav and Levi: one says a coin can be used for halipin (formal acquisition by exchange), the other says it cannot.

Rav Pappa explains the reasoning of the one who says coin cannot be used for halipin: because one's mind is on the form (צורתא) of the coin, and the form is liable to be nullified (by the government).

items.text: Proof from Mishnah: gold acquires silver
items.text_en: Proof from Mishnah: gold acquires silver
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove from the Mishnah that gold acquires silver through halipin, but rejects this, explaining it is through purchase (damim). It then brings a baraita to support the damim interpretation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's statement that gold acquires silver proves that coinage can serve as a medium of exchange (חליפין).
The Gemara rejects the proof, explaining that the Mishnah refers to purchase (דמים) rather than exchange, and cites a variant text that uses the term 'מחייב' (obligates) instead of 'קונה' (acquires).

The Gemara supports the interpretation of purchase (דמים) by noting that the Mishnah's continuation states silver does not acquire gold, which would be inconsistent if exchange (חליפין) were involved.
A baraita is cited that explicitly describes a case where silver does not acquire gold, reinforcing the purchase (דמים) interpretation and rejecting the exchange (חליפין) possibility.

items.text: Counter-proof from Mishnah's language
items.text_en: Counter-proof from Mishnah's language
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that if it is damim, the Mishnah should say 'nit'chayyev gavra' rather than 'nikneh kesef bechol makom shehu'. This supports the halipin interpretation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the Mishnah refers to damim (payment), it should say 'the person becomes liable' rather than 'the silver is acquired wherever it is'.

items.text: Rav Ashi's resolution: damim with specific coins
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's resolution: damim with specific coins
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves that it is damim, and 'bechol makom shehu' means 'as specified' – the seller can demand coins from a specific purse, not just any coins.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves that the Mishnah's case is indeed דמים (payment), and the phrase 'בכל מקום שהוא' means 'as specified' — the seller can demand coins from a specific purse, not just any coins.

items.text: Rav Pappa: coin can be acquired through halipin
items.text_en: Rav Pappa: coin can be acquired through halipin
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa argues that even according to the view that coin does not effect halipin, it can be acquired through halipin, analogous to fruit for Rav Nachman.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa argues that even according to the view that a coin does not effect חליפין (exchange acquisition), it can itself be acquired through חליפין, analogous to fruit for Rav Nachman.

items.text: Objection from a baraita
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita
items.desc_en: A baraita is brought that seems to contradict Rav Pappa's ruling, describing a case where one gives produce as a gift without money.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita describing a case where one standing in the granary without money gives produce as a gift, which seems to contradict Rav Pappa's ruling about the status of coins in exchange.

items.text: Gemara's initial proof that מטבע is not acquired by חליפין
items.text_en: Gemara's initial proof that מטבע is not acquired by חליפין
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that if one had coins in hand, he could redeem second tithe by giving them directly, implying coins are not acquired by חליפין. It rejects alternative methods (via sudar or land) and concludes that the Mishnah's case involves a person with no possessions, proving the point.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that if one had coins in hand, he could redeem second tithe by giving them directly, implying coins are not acquired by חליפין (exchange).

The Gemara objects that if coins could be acquired by חליפין, the Mishnah could have described acquisition via a sudar or land, but it rejects these possibilities because the person lacks such possessions.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah describes a person with no possessions, proving that מטבע (coin) is not acquired by חליפין.

items.text: Supporting statements from later Amoraim
items.text_en: Supporting statements from later Amoraim
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa retracted his earlier view, as illustrated by a story where he transferred money via acquisition of a doorstep. Ulla, Rav Asi, and Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan all explicitly state that a coin cannot serve as חליפין.

sub.text: Gemara's report of Rav Pappa's retraction
sub.text_en: Gemara's report of Rav Pappa's retraction
sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that Rav Pappa retracted his earlier view, illustrated by a story where he transferred money via acquisition of a doorstep.
Ulla explicitly states that a coin cannot serve as חליפין (exchange acquisition).
Rav Asi also states that a coin cannot serve as חליפין.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah cites Rabbi Yochanan, who also states that a coin cannot serve as חליפין.

items.text: Challenge from Rabbi Abba to Ulla
items.text_en: Challenge from Rabbi Abba to Ulla
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba challenges Ulla with a baraita: if a person has coins at home, he may ask a money-changer for coins to pay workers, promising to repay with better coins. If coins were not acquired by חליפין, this would be a prohibited loan. Ulla is silent.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba challenges Ulla with a baraita: if a person has coins at home, he may ask a money-changer for coins to pay workers, promising to repay with better coins; if coins were not acquired by חליפין (exchange), this would be a prohibited loan.
Ulla remains silent in response to the challenge.

items.text: First answer: the baraita deals with פרוטות
items.text_en: First answer: the baraita deals with פרוטות
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the baraita refers to פרוטות (small copper coins), which lack a minted face and are considered produce, thus can be acquired by חליפין. The language 'יפה דינר וטריסית' supports this, as it describes the coins as 'good' (produce-like).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the baraita deals with פרוטות (small copper coins) which lack a minted face and are considered produce, thus can be acquired by חליפין (exchange), and the language 'יפה דינר וטריסית' supports this.

items.text: Second answer by Rav Ashi: it is a promise to pay
items.text_en: Second answer by Rav Ashi: it is a promise to pay
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that since the person has coins at home, the transaction is not a loan but a promise to pay later, like saying 'lend me until my son comes' – thus no issue of חליפין arises.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the case involves coins and small change, and since the person has coins at home, it is like saying 'lend me until my son comes or until I find the key' – a promise to pay, not a חליפין (exchange) transaction.

items.text: Final challenge from a baraita and resolution
items.text_en: Final challenge from a baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita states that 'whatever is made money for another' – i.e., a coin – creates liability through חליפין, contradicting the earlier conclusion. Rav Yehuda explains that the baraita actually refers to the acquisition of the coin itself, not using it as a medium for חליפין.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita stating that 'whatever is made money for another' (a coin) creates liability through חליפין (exchange), challenging the conclusion that a coin cannot be acquired through חליפין.
Rav Yehuda resolves the contradiction by explaining that the baraita actually refers to the acquisition of the coin itself, not using it as a medium for חליפין.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and initial inference
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and initial inference
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all movable property can acquire one another through barter. The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's example that this applies even to produce, supporting the view that produce can effect acquisition.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all movable property can acquire one another through barter, and once one party takes possession, the other becomes obligated in the exchange.
The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's example that this applies even to produce, supporting the view that produce can effect acquisition.

items.text: Clarifying the Mishnah's intent
items.text_en: Clarifying the Mishnah's intent
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's example was not about coins but about produce, teaching that produce can also effect barter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the initial assumption that the Mishnah discussed coins, clarifying that the example of bartering an ox for a cow or a donkey for an ox demonstrates that produce can effect barter (חליפין).

items.text: Challenge from Rav Nachman's view
items.text_en: Challenge from Rav Nachman's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that this explanation works for Rav Sheishet, who holds that produce can effect barter, but for Rav Nachman, who holds that only a vessel can effect barter, the Mishnah's example must be reinterpreted as referring to the value of an animal, not the animal itself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's example works for Rav Sheishet, who holds that produce can effect barter, but challenges: for Rav Nachman, who holds that only a vessel can effect barter, what does the Mishnah's 'how so' example mean?
The Gemara resolves the challenge by reinterpreting the Mishnah's example as referring to the value (דמים) of an animal, not the animal itself, consistent with Rav Nachman's view.

items.text: Rav Nachman's reasoning and Rabbi Yochanan's principle
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's reasoning and Rabbi Yochanan's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rav Nachman follows Rabbi Yochanan, who holds that by Torah law money effects acquisition, but the Sages instituted meshichah to prevent loss. The distinction is made between common and uncommon cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is Rav Nachman's reasoning for his position that only a vessel (כלי) effects acquisition by חליפין (exchange), but not produce.

The Gemara answers that Rav Nachman follows Rabbi Yochanan, who holds that by Torah law money (מעות) effects acquisition, but the Sages instituted meshichah (משיכה) as the mode of acquisition to prevent the seller from saying 'your wheat was burned in the loft' after receiving payment.

The Gemara resolves that the Sages decreed meshichah only for a common case (מילתא דשכיחא) like produce, but not for an uncommon case (מילתא דלא שכיחא) like a vessel, which is why Rav Nachman distinguishes between them.

items.text: Reish Lakish's position and resolution
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's position and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers Reish Lakish, who holds meshichah is Torah law. If he agrees with Rav Sheishet, the Mishnah is straightforward; if he agrees with Rav Nachman, he must still resolve it like Rav Sheishet.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by considering Reish Lakish's view that meshichah is explicitly from the Torah, and notes that if he agrees with Rav Sheishet, he resolves the Mishnah like Rav Sheishet.
The Gemara questions how Reish Lakish could resolve the Mishnah if he agrees with Rav Nachman, who holds that produce does not effect exchange and coin does not acquire.
The Gemara resolves that Reish Lakish must necessarily resolve the Mishnah like Rav Sheishet, regardless of his own view.

items.text: Reish Lakish's ruling on coins and the necessity of both cases
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's ruling on coins and the necessity of both cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Reish Lakish's statement that even a bag of coins can acquire another bag of coins through barter. Rav Acha explains this refers to invalid coins. The Gemara explains why both cases of invalid coins (by kingdom and by province) are necessary.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah that movable property acquires one another through barter, and Reish Lakish's statement that even a bag of coins can acquire another bag of coins through barter.
Rav Acha explains that Reish Lakish's statement refers specifically to invalid coins, one disqualified by the kingdom and one disqualified by the province.

The Gemara explains why both cases of invalid coins are necessary: if only kingdom-disqualified coins were taught, one might think province-disqualified coins are still valid currency and cannot be acquired through barter.

The Gemara completes the analysis: if only province-disqualified coins were taught, one might think kingdom-disqualified coins are still usable privately and thus still currency, so both cases are necessary.

items.text: Rav Huna's statement on 'sell to me with these'
items.text_en: Rav Huna's statement on 'sell to me with these'
items.desc_en: The daf concludes with Rav Huna's ruling that if one says 'sell to me with these' (pointing to specific items), the buyer acquires the item.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah reports Rav Huna's ruling that if a buyer says 'sell to me with these' (pointing to specific coins or items), the buyer acquires the item immediately.

items.text: The case of 'sell to me with these' and the dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Abba
items.text_en: The case of 'sell to me with these' and the dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Abba
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case where a buyer says 'sell to me with these' and pays with specific coins. Rav Huna rules that the buyer acquires the item (since he is not particular about the coins, it is like barter) but can claim overcharge. Rav Abba reports Rav Huna's alternative view that the buyer acquires and cannot claim overcharge.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the case of 'sell to me with these' and states that the buyer acquires the item and can claim overcharge.
Rav Huna rules that the buyer acquires the item and can claim overcharge because the buyer said 'sell to me with these'.
Rav Abba reports Rav Huna's alternative view that the buyer acquires the item but cannot claim overcharge.

items.text: The case of barter with particularity: Rav Adda bar Ahavah's proof
items.text_en: The case of barter with particularity: Rav Adda bar Ahavah's proof
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether barter works when the parties are particular about the items. Rav Adda bar Ahavah brings a baraita about a barter of a cow for a donkey where the donkey dies before the cow's owner pulls the donkey. The baraita rules that the cow's owner does not acquire the donkey, proving that particularity in barter prevents acquisition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the parties are particular about the items in a barter, does the barter still effect acquisition?
Rav Adda bar Ahavah brings a baraita about a barter of a cow for a donkey where the donkey dies before the cow's owner pulls it, and the baraita rules the cow's owner does not acquire the cow.
The Gemara concludes from the baraita that when the parties are particular about the items in a barter, the barter does not effect acquisition.

items.text: Rava's rejection: The baraita is about a partial barter
items.text_en: Rava's rejection: The baraita is about a partial barter
items.desc_en: Rava rejects the proof, arguing that all barter involves particularity yet is valid. He explains that the baraita deals with a case where the barter is for multiple items (a donkey for a cow and a lamb), and the cow's owner only pulled the cow but not the lamb, so the pulling is incomplete.

sub.desc_en: Rava rejects the proof from the baraita, arguing that all barter involves particularity yet is valid, and explains that the baraita deals with a case of a partial barter (a donkey for a cow and a lamb) where the pulling was incomplete.

items.text: The implication of Rav Huna's view on whether coins can be used for barter
items.text_en: The implication of Rav Huna's view on whether coins can be used for barter
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rav Huna's ruling that 'sell to me with these' acquires but allows overcharge implies that coins can serve as barter (חליפין). It answers that Rav Huna follows Rabbi Yochanan, who holds that by Torah law money acquires, but the Sages instituted meshichah to prevent loss. Since the buyer is not particular, the Sages did not apply their decree. Mar Huna bar Rav Nachman reports that Rav Huna explicitly said coins cannot be used for barter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rav Huna's ruling that 'sell to me with these' acquires but allows overcharge implies that coins can be used as barter (חליפין).

The Gemara answers that Rav Huna follows Rabbi Yochanan, who holds that by Torah law money acquires, but the Sages instituted meshichah to prevent loss; since the buyer is not particular, the Sages did not apply their decree.

sub.text: Mar Huna bar Rav Nachman's report to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Mar Huna bar Rav Nachman's report to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Mar Huna bar Rav Nachman reports to Rav Ashi that Rav Huna explicitly said coins cannot be used for barter (חליפין).

items.text: The dispute between Rav and Levi: whose vessel effects the barter?
items.text_en: The dispute between Rav and Levi: whose vessel effects the barter?
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the mechanism of barter: Rav says the vessel of the buyer (קונה) effects the acquisition, while Levi says it is the vessel of the seller (מקנה). Rav Huna from Diskarta challenges Levi's view, arguing that it would allow land to be acquired with a cloak, contradicting the rule that movable property is acquired with land, not vice versa. Rava defends Levi, explaining that the seller's intent to please the buyer causes him to transfer ownership.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: by what means does one acquire through barter (חליפין)?
Rav states that the vessel of the buyer (קונה) effects the acquisition, because the buyer's satisfaction causes him to complete the transfer.
Levi states that the vessel of the seller (מקנה) effects the acquisition, as will be explained later.
Rav Huna from Diskarta objects to Levi's view, arguing that it would allow land to be acquired with a cloak, contradicting the rule that movable property is acquired with land, not vice versa.
Rava defends Levi, explaining that the seller's intent to please the buyer causes him to transfer ownership, so the cloak does not directly acquire the land.

items.text: The biblical source for barter and the dispute between Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet
items.text_en: The biblical source for barter and the dispute between Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse from Ruth about the shoe (נעל) as the source for barter. A dispute arises: Rav Nachman holds that only a vessel (like a shoe) can be used for barter, not produce, based on the word 'na'alo'. Rav Sheshet argues that any item can be used, based on the phrase 'to confirm every matter'. Rav Sheshet limits this to items that are defined (מסוים), excluding half-pomegranates.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verse from Ruth (Ruth 4:7) as the source for barter (תמורה), explaining that 'ge'ulah' refers to sale and 'temurah' to barter.
The Gemara asks who gave the shoe to whom in the verse, and records a dispute: Rabbi Yehuda holds that the redeemer (גואל) gave it to Boaz.
A baraita states that acquisition is performed with a vessel (כלי) even if it is not worth a perutah, and Rav Nachman limits this to a vessel, not produce.
Rav Sheshet argues that even produce can be used for acquisition, while Rav Nachman derives from the word 'na'alo' (his shoe) that only a shoe-like item (a vessel) is valid.

The Gemara asks Rav Sheshet's reasoning, who cites the phrase 'to confirm every matter' (לְקַיֵּם כָּל דָּבָר), and then objects that Rav Nachman could also use that phrase to include all items acquired with a shoe.
Rav Sheshet resolves that just as 'na'alo' refers to a defined item (דָּבָר הַמְסוּיָּים), so too any defined item is valid, excluding half-pomegranates and half-nuts.

items.text: The practical formula for a kinyan today
items.text_en: The practical formula for a kinyan today
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet bar Rav Idi explains that the standard formula in documents today is 'with a vessel fit to acquire with it', which excludes Rav Sheshet's view (produce) and Shmuel's view (coins).

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet bar Rav Idi explains that the standard formula in documents today ('with a vessel fit to acquire with it') excludes Rav Sheshet's view (produce) and Shmuel's view (coins).

items.text: Interpretation of the verse's extra words
items.text_en: Interpretation of the verse's extra words
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the exegetical function of the words 'לְמִקְנְיָא' and 'בֵּיהּ' in the verse, with Rav Papa and Rav Zevid (or Rav Ashi) offering different opinions on what is excluded.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the word 'לְמִקְנְיָא' excludes a Levite's acquisition by a kidney, teaching that the verse refers to an actual acquisition (מקנה) rather than a transfer (אקנויי).
Rav Papa interprets the word 'בֵּיהּ' as excluding coinage from the acquisition process.

sub.text: Rav Zevid or Rav Ashi's opinion
sub.text_en: Rav Zevid or Rav Ashi's opinion
sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid (or alternatively Rav Ashi) interprets the word 'בֵּיהּ' as excluding items forbidden for benefit.

An alternative version of the dispute assigns the exclusion of coinage to 'בֵּיהּ' and the exclusion of forbidden items to 'דְּכָשַׁר', while noting that the word 'מוֹרִיקָא' (a type of exchange) requires no exclusion.

items.text: Definition of asimon
items.text_en: Definition of asimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara defines 'asimon' as coins given as a token for the bathhouse, but a baraita contradicts this. Rabbi Yochanan resolves the contradiction by redefining asimon as a 'pulsa' (a small coin), and links this to Rabbi Dosa and Rabbi Yishmael's views.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'asimon' means.
Rav defines 'asimon' as coins given as a token for the bathhouse.
A baraita is cited that distinguishes between 'asimon' and 'coins given as a token for the bathhouse', contradicting Rav's definition.
Rabbi Yochanan redefines 'asimon' as a 'pulsa' (a small coin), resolving the contradiction.
Rabbi Yochanan links his view to Rabbi Dosa and Rabbi Yishmael, who both include items with a form for redemption of second tithe, and contrasts with Rabbi Akiva's broader inclusion.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan: Money acquires by Torah law, meshikha is a rabbinic decree
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan: Money acquires by Torah law, meshikha is a rabbinic decree
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that by Torah law money effects acquisition, but the Sages instituted meshikha as a safeguard against the seller's negligence in case of fire. The Gemara refines the reason to a case of unavoidable fire.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that by Torah law money acquires, but the Sages instituted meshikha (משיכה, pulling) as a decree lest the seller claim his wheat was burned in the loft.
The Gemara objects: ultimately, the arsonist must pay, so the seller's claim is false.
The Gemara refines the reason: the decree is for a case of unavoidable fire, where the seller would not exert himself to save goods that are no longer his.

items.text: Reish Lakish: Meshikha is from the Torah
items.text_en: Reish Lakish: Meshikha is from the Torah
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish argues that meshikha is explicitly derived from the verse 'אוֹ קָנֹה מִיַּד עֲמִיתֶךָ', indicating acquisition from hand to hand. Rabbi Yochanan counters that the verse excludes land from ona'ah. Reish Lakish retorts that the extra 'אוֹ קָנֹה' teaches meshikha, while Rabbi Yochanan uses it to include the seller's ona'ah.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish opens by asserting that meshikha (acquisition by pulling) is explicitly derived from the Torah.
The Gemara asks for the scriptural basis of Reish Lakish's position.
The Gemara explains that Reish Lakish derives meshikha from the verse 'אוֹ קָנֹה מִיַּד עֲמִיתֶךָ', indicating acquisition from hand to hand.
Rabbi Yochanan counters that the word 'מִיַּד' excludes land from the law of ona'ah (overreaching).
Reish Lakish retorts that if the verse only intended to exclude land, it could have omitted 'אוֹ קָנֹה'; its inclusion must teach meshikha.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that 'אוֹ קָנֹה' is needed to include the seller's ona'ah, as taught in a baraita.
The Gemara resolves that Reish Lakish derives both meshikha and the seller's ona'ah from the same verse.

items.text: Proof from Rabbi Shimon's mishnah
items.text_en: Proof from Rabbi Shimon's mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove that money acquires from Rabbi Shimon's statement that the seller can retract. Reish Lakish deflects by saying he was speaking according to the Rabbis, not Rabbi Shimon. The difference between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis is explained via Rav Chisda's enactment of meshikha for buyers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Shimon's mishnah that the seller can retract, and argues that this proves money acquires, because otherwise the buyer could also retract.
Reish Lakish deflects the proof by stating that his position was stated according to the Rabbis, not according to Rabbi Shimon.

The Gemara explains that according to Reish Lakish the difference between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis is clear, and according to Rabbi Yochanan the difference lies in Rav Chisda's enactment of meshikha for buyers.

items.text: Proof from the 'Aval' statement
items.text_en: Proof from the 'Aval' statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita that curses one who reneges on a verbal commitment, implying that money alone does not complete the sale, so the 'Aval' is justified. The Gemara questions whether one is punished for mere words, citing another baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that curses one who reneges on a verbal commitment, implying that money alone does not complete the sale, so the 'Aval' is justified.
The Gemara questions: if money does not acquire, why is the baraita placed under 'Aval' (a restrictive clause)?
The Gemara answers that the curse is due to mere words, not monetary acquisition.
The Gemara objects: is one really punished for mere words, citing another baraita that suggests otherwise.

items.text: Mishnah: Verbal commitment and the principle of 'no spirit of the sages'
items.text_en: Mishnah: Verbal commitment and the principle of 'no spirit of the sages'
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that one who reneges on a verbal agreement is subject to divine punishment, and the sages are displeased with such a person.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon states that despite the rule that a cloak acquires a gold dinar but not vice versa, one who reneges on a verbal commitment will be punished by God, who punished the generations of the flood, the dispersion, Sodom, and Egypt.
The mishnah concludes that one who negotiates verbally does not acquire, and one who reneges is not favored by the sages.

items.text: Rava's distinction regarding 'but' and 'no spirit'
items.text_en: Rava's distinction regarding 'but' and 'no spirit'
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the phrase 'no spirit of the sages is pleased with him' applies only when money was not exchanged; if money was given, the stricter 'but' clause applies.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the Mishnah's two clauses by distinguishing: the stricter 'but' clause applies only when money was exchanged, while the milder 'no spirit of the sages is pleased with him' applies when no money was given.

items.text: Rava cites a verse supporting Reish Lakish about meshikha
items.text_en: Rava cites a verse supporting Reish Lakish about meshikha
items.desc_en: Rava brings a verse about theft and deposit to show that the Torah requires meshikha for acquisition, as the term 'temurat yad' (a deposit for a loan) is not returned, implying it lacks meshikha.

sub.desc_en: Rava announces that both a verse and a baraita support Reish Lakish's position, then cites the verse about theft and deposit and explains the terms 'תשמת יד' and 'עשק' via Rav Chisda.
The gemara asks why the verse does not mention returning the 'תשמת יד' (deposit for a loan), implying that meshikha is required for acquisition.

items.text: Rav Pappa's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa challenges Rava, suggesting that the verse might refer to a case of theft where the item was returned as a deposit. The Gemara resolves that since the Torah did not explicitly return 'temurat yad', it supports Reish Lakish.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa objects to Rava that the verse might be referring to theft (עושק) where the item was returned, and the case involves one who took the item and then redeposited it with the owner.
The Gemara objects that this scenario is simply a deposit (פיקדון), not theft, and the verse already lists deposit separately.

The Gemara resolves that since the Torah did not explicitly return 'תשמת יד' (a deposit designated for a loan), this omission supports Reish Lakish's position that such a transaction requires משיכה (physical acquisition).

items.text: Baraita includes 'temurat yad' for oath, but not for return
items.text_en: Baraita includes 'temurat yad' for oath, but not for return
items.desc_en: A baraita from Rabbi Shimon shows that 'temurat yad' is included for the oath of deposit, but the verse does not explicitly return it, supporting the need for meshikha.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the claim that the verse did not return 'תשומת יד' (a deposit by hand), citing a baraita of Rabbi Shimon.
Rabbi Shimon's baraita, transmitted by Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha citing Rav, derives that 'תשומת יד' is included for the oath but not for return.
The Gemara concludes that although the baraita includes 'תשומת יד' for the oath, the verse explicitly did not return it, supporting the need for meshikha.

items.text: Baraita about a bath attendant supports meshikha
items.text_en: Baraita about a bath attendant supports meshikha
items.desc_en: A baraita states that giving an object to a bath attendant (balan) constitutes me'ilah, but Rav says this is only because no meshikha is needed; for other artisans, meshikha is required. A contradiction with a baraita about a barber is resolved by distinguishing between a Jewish and a Gentile barber.

sub.desc_en: The gemara cites a baraita that giving an object to a bath attendant (בלן) constitutes me'ilah (מעילה), supporting the need for meshikha (משיכה) in acquisition.
Rav explains that the baraita applies only to a bath attendant, who does not require meshikha (משיכה); for other artisans, me'ilah (מעילה) does not occur until meshikha is performed.

The gemara objects by citing a baraita that giving to a barber also constitutes me'ilah (מעילה), even though a barber normally requires meshikha (משיכה); the gemara resolves that the baraita refers to a Gentile barber, who is not subject to meshikha.

A second baraita explicitly states that for a barber, carpenter, or any artisan, me'ilah (מעילה) does not occur until meshikha (משיכה) is performed, confirming the distinction between a Jewish and Gentile barber.

items.text: Rav Nachman's principle and Levi's test
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's principle and Levi's test
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman states that by Torah law, money acquires, and Levi tested this with a baraita about a perfume seller, finding that giving money constitutes me'ilah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman states that by Torah law, money alone effects acquisition (מעות קונות).
Levi tested Rav Nachman's principle against his own baraita and found support: giving money to a perfume seller (סיטון) constitutes me'ilah (מעילה), proving money alone transfers ownership.

items.text: Resolution of the contradiction for Reish Lakish
items.text_en: Resolution of the contradiction for Reish Lakish
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a contradiction for Reish Lakish by attributing the earlier statement to Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction for Reish Lakish by attributing the earlier statement to Rabbi Shimon.

items.text: Dispute between Abaye and Rava about the curse of 'מי שפרע'
items.text_en: Dispute between Abaye and Rava about the curse of 'מי שפרע'
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava argue whether one who backs out of a deal is merely informed about the curse of 'מי שפרע' or actually cursed. Abaye cites the verse 'וְנָשִׂיא בְעַמְּךָ לֹא תָאֹר' to support his view, while Rava interprets 'בְּעַמְּךָ' to mean one who acts like your people.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a dispute: Abaye says we inform the reneger about the curse of 'מי שפרע', while Rava says we actually curse him.
Abaye cites the verse 'וְנָשִׂיא בְעַמְּךָ לֹא תָאֹר' to support his view that one may not curse a Jew, only inform him.
Rava interprets 'בְּעַמְּךָ' to mean one who acts like your people, allowing cursing of one who does not act properly.

items.text: Proof from Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef's case
items.text_en: Proof from Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef's case
items.desc_en: Rava brings a proof from a case where Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef gave money for salt, and when the price increased, Rabbi Yochanan told him to either give the salt or accept the curse. The Gemara explains that Rabbi Chiya had given an earnest deposit (ערבון), and Rabbi Yochanan ruled that it acquires the entire item.

sub.desc_en: Rava introduces a proof from the case of Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef who gave money for salt.
The salt price rose, and Rabbi Yochanan told Rabbi Chiya to either give the salt or accept the curse of 'Mi sheparah'.
The Gemara objects that if the curse is merely a warning, Rabbi Chiya would not have needed it, and if it is a curse, he would not have accepted it.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Chiya had given an earnest deposit (ערבון), and Rabbi Yochanan ruled that it acquires the entire item.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan about ערבון
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan about ערבון
items.desc_en: Rav and Rabbi Yochanan explicitly dispute whether an earnest deposit acquires only the corresponding portion or the entire item.

sub.desc_en: The gemara states a dispute: Rav says an earnest deposit (ערבון) acquires only the corresponding portion, while Rabbi Yochanan says it acquires the entire item.

items.text: Support from a baraita about earnest deposit
items.text_en: Support from a baraita about earnest deposit
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Yehuda dispute the effect of an earnest deposit, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel distinguishes between a case where the deposit is explicitly designated and a standard sale. The baraita suggests that in a standard sale, the deposit acquires the entire item.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about an earnest deposit with conditional forfeiture, and notes that Rabbi Yosei's position aligns with his view that an אסמכתא (conditional commitment) is binding.
Rabbi Yehuda states that the deposit only acquires the item up to the value of the deposit itself.

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel distinguishes between a case where the deposit is explicitly designated to acquire the item, and a standard sale where paying part of the price acquires the entire property, and the Gemara infers that the same rule applies to movable property.

items.text: Rejection of the support for movables
items.text_en: Rejection of the support for movables
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof, explaining that land is different because full payment acquires it, whereas movables are only acquired to invoke the curse of 'מי שפרע', so the deposit does not acquire the entire item.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the attempted proof, explaining that land is different because full payment acquires it outright, whereas movables are only acquired to invoke the curse of 'מי שפרע', so the deposit does not acquire the entire item.

items.text: Comparison with a dispute about a pledge and shemittah
items.text_en: Comparison with a dispute about a pledge and shemittah
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to compare the dispute to a tannaitic dispute between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi regarding whether a pledge exempts from shemittah, questioning the scope of the exemption.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes comparing the dispute to a tannaitic dispute between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi regarding whether a pledge exempts from shemittah.
The Gemara asks what the scope of the exemption is according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, suggesting it might be only against the value of the pledge.

The Gemara objects that if Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's exemption is only against the pledge, then Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi would hold that even the excess debt is exempt, which is inconsistent with the earlier dispute.

items.text: Reinterpreting the dispute between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi
items.text_en: Reinterpreting the dispute between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests a new interpretation of the dispute: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that a pledge acquires the entire debt, while Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi holds that it acquires only the portion against which it was taken. This explains why Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says the debt is not entirely subject to shemittah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the purpose of holding a pledge if it does not affect the shemittah exemption, and proposes that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel means the debt is not entirely remitted, while Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi means only the portion without a pledge is remitted.
The Gemara resolves that the dispute is about whether a pledge acquires the entire debt (Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel) or only the portion against which it was taken (Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi).

items.text: Alternative interpretation: Pledge as a mere reminder
items.text_en: Alternative interpretation: Pledge as a mere reminder
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the previous interpretation and offers another: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says the portion with a pledge is not subject to shemittah, while Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi holds even that portion is subject to shemittah. The pledge is only a reminder of the debt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the previous interpretation and offers an alternative: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says the portion with a pledge is not subject to shemittah, while Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi holds even that portion is subject to shemittah, and the pledge is merely a reminder of the debt.

items.text: Story of Rav Kahana and the dispute over verbal commitments
items.text_en: Story of Rav Kahana and the dispute over verbal commitments
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana gave money for flax, which later appreciated. Rav ruled that he must give the sellers only the amount he held, and the rest is mere words, which have no legal consequence. This is based on a dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan: Rav says verbal commitments do not incur a breach of faith, while Rabbi Yochanan says they do.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Rav Kahana gave money for flax, which later appreciated; Rav ruled that he must give only the amount he held, and the rest is mere words (דברים) with no breach of faith.
The Gemara cites the dispute: Rav says verbal commitments do not incur a breach of faith, while Rabbi Yochanan says they do.

items.text: Support for Rabbi Yochanan from a baraita and a Mishnah
items.text_en: Support for Rabbi Yochanan from a baraita and a Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita from Rabbi Yosei bar Yehudah about 'hin tzedek' and a Mishnah from Rabbi Shimon about the Flood generation, both implying that verbal commitments are binding and that breaking them is a serious matter. This challenges Rav's position.

sub.text: Supporting baraita from Rabbi Yosei bar Yehudah
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita from Rabbi Yosei bar Yehudah
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita from Rabbi Yosei bar Yehudah who expounds the verse 'הִין צֶדֶק' (a righteous hin-measure) to teach that one's 'yes' and 'no' must both be righteous, implying verbal commitments are binding.
Abaye explains that the baraita means one should not speak one thing with the mouth while thinking another in the heart, reinforcing the seriousness of verbal commitments.

The Gemara cites a Mishnah from Rabbi Shimon stating that although a cloak acquires a gold dinar and not vice versa, one who reneges on a verbal commitment will be punished by the One who punished the Flood and Dispersion generations.

items.text: Resolving the contradiction: Tannaitic dispute and the case of workers
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction: Tannaitic dispute and the case of workers
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the sources represent a Tannaitic dispute. It cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Yochanan ben Matya told his son to retract a promise of lavish meals to workers because they rely on the father, not the son. The Gemara explains that before work begins, workers do not rely on the promise, so retraction is allowed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by asserting it is a Tannaitic dispute, citing the Mishnah where Rabbi Yochanan ben Matya instructs his son to retract a lavish meal promise to workers before they start work.
The Gemara objects: if mere words carry a violation of 'מחוסרי אמנה (breach of faith), how could Rabbi Yochanan ben Matya tell his son to retract?
The Gemara answers that the case is different because the workers themselves did not rely on the son's promise, knowing they rely on the father.
The Gemara objects: if so, even after they started work, retraction should be allowed.
The Gemara answers that once work begins, the workers certainly rely on the promise, assuming the son spoke with the father's consent.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's own ruling on gifts and the case of maaser
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's own ruling on gifts and the case of maaser
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yochanan really holds that verbal commitments are binding, citing his ruling that one may retract a promise of a gift. Rav Pappa explains that for a small gift, the recipient relies on it. The Gemara then discusses a case of maaser where a Levi can separate terumat maaser based on a verbal promise, implying the promise is binding. The Gemara resolves this by suggesting the Levi had already taken the produce and redeposited it, but a counter-argument shows this is not the case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yochanan really holds that verbal commitments are binding, citing his ruling that one may retract a promise of a gift.
Rav Pappa explains that Rabbi Yochanan concedes that for a small gift, the recipient relies on the promise, making it binding.

sub.text: Rabbi Avahu's citation of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Avahu's citation of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Avahu's report that Rabbi Yochanan ruled a Levi may separate תרומת מעשר (the priestly portion from the tithe) based on a verbal promise, implying the promise is binding.

The Gemara resolves by suggesting the Levi had already taken the produce and redeposited it, but a counter-argument from the continuation shows this is not the case, concluding that the promise is indeed binding.

items.text: Story of the sesame buyers and the principle of 'Mi shepara'
items.text_en: Story of the sesame buyers and the principle of 'Mi shepara'
items.desc_en: A man gave money for sesame, which appreciated. The sellers tried to back out, but the buyer refused to take his money back, and the money was stolen. Rava ruled he is not even a shomer chinam. The rabbis asked if the sellers should be subject to 'Mi shepara', and Rava agreed. The Gemara then praises Rav Tavut or Rav Shmuel bar Zutra for never breaking his word, illustrated by a story where he would not sell sesame on Shabbat eve.

sub.desc_en: A man gave money for sesame, which appreciated; the sellers tried to back out, but the buyer refused to take his money back, and the money was stolen.
Rava ruled that since the buyer refused to take his money back, he is not even a shomer chinam (unpaid bailee).
The rabbis asked Rava whether the sellers should be subject to 'Mi shepara' (the curse of the one who punished the generation of the flood).
Rava agreed that the sellers should be subject to 'Mi shepara'.
Rav Pappei reported that Ravina heard from a rabbi named Rav Tavut (or Rav Shmuel bar Zutra) that he would never break his word even for all the world's wealth.
Rav Tavut illustrated his integrity with a story: on Shabbat eve, a man came asking to buy sesame, and he would not sell because he had already given his word.

items.text: The 'Here is the house' case and Rava's ruling
items.text_en: The 'Here is the house' case and Rava's ruling
items.desc_en: A man left money as a deposit with another, who said 'here is the house' (i.e., leave it here). The money was stolen. Rava ruled that the bailee is not even a gratuitous bailee (shomer hinam), let alone a paid bailee. The Gemara notes that the Rabbis asked Rava about accepting a 'Mi shepara' curse, but the depositor denied the whole incident.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts a case where a depositor asked the bailee to hold money, the bailee said 'here is the house,' and the money was stolen.
Rava rules that saying 'here is the house' does not even make one a gratuitous bailee (שומר חנם), let alone a paid bailee.
The Rabbis asked Rava whether the bailee should have accepted a 'Mi shepara' curse, but the depositor denied the whole incident.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's ruling on who may retract
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's ruling on who may retract
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon says that the one who holds the money has the upper hand. A beraita elaborates: this is only when both money and produce are with the seller, but if money is with the seller and produce with the buyer, the seller cannot retract because the buyer's money is in his hand. The Gemara corrects the text to refer to the value of the money.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Rabbi Shimon's ruling that the one who holds the money has the upper hand.

A baraita elaborates that Rabbi Shimon's rule applies only when both money and produce are with the seller; if the buyer has the produce, the seller cannot retract because the buyer's money is in his hand.
The Gemara objects that the baraita's phrase 'his money is in his hand' is problematic because the money is actually in the seller's hand.
The Gemara corrects the text to read 'because the value of his money is in his hand,' referring to the buyer's claim on the money's worth.

items.text: Rava's explanation: produce in the buyer's rented loft
items.text_en: Rava's explanation: produce in the buyer's rented loft
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why this case is not obvious. Rava explains that the case is where the buyer's loft is rented to the seller. The reason the Sages instituted meshikhah (pulling) was a decree lest the seller say 'your wheat burned in the loft'. Here, since the produce is in the buyer's domain, even if a fire breaks out, the buyer would have to exert himself to save it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why this case is not obvious (פְּשִׁיטָא).
Rava explains that the case involves the buyer's loft rented to the seller, so the buyer must exert himself to save the produce, justifying the Sages' decree of meshikhah (pulling).

items.text: Wine buyer retracts due to bad news: Rav Chisda's ruling
items.text_en: Wine buyer retracts due to bad news: Rav Chisda's ruling
items.desc_en: A man paid for wine but then heard that officials were coming to confiscate it. He asked for his money back. Rav Chisda ruled that just as the Sages instituted meshikhah for sellers, so they instituted it for buyers—so the buyer can retract until he performs meshikhah.

sub.desc_en: A man paid for wine and then heard that officials were coming to confiscate it.
The buyer demands his money back, saying he no longer wants the wine.
Rav Chisda rules that just as the Sages instituted meshikhah (drawing) for sellers, so they instituted it for buyers, so the buyer can retract until he performs meshikhah.

items.text: Mishnah: The law of ona'ah and Rabbi Tarfon's ruling
items.text_en: Mishnah: The law of ona'ah and Rabbi Tarfon's ruling
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the forbidden overcharge (ona'ah) is 4 silver coins per sela (24 coins), i.e., one-sixth of the purchase. The buyer may return it until he shows it to a merchant or relative. Rabbi Tarfon in Lod ruled the overcharge is 8 silver coins per sela, i.e., one-third. The merchants of Lod rejoiced, but when he added that the retraction period is all day, they asked him to let them be as they were, and they reverted to the Sages' opinion.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the basic law of ona'ah (overcharge): the forbidden overcharge is four silver coins per sela (24 coins), i.e., one-sixth of the purchase, and the buyer may return it until he shows it to a merchant or relative.

The Mishnah reports that Rabbi Tarfon in Lod ruled the overcharge is eight silver coins per sela (one-third), the merchants rejoiced, but when he added that retraction is permitted all day, they asked to revert to the Sages' opinion.

items.text: Gemara: Rav and Shmuel dispute the measure of ona'ah
items.text_en: Gemara: Rav and Shmuel dispute the measure of ona'ah
items.desc_en: Rav says the Mishnah measures one-sixth of the item's value (mikach); Shmuel says it measures one-sixth of the money paid. They agree on cases where there is a clear one-sixth disparity from both sides. The dispute is when the disparity is one-sixth from one side only: Shmuel says it's overcharge, Rav says it's voidance of sale if the item is cheaper, and forgiveness if the item is more expensive.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports a dispute: Rav says the Mishnah's measure of one-sixth is of the item's value (מקח), while Shmuel says it is of the money paid (מעות).
The Gemara notes that both agree when the disparity is one-sixth from both sides (e.g., item worth 5 sold for 6, or worth 7 sold for 6), it is overcharge (אונאה).

The Gemara states that the dispute is when the disparity is one-sixth from one side only: for Shmuel (following money) both cases are overcharge; for Rav (following item value), worth 5 sold for 6 is voidance of sale (ביטול מקח), and worth 7 sold for 6 is forgiveness (מחילה).

Shmuel clarifies that forgiveness and voidance of sale apply only when there is no one-sixth disparity from either side; but when there is a one-sixth disparity from one side, it is overcharge (אונאה).

items.text: Gemara: Analyzing the Mishnah to determine Rav and Shmuel's views
items.text_en: Gemara: Analyzing the Mishnah to determine Rav and Shmuel's views
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove Shmuel's position from the Mishnah's numbers: buying worth 20 for 24 involves a one-sixth overcharge of the money, implying the measure is money. It refutes this by positing a case where the item is worth 24 and sold for 20, making the buyer the victim. The same is done for Rabbi Tarfon's ruling. The Gemara concludes with a baraita supporting Shmuel: if one sold something worth 5 for 6, the buyer (the victim) has the upper hand.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove Shmuel's position from the Mishnah's numbers: buying worth 20 for 24 involves a one-sixth overcharge of the money, implying the measure is money.
The Gemara refutes this by positing a case where the item is worth 24 and sold for 20, making the buyer the victim.
The Gemara objects that in that case the seller is the victim, and cites Rav Nachman's ruling that the seller can always retract.
The Gemara reinterprets the Mishnah's numbers and attempts to prove Shmuel's position from Rabbi Tarfon's ruling.
The Gemara refutes this by positing a case where the item is worth 24 and sold for 16, making the seller the victim.
The Gemara objects that in that case the seller is the victim, and again cites Rav Nachman's ruling.
The Gemara resolves the difficulty by reinterpreting the case as selling worth 24 for 32, where the buyer is the victim and the Mishnah's numbers fit Shmuel's view.
A baraita supports Shmuel: if one sold something worth 5 for 6, the buyer (the victim) has the upper hand.

items.text: Baraita supporting Shmuel: buyer has the upper hand
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Shmuel: buyer has the upper hand
items.desc_en: A beraita teaches: one who was overcharged (the victim) has the upper hand. For example, if one sold something worth 5 for 6, the buyer is the victim and may demand either his money back or the return of the overcharge. The text breaks off after this example.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Shmuel's position: the victim of overcharging has the upper hand, illustrated by the case where the buyer is the victim and may demand either his money back or the return of the overcharge.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if an item worth six was sold for five, and the seller was the one who was overcharged, the seller has the upper hand: he can demand either the return of the item or the refund of the overcharge.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule for a sale where the item's value is six and the price is five: the seller who was overcharged has the upper hand to demand either the return of the item or the refund of the overcharge.

items.text: Gemara's question about less than a sixth
items.text_en: Gemara's question about less than a sixth
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether less than a sixth (פחות משתות) is immediately forgiven (מחילה) or only after showing to a merchant or relative. It then clarifies the difference between exactly a sixth and less than a sixth: with exactly a sixth, the victim can either cancel the sale or keep it and demand the overcharge; with less than a sixth, the sale is valid and the overcharge is returned.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether less than a sixth (פחות משתות) is immediately forgiven (מחילה) or only after showing to a merchant or relative.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between exactly a sixth and less than a sixth.

The Gemara explains that with exactly a sixth the victim can either cancel the sale or keep it and demand the overcharge, while with less than a sixth the sale is valid and the overcharge is returned.

items.text: Resolution attempt and comparison with Rabbi Tarfon
items.text_en: Resolution attempt and comparison with Rabbi Tarfon
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to resolve the question by citing a case where the Sages reverted to the opinion of the Rabbis. It then compares less than a sixth for the Rabbis to less than a third for Rabbi Tarfon, arguing that if less than a sixth is only forgiven after showing, then the reversion makes sense; but if it is immediately forgiven, the reversion is problematic.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to resolve the question by citing a case where the Sages reverted to the opinion of the Rabbis.
The Gemara compares less than a sixth for the Rabbis to less than a third for Rabbi Tarfon, arguing that if less than a sixth is only forgiven after showing, then the reversion makes sense.
The Gemara objects that if less than a sixth is immediately forgiven, the reversion is problematic.

items.text: Question on Rabbi Tarfon's ruling and the Sages' joy
items.text_en: Question on Rabbi Tarfon's ruling and the Sages' joy
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Sages initially rejoiced at Rabbi Tarfon's ruling but later retracted, given that for Rabbi Tarfon the overcharge is immediately forgiven. It then clarifies that for Rabbi Tarfon, an overcharge between one-sixth and one-third is like exactly one-sixth for the Sages, prompting a further question on what they rejoiced about initially.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Sages retracted from Rabbi Tarfon's ruling, given that for Rabbi Tarfon the overcharge is immediately forgiven, so his leniency should be even greater.
The Gemara clarifies that for Rabbi Tarfon, an overcharge between one-sixth and one-third is equivalent to exactly one-sixth for the Sages, not to less than one-sixth.
The Gemara asks: if so, what did the Sages initially rejoice about, since Rabbi Tarfon's ruling is no more lenient than their own?

items.text: First resolution: ביטול מקח forever for the Sages
items.text_en: First resolution: ביטול מקח forever for the Sages
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the Sages' joy and retraction prove that for the Sages, ביטול מקח lasts forever. If it were only until showing to a merchant, they would have rejoiced over the one-sixth itself being forgiveness for Rabbi Tarfon but overcharge for them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the Sages' joy and retraction prove that for the Sages, ביטול מקח (annulment of the sale) lasts forever, because when Rabbi Tarfon told them it was overcharge they rejoiced, but when he said 'all day' they retracted.
The Gemara objects that if the Sages' ביטול מקח were only until showing to a merchant, they would have rejoiced over the one-sixth itself being forgiveness for Rabbi Tarfon but overcharge for them.

items.text: The unresolved dilemma about ביטול מקח
items.text_en: The unresolved dilemma about ביטול מקח
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: for the Sages, does ביטול מקח last forever or only until showing to a merchant or relative? It further asks what difference exists between one-sixth and more than one-sixth if the right is limited, answering that for one-sixth only the victim can cancel, while for more than one-sixth both parties can cancel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an unresolved dilemma: for the Sages, does the right of ביטול מקח (cancellation of the sale) last forever or only until showing the item to a merchant or relative?
The Gemara asks: if the right is limited, what practical difference remains between one-sixth and more than one-sixth?
The Gemara answers: for one-sixth only the victim can cancel, while for more than one-sixth both parties can cancel.

items.text: Proof from the Sages' retraction
items.text_en: Proof from the Sages' retraction
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to resolve the dilemma by citing that the Sages retracted to the Sages' original view. If ביטול מקח were only until showing to a merchant, the retraction makes sense; but if it were forever, why would they retract from Rabbi Tarfon's more lenient ruling?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes to resolve the dilemma by citing the Sages' retraction to their original view.
The Gemara explains that if ביטול מקח (annulment of the sale) is only until showing to a merchant, the retraction makes sense.
The Gemara objects that if ביטול מקח were forever, the Sages would not have retracted from Rabbi Tarfon's more lenient ruling.

items.text: Rejection of the proof
items.text_en: Rejection of the proof
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof by stating that ביטול מקח is uncommon, so the Sages preferred Rabbi Tarfon's ruling which gave them a full day to cancel even for a one-sixth overcharge.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof by stating that ביטול מקח (annulment of the sale) is uncommon, so the Sages preferred Rabbi Tarfon's ruling which gave them a full day to cancel even for a one-sixth overcharge.

items.text: Rava's halakhic ruling
items.text_en: Rava's halakhic ruling
items.desc_en: Rava rules definitively: less than one-sixth – the sale stands; more than one-sixth – the sale is void; exactly one-sixth – the sale stands but the overcharge is returned. In all cases, the right to cancel lasts only until showing to a merchant or relative.

sub.desc_en: Rava issues a definitive halakhic ruling: less than one-sixth overcharge – the sale stands; more than one-sixth – the sale is void; exactly one-sixth – the sale stands but the overcharge is returned; in all cases the right to cancel lasts only until showing to a merchant or relative.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rava
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rava
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rava's ruling, with the same three categories. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi adds that the seller has the upper hand: he can choose to demand the item back or the overcharge. Both agree the right lasts until showing to a merchant or relative.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rava's ruling, stating the three categories of overcharge: less than a sixth, more than a sixth, and exactly a sixth, in the name of Rabbi Natan.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi adds that the seller has the upper hand, able to demand either the return of the item or the overpayment.
The baraita concludes that both parties have the right to retract only until showing the item to a merchant or relative.

items.text: Rav Nachman's distinction between buyer and seller
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's distinction between buyer and seller
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman states that the rule of limited time for cancellation applies only to the buyer, but the seller can cancel forever. The Gemara begins to cite a proof from the Sages' retraction.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman states that the rule of limited time for cancellation applies only to the buyer, but the seller can cancel forever.
The Gemara attempts to support Rav Nachman from the earlier story where the Sages retracted, arguing that only if the seller can cancel forever does the retraction make sense.

items.text: Gemara's question: Why did the Sages not enact a remedy for the seller?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why did the Sages not enact a remedy for the seller?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the seller is also considered like a buyer, what difference does it make? The Sages enacted a remedy for the buyer; they should also enact a remedy for the seller.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the seller is also considered like a buyer, why did the Sages not enact a remedy for the seller as they did for the buyer?

items.text: Story of Rami bar Chama's innkeeper and Rav Nachman's ruling
items.text_en: Story of Rami bar Chama's innkeeper and Rav Nachman's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates a story where an innkeeper sold a donkey and erred. Rami bar Chama told him to retract, but the innkeeper said he had waited longer than the time to show to a trader or relative. Rav Nachman ruled that only a buyer may retract indefinitely, but a seller may always retract because he does not hold the item and cannot easily know if he erred.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the story of Rami bar Chama's innkeeper who sold a donkey and erred, and Rami bar Chama told him to retract.
The innkeeper objects that he has waited longer than the time to show to a trader or relative, so he cannot retract.
Rav Nachman rules that only a buyer may retract within the time limit, but a seller may always retract because he does not hold the item and cannot easily know if he erred.

items.text: Two stories: buyer from a householder has no claim for ona'ah
items.text_en: Two stories: buyer from a householder has no claim for ona'ah
items.desc_en: Two similar stories are told: a man selling cloaks or baskets would ask for more than the value, and a buyer tried to pay the full asked price and then sue for overreaching. Rava and Rav Chisda each ruled that the law of ona'ah applies only to a buyer from a trader, not from a householder.

sub.desc_en: A story is told of a man selling silk strips who asked for six but would accept five and a half; a buyer decided to pay six and then sue for exploitation.
Rava ruled that the law of exploitation applies only to a buyer from a merchant, not from a householder.
A second similar story is told of a man selling jewelry who asked for sixty but would accept fifty-five; a buyer again tried to pay the full price and sue.
Rav Chisda similarly ruled that the law of exploitation does not apply to a buyer from a householder.

items.text: Rav Dimi and Rabbi Elazar approve; Rav Chisda explains the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rav Dimi and Rabbi Elazar approve; Rav Chisda explains the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi and Rabbi Elazar praised the ruling. The Gemara questions the Mishnah that says there is ona'ah for a trader as for a commoner. Rav Chisda explains: the Mishnah refers to a peddler (צדרייתי), but a householder does not sell his personal items unless at a high price.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi and Rabbi Elazar praise the ruling that a buyer from a homeowner has no claim of exploitation.
The Gemara questions the ruling by citing the Mishnah that says exploitation applies equally to a layman and a merchant, and asks whether 'layman' refers to a homeowner.
Rav Chisda explains that the Mishnah refers to a peddler (צדרייתי), but a homeowner does not sell his personal items unless at a high price.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara: Source for both buyer and seller having ona'ah
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara: Source for both buyer and seller having ona'ah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that both buyer and seller have a claim for ona'ah, and the same applies to a trader. The Gemara derives this from the verse 'When you sell... do not oppress' and 'Or buy... do not oppress', and explains why both verses are necessary.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that both the buyer and the seller have a claim for ona'ah (overcharge).
The Gemara asks: From where in the Torah are these matters derived?

The Gemara cites a baraita that derives the seller's ona'ah from the verse 'אוֹ קָנֹה ... אַל תּוֹנוּ' (or if you buy... do not oppress), in addition to the buyer's from 'וְכִי תִמְכְּרוּ... אַל תּוֹנוּ'.
The Gemara explains why both verses are necessary: each verse addresses a unique case where one might think the prohibition does not apply, so both are needed.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's opinion: a trader has no ona'ah; explanations
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's opinion: a trader has no ona'ah; explanations
items.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Rabbi Yehuda who says a trader has no ona'ah. Rav Nachman explains: it refers to a broker who knows the value and waived it, selling only because another opportunity arose. Rav Ashi says it means the trader is not subject to the law of ona'ah at all, and even less than the measure of ona'ah he may retract. A baraisa supports Rav Nachman.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yehuda's statement that a trader has no ona'ah, asking how being a trader alone exempts him.
Rav Nachman in the name of Rav explains that the Mishnah refers to a broker who knows the value and waived his rights, selling only because another opportunity arose.
The Gemara objects that even if the broker waived his rights, he is now retracting, so why is he exempt?
Rav Ashi explains that Rabbi Yehuda means the trader is not subject to the law of ona'ah at all, and even less than the measure of ona'ah he may retract.
A baraisa supports Rav Nachman's interpretation, stating that Rabbi Yehuda says a trader has no ona'ah because he is an expert.

items.text: Who is the Tanna of the Mishnah's last clause?
items.text_en: Who is the Tanna of the Mishnah's last clause?
items.desc_en: The Mishnah says the one who was wronged has the upper hand. The Gemara debates whether this follows Rabbi Natan or Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi. Rabbi Elazar is unsure. Rabbah says it is Rabbi Natan, and the baraisa also says 'if he wants'. Rava says it is Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, and the baraisa explains what the Mishnah omitted. Rav Ashi supports Rava.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna of the Mishnah's clause 'the one who was wronged has the upper hand', and suggests it is neither Rabbi Natan nor Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
The Gemara objects that if it were Rabbi Natan, the Mishnah says 'if he wants' but the baraisa does not; if it were Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, the Mishnah says 'buyer' but the baraisa says 'seller'.
A mnemonic sign (סימן) is inserted to aid memory of the following Amoraim's names: Zav, Rash.
Rabbi Elazar says he does not know who taught this law of ona'ah.
Rabbah says it is always Rabbi Natan, and the baraisa also says 'if he wants'.
Rava says it is always Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, and the baraisa explains what the Mishnah omitted.
