Rav Ashi supports Rava by noting that the Mishnah says 'both buyer and seller' but only explains the buyer, implying it omitted the seller.

items.text: Dispute: stipulating away the right to claim ona'ah
items.text_en: Dispute: stipulating away the right to claim ona'ah
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel argue about one who says 'on condition that you have no claim of ona'ah against me'. Rav says he still has a claim, Shmuel says he does not. The Gemara suggests they follow Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda regarding a condition that contradicts a Torah law. Rav explains that even Rabbi Yehuda only allows a condition when the party knowingly waives, but here the buyer does not know the extent of the overcharge.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute: Rav says that one who stipulates 'on condition that you have no claim of ona'ah against me' still has a claim, while Shmuel says he does not.
The Gemara suggests that Rav follows Rabbi Meir and Shmuel follows Rabbi Yehuda regarding a condition that contradicts a Torah law.
A baraita is cited: Rabbi Meir invalidates a condition that contradicts a Torah obligation, while Rabbi Yehuda upholds it in monetary matters.
Rav explains that even Rabbi Yehuda only allows a condition when the party knowingly waives, but here the buyer does not know the extent of the overcharge.

items.text: Gemara's question on Shmuel's position
items.text_en: Gemara's question on Shmuel's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Shmuel's earlier statement that even Rabbi Meir would agree that a stipulation waiving ona'ah is ineffective here because one does not know the exact overcharge at the time of the transaction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Shmuel's position by asking how one can waive an unknown overcharge.

items.text: Shmuel's response
items.text_en: Shmuel's response
items.desc_en: Shmuel clarifies that he holds even according to Rabbi Meir, but only because in the earlier case (overcharge by a third) the seller definitely uproots the transaction, whereas here one cannot say that anything is uprooted.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel clarifies that he holds even according to Rabbi Meir, but only because in the earlier case (overcharge by a third) the seller definitely uproots the transaction, whereas here one cannot say that anything is uprooted.

items.text: Rav Anan's report of Shmuel's distinction
items.text_en: Rav Anan's report of Shmuel's distinction
items.desc_en: Rav Anan reports that Shmuel explicitly distinguished between two formulations: 'on condition that you have no claim of ona'ah against me' is effective, but 'on condition that there is no ona'ah in this item' is not.

sub.desc_en: Rav Anan reports that Shmuel distinguished between two formulations: 'on condition that you have no claim of ona'ah against me' is effective, but 'on condition that there is no ona'ah in this item' is not.

items.text: Objection from a baraita
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that states that one who says 'on condition that you have no claim of ona'ah against me' has no ona'ah. This challenges Rav, who claimed to hold even according to Rabbi Yehuda, because the baraita seems to support Shmuel's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that states that one who says 'on condition that you have no claim of ona'ah against me' has no ona'ah, challenging Rav's position that he holds even according to Rabbi Yehuda.

items.text: Abaye's resolution
items.text_en: Abaye's resolution
items.desc_en: Abaye resolves the contradiction by explaining that Rav actually holds like Rabbi Meir, and Shmuel holds like Rabbi Yehuda, so the baraita is consistent with Shmuel's view.

sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves the contradiction by clarifying that Rav's position aligns with Rabbi Meir and Shmuel's with Rabbi Yehuda, making the baraita consistent with Shmuel's view.

items.text: Rava's alternative resolution
items.text_en: Rava's alternative resolution
items.desc_en: Rava resolves the contradiction differently: the baraita refers to a case where the seller specifies the true value, while the earlier dispute was about a general stipulation without specification. A supporting baraita is cited.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a general stipulation (סתם) and a case where the seller specifies the true value (מפרש).
A baraita is cited to support Rava's distinction: in a case where the seller or buyer explicitly states the true value and then stipulates no claim of overcharge, the stipulation is effective.

items.text: Baraita on the trustee and its explanation
items.text_en: Baraita on the trustee and its explanation
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that a trustee who buys and sells on trust must not calculate the bad items on trust and the good at market value, but must treat all consistently. He receives expenses for porter, camel, and inn, but not his own wage, since he already receives a commission of four per hundred. Rav Pappa explains the source of this commission.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that a trustee who buys and sells on trust must not calculate the bad items on trust and the good at market value, but must treat all consistently.
The baraita adds that the trustee receives expenses for porter, camel, and inn, but not his own wage, since he already received his commission from the seller.
The gemara asks: from where does the seller give the trustee his commission?
Rav Pappa explains that the commission comes from the sellers, who give the trustee four per hundred (4%) as a fee.

items.text: Opening Mishnah on coin deficiency
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah on coin deficiency
items.desc_en: The Mishnah begins a new topic: how much a sela may be deficient before it constitutes ona'ah, citing the opinions of Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, and beginning Rabbi Shimon's view.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens the topic by asking how deficient a sela coin may be before it constitutes ona'ah (overreaching).
Rabbi Meir states that the deficiency is four issarot, one issar per dinar.
Rabbi Yehuda states that the deficiency is four pundiyonot, one pundiyon per dinar.
The Mishnah begins to cite Rabbi Shimon's opinion, but the text cuts off at this point.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: limits of returning defective coins
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: limits of returning defective coins
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a coin defective by eight פונדיונות (two per dinar) may be returned. In cities, one may return it until showing it to a money changer; in villages, until Friday eve. If the seller recognizes the coin, he must accept it even after twelve months, but the buyer has only a complaint. The coin may be used for second tithe without concern, as it is merely ill will.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the limits for returning a defective coin and the time frames for doing so in cities and villages, and that the coin may be used for second tithe.

items.text: Gemara's contradiction and Rav Pappa's resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's contradiction and Rav Pappa's resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: elsewhere it asks how much a סלע must be deficient to constitute אונאה, implying a different measure. Rav Pappa resolves: our Tanna counts from bottom up, the external Tanna from top down.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from an external baraita that asks how much a סלע must be deficient to constitute אונאה, implying a different measure than our Mishnah.
Rav Pappa resolves the contradiction: our Tanna counts from bottom up (starting from the smallest deficiency), while the external Tanna counts from top down (starting from the largest deficiency).

items.text: Why dispute on סלע but not on טלית?
items.text_en: Why dispute on סלע but not on טלית?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Tannaim dispute about the measure for a סלע but not for a טלית (garment). Rava answers: the Tanna of טלית is Rabbi Shimon. Abaye says: regarding a טלית, one forgives up to a sixth, as people say 'it is pressed for you but worth it for your stomach'; regarding a סלע, since it cannot be used, one does not forgive.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Tannaim dispute about the measure for a סלע (coin) but not for a טלית (garment).
Rava answers that the Tanna of the טלית (garment) is Rabbi Shimon, who holds a lenient position that does not require a separate dispute.

Abaye answers that regarding a טלית (garment), one forgives up to a sixth because people say 'it is pressed for you but worth it for your stomach'; regarding a סלע (coin), since it cannot be used, one does not forgive.

items.text: Baraita: Tannaitic dispute on סלע deficiency and rules for defective coins
items.text_en: Baraita: Tannaitic dispute on סלע deficiency and rules for defective coins
items.desc_en: A baraita details the dispute: Rabbi Meir says four איסרות (an איסר per dinar), Rabbi Yehuda says four פונדיונות (a פונדיון per dinar), Rabbi Shimon says eight פונדיונות (two per dinar). Beyond that, one sells it at its value. It then states how much a coin may be reduced and still be retained: a סלע up to a שקל, a dinar up to a רובע. Less than that (an איסר) is forbidden to spend; one may not sell it to a merchant, robber, or murderer, but must pierce it and hang it on his child's neck.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the question of how much a סלע may be deficient before it constitutes אונאה (overcharge), and presents Rabbi Meir's position: four איסרות, one איסר per dinar.
Rabbi Yehuda states the deficiency threshold as four פונדיונות, one פונדיון per dinar.
Rabbi Shimon sets the threshold at eight פונדיונות, two per dinar.
If the coin is more deficient than these thresholds, one may sell it only at its actual value.
The baraita asks how much a coin may be reduced and still be retained, answering: a סלע up to a שקל, a dinar up to a רובע.
If the coin is reduced below that threshold (to an איסר), it is forbidden to spend it; one may not sell it to a merchant, robber, or murderer, but must pierce it and hang it on his child's neck.

items.text: Gemara's question on 'רובע' and support for Rabbi Ammi
items.text_en: Gemara's question on 'רובע' and support for Rabbi Ammi
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the baraita says for a סלע up to a שקל, and for a dinar up to a רובע. Abaye explains: 'רובע' means a quarter of a שקל. Rava supports this: it says 'רובע' not 'רביע'. The Gemara then asks why the dinar is tied to the שקל; it teaches incidentally that there is a dinar that comes from a שקל. This supports Rabbi Ammi, who says a dinar from a שקל may be retained, but from a סלע may not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the baraita sets different thresholds for a סלע (sela) and a דינר (dinar): for a סלע up to a שקל (shekel), but for a דינר up to a רובע (quarter).
Abaye explains that 'רובע' in the baraita means a quarter of a שקל (shekel), not a quarter of a דינר (dinar), thus the threshold is consistent.
Rava supports Abaye by noting that the baraita uses the term 'רובע' (quarter) rather than 'רביע' (a fourth), implying a specific quarter of a שקל.
The Gemara asks why the baraita ties the דינר (dinar) to the שקל (shekel) at all, rather than stating the threshold independently.
The Gemara answers that the baraita incidentally teaches that there exists a דינר (dinar) that comes from a שקל (shekel), i.e., a coin worth a quarter of a שקל.
The Gemara notes that this inference supports Rabbi Ammi, who rules that a דינר (dinar) that comes from a שקל (shekel) may be retained, but one that comes from a סלע (sela) may not.

items.text: Interpretation of 'less than an איסר'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'less than an איסר'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the baraita means by 'less than an איסר'. Abaye says: if a סלע is reduced more than the measure of אונאה (an איסר), it is forbidden. Rava objects: then even a tiny amount would be forbidden! Rather, Rava says: if a סלע is reduced by an איסר per dinar, it is forbidden, and the anonymous ruling follows Rabbi Meir.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the baraita means by 'less than an איסר'.
Abaye explains that the baraita means if a סלע is reduced more than the measure of אונאה (an איסר), it is forbidden.
Rava objects that if Abaye's interpretation were correct, even a tiny reduction would be forbidden.
Rava resolves that the baraita means if a סלע is reduced by an איסר per dinar, it is forbidden, and the anonymous ruling follows Rabbi Meir.

items.text: Baraita on a disqualified סלע and dispute between Rav Huna and Rabbi Ammi
items.text_en: Baraita on a disqualified סלע and dispute between Rav Huna and Rabbi Ammi
items.desc_en: A baraita from elsewhere discusses a disqualified סלע that one prepared for use as a weight: it becomes impure. It asks how much it may be reduced and still be retained: two dinars for a סלע; less than that, one must cut it up. The Gemara asks about more than that: Rav Huna says both less and more require cutting; Rabbi Ammi says less requires cutting, more may be retained. An objection is raised.

sub.desc_en: A baraita from elsewhere is cited: a disqualified סלע (coin) prepared as a weight becomes impure; it may be retained if reduced to two dinars, but less than that must be cut up.
The Gemara asks: what is the law for a reduction greater than two dinars (i.e., more than the permitted retention)?
Rav Huna rules: both less than two dinars and more than two dinars require cutting up the coin.
Rabbi Ammi rules: less than two dinars requires cutting, but more than two dinars may be retained.
The Gemara raises an objection against the positions of Rav Huna and Rabbi Ammi.

items.text: Clarifying the Mishnah's phrase 'more than that'
items.text_en: Clarifying the Mishnah's phrase 'more than that'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether 'more than that' means the coin depreciated more than the overcharge limit, and answers that it means it has not yet depreciated to the overcharge limit, so she sells it at its value.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's phrase 'more than that' means the coin depreciated more than the overcharge limit.
The Gemara answers that it means the coin has not yet depreciated to the overcharge limit, so she sells it at its value.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita on gradual depreciation
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita on gradual depreciation
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges with a baraita that allows keeping a coin until it depreciates to a shekel, implying gradual depreciation. The answer is that it fell into fire and depreciated all at once.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges with a baraita that allows keeping a coin until it depreciates to a shekel, implying gradual depreciation.
The Gemara answers that the coin fell into fire and depreciated all at once, not gradually.

items.text: Contradiction about piercing and hanging a defective coin
items.text_en: Contradiction about piercing and hanging a defective coin
items.desc_en: The Mishnah permits piercing and hanging the coin on a child's neck, but a baraita forbids it. Rabbi Elazar resolves the contradiction: the Mishnah refers to piercing in the middle, the baraita to piercing on the side.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's ruling that one may pierce a defective coin and hang it on a child's neck.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that forbids piercing and hanging the coin, requiring instead grinding, melting, cutting, or throwing it into the Dead Sea.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar (or Rav Huna citing Rabbi Elazar)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar (or Rav Huna citing Rabbi Elazar)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar resolves the contradiction: the Mishnah permits piercing in the middle of the coin, while the baraita forbids piercing on the side.

items.text: Time limit for returning a defective coin vs. a garment
items.text_en: Time limit for returning a defective coin vs. a garment
items.desc_en: The Mishnah distinguishes between cities (until showing a money changer) and villages (until Friday eve). The Gemara asks why a coin has different rules than a garment. Abaye and Rava offer explanations based on expertise and availability of experts.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah distinguishes between cities and villages for returning a defective coin (סלע) but not for a garment (טלית).
Abaye answers that the Mishnah's ruling about a garment also applies only in cities, so there is no distinction.
Rava explains that everyone is expert in a garment, so no time limit is needed; but a coin requires a money changer, so the time limit depends on access to one.

items.text: The case of recognizing the coin after twelve months
items.text_en: The case of recognizing the coin after twelve months
items.desc_en: The Mishnah says if one recognizes the coin even after twelve months, he must accept it. The Gemara questions this given the earlier time limits. Rav Chisda answers that this is a pious measure, and the Gemara clarifies that the complaint applies to the one who returns it, not the pious recipient.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling about returning a coin after twelve months, given the earlier time limits for cities and villages.
Rav Chisda answers that the Mishnah teaches a pious measure, and the Gemara objects by questioning to whom the grievance applies.
The Gemara resolves that the grievance applies to the one who returns the coin, not the pious recipient who refuses to accept it.

items.text: The coin given to second tithe and the 'evil spirit'
items.text_en: The coin given to second tithe and the 'evil spirit'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah says one may give the defective coin for second tithe without concern, as it is only an 'evil spirit'. Rav Pappa deduces that one who hoards coins is called an 'evil spirit', but only if they circulate.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may give the defective coin for second tithe without concern, as the refuser is merely an 'evil spirit'.
Rav Pappa deduces that one who hoards coins is called an 'evil spirit', but only if the coins still circulate.

items.text: Support for Chizkiya's ruling on redeeming second tithe
items.text_en: Support for Chizkiya's ruling on redeeming second tithe
items.desc_en: The Gemara supports Chizkiya's statement that when redeeming second tithe, one redeems it at its full value, but when changing it, one changes it at its current value. The Gemara clarifies that 'at its full value' means at the rate of a good coin, not devaluing it twice.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a support for Chizkiya's ruling that when redeeming second tithe one redeems at full value, but when changing it one changes at current value.
The Gemara asks what Chizkiya's statement means, and clarifies that even though when redeeming one uses the current value, when changing one uses the full value.

The Gemara objects that Chizkiya's ruling seems to devalue second tithe, contradicting his own statement that second tithe worth less than a perutah can be redeemed on earlier coins because one cannot precisely limit one's money.
The Gemara resolves that 'at its full value' means at the rate of a good coin, not devaluing it twice.

items.text: Chizkiya's original statement and a challenge
items.text_en: Chizkiya's original statement and a challenge
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Chizkiya's statement about redeeming second tithe worth less than a perutah, and then challenges it with a baraita about terumah and first fruits that require death and the fifth.

sub.desc_en: Chizkiya states that second tithe worth less than a perutah can be redeemed by declaring it and its fifth nullified onto earlier coins, because one cannot precisely limit his coins.
The Gemara challenges Chizkiya by citing a baraita that terumah and first fruits incur death and the fifth, implying that second tithe should similarly require strict handling.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the stringencies of terumah and bikurim that do not apply to ma'aser sheni, including that they are forbidden to non-priests, are priestly property, are nullified in one in a hundred, require hand-washing and sunset for purity.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the stringencies of תרומה (priestly portion) and ביכורים (first fruits) that do not apply to מעשר שני (second tithe).

items.text: Gemara's initial inference and challenge
items.text_en: Gemara's initial inference and challenge
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's phrase 'what is not the case with ma'aser' that ma'aser is nullified in a majority, but this contradicts Hezekiah's principle that something with a permitted alternative cannot be nullified at all.

sub.desc_en: The gemara infers from the Mishnah's wording that מעשר (second tithe) is nullified in a simple majority (רוב), and objects that if Chizkiyah's principle holds, this would be a דבר שיש לו מתירין (an item that can become permitted) which is never nullified even in a thousand.

The Gemara objects: if Hezekiah's principle holds — that something with a permitted alternative (דבר שיש לו מתירין) cannot be nullified even in a thousand — then ma'aser, which has a permitted alternative, should not be nullified at all.

items.text: Rejection of the inference
items.text_en: Rejection of the inference
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's phrase necessarily implies nullification in a majority; perhaps it means ma'aser is not nullified at all. It argues that the Mishnah only lists stringencies of terumah, not leniencies, but the mention of 'they are priestly property' is a leniency, so the inference stands.

sub.desc_en: The gemara challenges the inference: perhaps the Mishnah means that מעשר is not nullified at all, not that it is nullified in a majority; but then notes that the Mishnah only lists stringencies of תרומה, not leniencies, yet it includes 'they are priestly property' which is a leniency for the priest.

The Gemara rejects the objection, arguing that the Mishnah only lists stringencies of תרומה (priestly portion), not leniencies, but the mention of 'they are priestly property' is a leniency, so the inference stands.

items.text: Support from a baraita
items.text_en: Support from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that explicitly states ma'aser sheni is nullified in a majority, specifically when it lacks a perutah's value and has entered and left Jerusalem. This contradicts Hezekiah's principle, as one could redeem it with first-year money, but the baraita says it is not redeemed.

sub.desc_en: The gemara rejects the objection by citing an explicit baraita that מעשר שני is nullified in a majority, specifically when it has no value of a פרוטה (small coin) and has entered and left Jerusalem.
The gemara objects: if Chizkiyah's principle holds, why not redeem the מעשר on the original coins, since the owner did not redeem it.

items.text: Attempt to combine with other ma'aser
items.text_en: Attempt to combine with other ma'aser
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests bringing another ma'aser to combine with the deficient one, but rejects this because biblical and rabbinic laws do not combine.

sub.desc_en: The gemara answers: one could bring another מעשר that has value and combine them, but biblical and rabbinic law do not combine.
The Gemara rejects the suggestion because biblical and rabbinic laws do not combine.

items.text: Concern about bringing definite produce
items.text_en: Concern about bringing definite produce
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions what type of ma'aser could be brought, fearing one might bring definite (untithed) produce.

sub.desc_en: The gemara objects: what kind of מעשר would one bring? Perhaps one might bring definite (unredeemed) מעשר.

items.text: Attempt with two perutahs
items.text_en: Attempt with two perutahs
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests using two perutahs to redeem the ma'aser, but explains that a half-perutah does not effect redemption, leaving a biblical-rabbinic mixture that does not combine.

sub.desc_en: The gemara proposes bringing two פרוטות (small coins) and redeeming the מעשר on one and a half, but rejects this because a half-פרוטה does not effect redemption, leaving a mixture of biblical and rabbinic law that does not combine.
The Gemara rejects the proposal: a half-perutah cannot effect redemption, leaving a mixture of biblical and rabbinic value that does not combine.

items.text: Final analysis of the baraita's conditions
items.text_en: Final analysis of the baraita's conditions
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers using an issar coin but fears one might come to use perutahs. It then questions why the baraita specifies 'entered and left Jerusalem' – if it entered, why not re-enter? It answers that it became impure, and cites Rabbi Elazar that impure ma'aser sheni may be redeemed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests using an issar coin to redeem the ma'aser sheni, but rejects it due to concern that one might come to use perutahs instead.
The Gemara questions why the baraita specifies 'entered and left Jerusalem' – if it entered, why not re-enter it?
The Gemara answers that the ma'aser sheni became impure, and cites Rabbi Elazar that impure ma'aser sheni may be redeemed.

items.text: Opening proof that 'שאת' means eating
items.text_en: Opening proof that 'שאת' means eating
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse to prove that the word 'שאת' in the context of Jerusalem refers to eating, based on the verse about Joseph's portions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse to prove that the word 'שאת' in the context of Jerusalem refers to eating, based on the verse about Joseph's portions.

items.text: Question about purchased second tithe and Rabbi Yehuda's view
items.text_en: Question about purchased second tithe and Rabbi Yehuda's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the mishnah refers to second tithe that 'left' Jerusalem, suggesting it might be about purchased second tithe, but then notes that such tithe can be redeemed if impure, unless it follows Rabbi Yehuda who says it must be buried.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the mishnah's case is about second tithe purchased with money (לקוח בכסף מעשר שני), not about pure second tithe.
The Gemara objects that even purchased second tithe can be redeemed if impure, citing a mishnah that permits redemption.
The Gemara answers that the mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda, who rules that such tithe must be buried (יקבר) and cannot be redeemed.

items.text: Rejection: it refers to pure tithe whose walls fell
items.text_en: Rejection: it refers to pure tithe whose walls fell
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the previous approach, explaining that the mishnah deals with pure tithe, and 'left' means its walls fell. Rava's distinction between biblical and rabbinic walls is cited, but the Gemara concludes that the rabbis did not distinguish between existing and fallen walls.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the identification with Rabbi Yehuda, arguing that the mishnah's use of 'יצא' (went out) is problematic, and instead explains that the mishnah deals with pure tithe and 'יצא' means its walls fell.
Rava's distinction is cited: the wall for eating is biblical, but the walls for absorbing (קליטה) are rabbinic, and the rabbis only decreed when walls exist, not when they have fallen.
The Gemara concludes that the rabbis did not distinguish between existing and fallen walls in this context.

items.text: Rav Huna bar Yehuda's alternative: a single case of tithe without a perutah
items.text_en: Rav Huna bar Yehuda's alternative: a single case of tithe without a perutah
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehuda citing Rav Sheshet explains that the mishnah refers to second tithe lacking a perutah's worth that entered and left Jerusalem. The Gemara questions why it cannot be re-entered and eaten, and answers that the walls fell. It then questions redemption, citing Rava's distinction again, concluding that the rabbis did not distinguish.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Yehuda citing Rav Sheshet
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Yehuda citing Rav Sheshet
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehuda in the name of Rav Sheshet asserts that the mishnah teaches a single case: second tithe lacking a perutah's worth that entered Jerusalem and then left.
The Gemara asks why the tithe cannot simply be brought back into Jerusalem and eaten there.
The Gemara answers that the walls of Jerusalem have fallen, so the tithe cannot be re-entered and eaten.
The Gemara further asks why the tithe cannot be redeemed (פדיון) instead.

The Gemara invokes Rava's distinction: the wall's function for eating is biblical, but for absorbing (קליטה) is rabbinic; the rabbis only decreed absorption when walls exist, not when they have fallen.
The Gemara concludes that the rabbis did not distinguish between cases where walls exist and where they do not, so redemption is not possible.

items.text: Clarification: why specify 'without a perutah'?
items.text_en: Clarification: why specify 'without a perutah'?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the mishnah specifies 'without a perutah's worth', since even if it had value, the walls would have absorbed it. It answers that the mishnah is not necessary for the case with value, but teaches that even without value, the walls do not absorb it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the mishnah specifies 'without a perutah's worth', since even if it had value, the walls would have absorbed it.
The Gemara answers that the mishnah is not necessary for the case with value, but teaches that even without value, the walls do not absorb it.

items.text: Baraita and dispute about the minimum for redemption
items.text_en: Baraita and dispute about the minimum for redemption
items.desc_en: A baraita derives from a verse that second tithe without a perutah's worth cannot be redeemed. A dispute follows: Rav Ami and Rabbi Yochanan say 'without a perutah' refers to the principal, while Rav Asi and Resh Lakish say it refers to the fifth.

sub.desc_en: A baraita derives from the verse 'if a man redeems from his tithe' that second tithe without a perutah's worth cannot be redeemed.
The gemara reports a dispute: Rav Ami and Rabbi Yochanan say 'without a perutah' refers to the principal, while Rav Asi and Resh Lakish say it refers to the fifth.

items.text: Challenge to the view that the principal lacks a perutah
items.text_en: Challenge to the view that the principal lacks a perutah
items.desc_en: A baraita states that second tithe without a perutah's worth may be redeemed by saying 'it and its fifth are redeemed on the first money'. This supports the view that the fifth lacks a perutah, but challenges the view that the principal lacks a perutah, since the baraita says 'it is enough' (דיו), implying the principal has value.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: second tithe lacking a perutah's worth may be redeemed by saying 'it and its fifth are redeemed on the first money'.

The gemara explains that the baraita's word 'דיו' (it is enough) supports the view that the fifth lacks a perutah, but challenges the view that the principal lacks a perutah, since 'דיו' implies the principal has value.

items.text: Inquiry: is the fifth calculated from within or without?
items.text_en: Inquiry: is the fifth calculated from within or without?
items.desc_en: The Gemara inquires whether the fifth is added from within (one-fifth of the total) or from without (one-fifth of the principal). Ravina brings a proof from a mishna about owners adding a fifth when redeeming, implying the fifth is added on top of the principal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the fifth (חומש) is calculated from within (one-fifth of the total) or from without (one-fifth of the principal).
Ravina brings a proof from a mishna where owners add a fifth when redeeming, implying the fifth is added on top of the principal.

The mishna gives an example where one pledges twenty-one, showing the fifth is added externally (one-fifth of twenty is four, making twenty-four, not twenty-one; the example is cited to illustrate the principle).

items.text: Mishnah: Calculation of redemption payments
items.text_en: Mishnah: Calculation of redemption payments
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a table of redemption values for a field, showing that when the owner redeems it, they pay the principal plus an additional fifth. The Gemara infers from the last case that the fifth is added on top of the principal (חומשא מלבר).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a table of redemption values for a field, showing that when the owner redeems it, they pay the principal plus an additional fifth.
The Gemara infers from the last case that the fifth is added on top of the principal (חומשא מלבר).

items.text: Tannaic dispute on the calculation of the fifth
items.text_en: Tannaic dispute on the calculation of the fifth
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a dispute between Rabbi Yoshiya and Rabbi Yonatan regarding the interpretation of the verse 'וְיָסַף חֲמִשִׁתוֹ עָלָיו'. Rabbi Yoshiya holds that the fifth is one-fifth of the total (so principal plus fifth equals five parts), while Rabbi Yonatan holds it is one-fifth of the principal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a Tannaic dispute regarding the interpretation of the verse 'וְיָסַף חֲמִשִׁתוֹ עָלָיו', presenting Rabbi Yoshiya's position that the principal and its fifth together equal five parts.
Rabbi Yonatan argues that the fifth is one-fifth of the principal, not of the total.

items.text: Question: Does the fifth impede redemption?
items.text_en: Question: Does the fifth impede redemption?
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: Is the additional fifth indispensable (מעכב) for the redemption, or not? It presents two possibilities: either the owner redeems with four units for a four-unit principal and adds the fifth separately (fifth not indispensable), or redeems with five units for a four-unit principal (fifth indispensable).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: Is the additional fifth (חומש) indispensable (מעכב) for the redemption of consecrated property, or not? It presents two possibilities: either the owner redeems with four units for a four-unit principal and adds the fifth separately (fifth not indispensable), or redeems with five units for a four-unit principal (fifth indispensable).

items.text: Proof from demai produce
items.text_en: Proof from demai produce
items.desc_en: Ravina brings a proof from the law of demai (doubtfully tithed produce): demai has no requirement for a fifth or for removal (ביעור), but it does have a principal. The Gemara explains that the principal, which is indispensable in Torah law, applies even rabbinically, but the fifth, which is not indispensable in Torah law, does not apply rabbinically.

sub.desc_en: Ravina brings a proof from the law of demai (doubtfully tithed produce): demai has no requirement for a fifth or for removal (ביעור), but it does have a principal.
The Gemara explains that the principal, which is indispensable in Torah law, applies even rabbinically, but the fifth, which is not indispensable in Torah law, does not apply rabbinically.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua about eating after paying principal
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua about eating after paying principal
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where if one paid the principal but not the fifth, Rabbi Eliezer says he may eat (the redeemed produce), while Rabbi Yehoshua says he may not. Rabbi declares that Rabbi Eliezer's view applies on Shabbat and Rabbi Yehoshua's on weekdays. The Gemara initially suggests they dispute whether the fifth is indispensable, but Rav Papa explains that all agree it is not indispensable; rather, they dispute whether we suspect the owner might be negligent (פשיעותא) and not pay the fifth later.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer permits eating after paying the principal but not the fifth, Rabbi Yehoshua forbids it, and Rabbi declares each view applies in a different context.
The Gemara infers from Rabbi's statement that the dispute applies both on Shabbat and on weekdays.
The Gemara suggests the dispute is about whether the fifth (חומש) is indispensable (מעכב).
Rav Papa rejects the suggestion, explaining that all agree the fifth is not indispensable; the dispute is about whether we suspect the owner might be negligent (פשיעותא) and fail to pay later.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's statement about consecrated property and Shabbat
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's statement about consecrated property and Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says that all agree regarding consecrated property (הקדש) that if one paid the principal, the redemption is effective because the treasurers pursue him in the market. The Gemara challenges this with a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages dispute whether redemption is effective without the fifth. Rabbi Yochanan then clarifies that all agree specifically on Shabbat regarding consecrated property, because of the verse 'וְקָרָאתָ לַשַּׁבָּת עֹנֶג' and because the treasurers pursue him.

sub.desc_en: רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) states that all agree regarding consecrated property (הקדש) that if one paid the principal, the redemption is effective because the treasurers pursue him in the market.

The Gemara challenges with a baraita where רבי אליעזר (Rabbi Eliezer) and the Sages dispute whether redemption is effective without the fifth, and Rabbi says the statements appear correct for different contexts.
The Gemara infers from Rabbi's statement that the Sages disagree even regarding consecrated property (הקדש), contradicting רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan)'s claim of universal agreement.

רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) clarifies that all agree specifically on שבת (Shabbat) regarding consecrated property (הקדש), because of the verse 'וְקָרָאתָ לַשַּׁבָּת עֹנֶג' and because the treasurers pursue him.

items.text: Questions about the fifth regarding land, terumah, and asimon
items.text_en: Questions about the fifth regarding land, terumah, and asimon
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama raises three questions: whether the fifth of consecrated property can be redeemed on land (since the principal cannot), whether the fifth of terumah can be paid from non-chullin (since the principal must be from chullin), and whether the fifth of ma'aser can be redeemed on asimon (uncoined metal). Rava answers with a verse that the fifth is like the principal itself. Ravina supports this from a mishnah about one who steals terumah.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks whether the additional one-fifth of consecrated property can be desacralized with land, given that the principal cannot.
Rami bar Chama asks whether the additional one-fifth of terumah can be paid from non-chullin, since the principal must be from chullin.
Rami bar Chama asks whether the additional one-fifth of ma'aser can be desacralized with an asimon (uncoined metal), since the principal cannot.
Rava resolves all three questions by citing the verse 'עליו' (upon it), which includes the additional one-fifth in the same legal status as the principal.
Ravina supports Rava's ruling by citing a mishnah about one who steals terumah, which shows that the additional one-fifth follows the same rules as the principal.

items.text: Initial inference from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Initial inference from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that the added fifth is like the principal (חומשו כמותו), meaning that a fifth is added to the fifth itself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that the added fifth is like the principal (חומשו כמותו), meaning that a fifth is added to the fifth itself.

items.text: Comparison of גזל, תרומה, and מעשר
items.text_en: Comparison of גזל, תרומה, and מעשר
items.desc_en: Rava cites verses and Mishnayot for גזל and תרומה, showing that both add a fifth on a fifth, but for מעשר there is no verse, no Mishnah, and no question raised.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens by citing the verse for גזל (theft) and the Mishnah that one adds a fifth on a fifth, establishing the pattern.
Rava cites the verse for תרומה (priestly portion) and the Mishnah that one who eats it pays a fifth on a fifth, showing the same pattern.
Rava notes that for מעשר (tithe) there is no verse, no Mishnah, and no question was raised about adding a fifth on a fifth.

items.text: Question regarding הקדש and the added fifth
items.text_en: Question regarding הקדש and the added fifth
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that for הקדש, a verse says 'וְיָסַף חֲמִישִׁית', but the Mishnah only mentions one fifth, not a fifth of a fifth. It then questions whether the extra vav in 'וְיָסַף' for תרומה yields 'חֲמִישִׁתָיו' (plural), while for הקדש it yields only 'חֲמִשִׁתוֹ' (singular).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that for הקדש (sanctified property), the verse says 'וְיָסַף חֲמִישִׁית' (and he shall add a fifth), and the Mishnah teaches that one adds a fifth, but does not teach a fifth of a fifth, raising the question of whether the added fifth applies recursively.

The Gemara analyzes that for תרומה (priestly portion), the extra vav in 'וְיָסַף' yields 'חֲמִישִׁתָיו' (plural, implying multiple fifths), while for הקדש, even with the vav, the word remains 'חֲמִשִׁתוֹ' (singular), suggesting only one fifth is added.

items.text: Objection and resolution via Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
items.text_en: Objection and resolution via Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that even if only one fifth is added, it could apply to a second redemption of הקדש. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules that only the first redemption of הקדש adds a fifth, not the second. Rava confirms that the fifth is like the initial consecration.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that even if only one fifth is added, it could apply to a second redemption of הקדש (consecrated property), and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules that only the first redemption adds a fifth, not the second.

sub.text: Rav Papi to Ravina citing Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Papi to Ravina citing Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Papi tells Ravina that Rava said the fifth is like the initial consecration, resolving the objection.

items.text: Final resolution via Abaye
items.text_en: Final resolution via Abaye
items.desc_en: Rav Tavyomi in the name of Abaye resolves the question by noting that the verse 'וְיָסַף חֲמִישִׁית כֶּסֶף עֶרְכְּךָ' compares the fifth to the principal redemption money, so just as the principal adds a fifth, so too the fifth adds a fifth.

sub.text: Rav Tavyomi in the name of Abaye
sub.text_en: Rav Tavyomi in the name of Abaye
sub.desc_en: Rav Tavyomi in the name of Abaye resolves the question by citing the verse 'וְיָסַף חֲמִישִׁית כֶּסֶף עֶרְכְּךָ' and arguing that just as the principal redemption money adds a fifth, so too the fifth itself adds a fifth.

items.text: Source for Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's ruling
items.text_en: Source for Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's ruling
items.desc_en: Rava explains Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's reasoning: the verse 'וְאִם הַמַּקְדִּישׁ יִגְאַל אֶת בֵּיתוֹ' implies only the original consecrator (המקדיש) adds a fifth, not one who subsequently consecrates (המתפיס).

sub.desc_en: The gemara cites Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's ruling: one adds a fifth (חומש) only on the first consecration (הקדש ראשון), not on a second consecration (הקדש שני).

Rava explains the scriptural basis: the verse 'וְאִם הַמַּקְדִּישׁ יִגְאַל אֶת בֵּיתוֹ' (if the consecrator redeems his house) implies that only the original consecrator (המקדיש) adds a fifth, not one who subsequently consecrates (המתפיס).

items.text: Discussion of מעילה and the baraita
items.text_en: Discussion of מעילה and the baraita
items.desc_en: A baraita taught before Rabbi Elazar compares an unclean animal to other consecrated items regarding מעילה. Rabbi Elazar clarifies that the baraita refers to the added fifth, consistent with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi. Rav Ashi questions whether an unclean animal is subject to the initial consecration.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna recites a baraita before Rabbi Elazar, deriving from the verse about an unclean animal that only items whose initial consecration is fully for Heaven are subject to מעילה (misuse of consecrated property).

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar's question to the Tanna
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's question to the Tanna
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar questions the Tanna: the phrase 'כּוּלָּהּ לַשָּׁמַיִם' excludes קדשים קלים (lesser sanctities), but what does 'תְּחִילַּת הֶקְדֵּשׁ' (initial consecration) exclude?
Rabbi Elazar suggests that the baraita might be referring to the added fifth (חומש), consistent with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's ruling that only initial consecration adds a fifth.
The Tanna confirms that this is indeed what he meant.
Rav Ashi asks Ravina whether an unclean animal is subject to the initial consecration (i.e., whether it can be consecrated at all, given it cannot be offered).

items.text: Debate on adding a fifth for middle consecration
items.text_en: Debate on adding a fifth for middle consecration
items.desc_en: Rav Aha challenges Ravina: if a middle consecration exists, why not add a fifth? Ravina compares it to the end of consecration, which does not add a fifth. Rav Zutra objects, suggesting it should be compared to the beginning of consecration, which does add a fifth. Ravina defends his analogy: both are 'caught from what is caught'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Aha challenges Ravina: if a middle consecration exists, why not add a fifth? Ravina responds that it is like the end of consecration, which does not add a fifth.

sub.text: Rav Zutra bar Rav Mari's objection
sub.text_en: Rav Zutra bar Rav Mari's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Zutra objects: why compare middle consecration to the end, which does not add a fifth? It should be compared to the beginning, which does add a fifth, since both are 'a thing that has sanctity after it'.

Ravina defends his analogy: middle consecration is 'caught from what is caught' (נתפס מנתפס), like the end, not the beginning, which is 'a thing that has sanctity after it from a thing that has sanctity after it'.

items.text: Support from Rava's principle
items.text_en: Support from Rava's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rava's principle that 'the burnt-offering' refers to the first burnt-offering, and similarly 'the unclean' refers to the first unclean animal, supporting the analogy to the beginning of consecration.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rava's principle that 'the burnt-offering' refers to the first burnt-offering, and similarly 'the unclean' refers to the first unclean animal, supporting the analogy to the beginning of consecration.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's view: when one says 'this cow in place of a consecrated cow' without specifying a price, the consecration is redeemed but the sanctity rests on the top (the original). When a price is specified, the consecration is redeemed, and a fifth is added only to the first consecration, not the second.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's view: when one says 'this cow in place of a consecrated cow' without specifying a price, the consecration is redeemed but the sanctity rests on the top (the original).
The baraita continues: when a price is specified, the consecration is redeemed, and a fifth is added only to the first consecration, not the second.

items.text: Mishnah: The five perutah-values
items.text_en: Mishnah: The five perutah-values
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the five perutah-values in halakha: the admission (in an oath) is worth a perutah, a woman is betrothed with a perutah, one who benefits from consecration worth a perutah is liable for misuse, one who finds an object worth a perutah must announce it, and one who robs a fellow of a perutah and swears falsely must return it even to Media.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing the perutah-values in halakha: the admission (in an oath) is worth a perutah.
The Mishnah enumerates the five perutah-values: betrothal, misuse of consecrated property, finding lost property, and robbery with a false oath.

items.text: Gemara: Why repeat the oath laws?
items.text_en: Gemara: Why repeat the oath laws?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah repeats the laws of the claim (two silver) and admission (perutah) from the oath of judges. It answers that the latter part (the five perutah-values) is necessary.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah repeats the laws of the claim (two silver) and admission (perutah) from the oath of judges, since they were already taught.
The Gemara answers that the latter part of the Mishnah, listing the five perutah-values, is necessary and was not previously taught.

items.text: Debate on whether there is overcharge for perutot
items.text_en: Debate on whether there is overcharge for perutot
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah does not list overcharge (ona'ah) as a perutah. Rav Kahana says this teaches there is no overcharge for perutot. Levi argues there is overcharge for perutot, and his baraita lists overcharge as a perutah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah's list of five perutot does not include overcharge (אונאה) as a perutah.
Rav Kahana answers that the omission teaches there is no overcharge (אונאה) for perutot (small coins).
Levi objects, asserting that there is overcharge for perutot.
Levi cites his own baraita listing overcharge (אונאה) as a perutah among the five perutot.

items.text: Analysis of inclusions and exclusions in the lists
items.text_en: Analysis of inclusions and exclusions in the lists
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why our Tanna does not list 'sitting of the court' (it is included in robbery), and why Levi does not list 'lost object' (it is included in robbery). It further explains why our Tanna includes 'lost object' (to teach that even if it depreciates, one must announce), and why Levi includes 'sitting of the court' (to exclude Rav Ketina's view that courts adjudicate even less than a perutah). Finally, it asks why our Tanna does not list 'consecration' (the Mishnah deals with non-sacred items) and why not 'tithe' (according to the view that there is no perutah in its fifth).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why our Tanna does not list 'sitting of the court' among the five perutah cases.
The Gemara answers that 'sitting of the court' is included in the category of robbery (גזל).
The Gemara asks why Levi does not list 'lost object' among his five perutah cases.
The Gemara answers that 'lost object' is also included in the category of robbery (גזל).
The Gemara asks why Levi does not list 'consecration' among his five perutah cases.
The Gemara answers that Levi's list deals with non-sacred items (חולין), not consecrated items (קדשים).
The Gemara asks why our Tanna, who deals with consecrated items, does not list 'tithe' among his five perutah cases.
The Gemara answers that our Tanna follows the view that there is no perutah in the fifth of the tithe.
The Gemara asks why our Tanna does not list the fifth of the tithe as a perutah case.
The Gemara answers that our Tanna deals only with the principal (קרן), not with the added fifth (חומש).

items.text: Rav Ketina's statement challenged by Rava
items.text_en: Rav Ketina's statement challenged by Rava
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Ketina's statement that courts adjudicate even less than a perutah, and Rava challenges it from a verse: 'And that which he has sinned from the holy he shall repay'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ketina states that a court adjudicates even for a claim of less than a perutah.
Rava challenges Rav Ketina by citing the verse 'And that which he has sinned from the holy he shall repay', implying a minimum value for court involvement.

items.text: Court's completion of adjudication for less than a perutah
items.text_en: Court's completion of adjudication for less than a perutah
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies Rav Ketina's statement: if a court has already engaged with a case involving a perutah, they may complete it even for less than a perutah; the initial hearing requires a perutah, but the conclusion does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara initially interprets the baraita as including less than a perutah (פרוטה) for sacred redemption but not for ordinary cases.

Rav Ketina clarifies that if a court has already engaged with a case involving a perutah (פרוטה), they may complete the adjudication even for less than a perutah (פרוטה); the initial hearing requires a perutah (פרוטה), but the conclusion does not.

items.text: Mishnah: Five cases of adding a fifth
items.text_en: Mishnah: Five cases of adding a fifth
items.desc_en: The mishnah lists five categories where one adds a fifth (ḥomesh): eating terumah, terumat ma'aser, terumat ma'aser of demai, hallah, and bikurim; redeeming neta revai and ma'aser sheni; redeeming one's own hekdesh; benefiting from hekdesh worth a perutah; and stealing from a fellow and swearing falsely.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists five cases where an additional fifth (חומש) is added: eating terumah (תרומה), terumat maaser (תרומת מעשר), terumat maaser of demai (דמאי), challah (חלה), and bikurim (ביכורים); redeeming neta revai (נטע רבעי) and maaser sheni (מעשר שני); redeeming consecrated property; benefiting from hekdesh (הקדש); and stealing from a fellow and swearing falsely.

items.text: Rava's question about terumat ma'aser of demai
items.text_en: Rava's question about terumat ma'aser of demai
items.desc_en: Rava reports that Rabbi Elazar was troubled by the inclusion of terumat ma'aser of demai in the list, asking: Did the Sages make their enactments as strong as Torah law?

sub.text: Rava's question in the name of Rabbi Elazar
sub.text_en: Rava's question in the name of Rabbi Elazar
sub.desc_en: Rava reports that Rabbi Elazar questions why the Mishnah includes terumat maaser of demai (תרומת מעשר של דמאי), asking whether the Sages strengthened their own enactments to be like Torah law.

items.text: Answer: The mishnah follows Rabbi Meir
items.text_en: Answer: The mishnah follows Rabbi Meir
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel answers that the mishnah is Rabbi Meir's view, who holds that rabbinic enactments are as strong as Torah law. A baraita is cited where Rabbi Meir rules that a get brought from overseas without the formula 'written and signed in my presence' renders the child a mamzer, while the Sages disagree. The Gemara then explains that Rabbi Meir's position is consistent with his general principle, as stated by Rav Hamnuna in the name of Ulla: anyone who deviates from the coinage established by the Sages in gittin must divorce and the child is a mamzer.

sub.text: Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel answers that the mishnah follows Rabbi Meir, who holds that rabbinic enactments are as strong as Torah law.
A baraita is cited where Rabbi Meir rules that a get brought from overseas without the formula renders the child a mamzer, while the Sages disagree and prescribe a corrective procedure.
The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Meir would really require divorce and declare the child a mamzer merely for omitting the formula.

sub.text: Gemara's answer via Rav Hamnuna in the name of Ulla
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer via Rav Hamnuna in the name of Ulla
sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that Rabbi Meir's position is consistent with his general principle, as stated by Rav Hamnuna in the name of Ulla: anyone who deviates from the formula coined by the Sages in gittin must divorce and the child is a mamzer.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's objection from ma'aser sheni redemption
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's objection from ma'aser sheni redemption
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet raises an objection from a baraita where Rabbi Meir permits redeeming ma'aser sheni silver with copper, which seems to contradict the principle that rabbinic enactments are as strong as Torah law, since Torah law requires silver for redemption. The Gemara then cites a mishnah about mixing a selah of ma'aser sheni with hullin, implying that one cannot redeem silver with copper.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet raises an objection from a baraita where Rabbi Meir permits redeeming ma'aser sheni silver with copper, which seems to contradict the principle that rabbinic enactments are as strong as Torah law, since Torah law requires silver for redemption.
The Gemara cites a mishnah about mixing a selah of ma'aser sheni with hullin, implying that one cannot redeem silver with copper.

items.text: Opening statement on redeeming second tithe under duress
items.text_en: Opening statement on redeeming second tithe under duress
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah permits redeeming second tithe money from silver to copper only under duress, implying that without duress it is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's phrase 'under duress' that redeeming second tithe silver for copper is permitted only when pressed, not voluntarily.

items.text: Rabbi Meir's stringency on demai and the Sages' leniency
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's stringency on demai and the Sages' leniency
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef explains that although Rabbi Meir is lenient in redeeming second tithe, he is stringent regarding its consumption: only a storekeeper or householder may sell demai, but must tithe. The Sages permit anyone to sell or give demai without concern.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef states that Rabbi Meir, though lenient in redeeming second tithe, is stringent regarding its consumption.
A baraita is cited: Rabbi Meir permits selling demai only to a storekeeper or householder, but both must tithe.
The Sages permit anyone to sell or give demai without concern for tithing.

items.text: Ravina's objection from the baker's case
items.text_en: Ravina's objection from the baker's case
items.desc_en: Ravina raises an objection: Rabbi Meir allows tithing from hot bread for cold bread and from different batches, which seems to permit tithing from the obligated on the exempt. The Gemara questions why there is no concern for separating from the obligated on the exempt.

sub.desc_en: Ravina raises an objection by citing a baraita where Rabbi Meir permits tithing from hot bread for cold bread and from different batches, implying no concern for separating from the obligated on the exempt.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Ila'i's proof
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Ila'i's proof
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that tithing from cold for hot is justified by Rabbi Ila'i's proof from a verse that one can separate from inferior for superior.
The Gemara objects that even with multiple batches, one should worry about tithing from the obligated on the exempt.

items.text: Abaye's critique of Samuel's resolution
items.text_en: Abaye's critique of Samuel's resolution
items.desc_en: Abaye states that Rabbi Elazar's difficulty is valid, but Samuel's resolution is not, because Samuel compares death by Heaven to death by court, which is more severe.

sub.desc_en: Abaye rejects Samuel's resolution of Rabbi Elazar's difficulty, arguing that death by court (מיתת בית דין) is more severe than death by Heaven (מיתה בידי שמים), so the comparison fails.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's objection and Rav Yosef's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's objection and Rav Yosef's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet objects based on the verse 'you cannot eat within your gates', and Rav Yosef resolves it properly.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet objects to the previous discussion by citing the verse 'you cannot eat within your gates'.
Rav Yosef properly resolves Rav Sheshet's objection.

items.text: Ravina's support from the palter case and resolution
items.text_en: Ravina's support from the palter case and resolution
items.desc_en: Ravina attempts to support his objection from the case of a palter (wholesaler), but the Gemara distinguishes: a palter buys from multiple sellers, while a baker buys from one, so the concern does not apply.

sub.desc_en: Ravina objects that the case of a baker (נחתום) should be analogous to a palter (פלטר), citing the Mishnah where Rabbi Meir requires tithing from each batch even from a palter.

The Gemara resolves the objection by distinguishing that a palter buys from multiple sellers (creating a concern of mixing liable and exempt batches), while a baker buys from a single seller, so the concern does not apply.

items.text: Rava's defense of Samuel
items.text_en: Rava's defense of Samuel
items.desc_en: Rava argues that Samuel's resolution is valid because the term 'death' is used in a general sense.

sub.desc_en: Rava defends Samuel's resolution by arguing that the term 'death' is used in a general sense, so Samuel's distinction is valid.

items.text: Mishnah: Items exempt from ona'ah
items.text_en: Mishnah: Items exempt from ona'ah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items that have no claim of overcharge: slaves, documents, land, and consecrated property. They also have no double payment or four/five payment, and certain laws of bailees do not apply.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items exempt from the law of overcharge: slaves, documents, land, and consecrated property, and notes they are also exempt from certain other payments and oaths.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that consecrated items for which one is liable have ona'ah, while those not liable do not. Rabbi Yehuda adds that a Torah scroll, animal, and pearl have no ona'ah, but the Sages limit this to specific items.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule: consecrated items for which one is liable have ona'ah, while those not liable do not.
Rabbi Yehuda adds that a Torah scroll, animal, and pearl have no ona'ah.
The Sages object that the rule of no ona'ah was only stated for these specific items.

items.text: Gemara's derivation and exclusion of documents
items.text_en: Gemara's derivation and exclusion of documents
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse that only movable items subject to hand-to-hand transfer have ona'ah, excluding land, slaves, and documents. It then clarifies that selling documents for their paper does have ona'ah, countering Rav Kahana's view that small coins have no ona'ah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where are these matters (that certain items have no ona'ah) derived?
The Tanna derives from the verse that only items acquired hand-to-hand have ona'ah, excluding land, slaves, and documents.
The Gemara cites a baraita that selling documents for their paper has ona'ah, and clarifies that this counters Rav Kahana's view that small coins have no ona'ah.

items.text: Interpretation of 'yado' (his hand) in the verse
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'yado' (his hand) in the verse
items.desc_en: Rabba bar Memel challenges the literal interpretation of 'yado' in the verse, citing a case where it means 'his domain.' The Gemara reconciles this with other verses where 'yado' is literal, concluding that here it refers to domain.

sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Memel challenges the assumption that 'yado' (his hand) in the verse always means a literal hand.

Rabba bar Memel cites the verse 'וַיִּקַּח אֶת כָּל אַרְצוֹ מִיָּדוֹ' (he took all his land from his hand) where 'yado' must mean 'his domain,' not his literal hand, and applies the same interpretation here.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita on theft where 'yado' is literal, and the verse adds 'אִם הִמָּצֵא תִמָּצֵא' to include other domains.
The Gemara cites another baraita regarding 'וְנָתַן בְּיָדָהּ' (and placed in her hand) where 'yad' is literal, and the extra word 'וְנָתַן' extends to other domains.
The Gemara resolves that generally 'yado' means a literal hand, but in the context of the verse about ona'ah (overcharging), it must mean 'his domain' because a literal reading is impossible.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's question on rental
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's question on rental
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks whether rental has ona'ah, since the verse says 'sale' but not rental. Abaye answers that the term 'sale' is general and includes rental for its duration.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks whether rental has ona'ah (overcharge law), considering the verse mentions 'sale' but not rental.
Abaye answers that the term 'ממכר' (sale) is general and includes rental, since each day of rental is like a sale for that day.

items.text: Rava's question on grain sown in land
items.text_en: Rava's question on grain sown in land
items.desc_en: Rava asks whether grain sown in land has ona'ah, oath liability, and whether the Omer permits it. The Gemara clarifies the scenario: the seller claimed he sowed enough, but it was insufficient, and debates if the grain is considered like in a container or nullified by the land.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether grain that was sown in land is subject to ona'ah (overcharge law), considering whether it is like grain in a container or nullified by the land.
The Gemara clarifies the scenario, rejecting a case where the seller claimed a specific measure and witnesses contradicted him, because Rava's rule about fixed measures would apply regardless.
Rava refines the question to a case where the seller claimed he sowed enough but it was insufficient, asking whether the grain is considered like in a container or nullified by the land.
Rava asks whether one can take an oath regarding such sown grain, or whether it is nullified by the land and thus exempt from oath liability.

items.text: Clarification on the Omer's permission
items.text_en: Clarification on the Omer's permission
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves Rava's question about the Omer by distinguishing between grain that rooted before the Omer and grain harvested and replanted after the Omer but before rooting, concluding that the Omer does not permit it.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether the Omer permits grain that was sown after being harvested before the Omer.
The Gemara objects that the question seems already answered by a Mishnah: if the grain rooted before the Omer, the Omer permits it; if not, it is forbidden until the next Omer.
The Gemara cites the Mishnah that explicitly rules: grain that rooted before the Omer is permitted by the Omer; otherwise it is forbidden until the next Omer.

The Gemara resolves the question by specifying a case: the grain was harvested and replanted before the Omer, and the Omer passed over it without it having rooted before the Omer, so the Omer does not permit it.

items.text: Unresolved question about gleaning from hekdesh
items.text_en: Unresolved question about gleaning from hekdesh
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a teiku (undecided) question: when produce of hekdesh is scattered, is it considered like something thrown into a barrel (and thus permitted to glean and eat) or is it nullified by attachment to the ground?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an unresolved question (תיקו) about whether scattered hekdesh produce is considered like something thrown into a barrel (permitted to glean) or nullified by attachment to the ground.

items.text: Rava's report: R. Ammi's query and resolution on bitul mekach for hekdesh and land
items.text_en: Rava's report: R. Ammi's query and resolution on bitul mekach for hekdesh and land
items.desc_en: Rava reports that R. Ammi asked whether hekdesh and land, though exempt from ona'ah, are subject to bitul mekach. R. Nachman reports that R. Ammi resolved that they are. R. Yona and R. Yirmiyah, both citing R. Yochanan, disagree on whether this applies to hekdesh or only to land.

sub.desc_en: Rava reports that Rabbi Ammi asked whether hekdesh and land, though exempt from ona'ah, are subject to bitul mekach.

sub.text: Rav Nachman reporting Rabbi Ammi's resolution
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman reporting Rabbi Ammi's resolution
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman reports that Rabbi Ammi resolved that hekdesh and land have bitul mekach.

sub.text: Rabbi Yona and Rabbi Yirmiyah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yona and Rabbi Yirmiyah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yona and Rabbi Yirmiyah, both citing Rabbi Yochanan, disagree on whether the ruling applies to hekdesh or only to land.

items.text: Clarifying the positions: hekdesh vs. land
items.text_en: Clarifying the positions: hekdesh vs. land
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the logic: the one who says the ruling applies to hekdesh certainly includes land; the one who says it applies to land excludes hekdesh, citing Shmuel's principle that hekdesh worth a maneh can be redeemed for a perutah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the one who says the ruling applies to hekdesh certainly includes land.
The Gemara explains that the one who says it applies to land excludes hekdesh.
The Gemara cites Shmuel's principle that hekdesh worth a maneh can be redeemed for a perutah, supporting the exclusion of hekdesh.

items.text: Mishnah on blemished consecrated animal and dispute between R. Yochanan and Resh Lakish
items.text_en: Mishnah on blemished consecrated animal and dispute between R. Yochanan and Resh Lakish
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah: if a consecrated animal with a blemish is redeemed, it goes out to non-sacred status but requires valuation. R. Yochanan says the going out is Torah law, but the valuation is rabbinic; Resh Lakish says even the valuation is Torah law.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah: if a consecrated animal with a blemish is redeemed, it goes out to non-sacred status but requires valuation.
Rabbi Yochanan states that the going out to non-sacred status is Torah law, but the valuation is rabbinic.
Resh Lakish argues that even the valuation is Torah law.

items.text: Gemara's analysis: which case are they discussing?
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis: which case are they discussing?
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether the dispute is about ona'ah or bitul mekach. If it's about ona'ah, Resh Lakish's position contradicts the Mishnah that hekdesh has no ona'ah. If it's about bitul mekach, R. Yochanan's position contradicts his own statement that bitul mekach applies. The Gemara resolves by flipping the attributions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what case the dispute is about, and raises the possibility that if it is about the standard overcharge (כדי אונאה), Resh Lakish's position would contradict the Mishnah that hekdesh has no אונאה (overcharge).
The Gemara alternatively considers that the dispute is about ביטול מקח (annulment of the sale), but then Rabbi Yochanan's position would contradict his own statement that hekdesh has ביטול מקח.
The Gemara resolves by flipping the attributions: Rabbi Yochanan's statement is assigned to Resh Lakish, and Resh Lakish's statement to Rabbi Yochanan.

items.text: First explanation: dispute over Shmuel's principle
items.text_en: First explanation: dispute over Shmuel's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the dispute between R. Yochanan and Resh Lakish is about whether to accept Shmuel's ruling that hekdesh can be redeemed for a perutah. One master accepts it, the other does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the dispute between R. Yochanan and Resh Lakish is about, and suggests it revolves around Shmuel's principle.
The Gemara explains that one master (R. Yochanan) accepts Shmuel's ruling that hekdesh can be redeemed for a perutah, and the other (Resh Lakish) does not.

items.text: Second explanation: both accept Shmuel, dispute about lechatchilah
items.text_en: Second explanation: both accept Shmuel, dispute about lechatchilah
items.desc_en: Alternatively, both accept Shmuel's principle, but they disagree whether it applies only after the fact (b'di'avad) or even initially (lechatchilah).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes an alternative explanation: both Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish accept Shmuel's principle, but they disagree about whether it applies only after the fact (בדיעבד) or even לכתחילה (the ideal standard).

items.text: Third explanation: dispute about Rav Chisda's interpretation of 'no ona'ah'
items.text_en: Third explanation: dispute about Rav Chisda's interpretation of 'no ona'ah'
items.desc_en: A final alternative: the dispute is about the meaning of 'they have no ona'ah' – whether it means they are not subject to the laws of ona'ah at all (and thus even bitul mekach does not apply) or something else. The daf ends mid-explanation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a third alternative: the dispute is about Rav Chisda's interpretation of 'they have no ona'ah' – meaning they are not subject to the laws of ona'ah at all, and the daf ends mid-explanation.

items.text: Gemara's initial claim about ona'ah
items.text_en: Gemara's initial claim about ona'ah
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that even less than the measure of ona'ah (one-sixth) is subject to return, implying that the law of ona'ah applies broadly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asserts that even less than the measure of ona'ah (one-sixth) is subject to return, implying broad applicability of the law.

items.text: Objection from a baraita and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita stating that ribbit and ona'ah do not apply to hekdesh. It resolves by interpreting the baraita as referring to the 'law of ona'ah' (i.e., the prohibition) rather than monetary restitution. The Gemara then questions why the baraita only mentions a stringency for hedyot and not for hekdesh, and concludes that the baraita lists only one stringency for hedyot, not for hekdesh.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that states ribbit and ona'ah apply to a commoner (הדיוט) but not to hekdesh.
The Gemara resolves the objection by interpreting the baraita as referring to the 'law of ona'ah' (דין אונאה) rather than monetary restitution, consistent with the earlier resolution of the mishnah.
The Gemara questions why the baraita's continuation only mentions a stringency for hedyot (ribbit) and not a stringency for hekdesh (ona'ah).
The Gemara answers that the baraita only lists one stringency for hedyot, not for hekdesh, so the omission is consistent.

items.text: Question about ribbit with hekdesh
items.text_en: Question about ribbit with hekdesh
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how ribbit could apply to hekdesh, suggesting a case where the treasurer lends money with interest, but notes that the treasurer would have misappropriated funds, rendering the money secular.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how ribbit (interest) could apply to hekdesh (consecrated property), and suggests a case where the treasurer (גזבר) lends money with interest, but immediately rejects it because the treasurer would have misappropriated the funds (מעל), rendering the money secular (חולין).

items.text: Rav Hoshaya's answer: supply of flour
items.text_en: Rav Hoshaya's answer: supply of flour
items.desc_en: Rav Hoshaya explains that the case involves someone who undertook to supply flour at four se'ahs per selah, and the price dropped to three; he must supply at four, because the hand of hekdesh is on the upper side.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hoshaya answers that the case involves a supplier of flour who must give at the higher rate because the hand of hekdesh is on the upper side.

items.text: Rav Pappa's answer: building stones
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's answer: building stones
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa offers an alternative explanation: the case involves building stones entrusted to the treasurer, following Shmuel's principle that one builds with mortar and then consecrates.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa answers that the case involves building stones entrusted to the treasurer, citing Shmuel's principle that one builds with mortar and then consecrates.

items.text: Derivation that double payment does not apply to hekdesh
items.text_en: Derivation that double payment does not apply to hekdesh
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from a brayta using the hermeneutic principle of כלל ופרט וכלל that the law of double payment (for theft) applies only to movable property with intrinsic monetary value, excluding land, slaves, documents, and hekdesh (based on the word 'רֵעֵהוּ').

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where are these matters (that hekdesh is exempt from double payment) derived?
The Gemara cites a baraita that applies the hermeneutic principle of כלל ופרט וכלל (general, particular, general) to the verse about theft, establishing the framework for the derivation.
The Gemara resolves that the rule limits double payment to movable property with intrinsic monetary value, excluding land, slaves, documents, and hekdesh, based on the word 'רֵעֵהוּ' (your fellow).

items.text: Derivation that four/five-fold payment does not apply to hekdesh
items.text_en: Derivation that four/five-fold payment does not apply to hekdesh
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Torah mandates four/five-fold payment for theft of an ox or sheep, not three/four-fold, implying that hekdesh is excluded.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah states that four/five-fold payment does not apply to hekdesh, and answers that the Torah mandated four/five-fold payment for theft of an ox or sheep, not three/four-fold, thereby excluding hekdesh.

items.text: Derivation that bailee oaths do not apply to hekdesh
items.text_en: Derivation that bailee oaths do not apply to hekdesh
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from a brayta using כלל ופרט וכלל that the laws of an unpaid bailee (who swears) and a paid bailee (who pays) apply only to movable property with intrinsic value, excluding land, slaves, documents, and hekdesh (based on 'רֵעֵהוּ').

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where are these matters derived regarding the unpaid bailee not taking an oath?
The baraita cites the verse for the unpaid bailee, applying the rule of generalization-detail-generalization to limit the law to movable property with intrinsic monetary value.

The Gemara concludes that land, slaves, documents, and consecrated property are excluded from the unpaid bailee's oath, the latter because the verse says 'רֵעֵהוּ' (his neighbor), not consecrated property.
The Gemara asks: From where are these matters derived regarding the paid bailee not paying?
The baraita cites the verse for the paid bailee, applying the same rule of generalization-detail-generalization to limit the law to movable property with intrinsic monetary value.

The Gemara concludes that land, slaves, documents, and consecrated property are excluded from the paid bailee's liability, the latter because the verse says 'רֵעֵהוּ' (his neighbor), not consecrated property.

items.text: Contradiction regarding shekalim sent by townspeople
items.text_en: Contradiction regarding shekalim sent by townspeople
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a mishna about townspeople who sent their shekalim (half-shekel donations) and they were stolen or lost, discussing the status after the terumah was taken.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a mishna about townspeople who sent their shekalim (half-shekel donations) and they were stolen or lost.
The Gemara begins to present the condition of the mishna: if this occurred after the תרומה (priestly portion) was taken from the chamber.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if Temple funds are lost or stolen, the treasurers swear an oath, and if not, the townspeople swear and contribute replacement funds. If the original funds are later found or returned, they are considered shekels but do not count for the next year.
