sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rules for oaths and replacement funds when Temple shekels are lost or stolen.

items.text: Gemara's first question and answers
items.text_en: Gemara's first question and answers
items.desc_en: Shmuel explains that the Mishnah deals with a paid custodian who swears to receive his fee. Rabba clarifies that the oath is taken before the townspeople in the presence of the treasurers to avoid suspicion. The Gemara objects that a paid custodian is liable for theft and loss, and Rabba answers that the case involves armed bandits or a shipwreck.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel explains that the Mishnah deals with a paid custodian (נושא שכר) who swears to receive his fee.
The Gemara objects that if the oath is for the fee, the Mishnah should say they swear to the townspeople, not to the treasurers.
Rabba clarifies that the oath is taken before the townspeople in the presence of the treasurers to avoid suspicion and prevent them from being called negligent.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah mentions theft and loss, for which a paid custodian is liable, so even if they don't pay, they should at least lose their fee.
Rabba answers that the case involves armed bandits (ליסטים מזוין) for theft and a shipwreck for loss, which are exempt for a paid custodian.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan attributes the Mishnah to Rabbi Shimon, who holds that consecrated property for which one is liable has the laws of overreaching and requires an oath.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan attributes the Mishnah to Rabbi Shimon, who holds that consecrated property for which one is liable has the laws of overreaching and requires an oath.

items.text: Objection to Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Objection to Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that after terumah has been separated, the consecrated items are not under the custodian's liability, as a baraita teaches that one may separate terumah on behalf of lost or future produce.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that after the terumah is separated, the funds are consecrated property for which one is not liable, citing a baraita that terumah can be set aside for lost or future collections.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's resolution
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar explains that the oath is a rabbinic enactment to prevent people from treating consecrated property lightly.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar explains that the oath is a rabbinic enactment to prevent people from treating consecrated property lightly.

items.text: Contradiction about paid watchman's liability on Shabbat
items.text_en: Contradiction about paid watchman's liability on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Chama raises a contradiction: the Mishnah says a paid custodian does not pay, but a baraita states that a worker hired to watch an animal on Shabbat has liability on Shabbat if paid for Shabbat. The Gemara initially suggests this means he must pay, but Rav Sheshet and Rabbi Yochanan explain that it means he loses his wages, and this applies only if he explicitly accepted liability.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a paid custodian does not pay for lost or stolen consecrated items.

sub.text: Rav Yosef bar Chama's contradiction to Rabba
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef bar Chama's contradiction to Rabba
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Chama raises a contradiction: the Mishnah says a paid custodian does not pay, but a baraita states that a worker hired to watch an animal on Shabbat has liability on Shabbat if paid for Shabbat, implying he must pay.
The Gemara answers that the baraita means he loses his wages, not that he pays; but then questions how this applies to the first clause where no wages are given, and Rabba remains silent.

sub.text: Rav Sheshet and Rabbi Yochanan's resolution
sub.text_en: Rav Sheshet and Rabbi Yochanan's resolution
sub.desc_en: Rabba asks if Rav Yosef bar Chama has heard anything about this; Rav Yosef bar Chama reports that Rav Sheshet and Rabbi Yochanan both said the baraita applies only when the worker explicitly accepted liability (קנו מידו).

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's principle and a baraita
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's principle and a baraita
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon states that consecrated property for which one is liable has the laws of overreaching, while property not under liability does not. A baraita taught before Rabbi Yitzchak bar Abba derives this from verses, but he dismisses it as irrelevant.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon states the principle that consecrated property for which one bears liability is subject to the laws of overreaching (אונאה), while property for which one bears no liability is not.

sub.text: Baraita taught before Rabbi Yitzchak bar Abba
sub.text_en: Baraita taught before Rabbi Yitzchak bar Abba
sub.desc_en: A Tanna recites a baraita before Rabbi Yitzchak bar Abba that derives Rabbi Shimon's distinction from the verses 'בה' וכחש' (in God and lied) for liable consecrated property and 'בעמיתו וכחש' (in his fellow and lied) for exempt property.
Rabbi Yitzchak bar Abba dismisses the baraita as irrelevant, saying 'כלפי ליא' (against what? / what is it directed at?).

items.text: Gemara's resolution of the earlier dispute about liability for consecrated items
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution of the earlier dispute about liability for consecrated items
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a previous contradiction by explaining that the Tanna Kamma distinguishes between items for which one bears responsibility (liable for ona'ah) and those for which one does not (exempt), based on the verses 'bah' and 'ba'amito'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous assumption, asking if the Tanna Kamma's position should be reversed.

The Gemara answers that the Tanna Kamma distinguishes between consecrated items for which one bears responsibility (liable for ona'ah) and those for which one does not (exempt), based on the verses 'bah' and 'ba'amito'.

items.text: Mishnah: Rabbi Yehuda's exceptions to ona'ah
items.text_en: Mishnah: Rabbi Yehuda's exceptions to ona'ah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Rabbi Yehuda exempts a seller of a Torah scroll, a pearl, and an animal from the laws of ona'ah, with a baraita explaining the reasons: the Torah scroll has no fixed price, and the animal and pearl are desired for their match.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Yehuda's position that a Torah scroll, a pearl, and an animal have no ona'ah because their value is subjective or because one wants to match them.
A baraita explains the reasons: the Torah scroll has no fixed price, and the animal and pearl are desired for their match.

items.text: Gemara's challenge and resolution regarding Rabbi Yehuda's view
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge and resolution regarding Rabbi Yehuda's view
items.desc_en: The Sages challenge Rabbi Yehuda: doesn't everyone desire a match? The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between items that are significant to the buyer and those that are not. Amemar limits the exemption to the item's value.

sub.desc_en: The Sages object that one wants to match all items, not just these, and Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between what is significant to him and what is not.
Amemar answers that the exemption applies only up to the item's market value.
Amemar limits the exemption from אונאה (overcharge) to the item's value, meaning the buyer is only protected up to the item's worth.

items.text: Baraita: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's additional exceptions
items.text_en: Baraita: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's additional exceptions
items.desc_en: A baraita adds that Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira exempts a horse, sword, and shield sold in wartime from ona'ah because they are life-saving items.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's position that a horse, sword, and shield sold in wartime have no ona'ah because they are life-saving items.

items.text: Mishnah: Ona'at devarim (verbal wronging)
items.text_en: Mishnah: Ona'at devarim (verbal wronging)
items.desc_en: The Mishnah introduces the concept of verbal wronging, listing examples: asking a price without intent to buy, reminding a penitent of past sins, or reminding a convert of their ancestors' deeds, citing the verse 'And you shall not wrong a convert.'

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that just as there is ona'ah in buying and selling, so too there is ona'ah in speech, listing examples of forbidden verbal wrongs.

items.text: Gemara: Baraita expanding on verbal wronging
items.text_en: Gemara: Baraita expanding on verbal wronging
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives the prohibition of verbal wronging from the verse 'You shall not wrong one another,' distinguishing it from monetary wronging. It provides additional examples: not reminding a convert of their past, not taunting a sufferer like Job's friends, and not directing a buyer to a seller who never sells.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by citing the verse 'לֹא תוֹנוּ אִישׁ אֶת עֲמִיתוֹ' and asserts that it refers to verbal wronging, not monetary wronging.
The baraita provides examples of verbal wronging: not reminding a penitent of past sins, not taunting a convert about his ancestry, and not mocking a convert who comes to learn Torah.
The baraita continues with examples: not taunting a sufferer or one who buries his children, as Job's friends did.
The baraita gives a final example: not directing buyers to a seller who never sells, and Rabbi Yehuda adds not to gaze at merchandise without money, as this is a matter of the heart.

items.text: Debate on the severity of verbal versus monetary wronging
items.text_en: Debate on the severity of verbal versus monetary wronging
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai states that verbal wronging is greater than monetary wronging because it includes the phrase 'fear of God.' Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani offer alternative reasons: one affects the body, the other money; one can be compensated, the other cannot.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai states that verbal ona'ah is greater than monetary ona'ah because the former includes the phrase 'וְיָרֵאתָ מֵאֱלֹהֶיךָ' (fear of God) and the latter does not.
Rabbi Elazar adds that verbal ona'ah affects the body while monetary ona'ah affects only money, and Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani adds that verbal ona'ah cannot be restored.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani adds that verbal ona'ah cannot be restored, unlike monetary ona'ah.

items.text: The severity of public humiliation: like shedding blood
items.text_en: The severity of public humiliation: like shedding blood
items.desc_en: A baraita taught before Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak states that one who whitens a friend's face in public is as if shedding blood. The Gemara discusses this, and Rabbi Chanina lists three who descend to Gehinnom and do not ascend: one who commits adultery, one who publicly shames another, and one who gives a derogatory nickname.

sub.text: Tanna before Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak
sub.text_en: Tanna before Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak
sub.desc_en: A Tanna recites a baraita before Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak stating that one who whitens a friend's face in public is as if shedding blood, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak confirms this by noting the visible color change.
Abaye asks Rav Dimi what they are especially careful about in the West (Eretz Yisrael) regarding interpersonal conduct.
Rav Dimi answers that they are especially careful about whitening faces (public humiliation).
Rabbi Chanina states that everyone descends to Gehinnom except for three types of people.
The Gemara objects that it cannot be that everyone descends to Gehinnom.
The Gemara corrects the statement: all who descend to Gehinnom ascend except for three who descend and do not ascend.
The Gemara lists the three who descend and do not ascend: one who commits adultery, one who publicly shames another, and one who gives a derogatory nickname.
The Gemara questions whether giving a derogatory nickname is the same as public humiliation.
The Gemara answers that giving a nickname is worse because it includes the element of using the person's name in the insult.

items.text: Introduction to the next statement by Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Introduction to the next statement by Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new statement by Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, which will continue in the following segments.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan begins a new statement (the content is cut off in the source).

items.text: The severity of public embarrassment compared to adultery
items.text_en: The severity of public embarrassment compared to adultery
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that it is better for a person to commit a possible sin with a married woman than to embarrass someone in public. It derives this from Rava's exposition of David's lament, where David says that even when his enemies discussed his sin with Bathsheba, he could respond that he still has a share in the World to Come, but one who embarrasses another has no share.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that it is preferable for a person to commit a possible sin with a married woman than to publicly embarrass another.
The Gemara asks for the source of this principle.
The Gemara cites Rava's exposition of David's lament, where David says that even if his enemies tore his flesh, his blood would not flow to the ground.
David continues that even when his enemies discuss his sin with Bathsheba, he can respond that he still has a share in the World to Come, but one who embarrasses another has no share.

items.text: Support from Tamar's example
items.text_en: Support from Tamar's example
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra bar Toviya in the name of Rav (or other authorities) states that it is better to throw oneself into a fiery furnace than to embarrass another in public, citing Tamar who was taken out to be burned but sent a message to her father-in-law rather than publicly shaming him.

sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra bar Toviya in the name of Rav (or alternative attributions) states the principle that it is better to throw oneself into a fiery furnace than to embarrass another in public.
The gemara cites the source for this principle from Tamar, who was taken out to be burned but sent a message to her father-in-law rather than publicly shaming him.

items.text: Ona'ah of one's wife and the power of tears
items.text_en: Ona'ah of one's wife and the power of tears
items.desc_en: Rav Chinana bar Rav Idi interprets the verse 'Do not oppress your fellow' as referring to one who is with you in Torah and mitzvot. Rav advises being careful with ona'ah of one's wife because her tears are frequent and her oppression is close. Rabbi Elazar adds that since the Temple's destruction, the gates of prayer are locked but the gates of tears are not.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chinana bar Rav Idi interprets the verse 'וְלֹא תוֹנוּ אִישׁ אֶת עֲמִיתוֹ' (Do not oppress your fellow) as referring to one who is with you in Torah and mitzvot.
Rav advises that one should always be careful with ona'ah (oppression) of one's wife because her tears are frequent and her oppression is close.
Rabbi Elazar adds that since the Temple's destruction, the gates of prayer are locked but the gates of tears are not, citing the verse 'אֶל דִּמְעָתִי אַל תֶּחֱרַשׁ' (Do not be silent to my tears).

items.text: Following a wife's advice: worldly vs. household matters
items.text_en: Following a wife's advice: worldly vs. household matters
items.desc_en: Rav states that one who follows his wife's advice falls into Gehinnom, citing Ahab. Rav Pappa questions this based on the folk saying to listen to one's wife. The Gemara resolves that this applies to worldly matters (or heavenly matters), but not to household matters.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that one who follows his wife's advice falls into Gehinnom, citing the verse about Ahab.
Rav Pappa questions Rav's statement by citing the folk saying that one should listen to his wife's advice.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: Rav's warning applies to worldly matters, while the folk saying applies to household matters.
An alternative version distinguishes between heavenly matters (where one should not follow a wife's advice) and worldly matters (where one may).

items.text: The gates of ona'ah are never locked
items.text_en: The gates of ona'ah are never locked
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda teaches that all gates are locked except the gates of ona'ah (oppression), citing a verse. Rabbi Elazar adds that everything is exacted through an agent except ona'ah. Rabbi Avahu lists three things before which the curtain (pargod) is not locked: ona'ah, theft, and idolatry, each with scriptural support.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda teaches that all gates are locked except the gates of ona'ah (oppression), citing the verse 'הנה ה' נצב על חומת אנך ובידו אנך'.
Rabbi Elazar adds that everything is exacted through an agent except ona'ah, citing the same verse.
Rabbi Avahu lists three things before which the curtain (פרגוד) is not locked: ona'ah, theft, and idolatry, each with scriptural support.

items.text: The importance of grain and honoring one's wife
items.text_en: The importance of grain and honoring one's wife
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda advises being careful with grain in the house, as strife only comes over grain. Rav Pappa cites a folk saying. Rav Chinana bar Pappa adds that Israel became poor only over grain. Rabbi Chelbo says one should always honor his wife, as blessing comes only through her, and Rava told the people of Mehoza to honor their wives to become wealthy.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda advises that one should always be careful with grain in his house, as strife only comes over grain, citing a verse.
Rav Pappa supports Rav Yehuda with a folk saying that when barley is gone from the jar, strife comes knocking at the house.
Rav Chinana bar Pappa adds that Israel became poor only over grain, citing verses about the Midianite oppression.
Rabbi Chelbo says one should always honor his wife, as blessing comes only through her, citing the verse about Avraham benefiting because of Sarah.
Rava tells the people of Mehoza to honor their wives in order to become wealthy, supporting Rabbi Chelbo's statement.

items.text: Mishnah: A stove made of coils with sand between them
items.text_en: Mishnah: A stove made of coils with sand between them
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah: If one cut a stove into coils and placed sand between each coil, Rabbi Eliezer declares it pure (not susceptible to impurity), while the Sages declare it impure.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited: a stove cut into coils with sand between them is deemed pure by Rabbi Eliezer and impure by the Sages.

items.text: Introduction to the Oven of Akhnai
items.text_en: Introduction to the Oven of Akhnai
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the oven is called 'of Akhnai' and introduces the dispute: Rabbi Eliezer brought all possible proofs but was not accepted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the oven is called 'of Akhnai': it was surrounded by arguments like a snake (עכנא) and declared impure.
A baraita reports that on that day Rabbi Eliezer brought every possible answer but was not accepted.

items.text: First two miracles: carob tree and aqueduct
items.text_en: First two miracles: carob tree and aqueduct
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer calls upon a carob tree and an aqueduct to prove his halakhic position, but the Sages reject these proofs as inadmissible.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer invokes a carob tree as a sign that the halakha (הלכה) follows him, and the tree miraculously uproots itself.
The Sages reject the carob tree's testimony as an inadmissible proof.
Rabbi Eliezer then invokes an aqueduct as a sign, and the water flows backward.
The Sages reject the aqueduct's testimony as an inadmissible proof.

items.text: Third miracle: walls of the study hall
items.text_en: Third miracle: walls of the study hall
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer calls upon the walls of the study hall, which begin to fall. Rabbi Yehoshua rebukes the walls, and they remain tilted.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer calls upon the walls of the study hall to prove his halachic position, and the walls begin to tilt.
Rabbi Yehoshua rebukes the walls, asserting that halachic debate among sages is not for walls to decide, and the walls remain tilted out of respect for both rabbis.
The walls remain tilted, neither falling nor straightening, as a permanent testament to the dispute.

items.text: Bat Kol and the principle 'Not in Heaven'
items.text_en: Bat Kol and the principle 'Not in Heaven'
items.desc_en: A Bat Kol declares that the law follows Rabbi Eliezer, but Rabbi Yehoshua cites Deuteronomy 30:12 to assert that the Torah is not in heaven. Rabbi Yirmeya explains that we follow the majority. Rabbi Nathan asks Elijah what God did, and He rejoiced that His children prevailed.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer invokes a heavenly sign to prove his halachic position.
A Bat Kol (heavenly voice) declares that the law follows Rabbi Eliezer everywhere.
Rabbi Yehoshua objects by citing the verse 'It is not in heaven' (Deuteronomy 30:12).
Rabbi Yirmeya explains that since the Torah was given at Sinai, we follow the majority (אחרי רבים להטות) and do not heed a Bat Kol.
Rabbi Nathan asks Elijah what God did at that moment, and Elijah reports that God smiled and said, 'My children have prevailed over Me.'

items.text: Excommunication of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva's mission
items.text_en: Excommunication of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva's mission
items.desc_en: The Sages burn all items Rabbi Eliezer had declared pure and excommunicate him. Rabbi Akiva volunteers to inform him, dressing in mourning and sitting at a distance.

sub.desc_en: The Sages burn all items Rabbi Eliezer had declared pure.
The Sages excommunicate Rabbi Eliezer and ask who will inform him.
Rabbi Akiva volunteers to inform Rabbi Eliezer, fearing an unworthy messenger would cause disaster.
Rabbi Akiva dresses in mourning and sits at a distance from Rabbi Eliezer.

sub.text: Dialogue between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva
sub.text_en: Dialogue between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer asks why Rabbi Akiva came, and Rabbi Akiva hints that the colleagues are distancing themselves from him.
Rabbi Eliezer tears his garments, removes his shoes, and sits on the ground in mourning.

items.text: Punishments and Rabban Gamliel's prayer
items.text_en: Punishments and Rabban Gamliel's prayer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer's tears cause crop damage and fires. Rabban Gamliel, at sea, prays that the dispute was for God's honor, and the storm subsides.

sub.desc_en: The narrative describes that Rabbi Eliezer's tears caused a third of the world's crops to be blighted, and wherever he cast his eyes, fire broke out.
The narrative shifts to Rabban Gamliel, who was at sea and a wave threatened to drown him.
Rabban Gamliel prays, declaring that his actions were for God's honor, and the sea calms.

items.text: Ima Shalom prevents Rabbi Eliezer's prayer
items.text_en: Ima Shalom prevents Rabbi Eliezer's prayer
items.desc_en: Ima Shalom, Rabbi Eliezer's wife and Rabban Gamliel's sister, prevents him from falling on his face in prayer. She explains that all gates are locked except those of ona'ah (oppression).

sub.desc_en: Introduces Ima Shalom as Rabbi Eliezer's wife and Rabban Gamliel's sister, and notes that after the incident she prevented Rabbi Eliezer from falling on his face in prayer.
Explains that on that day it was Rosh Chodesh and she confused the full and deficient months, or alternatively a poor person came to the door and she gave him bread.
Ima Shalom finds Rabbi Eliezer fallen on his face in prayer and tells him he has killed her brother (Rabban Gamliel).
At that moment a shofar blast from Rabban Gamliel's house announces his death, confirming Ima Shalom's words.
Rabbi Eliezer asks Ima Shalom how she knew that his prayer would cause Rabban Gamliel's death.
Ima Shalom answers that she received a tradition from her grandfather's house: all gates of prayer are locked except the gates of ona'ah (oppression).

items.text: Laws of oppressing a convert
items.text_en: Laws of oppressing a convert
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the prohibitions against oppressing a convert, noting that one who does so violates multiple negative commandments. Rabbi Eliezer HaGadol explains the many warnings, and Rabbi Nathan gives a moral lesson.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that one who oppresses a convert violates three negative commandments, and one who pressures him violates two.
The Gemara questions why the baraita counts three prohibitions for oppression but only two for pressure, noting that three verses also appear for pressure.
The Gemara resolves that both oppression and pressure actually involve three prohibitions, correcting the baraita's initial count.
Rabbi Eliezer HaGadol explains that the Torah warns about the convert in 36 or 46 places because the convert has a bad tendency (to revert to idolatry).

Rabbi Nathan teaches that one should not point out a flaw in another that one has oneself, illustrated by the folk saying about not telling a friend to hang a small fish when one's own basket has a large one.

items.text: Mishnah: Prohibition of mixing produce
items.text_en: Mishnah: Prohibition of mixing produce
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not mix different types of produce, even new with new.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the prohibition of mixing different types of produce, even new with new.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Prohibitions on mixing and deceptive sales
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Prohibitions on mixing and deceptive sales
items.desc_en: The Mishnah prohibits mixing old and new produce, but allows mixing harsh and sweet wine because it improves it. It also restricts selling diluted wine without disclosure and prohibits selling to a retailer even with disclosure to prevent fraud.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the prohibition against mixing old and new produce, but permits mixing harsh and sweet wine because it improves the wine.
The Mishnah adds that one may not mix wine sediment into wine, but may give the sediment separately.
The Mishnah rules that one who diluted wine with water must disclose it to a retail buyer, and may not sell to a wholesaler even with disclosure, but where the custom is to add water, one may do so.
The Mishnah permits a merchant to mix produce from five granaries or wine from five vats into one container, provided he does not intend to deceive.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying the Mishnah's rulings on mixing and wine
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying the Mishnah's rulings on mixing and wine
items.desc_en: The Gemara expands on the Mishnah, stating that even mixing new from three years with old from four is prohibited. Rabbi Elazar notes that 'BeEmet Amru' indicates a halakha. Rav Nachman limits the wine mixing allowance to between the vats. Rav Pappa and Rav Acha offer explanations for current practice.

sub.desc_en: A baraita expands the Mishnah's prohibition: not only old from three years with new from four is forbidden, but even new from three with old from four, because one wants to age the wine.
Rabbi Elazar rules that any Mishnah using the phrase 'BeEmet Amru' (in truth they said) is a binding halakha (הלכה).
Rav Nachman limits the allowance of mixing harsh and sweet wine to between the vats (בין הגיתות), not in the market.
The Gemara asks: nowadays, why do merchants mix wine not between the vats, contrary to Rav Nachman's ruling?
Rav Pappa answers that customers know and willingly forgo the prohibition.
Rav Acha offers an alternative answer: the lenient practice follows Rabbi Acha, who permits mixing in a case where the taste is discernible (דבר הנטעם).

items.text: Gemara: Resolving contradiction in the Mishnah about wine lees
items.text_en: Gemara: Resolving contradiction in the Mishnah about wine lees
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's apparent contradiction: it forbids mixing wine lees with wine but then says one may give the lees. Rav Yehuda explains that the prohibition is mixing lees from one day with wine from another, but one may give the lees separately. A baraita supports this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's apparent contradiction: it forbids mixing wine lees with wine, yet says one may give the lees; the Mishnah's later clause requiring disclosure for diluted wine implies the earlier clause permits giving lees without disclosure, contradicting the prohibition.
Rav Yehuda resolves the contradiction: the prohibition refers to mixing lees from one day with wine from another day, but one may give the lees separately.
A baraita citing Rabbi Yehuda supports Rav Yehuda's distinction: one may not mix lees of yesterday with today's wine, but may mix lees of the same day.

items.text: Gemara: Rava's case and the ruling on diluted wine
items.text_en: Gemara: Rava's case and the ruling on diluted wine
items.desc_en: Rava sends back wine that was not tasty, and Abaye objects citing the Mishnah's prohibition on selling to a retailer. Rava defends himself, saying his mixture is known. The Gemara then discusses the custom of adding water to wine, with a baraita specifying proportions.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who mixed water into his wine may not sell it in a shop unless he informs the buyer.
The Gemara relates that Rava had wine brought from a shop, tasted it, found it not sweet, and sent it back to the shop.
Abaye objects that the Mishnah prohibits selling even to a retailer, even if the retailer is informed.
Rava defends himself, saying his mixture is known, and if one fears the retailer might dilute it further and sell it, there would be no end to the matter.
The Gemara cites a baraita that in places where it is customary to add water to wine, one may add up to half, a third, or a quarter.
Rav rules that this leniency was taught only for the period between the winepresses (when wine is new and raw).

items.text: Mishnah: Prohibitions on enticing children and price manipulation
items.text_en: Mishnah: Prohibitions on enticing children and price manipulation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah records a dispute: Rabbi Yehuda prohibits giving nuts to children to attract them, while the Sages permit it. It also prohibits lowering prices, with the Sages praising such acts. Abba Shaul prohibits sorting beans, but the Sages permit it, except when done deceptively.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda prohibits a storekeeper from distributing roasted ears of grain and nuts to children, because it habituates them to come to him.
The Sages permit distributing nuts and grains to children.
The Mishnah states that one may not lower the market price.
The Sages say that one who lowers prices is remembered for good.

sub.text: Mishnah: Abba Shaul's position on sorting beans
sub.text_en: Mishnah: Abba Shaul's position on sorting beans
sub.desc_en: Abba Shaul prohibits sorting beans.
The Sages permit sorting beans.

sub.text: Mishnah: Sages' exception for deceptive sorting
sub.text_en: Mishnah: Sages' exception for deceptive sorting
sub.desc_en: The Sages agree that one may not sort from the top of the bin, as that is merely deceiving the eye.
The Mishnah concludes that one may not groom a person, an animal, or vessels.

items.text: Gemara: Reasoning of the Sages on the Mishnah's disputes
items.text_en: Gemara: Reasoning of the Sages on the Mishnah's disputes
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Sages' reasoning: the storekeeper can argue he gives nuts while the customer gives other items. It then asks for the rationale behind the Sages' lenient view on lowering prices, implying a question about their position.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the reasoning of the Sages who permit the storekeeper to distribute nuts and lower prices.
The Gemara explains that the storekeeper can argue: I distribute nuts, and you distribute other items (so there is no unfair inducement).
The Gemara asks what is the reasoning of the Sages who permit lowering prices, implying a question about their position.

items.text: Reason for the Mishnah's prohibition of clearing bran
items.text_en: Reason for the Mishnah's prohibition of clearing bran
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's prohibition of clearing bran from the mouth of a sieve is because it creates a deceptive appearance of abundance.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's prohibition of clearing bran from the sieve is because it creates a deceptive appearance of abundance.

items.text: Abba Shaul and the Sages on clearing grits
items.text_en: Abba Shaul and the Sages on clearing grits
items.desc_en: The Mishnah records a dispute: Abba Shaul prohibits clearing grits, while the Sages permit it. The Gemara identifies the Sages as Rabbi Acha, who permits anything visible.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Abba Shaul prohibits clearing grits on Shabbat, while the Sages permit it.
The Gemara identifies the anonymous Sages as Rabbi Acha, who permits handling anything visible.

items.text: Prohibition of perakmus and its definition
items.text_en: Prohibition of perakmus and its definition
items.desc_en: The Mishnah prohibits perakmus (smoothing) for people, animals, and vessels. A baraita elaborates: one may not smooth an animal, blow into entrails, or soak meat in water. The Gemara defines 'smoothing' as either using 'mayya dechizra' (a type of water) or 'mazkefta' (a tool).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the prohibition of perakmus (smoothing) for people, animals, and vessels.
A baraita elaborates the prohibition: one may not smooth an animal, blow into entrails, or soak meat in water.
The Gemara asks the meaning of the term 'mesharbetin' (smoothing) in the baraita.
The local tradition explains that 'mesharbetin' refers to using 'mayya dechizra' (a type of water) for smoothing.
Ze'iri in the name of Rav Kahana explains that 'mesharbetin' refers to using a tool called 'mazkefta' (a smoothing tool).

items.text: Amoraic leniencies and resolution with the Mishnah
items.text_en: Amoraic leniencies and resolution with the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Several Amoraim permitted specific practices: Shmuel allowed placing garlic on a cloak, Rav Yehuda allowed smoothing silk, Rabbah allowed beating garments, Rava allowed smoothing arrows, and Rav Pappa bar Shmuel allowed smoothing baskets. The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction with the Mishnah: the Mishnah refers to new items, while these leniencies apply to old items.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara lists five lenient practices by Amoraim: Shmuel allowed placing garlic on a cloak, Rav Yehuda allowed smoothing silk, Rabbah allowed beating garments, Rava allowed smoothing arrows, and Rav Pappa bar Shmuel allowed smoothing baskets.
The Gemara objects that these leniencies contradict the Mishnah which prohibits smoothing (פירכוס) for people, animals, and vessels.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the Mishnah's prohibition applies to new items, while the Amoraim's leniencies apply to old items.

items.text: Story of the old slave and perakmus of a person
items.text_en: Story of the old slave and perakmus of a person
items.desc_en: The Gemara illustrates perakmus of a person with a story: an old slave dyed his hair and beard, then came before Rava to be sold. Rava refused, citing the verse 'let the poor be members of your household.' The slave then went to Rav Pappa bar Shmuel, who bought him. Later, when the slave asked for water, Rav Pappa had his hair and beard whitened, and the slave remarked he was older than Rav Pappa's father. Rav Pappa applied the verse 'the righteous is delivered from trouble, and another comes in his stead.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what constitutes perakmus (freshening up) of a person.
The Gemara illustrates with a story: an old slave dyed his hair and beard and came to Rava to be sold, but Rava refused, citing the verse 'let the poor be members of your household.'

The slave then went to Rav Pappa bar Shmuel, who bought him; later, when the slave asked for water, Rav Pappa had his hair and beard whitened, and the slave remarked he was older than Rav Pappa's father, prompting Rav Pappa to apply the verse 'the righteous is delivered from trouble, and another comes in his stead.'

items.text: Conclusion of the previous chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the previous chapter
items.desc_en: The standard formula 'hadaran alakh' marks the end of the previous chapter.

sub.desc_en: The standard closing formula 'hadaran alakh' marks the end of the previous chapter.

items.text: Mishnah: Definitions of neshekh and tarbit
items.text_en: Mishnah: Definitions of neshekh and tarbit
items.desc_en: The Mishnah defines neshekh as lending a sela for five dinarim, or two se'ah of wheat for three, which is prohibited because it bites. Tarbit is increasing through produce, illustrated by a case where one buys wheat at a fixed price and later the price rises, and the seller offers wine instead at the higher price, but has no wine.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by defining neshekh as lending a sela for five dinarim or two se'ah of wheat for three, which is prohibited because it bites.

The Mishnah defines tarbit as increasing through produce, illustrating with a case where one buys wheat at a fixed price, the price rises, and the seller offers wine at the higher price but has no wine.

items.text: Gemara: Are neshekh and tarbit distinct prohibitions?
items.text_en: Gemara: Are neshekh and tarbit distinct prohibitions?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah distinguishes neshekh and tarbit if they are both biblical usury. It attempts to find cases of neshekh without tarbit and vice versa, but each attempt fails. Rava concludes that one cannot find neshekh without tarbit or tarbit without neshekh; the Torah separated them only to violate two negative commandments.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah distinguishes neshekh and tarbit if both are biblical usury, given that the verses use distinct terms.
The Gemara objects that perhaps there are cases of neshekh without tarbit and tarbit without neshekh, and asks for an example of neshekh without tarbit.
The Gemara proposes a case of neshekh without tarbit: lending 100 at 120 when the market value of a danka (a small coin) changes, so the lender gains but the borrower does not profit.
The Gemara refutes the case: if one follows the initial value, both neshekh and tarbit exist; if one follows the final value, neither exists.
The Gemara proposes a case of tarbit without neshekh: lending 100 at 100 when the market value of a danka changes to a chumsha (a fifth), so the borrower profits but the lender does not bite.
The Gemara refutes the case: if one follows the initial value, neither exists; if one follows the final value, both neshekh and tarbit exist.
Rava concludes that one cannot find neshekh without tarbit or tarbit without neshekh; the Torah separated them only to violate two negative commandments.

items.text: Baraita: Derivation of neshekh and tarbit for food and money
items.text_en: Baraita: Derivation of neshekh and tarbit for food and money
items.desc_en: A baraita derives from verses that neshekh applies to food and tarbit to money, expanding the prohibitions beyond the literal readings.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites verses to derive that the prohibition of neshekh applies to food and tarbit to money, and vice versa, through the phrase 'neshekh okhel' and 'neshekh kesef'.

items.text: Gezerah shavah linking borrower and lender
items.text_en: Gezerah shavah linking borrower and lender
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that the verse 'neshekh kol davar asher yishakh' teaches that the prohibition applies to all forms of interest. A gezerah shavah on the word 'neshekh' extends the prohibition from borrower to lender, covering money, food, and anything else.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the verse about נשך (interest) on money is already covered by the prohibition 'לֹא תַשִּׁיךְ לְאָחִיךָ' (do not lend with interest to your brother), then apply the verse to interest on food instead.
The Gemara asks: from the verse we only learn about the borrower; how do we derive the prohibition for the lender?

The Gemara answers with a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy): the word 'נשך' appears both by the borrower and the lender, teaching that the prohibition applies equally to money, food, and any form of interest, and the verse 'נשך כל דבר אשר ישך' (interest of any thing that bears interest) includes all items.

items.text: Ravina's alternative reading and the necessity of the gezerah shavah
items.text_en: Ravina's alternative reading and the necessity of the gezerah shavah
items.desc_en: Ravina argues that the verses themselves, when read with a different punctuation, already teach that interest applies to both money and food, making the gezerah shavah unnecessary except to include 'neshekh kol davar' for the lender. The Gemara clarifies that the Tanna's use of 'ne'emar' is a rhetorical device.

sub.desc_en: Ravina argues that the verses, when read with a different punctuation, already teach that interest applies to both money and food, making the gezerah shavah unnecessary.
The Gemara objects that the Tanna explicitly uses the phrase 'ne'emar' (it was said), indicating reliance on a gezerah shavah, not a simple reading.

The Gemara clarifies that the Tanna's use of 'ne'emar' is a rhetorical device: the gezerah shavah would have been necessary had the verse been written differently, but now it is only needed to include 'neshekh kol davar' for the lender.

items.text: Rava's question: Why separate negative commandments?
items.text_en: Rava's question: Why separate negative commandments?
items.desc_en: Rava asks why the Torah needed separate negative commandments for interest, theft, and overcharging (ona'ah). The Gemara explains that each is unique: interest is a novelty, theft is against the victim's will, and overcharging involves forgiveness.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks why the Torah needed separate negative commandments for interest (ריבית), theft (גזל), and overcharging (אונאה).

The Gemara explains that each prohibition is needed: interest is a novelty (חידוש) because it applies even to a borrower, theft is against the victim's will (בעל כורחיה), and overcharging might otherwise be permitted because the victim forgives.
The Gemara continues: if the Torah had only written the prohibition for theft, one might think overcharging is permitted because the victim does not know and forgives.
The Gemara concludes: if the Torah had only written the prohibition for overcharging, one might think theft is permitted because the victim does not know and forgives.

items.text: Attempt to derive one prohibition from the others
items.text_en: Attempt to derive one prohibition from the others
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to derive the prohibition of theft from interest and overcharging, but the arguments fail because each has a unique feature. The common element is that all involve taking something that belongs to another, so theft is included.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that one prohibition cannot be derived from another, and proposes deriving one from two.
The Gemara objects that if the Torah had not written the prohibition of interest, it could not be derived from theft and overcharging because interest is given willingly.
The Gemara objects that if the Torah had not written the prohibition of overcharging, it could not be derived from theft and interest because theft and interest do not involve a standard sale.
The Gemara objects that if the Torah had not written the prohibition of theft, it could not be derived from interest and overcharging because each has a unique feature that the other lacks.
The Gemara resolves that the common element among all three is that they involve taking what belongs to another, so theft is included.

items.text: Purpose of the negative commandment for theft
items.text_en: Purpose of the negative commandment for theft
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the negative commandment for theft is needed for withholding a worker's wages, which is already prohibited elsewhere, to add a second negative commandment. The daf ends with a question about applying this to interest and overcharging.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the negative commandment for theft (לָאו בְּגָזֵל) is needed for the case of withholding a worker's wages (כּוֹבֵשׁ שְׂכַר שָׂכִיר).

The Gemara objects that withholding wages is already explicitly prohibited by the verse 'לֹא תַעֲשֹׁק שָׂכִיר עָנִי וְאֶבְיוֹן', so the additional negative commandment is only to make the violator liable for two negative commandments.

The Gemara questions why the negative commandment for theft is not applied to interest (רִבִּית) and overcharging (אוֹנָאָה) to make the violator liable for two negative commandments, since the matter is learned from its context (דָּבָר הַלָּמֵד מֵעִנְיָינוֹ).

items.text: Gemara's question on the prohibition of theft in the context of a hired worker
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the prohibition of theft in the context of a hired worker
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah wrote 'You shall not steal' in the context of a hired worker, and answers that it prohibits stealing with intent to cause loss or to repay double.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah wrote 'You shall not steal' in the context of a hired worker, and answers that it prohibits stealing with intent to cause loss or to repay double.

items.text: Rav Yemar and Rav Ashi on the prohibition of weights
items.text_en: Rav Yemar and Rav Ashi on the prohibition of weights
items.desc_en: Rav Yemar asks why the Torah wrote a separate prohibition for weights, and Rav Ashi explains it forbids hiding weights in salt; the Gemara clarifies it is a distinct prohibition from theft.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yemar asks Rav Ashi why the Torah wrote a separate prohibition for dishonest weights.
Rav Ashi answers that the prohibition is for hiding weights in salt to make them heavier.
The Gemara objects that hiding weights in salt is simply outright theft, so why a separate prohibition?
The Gemara resolves that the separate prohibition is to make one liable from the moment of making the weights, before any theft occurs.

items.text: Baraita on measures, weights, and liquids
items.text_en: Baraita on measures, weights, and liquids
items.desc_en: A baraita expounds the verse 'Do not commit injustice in judgment, measure, weight, or liquid measure,' detailing specific prohibitions and a kal vachomer argument from a small liquid measure to larger ones.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verse and explains each term: 'במדה' refers to land measurement, 'במשקל' forbids salting weights, and 'ובמשורה' forbids frothing liquid measures.

The gemara adds a kal vachomer argument: if the Torah is strict about a small liquid measure (one thirty-third of a log), then certainly it is strict about larger measures like the hin, half-hin, log, and quarter-log.

items.text: Rava's question on the Exodus in three contexts
items.text_en: Rava's question on the Exodus in three contexts
items.desc_en: Rava asks why the Torah mentions the Exodus in the contexts of interest, fringes, and weights, and answers that God, who distinguished between firstborn and non-firstborn drops in Egypt, will punish those who circumvent these laws.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks why the Torah mentions the Exodus in three distinct contexts: interest, fringes, and weights.

The Holy One, blessed be He, declares that He who distinguished between the drop of the firstborn and the non-firstborn in Egypt will punish those who circumvent the laws of interest, weights, and fringes.

items.text: Ravina and Rav Chanina on the Exodus regarding creeping creatures
items.text_en: Ravina and Rav Chanina on the Exodus regarding creeping creatures
items.desc_en: Rav Chanina asks why the Exodus is mentioned regarding creeping creatures; Ravina answers that God will punish those who mix unclean fish innards with clean ones. Ravina then questions the use of 'HaMa'aleh' (the One who brought up), and the Gemara cites a teaching of Rabbi Yishmael that the Exodus alone justifies Israel's distinction from creeping creatures, even if the reward is not greater than for other commandments.

sub.desc_en: The narrator sets the scene: Ravina arrived at Sura on the Euphrates.
Rav Chanina asks Ravina why the Torah mentions the Exodus from Egypt in the context of creeping creatures.
Ravina answers that God, who distinguished between the firstborn and non-firstborn in Egypt, will punish those who mix innards of unclean fish with clean fish and sell them to Israel.
Ravina then questions why the Torah specifically uses the term 'המעלה' (the One who brought up) in this context.

sub.text: Ravina's second answer (citing Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael)
sub.text_en: Ravina's second answer (citing Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael)
sub.desc_en: Ravina answers by citing the school of Rabbi Yishmael: God says that even if He had only brought Israel out of Egypt for this reason—that they do not become impure through creeping creatures—it would have been sufficient.
Ravina objects: Is the reward for this commandment greater than that for the prohibitions of interest, tzitzit, and weights?
Ravina resolves that even though the reward is not greater, the prohibition is emphasized because creeping creatures are repulsive to eat.

items.text: Distinction between Torah-level interest and rabbinic dust of interest
items.text_en: Distinction between Torah-level interest and rabbinic dust of interest
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the Mishnah's definition of תרבית and asks if all previously discussed cases are interest. Rabbi Avahu and Rava answer that until this point is Torah-level interest, and from here onward is rabbinic dust of interest, with a proof from the verse 'The wicked man prepares and the righteous wears.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether all the cases discussed until now are not interest, given the Mishnah's definition of תרבית.
Rabbi Avahu and Rava answer that the cases up to this point are Torah-level interest, and from here onward are rabbinic dust of interest.
The Gemara objects that the verse 'The wicked man prepares and the righteous wears' applies even to the earlier cases, not just the later ones.
The Gemara resolves that the earlier cases are fixed interest (ריבית קצוצה) and the later ones are dust of interest (אבק ריבית).

items.text: Debate on whether courts compel repayment of interest
items.text_en: Debate on whether courts compel repayment of interest
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yochanan debate whether fixed interest (ribbit ketzutzah) and dust of interest (avak ribbit) are recoverable through courts. Rabbi Yochanan holds even fixed interest is not recoverable, citing verses that it is given to death or fear, not repayment. Rava compares interest lenders to murderers. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains Rabbi Elazar's view.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that fixed interest (ribbit ketzutzah) is recoverable through courts, but dust of interest (avak ribbit) is not.
Rabbi Yochanan argues that even fixed interest is not recoverable through courts.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak's explanation for Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak's explanation for Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak explains Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning: the verse 'בַּנֶּשֶׁךְ נָתַן... וָחָי לֹא יִחְיֶה' indicates that interest is given to death, not to repayment.

sub.text: Rav Adda bar Ahava's alternative proof
sub.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava's alternative proof
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava cites a different verse: 'אֶל תִּקַּח מֵאִתּוֹ נֶשֶׁךְ וְתַרְבִּית וְיָרֵאתָ מֵאֱלֹהֶיךָ' — interest is given to fear, not to repayment.
Rava derives from the verse 'מוֹת יוּמָת דָּמָיו בּוֹ יִהְיֶה' that interest lenders are equated to murderers, and just as murderers are not subject to repayment, so too interest lenders are not.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's explanation for Rabbi Elazar
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's explanation for Rabbi Elazar
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak begins to explain Rabbi Elazar's reasoning by citing a verse.

items.text: The principle of 'and your brother shall live with you'
items.text_en: The principle of 'and your brother shall live with you'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the verse 'and your brother shall live with you' teaches that one's own life takes precedence over another's, as derived by Rabbi Akiva from the story of two travelers with one water flask.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse 'וְחֵי אָחִיךָ עִמָּךְ' (and your brother shall live with you) and notes that it returns the principle that one's own life takes precedence.
The Gemara asks: What does Rabbi Yochanan do with this verse?
The Gemara answers that the verse is needed for the baraita about two travelers with one flask of water.
Ben Petora taught that it is better for both to drink and die rather than one see the other's death.
Rabbi Akiva came and taught that the verse 'וְחֵי אָחִיךָ עִמָּךְ' means your life takes precedence over your friend's life.

items.text: Objection from inherited interest money
items.text_en: Objection from inherited interest money
items.desc_en: A baraita states that children who inherit interest money from their father are not required to return it, implying the father would have been obligated. The Gemara explains that the father is also exempt, but the baraita mentions the children due to the latter clause about returning specific items out of respect for their father.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that children inheriting interest money are not required to return it, implying the father would have been obligated.

The Gemara answers that the father is also exempt, but the baraita mentions the children because the latter clause about returning specific items out of respect for their father requires the children as the subject.

items.text: The exception for a repentant father
items.text_en: The exception for a repentant father
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how children can return items out of respect for a wicked father, citing the verse 'do not curse a prince among your people'. Rabbi Pinchas explains that the father had repented but died before returning the money.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how children can be obligated to return items out of respect for a wicked father, citing the verse 'do not curse a prince among your people' which limits honor to one who acts like your people.

sub.text: Rabbi Pinchas in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rabbi Pinchas in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Pinchas answers that the father had repented (עשה תשובה) but died before he could return the money, so the children return it out of respect for their repentant father.

items.text: Second objection: robbers and usurers must return
items.text_en: Second objection: robbers and usurers must return
items.desc_en: Another baraita states that robbers and usurers must return what they took, even after collecting. The Gemara clarifies that 'robbers' here refers to usurers, and the baraita seems to contradict the previous one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita stating that robbers and usurers must return what they took, even after collecting.
The Gemara questions the baraita's phrasing, noting that for robbers the concept of 'even though they collected' is irrelevant.
The Gemara resolves the difficulty by explaining that 'robbers' in the baraita actually refers to usurers.

items.text: The dispute between Tannaim
items.text_en: The dispute between Tannaim
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by attributing the views to different Tannaim: Rabbi Nehemya and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov exempt the lender and guarantor from returning, while the first Tanna obligates them. The debate centers on whether a loan document is considered as already collected (גבוי) or not, and whether the act of writing the document itself is significant (שומא מילתא היא).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a Tannaitic dispute: Rabbi Nehemya and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov exempt the lender and guarantor from returning, and the Gemara asks whether the phrase 'קום עשה' (arise and perform) means they must return the money.
The Gemara clarifies that the first Tanna does not require return; rather, 'קום עשה' means to tear up the loan document.
The Gemara questions the underlying assumption: if a loan document is considered as already collected (כגבוי), the prohibition was already violated; if not, tearing the document does nothing.
The Gemara resolves that the document is not considered as already collected, but the act of writing the document itself (שומא מילתא היא) is significant.

items.text: Proof from Mishnah: witnesses violate a negative commandment
items.text_en: Proof from Mishnah: witnesses violate a negative commandment
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a Mishnah listing those who violate a negative commandment for usury, including witnesses. Since witnesses do no physical act, this proves that the document itself (שומא) is significant, supporting the view that the lender must return.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a Mishnah listing those who violate a negative commandment for usury, including witnesses, to prove that the document itself (שומא) is significant, supporting the view that the lender must return.

items.text: Rav Safra's principle and challenges
items.text_en: Rav Safra's principle and challenges
items.desc_en: Rav Safra states that in cases where gentile courts would collect from the borrower, Jewish courts require the lender to return; where gentile courts would not collect, Jewish courts do not require return. Abaye and Ravina challenge this with the cases of 'se'ah be-se'ah' and a mortgage without deduction, but the Gemara distinguishes them as being treated as a deposit or sale.

sub.desc_en: Rav Safra states a general principle: where gentile courts would collect from the borrower, Jewish courts require the lender to return; where gentile courts would not collect, Jewish courts do not require return.
Abaye challenges Rav Yosef by citing the case of 'סאה בסאה' (a se'ah for a se'ah), where gentile courts would collect but Jewish courts do not require return, contradicting Rav Safra's principle.
Rav Yosef answers that the case of 'סאה בסאה' is treated as a deposit (פיקדון) by gentile law, not a loan, so it does not undermine Rav Safra's principle.
Ravina challenges Rav Ashi with the case of a mortgage without deduction (משכנתא בלא נכייתא), where gentile courts would collect but the status under Jewish law is unclear.

items.text: Distinction between fixed and other interest
items.text_en: Distinction between fixed and other interest
items.desc_en: Rav Safra explains that the Mishnah's rule about returning interest applies only to fixed interest (ריבית קצוצה), where gentile courts would extract it, but not to early or late interest (ריבית מוקדמת, ריבית מאוחרת), where they would not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement that in Jewish courts we do not return interest from lender to borrower, noting that gentile courts treat it as a sale.

Rav Safra explains that the Mishnah's rule applies only to fixed interest (ריבית קצוצה), where gentile courts would extract it, but not to early or late interest (ריבית מוקדמת, ריבית מאוחרת), where they would not.

items.text: Question on the Mishnah's case
items.text_en: Question on the Mishnah's case
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's scenario where the buyer has no wine, citing a baraita that allows fixing a price once the market rate is established, even if the seller lacks the produce, as long as others have it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's case: why does it specify that the buyer has no wine, since the price was already fixed when the market rate was established?
The Gemara cites a baraita that permits fixing a price once the market rate is established, even if the seller lacks the produce, as long as others have it.

items.text: Rabbah's answer: case of debt repayment
items.text_en: Rabbah's answer: case of debt repayment
items.desc_en: Rabbah answers that the Mishnah deals with a case where the buyer comes to owe the seller the money for the produce, as in a baraita where a creditor asks for his money and the debtor offers wheat at the current rate, which is prohibited because it is not like his money coming to hand.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah answers that the Mishnah deals with a case where the buyer comes to owe the seller the money for the produce, citing a baraita where a creditor asks for his money and the debtor offers wheat at the current rate, which is prohibited because it is not like his money coming to hand.

items.text: Abaye's objection and alternative explanation
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Abaye objects that if the issue is that the money is not coming to hand, then even if the seller has the wheat it should be prohibited, so he explains the Mishnah according to Rav Safra's teaching in the school of Rabbi Chiyya.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that if the issue is that the money is not coming to hand (דְּלָא כְּאִיסָּרוֹ הַבָּא לְיָדוֹ), then even if the seller has the wheat it should be prohibited.

Abaye resolves the difficulty by explaining the Mishnah according to Rav Safra's teaching in the school of Rabbi Chiyya, which distinguishes cases based on whether the transaction is a genuine sale or a disguised loan.

items.text: Rav Safra's baraita and its application
items.text_en: Rav Safra's baraita and its application
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Safra's baraita about permitted and forbidden cases due to the appearance of interest, and applies it to the Mishnah: if the borrower has wine to give at the fixed price, it is permitted; if not, it appears as interest.

sub.desc_en: Rav Safra cites a baraita from the school of Rabbi Chiyya listing cases that are permitted but forbidden due to the appearance of interest (הערמת רבית).

The baraita gives an example: one asks for a loan of a maneh, the other gives wheat worth a maneh and then buys it back for 24 selas — the transaction is permitted but forbidden as an evasion of interest.
The Gemara applies the baraita to the Mishnah: if the borrower has wine to give at the fixed price, it is a legitimate sale; if not, it appears as interest.

items.text: Rava's objection and correction of the Mishnah's wording
items.text_en: Rava's objection and correction of the Mishnah's wording
items.desc_en: Rava objects that the Mishnah's language is imprecise, requiring emendations to 'the money for my wheat' and 'which I sold to you', and then questions the case of wine when the Mishnah already mentions a fixed price, concluding with a cryptic remark about Rabbi Oshaya.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects that the Mishnah's phrase 'give me my wheat' should be emended to 'the money for my wheat'.
Rava objects that the Mishnah's phrase 'which I am selling' should be emended to 'which I sold to you'.

Rava objects that the Mishnah's phrase 'your wheat is established upon me at thirty dinars' is redundant, and explains the intended meaning as 'with the money of your wheat which you established upon me at thirty dinars'.
Rava questions why the Mishnah mentions a case where the borrower has no wine, when it already stated a fixed price at the market rate.
Rava cryptically remarks that when he dies, Rabbi Oshaya will come out to meet him, implying that Rabbi Oshaya's teaching resolves the difficulty.

items.text: Baraita of Rabbi Oshaya
items.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Oshaya
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita of Rabbi Oshaya that describes a scenario where a creditor agrees to take produce from the debtor at the current market price, and later converts it to other produce. The baraita rules that if the debtor has the produce, it is permitted; if not, it is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with a scenario: a creditor demands his money to buy wheat, and the debtor offers wheat at the current market price.

The baraita extends the scenario through multiple produce conversions and rules: if the debtor has the produce, it is permitted; if not, it is forbidden, and explains the meaning of 'לקח' (took) as taking in exchange for his loan.

items.text: Rava's three inferences
items.text_en: Rava's three inferences
items.desc_en: Rava derives three principles from Rabbi Oshaya's baraita: that one may appoint a loan on produce (not considered like the prohibited 'issar' that comes to his hand), that the leniency applies only when the seller has the produce, and that Rabbi Yannai's ruling is supported.

sub.desc_en: Rava announces that he derives three principles from Rabbi Oshaya's baraita.
Rava infers that one may appoint a loan on produce, and it is not considered like the prohibited 'issar' (a coin that comes to his hand).
Rava infers that the leniency applies only when the seller actually has the produce in his possession.
Rava infers that Rabbi Yannai's ruling—that there is no difference between the produce itself and its monetary value—is supported by the baraita.

items.text: Objection and resolution by Rav Huna and Shmuel
items.text_en: Objection and resolution by Rav Huna and Shmuel
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from the baraita's ruling that it is permitted only if the seller has the produce. Rav Huna explains that it refers to a case where the buyer already pulled the produce, or designated a corner for it. Shmuel attributes the baraita to Rabbi Yehuda, who permits 'one-sided interest'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from the baraita of Rabbi Oshaya, which rules that all such transactions are permitted only if the seller has the produce in his possession.
Rav Huna in the name of Rav answers that the baraita refers to a case where the buyer already pulled (משך) the produce, acquiring it.
The Gemara objects that if the buyer already pulled the produce, the permission is obvious and does not need to be stated.

Rav Huna resolves the objection by explaining that the baraita refers to a case where the seller designated a specific corner (קרן זווית) for the buyer, which is a weaker form of acquisition that still permits the transaction.
Shmuel answers that the baraita follows Rabbi Yehuda, who permits 'one-sided interest' (צד אחד בריבית), where only one party risks ribbis.

items.text: Shmuel's attribution to Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Shmuel's attribution to Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: Shmuel identifies the baraita as following Rabbi Yehuda, who permits 'one-sided interest'. A supporting baraita is cited where Rabbi Yehuda permits a sale arrangement even when the buyer eats the produce, citing a precedent with Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel identifies the baraita as following Rabbi Yehuda, who permits 'one-sided interest' (צד אחד בריבית).
A baraita is cited: a creditor who makes a field sale arrangement is permitted when the seller eats the produce, but Rabbi Yehuda permits even when the buyer eats the produce.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehuda's precedent and Sages' response
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's precedent and Sages' response
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda cites a precedent with Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya where the buyer ate the produce, but the Sages reject it, claiming the seller actually ate the produce.

items.text: Dispute between Abaye and Rava
items.text_en: Dispute between Abaye and Rava
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava debate the precise point of dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages: Abaye says it is about 'one-sided interest', while Rava says it is about interest with intent to return. Rava then notes that according to Rabbi Yannai, the leniency applies even to the produce's value.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the practical difference between the positions of Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages.
Abaye answers that the dispute concerns צד אחד בריבית (one-sided interest), where only one party might gain interest.
Rava answers that the dispute concerns ריבית על מנת להחזיר (interest with intent to return the principal).
Rava notes that according to Rabbi Yannai's principle, the leniency applies even to the value of the produce.

items.text: Opening statement: the leniency of paskin al sha'ar shebashuk
items.text_en: Opening statement: the leniency of paskin al sha'ar shebashuk
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that one may fix a price based on the market gate rate even if the seller does not currently have the produce, because the buyer could say 'what benefit did you give me?' since he could have bought it at that rate anyway.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the principle that one may fix a price based on the market gate rate (פוסקין על שער שבשוק) even if the seller does not currently have the produce, because the buyer could say 'what benefit did you give me?' since he could have bought it at that rate anyway.

items.text: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna's objection from a baraita
items.text_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna's objection from a baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua object to Rava: a baraita states that all such transactions are permitted only if the seller has the produce, otherwise forbidden. Rava distinguishes: there it is a loan (interest prohibition), here it is a sale.

sub.text: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua's objection to Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua's objection to Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua object to Rava by citing a baraita that states all such transactions are permitted only if the seller has the produce, but forbidden if he does not.
Rava answers that the baraita refers to a loan (הלוואה), whereas here it is a sale (זביני), so the restriction does not apply.

items.text: Rabbah and Rav Yosef's rationale for the leniency
items.text_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef's rationale for the leniency
items.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef explain the Sages' reasoning: the buyer can say 'I took your favor and threw it on the thorns' – what benefit did you give me? If I had money, I would have bought at the gate rate anyway.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef explain the rationale for the leniency: the buyer can say 'you took my favor and threw it on the thorns' because if he had money in hand he could have bought the produce cheaply at the market rate.

items.text: Abaye's challenge and Rav Yosef's response
items.text_en: Abaye's challenge and Rav Yosef's response
items.desc_en: Abaye asks: if so, why not permit lending a se'ah for a se'ah (interest)? The borrower could say 'what benefit did you give me?' since the wheat might have sprouted in the field. Rav Yosef replies: there it is a loan, here a sale.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that if this reasoning is valid, then borrowing a se'ah for a se'ah (a loan of produce) should also be permitted, since the borrower could similarly say 'you took my favor and threw it on the thorns' — but that is forbidden as interest.
Rav Yosef answers that the distinction is between a loan (הלוואה), which is forbidden, and a sale (זביני), which is permitted.

items.text: Ada bar Abba's question about the broker's fee
items.text_en: Ada bar Abba's question about the broker's fee
items.desc_en: Ada bar Abba asks Rava: doesn't the buyer need to pay a broker's fee, so the seller does give benefit? Rava and Rav Ashi answer that the buyer also pays the broker, or the broker's fee is paid by the buyers collectively.

sub.text: Adda bar Abba's objection to Rava
sub.text_en: Adda bar Abba's objection to Rava
sub.desc_en: Adda bar Abba objects that the buyer still needs to pay a broker's fee (ספסירא) to obtain the produce at the market rate, so the seller does provide a benefit.
Rava answers that the seller also gives the buyer money for the broker's fee, so there is no net benefit.
Rav Ashi answers that the buyer's own money effectively performs the brokerage for him, so no extra benefit is conferred.

items.text: Rabbah and Rav Yosef's ruling on showing oneself at the storehouse
items.text_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef's ruling on showing oneself at the storehouse
items.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef rule that one who gives money for sharp produce must show himself at the storehouse. The Gemara clarifies this is for accepting the curse 'Mi shepara' – the buyer must appear so the seller's mind is settled, knowing the buyer didn't find better produce elsewhere. Rav Ashi adds that even if he meets him in the market, it suffices.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef rule that one who gives money for sharp produce must show himself at the storehouse.
The Gemara questions the purpose of showing oneself: if for acquisition, it is not effective; if for accepting the curse 'Mi shepara', even without showing oneself the buyer accepts it.

The Gemara answers that the purpose is indeed for accepting the curse 'Mi shepara', but the buyer must show himself so the seller's mind is settled, knowing the buyer didn't find better produce elsewhere.
Rav Ashi adds that even if the seller meets the buyer in the market and tells him, it suffices to settle his mind.

items.text: Rav Nachman's first rule: all aggar natar is forbidden
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's first rule: all aggar natar is forbidden
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman states the general principle: any payment for waiting (interest) is forbidden. He then gives an example: one who gives money for wine at four measures and later receives five – if the seller has the wine, it's permitted; if not, forbidden. The Gemara clarifies that even if the seller has credit in the city, since collection is uncertain, it is considered as if he does not have it.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman states the general principle that any payment for waiting (אגר נטר) is forbidden, and gives an example: one who gives money for wine at four measures and later receives five – if the seller has the wine, it's permitted; if not, forbidden.
The Gemara objects that Rav Nachman's ruling is obvious, then clarifies that it is needed only when the seller has credit (אשרי) in the city.

The Gemara resolves that even though the seller has credit in the city, since collection requires effort (מחסרי גוביינא), it is considered as if he does not have the wine, so the transaction is forbidden.

items.text: Rav Nachman's rule on returning excess payment due to miscalculation
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's rule on returning excess payment due to miscalculation
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules: one who lends coins to a friend and finds extra must return it if the mistake is due to a common miscalculation (da'at to'ah); otherwise it is a gift. Rav Acha bar Rav Yosef begins to define 'da'at to'ah'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that one who lends coins and finds extra must return it if the mistake is due to a common miscalculation (da'at to'ah), otherwise it is a gift.
The gemara asks for a definition of 'da'at to'ah' (common miscalculation), and Rav Acha bar Rav Yosef begins to answer.

items.text: Gemara's question about a powerful person who refuses gifts
items.text_en: Gemara's question about a powerful person who refuses gifts
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava asks Rav Ashi what to do if a powerful person refuses a gift, implying the transaction might be a disguised loan. Rav Ashi responds that the lender might have stolen from the borrower and concealed it in the account, citing a baraita that one who steals and conceals it in an account is exempt.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava asks Rav Ashi what to do if a powerful person refuses a gift, implying the transaction might be a disguised loan.
Rav Ashi responds that the lender might have stolen from the borrower and concealed it in the account, citing a baraita that one who steals and conceals it in an account is exempt.

items.text: Second scenario: a stranger with no prior dealings
items.text_en: Second scenario: a stranger with no prior dealings
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava asks about a stranger with no prior dealings. Rav Ashi answers that perhaps someone else stole from the stranger and told him to conceal it in the account with the lender.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava asks about a stranger with no prior dealings with the lender, what is the halacha if he gives a gift to conceal stolen money in an account.
Rav Ashi answers that perhaps someone else stole from the stranger and told him to conceal the stolen money in the account with the lender.

items.text: Rav Kahana's report of Rav's ruling on selling produce by the vine
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's report of Rav's ruling on selling produce by the vine
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana recounts hearing Rav say 'קָרֵי קָרֵי' without understanding. Later he learns that Rav ruled: if one gives money to a gardener for ten immature vines and the gardener says he will give full-grown ones, if they exist it is permitted, if not it is forbidden. The Gemara notes this is obvious, but the ruling teaches that even though they grow naturally, it is still forbidden if they do not yet exist.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana recounts hearing Rav say 'קָרֵי קָרֵי' without understanding what he meant.

Others explain that Rav ruled: if one gives money to a gardener for ten immature vines (קָרֵי) and the gardener promises full-grown ones (בְּנֵי גַרְמִידָא), if they exist it is permitted, if not it is forbidden.
The Gemara notes the ruling is obvious, but explains that Rav teaches that even though the vines grow naturally (מִמֵּילָא קָא רָבוּ), it is still forbidden if they do not yet exist.

items.text: Supporting baraita about selling future produce
items.text_en: Supporting baraita about selling future produce
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that matches Rav's ruling: if one says 'what my goats will milk is sold to you' it is permitted, but if he specifies a quantity it is forbidden, even though the produce grows naturally, because it does not yet exist.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that Rav's ruling aligns with a specific Tanna (baraita).
The baraita states that selling future produce without specifying a quantity is permitted.
The baraita continues that specifying a quantity renders the sale forbidden, even though the produce grows naturally, because it does not yet exist.

items.text: Rava's alternative view and resolution
items.text_en: Rava's alternative view and resolution
items.desc_en: Some say Rava ruled that since the produce grows naturally it is permitted, contradicting the baraita. The Gemara resolves that in the baraita the produce is not from the same source (one vine is taken and another replaces it), whereas in Rav's case the growth is from the same vine.

sub.desc_en: Some say Rava ruled that since the produce grows naturally (ממילא), it is permitted.
The Gemara objects: but the baraita explicitly forbids a fixed amount even when the produce grows naturally.
The Gemara resolves that in the baraita the produce is not from the same source (one vine is taken and another replaces it), whereas in Rav's case the growth is from the same vine.

items.text: Abaye's ruling on a conditional sale of wine
items.text_en: Abaye's ruling on a conditional sale of wine
