items.desc_en: Abaye permits a person to say to another: take four zuz for a barrel of wine, if it turns sour it is your responsibility, if it appreciates or depreciates it is mine. Rav Sherevya questions this.

sub.desc_en: Abaye permits a conditional sale of wine where the buyer assumes risk of spoilage but the seller retains profit or loss from price changes.
Rav Sherevya questions Abaye's ruling, though the text breaks off before stating the content of the question.

items.text: Conclusion of previous sugya
items.text_en: Conclusion of previous sugya
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the previous discussion about a transaction that is close to profit and far from loss, stating that since the seller accepts the risk of price drops, it is equally close to both profit and loss.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that since the seller accepts the risk of price drops, the transaction is equally close to profit and loss.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who lends money to another may not live in the borrower's courtyard for free, nor rent it at a discount, because this constitutes ribbit.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a lender may not live in the borrower's courtyard for free or rent it at a discount, because this constitutes ribbit (usury).

items.text: Rav Nachman's ruling and its novelty
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling and its novelty
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Minyomei quotes Rav Nachman: although one who lives in another's courtyard without permission need not pay rent, if the owner lent him money and he lives there, he must pay. The Gemara questions what this adds to the Mishnah, and explains that it applies even to a courtyard not typically rented and a person not accustomed to renting.

sub.text: Rav Yosef bar Minyomei quoting Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef bar Minyomei quoting Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Minyomei quotes Rav Nachman's ruling: one who lives in another's courtyard without permission need not pay rent, but if the owner lent him money and he lives there, he must pay.
The Gemara questions what novelty Rav Nachman adds, citing the Mishnah that already forbids living in the borrower's courtyard for free or renting at a discount due to ribbis (usury).

The Gemara explains the novelty: from the Mishnah one might think the prohibition applies only to a courtyard typically rented and a person accustomed to renting, but Rav Nachman teaches that it applies even to a courtyard not typically rented and a person not accustomed to renting.

items.text: Alternative version of Rav Nachman's statement
items.text_en: Alternative version of Rav Nachman's statement
items.desc_en: An alternative version states Rav Nachman's ruling as: 'Lend me money and live in my courtyard' requires payment. The Gemara explains the difference: the first version (he lent him) implies the second (lend me) is even more obvious, while the second version limits the obligation to cases where the borrower initiated the arrangement.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version cites Rav Nachman's ruling: 'Lend me money and live in my courtyard' requires payment.

The Gemara explains the difference between the two versions: the first version (he lent him) implies the second (lend me) is even more obvious, while the second version limits the obligation to cases where the borrower initiated the arrangement.

items.text: Story of Rav Yosef bar Chama and his son Rava
items.text_en: Story of Rav Yosef bar Chama and his son Rava
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Chama would seize slaves of debtors and make them work. His son Rava questioned this, and Rav Yosef bar Chama cited Rav Nachman that a slave is not worth his feed. Rava countered that Rav Nachman only referred to his own dancing slave, not others. Rav Yosef bar Chama then cited Rav Daniel bar Rav Katina quoting Rav that one who seizes another's slave and works him is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The gemara reports that Rav Yosef bar Chama would seize slaves of debtors and make them work.
Rava, his son, asks Rav Yosef bar Chama why he acts this way.

sub.text: Rav Yosef bar Chama's first answer
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef bar Chama's first answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Chama answers that he follows Rav Nachman, who said a slave is not worth his feed.
Rava objects that Rav Nachman only referred to his own dancing slave Daru, not to other slaves.

sub.text: Rav Yosef bar Chama's second answer
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef bar Chama's second answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Chama answers that he follows the statement of Rav Daniel bar Rav Katina quoting Rav that one who seizes another's slave and works him is exempt.

items.text: Gemara's discussion on interest through rent
items.text_en: Gemara's discussion on interest through rent
items.desc_en: The Gemara continues a previous discussion about a debtor living in the creditor's courtyard. It cites Rav Nachman's ruling that if a debtor lives in the creditor's courtyard without permission, he need not pay rent, but if he borrowed money and lives there, he must pay rent, as it would otherwise appear as interest.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a statement about the debtor's preference that his slaves not be idle, setting the context for the discussion.

sub.text: Rav Yosef bar Minyomi citing Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef bar Minyomi citing Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Minyomi in the name of Rav Nachman rules that a debtor living in the creditor's courtyard without permission need not pay rent, but if he borrowed money and lives there, he must pay rent to avoid the appearance of interest.

items.text: Abaye and Rava dispute on recovering interest when prices change
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava dispute on recovering interest when prices change
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava argue about a case where a debtor owes interest and the market price of wheat drops. Abaye holds that only the principal (four gerivai) is recovered, while the extra is considered a discount. Rava holds that all five gerivai are recovered because the entire transaction was tainted with interest from the start.

sub.desc_en: Abaye states that when a debtor owes interest and wheat prices drop, only the principal (four gerivai) is recovered, and the extra is considered a discount.
Rava argues that all five gerivai are recovered because the entire transaction was tainted with interest from the start.

items.text: Abaye and Rava dispute on recovering a cloak given as interest
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava dispute on recovering a cloak given as interest
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava argue about a case where a debtor gave a cloak as part of an interest debt. Abaye holds that only the principal (four zuz) is recovered, not the cloak. Rava holds that the cloak is also recovered, to prevent people from saying that the cloak is interest.

sub.desc_en: Abaye rules that when a debtor gave a cloak as part of an interest debt of four zuz, only the four zuz are recovered from him, not the cloak.
Rava disagrees and rules that the cloak is also recovered, to prevent people from saying that the cloak he is wearing is interest.

items.text: Rava's ruling on interest through rent and Rav Acha's objection
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on interest through rent and Rav Acha's objection
items.desc_en: Rava rules that if a debtor rents a courtyard worth ten zuz for twelve zuz due to an interest debt, only twelve zuz are recovered. Rav Acha from Difti objects, arguing the debtor could claim the rent was based on the courtyard's value at the time, but the Gemara rejects this because the debtor accepted the terms.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that if a debtor owes twelve zuz of interest and rents a courtyard worth ten zuz for twelve zuz, only twelve zuz are recovered from him.
Rav Acha from Difti objects that the debtor could claim the rent was based on the courtyard's value at the time, which has since decreased.
The Gemara rejects the objection because the debtor accepted the terms willingly, so he cannot later claim a lower value.

items.text: Mishnah: Permissible to increase rent, forbidden to increase sale price
items.text_en: Mishnah: Permissible to increase rent, forbidden to increase sale price
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may charge more for rent if paid later, but not for a sale. Examples: renting a courtyard for ten selaim a year if paid now, or a selah per month if paid monthly, is permitted. Selling a field for 1000 zuz now or 1200 maneh at harvest time is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule that one may increase the price for deferred rent but not for a deferred sale, and gives examples.

items.text: Gemara explains the distinction between rental and sale
items.text_en: Gemara explains the distinction between rental and sale
items.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef explain that rent is only due at the end, so paying early is a discount, not interest. In a sale, the seller needs money now, so charging more later is interest for waiting. Rava adds that the verse 'as a hired worker year by year' implies rent is paid at the end of the period.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah distinguishes between rental (permitted) and sale (forbidden) regarding early payment discounts.
Rabbah and Rav Yosef explain that rent is only due at the end, so paying early is a discount, not interest; in a sale, the seller needs money now, so charging more later is interest for waiting.
Rava adds that the verse 'as a hired worker year by year' implies rent is paid at the end of the period, supporting the distinction.

items.text: Rav Nachman permits 'tarsha' (advance payment for produce) and defends it
items.text_en: Rav Nachman permits 'tarsha' (advance payment for produce) and defends it
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman permits tarsha (paying in advance for produce at a lower price). Rami bar Chama objects from the Mishnah's prohibition of selling a field for more later. Rav Nachman distinguishes: there the price is fixed, here it is not fixed (the buyer takes the risk of price fluctuation).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one sells a field for payment at the threshing floor for twelve maneh, it is forbidden.
Rav Nachman rules that tarsha (advance payment for produce at a lower price) is permitted.
Rami bar Chama (or Rav Ukva bar Chama) objects to Rav Nachman from the Mishnah's explicit prohibition of selling a field for more later.
Rav Nachman distinguishes: there the price is fixed (so the extra payment is clearly interest), here the price is not fixed (the buyer takes the risk of price fluctuation).

items.text: Rav Papa and Rav Chama justify their own tarsha practices
items.text_en: Rav Papa and Rav Chama justify their own tarsha practices
items.desc_en: Rav Papa permits his own tarsha because he doesn't need the money and his wine doesn't spoil, so he is just doing a favor for the buyer. Rav Sheishet objects, arguing that if the buyers had money they would pay the current price, but since they don't, they pay the future higher price. Rav Chama permits his tarsha because he benefits from the buyers storing their goods in his domain, avoiding taxes and market fees.

sub.desc_en: Rav Papa declares his own tarsha (advance payment for future delivery) permitted, because his wine does not spoil and he does not need the money, so he is merely doing a favor for the buyer.

Rav Sheishet objects to Rav Papa's reasoning, arguing that the buyers would pay the current price if they had money, but since they lack funds, they pay the future higher price, which constitutes interest.

Rav Chama justifies his own tarsha as permitted because the buyers benefit by storing their goods in his domain, thereby avoiding taxes and market fees, so the arrangement is a mutual benefit rather than interest.

items.text: Halakhic ruling on earlier opinions
items.text_en: Halakhic ruling on earlier opinions
items.desc_en: The Gemara rules in accordance with Rav Chama, Rabbi Elazar, and Rabbi Yannai, who said that there is no difference between the principal and its proceeds in terms of ribbis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rules in accordance with Rav Chama, Rabbi Elazar, and Rabbi Yannai, who hold that there is no difference between the principal and its proceeds regarding ribbis.

items.text: Mishnah: Conditional sale and mortgage
items.text_en: Mishnah: Conditional sale and mortgage
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases where a seller receives partial payment and allows the buyer to pay later, or a borrower mortgages his field with a condition that it becomes the lender's if not redeemed within three years. The latter is permitted, as was the practice of Beitos ben Zonin with rabbinic approval.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases of conditional sale and mortgage, including the practice of Beitos ben Zonin with rabbinic approval.

items.text: Gemara: Who eats the produce?
items.text_en: Gemara: Who eats the produce?
items.desc_en: Rav Huna and Rav Anan debate who consumes the produce in a conditional sale. They are not in dispute: one case is where the seller says 'when you bring the money, acquire it' (seller eats), the other where he says 'from now' (produce is divided).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who eats the produce in a conditional sale where the buyer has paid only part of the price.
Rav Huna answers that the seller eats the produce.
Rav Anan answers that the produce is divided between seller and buyer.

The Gemara resolves that the two opinions are not in dispute: Rav Huna's case is where the seller said 'when you bring the money, acquire it' (seller eats), and Rav Anan's case is where he said 'when you bring the money, acquire it from now' (produce is divided).

items.text: Baraita of Rav Safra and Rava's elaboration
items.text_en: Baraita of Rav Safra and Rava's elaboration
items.desc_en: Rav Safra taught a baraita from the school of Rabbi Chiya listing four scenarios: both permitted, both forbidden, seller permitted and buyer forbidden, buyer permitted and seller forbidden. Rava explains each: both permitted when he says 'acquire at the value of your zuz'; both forbidden when he says 'when you bring, acquire from now'; seller permitted when he says 'when you bring, acquire'; buyer permitted when he says 'acquire from now and the money will be a loan with you'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Safra teaches a baraita from the school of Rabbi Chiya listing four scenarios regarding ribbit (usury) in land sales.
Rava explains the first two scenarios: both permitted when the seller says 'acquire at the value of your zuz', both forbidden when he says 'when you bring, acquire from now'.
Rava explains the remaining two scenarios: seller permitted when he says 'when you bring, acquire', buyer permitted when he says 'acquire from now and the money will be a loan with you'.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna of 'both forbidden'
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna of 'both forbidden'
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua identifies the Tanna who holds both are forbidden as not Rabbi Yehuda, since Rabbi Yehuda permits 'one side of ribbis'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna is the source of the ruling that both parties are forbidden in the case of a conditional sale.
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua answers that the Tanna is not Rabbi Yehuda, because Rabbi Yehuda permits צד אחד בריבית (one side of ribbis).

items.text: Mishnah: Mortgage with right of first refusal
items.text_en: Mishnah: Mortgage with right of first refusal
items.desc_en: If one mortgages a house or field and stipulates that the borrower may only sell it to the lender at a fixed price, it is forbidden; if at its market value, it is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one mortgages a house or field and stipulates that the borrower may only sell it to the lender at a fixed price, it is forbidden; if at its market value, it is permitted.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna of 'at these prices'
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna of 'at these prices'
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua again identifies the Tanna who forbids 'at these prices' as not Rabbi Yehuda, who permits 'one side of ribbis'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna is the source for the ruling that 'at these prices' is forbidden.
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua answers that the Tanna is not Rabbi Yehuda, who permits 'one side of ribbis'.

items.text: Mishnah: Conditional sale with right of return and Rava's distinction
items.text_en: Mishnah: Conditional sale with right of return and Rava's distinction
items.desc_en: If a seller says 'when I have money, return it to me' it is forbidden; if he says 'when you have money, I will return it to you' it is permitted. Rava explains: the first case is forbidden because the seller did not stipulate from his own initiative (the buyer may feel compelled), while the second is permitted because the buyer initiates the condition.

items.text: Story of a sale without guarantee and Amemar's comment
items.text_en: Story of a sale without guarantee and Amemar's comment
items.desc_en: A man sold a field without guarantee; seeing the buyer distressed, he promised to compensate him if the field was seized. Amemar begins to comment on this case.

sub.desc_en: The gemara recounts a story of a man who sold a field without guarantee and saw the buyer distressed.
The seller promises to compensate the buyer with the field's value, improvements, and produce if it is seized.
Amemar begins to comment on this case.

items.text: Rav Ashi's explanation of the seller's intent
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's explanation of the seller's intent
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains to Amemar that the reason the seller's statement is considered mere talk is because the buyer is the one who needs to retract, but here the seller is retracting, so it is mere talk.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains to Amemar that the seller's statement is mere talk (פטומי מילי) because the seller, not the buyer, is retracting.

items.text: Analysis of the Mishnah and Rava's distinction
items.text_en: Analysis of the Mishnah and Rava's distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that 'when you have money I will return it' is permitted, noting that here the seller retracts. Rava explains that in the latter clause, the seller said 'of his own accord', implying that without such a statement, it is not mere talk. The Gemara then notes that this was stated as if he said 'of his own accord'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that 'when you have money I will return it' is permitted, noting that here the seller retracts.
Rava explains that in the latter clause, the seller said 'of his own accord', implying that without such a statement, it is not mere talk.
The Gemara concludes that this was stated as if he said 'of his own accord'.

items.text: Case of a dying man and his wife's promise
items.text_en: Case of a dying man and his wife's promise
items.desc_en: A dying man wrote a get for his wife, groaned, and she promised to be his if he recovered. Rav Zevid says this is mere talk. Rav Acha from Difti questions Ravina: if not mere talk, what could it be? The Gemara concludes that it teaches that he gave the get based on her intent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case: a dying man wrote a get for his wife, groaned, and she promised to be his if he recovered.
Rav Zevid rules that the wife's promise is mere talk (פטומי מילי) and does not create a condition.

sub.text: Rav Acha from Difti to Ravina
sub.text_en: Rav Acha from Difti to Ravina
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha from Difti questions Ravina: if not mere talk, what could it be? The wife cannot impose a condition on the get.
The Gemara concludes that the case teaches that the husband gave the get based on her intent, not that she imposed a condition.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Nachman on loan secured by field
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Nachman on loan secured by field
items.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that if one lends money on a field, at the time of giving the money the lender acquires the entire field, but afterward only acquires the value of his money. Rav Nachman says even afterward he acquires the entire field.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that if one lends money on a field, at the time of giving the money the lender acquires the entire field, but afterward only acquires the value of his money.
Rav Nachman disputes Rav Huna, ruling that even after giving the money the lender acquires the entire field.

items.text: Rav Nachman's ruling and Rav Yehuda's objection
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling and Rav Yehuda's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman acted according to his ruling before the Exilarch, and Rav Yehuda tore up the document. The Exilarch complained, and Rav Yehuda defended himself, saying a great man saw a reason and tore it. Alternatively, he said everyone is a child compared to him in law.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman acted according to his ruling before the Exilarch, and Rav Yehuda tore up the document; the Exilarch complained to Rav Yehuda.
Rav Yehuda defended himself, saying a great man saw a reason and tore it; alternatively, he said everyone is a child compared to him in law.

items.text: Rav Nachman's retraction and Rava's objection
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's retraction and Rava's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman later retracted, saying even at the time of giving the money the lender acquires nothing. Rava objected from a Mishnah: if one says 'if you do not give me from now until three years, it is mine' – it is his!

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman retracts his earlier position, now ruling that even at the time of giving the money the lender acquires nothing.
Rava objects to Rav Nachman's retraction by citing a Mishnah: if one says 'if you do not give me from now until three years, it is mine' – it is his!

items.text: Asmakhta dispute and resolution
items.text_en: Asmakhta dispute and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman says asmakhta (a conditional commitment) effects acquisition, while Minyomi says it does not. The Gemara questions Minyomi from the Mishnah, and answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yosei, who holds asmakhta effects acquisition.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman states his position that an אסמכתא (conditional commitment) effects acquisition.
Minyomi states his opposing position that an אסמכתא does not effect acquisition.
The Gemara raises a difficulty for Minyomi from the Mishnah, which implies that an אסמכתא does effect acquisition.
The Gemara resolves the difficulty by explaining that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yosei, who holds that an אסמכתא effects acquisition.

items.text: Alternative explanation for the earlier ruling
items.text_en: Alternative explanation for the earlier ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation for the previous ruling: the seller said 'acquire from now' (k'nei me'achshav), making the sale effective immediately.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation for the earlier ruling: the seller said 'acquire from now' (קְנִי מֵעַכְשָׁיו), making the sale effective immediately.

items.text: The Nehardeans' ruling on asmachta and Rav Ashi's clarification
items.text_en: The Nehardeans' ruling on asmachta and Rav Ashi's clarification
items.desc_en: Mar Yanuka and Mar Kashisha report in the name of Rav Nachman that asmachta is valid if the condition is fulfilled within the specified time, but not after. Rav Ashi questions this, suggesting they meant that if found within the time and told to acquire, it is valid; after the time, it is not, due to embarrassment. The Gemara concludes that even within the time it is not valid, and the statement was made to avoid being bothered later.

sub.text: Mar Yanuka and Mar Kashisha reporting in the name of Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Mar Yanuka and Mar Kashisha reporting in the name of Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Mar Yanuka and Mar Kashisha report to Rav Ashi the Nehardean ruling in the name of Rav Nachman that an asmachta (conditional commitment) is valid if fulfilled within the specified time, but not after.
Rav Ashi questions the Nehardeans' statement, pointing out that the rule 'within the time acquires, after the time does not acquire' is obvious for any conditional transaction.

Rav Ashi suggests that the Nehardeans meant that if the debtor is found within the time and told 'acquire', he acquires, but after the time he does not, because the debtor's statement is motivated by embarrassment.
The Gemara concludes that even within the time the asmachta does not effect acquisition, and the statement 'acquire' was only made to avoid being bothered later.

items.text: Rav Pappa's distinction based on the debtor's circumstances
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's distinction based on the debtor's circumstances
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa rules that asmachta sometimes is valid and sometimes not: if the debtor was found drinking beer (indicating he has money), it is valid; if he was found turning over coins (looking for money), it is not.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa introduces a distinction: an asmachta (conditional commitment) is valid if the debtor was found drinking beer (indicating wealth), but invalid if he was found turning over coins (indicating poverty).

items.text: Rav Acha's objection and Ravina's alternative criterion
items.text_en: Rav Acha's objection and Ravina's alternative criterion
items.desc_en: Rav Acha from Difti objects to Rav Pappa's distinction, suggesting the debtor might drink to calm his nerves or someone else might have lent him money. Ravina instead rules that if the debtor is particular about the price, it is certainly valid.

sub.text: Rav Acha from Difti's objection to Ravina
sub.text_en: Rav Acha from Difti's objection to Ravina
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha from Difti objects to Rav Pappa's distinction by suggesting that the debtor might drink to calm his nerves or that someone else might have lent him money.
Ravina rules that if the debtor is particular about the price, the transaction is certainly valid.

items.text: Another objection and Rav Pappa's alternative criterion
items.text_en: Another objection and Rav Pappa's alternative criterion
items.desc_en: Rav Acha from Difti objects again, suggesting the debtor might be particular about the land's value not being diminished. Rav Pappa then rules that if the debtor is particular about the land, it is certainly valid.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha from Difti objects to Ravina's criterion, suggesting the debtor might be particular about the land's value not being diminished.
Rav Pappa rules that if the debtor is particular about the land itself (not just its value), the acquisition is certainly valid.

items.text: Rav Pappa's ruling on asmachta as a lien
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's ruling on asmachta as a lien
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa rules that even though asmachta does not effect a sale, it can serve as a lien (apoteiki) to collect from the property. Rav Huna bar Natan and Mar Zutra question this, and the Gemara clarifies that the lien means the creditor can only collect from that specific property.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa rules that even though asmachta does not effect a sale, it can serve as a lien (apoteiki) to collect from the property.
Rav Huna bar Natan questions whether the seller explicitly said 'acquire for collection,' and Mar Zutra adds that even if he did, asmachta should still not effect a lien.
The Gemara clarifies that Rav Pappa's lien means the creditor can only collect from that specific property, not that the property is acquired as a sale.

items.text: Case of a sale with guarantee and the dispute over payment from superior land
items.text_en: Case of a sale with guarantee and the dispute over payment from superior land
items.desc_en: A man sold land with a guarantee, and when it was seized, he tried to collect from the buyer's superior land. Rav Pappa thought he could, but Rav Acha from Difti objected, saying the seller only promised payment from the superior land that existed at the time, and now the buyer has other superior land.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a case: a man sold land with a guarantee (אחריות), and when it was seized, he tried to collect from the buyer's superior land (עידית).
Rav Pappa thought the seller could collect from the buyer's current superior land, since the buyer had promised payment from 'superior land' and such land now exists.

sub.text: Rav Acha from Difti's objection to Ravina
sub.text_en: Rav Acha from Difti's objection to Ravina
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha from Difti objects: the seller can argue that his promise referred only to the superior land that existed at the time of the sale, and now the buyer has other superior land, so the seller cannot collect from the current one.

items.text: Case of asmachta on wine and Rav Huna's ruling
items.text_en: Case of asmachta on wine and Rav Huna's ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana owed money to Rav bar Sheva, who said if not paid by a certain date, collect from this wine. Rav Pappa thought wine, being for sale, is like money, so asmachta applies. Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua ruled in the name of Rabba that any conditional statement (kol d'ei) is not valid.

sub.desc_en: Introduces the case: Rav bar Sheva was owed money by Rav Kahana, who said if not paid by a certain date, collect from this wine.
Rav Pappa thought that since wine is for sale, it is like money, so the rule of אסמכתא (conditional commitment) not acquiring should not apply.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's ruling
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's ruling
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua rejected Rav Pappa's reasoning, ruling in the name of Rabba that any conditional statement (כל דאי) does not effect acquisition.

items.text: Rav Nachman's ruling on asmachta and the dispute about retroactive cancellation
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling on asmachta and the dispute about retroactive cancellation
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that since asmachta is invalid, the land and its fruits revert. The Gemara questions whether this implies Rav Nachman holds that mistaken forgiveness is not forgiveness. It then cites a dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Nachman about selling dates of a palm tree, and Rav Nachman's distinction between a sale and a loan. Rava's statement begins but is cut off.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that since asmachta (a conditional commitment) does not effect acquisition, the land and its fruits revert to the seller.
The Gemara questions whether Rav Nachman's ruling implies that mistaken forgiveness (מחילה בטעות) is not valid forgiveness.
The Gemara cites a dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Nachman about selling dates of a palm tree, where Rav Nachman holds that even after the dates come into existence, the seller can retract.
Rav Nachman clarifies that in the sale case, if the buyer actually took and consumed the dates, we do not extract them, because that is a sale, whereas here it is a loan, so the fruits revert.
Rava begins to speak, but the statement is cut off at the section boundary.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of mistaken forgiveness and the Aylonit case
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of mistaken forgiveness and the Aylonit case
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts a story where Rav Nachman was about to establish the law of ona'ah (overcharge) but was challenged by the case of an Aylonit (a woman incapable of bearing children) who forgave her ketubah. The Gemara initially thought this was a case of mistaken forgiveness, but then clarifies that the Aylonit's forgiveness is valid because she benefits from being considered married. The Gemara concludes that neither the ona'ah nor the Aylonit case serve as a proof or refutation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Rav Nachman was about to establish the law of ona'ah (overcharge) but was challenged by the case of an Aylonit (a woman incapable of bearing children) who forgave her ketubah, initially thinking it was mistaken forgiveness, but then clarifying that the Aylonit's forgiveness is valid because she benefits from being considered married.
The Gemara cites a baraita that a woman who refuses marriage, a secondary wife, and an Aylonit have no ketubah, no fruit, no sustenance, and no worn garments.
The Gemara concludes that neither the ona'ah case serves as a refutation nor the Aylonit case serves as support for Rav Nachman.

The Gemara explains that the ona'ah case is not a refutation because the borrower did not know about the overcharge, and the Aylonit case does not support Rav Nachman because she benefits from being considered married.

items.text: Case of a woman asking an agent to buy land from relatives
items.text_en: Case of a woman asking an agent to buy land from relatives
items.desc_en: A woman tells a man to buy land for her from her relatives. He does so, and then asks if she would sell it back to him if he had money. She replies 'You and the donkey are brothers' (a dismissive phrase). Rava bar Rav Huna explains that such a statement indicates the seller does not fully intend to transfer ownership, so the sale is not final.

sub.desc_en: A woman tells an agent to buy land from her relatives; after the purchase, the agent asks if she would sell it back, and she dismissively replies 'You and the donkey are brothers.'
Rava bar Rav Huna rules that the woman's dismissive phrase indicates she did not fully intend to transfer ownership, so the sale is not final.

items.text: Question about the status of produce consumed in such a transaction
items.text_en: Question about the status of produce consumed in such a transaction
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the produce consumed by the agent (who bought the land and then effectively repurchased it) is considered fixed interest (רבית קצוצה) that can be recovered in court, or mere dust of interest (אבק רבית) that cannot. Rava bar Rav Huna and Rava both rule that it is אבק רבית and not recoverable in court.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the produce consumed by the agent is considered fixed interest (רבית קצוצה) that can be recovered in court, or mere dust of interest (אבק רבית) that cannot.

sub.text: Rava bar Rav Huna and Rava
sub.text_en: Rava bar Rav Huna and Rava
sub.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Huna and Rava both rule that the produce is dust of interest (אבק רבית) and cannot be recovered in court.

items.text: Abaye's comparison to a mortgage (משכנתא)
items.text_en: Abaye's comparison to a mortgage (משכנתא)
items.desc_en: Abaye asks Rava whether this case is analogous to a mortgage (משכנתא) where the lender consumes produce without a fixed term. The reason there is that no fixed amount was stipulated; here too no fixed amount was stipulated. Alternatively, perhaps a mortgage is a sale, while this is a loan. Rava responds that the reason is the lack of a fixed term, so here too it is not fixed interest.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks Rava whether the case of a mortgage (משכנתא) where the lender consumes produce without a fixed term is analogous to the current case, since both lack a fixed stipulation, or whether a mortgage is a sale while this is a loan.
Rava responds that the reason in the mortgage case is the lack of a fixed term, so here too, since no fixed amount was stipulated, it is not considered fixed interest.

items.text: Rav Papi reports a contrary ruling by Ravina
items.text_en: Rav Papi reports a contrary ruling by Ravina
items.desc_en: Rav Papi reports that Ravina actually ruled in practice contrary to Rava bar Rav Huna, calculating and recovering the produce consumed.

sub.desc_en: Rav Papi reports that Ravina performed a practical ruling, calculating and recovering the produce consumed, contrary to Rava bar Rav Huna's position.

items.text: Mar bar Rav Yosef's ruling on mortgages in different locations
items.text_en: Mar bar Rav Yosef's ruling on mortgages in different locations
items.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Yosef, citing Rava, rules that in a place where mortgages are normally redeemed, if the lender consumed produce equal to the loan amount, he is removed; if he consumed more, the excess is not recovered and not offset between notes. However, for orphans, if he consumed more, the excess is recovered and offset between notes.

sub.text: Mar bar Rav Yosef citing Rava
sub.text_en: Mar bar Rav Yosef citing Rava
sub.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Yosef, citing Rava, opens with the ruling that in a place where mortgages are redeemed, if the lender consumed produce equal to the loan amount, he is removed.

sub.text: Mar bar Rav Yosef citing Rava
sub.text_en: Mar bar Rav Yosef citing Rava
sub.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Yosef continues: if the lender consumed more than the loan amount, the excess is not recovered and not offset between notes.

sub.text: Mar bar Rav Yosef citing Rava
sub.text_en: Mar bar Rav Yosef citing Rava
sub.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Yosef adds a special rule for orphans: if the lender consumed more than the loan amount, the excess is recovered and offset between notes.

items.text: Rav Ashi's refinement and practical ruling for orphans
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's refinement and practical ruling for orphans
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi argues that since consuming excess produce is not recovered, even consuming the principal amount should not lead to removal without payment, because removal without payment is itself recovery of interest, which is אבק רבית and not recovered in court. He then applied this ruling in practice for minor orphans.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi argues that since consuming excess produce is not recovered, even consuming the principal amount should not lead to removal without payment, because removal without payment is itself recovery of interest, which is אבק רבית (dust of interest) and not recovered in court.
Rav Ashi applied this ruling in practice for minor orphans.

items.text: Rava's ruling on eating produce from a mortgage in a place where the creditor is repaid
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on eating produce from a mortgage in a place where the creditor is repaid
items.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Yosef states in the name of Rava that in a place where the creditor is repaid (i.e., can be forced to return the field), he may only eat the produce with a deduction (בנכייתא). A Torah scholar should not eat even with a deduction, but only through a fixed-term arrangement (בקיצותא).

sub.text: Rava bar Rav Yosef citing Rava
sub.text_en: Rava bar Rav Yosef citing Rava
sub.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Yosef rules in the name of Rava that in a place where the creditor is repaid, he may eat produce only with a deduction (בנכייתא), and a Torah scholar should eat only through a fixed-term arrangement (בקיצותא).

items.text: Dispute about the permissibility of a fixed-term arrangement (קיצותא)
items.text_en: Dispute about the permissibility of a fixed-term arrangement (קיצותא)
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rava's ruling assumes that a fixed-term arrangement (קיצותא) is permitted, but there is a dispute between Rav Acha and Ravina about this. One says it is permitted, the other says it is forbidden. The Gemara explains what a fixed-term arrangement is: the creditor says he will eat the produce without deduction for five years, and thereafter will deduct all the produce. An alternative version reverses the terms.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty: Rava's ruling that a Torah scholar may eat only via a fixed-term arrangement (קיצותא) works only for the one who permits קיצותא, but what can be said for the one who forbids it?
The Gemara cites the dispute between Rav Acha and Ravina about whether a fixed-term arrangement (קיצותא) is permitted or forbidden.
The Gemara explains what a fixed-term arrangement (קיצותא) is: the creditor says he will eat the produce without deduction for five years, and thereafter will deduct all the produce.

items.text: Reconciling the dispute and the practice in Sura
items.text_en: Reconciling the dispute and the practice in Sura
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the one who forbids in the first version permits in the second, and the one who forbids in the second version—how can he eat? He may eat like the mortgage of Sura, where they write: 'Upon completion of these years, this land shall go out without money.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes the contradiction: the one who forbids in the first version permits in the second, so how can the one who forbids in the second version eat?
The Gemara answers that he may eat like the mortgage of Sura, where they write that after these years the land will go out without money.

items.text: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna's ruling on the legal status of a mortgage
items.text_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna's ruling on the legal status of a mortgage
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua both say: In a place where the creditor is repaid, the creditor cannot collect from it, the firstborn does not take a double portion from it, and the Sabbatical year cancels it. In a place where the creditor is not repaid, the creditor can collect from it, the firstborn takes a double portion, and the Sabbatical year does not cancel it.

sub.text: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua rule that in a place where the creditor is repaid, the mortgage is not collected by creditors, the firstborn does not take a double portion, and the Sabbatical year cancels it.

sub.text: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua
sub.desc_en: They contrast the opposite case: in a place where the creditor is not repaid, the creditor can collect, the firstborn takes a double portion, and the Sabbatical year does not cancel it.

items.text: Mar Zutra's addition regarding repayment and acquisition
items.text_en: Mar Zutra's addition regarding repayment and acquisition
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra says in the name of Rav Pappa: In a place where the creditor is repaid, they can force him to return even dates from the palm tree. If he collected them with stalks, he acquires them. According to the one who says that the buyer's property is in the seller's domain, even if he did not collect them with stalks, he acquires them.

sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra states in the name of Rav Pappa that in a place where the creditor is repaid, they can force him to return even dates from the palm tree.
Mar Zutra adds that if the creditor collected the dates with stalks, he acquires them.
Mar Zutra concludes that according to the opinion that the buyer's property is in the seller's domain, even without collecting with stalks, the creditor acquires them.

items.text: Dispute about whether a formal acquisition is needed when the creditor says he will not be repaid
items.text_en: Dispute about whether a formal acquisition is needed when the creditor says he will not be repaid
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: In a place where the creditor is repaid, if he says 'I will not be repaid,' it is obvious that he is not repaid. But in a place where he is not repaid, if he says 'I will be repaid,' does he need to make a formal acquisition from him? Rav Pappa says no, Rav Sheshet bar Rav Idi says yes. The halakha is that he needs to make a formal acquisition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara poses a question: in a place where the creditor is normally repaid, if he says he will not be repaid, it is obvious; but in a place where he is not repaid, if he says he will be repaid, does he need a formal acquisition (קניין) from him or not?
Rav Pappa rules that no formal acquisition is needed from the creditor.
Rav Sheshet bar Rav Idi rules that a formal acquisition is required from the creditor.
The Gemara concludes that the halakha (הלכה) follows Rav Sheshet bar Rav Idi: a formal acquisition is needed.

items.text: Dispute about eating produce when the debtor says he will bring money
items.text_en: Dispute about eating produce when the debtor says he will bring money
items.desc_en: If the debtor says 'I will go and bring money,' the creditor may not eat. If he says 'I will trouble myself and bring money,' Ravina says he may eat, but Mar Zutra bar Rav Mari says he may not. The halakha is that he may not eat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the first case: if the debtor says 'I will go and bring money,' the creditor may not eat the produce.
The Gemara presents the second case: if the debtor says 'I will trouble myself and bring money,' Ravina permits eating.
Mar Zutra bar Rav Mari objects and rules that even in the second case the creditor may not eat.
The halakha is decided: the creditor may not eat in either case.

items.text: Practices of the Amoraim and Mar Zutra's explanation
items.text_en: Practices of the Amoraim and Mar Zutra's explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana, Rav Pappa, and Rav Ashi did not eat with a deduction (בנכייתא). Ravina ate with a deduction. Mar Zutra explains the reasoning of the one who eats with a deduction: it is like a field that is an ancestral holding (שדה אחוזה), where even though one eats much produce, the Merciful One said...

sub.desc_en: Reports that Rav Kahana, Rav Pappa, and Rav Ashi did not eat with a deduction (בנכייתא), while Ravina did eat with a deduction.

Mar Zutra explains the reasoning of the one who eats with a deduction: it is analogous to a field that is an ancestral holding (שדה אחוזה), where even though one eats much produce, the Merciful One said...

items.text: Distinction between redemption of ancestral field and loan
items.text_en: Distinction between redemption of ancestral field and loan
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves an apparent contradiction by distinguishing between an ancestral field (which is considered consecrated and redeemed at a fixed price) and a loan (which appears as usury). The one who permits the practice argues that the case is like the redemption of an ancestral field, while the one who prohibits it argues that a loan appears as usury.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: if one can redeem an ancestral field for four zuz, why should a loan be different?
The one who prohibits answers that an ancestral field is consecrated and the Torah fixed its redemption price, whereas a loan appears as usury.

items.text: Rav Ashi's traditions about standard collateral
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's traditions about standard collateral
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi reports two traditions from the elders of Meḥasya: first, that a standard collateral agreement is for one year, meaning the borrower can redeem within the year but not after; second, that the term 'משכנתא' implies the collateral is near the lender, which has implications for the law of the adjacent neighbor (בר מצרא).

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi reports the first tradition from the elders of Meḥasya: a standard collateral agreement (משכנתא) is for one year, meaning the borrower can redeem within the year but not after.
Rav Ashi reports the second tradition from the elders of Meḥasya: the term 'משכנתא' implies the collateral is near the lender, which has implications for the law of the adjacent neighbor (בר מצרא).

items.text: Rava's rejection of three practices
items.text_en: Rava's rejection of three practices
items.desc_en: Rava declares that the halakha does not follow the practices of the Ṭarsei of Pappunya, the documents of Meḥoza, or the leases of Narsha.

sub.desc_en: Rava declares that the halakha does not follow the practices of the Ṭarsei of Pappunya, the documents of Meḥoza, or the leases of Narsha.

items.text: Explanation of Ṭarsei Pappunai and documents of Meḥoza
items.text_en: Explanation of Ṭarsei Pappunai and documents of Meḥoza
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Ṭarsei Pappunai refers to the documents of Rav Pappa. The documents of Meḥoza involve writing the profit as part of the principal, which is problematic. Mar bar Ameimar reports that his father (Ameimar) would do this and trust the parties, but Rav Ashi questions what happens if the lender dies and the document falls before orphans, leading to a tragic outcome.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Ṭarsei Pappunai refers to the documents of Rav Pappa.
The Gemara describes the problematic documents of Meḥoza, where the profit is written as part of the principal, raising the question of whether profit is guaranteed.

sub.text: Mar bar Ameimar's report and Rav Ashi's question
sub.text_en: Mar bar Ameimar's report and Rav Ashi's question
sub.desc_en: Mar bar Ameimar reports that his father Ameimar would do this and trust the parties, but Rav Ashi questions what happens if the lender dies and the document falls before orphans, leading to a tragic outcome.

items.text: Explanation of leases of Narsha and the current practice
items.text_en: Explanation of leases of Narsha and the current practice
items.desc_en: The leases of Narsha involve a person mortgaging his land and then leasing it back, which is problematic because the acquisition is not clear. The current practice is to write that they performed a kinyan and waited a while before leasing it back, which is valid to prevent the locking of the door before borrowers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara describes the problematic leases of Narsha, where a person mortgages his land and then leases it back from the creditor.
The Gemara questions when the creditor actually acquires the land so that he can lease it back to the debtor.

The Gemara explains that the current practice is to write that they performed a formal acquisition (קִנְיָן) and waited a while before leasing it back, which is valid to prevent the locking of the door before borrowers.
The Gemara concludes that this practice is not a valid arrangement (i.e., it is still problematic).

items.text: Mishnah: Restrictions on partnerships to avoid usury
items.text_en: Mishnah: Restrictions on partnerships to avoid usury
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not appoint a storekeeper on a profit-sharing basis, nor give money to buy produce on a profit-sharing basis, unless the investor pays the worker's wage. Similarly, one may not place chickens or appraise calves and foals on a profit-sharing basis unless paying for labor and feed. However, one may accept calves and foals on a profit-sharing basis and raise them until they are one-third grown, and a donkey until it can carry a load.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by forbidding appointing a storekeeper or giving money for produce on a profit-sharing basis unless the investor pays the worker's wage.
The Mishnah extends the restriction to placing chickens or appraising calves and foals on a profit-sharing basis unless the investor pays for labor and feed.
The Mishnah concludes by permitting accepting calves and foals on a profit-sharing basis and raising them until one-third grown, and a donkey until it can carry a load.

items.text: Gemara's question about the wage of an idle worker
items.text_en: Gemara's question about the wage of an idle worker
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: What is meant by 'the wage of an idle worker'? It cites a Tanna who specifies that the compensation is like that of an idle worker, and the Gemara seeks clarification.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Tanna who states that the compensation is 'like that of an idle worker' and then asks for clarification of what this phrase means.

items.text: Abaye's principle and the need for both cases
items.text_en: Abaye's principle and the need for both cases
items.desc_en: Abaye states that the compensation for a caretaker is calculated as a 'idle worker' of that specific trade. The Gemara explains that both the case of a shopkeeper (חנוני) and the case of money to buy produce (מעות ליקח בהן פירות) are necessary to teach, because each case might have been assumed differently without the other.

sub.desc_en: Abaye states that the compensation for a caretaker is calculated as a 'idle worker' of that specific trade.

The Gemara explains that the case of a shopkeeper (חנוני) alone would have been insufficient, because one might have thought that only a shopkeeper, whose work is light, receives the idle-worker rate, but not one who handles money to buy produce, whose work is heavy.

The Gemara explains that the case of money to buy produce alone would also have been insufficient, because one might have thought that only that case requires the idle-worker rate, but a shopkeeper might be paid with a mere token, like dipping a fig in brine; therefore both cases are necessary.

items.text: Parenthetical: How many goats and chickens raise a sign
items.text_en: Parenthetical: How many goats and chickens raise a sign
items.desc_en: A brief parenthetical note inserted in the text, likely a scribal or editorial comment, asking how many goats and chickens are needed to raise a sign (i.e., to indicate ownership or a transaction).

sub.desc_en: A parenthetical note inserted in the text, asking how many goats and chickens are needed to raise a sign (i.e., to indicate ownership or a transaction).

items.text: Tannaitic dispute on the amount of compensation
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute on the amount of compensation
items.desc_en: A baraita records a dispute: Rabbi Meir says the compensation is fixed regardless of the amount of work; Rabbi Yehuda says even minimal acts like dipping a fig in brine or eating a single dried fig constitute full compensation; Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai says the owner pays the caretaker his full compensation.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with a question about the amount of compensation, and records Rabbi Meir's position that it is fixed regardless of the amount of work.
Rabbi Yehuda states that even minimal acts like dipping a fig in brine or eating a single dried fig constitute full compensation.
Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai rules that the owner pays the caretaker his full compensation.

items.text: Dispute about assessing animals for sharecropping
items.text_en: Dispute about assessing animals for sharecropping
items.desc_en: Another baraita discusses which animals are assessed for sharecropping: the first Tanna says goats, sheep, and anything that does not produce and eat are not assessed; Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda says goats, sheep, and chickens are assessed because they produce milk, wool, and eggs. The Gemara explains that the dispute is about incidental benefits (נסיובי ותותרי), not about wool and milk which all agree are compensation.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the first Tanna's ruling: goats, sheep, and anything that does not produce and eat are not assessed for sharecropping.
Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda counters: goats, sheep, and chickens are assessed because they produce milk, wool, and eggs respectively.
The Gemara questions the first Tanna: are wool and milk not considered compensation for labor and food?
The Gemara resolves: the dispute is only about incidental benefits (נסיובי ותותרי), not about wool and milk which all agree are compensation.
The Gemara explains that the first Tanna follows Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai (who requires full payment), while Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda follows his father Rabbi Yehuda (who accepts minimal compensation).

items.text: Case of a woman renting a hen to a friend
items.text_en: Case of a woman renting a hen to a friend
items.desc_en: A baraita presents a case where a woman says to her friend: 'My hen and your eggs, and we will split the chicks.' Rabbi Yehuda permits it, Rabbi Shimon forbids it. The Gemara asks: Doesn't Rabbi Yehuda require compensation for labor and expenses? The answer is that there are 'muzarot' eggs (eggs that are laid without a rooster, thus the hen's work is minimal).

sub.desc_en: A baraita presents a case where a woman rents a hen to a friend, or proposes a partnership: 'My hen and your eggs, and we split the chicks' — Rabbi Yehuda permits it, Rabbi Shimon forbids it.
The Gemara asks: Does Rabbi Yehuda not require compensation for labor and expenses (שְׂכַר עֲמָלוֹ וּמְזוֹנוֹ) in this arrangement?
The Gemara answers: There are 'muzarot' eggs (eggs laid without a rooster, which require minimal effort from the hen), so the hen's work is negligible and no compensation is needed.

items.text: Dispute about raising the porter's fee for animals
items.text_en: Dispute about raising the porter's fee for animals
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses the custom of raising the porter's fee for animals: the first Tanna says one follows the local custom; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says one assesses a calf with its mother and a foal with its mother even where the custom is to raise the fee. The Gemara asks: Doesn't Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel require compensation for labor and expenses? The answer is that there are droppings (גללים) which serve as compensation. The other side argues that droppings are ownerless.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the rule: where the custom is to raise the porter's fee for animals, one follows the custom; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says one assesses a calf with its mother and a foal with its mother even where the custom is to raise the fee.
The Gemara asks: Does Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel not require compensation for the worker's labor and expenses?
The Gemara answers: There are droppings (גללים) which serve as compensation for the worker's labor.
The other side objects: Droppings are ownerless (הפקר) and therefore cannot serve as valid compensation.

items.text: Rav Nachman's ruling on the halakha
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling on the halakha
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel in their respective disputes.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel in their respective disputes.

items.text: Case of the sons of Rav Ilish and a problematic contract
items.text_en: Case of the sons of Rav Ilish and a problematic contract
items.desc_en: A story: The sons of Rav Ilish had a contract that stated 'half the profit, half the loss.' Rava comments that Rav Ilish was a great man and would not have allowed a prohibition. The Gemara begins to analyze the contract: if half the profit, then two-thirds of the loss? (The text cuts off at this point on the amud.)

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a story: the sons of Rav Ilish had a contract that stated 'half the profit, half the loss.'
Rava asserts that Rav Ilish was a great man and would not have allowed a prohibition to occur.
The Gemara begins to analyze the contract: if half the profit, then two-thirds of the loss? (The text cuts off.)

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's ruling on loss and profit
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's ruling on loss and profit
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines the Mishnah's statement that if the investor takes half the loss, he gets two-thirds of the profit. Rav Kahana reports a tradition from Rav Zevid suggesting this might be a specific case, and Rav Nachman's ruling that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda is reinterpreted as a mere suggestion of a method, not a binding ruling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by quoting the Mishnah's rule: if the investor takes half the loss, he gets two-thirds of the profit.
Rav Kahana reports that he recited this teaching before Rav Zevid, who suggested it might refer to a specific case involving a person named Rav Ilish who was a minor partner.
Rav Nachman rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda's opinion.
Rav Nachman clarifies that his statement was not a binding halakhic ruling but merely a suggestion of a method (שיטה).

items.text: Rav and Shmuel dispute the 'surplus of a third'
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel dispute the 'surplus of a third'
items.desc_en: Rav permits taking a surplus of a third as profit, while Shmuel initially says if no surplus is found the worker goes empty-handed, but then amends to say the investor should stipulate a fixed dinar payment.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that taking a surplus of a third as profit is permitted.
Shmuel initially says that if no surplus of a third is found, the worker goes home empty-handed.
Shmuel amends his position and says the investor should stipulate a fixed payment of one dinar.

items.text: Gemara questions Rav's consistency and offers resolution
items.text_en: Gemara questions Rav's consistency and offers resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav's position by citing a case where Rav allowed a calf's head as payment, suggesting it implies a fixed payment. It resolves by explaining that Rav's statement applies only when the investor has his own animal, and the calf's head case is an alternative arrangement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav's consistency by asking whether he holds that one may not fix a dinar payment, citing the case of the calf's head where Rav seemingly allowed a fixed payment.
The Gemara offers a first answer: the calf's head case was an alternative arrangement where the investor could choose either the surplus or the calf's head, not a fixed payment.

The Gemara offers an alternative answer: Rav's statement applies only when the investor has his own animal, and the calf's head case is explained by the folk saying 'one who tends a bull tends bulls.'

items.text: Story of Rabbi Elazar and his sharecropper
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Elazar and his sharecropper
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar from Hagronya buys an animal and gives it to his sharecropper to fatten, paying him with the head and half the profit. His wife suggests partnership, leading to a dispute over the tail. Rabbi Elazar explains that previously it looked like interest, but now as partners, extra work is expected.

sub.desc_en: The gemara narrates that Rabbi Elazar from Hagronya bought an animal and gave it to his sharecropper to fatten, paying him with the head and half the profit.
Rabbi Elazar's wife suggests that if he enters a partnership with the sharecropper, the sharecropper would also give him the tail.
Rabbi Elazar goes and buys a share in the animal with the sharecropper, and the sharecropper gives him a portion of the tail.
The sharecropper proposes that they also divide the head, implying he wants a share of it now that they are partners.
Rabbi Elazar objects, pointing out that even originally the sharecropper did not receive a share of the head.

Rabbi Elazar explains that previously, giving extra compensation would have appeared as ribbit (interest), but now as partners, the sharecropper's extra work is expected, as people say a sharecropper is naturally subservient to the landowner to bring him pasture.

items.text: Baraita on the duration of care for a purchased animal
items.text_en: Baraita on the duration of care for a purchased animal
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one who purchases an animal from a friend must care for it for a set period: 18 months for donkeys, 24 for goats. The partner cannot force division during that time, and the care differs each year.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating the rule: one who purchases an animal must care for it for a set period (18 months for donkeys, 24 for goats), and the partner cannot force division during that time, though care differs each year.

items.text: Baraita on caring for offspring and division of profit
items.text_en: Baraita on caring for offspring and division of profit
items.desc_en: Another baraita specifies the care period for offspring: 30 days for small animals, 50 for large, with Rabbi Yosei requiring three months for small due to delicate teeth. After that, the partner takes his half and half of the other's half.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating the general rule for how long one must care for offspring: 30 days for small animals (דקה) and 50 for large (גסה).
Rabbi Yosei requires three months for small animals because their teeth are delicate, necessitating more intensive care.
After the care period, the partner takes his own half and half of the other partner's half, defining the profit division.

items.text: Rav Menashya bar Gadda's practice challenged by Abaye
items.text_en: Rav Menashya bar Gadda's practice challenged by Abaye
items.desc_en: Rav Menashya bar Gadda took half his share and half of the other's half, but Abaye questions who authorized this, noting that in a place where it is customary to raise animals, one must follow the custom.

sub.desc_en: Rav Menashya bar Gadda took his half and half of the other's half from the partnership.
Abaye asks Rav Menashya bar Gadda who authorized him to take that extra portion.
Abaye further objects that in a place where it is customary to raise animals, one must follow the custom, implying Rav Menashya bar Gadda violated the local practice.

items.text: Cases of partners dividing without consent and Rav Pappa's rulings
items.text_en: Cases of partners dividing without consent and Rav Pappa's rulings
items.desc_en: Two cases are brought before Rav Pappa: one where a partner divided coins without the other's knowledge, and another where a partner divided wine. Rav Pappa rules that coins are considered already divided, but for wine, the division is invalid without consent.

sub.desc_en: A case is brought before Rav Pappa: two partners in business, one divided coins without the other's knowledge.
Rav Pappa asks what difference it makes that the division was done without consent.
Rav Pappa cites Rav Nachman's principle that coins are considered as if already divided, so the division is valid.
A second case is brought before Rav Pappa: partners bought wine together, and one divided it without the other's knowledge.
Rav Pappa asks who authorized the division of the wine.
The partner objects that Rav Pappa's ruling on coins seems to follow his own reasoning, implying the wine division should also be valid.

items.text: Gemara's question about informing the borrower
items.text_en: Gemara's question about informing the borrower
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether one must inform the borrower about the quality of coins or wine when lending, and concludes that for wine, everyone knows there is good and bad, so no need to inform.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether one must inform the borrower about the quality of coins when lending, questioning if one would take good coins and leave deficient ones.
The answer is that for wine, everyone knows there is good and bad, so no need to inform; for coins, one must inform.

items.text: Rav Nachman's ruling on coins
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling on coins
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman states that coins are considered as if they are divided; if both are good or both are heavy, it's fine, but if one is good and the other heavy, it's forbidden.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that coins are considered as if divided; exchanging good for good or heavy for heavy is permitted, but good for heavy is forbidden.

items.text: Rav Chama's practice and its justification
items.text_en: Rav Chama's practice and its justification
items.desc_en: Rav Chama would lend coins for a fixed term, and his coins were exhausted. He thought it was like a hoe (which returns intact), but the Gemara distinguishes: a hoe returns and its depreciation is known, coins do not return intact and their depreciation is unknown.

sub.desc_en: Describes Rav Chama's practice of lending coins for a fixed daily fee, which exhausted his coins.
Rav Chama reasoned that his practice should be permitted, comparing it to lending a hoe (מרא) which returns intact.
The Gemara rejects the comparison: a hoe returns intact and its depreciation is known, but coins do not return intact and their depreciation is unknown, making the fee prohibited as ribbit (usury).

items.text: Rava's principle of 'shekhar amirah'
items.text_en: Rava's principle of 'shekhar amirah'
items.desc_en: Rava permits one to say to another: 'Take these four zuz and lend so-and-so money,' because the Torah only forbids interest from borrower to lender. Similarly, one can say: 'Take four zuz and tell so-and-so to lend me money,' as this is payment for speech. The Gemara brings a story about Abba Mar who took a basket of clay from potters and asked his father to lend them money; the rabbis questioned it, but Rav Papa justified it as payment for speech.

sub.desc_en: Rava permits one to say to another: 'Take these four zuz and lend so-and-so money,' because the Torah only forbids interest from borrower to lender.
Rava adds that one may say: 'Take four zuz and tell so-and-so to lend me money,' because this is payment for speech (שְׂכַר אֲמִירָה).
The Gemara brings a story: Abba Mar took a basket of clay from potters and asked his father Rav Papa to lend them money; the rabbis questioned whether this was interest.
Rav Papa justifies it as payment for speech (שְׂכַר אֲמִירָה), not forbidden interest, and permits it.

items.text: Mishnah: Evaluating animals and fields for sharecropping
items.text_en: Mishnah: Evaluating animals and fields for sharecropping
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may evaluate a cow, donkey, or any working and eating animal for half-profit sharecropping. In places where they customarily divide offspring immediately, they do so; where they raise them, they raise them. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that one may evaluate a calf with its mother, a foal with its mother, and may 'hafriz' (increase the rent) on his field without concern for interest.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule of evaluating animals for half-profit sharecropping and the local custom regarding dividing or raising offspring.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that one may evaluate a calf with its mother and a foal with its mother, and may increase the rent on his field without concern for interest.

items.text: Gemara: Explanation of 'hafriz' on a field
items.text_en: Gemara: Explanation of 'hafriz' on a field
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the case of 'hafriz' on a field: if one rents a field for ten kor of wheat per year and says 'give me 200 zuz to improve it, and I will give you twelve kor per year,' it is permitted. However, one may not 'hafriz' on a store or a ship.

sub.desc_en: The baraita defines the permitted case of 'hafriz' on a field: a tenant who rents for ten kor and offers to improve the field for 200 zuz in exchange for raising the rent to twelve kor.
The baraita adds that the leniency of 'hafriz' does not apply to a store or a ship.

items.text: Rav Nachman's exception for store and ship
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's exception for store and ship
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha says that sometimes one may 'hafriz' on a store to paint a picture in it, or on a ship to make an 'iskarya' (a cabin), because these improvements increase the rental value.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha states an exception to the rule that one may not 'hafriz' (advance money for future rent) on a store or ship, permitting it when the improvement increases the rental value.

items.text: Rav's ruling on ship rental and the final halakha
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on ship rental and the final halakha
items.desc_en: Rav says about a ship: 'agrah u'fagra' (rent and body). Rav Kahana and Rav Asi object: if rent, then not body; if body, then not rent. Rav is silent. Rav Sheshet explains Rav's silence: he didn't know the baraisa that permits receiving 'tzon barzel' from gentiles and the case of evaluating a cow for 30 dinars with a monthly payment. Rav Papa concludes the halakha: a ship is 'agrah u'fagra'.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that a ship is considered both rent and body (the renter bears both rental fee and liability for the ship's body).
Rav Kahana and Rav Asi object to Rav: if it is rent, it cannot be body; if it is body, it cannot be rent — the two are mutually exclusive.
Rav remains silent in response to the objection.

Rav Sheshet explains Rav's silence: Rav was unaware of the baraisa that permits receiving 'צאן ברזל' (iron flock) from gentiles and the case of evaluating a cow for 30 dinars with a monthly payment, because the cow was not made into money while alive.
Rav Papa concludes the halakha (הלכה) that a ship is indeed both rent and body (אגרא ופגרא).

items.text: Opening anecdote about the practice of Kufra
items.text_en: Opening anecdote about the practice of Kufra
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the people of Kufra would set wages at the time of pulling and depreciation at the time of breaking, and questions whether this depends on custom, concluding that it is based on a taught Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports the custom of the people of Kufra to set wages at the time of pulling and depreciation at the time of breaking.
The Gemara questions whether the matter depends on mere custom.
The Gemara answers that it is based on a taught Mishnah, so it is a binding custom.

items.text: Rav Anan's ruling on orphan funds
items.text_en: Rav Anan's ruling on orphan funds
items.desc_en: Rav Anan quotes Shmuel that orphan funds may be lent with interest. Rav Nachman objects, arguing that orphans should not be permitted to consume what is not theirs, and asks for the actual precedent.

sub.desc_en: Rav Anan reports in the name of Shmuel that orphan funds may be lent with interest.
Rav Nachman objects that orphans should not be permitted to consume what is not theirs, and that they should follow their guardians for support.

sub.text: Rav Anan's request for the precedent
sub.text_en: Rav Anan's request for the precedent
sub.desc_en: Rav Anan asks Rav Nachman to tell him the actual details of the precedent.

items.text: The precedent of Mar Ukva's chest
items.text_en: The precedent of Mar Ukva's chest
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman describes a practice in Shmuel's house involving a chest of Mar Ukva's children: they would weigh and give, weigh and take, taking both wages and depreciation, but not both simultaneously.

sub.text: Rav Nachman's description of the precedent
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman's description of the precedent
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman describes the practice in Shmuel's house with Mar Ukva's children's chest: they would weigh and give, weigh and take.

sub.text: Rav Nachman's explanation of the arrangement
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman's explanation of the arrangement
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman explains that they took either wages or depreciation, but not both simultaneously.

items.text: Rav Nachman's extension to adults
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's extension to adults
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that such a practice is even permitted for adults, since they accept the risk of depreciation of the copper, whose value decreases as it is smelted.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman responds that even adults may use this arrangement because they accept the risk of the copper's depreciation as it is smelted.

items.text: Rav Chisda's ruling on near-profit far-loss
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's ruling on near-profit far-loss
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda (or Rav Sheishes) states that orphan funds may be lent in a manner that is close to profit and far from loss.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda (or Rav Sheishes) rules that orphan funds may be lent in a manner that is close to profit and far from loss.

items.text: Baraita on the three types of lenders
items.text_en: Baraita on the three types of lenders
items.desc_en: A baraita classifies lenders: close to profit and far from loss is wicked; close to loss and far from profit is pious; equally close or far is the measure of an average person.

sub.desc_en: The baraita classifies three types of lenders: one close to profit and far from loss is wicked, one close to loss and far from profit is pious, and one equally close or far is the measure of an average person.

items.text: Rabbah's question and Mar's advice on orphan funds
items.text_en: Rabbah's question and Mar's advice on orphan funds
items.desc_en: Rabbah asks Rav Yosef how to handle orphan funds; Rav Yosef suggests placing them in court and giving out one coin at a time, but Rabbah objects that the principal is consumed. Mar then advises finding a man with refined gold, taking the gold, and lending it close to profit and far from loss, but not a marked item lest it be a deposit claimed by its owner.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah asks Rav Yosef how to handle orphan funds.
Rav Yosef suggests placing the funds in court and giving out one coin at a time.
Rabbah objects that the principal is consumed by this method.
Mar asks Rabbah how to proceed instead.
Mar advises finding a man with refined gold, taking the gold, and lending it close to profit and far from loss.
Mar adds that a marked item should not be used, lest it be a deposit claimed by its owner via identifying marks.

items.text: Rav Ashi's alternative method
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's alternative method
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi questions what to do if no one has refined gold, and proposes finding a trustworthy person with stable assets who fears Torah law and rabbinic bans, and lending the funds in court.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi raises the problem: if no one with refined gold is found, should the orphans' money just sit idle?
Rav Ashi proposes an alternative: find a trustworthy person with stable assets who fears Torah law and rabbinic bans, and lend the funds in court.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not accept 'iron sheep' from a Jew because it constitutes interest, but may do so from a gentile or a resident alien. A Jew may lend or borrow with interest from a gentile, and may lend a gentile's money with the gentile's knowledge but not with the Jew's knowledge.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that one may not accept 'iron sheep' (a guaranteed investment) from a Jew because it constitutes interest.
The Mishnah permits accepting 'iron sheep' from a gentile or a resident alien (גר תושב).
The Mishnah concludes that a Jew may lend a gentile's money with the gentile's knowledge but not with the Jew's knowledge.

items.text: Gemara's first question
items.text_en: Gemara's first question
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah implies that the animal is under the receiver's ownership, citing a contradiction from a baraita that says offspring of 'iron sheep' from a gentile are exempt from the firstborn status.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah implies that the animal is under the receiver's ownership, citing a contradiction from a baraita that says offspring of 'iron sheep' from a gentile are exempt from the firstborn status.

items.text: Abaye's resolution
items.text_en: Abaye's resolution
items.desc_en: Abaye resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between cases: one where the receiver accepts liability for loss and depreciation, and one where he does not.

sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between cases: one where the receiver accepts liability for loss and depreciation, and one where he does not.

items.text: Rava's objection and alternative
items.text_en: Rava's objection and alternative
items.desc_en: Rava objects to Abaye's distinction, arguing that if the owner accepts liability, it is not called 'iron sheep'. He further points out that the Mishnah's continuation should have distinguished explicitly. He implies that the Mishnah's leniency applies only when the receiver does not accept liability.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects to Abaye's distinction, arguing that if the owner accepts liability for loss and depreciation, the arrangement cannot be called 'צאן ברזל' (iron sheep) at all.

Rava further objects that the Mishnah's continuation should have distinguished explicitly between cases where the receiver does or does not accept liability, implying that the Mishnah's leniency applies only when liability is not accepted.

items.text: Rava's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rava's alternative explanation
