items.desc_en: Rava explains that both cases involve the receiver not accepting liability, yet the offspring are exempt from the firstborn status because the gentile can seize the animal or its offspring if the Jew does not pay, giving the gentile a hand in the middle, which exempts from the firstborn status.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the contradiction by explaining that in both cases the receiver does not accept liability for loss or depreciation, yet the offspring are exempt from firstborn status because the gentile can seize the animal or its offspring if the Jew does not pay, giving the gentile a hand in the middle.

items.text: Interpretation of a verse about interest
items.text_en: Interpretation of a verse about interest
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse about one who increases his wealth through interest, and Rav interprets 'he who graciously gives to the poor' as referring to King Shapur.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse from Proverbs about one who increases wealth through interest and gives to the poor.
The Gemara asks the meaning of the phrase 'he who graciously gives to the poor' in the verse.
Rav interprets the verse as referring to King Shapur, who took interest from non-Jews and gave it to the poor.

items.text: Discussion on interest with gentiles
items.text_en: Discussion on interest with gentiles
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman reports that Huna said the verse applies even to interest from a gentile. Rava challenges this with the verse 'to the gentile you may lend with interest', interpreting it as a command. The Gemara clarifies that the verse is needed to exclude a brother, and to establish both a positive and negative commandment.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman reports that Huna said the verse applies even to interest from a gentile.
Rava challenges Rav Nachman by citing the verse 'לַנׇּכְרִי תַשִּׁיךְ' (to the gentile you may lend with interest), interpreting it as a command.
The Gemara clarifies that the word is 'תַּשִּׁיךְ' (you shall lend with interest), not 'תִּשּׁוֹךְ' (you shall bite).
The Gemara asks: is it not necessary to interpret the verse otherwise?
The Gemara explains that the verse is needed to exclude a brother from the permission.
The Gemara objects that the prohibition regarding a brother is already explicitly written in the verse 'וּלְאָחִיךְ לֹא תַשִּׁיךְ' (and to your brother you shall not lend with interest).
The Gemara resolves that the verse establishes both a positive and a negative commandment regarding interest with a brother.

items.text: Objection from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Objection from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rava raises an objection from the Mishnah which permits borrowing and lending with interest from gentiles and resident aliens. Rav Chiya bar Rav Huna responds that the permission is only needed for a specific case, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: Rava raises an objection from the Mishnah which explicitly permits borrowing and lending with interest from gentiles and resident aliens.

sub.text: Rav Chiya bar Rav Huna's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Chiya bar Rav Huna's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiya bar Rav Huna responds that the Mishnah's permission is only needed for a specific case, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Ravina's explanation of the leniency for Torah scholars
items.text_en: Ravina's explanation of the leniency for Torah scholars
items.desc_en: Ravina explains that the earlier ruling allowing a Torah scholar to lend with interest applies specifically to Torah scholars, because the rabbinic decree was only to prevent learning from the borrower's actions, and a Torah scholar will not learn from such actions.

sub.desc_en: Ravina explains that the earlier ruling applies specifically to Torah scholars, because the rabbinic decree was only to prevent learning from the borrower's actions, and a Torah scholar will not learn from such actions.

items.text: Priority in lending: Jew vs. gentile, poor vs. rich
items.text_en: Priority in lending: Jew vs. gentile, poor vs. rich
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about priorities in lending: a Jew takes precedence over a gentile, a poor person over a rich one, and one's own poor over those of another city. Rav Nachman clarifies that the priority of a Jew over a gentile applies even if the Jew would borrow without interest and the gentile would pay interest.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited, attributed to Rav Yosef, establishing priorities in lending: a Jew over a gentile, a poor person over a rich one, and one's own poor over those of another city.
The Gemara questions why the baraita states the obvious priority of a Jew over a gentile.
Rav Nachman explains that the baraita is necessary to teach that a Jew takes precedence even when lending to a gentile would yield interest and lending to a Jew would be interest-free.

items.text: The severity of lending with interest and the fate of usurers
items.text_en: The severity of lending with interest and the fate of usurers
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosi describes the blindness of usurers who deny God by documenting the loan. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar cites a verse that one who lends without interest will never falter, implying that usurers' assets will falter. Rabbi Elazar distinguishes between those who falter and rise and those who falter and do not rise.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosi opens by describing the blindness of usurers, who bring witnesses and scribes to document the loan, thereby denying God.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar cites a verse that one who lends without interest will never falter, implying that usurers' assets will falter.
The Gemara objects that we see people who do not lend with interest also have their assets falter.
Rabbi Elazar resolves the objection by distinguishing between those who falter and rise (non-usurers) and those who falter and do not rise (usurers).

items.text: Interpretation of a verse about the righteous being swallowed
items.text_en: Interpretation of a verse about the righteous being swallowed
items.desc_en: Rav Huna interprets the verse 'Why do You look at traitors and remain silent when the wicked swallows one more righteous than he?' to mean that a wicked person swallows one who is more righteous than himself, but not a completely righteous person.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna interprets the verse to mean that a wicked person swallows one who is more righteous than himself, but not a completely righteous person.

items.text: The status of a ger toshav regarding sale and interest
items.text_en: The status of a ger toshav regarding sale and interest
items.desc_en: Rabbi states he does not know the meaning of 'ger tzedek' in the context of sale and 'ger toshav' in the context of interest. The Gemara explains the verses regarding a Hebrew slave sold to a ger, and questions whether a ger can acquire a Hebrew slave. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between acquisition and legal status. The discussion includes a baraita about a woman acquiring slaves and a digression about a widow and a dog.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi states he does not know the meaning of 'ger tzedek' in the context of sale and 'ger toshav' in the context of interest.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the sale context
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the sale context
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the verses regarding a Hebrew slave sold to a ger, distinguishing between ger tzedek, ger toshav, a gentile, and one sold to idolatry itself.
The Gemara questions whether a ger can acquire a Hebrew slave, citing a baraita that a ger is not acquired as a Hebrew slave and a woman and ger do not acquire a Hebrew slave.
The Gemara explains that a ger cannot be acquired as a Hebrew slave because the verse requires return to family, and a woman and ger do not acquire due to propriety and tradition.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between acquisition and legal status: a ger does not acquire a Hebrew slave but his legal status is like a Jew, yet he can acquire with the status of a gentile.
A baraita supports the distinction: a slave with a pierced ear or sold to a gentile does not serve the son or daughter.

sub.text: Gemara's question about Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
sub.text_en: Gemara's question about Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the baraita conflicts with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who says a woman can acquire slaves, and resolves that the baraita refers to a Hebrew slave while Rabban Shimon refers to a Canaanite slave.
The Gemara explains the distinction: a Hebrew slave is modest for a woman, while a Canaanite slave is immodest.
The Gemara digresses to discuss Rav Yosef's teaching that a widow should not raise a dog or host a student, explaining that the dog's attachment is due to the morsel she throws it.

items.text: The prohibition of interest with a ger toshav and the allowance of being a guarantor
items.text_en: The prohibition of interest with a ger toshav and the allowance of being a guarantor
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions a contradiction: a verse prohibits taking interest from a ger toshav, but a baraita allows lending to and borrowing from a ger toshav with interest. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves this by noting the verse says 'from him' (singular), referring to a Jew, not a ger toshav. The baraita then teaches that one may be a guarantor for a ger toshav.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: a verse prohibits taking interest from a ger toshav, but a baraita permits lending to and borrowing from a ger toshav with interest.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the contradiction by noting that the verse says 'from him' (singular), referring to a Jew, not a ger toshav.
The baraita teaches that although one may not take interest from a ger toshav, one may serve as a guarantor for him.

items.text: Initial question on the guarantor's liability
items.text_en: Initial question on the guarantor's liability
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the earlier Mishnah's ruling about a guarantor: if the guarantor is for a Jew, he violates the prohibition of usury along with the lender and borrower. If for a gentile, since gentile law pursues the guarantor, the guarantor himself is paying interest.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling: if the guarantor is for a Jew, he violates the prohibition of usury along with the lender and borrower; if for a gentile, since gentile law pursues the guarantor, the guarantor himself is paying interest.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's resolution: accepting Jewish law
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's resolution: accepting Jewish law
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet answers that the case is where the guarantor accepted to be judged by Jewish law. The Gemara objects that if so, he should also not take interest. Rav Sheshet clarifies: he accepted for this (the guarantee) but not for that (the interest).

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet answers that the case is where the guarantor accepted to be judged by Jewish law.
The Gemara objects that if he accepted Jewish law, he should also not take interest.
Rav Sheshet clarifies that the guarantor accepted Jewish law for the guarantee but not for the interest.

items.text: Baraita: Jew lending gentile's money with gentile's knowledge
items.text_en: Baraita: Jew lending gentile's money with gentile's knowledge
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: A Jew may lend a gentile's money with the gentile's knowledge but not with a Jew's knowledge. Examples are given: if a Jew borrowed from a gentile with interest and another Jew offers to repay him in the same manner, it is forbidden unless the gentile is made the creditor. The reverse case is also discussed.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the general rule: a Jew may lend a gentile's money with the gentile's knowledge but not with a Jew's knowledge.
The baraita gives the first case: a Jew who borrowed from a gentile with interest is forbidden to have another Jew repay the gentile in the same manner, unless the gentile is made the creditor.
The baraita gives the reverse case: a gentile who borrowed from a Jew with interest is permitted to have another Jew repay the Jew in the same manner, but forbidden if the Jew is made the creditor.

items.text: Gemara's difficulty with the first clause
items.text_en: Gemara's difficulty with the first clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the first clause: since a gentile has no agency (shlichut), the Jew who pays the gentile's debt is actually paying interest himself, so why is it permitted?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the first clause: since a gentile has no agency (שליחות), the Jew who pays the gentile's debt is actually paying interest himself, so why is it permitted?

items.text: Rav Huna bar Manoach and Rav Pappa's answers
items.text_en: Rav Huna bar Manoach and Rav Pappa's answers
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Manoach in the name of Rav Acha bar Rav Ika answers that the case is where the gentile said: 'Place them on the ground and be free.' The Gemara objects that this is obvious. Rav Pappa answers that it is where the Jew took and gave by hand, teaching that the gentile gives on the Jew's account.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Manoach citing Rav Acha bar Rav Ika
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Manoach citing Rav Acha bar Rav Ika
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Manoach answers that the case is where the gentile said: 'Place them on the ground and be free.'
The Gemara objects that this answer is obvious and asks what novelty it teaches.
Rav Pappa answers that the case is where the Jew took and gave by hand.
The Gemara again objects that this is still obvious.
The Gemara resolves that the novelty is that one might have thought the gentile gives on the Jew's account, so the teaching informs us otherwise.

items.text: Rav Ashi's first version: agency for gentiles in all Torah except terumah
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's first version: agency for gentiles in all Torah except terumah
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi says that the principle 'no agency for a gentile' applies only to terumah, but in the entire Torah a gentile can be an agent. The Gemara rejects this, arguing that agency for all Torah is derived from terumah, so Rav Ashi's statement is a difficulty.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi states that the principle 'no agency for a gentile' applies only to תרומה (priestly portion), but in the entire Torah a gentile can be an agent.

The Gemara objects that Rav Ashi's statement is a difficulty, asking why תרומה (priestly portion) is different and citing the verse 'אַתֶּם' (you) and 'גַּם אַתֶּם' (also you) to show that agency requires being part of the covenant (בני ברית).
The Gemara concludes that agency for the entire Torah is derived from תרומה (priestly portion) by a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy), so Rav Ashi's statement is indeed a difficulty and is rejected.

items.text: Rav Ashi's second version: gentiles as agents for us but not vice versa
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's second version: gentiles as agents for us but not vice versa
items.desc_en: An alternative version: Rav Ashi says that the lack of agency applies only when gentiles act for us, but we can be agents for them. The Gemara rejects this too, since the verse requires agents to be 'sons of the covenant'.

sub.text: Alternative version (איכא דאמרי) of Rav Ashi's statement
sub.text_en: Alternative version (איכא דאמרי) of Rav Ashi's statement
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi states that the principle of no agency for a gentile applies only when they act for us, but we can be agents for them.
The Gemara objects: why should gentiles not be agents for us? Because the verse 'אתם' (you) includes only those who are 'בני ברית' (members of the covenant).
The Gemara objects further: the same verse requires the agent to be a 'בן ברית' (member of the covenant), so even we cannot be agents for them, rendering Rav Ashi's statement a rejected error.

items.text: Ravina's answer: rabbinic acquisition (zekiyah) for gentiles
items.text_en: Ravina's answer: rabbinic acquisition (zekiyah) for gentiles
items.desc_en: Ravina answers that although a gentile has no biblical agency, he has rabbinic acquisition (zekiyah), similar to a minor. The Gemara begins to compare this to a minor who lacks agency.

sub.desc_en: Ravina answers that although a gentile has no biblical agency (שליחות), he does have rabbinic acquisition (זכייה), analogous to a minor who also lacks agency.

items.text: Gemara's objection and resolution regarding a convert's acquisition
items.text_en: Gemara's objection and resolution regarding a convert's acquisition
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that a convert has rabbinic acquisition, so the earlier case should be no different. It resolves that a Jew can become an agent, but a gentile cannot, so the convert's status changes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that since a convert has rabbinic acquisition (זכייה מדרבנן), the earlier case should be no different.
The Gemara resolves that a Jew can become an agent (שליחות), but a gentile cannot, so the convert's status changes.

items.text: Baraita on a Jew lending to a gentile with interest and conversion
items.text_en: Baraita on a Jew lending to a gentile with interest and conversion
items.desc_en: A baraita rules that if a Jew lent to a gentile with interest and the debt was folded into a loan before conversion, the lender collects both principal and interest; if after conversion, only principal. Rabbi Yosei says the lender always collects both, and Rava cites Rav Huna that the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei to avoid suspicion that the convert converted for the money.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the case of a Jew who borrowed from a gentile with interest and folded the debt into a loan before conversion, ruling that if done before conversion the lender collects both principal and interest, but if after conversion only principal.
The baraita adds the parallel case of a gentile who borrowed from a Jew with interest and then converted, applying the same distinction.
Rabbi Yosei disagrees and rules that in the gentile-borrower case, the lender always collects both principal and interest regardless of when the debt was folded.

sub.text: Rava citing Rav Chisda citing Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Rava citing Rav Chisda citing Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Rava transmits a tradition from Rav Chisda citing Rav Huna that the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei.
Rava explains Rabbi Yosei's reasoning: to prevent people from saying that the convert converted for the sake of the money.

items.text: Baraita on a promissory note with interest
items.text_en: Baraita on a promissory note with interest
items.desc_en: A baraita states that if a note includes interest, Rabbi Meir penalizes the lender by forfeiting both principal and interest, while the Sages say he collects principal but not interest. The dispute is whether we penalize permissible money because of prohibited money.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that if a promissory note includes interest, Rabbi Meir penalizes the lender by forfeiting both principal and interest.
The Sages argue that the lender collects the principal but not the interest.
The Gemara asks what is the underlying dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Meir holds we penalize permissible money because of prohibited money, while the Sages hold we do not.

items.text: Gemara on early-dated and late-dated notes
items.text_en: Gemara on early-dated and late-dated notes
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why early-dated notes are invalid, since they could still be collected from the later date. Resh Lakish says this is a dispute and follows Rabbi Meir, while Rabbi Yochanan says even the Sages agree, due to a decree lest the lender collect from the earlier date.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why early-dated promissory notes are invalid, since they could still be collected from the later date.
Resh Lakish answers that the mishnah is taught as a dispute and follows Rabbi Meir's position.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that even the Sages agree the notes are invalid, due to a decree lest the lender collect from the earlier date.

items.text: Case of a pledged orchard and the nature of the sale
items.text_en: Case of a pledged orchard and the nature of the sale
items.desc_en: A man pledged his orchard to another who consumed its produce for three years. The pledgee threatened to claim it was purchased if not sold. The owner then transferred it to his minor son and sold it to the pledgee. The Gemara questions whether the sale is valid and whether the money is like a loan with a lien or an oral loan. Abaye connects this to Rabbi Asi's ruling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a case: a man pledged his orchard to another, who consumed its produce for three years, then threatened to claim it was purchased if not sold.
The owner transferred the orchard to his minor son and then sold it to the pledgee.
The Gemara questions whether the sale is valid and whether the money is like a loan with a lien (מלוה בשטר) or an oral loan (מלוה על פה).
Abaye connects the case to Rabbi Asi's ruling, implying the answer lies in that precedent.

items.text: Opening Mishnah (continued from previous daf)
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah (continued from previous daf)
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who admits to a debt document does not need to validate it, and can collect from liened property.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who admits to a debt document does not need to validate it, and can collect from liened property.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: Rava distinguishes the case from others where the document was not given to be written. Marimar and Ravina discuss Rabbi Yochanan's decree, and the Gemara addresses a baraita about land improvement, concluding that the cases differ because here the debtor seeks to evade payment.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects to the comparison, arguing that in the Mishnah's case the document was given to be written, whereas here it was not.

Ravina challenges Marimar: if Rabbi Yochanan's decree about collecting from an earlier date applies, why isn't it considered 'not given to be written'? Marimar responds that it is given to be written from the second date, unlike here where it is not given to be written at all.

The Gemara raises a baraita about land improvement where the robber collects the principal from liened property and the improvement from free property, questioning why this is not considered 'not given to be written'.
The Gemara resolves that in the land improvement case the robber can appease the owner and uphold the document, whereas here the debtor seeks to evade payment, so the document is upheld.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of fixing prices for produce
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of fixing prices for produce
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may not fix a price for produce until the market price is published. Once published, one may fix a price even if the seller does not have the produce. Exceptions are made for the first buyer of the harvest, and for certain items like eggs and lime. Rabbi Yosei and the Sages dispute regarding manure, and Rabbi Yehuda adds a condition about the high market price.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the general rule: one may not fix a price for produce until the market price is published, but once published, one may fix a price even if the seller does not have the produce.
The Mishnah lists exceptions: the first buyer of the harvest may fix a price on the sheaf, grape-basket, olive-vat, potter's eggs, and lime once it is sunk in the kiln.
The Mishnah records a dispute: one may fix a price for manure year-round; Rabbi Yosei restricts it to when the seller has manure in the ash-heap, while the Sages permit it unconditionally.
The Mishnah concludes with Rabbi Yehuda's ruling: even if one did not fix a price at the high market price, the buyer may demand either the produce at that price or his money back.

items.text: Gemara: Rabbi Yochanan's statement on the market price
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabbi Yochanan's statement on the market price
items.desc_en: Rabbi Asi quotes Rabbi Yochanan that one may not fix a price based on the market price in the street. Rabbi Zeira asks if this applies even to a 'dormus' (a large market), and Rabbi Asi clarifies it applies only to small towns where gates are not fixed. The Gemara then reconciles this with the Mishnah by explaining the Mishnah refers to wheat from storehouses with long gates.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Asi states in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that one may not fix a price based on the market price in the street.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira's question to Rabbi Asi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's question to Rabbi Asi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks Rabbi Asi whether Rabbi Yochanan's ruling applies even to a large market (דורמס).
Rabbi Asi clarifies that Rabbi Yochanan's ruling applies only to small towns where the gates are not fixed.
The Gemara reconciles the Mishnah with Rabbi Yochanan's ruling by explaining that the Mishnah refers to wheat from storehouses with long gates.

items.text: Baraita: Details of fixing prices
items.text_en: Baraita: Details of fixing prices
items.desc_en: A baraita elaborates on the Mishnah: one may not fix a price until the market price is published, but once published, one may fix a price even if the seller does not have the produce. If there are new and old produce at different prices, one must wait for the market price for each. Similarly, if there are pickers and sellers at different prices, one must wait for the market price for each.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating the rule: one may not fix a price until the market price is published, but once published, one may fix a price even if the seller does not have the produce.
The baraita adds a detail: if new and old produce are sold at different prices, one must wait for the market price for each type.
The baraita adds another detail: if pickers and sellers have different prices, one must wait for the market price for each group.

items.text: Rav Nachman and Rava on pickers' prices
items.text_en: Rav Nachman and Rava on pickers' prices
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that one may fix a price for pickers at the pickers' market price. Rava questions why a homeowner cannot borrow from a picker like a picker does from another picker. Rav Nachman explains that it is beneath the homeowner's dignity to borrow from a picker, or alternatively, one who gives money to a homeowner expects good produce.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that one may fix a price for pickers at the pickers' market price.
Rava questions why a homeowner cannot borrow from a picker like a picker does from another picker.
Rav Nachman answers that it is beneath the homeowner's dignity to borrow from a picker.
Rav Nachman offers an alternative explanation: one who gives money to a homeowner expects good produce.

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling on borrowing based on market price
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling on borrowing based on market price
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet quotes Rav Huna that one may not borrow based on the market price in the street. Rav Yosef bar Chama questions this, citing a case where Rav Huna permitted students to borrow in Tishrei and repay in Tevet because they could buy and repay. The Gemara explains that initially Rav Huna held that one may not borrow, but after hearing Rabbi Shmuel bar Chiya quoting Rabbi Elazar that one may borrow, he retracted.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet reports Rav Huna's ruling that one may not borrow based on the market price in the street.

sub.text: Rav Yosef bar Chama (or Rav Yosei bar Abba) questioning Rav Sheshet
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef bar Chama (or Rav Yosei bar Abba) questioning Rav Sheshet
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Chama challenges Rav Sheshet by citing a case where Rav Huna permitted students to borrow in Tishrei and repay in Tevet, because they could buy wheat and repay.
The Gemara explains that initially Rav Huna held that one may not borrow, but after hearing Rabbi Shmuel bar Chiya quoting Rabbi Elazar that one may borrow, he retracted.

items.text: Baraita: Transporting a bundle
items.text_en: Baraita: Transporting a bundle
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses a case where one transports a bundle from place to place and a friend offers to pay the local rate for it.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents a case where one transports a bundle and a friend offers to pay the local rate for it.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and related baraita
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and related baraita
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if produce is in the seller's domain, it is permitted to sell on credit at a higher price, but in the buyer's domain it is forbidden. A baraita adds that if a transporter is asked to deliver produce in exchange for future produce elsewhere, it is permitted only if the transporter has produce at that location. The baraita also notes that transporters may charge more in expensive places without concern for interest.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule that selling produce on credit at a higher price is permitted when the produce is in the seller's domain, but forbidden when in the buyer's domain.

A baraita elaborates that a transporter may receive future produce in exchange for current delivery only if he has produce at the destination, and transporters may charge more in expensive places without concern for interest.

items.text: Gemara's question and two explanations
items.text_en: Gemara's question and two explanations
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why transporters are permitted to charge more in expensive places. Rav Pappa says it is because they are pleased to have the merchants reveal the market price. Rav Acha bar Rav Ika says it is because they are pleased that the merchants come to them. The difference between them is a new merchant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the transporters are permitted to charge the same price in expensive places as in cheap ones.
Rav Pappa explains that the transporters are pleased because the merchants reveal the market price (תַּרְעָא) to them.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika explains that the transporters are pleased because the merchants come to them (מוֹזְלִי גַּבַּיְיהוּ).
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two explanations.

The Gemara resolves that the difference is a new merchant (תַּגָּרָא חַדְתָּא): according to Rav Pappa, the transporters benefit from the price revelation even from a new merchant; according to Rav Acha bar Rav Ika, they only benefit if the merchant comes to them, not a new one.

items.text: Case of Rav's arrangement with transporters
items.text_en: Case of Rav's arrangement with transporters
items.desc_en: The Gemara describes a practice in Sura and Kafri where transporters travel in groups. Rav would give money to transporters, accept responsibility for road accidents, and take five out of six units of profit. The Gemara asks why he does not take six, and answers that an important person is different.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara describes the practice in Sura and Kafri where transporters travel in groups, and Rav's arrangement to give them money, accept responsibility for road accidents, and take five out of six units of profit.
The Gemara asks why Rav takes only five units of profit instead of six, given that he bears the risk of road accidents.
The Gemara answers that an important person (אדם חשוב) is different, implying that Rav's stature allowed him to accept a lower profit share without it appearing as interest.

items.text: Inquiry about flax scrapings
items.text_en: Inquiry about flax scrapings
items.desc_en: Rabbi Asi asked Rabbi Yochanan whether one may do similarly with flax scrapings. Rabbi Yochanan replied that Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei sought to do so with linen garments, but Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi) did not allow him. An alternative version says Rabbi sought to do so with scrapings, but Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei did not allow him.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Asi asks Rabbi Yochanan whether one may do similarly with flax scrapings (גרוטאות).
Rabbi Yochanan replies that Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei sought to do so with linen garments, but Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi) did not allow him.
An alternative version states that Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi) sought to do so with scrapings, but Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei did not allow him.

items.text: Dispute about orchards and Rav's concession
items.text_en: Dispute about orchards and Rav's concession
items.desc_en: Rav forbade and Shmuel permitted leasing an orchard for a fixed amount of produce. Rav reasoned that since the orchard's value is higher upfront, it appears as interest for waiting. Shmuel permitted it because there is uncertainty about the yield, so it does not appear as interest. Rav Shimi bar Chiya added that Rav concedes in the case of oxen, whose loss is great.

sub.desc_en: The gemara reports that Rav forbade and Shmuel permitted leasing an orchard for a fixed amount of produce, with each giving their reasoning: Rav because the orchard's value is higher upfront (appearing as interest for waiting), and Shmuel because the yield is uncertain (so it does not appear as interest).
Rav Shimi bar Chiya adds that Rav concedes in the case of oxen, whose potential loss is great, implying that the arrangement is permitted there.

items.text: Shmuel's instruction to flax workers
items.text_en: Shmuel's instruction to flax workers
items.desc_en: Shmuel told flax workers to overturn the land so that they acquire the land itself, otherwise their payment would be considered a loan and forbidden as interest.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel instructs flax workers to overturn the land to acquire it, otherwise their payment would be considered a loan and forbidden as interest.

items.text: Rava's arrangement with field guards and the rabbis' challenge
items.text_en: Rava's arrangement with field guards and the rabbis' challenge
items.desc_en: Rava told field guards to overturn in the barns so that their wages are not paid until that time, since wages are only paid at the end, and at that time they are giving him a discount. The rabbis challenged Rava, saying he was eating interest because everyone else pays four and settles with the sharecropper in Nisan, while Rava waits until Iyar and takes six. Rava replied that they act unjustly by settling early, causing loss to the sharecropper, whereas he waits and benefits them.

sub.desc_en: Rava instructs field guards to overturn in the barns so their wages are not paid until the end, at which point they give him a discount.
The rabbis object that Rava is eating interest (ריבית), since everyone else pays four and settles with the sharecropper in Nisan, while Rava waits until Iyar and takes six.
Rava replies that the rabbis act unjustly by settling early, causing loss to the sharecropper, whereas he waits until Iyar and benefits them.

items.text: Case of Rav Mari bar Rachel and the gentile's house
items.text_en: Case of Rav Mari bar Rachel and the gentile's house
items.desc_en: Rav Mari bar Rachel had mortgaged a house from a gentile, who later sold it to Rava. Rav Mari collected rent for twelve months and offered it to Rava, explaining that the standard mortgage term is one year. Rava responded that had he known of the mortgage, he would not have bought it, and he will not take rent until the gentile repays the loan.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mari bar Rachel mortgaged a house from a gentile, who later sold it to Rava; after collecting rent for a year, Rav Mari offers the rent to Rava, explaining the standard mortgage term.
Rava replies that had he known of the mortgage he would not have bought the house, and he will not take rent until the gentile repays the loan.

items.text: Rava bar Nish's question about wine and interest
items.text_en: Rava bar Nish's question about wine and interest
items.desc_en: Rava bar Nish asked Rav Ashi about rabbis who appear to take interest by giving money for wine in Tishrei and selecting it in Tevet. Rav Ashi explained that they are paying for wine, not for the delay, as they choose from the wine at the time of selection.

sub.desc_en: Rava bar Nish asks Rav Ashi how the rabbis are permitted to give money for wine in Tishrei and select it in Tevet, which appears to be interest.
Rav Ashi answers that they are paying for the wine itself, not for the delay, because they choose the wine at the time of selection based on its current value.

items.text: Ravina's case with the date-growers and tax
items.text_en: Ravina's case with the date-growers and tax
items.desc_en: Ravina gave money to date-growers who poured extra dates for him. He asked Rav Ashi if this was permitted. Rav Ashi said yes, as they are waiving the extra. Ravina objected that the land is not theirs, but Rav Ashi explained that the land is liened for the tax, and the king says whoever pays the tax may eat from the land.

sub.desc_en: Ravina gave money to date-growers who poured extra dates for him.
Ravina came before Rav Ashi and asked if taking the extra dates is permitted.
Rav Ashi answered that it is permitted because the growers are waiving the extra dates.
Ravina objected that the land is not owned by the date-growers, so they cannot waive the extra dates.
Rav Ashi resolved that the land is liened for the tax, and the king's rule is that whoever pays the tax may eat from the land.

items.text: Rav Papa's question about tax collectors and interest
items.text_en: Rav Papa's question about tax collectors and interest
items.desc_en: Rav Papa asked Rava about rabbis who give money for people's tax and then collect extra. Rava initially declined to answer, then cited Rav Sheshet that the tax collectors' authority is from the king's document, and the king says whoever does not pay tax shall be enslaved to whoever pays it.

sub.desc_en: Rav Papa asks Rava about rabbis who give money for people's tax and then collect extra, implying it looks like interest.
Rava initially declines to answer, saying he will not discuss this matter while there is a dying person present.
Rava cites Rav Sheshet that the tax collectors' authority is from the king's document, and the king decrees that whoever does not pay tax shall be enslaved to whoever pays it.

items.text: Rav Se'orum's enforcement and the baraita
items.text_en: Rav Se'orum's enforcement and the baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Se'orum would seize people who did not behave properly and bring them to Rava's prison. Rava approved, citing a baraita that one may enslave someone who does not follow the proper path, but not one who does.

sub.desc_en: Rav Se'orum would seize people who did not behave properly and bring them to Rava's prison.
Rava approved, citing a baraita that one may enslave someone who does not follow the proper path, but not one who does.

items.text: Rav Hama's ruling on agency for wine and the debate
items.text_en: Rav Hama's ruling on agency for wine and the debate
items.desc_en: Rav Hama ruled that one who takes money to buy wine for another and fails to do so must compensate for the lost profit. Amemar qualified this to generic wine, but Rav Ashi rejected even that, calling it an asmachta that does not acquire. The Gemara questions Rav Ashi from a mishna about a contractor's penalty.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hama rules that one who takes money to buy wine for another and negligently fails to do so must compensate for the lost profit as if the wine were sold at the wholesale market of Zulshafat.

Amemar qualifies Rav Hama's ruling, stating it applies only to generic wine (יַיִן סְתָם), but not to a specific wine (יַיִן זֶה), since one cannot guarantee that the specific wine will be sold to him.
Rav Ashi rejects even Amemar's qualification, ruling that even generic wine is not compensable because the agreement is an אסמכתא (a conditional commitment that does not effect acquisition).
The Gemara questions Rav Ashi's position by citing a mishna that imposes a penalty on a contractor who fails to perform, suggesting that such commitments are binding despite being an אסמכתא.

items.text: Rava's ruling on joint agency for purchase
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on joint agency for purchase
items.desc_en: Rava rules that when three people give money to one person to buy something for them, and he buys for one of them, he buys for all of them, unless each one sealed his own money separately.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces the case: here, the money is not in his possession (i.e., the agent does not own it).
Rava rules that when three people give money to one agent to buy something, the purchase is for all unless each sealed his money separately.

items.text: The legal force of סיטומתא
items.text_en: The legal force of סיטומתא
items.desc_en: Rav Pappi reports in Rava's name that a customary mark (סיטומתא) effects acquisition. Rav Chaviva holds it effects actual acquisition, while the Rabbis hold it only obligates the seller to accept the curse of 'mi shepara'. The halakha follows the Rabbis, except where local custom treats it as actual acquisition.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappi reports in Rava's name that a customary mark (סיטומתא) effects acquisition.
The Gemara asks: for what halachic purpose does this acquisition apply?
Rav Chaviva holds that the mark effects actual acquisition (מקני ממש).
The Rabbis hold that the mark only obligates the seller to accept the curse of 'mi shepara' (מי שפרע).
The halakha follows the Rabbis (obligation to accept 'mi shepara'), except where local custom treats the mark as actual acquisition.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on fixing price for unprocessed produce
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on fixing price for unprocessed produce
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel dispute whether one may fix a price for produce that still requires processing. Rav distinguishes between two and three missing stages, while Shmuel distinguishes between human-dependent and heaven-dependent stages.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one was the first among the reapers, he may fix a price for produce.
Rav rules that if only two stages of processing are missing, one may fix a price; if three are missing, one may not.
Shmuel rules that if the missing stages depend on human action, even a hundred stages are permitted; if they depend on heaven, even one stage is forbidden.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's cases in light of Rav and Shmuel
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's cases in light of Rav and Shmuel
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines each case in the Mishnah where one may fix a price, showing how it aligns with Rav's and Shmuel's positions, often by explaining that the missing stages are performed by the seller or are not heaven-dependent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the Mishnah's case of fixing a price on the stack fits Rav's rule, since the grain still requires multiple heaven-dependent stages.
The Gemara answers that the case is where the grain has already been spread in the sun and dried.
The Gemara asks how the Mishnah's case fits Shmuel's position, since threshing (מִידְרֵא) is a heaven-dependent stage.
The Gemara answers that threshing can be done by winnowing (נָפְווֹתָא), which is a human action.
The Gemara asks how the Mishnah's case of the winepress vat fits, since it requires pressing, treading, and drawing off.
The Gemara cites Rabbi Chiyya's baraita that the Mishnah refers to the heap (כּוֹמֶר) of grapes, not the vat, reducing the missing stages.
The Gemara objects that even with the heap, three stages are still missing.
The Gemara answers that in a place where the buyer himself draws off the wine, that stage is not considered a missing step.
The Gemara asks how the Mishnah's case of the olive press fits, since it requires pressing, bringing to the press, treading, and drawing off.
The Gemara cites Rabbi Chiyya's baraita that the Mishnah refers to the heap of olives, not the press.
The Gemara objects that even with the heap, three stages are still missing.
The Gemara answers that in a place where the buyer himself draws off the oil, that stage is not counted.
The Gemara asks how the Mishnah's case of the potter's clods fits, since they require wrapping, drying, firing, and removing.
The Gemara answers that the case is where the clods are already wrapped and dried.
The Gemara objects that even so, three stages remain (firing, removing, and grinding).
The Gemara answers that in a place where the buyer himself removes the pottery from the kiln, that stage is not counted.
The Gemara asks how the Mishnah's case of lime fits, since it requires burning, removing, and grinding.
The Gemara answers that in a place where the buyer himself grinds the lime, that stage is not counted.
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies 'from when he sinks it in the kiln' according to Shmuel, who permits fixing a price even for many human-dependent stages.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah should be read as 'from when it is fit to sink it in the kiln', not after actual sinking.

items.text: Tosefta on potter's clay and Amemar's practice
items.text_en: Tosefta on potter's clay and Amemar's practice
items.desc_en: A Tosefta records a dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yossi about fixing a price for potter's clay. Amemar's practice of giving money when clay is brought is analyzed in light of this dispute, concluding that in his locale clay was scarce, so he relied on the delivery.

sub.desc_en: A Tosefta is cited: Rabbi Meir forbids fixing a price for potter's clay until the vessels are made, while Rabbi Yossi permits it for black clay because it is always available.
The gemara questions Amemar's practice of giving money when clay is brought, asking which Tanna he follows, since both positions seem to contradict his practice.
The gemara resolves that Amemar follows Rabbi Yossi, but in his locale clay was scarce (עֲשִׁיק עַפְרָא), so he only gives money when clay is actually delivered, otherwise his mind is not settled.

items.text: Beginning of discussion on fixing price for manure all year
items.text_en: Beginning of discussion on fixing price for manure all year
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states one may fix a price for manure all year. The Gemara begins to question why this is not redundant with the first Tanna, and Rava starts to answer.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may fix a price for manure all year long.
The Gemara asks why this ruling is not redundant with the first Tanna's statement.
Rava begins to answer the question, though the full answer is cut off at the section boundary.

items.text: Opening Mishnah excerpt
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah excerpt
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that during the rainy season there is a difference, and one may stipulate with him at the highest market rate.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that during the rainy season there is a difference between the market rate and the credit price, and one may stipulate with the seller at the highest market rate.

items.text: Rav Pappa's ruling on a dowry case
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's ruling on a dowry case
items.desc_en: A man gave money for his wife's dowry, and the value dropped. Rav Pappa rules that if he fixed the price at the highest rate, he takes according to the current value; if not, he takes according to the original value. The Rabbis object that money does not effect acquisition, so Rav Pappa clarifies he meant the 'Mi shePara' curse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a case: a man gave money for his wife's dowry, the value dropped, and the parties came before Rav Pappa.
Rav Pappa rules: if the man fixed the price at the highest rate, he takes according to the current value; if not, he takes according to the original value.
The Rabbis object: since money does not effect acquisition, how can the man take according to the original value?
Rav Pappa clarifies that he meant the 'Mi shePara' curse: if the seller backs out, he receives the curse; if the buyer backs out, he receives it.

items.text: Ravina's challenge: which Tanna is the Rabbis disagreeing with?
items.text_en: Ravina's challenge: which Tanna is the Rabbis disagreeing with?
items.desc_en: Ravina questions whether the Rabbis who disagree with Rabbi Shimon (who holds money acquires) are the same as those in the case. He suggests that if it is Rabbi Shimon's view, then the ruling would differ, but according to the Rabbis, the buyer's intention is always based on the current low price.

sub.desc_en: Ravina challenges Rav Pappa's assumption that the Rabbis who disagree with Rabbi Shimon are the ones behind the ruling, arguing that if it were Rabbi Shimon's view (that money acquires), the ruling would differ, but according to the Rabbis, the buyer's intention is always based on the current low price.

items.text: Rav Pappa's response: Rabbi Shimon's view limited to one market
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's response: Rabbi Shimon's view limited to one market
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa argues that Rabbi Shimon's principle (money acquires) applies only when there is one market price, but here there are two prices (high and low). He supports this by noting that otherwise Rabbi Shimon would have no 'Mi shePara' for a buyer, which contradicts a baraita.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa responds that Rabbi Shimon's principle (money acquires) applies only when there is one market price (חד תרעא), but here there are two prices (תרי תרעי), so Rabbi Shimon would not apply it.
Rav Pappa argues that if Rabbi Shimon applied his view to two prices, there would be no 'Mi shePara' (curse) for a buyer according to Rabbi Shimon, which contradicts a baraita.
The Gemara objects: perhaps indeed Rabbi Shimon has no 'Mi shePara' for a buyer, as a baraita states that in all cases the Sages instituted 'Mi shePara'.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita's phrase 'in any case' means both buyer and seller receive 'Mi shePara', but Rabbi Shimon's view is limited to one market price, not two.

items.text: Rav Acha's question and Rav Ashi's answer
items.text_en: Rav Acha's question and Rav Ashi's answer
items.desc_en: Rav Acha asks why the agent is not considered a messenger from the outset, and Rav Ashi answers that this case involves a merchant who buys and sells.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha asks Rav Ashi why the agent is not considered a messenger (שליח) from the outset, which would preclude any price fluctuation issue.
Rav Ashi answers that this case involves a merchant (תגרא) who buys and sells, so the agent is not a simple messenger but a party to the transaction.

items.text: Mishnah: lending wheat to sharecroppers for seed
items.text_en: Mishnah: lending wheat to sharecroppers for seed
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may lend wheat to sharecroppers for seed but not for food, and recounts Rabban Gamliel's practice of taking at the cheap rate even when prices changed, though not as law but as stringency.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may lend wheat to sharecroppers for seed but not for food, and recounts Rabban Gamliel's practice of taking at the cheap rate even when prices changed, though not as law but as stringency.

items.text: Gemara: dispute between Tanna of our Mishnah and external Tanna
items.text_en: Gemara: dispute between Tanna of our Mishnah and external Tanna
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a baraita that distinguishes between when the sharecropper has not yet descended (permitted) and when he has descended (forbidden). Rava explains the difference based on regional custom: in the Tanna of our Mishnah's place, the sharecropper provides seed, so he can always be dismissed; in the external Tanna's place, the landowner provides seed, so if the sharecropper has descended and cannot be dismissed, it is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that permits lending wheat for seed to a sharecropper only if he has not yet descended to work, but forbids it if he has descended.
The Gemara asks why the Tanna of our Mishnah does not distinguish between the sharecropper having descended or not, while the external Tanna does.
Rava, citing Rabbi Idi, explains that in the place of our Mishnah's Tanna, the sharecropper provides seed, so even after descending he can be dismissed, and the loan is permitted.
Rava concludes that in the external Tanna's place, the landowner provides seed, so if the sharecropper has descended and cannot be dismissed, the loan is forbidden.

items.text: Beginning of a new baraita
items.text_en: Beginning of a new baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita that begins 'A person may say to his fellow...'

sub.desc_en: The baraita begins with the rule that a person may say to his fellow.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's clarification
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's clarification
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one lends a kor of wheat and sets a price, but prices fall, the borrower gives wheat; if prices rise, he gives money. The Gemara questions this, and Rav Sheshet explains that the Mishnah refers to a case where no price was set.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: if one lends a kor of wheat and sets a price, the borrower gives wheat if prices fall, or money if prices rise.

items.text: Mishnah: Prohibition of lending with future delivery
items.text_en: Mishnah: Prohibition of lending with future delivery
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may not say 'Lend me a kor of wheat and I will give it to you at the threshing floor' due to interest concerns, but one may lend until a specific time. Hillel forbids even that, and similarly prohibits a woman from lending a loaf to her friend without setting a price.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may not say 'Lend me a kor of wheat and I will repay you at the threshing floor,' but may say 'Lend me until my son comes' or 'until I find the key'; Hillel forbids even that, and similarly forbids a woman lending a loaf to her friend without setting a price, lest prices rise and they come to ribbit (usury).
The Mishnah states the basic rule: one may not lend produce with future delivery at a fixed price, but may lend until a specific time.
Hillel forbids even lending until a specific time, and extends the prohibition to a woman lending a loaf to her friend without setting a price.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rabbi Yitzchak
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rabbi Yitzchak
items.desc_en: Rav Huna says one may only borrow a measure if he has that measure in his possession. Rabbi Yitzchak permits borrowing many korin even if he has only one se'ah. A baraita supports Rabbi Yitzchak, stating that if one has a drop of wine or oil, he may borrow many drops.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna states that one may only borrow a measure of grain if he has that same measure in his possession.
Rabbi Yitzchak permits borrowing many korin (large measures) even if one has only one se'ah (small measure) in his possession.
Rabbi Chiyya teaches a baraita supporting Rabbi Yitzchak: if one has no drop of wine or oil, he may not borrow; but if he has a drop, he may borrow many drops.

items.text: Halakhic ruling on Hillel's opinion
items.text_en: Halakhic ruling on Hillel's opinion
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman quotes Shmuel that the halakha follows Hillel's stringent view, but then states that the accepted halakha does not follow Hillel.

sub.text: Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman reports in Shmuel's name that the halacha (binding law) follows Hillel's stringent view, but then states that the final halacha does not follow him.
Rav Nachman reports in the name of Shmuel that the binding law (הלכה) follows Hillel's stringent opinion.
The Gemara concludes that the accepted halakha (הלכה) does not follow Hillel's view.

items.text: Dispute between Hillel and the Sages on women lending
items.text_en: Dispute between Hillel and the Sages on women lending
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel that Hillel forbids a woman from lending a loaf without setting a price, but the Sages permit lending and repaying without specifying a price.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in Shmuel's name that Hillel's ruling is his own view, but the Sages permit borrowing and repaying without specifying a price.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's statement on partners and interest
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's statement on partners and interest
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel that partners who are particular with each other violate several prohibitions, including lending and repaying on Yom Tov, and according to Hillel, also interest.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in Shmuel's name that members of a group who are exacting with each other violate several prohibitions, and according to Hillel also the prohibition of ribbit (usury).

items.text: Permissibility for Torah scholars to lend with interest
items.text_en: Permissibility for Torah scholars to lend with interest
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel that Torah scholars may lend to each other with interest, as they know it is forbidden and intend it as a gift. Shmuel himself borrowed peppers with interest from his father.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in Shmuel's name that Torah scholars are permitted to borrow from each other with ribbit (usury), because they know it is forbidden and intend it as a gift.
Shmuel himself asks Abahu bar Ihi to lend him 100 peppercorns for 120, demonstrating the practice.

items.text: Rav's ruling on lending to family with interest
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on lending to family with interest
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Rav that one may lend to his children and household with interest to teach them the taste of interest, but this is rejected because it may lead to becoming accustomed to it.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in Rav's name that one may lend to his sons and household members with ribbit (usury) to accustom them to the taste of ribbit.
The Gemara rejects this ruling, because it might lead to habitual sin.

items.text: Mishnah: Permitted and prohibited exchanges of labor
items.text_en: Mishnah: Permitted and prohibited exchanges of labor
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may say to another 'Weed with me and I will weed with you' or 'Hoe with me and I will hoe with you,' but not 'Weed with me and I will hoe with you' because that constitutes interest.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may say to another 'Weed with me and I will weed with you' or 'Hoe with me and I will hoe with you,' but may not say 'Weed with me and I will hoe with you' or 'Hoe with me and I will weed with you.'

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Types of interest and transgressors
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Types of interest and transgressors
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists forms of interest: interest for waiting (ribbit me'ucheret) and early interest (ribbit mukdemet), as well as verbal interest (ribbit devarim). It then lists those who violate the prohibition: lender, borrower, guarantor, witnesses, and according to the Sages, the scribe, citing multiple verses.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with a general rule about hiring workers for dry and rainy seasons.
Rabban Gamliel defines early interest (ribbit mukdemet) and late interest (ribbit me'ucheret) with examples.
Rabbi Shimon introduces the concept of verbal interest (ribbit devarim), forbidding speech that benefits the lender.
The Mishnah lists those who violate the prohibition against interest: lender, borrower, guarantor, witnesses, and according to the Sages, the scribe, citing multiple verses.

items.text: Gemara: Prohibition of greeting a debtor
items.text_en: Gemara: Prohibition of greeting a debtor
items.desc_en: A beraita cites Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, who derives from the verse 'neshekh kol davar asher yishakh' that even greeting a debtor is forbidden if one is not accustomed to doing so.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, who derives from the verse 'neshekh kol davar asher yishakh' that even greeting a debtor is forbidden if one is not accustomed to doing so.

items.text: Abaye's analysis of transgressions
items.text_en: Abaye's analysis of transgressions
items.desc_en: Abaye specifies which prohibitions each party violates: the lender violates all, the borrower violates 'lo tashikh' and 'lifnei iver', while the guarantor and witnesses only violate 'lo tasimun alav neshekh'.

sub.desc_en: Abaye opens by stating that the lender violates all the prohibitions.
Abaye specifies that the borrower violates 'לֹא תַשִּׁיךְ' (do not lend with interest) and 'לִפְנֵי עִוֵּר' (placing a stumbling block).
Abaye concludes that the guarantor and witnesses only violate 'לֹא תְשִׂימוּן עָלָיו נֶשֶׁךְ' (do not place interest upon him).

items.text: Beraita: Usurers' loss and heresy
items.text_en: Beraita: Usurers' loss and heresy
items.desc_en: A beraita of Rabbi Shimon states that usurers lose more than they gain and even cause people to call Moses a fool and his Torah false, claiming that if Moses knew there was profit, he would not have written the prohibition.

sub.desc_en: A beraita of Rabbi Shimon teaches that usurers lose more than they gain and even cause people to call Moses a fool and his Torah false, claiming that if Moses knew there was profit, he would not have written the prohibition.

items.text: Prohibition of passing before a debtor and the severity of lending without witnesses
items.text_en: Prohibition of passing before a debtor and the severity of lending without witnesses
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi teaches that one who knows a debtor cannot repay is forbidden to pass before him, derived from 'lo tiheyeh lo k'nosheh'. Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi add that such a lender is as if judged in two courts, citing a verse.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi teaches that one who knows a debtor cannot repay is forbidden to pass before him, derived from the verse 'לֹא תִהְיֶה לוֹ כְּנֹשֶׁה' (you shall not be to him as a creditor).

sub.text: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi's statement
sub.text_en: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi's statement
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi add that such a lender is as if judged in two courts, citing the verse 'הִרְכַּבְתָּ אֱנוֹשׁ לְרֹאשֵׁנוּ בָּאנוּ בָאֵשׁ וּבַמַּיִם' (You have caused men to ride over our heads; we went through fire and water).

items.text: Lending without witnesses and the story of Ravina
items.text_en: Lending without witnesses and the story of Ravina
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav says lending without witnesses violates 'lifnei iver', and Reish Lakish says it brings a curse. The Gemara recounts that Rav Ashi sent Ravina money to buy land, insisting on witnesses even for himself, lest he forget and cause a curse.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states that lending money without witnesses violates the prohibition of ולפני עור לא תתן מכשל (placing a stumbling block before the blind).
Reish Lakish adds that such a lender brings a curse upon himself, citing the verse 'תאלמנה שפתי שקר' (let the lying lips be silenced).

sub.text: Story of Rav Ashi and Ravina
sub.text_en: Story of Rav Ashi and Ravina
sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Rav Ashi sent Ravina money to buy land, insisting on witnesses and a document even for himself, lest he forget and bring a curse.

items.text: Three who cry out and are not answered
items.text_en: Three who cry out and are not answered
items.desc_en: A beraita lists three who cry out but are not answered: one who lends without witnesses, one who acquires a master for himself, and one whose wife rules over him. The Gemara explains 'acquires a master' as various cases: transferring assets to a gentile, writing property to children in his lifetime, or staying in a bad place.

sub.desc_en: The beraita lists three types of people who cry out but are not answered: one who lends without witnesses, one who acquires a master for himself, and one whose wife rules over him.
The Gemara asks: what does 'acquires a master for himself' mean?
Three explanations are given: transferring assets to a gentile, writing property to children in his lifetime, or staying in a bad place instead of moving elsewhere.

items.text: Mishnah: Hiring workers who renege
items.text_en: Mishnah: Hiring workers who renege
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if hired workers deceive each other, they have only a complaint. However, for lost items like bringing flutes to a wedding or funeral, or workers to raise flax, if there is no one else, the employer may hire others at their expense or deceive them. If workers renege, their hand is on the bottom (they lose).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that if hired workers deceive each other, they have only a complaint (תַּרְעוֹמֶת) against each other.

The Mishnah lists exceptions: for lost items like bringing flutes to a wedding or funeral, or workers to raise flax, if there is no one else, the employer may hire others at their expense or deceive them.
The Mishnah concludes that if workers renege, their hand is on the bottom (יָדָם עַל הַתַּחְתּוֹנָה), meaning they lose their wages or are paid the minimum.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the homeowner reneges, or if either party changes the terms, the reneging party is at a disadvantage.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the homeowner reneges or changes the terms, the reneging party is at a disadvantage.

items.text: Gemara's initial question and scenario
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question and scenario
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah says 'they misled each other' not 'they reneged', implying the workers misled each other. It posits a case where the homeowner told the agent to hire workers at four, but the agent told them three.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah says 'they misled each other' not 'they reneged', implying the workers misled each other, and posits a case where the homeowner told the agent to hire workers at four, but the agent told them three.

items.text: Analysis of possible scenarios
items.text_en: Analysis of possible scenarios
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers two scenarios: if the agent promised less than the homeowner said, the workers accepted willingly; if the agent promised more, the agent must pay the difference from his own pocket, as per a baraita about a worker hired for one field but shown another.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what are the circumstances? If the homeowner said four and the agent said three, the workers accepted willingly, so why would they complain?
The Gemara asks: if the homeowner said three and the agent said four, and the agent said 'your wages are on me,' he would pay from his own pocket, so why would they complain?
The Gemara cites a baraita: one who hires a worker for his own field but shows him another's field must pay the worker in full and then collect from the field owner only what the worker benefited.

items.text: Refinement of the case
items.text_en: Refinement of the case
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the case is where the agent said 'your wages are on the homeowner'. The workers complain that had they known the true wage, they would have worked harder or found better work.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the difficulty by specifying that the agent told the workers 'your wages are on the homeowner', so the agent is not personally liable.
The Gemara asks: why don't the workers just see the market rate and realize they were misled?
The Gemara answers that the market is not uniform: some workers hire for four and some for three, so the workers claim they would have exerted themselves for the higher wage.

items.text: Alternative explanations
items.text_en: Alternative explanations
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers two alternative explanations: one focusing on the homeowner's embarrassment, and another where the workers claim they would have done better work for the higher wage, but the quality of work is not easily assessed (e.g., in a leaky boat).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation that the case involves the homeowner's embarrassment (זילותא) if he hired at a lower wage.
The Gemara offers another alternative explanation that the workers claim they would have done better work for the higher wage, but the quality is not assessable (e.g., caulking a leaky boat).

items.text: Another scenario: agent underpromises
items.text_en: Another scenario: agent underpromises
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers the case where the homeowner said four and the agent said three; the workers might claim the agent violated the verse 'Do not withhold good from its owners' by not telling them the truth.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes an alternative scenario where the homeowner said four and the agent said three, and the workers might claim the agent violated the verse 'Do not withhold good from its owners' by not telling them the truth.

items.text: Question of reliance on the agent's word
items.text_en: Question of reliance on the agent's word
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: if the homeowner said three and the agent said four, and the workers say 'as the homeowner said', do they rely on the agent's word or the homeowner's?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the straightforward case: if the homeowner said three and the agent said four, and the workers say 'as the homeowner said', their intent is clearly to benefit the agent by reducing his payment.

The Gemara raises the dilemma: if the homeowner said four and the agent said three, and the workers say 'as the homeowner said', do they rely on the agent's word that he indeed said four, or do they rely directly on the homeowner's original statement?

items.text: Proof from a case of divorce
items.text_en: Proof from a case of divorce
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a proof from a case where a husband says 'bring my get' and the wife says 'accept my get', and the agent says 'here it is as she said'. Rav Nachman says she is not divorced even if the get reaches her hand, showing reliance on the agent's word.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a proof from a case of divorce: a husband says 'bring my get', the wife says 'accept my get', and the agent says 'here it is as she said'.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuh citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuh citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules in the name of Rav that even if the get reaches her hand, she is not divorced, showing the agent relies on the husband's words.
The Gemara infers from Rav Nachman's ruling that the agent relies on the husband's words, not the wife's, because if he relied on her words she would be divorced upon receipt.
Rav Ashi begins to speak, marking a shift in the discussion.

items.text: Gemara's initial objection and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's initial objection and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects to the baraita's ruling that workers who mislead the homeowner have only a complaint, citing a case where a husband says 'accept my get' and the wife says 'bring my get', and Rav Nachman rules she is divorced when the get reaches the husband's hand, relying on her words. The Gemara resolves that the case is different because the agent nullified his agency entirely.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the baraita's ruling contradicts a case where a husband says 'accept my get' and a wife says 'bring my get', and Rav Nachman rules the wife is divorced when the get reaches the husband's hand, relying on her words.
The Gemara resolves that the case there is different because the agent nullified his agency entirely, saying 'I am an agent for acceptance, not for delivery'.

items.text: Alternative answer: the tanna calls 'misled' also 'returned'
items.text_en: Alternative answer: the tanna calls 'misled' also 'returned'
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative answer: the tanna of the baraita also calls 'returned' (חזרו) as 'misled' (הטעו), citing a baraita where craftsmen mislead the homeowner or vice versa, and they have only a complaint.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative answer: the tanna of the baraita also calls 'returned' (חזרו) as 'misled' (הטעו), citing a baraita where craftsmen mislead the homeowner or vice versa, and they have only a complaint.

items.text: Baraita detailing when workers are paid fully
items.text_en: Baraita detailing when workers are paid fully
items.desc_en: The baraita specifies cases where workers who went and did not find work are paid in full, but not equally to those who worked. It discusses when they began work, the assessment of partial work, and the case of perishable goods where the homeowner can hire others or deceive them.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by distinguishing cases where workers did not go to work, and then states that if they went and found no work, they receive full pay, but not equal to those who worked.
The baraita distinguishes cases where workers began work, stating that they are assessed for what they did.
The baraita gives an example of how to assess partial work: if the work was worth six dinars, they receive a sela, or they may finish and receive two selas.
Rabbi Dosa argues that the assessment should be based on what remains to be done, with a different calculation.
The baraita states that for perishable goods, the homeowner may hire others or deceive the workers, with a limit on hiring costs.
The baraita concludes that if other workers are available, the homeowner has only a complaint against the original workers.

items.text: Rav's objection to the baraita's ruling
items.text_en: Rav's objection to the baraita's ruling
items.desc_en: A tanna taught before Rav that the homeowner gives them full wages. Rav objected, citing his teacher 'Chavivi' who would only give them the wage of a idle worker, and noted the baraita itself says one who comes laden is not like one who comes empty. The Gemara says the baraita was not completed before Rav.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna taught before Rav that the homeowner gives the workers full wages.
Rav objected, citing his teacher Chavivi who would only give them the wage of an idle worker.

sub.text: Rav's supporting evidence from the baraita
sub.text_en: Rav's supporting evidence from the baraita
sub.desc_en: Rav noted that the baraita itself distinguishes between one who comes laden and one who comes empty, implying only reduced wages.
The Gemara explains that the baraita was not completed before Rav, so the objection was based on an incomplete text.

items.text: Alternative version of Rav's objection
items.text_en: Alternative version of Rav's objection
items.desc_en: Some say the baraita was completed before Rav, and he said: Chavivi said I would give them nothing at all, and you say like an idle worker? But that is difficult.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces an alternative version: some say the baraita was completed before Rav, and he responded accordingly.
Rav, citing Chavivi, objects that he would give the workers nothing at all, not even the idle worker's wage.
Rav challenges the baraita: you say to pay like an idle worker, but Chavivi says nothing at all — so the baraita is difficult.

items.text: Resolution: distinction based on whether the field was irrigated
items.text_en: Resolution: distinction based on whether the field was irrigated
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction: one case where the field was irrigated from the previous night, the other where it was not. Rava illustrates: if one hired workers for hoeing and rain filled the field with water, if the field was irrigated from the previous night...

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a case where the field was irrigated from the previous night and one where it was not.
Rava illustrates the resolution with a case: if one hired workers for hoeing and rain filled the field with water, the ruling depends on whether the field was irrigated from the previous night.

items.text: Mishnah: Loss from workers vs. loss from homeowner
items.text_en: Mishnah: Loss from workers vs. loss from homeowner
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a worker's loss occurs (e.g., due to rain), it is the worker's loss, but if the homeowner did not fence his field, the loss is the homeowner's, and he pays the workers like idle workers.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: loss from workers is theirs, but if the homeowner did not fence his field, the loss is his and he pays them as idle workers.

items.text: Rava's three rulings on interrupted work
items.text_en: Rava's three rulings on interrupted work
items.desc_en: Rava gives three cases: (1) If rain comes, it's the workers' loss; if a river comes, it's the homeowner's loss. (2) If a river dries up mid-day, whether the loss is the workers' depends on whether it was foreseeable. (3) If work finishes early, the homeowner must give them work of equal or lesser difficulty, but not harder work, and pays full wages.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that if rain comes, the workers bear the loss; if a river comes, the homeowner bears the loss and pays them like idle workers.
Rava rules that if a river dries up mid-day, the loss falls on the workers unless the river's drying was foreseeable and the workers are locals, in which case the homeowner bears the loss.
Rava rules that if work finishes early, the homeowner must give them work of equal or lesser difficulty, but not harder work, and pays full wages.

items.text: Gemara's question and answer on Rava's third ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's question and answer on Rava's third ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rava requires full payment; why not pay them as idle workers? It answers that Rava spoke about the weak people of Mehoza, who would become ill if they didn't work.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rava requires full payment; why not pay them as idle workers (פועל בטל)?
The Gemara answers that Rava spoke about the weak people of Mehoza (אכלושי דמחוזא), who would become ill if they didn't work.

items.text: Rabbis' opinion: Appraise the work done
items.text_en: Rabbis' opinion: Appraise the work done
items.desc_en: The Rabbis hold that the worker's hand is on top, so if the work is worth six dinars, they get a sela (four dinars). The Gemara clarifies cases where the work became more expensive or cheaper, and what the parties can claim.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the Rabbis' opinion: they appraise the work done, and if it was worth six dinars, the employer gives them a sela (four dinars), because the worker's hand is on top.

The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needed to state the obvious case where the workers could finish the job and take two sela'im, and explains it is needed for a case where the work became more expensive and the employer appeased the workers.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah teaches that the employer can say he appeased them only with the intent of providing better food and drink, not to increase their wage.

The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needed to state the case where the work became cheaper and the employer gives a sela, and explains it is needed for a case where the work was originally cheap and they were hired for extra zuz, but later the work became expensive and stood at the extra zuz.
