The Gemara explains that the Mishnah teaches that the employer can say he promised the extra zuz only because the workers were unaware of the current market rate, but now that they know, they must accept the lower rate.

items.text: Rabbi Dosa's opinion: Appraise what will be done
items.text_en: Rabbi Dosa's opinion: Appraise what will be done
items.desc_en: Rabbi Dosa holds that the worker's hand is on the bottom, so if the work is worth six dinars, they get a shekel (two dinars). The Gemara clarifies cases where the work became cheaper or more expensive, and what the parties can claim.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Dosa states his opinion that the worker's hand is on the bottom, so if the work is worth six dinars they receive a shekel (two dinars).

The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needs to state the obvious case where workers complete the work and receive two selas, and explains it deals with a scenario where the work became cheaper and the employer tried to renegotiate.
The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah teaches that workers can respond to the employer's attempt to reduce wages by saying they intended to do high-quality work for the original wage.

The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needs to state the obvious case where the work is worth a sela and the employer pays a sela, and Rav Huna bar Rav Nathan explains it deals with a scenario where workers initially discounted their wages and then the work became cheaper.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Rav Nathan's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Nathan's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Nathan explains that the Mishnah teaches that workers can respond to the employer's attempt to further reduce wages by saying the initial discount was only because the market rate was not yet known.

items.text: Rav rules like Rabbi Dosa, with a contradiction
items.text_en: Rav rules like Rabbi Dosa, with a contradiction
items.desc_en: Rav rules like Rabbi Dosa, but the Gemara objects that Rav also said a worker can retract even mid-day, implying the worker's hand is on top. The Gemara begins to resolve this by distinguishing between hired labor and contract work, citing a baraita.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Dosa's position.
The Gemara objects that Rav elsewhere said a worker can retract even mid-day, which seems to contradict Rabbi Dosa's view that the worker's hand is on the bottom.
The Gemara proposes that Rabbi Dosa distinguishes between hired labor (שְׂכִירוּת) and contract work (קַבְּלָנוּת), but immediately questions whether he actually makes such a distinction.
The Gemara cites a baraita about a hired worker who hears of a death or is overcome by heat mid-day, which begins to address the distinction between hired and contracted workers.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a worker is hired as a day laborer, he receives his wages; if he is a contractor, he receives his contracting fee.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: a day laborer receives his wages, a contractor receives his contracting fee.

items.text: Gemara's identification of the Mishnah's author
items.text_en: Gemara's identification of the Mishnah's author
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions who authored the Mishnah. It suggests it cannot be the Rabbis, as they hold that the worker's hand is on top even without an unavoidable circumstance. It concludes it must be Rabbi Dosa, and then Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains the case is about a lost object.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who authored the Mishnah, suggesting it cannot be the Rabbis because they hold that the worker's hand is on top even without an unavoidable circumstance.
The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah must be Rabbi Dosa, and infers that for Rabbi Dosa there is no difference between a hired worker and a contractor.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the case involves a lost object, and all agree on the ruling.

items.text: Proof from the Mishnah about one who reneges
items.text_en: Proof from the Mishnah about one who reneges
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a proof from the Mishnah that states 'all who renege, their hand is on the bottom', and asks if this comes to include a worker according to Rabbi Dosa.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's rule that one who reneges is at a disadvantage and asks whether the phrase 'all who renege' comes to include a worker according to Rabbi Dosa.

items.text: Resolution: Rabbi Dosa said two things
items.text_en: Resolution: Rabbi Dosa said two things
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Dosa said two things, and Rav agrees with him on one and disagrees on the other.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Dosa said two things, and Rav agrees with him on one and disagrees on the other.

items.text: Alternative explanation: the case of selling a field
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: the case of selling a field
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation that the Mishnah's ruling about 'all who renege' refers to a case where one sold a field and gave partial payment, detailing the laws of who can renege and from what quality of land they collect.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an alternative explanation that the Mishnah's phrase 'all who renege' refers to a case where one sold a field and gave partial payment, citing a baraita that when the seller reneges the buyer has the upper hand.

The baraita details the options for the reneging party: the buyer can demand his money or land of equivalent value, collecting from the best land when the seller reneges, and the seller can return the money or give inferior land when the buyer reneges.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel teaches that the parties should be instructed not to renege by writing a document acknowledging the debt, which effects acquisition even after many years.

items.text: Discussion on the quality of land for collection
items.text_en: Discussion on the quality of land for collection
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the seller collects from the best quality land, and suggests it should be from intermediate land like a creditor. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains it means the best of that field, and Rav Acha bar Rav Ika says it is because the seller is like a damaged party who collects from the best.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the seller collects from the best quality land (עידית), arguing that he should be like a creditor who collects from intermediate land, and noting that the land itself was given for the money.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the reference is to the best quality within that specific field, not the seller's general property.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika argues that even if it means the seller's best land, the seller is like a damaged party (ניזק) who collects from the best, because a seller typically discounts his property.

items.text: Analysis of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statement and the law of earnest money
items.text_en: Analysis of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statement and the law of earnest money
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's requirement for a written document, and brings a baraita about earnest money where conditions are effective according to Rabbi Yossi. It distinguishes between cases where the buyer goes back and forth over the money and where he does not, citing Rava's principle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's requirement for a written document implies that without it, the buyer does not acquire the field.
The Gemara cites a baraita about earnest money where conditions are effective according to Rabbi Yossi, who holds that an אסמכתא (conditional commitment) is binding.
Rabbi Yehuda states that the buyer only acquires the portion corresponding to the earnest money given.

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel distinguishes between a case where the buyer says 'my earnest money shall acquire' (only the portion is acquired) and a standard sale with partial payment (the entire field is acquired, with the balance owed).

The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction between the baraita and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statement by distinguishing between cases where the buyer goes back and forth over the money (no acquisition) and where he does not (acquisition).
Rava states the general principle: if the buyer goes back and forth over the money, he does not acquire; if he does not, he acquires.

items.text: Rava's ruling on partial repayment and a case about a donkey
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on partial repayment and a case about a donkey
items.desc_en: Rava rules on partial repayment of a loan, and then a case is brought about a man who sold a donkey and was owed one zuz, with the buyer going back and forth. Rav Ashi deliberates, and Rav Mordechai reports from Avimi that one zuz is like many zuzim and the buyer does not acquire. Rav Acha bar Rav Yosef challenges this, and Rav Ashi suggests reconciling the conflicting reports.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that partial repayment of a loan is valid repayment, but the lender has a grievance (תַּרְעוֹמֶת) against the borrower for causing loss.
A case is brought about a man who sold a donkey and was owed one zuz, with the buyer going back and forth; Rav Ashi deliberates whether in such a case the buyer acquires or not.

sub.text: Rav Mordechai citing Avimi from Hagronya in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Mordechai citing Avimi from Hagronya in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Mordechai reports to Rav Ashi that Avimi from Hagronya said in the name of Rava that one zuz is like many zuzim (זוּזָא כְּזוּזֵי דָּמֵי) and the buyer does not acquire.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Yosef's challenge
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Yosef's challenge
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Yosef challenges Rav Ashi, noting that a conflicting report in the name of Rava says the buyer does acquire.
Rav Ashi suggests reconciling the conflicting reports by interpreting the lenient ruling as referring to a seller of a field (where the land is substantial), not a donkey.

items.text: Gemara's question on selling due to distress
items.text_en: Gemara's question on selling due to distress
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a seller who could have found a buyer at a lower price but didn't bother, and instead sold at a higher price while still seeking money, is considered a forced seller (like one selling his field because of its poor quality) or not. The question remains unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara poses an unresolved question (תיקו) about whether a seller who could have found a buyer at a lower price but didn't bother, and instead sold at a higher price while still seeking money, is considered a forced seller (like one selling his field because of its poor quality) or not.

items.text: Rav Nachman's ruling on hiring replacements
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling on hiring replacements
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a hired worker (e.g., a donkey driver or potter) reneges, the employer can hire others at the worker's expense. Rav Nachman limits this to the amount of the original worker's wages. Rava objects with a baraita that specifies up to forty or fifty zuz, and Rav Nachman explains that baraita refers to a case where the employer already has a package in hand.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a hired worker reneges, the employer may hire replacements at the worker's expense, and asks up to what amount.
Rav Nachman rules that the employer may hire replacements only up to the amount of the original worker's wages.
Rava objects by citing a baraita that specifies the employer may hire replacements up to forty or fifty zuz, not limited to the original wages.
Rav Nachman resolves the objection by explaining that the baraita refers to a case where the employer already has a package in hand, so the higher limit applies.

items.text: Mishnah: liability for deviating from the route
items.text_en: Mishnah: liability for deviating from the route
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases where a renter deviates from the agreed route (mountain vs. valley). If the donkey dies, the renter is liable even if the distances are equal. It then distinguishes between slipping and overheating, depending on the deviation.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases of hiring a donkey for mountain or valley travel, with liability rules for death or slipping depending on deviation from the agreed route.

items.text: Mishnah: cases of blinding or conscription
items.text_en: Mishnah: cases of blinding or conscription
items.desc_en: The Mishnah continues: if the donkey goes blind or is conscripted for royal service, the renter can say 'it is before you' and is exempt. But if it dies or breaks a limb, he must provide another donkey.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if a hired donkey becomes blind or is conscripted, the hirer may say 'here is yours before you,' but if it dies or breaks, the hirer must provide another donkey.

items.text: Gemara's question and answers on the Mishnah's distinction
items.text_en: Gemara's question and answers on the Mishnah's distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the first clause of the Mishnah (mountain/valley deviation) does not distinguish between slipping and overheating, while the second clause (blinding/conscription) does. The school of Rabbi Yannai answers that the first case involves death from the air (climate), so both are equally fatal. Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina says it's about a specific illness (ubtzana). Rabbah says it's about a snake bite. Rabbi Chiya bar Abba cites Rabbi Yochanan that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Meir, who holds that any deviation from the owner's intent imposes liability.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the first clause of the Mishnah (mountain/valley deviation) does not distinguish between slipping and overheating, while the second clause (blinding/conscription) does.
The school of Rabbi Yannai answers that the first case involves death from the air (climate), so both mountain and valley air are equally fatal.
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina says the first case is about death from a specific illness (אובצנא, a type of fever or inflammation).
Rabbah says the first case is about a snake bite, which is equally fatal regardless of terrain.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba cites Rabbi Yochanan that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Meir, who holds that any deviation from the owner's intent imposes liability.

items.text: The principle that deviating from the owner's intent is robbery
items.text_en: The principle that deviating from the owner's intent is robbery
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks to identify which Rabbi Meir holds that one who deviates from the owner's intent is called a robber. It considers three possible sources: the dyer (Mishnah), the Purim collection (baraita), and the case of a poor person given money for a specific garment. Each is rejected because of a distinguishing factor, until the Gemara concludes from the last source that the principle is indeed that one who deviates is called a robber.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with the principle that one who deviates from the owner's intent is called a robber.
The Gemara asks which Rabbi Meir holds this principle, first suggesting the dyer Mishnah where Rabbi Meir rules the dyer pays the wool's value.
Rabbi Yehuda offers a different ruling in the dyer case, based on the relative value of the improvement versus the expense.
The Gemara rejects the dyer case as a source, because there the dyer acquires the wool through a change in the object (שינוי מעשה).
The Gemara suggests the Purim collection baraita as another possible source for Rabbi Meir's principle.

sub.text: Rabbi Eliezer citing Rabbi Yaakov in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer citing Rabbi Yaakov in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer, citing Rabbi Yaakov in the name of Rabbi Meir, rules that Purim collection funds are restricted to Purim use, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel is lenient.
The Gemara rejects the Purim collection case because the donor gives specifically for Purim, not for any other purpose.
The Gemara suggests the baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar citing Rabbi Meir, where a poor person given a dinar for a specific garment may not buy a different one.
The Gemara objects that the poor person's restriction might be due to suspicion (חשד) that the poor person misappropriated the funds.
The Gemara concludes that since the baraita says 'because he deviates from the owner's intent' rather than 'because of suspicion', the principle is indeed that one who deviates is called a robber.

items.text: Clarifying the term 'הִבְרִיקָה'
items.text_en: Clarifying the term 'הִבְרִיקָה'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah uses the term 'וְהִבְרִיקָה' for a donkey that becomes incapacitated. The Gemara explains that in the West they translate it as 'נְהוֹרִיתָא' (lamp, i.e., a disease), while Rava says it means 'אַבְזְקָת' (a type of seizure). A story is told about a man who used this word in a dangerous context.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the meaning of the term 'וְהִבְרִיקָה' used in the Mishnah for a donkey that becomes incapacitated.
In the West (Eretz Yisrael) they translate 'וְהִבְרִיקָה' as 'נְהוֹרִיתָא' (lamp, a disease causing lameness).
Rava says the term means 'אַבְזְקָת' (a type of seizure or spasm).

A story is told about a man who used the word 'אַבְזְקָת' in a dangerous context regarding the king's robes, leading to his execution or release depending on whether he specified silver or gold plates.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on a donkey commandeered by the government
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on a donkey commandeered by the government
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a hired donkey is commandeered (אנגריא), the renter says 'here is yours before you' and is exempt. Rav limits this to a temporary conscription, but for a permanent one he must provide another donkey. Shmuel distinguishes based on whether the donkey was taken on the road or not. A baraita is brought that seems to contradict Shmuel, but he resolves it by aligning with Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's opinion or by emending the baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a hired donkey is commandeered (אנגריא), the renter says 'here is yours before you' and is exempt.
Rav limits the Mishnah's exemption to a temporary conscription (אנגריא חוזרת), but for a permanent one he must provide another donkey.
Shmuel distinguishes based on whether the donkey was taken on the road (בדרך הליכתה) or not, regardless of the conscription's permanence.
A baraita is brought that states if the donkey died or was commandeered (אנגריא), the renter is liable to provide another donkey, seemingly contradicting Shmuel.
The Gemara notes that the baraita does not contradict Rav (who distinguishes temporary vs. permanent), but it does contradict Shmuel.
The Gemara suggests that Shmuel could resolve the contradiction by distinguishing whether the donkey was taken on the road or not.
The Gemara objects that the baraita's continuation (Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's distinction) implies the first Tanna does not distinguish, so Shmuel's resolution fails.
Shmuel resolves the contradiction by aligning his opinion with Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's distinction.
Shmuel alternatively emends the baraita to say the entire text is Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's opinion, with the distinction inserted.

items.text: Opening baraita: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's ruling
items.text_en: Opening baraita: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's ruling
items.desc_en: The baraita states Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's opinion: if the donkey was taken while walking normally, the renter says 'yours is before you'; otherwise, he must provide another donkey.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's ruling: if the donkey was taken while walking normally, the renter says 'yours is before you'; otherwise, he must provide another donkey.

items.text: Gemara's challenge: contradiction with the mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge: contradiction with the mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the baraita can be attributed to Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, since the mishnah's first clause says the renter says 'yours is before you' for a donkey that becomes lame or insane, while Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar elsewhere requires providing another donkey in such cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the attribution of the baraita to Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar by citing the mishnah's first clause, which says the renter says 'yours is before you' for a lame or insane donkey, while Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar elsewhere requires providing another donkey in such cases.

items.text: Resolution: distinction for riding
items.text_en: Resolution: distinction for riding
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna distinguishes: renting for riding is different. Rav Pappa adds that glass vessels are like riding.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna resolves the contradiction by distinguishing that renting a donkey for riding is different from renting it for carrying goods.
Rav Pappa adds that glass vessels are analogous to riding, since they require careful handling and thus the same distinction applies.

items.text: Rav's ruling on partial rent and complaint
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on partial rent and complaint
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna quotes Rav: if a donkey rented for riding dies mid-journey, the renter pays half the rent and the owner has only a complaint. The Gemara questions this: if donkeys are available for rent, why only a complaint? If not, the owner should get full rent. The Gemara answers that it's a case where donkeys are not available, and the owner can say 'if you had wanted to come this far, wouldn't you have paid rent?'

sub.text: Rabbah bar Rav Huna citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna quotes Rav: if a donkey rented for riding dies mid-journey, the renter pays half the rent and the owner has only a complaint.
The Gemara questions the ruling: if donkeys are available for rent, why only a complaint? If not, the owner should get full rent.
The Gemara answers that it is a case where donkeys are not available, and the owner can say 'if you had wanted to come this far, wouldn't you have paid rent?'

items.text: Distinction between renting a specific donkey and a general donkey
items.text_en: Distinction between renting a specific donkey and a general donkey
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if he said 'a donkey' (unspecified), the owner must provide another donkey; if 'this donkey', and its carcass has value, he should buy another. The Gemara clarifies: it's when the carcass has insufficient value to buy, but enough to rent. Rav's view is that we do not deplete the principal (קרנא).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if he said 'a donkey' (unspecified), the owner must provide another donkey; if 'this donkey', and its carcass has value, he should buy another.
The Gemara clarifies: it's when the carcass has insufficient value to buy, but enough to rent; Rav's view is that we do not deplete the principal (קרנא).

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on using principal
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on using principal
items.desc_en: An amoraic dispute: if a rented donkey dies mid-journey, Rav says if the carcass can buy another, buy; if only to rent, do not rent. Shmuel says even rent. They disagree on whether we deplete the principal (קרנא).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the amoraic dispute: if a rented donkey dies mid-journey, Rav rules that if the carcass can buy another donkey, buy; if only to rent, do not rent; Shmuel rules that even renting is permitted.
The Gemara explains the dispute: Rav holds we do not deplete the principal (קרנא), while Shmuel holds we do deplete the principal.

items.text: Objection from a baraita about a tree and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita about a tree and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita about a tree that dried up or was cut: both are forbidden to use it, and one should buy land with its value and eat the produce. This seems to deplete the principal when the land returns at Jubilee. The Gemara resolves: it's a sale for sixty years (which does not return at Jubilee), or when Jubilee is not observed. Further, even if Jubilee is observed, the principal may not be depleted if the mortgage ends before Jubilee or the debtor redeems early.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita about a tree that dried up or was cut: both are forbidden to use it, and one should buy land with its value and eat the produce, which seems to deplete the principal when the land returns at Jubilee.

The Gemara answers that the baraita deals with a sale for sixty years, which does not return at Jubilee, citing Rav Chisda quoting Rav Katina's derivation from the verse 'וְהָאָרֶץ לֹא תִמָּכֵר לִצְמִיתוּת'.
The Gemara objects that even after sixty years the land returns to its owner, depleting the principal, and suggests that if Jubilee were observed, one could sell the wood and take the money.
The Gemara resolves that the objection is not difficult, because the mortgage may end before Jubilee or the debtor may redeem it early, so the principal is not necessarily depleted.

items.text: Baraita about a sunken ship and Rabbi Natan's ruling
items.text_en: Baraita about a sunken ship and Rabbi Natan's ruling
items.desc_en: A baraita: if a rented ship sinks mid-journey, Rabbi Natan says if the renter paid, he does not get a refund; if he didn't pay, he does not pay. The Gemara questions: if it's a specific ship and unspecified wine, why no refund? He could say 'give me a ship, I'll bring my wine.' If it's an unspecified ship and specific wine, why not pay?

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: if a rented ship sinks mid-journey, Rabbi Natan rules that if the renter paid he does not get a refund, and if he did not pay he does not pay.
The Gemara questions the baraita's logic: if it is a specific ship and unspecified wine, why no refund? And if it is an unspecified ship and specific wine, why no payment?

items.text: Gemara on the Mishnah's earlier case: returning a boat mid-journey
items.text_en: Gemara on the Mishnah's earlier case: returning a boat mid-journey
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa qualifies the Mishnah's case: the renter can demand the boat only if it is a specific boat with specific wine; but if both are unspecified, the loss is split.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the renter can demand the specific boat and wine from the owner.
Rav Pappa qualifies that this applies only when both boat and wine are specified; if both are unspecified, the loss is split.

items.text: Tosefta on returning a boat mid-route, and Gemara's analysis
items.text_en: Tosefta on returning a boat mid-route, and Gemara's analysis
items.desc_en: A baraita states that if a renter returns a boat mid-route, he pays only for half the journey and the owner has only a complaint. The Gemara questions this: if the owner can rehire it, why complaint? If not, he should pay full fare. The Gemara resolves that the complaint is over wear and tear of the boat; the renter's claim for loss of future earnings is not monetary.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: if a renter unloads a boat mid-journey, he pays half the rent and only has a complaint; the Gemara questions whether this applies when the owner can re-rent it.
The Gemara explains that even when the owner can re-rent, the complaint is valid due to wear and tear on the boat, which would be a monetary claim.
The Gemara reinterprets 'unloaded' as unloading the cargo, and the complaint is due to change of mind or to avoid extra expense.
The Gemara objects: if wear and tear is a valid claim, it should be a monetary claim, not just a complaint.

The Gemara resolves: 'פְּרָקָהּ' means the renter unloaded his cargo from the boat, and the complaint is over inconvenience (שִׁנּוּי דַּעְתָּא) or lost opportunity for extra profit (אַשְׁלָא יַתִּירָא).

items.text: Tosefta on donkey rental: what the rider and the donkey-driver may load
items.text_en: Tosefta on donkey rental: what the rider and the donkey-driver may load
items.desc_en: A baraita specifies that the rider may place his clothing, flask, and food for the journey; the donkey-driver may place barley, straw, and his own food for the day. The Gemara questions why the driver can restrict the rider's load when supplies are available. Rav Pappa answers that the distinction is based on who normally bothers to buy from shop to shop (the driver) versus who does not (the rider).

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: a renter of a donkey may load his clothing and provisions for the journey, but beyond that the donkey driver may object; the driver loads barley and straw for the day, beyond which the renter may object.
The Gemara questions the baraita: if provisions are available for purchase, why should either party object; if not, why should either be allowed to object?
Rav Pappa explains that the baraita refers to a case where provisions are available but require effort to buy from inn to inn; the driver is accustomed to such effort, but the renter is not.

items.text: Tosefta on who may ride a donkey hired for a man, and Abaye's inference
items.text_en: Tosefta on who may ride a donkey hired for a man, and Abaye's inference
items.desc_en: A baraita rules that a donkey hired for a man may not be ridden by a woman, but a donkey hired for a woman may be ridden by a man; and a woman, whether large, small, pregnant, or nursing, is allowed. The Gemara questions the redundancy of 'pregnant' and 'nursing'. Rav Pappa explains it means a woman who is both pregnant and nursing. Abaye infers that a daughter is heavier than her mother (i.e., pregnancy adds weight), with practical relevance for sales.

sub.desc_en: A baraita rules that a donkey hired for a man may not be ridden by a woman, but a donkey hired for a woman may be ridden by a man; and a woman, whether large, small, pregnant, or nursing, is allowed.
The Gemara questions the redundancy of listing both 'pregnant' and 'nursing' in the baraita.
Rav Pappa explains that the baraita refers to a woman who is both pregnant and nursing.
Abaye infers from the baraita that a daughter (fetus) is heavier than her mother (i.e., pregnancy adds weight), with practical relevance for sales.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: changing the terrain or crop
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: changing the terrain or crop
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one rents a cow to plow in the mountain and plows in the valley, and the plow breaks, he is exempt; if the reverse, he is liable. Similarly, if he rents to thresh legumes and threshes grain, he is exempt; if the reverse, he is liable because legumes are slippery.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents two pairs of cases: (a) renting a cow to plow on mountain vs. valley terrain, and (b) renting to thresh legumes vs. grain, stating the hirer's liability or exemption based on whether the change increased the risk.

items.text: Gemara: who pays for the breakage?
items.text_en: Gemara: who pays for the breakage?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who pays when the animal is not changed. Rav Pappa says the one holding the plow pays; Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi says the one holding the vessel pays. The halakha follows the latter, and if they hold a pair of gundrei, both pay.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who pays for breakage when the animal was not changed from the agreed task.
Rav Pappa says the one holding the plow pays.
Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi says the one holding the vessel pays.
The halakha is ruled in accordance with Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi that the vessel-holder pays.
If they hold a pair of gundrei (a double plow), both pay.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on sale with multiple defects
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on sale with multiple defects
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that if one sells an animal and lists many bad traits, but it has only one defect among them, it is a mistaken transaction. If it has that defect and another, it is not. A baraita supports this with a similar case of a maidservant.

sub.desc_en: רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) rules that if one sells a cow listing many defects but it has only one defect among them, it is a mistaken transaction; if it has that defect and another unspecified defect, it is not.
A ברייתא (baraita) supports this with a parallel case of selling a maidservant with multiple defects, applying the same distinction.

items.text: Rav Acha's question and Rava's answer
items.text_en: Rav Acha's question and Rava's answer
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava asks Rav Ashi: if the animal had all the listed defects, what is the law? Rav Mordechai reports in Rava's name that it is not a mistaken transaction.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava asks Rav Ashi: if the animal had all the listed defects, what is the law?

sub.text: Rav Mordechai's report in Rava's name
sub.text_en: Rav Mordechai's report in Rava's name
sub.desc_en: Rav Mordechai reports in Rava's name that if the animal had all the defects, it is not a mistaken transaction.

items.text: Second Mishnah: changing the load
items.text_en: Second Mishnah: changing the load
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one rents a donkey to bring wheat and brings barley, he is liable; if he brings straw instead of grain, he is liable because straw's bulk is as heavy as the load. If he rents for a letekh of wheat and brings a letekh of barley, he is exempt. If he adds to the load, he is liable. Sumchus says in Rabbi Meir's name: a se'ah for a camel, three kav for a donkey.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the laws of liability when a renter changes the load on a donkey, including the rule that straw's bulk is as heavy as the load, and Sumchus quotes Rabbi Meir's measure for additional load.

items.text: Abaye and Rava debate the Mishnah's wording
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava debate the Mishnah's wording
items.desc_en: Abaye says the Mishnah reads 'קָשֶׁה כְּמַשָּׂאוֹי' (hard as its load), meaning straw's bulk equals the weight, so adding three kav makes one liable. Rava says it reads 'קָשֶׁה לְמַשָּׂאוֹי' (hard for its load), meaning weight equals weight, and the bulk is an addition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between Abaye and Rava over the correct reading of the Mishnah's phrase regarding straw's bulk.
Abaye holds that the Mishnah reads 'קָשֶׁה כְּמַשָּׂאוֹי' (hard as its load), meaning straw's bulk equals the weight of grain, so adding three kav makes one liable.
Rava holds that the Mishnah reads 'קָשֶׁה לְמַשָּׂאוֹי' (hard for its load), meaning weight equals weight, and the bulk of straw is an addition that triggers liability.

items.text: Gemara's challenge and resolution on the addition
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge and resolution on the addition
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: does the Mishnah's 'if he added' mean three kav? It notes the explicit statement of Sumchus about a se'ah for a camel and three kav for a donkey. The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah refers to a case where the type is not changed, and Sumchus's measure applies there.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: from the Mishnah's statement that if one added to the load he is liable, does this not imply the addition is three kav?
The Gemara rejects this: no, the addition is a se'ah, not three kav.
The Gemara objects: but the Mishnah itself teaches that Sumchus says in the name of Rabbi Meir that the addition is a se'ah for a camel and three kav for a donkey.
The Gemara resolves: the Mishnah's statement about Sumchus's measure applies to a case where the type is not changed, e.g., wheat for wheat or barley for barley.

items.text: Incomplete continuation
items.text_en: Incomplete continuation
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins another challenge with 'תָּא שְׁמַע' but the text cuts off mid-sentence.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins to bring a supporting baraita as a challenge, but the text is cut off mid-sentence.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's measure
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's measure
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the Mishnah says sixteen barleycorns are liable, but three kavs are exempt. Abaye resolves this by explaining the case is about a hidden loss (מחיקתא).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points out a contradiction: the Mishnah imposes liability for a loss of sixteen barleycorns but exempts for three kavs, implying an inconsistency in the measure.
Abaye resolves the contradiction by explaining that the Mishnah's case involves a hidden loss (מחיקתא), where the measure is different.

items.text: Baraita on porter and ship loads, and Gemara's analysis
items.text_en: Baraita on porter and ship loads, and Gemara's analysis
items.desc_en: A baraita states standard loads: a kav for a porter, an adriv for a weaver, a kor for a ship, three korim for a large burani. The Gemara questions why a porter would not notice a kav's weight, and Abaye, Rava, and Rav Ashi offer explanations.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states standard loads: a kav for a porter, an adriv for a weaver, a kor for a ship, three korim for a large burani.
The Gemara questions why a porter would not notice the weight of a kav and simply discard it.
Abaye explains that the case is where the porter immediately beat the load onto his back, so he does not notice the extra weight.
Rava answers that even without immediate beating, the case involves extra wages, so the porter tolerates the extra weight.
Rav Ashi answers that the porter thinks the extra weight is due to his own weakness, so he does not realize it is an overload.

items.text: Rav Pappa's inference about ship capacity
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's inference about ship capacity
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa infers from the baraita that a standard ship holds thirty korim, and this is relevant for sales.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa infers from the baraita that an average ship holds thirty korim, and notes the practical implication for buying and selling (למקח וממכר).
The gemara asks what practical halachic difference this inference has.
The gemara answers that this inference is relevant for sales transactions involving ships.

items.text: Mishnah: Classification of guardians
items.text_en: Mishnah: Classification of guardians
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all craftsmen are paid guardians; if they say 'take yours and bring money' they become unpaid guardians; 'guard for me and I'll guard for you' is paid; 'guard for me' and 'leave before me' is unpaid; a lender on a pledge is a paid guardian; Rabbi Yehuda and Abba Shaul offer alternative views.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that all craftsmen are paid guardians, then lists cases where they become unpaid guardians.
The Mishnah continues with the rule that a lender on a pledge is a paid guardian, and records the alternative views of Rabbi Yehuda and Abba Shaul.

items.text: Gemara: Does the Mishnah align with Rabbi Meir?
items.text_en: Gemara: Does the Mishnah align with Rabbi Meir?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks if the Mishnah (which treats craftsmen as paid guardians) contradicts Rabbi Meir, who says a renter is like an unpaid guardian. It offers several answers: the craftsman benefits from being chosen over others, or from a small extra payment, or from not having to chase his fee. Alternatively, it cites a variant baraita where Rabbi Meir says a renter is a paid guardian.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah, which treats craftsmen as paid guardians (שומר שכר), contradicts Rabbi Meir, who rules that a renter (שוכר) is like an unpaid guardian (שומר חנם).
The Gemara answers that even according to Rabbi Meir, the craftsman is a paid guardian because he benefits from the craftsman being chosen over others (הנאה דקא שביק כולי עלמא ואגיר ליה לדידיה).
The Gemara objects that the same reasoning would apply to a renter (שוכר), who also benefits from being chosen, contradicting Rabbi Meir's own position.
The Gemara offers a second answer: the craftsman is a paid guardian because he receives a small extra payment (הנאה דקא יהיב ליה טפי פורתא) beyond the standard fee.
The Gemara objects that a renter also pays a small extra amount, so the same reasoning would apply to a renter.
The Gemara offers a third answer: the craftsman is a paid guardian because he benefits from not having to chase his fee (הנאה דתפיס ליה אאגריה, דלא בעי למיעל ולמיפק אזוזי).

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by citing a variant baraita transmitted by Rabba bar Avuh, where Rabbi Meir rules that a renter is a paid guardian (שומר שכר) and Rabbi Yehuda rules that he is an unpaid guardian (שומר חנם).

items.text: Gemara: 'Take yours and bring money' and the borrower's return
items.text_en: Gemara: 'Take yours and bring money' and the borrower's return
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a related teaching: if a borrower says 'send' and the animal dies, he is liable. Rafram bar Pappa says this only applies if returned within the loan period; after, he is exempt. Rav Nachman bar Pappa challenges this from the Mishnah's rule on 'take yours and bring money'.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of a parallel Mishnah
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of a parallel Mishnah
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a parallel Mishnah about a borrower who returns an animal and its liability status.
The Gemara cites a baraita about a borrower who says 'send' and the animal dies, establishing liability during the return.

sub.text: Rafram bar Pappa citing Rav Chisda
sub.text_en: Rafram bar Pappa citing Rav Chisda
sub.desc_en: Rafram bar Pappa citing Rav Chisda limits the liability to returns within the loan period; after the period, the borrower is exempt.

Rav Nachman bar Pappa challenges Rav Chisda's distinction by citing the Mishnah's rule that after 'take yours and bring money,' the watchman is an unpaid watchman, implying the borrower's liability continues.

items.text: Gemara's question on גמרתיו vs. טול את שלך
items.text_en: Gemara's question on גמרתיו vs. טול את שלך
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the phrase גמרתיו implies a paid guardian (שומר שכר) or unpaid guardian (שומר חנם). It argues that if גמרתיו were unpaid, the Mishnah should have taught it instead of טול את שלך, which is a more lenient case. The Gemara then explains that טול את שלך was necessary to counter a possible assumption that even unpaid status is lost.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the phrase גמרתיו (I have finished with it) implies a paid guardian (שומר שכר) or an unpaid guardian (שומר חנם), arguing that if it were unpaid, the Mishnah should have taught it instead of the more lenient case of טול את שלך (take yours).
The Gemara answers that the case of טול את שלך was necessary to counter a possible assumption that even unpaid guardian status is lost.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Pappa's alternative version
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Pappa's alternative version
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Pappa presents an alternative version of the discussion, asserting that the Mishnah's ruling on טול את שלך implies the same for גמרתיו. The Gemara rejects this, noting that טול את שלך is different.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Pappa cites a baraita supporting that the same rule applies to גמרתיו, but the Gemara rejects this, distinguishing the case of טול את שלך.
The Gemara rejects the inference, noting that the case of טול את שלך is different and does not extend to גמרתיו.

items.text: Huna Mar bar Marimar's contradiction and resolution
items.text_en: Huna Mar bar Marimar's contradiction and resolution
items.desc_en: Huna Mar bar Marimar raises a contradiction between the Mishnah (which implies גמרתיו is like טול את שלך) and a baraita about a borrower who returns the animal and it dies. Rafram bar Pappa in the name of Rav Chisda resolves: the baraita applies only if the return is within the loan period; after the period, the borrower is exempt.

sub.text: Huna Mar bar Marimar's challenge before Ravina
sub.text_en: Huna Mar bar Marimar's challenge before Ravina
sub.desc_en: Huna Mar bar Marimar raises a contradiction between the Mishnah and a baraita about a borrower who returns the animal, and Rafram bar Pappa in the name of Rav Chisda resolves it by distinguishing between returning within the loan period and after it.

sub.text: Rafram bar Pappa in the name of Rav Chisda's resolution
sub.text_en: Rafram bar Pappa in the name of Rav Chisda's resolution
sub.desc_en: Rafram bar Pappa in the name of Rav Chisda resolves the contradiction by distinguishing: the baraita's liability applies only if the return occurs within the loan period; after the loan period, the borrower is exempt.

items.text: Inquiry about the exempted borrower's status
items.text_en: Inquiry about the exempted borrower's status
items.desc_en: The Gemara inquires whether the borrower who returns the animal after the loan period is exempt from borrower liability but still liable as a paid guardian, or even exempt from that. Ameimar rules that he is liable as a paid guardian because he benefited from the loan.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether after the loan period the guardian is exempt from borrower liability but liable as a paid guardian, or even exempt from paid guardian status; Amemar rules he is liable as a paid guardian because he benefited from the use.
Ameimar rules that the borrower is liable as a paid guardian because he benefited from the loan.

items.text: Supporting baraita for Ameimar
items.text_en: Supporting baraita for Ameimar
items.desc_en: A baraita supports Ameimar: a person who takes utensils from a craftsman to send to his father-in-law, with an agreement to pay if accepted or pay for benefit if not, is liable for accidents on the way there but exempt on the return, because the return is like a paid guardian.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Amemar's ruling: one who takes vessels from a craftsman to send to his father-in-law is liable for accidents on the outward journey but exempt on the return, because the return is like a paid carrier.

items.text: Case of the donkey seller and Rav Nachman's ruling
items.text_en: Case of the donkey seller and Rav Nachman's ruling
items.desc_en: A man sold a donkey to another, agreeing to take it to a place to sell; if not sold, he would return it. The donkey was lost on the return. Rav Nachman held him liable. Rabba objected based on the baraita that return is exempt. Rav Nachman replied that this return is like the going, because the seller would have sold it if he found a buyer.

sub.text: Story of the donkey seller before Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Story of the donkey seller before Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: A man sold a donkey to his friend with an agreement to bring it to a certain place for sale; when it was not sold and was lost on the return, Rav Nachman held him liable.
Rabba objects to Rav Nachman's ruling, citing the baraita that on the return journey one is exempt because he is like a paid carrier.
Rav Nachman answers that this return is considered a going because if he had found a buyer on the way back, he would have sold it.

items.text: Reciprocal guardianship as paid guardians
items.text_en: Reciprocal guardianship as paid guardians
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that saying 'guard for me and I will guard for you' makes one a paid guardian. The Gemara questions why this is not considered guardianship with the owner (שמירה בבעלים). Rav Pappa explains it refers to guarding on different days. A baraita extends this to other reciprocal arrangements.

sub.text: Gemara's question on 'שמור לי ואשמור לך'
sub.text_en: Gemara's question on 'שמור לי ואשמור לך'
sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why 'guard for me and I will guard for you' makes one a paid guardian, since it seems to be a case of שמירה בבעלים (guardianship with the owner present), which normally exempts.
Rav Pappa answers that the case is where one says 'guard for me today and I will guard for you tomorrow,' so the owner is not present during the guarding period.
Rav Pappa explains that the Mishnah refers to guarding on different days, so the owner is not present during the guardianship.

items.text: Case of the bakers and Rav Pappa's ruling
items.text_en: Case of the bakers and Rav Pappa's ruling
items.desc_en: Bakers who took turns baking asked one to bake; he asked them to watch his cloak. They neglected it and it was stolen. Rav Pappa held them liable. The Rabbis objected that this is negligence with the owner (פשיעה בבעלים). Rav Pappa was embarrassed, but later it was revealed that the baker was drunk at the time, so it was not with the owner. The Gemara discusses the implications.

sub.desc_en: Introduces the case of bakers who took turns baking; one baker asked them to watch his cloak while he baked.
The bakers neglected the cloak and it was stolen; Rav Pappa held them liable.
The Rabbis objected that this is negligence with the owner (פשיעה בבעלים), and Rav Pappa was embarrassed.
It was later revealed that the baker was drunk at the time, so the case was not one of negligence with the owner.
The Gemara questions: according to the view that negligence with the owner exempts, the embarrassment is understandable, but according to the view that it obligates, why was Rav Pappa embarrassed?

The Gemara resolves: that day was not the baker's turn, so they asked him to bake for them, and he said 'for this wage that I bake for you, watch my cloak' — thus it was not a case of negligence with the owner.

items.text: Case of the donkey and the stolen load
items.text_en: Case of the donkey and the stolen load
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa initially holds the borrowers liable, but the rabbis point out that this is a case of shemirah biba'alim (the owner was with them at the time), causing Rav Pappa to be embarrassed. Later it is revealed that the owner was drunk, which may affect the ruling.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a case where a donkey was stolen while the borrowers were using it.
Rav Pappa initially rules that the borrowers are liable for the theft.
The rabbis object that this is a case of שמירה בבעלים (the owner was with them at the time), which exempts the borrowers.
Rav Pappa is embarrassed by the objection.
It is later revealed that the owner was drunk at the time, which may affect the ruling regarding שמירה בבעלים.

items.text: Case of the tall man and the short man
items.text_en: Case of the tall man and the short man
items.desc_en: A tall man riding a donkey and a short man walking exchange garments; the tall man's garment is swept away by the river. Rava holds the tall man liable, but the rabbis object that this is she'elah biba'alim (the owner was with him). Rava is embarrassed, but later it is revealed that the tall man took the garment without the short man's knowledge.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case: a tall man riding a donkey and a short man walking exchange garments, and the tall man's garment is swept away by the river.

Rava holds the tall man liable, but the rabbis object that this is שְׁאֵלָה בִּבְעָלִים (the owner was with him), causing Rava embarrassment; later it is revealed that the tall man took the garment without the short man's knowledge.

items.text: Case of the donkey hired with a route condition
items.text_en: Case of the donkey hired with a route condition
items.desc_en: A man hires out his donkey and instructs the hirer not to go via the river road. The hirer goes that way and the donkey dies, but claims there was no water. Rava says he could have simply lied and said he went the other way, so why admit to the forbidden route? Abaye objects that in the presence of witnesses, one does not say 'why lie'.

sub.desc_en: The narrator presents the case: a man hires out his donkey with a route condition, the hirer goes the forbidden route, the donkey dies, and the hirer admits to the route but claims there was no water.
Rava asks why the hirer would admit to the forbidden route when he could have simply lied and said he went the permitted route.
Abaye objects that in the presence of witnesses, the principle 'why lie' does not apply.

items.text: The status of 'hanach' without specification
items.text_en: The status of 'hanach' without specification
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one says 'shmor li' and the other says 'hanach lefanai', he is an unpaid bailee. Rav Huna adds that 'hanach lefanecha' makes him neither an unpaid nor a paid bailee. A question arises about 'hanach' without specification. The Gemara attempts to resolve it from the Mishnah but concludes it is inconclusive.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one says 'guard for me' and the other says 'place before me', he is an unpaid bailee.
Rav Huna adds that if one says 'place before you', he is neither an unpaid nor a paid bailee.
The Gemara asks about the status of 'hanach' without specification.
The Gemara attempts to resolve from the Mishnah that unspecified 'hanach' means nothing.
The Gemara objects that from Rav Huna's statement, unspecified 'hanach' might be an unpaid bailee.
The Gemara concludes that no definitive resolution can be derived from this source.

items.text: Comparison with the Tannaitic dispute about entering a courtyard
items.text_en: Comparison with the Tannaitic dispute about entering a courtyard
items.desc_en: The Gemara compares the case of 'hanach' to a dispute between the Rabbis and Rabbi Yehuda about one who brings an item into a homeowner's courtyard. The Rabbis hold the homeowner liable if he accepted responsibility, while Rabbi Yehuda says he is never liable unless he explicitly accepts. The Gemara explains that the cases differ because a courtyard is inherently guarded, whereas a public market is not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes comparing the case of 'הנח' (leave it) to a Tannaitic dispute about entering a courtyard, where the Rabbis hold the homeowner liable if he accepted responsibility, and Rabbi Yehuda says he is never liable unless he explicitly accepts.

The Gemara rejects the comparison, explaining that the Rabbis' position in the courtyard case is because a courtyard is inherently guarded (בת נטורי), so 'enter' implies acceptance of responsibility, whereas a public market (שוקא) is not guarded, so 'leave' means 'leave and guard yourself'.

The Gemara offers an alternative rejection: Rabbi Yehuda's position in the courtyard case is because entering requires permission, so granting permission is only for entry, not for guarding; but here, 'leave' implies 'leave and I will guard', since if it meant 'leave and guard yourself', the owner would need explicit permission to sit in the market.

items.text: The lender's liability for a pledged object
items.text_en: The lender's liability for a pledged object
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who lends money on a pledge is a paid bailee. The Gemara questions whether this aligns with Rabbi Eliezer's view that the lender can swear and collect his debt if the pledge is lost. Rabbi Akiva holds that the lender loses his money. The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction by distinguishing between a pledge taken at the time of the loan and one taken later.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who lends money on a pledge is a paid bailee (שומר שכר).
The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah contradicts Rabbi Eliezer's view that the lender can swear and collect his debt if the pledge is lost.

A baraita is cited: Rabbi Eliezer says the lender swears and collects; Rabbi Akiva says the lender loses his money if the pledge is lost, but if the pledge was given after the loan, all agree the money is lost.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a pledge taken at the time of the loan (where the Mishnah applies) and one taken later (where Rabbi Eliezer's ruling applies).

items.text: Initial contradiction and resolution
items.text_en: Initial contradiction and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction in the Mishnah: it first states that one who lends on a collateral is a paid guardian, but then implies a distinction between money and produce. The resolution is that the first clause refers to a loan of produce, while the second clause refers to a loan of money.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the Mishnah first states that one who lends on a collateral is a paid guardian, but the second clause implies a distinction between money and produce.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the first clause refers to a loan of produce, while the second clause refers to a loan of money.

items.text: Challenge and reworking of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Challenge and reworking of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the resolution by noting that Rabbi Yehuda's statement in the Mishnah explicitly distinguishes between money and produce, implying the first Tanna does not. It then reinterprets the entire Mishnah as Rabbi Yehuda's view, with a missing clause: the first part applies to produce, and Rabbi Yehuda adds his own distinction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous resolution by noting that the Mishnah's explicit distinction between money and produce in Rabbi Yehuda's statement implies the first Tanna does not distinguish between them.
The Gemara reinterprets the entire Mishnah as Rabbi Yehuda's view, with a missing clause: the first part applies to produce, and Rabbi Yehuda adds his own distinction.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah is not in accordance with Rabbi Akiva, but rather with Rabbi Eliezer, based on the distinction between money and produce.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah is not in accordance with Rabbi Akiva, but rather with Rabbi Eliezer, based on the distinction between money and produce.

items.text: First explanation: dispute over Shmuel's principle
items.text_en: First explanation: dispute over Shmuel's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the dispute is about a collateral worth less than the loan, and whether Shmuel's ruling applies: if the collateral is lost, the debt is lost.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the dispute in the Mishnah concerns a collateral worth less than the loan, and revolves around Shmuel's principle.
The Gemara cites Shmuel's ruling that if a borrower gave a collateral worth less than the loan, the loss of the collateral cancels the entire debt.

items.text: Second explanation: dispute over Rabbi Yitzchak's principle
items.text_en: Second explanation: dispute over Rabbi Yitzchak's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the first explanation, positing that all agree with Shmuel when the collateral is insufficient. Instead, the dispute is when the collateral is worth the loan amount, and revolves around Rabbi Yitzchak's principle that a creditor acquires the collateral.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the dispute in the Mishnah is not about Shmuel's principle, but about Rabbi Yitzchak's principle when the collateral is worth the loan amount.
Rabbi Yitzchak cites a verse to prove that a creditor acquires the collateral (קנה משכון).

items.text: Refinement and final explanation: dispute over guardian of a lost object
items.text_en: Refinement and final explanation: dispute over guardian of a lost object
items.desc_en: The Gemara refines the second explanation: Rabbi Yitzchak's principle applies only to a collateral taken after the loan, not at the time of the loan. All agree on that. The dispute here is about a collateral taken at the time of the loan, and it parallels the dispute between Rabbah and Rav Yosef regarding the status of a finder-guardian.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the application of Rabbi Yitzchak's principle, noting that he only spoke of a collateral taken after the loan, not at the time of the loan.

The Gemara resolves that all agree on Rabbi Yitzchak's principle for collateral taken after the loan; the dispute here concerns collateral taken at the time of the loan, which parallels the dispute between Rabbah and Rav Yosef regarding the status of a finder-guardian (שומר אבדה).

items.text: Conclusion: the dispute is not about the finder-guardian
items.text_en: Conclusion: the dispute is not about the finder-guardian
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the dispute is not about the finder-guardian, as all agree with Rav Yosef that a finder-guardian is a paid guardian. The actual dispute remains unresolved in this segment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the suggestion that Rav Yosef's view is disputed by Tanna'im, concluding that all agree with Rav Yosef regarding the finder-guardian, and the actual dispute remains unresolved.

items.text: Dispute over the lender's status as a paid or unpaid bailee
items.text_en: Dispute over the lender's status as a paid or unpaid bailee
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the underlying dispute between the two opinions in the Mishnah: one holds that lending is a mitzvah, making the lender a paid bailee; the other holds that the lender acts for his own benefit, making him an unpaid bailee.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's dispute about the lender's status as a paid or unpaid bailee hinges on whether lending is a mitzvah (commandment) or done for the lender's own benefit.

items.text: Abba Shaul's ruling on renting out a poor man's collateral
items.text_en: Abba Shaul's ruling on renting out a poor man's collateral
items.desc_en: Abba Shaul permits renting out a poor man's collateral, with the rental reducing the debt. Rav Chanan bar Ami cites Shmuel that the halakha follows Abba Shaul, but only for tools like a pickaxe and ax whose rental is high and depreciation low.

sub.desc_en: Abba Shaul rules that one may rent out a poor man's collateral, with the rental reducing the debt.

sub.text: Rav Chanan bar Ami citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Chanan bar Ami citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Chanan bar Ami reports in the name of Shmuel that the binding law (הלכה) follows Abba Shaul.
The gemara qualifies that Abba Shaul's leniency applies only to tools like a pickaxe and ax, whose rental fee is high and depreciation low.

items.text: Mishnah: Porter who breaks a barrel
items.text_en: Mishnah: Porter who breaks a barrel
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a porter breaks a barrel while moving it, both a paid and unpaid bailee swear (that they were not negligent). Rabbi Eliezer says both swear, but he wonders if they can indeed swear.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that if a porter breaks a barrel while moving it, both a paid and unpaid bailee swear they were not negligent.
Rabbi Eliezer agrees that both swear, but expresses doubt whether they can indeed swear.

items.text: Baraita with three opinions
items.text_en: Baraita with three opinions
items.desc_en: A baraita presents the dispute: Rabbi Meir says both swear; Rabbi Yehuda says an unpaid bailee swears but a paid bailee pays; Rabbi Eliezer says both swear but he doubts they can.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with Rabbi Meir's position: both an unpaid bailee (שומר חנם) and a paid bailee (שומר שכר) who break a barrel while moving it swear they were not negligent.
Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes: the unpaid bailee swears he was not negligent, but the paid bailee must pay compensation.
Rabbi Eliezer agrees with Rabbi Meir that both swear, but expresses doubt whether they can legitimately take such an oath.

items.text: Contradiction from another baraita on stumbling
items.text_en: Contradiction from another baraita on stumbling
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Meir holds that stumbling is not negligence, citing a baraita where Rabbi Meir obligates payment for damages from a fallen jug or camel, while the Sages exempt. The Gemara notes it is established that they dispute about stumbling as negligence.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Meir holds that stumbling is not negligence, based on the baraita where he obligates payment for a broken jug or fallen camel.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Meir obligates payment for damages from a fallen jug or camel, while the Sages exempt, indicating a dispute about stumbling as negligence.
The Gemara resolves that it is established that Rabbi Meir and the Sages dispute whether stumbling is considered negligence.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's resolution: different versions of the baraita
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's resolution: different versions of the baraita
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar resolves the contradiction by saying the baraita is broken: the one who taught this (the first baraita) did not teach that (the second). Rabbi Yehuda's opinion is that each bailee follows his own law; Rabbi Eliezer agrees with Rabbi Meir's ruling but doubts the oath's feasibility.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar resolves the contradiction by asserting that the baraita is broken: the one who taught the first version did not teach the second.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar explains that Rabbi Yehuda's position is that each bailee follows his own standard law: the unpaid bailee swears, the paid bailee pays.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar's explanation of Rabbi Eliezer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's explanation of Rabbi Eliezer
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar explains that Rabbi Eliezer agrees with Rabbi Meir's ruling in principle but expresses doubt whether both bailees can actually swear.

items.text: Gemara's difficulty: why would a paid bailee swear?
items.text_en: Gemara's difficulty: why would a paid bailee swear?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a paid bailee would swear, as even without negligence he must pay. It also questions the unpaid bailee's oath in a non-dangerous place, where he cannot claim no negligence.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: it is understandable that an unpaid bailee swears he was not negligent, but why does a paid bailee swear, since even without negligence he must pay?
The Gemara further asks: even regarding the unpaid bailee, if the accident occurred in a non-dangerous place, how can he swear he was not negligent?

items.text: Gemara's question on the oath and R' Yochanan's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the oath and R' Yochanan's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a bailee must swear if there are witnesses, citing Isi ben Yehuda's teaching that if there is a witness, the bailee brings proof and is exempt. R' Yochanan explains that this oath is a rabbinic enactment to encourage people to handle barrels for others.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a bailee must swear if there are witnesses, citing Isi ben Yehuda's teaching that if there is a witness, the bailee brings proof and is exempt.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that this oath is a rabbinic enactment to encourage people to handle barrels for others.

items.text: Rava's formulation of the oath and opinions of Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar
items.text_en: Rava's formulation of the oath and opinions of Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar
items.desc_en: Rava states the oath is 'that I did not break it intentionally.' Rabbi Yehuda says the unpaid bailee swears and the paid bailee pays, each according to their law. Rabbi Elazar agrees the ruling follows Rabbi Meir but doubts both can swear.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the bailee swears in this case.
Rava formulates the oath as 'that I did not break it intentionally.'
Rabbi Yehuda states that each bailee follows his standard law: the unpaid bailee swears and the paid bailee pays.
Rabbi Elazar agrees the ruling follows Rabbi Meir but doubts both bailees can swear.

items.text: Gemara's objection and resolution with Isi ben Yehuda
items.text_en: Gemara's objection and resolution with Isi ben Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: the unpaid bailee swears he did not neglect, but the paid bailee must pay even without negligence; even the unpaid bailee's oath only applies in a place of stumbling, but where there are witnesses, he should bring proof. It cites Isi ben Yehuda's teaching that if there is a witness, the bailee brings proof and is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the mishnah's oath for the paid bailee and the unpaid bailee in a non-stumbling place, and where witnesses exist.

sub.text: Supporting baraita of Isi ben Yehuda
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita of Isi ben Yehuda
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Isi ben Yehuda's baraita that if there is a witness, the bailee brings proof and is exempt.

items.text: First story: barrel broken in Mahoza
items.text_en: First story: barrel broken in Mahoza
items.desc_en: A man broke a barrel on a projection in Mahoza. Rava told him to bring proof and be exempt, as people are common there. Rav Yosef asked if this follows Isi, and Rava confirmed.

sub.desc_en: A man was carrying a barrel of wine in the marketplace of Mahoza and broke it on a projection.
Rava told the man to bring proof that he was not negligent and he would be exempt, because the marketplace is frequented by people.
Rav Yosef asked Rava whether his ruling follows the opinion of Isi ben Yehuda.
Rava confirmed that his ruling follows Isi, and that they hold like him.

items.text: Second story: barrels that turned sour
items.text_en: Second story: barrels that turned sour
items.desc_en: A man bought 400 barrels of wine for another, which turned sour. Rava told him to bring proof the wine was good originally. Rav Yosef asked if this follows Isi, and Rava confirmed.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a story: a man told his friend to buy 400 barrels of wine, which later turned sour.
Rava rules that since the souring of 400 barrels is a well-known event, the agent must bring proof the wine was originally good to be exempt.
Rav Yosef asks Rava whether this ruling follows the opinion of Isi ben Yehuda.
Rava confirms that the ruling is indeed in accordance with Isi, and that they hold like him.

items.text: Rav Chiyya bar Yosef's enactment for porters
items.text_en: Rav Chiyya bar Yosef's enactment for porters
items.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Yosef enacted in Sikra: if porters carrying on their shoulders break a barrel, they pay half, as it is close to accident and negligence; if carrying on a pole, they pay full.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Yosef enacted in Sikra that porters carrying on their shoulders who break a barrel pay half, as it is close to accident and negligence, while those carrying on a pole pay full.

items.text: Story of Rabba bar bar Chanan and the porters
items.text_en: Story of Rabba bar bar Chanan and the porters
items.desc_en: Porters broke Rabba bar bar Chanan's barrel; he took their cloaks. Rav told him to return them, citing 'walk in the way of good men.' The porters then complained of hunger, and Rav told Rabba to pay their wages, citing 'keep the paths of the righteous.'

sub.desc_en: Porters broke Rabba bar bar Chanan's barrel of wine, and he took their cloaks as compensation.
The porters came and complained to Rav about Rabba bar bar Chanan taking their cloaks.
Rav ordered Rabba to return the cloaks, citing the verse 'walk in the way of good men' (Proverbs 2:20).
Rabba questioned whether the law required returning the cloaks, but complied after Rav's answer.
The porters complained to Rav that they were poor, had worked all day, were hungry, and had nothing.
Rav ordered Rabba to pay the porters their wages, citing the verse 'keep the paths of the righteous' (Proverbs 2:20).

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chanan's second objection
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chanan's second objection
sub.desc_en: Rabba again questioned whether the law required paying wages, and Rav affirmed it with the same verse.

items.text: Mishnah: Hiring workers and local customs
items.text_en: Mishnah: Hiring workers and local customs
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one hires workers and stipulates early or late work, he cannot force them against local custom. Local custom determines food and sweets. A story about Rabbi Yochanan ben Matya's son who promised meals; his father said even a feast like Solomon's is insufficient, and he should stipulate only bread and legumes. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says all follows local custom.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule that hiring workers follows local custom regarding start and end times, food, and sweets.

sub.text: Story about Rabbi Yochanan ben Matya
sub.text_en: Story about Rabbi Yochanan ben Matya
sub.desc_en: A story illustrates that even a lavish meal does not fulfill the obligation to workers unless a stipulation is made before work begins.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel disagrees, stating that all follows local custom without need for explicit stipulation.

items.text: Gemara's clarification and Resh Lakish's statement
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification and Resh Lakish's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Mishnah's case: if the employer added to their wages, one might think the extra was for early work, but the workers say it was for quality work. Resh Lakish begins a statement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah's case is necessary, since it seems obvious.
The Gemara explains the case: the employer added to their wages, so one might think the extra was for early and late work.
The Gemara rejects that possibility, teaching that the workers can claim the extra was for quality work.
Resh Lakish begins a statement that continues beyond the section.

items.text: Opening baraita: worker's bread
items.text_en: Opening baraita: worker's bread
items.desc_en: The baraita teaches that a worker eats from his own bread when entering the field, but from the homeowner's when leaving, citing the verse about sunset and sunrise.

items.text: Gemara's question and answer about the baraita
items.text_en: Gemara's question and answer about the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how to determine the custom in a new city or for workers from elsewhere, and answers that the employer can stipulate they are hired as Torah-defined workers.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's allegorical derasha on Psalms
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's allegorical derasha on Psalms
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira (or some say Rav Yosef) interprets the verses about night and day as allegories for the righteous and wicked, their rewards and punishments in the world to come.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon confronts a police chief
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon confronts a police chief
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon finds a police chief arresting thieves and questions him, citing verses that compare thieves to wild animals, warning that he might catch the righteous and leave the wicked.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's advice on identifying thieves
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's advice on identifying thieves
items.desc_en: The police chief asks what to do, and Rabbi Elazar advises him to go to the tavern at the fourth hour and observe: if a man is a Torah scholar who fell asleep, he woke early to study; if a worker, he started work early; otherwise, he is a thief and should be arrested.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar appointed as thief-catcher; Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha's rebuke
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar appointed as thief-catcher; Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha's rebuke
items.desc_en: The matter reaches the king, who appoints Rabbi Elazar as the police chief. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha sends him a message calling him 'vinegar son of wine' and rebukes him for handing over God's people to execution.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's response and the incident with the laundryman
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's response and the incident with the laundryman
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar replies that he is removing thorns from the vineyard; Rabbi Yehoshua retorts that the vineyard owner should remove them. Later, a laundryman insults Rabbi Elazar, who orders his arrest.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's regret and the revelation of the laundryman's guilt
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's regret and the revelation of the laundryman's guilt
items.desc_en: After calming down, Rabbi Elazar tries to free the laundryman but cannot. He quotes a verse about guarding one's mouth. The laundryman is hanged, and Rabbi Elazar weeps beneath the gallows, but is told the man and his son committed a grave sin.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's joy in his intestines
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's joy in his intestines
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar places his hand on his intestines and expresses joy, confident that since they were involved in doubtful matters (like his rulings), they will surely be preserved from decay in certain ones.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's autopsy and the miraculous preservation of his fat
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's autopsy and the miraculous preservation of his fat
items.desc_en: Despite his joy, he is not fully appeased, so they give him a sleeping potion, bring him to a marble house, and cut open his abdomen, removing baskets of fat that do not putrefy even in summer, fulfilling the verse 'my flesh shall dwell in safety'.

items.text: Transition to Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Transition to Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: The narrative begins to shift to a similar story about Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei, indicating a parallel account.

items.text: Elijah's advice to Rabbi Yishmael
items.text_en: Elijah's advice to Rabbi Yishmael
items.desc_en: Elijah rebukes Rabbi Yishmael for handing over Jews to the Romans, and advises him to flee to Lodkiya.

sub.desc_en: Elijah encounters Rabbi Yishmael and rebukes him for handing over Jews to execution.
Rabbi Yishmael responds that he is compelled by royal decree.
Elijah advises Rabbi Yishmael to flee to Lodkiya, just as his father fled to Asia.

items.text: The matron's accusation and the rabbis' response
items.text_en: The matron's accusation and the rabbis' response
items.desc_en: A matron accuses Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Elazar of having children who are not theirs, due to their extreme beauty. They respond with verses, and the Gemara explains why they answered her at all.

sub.desc_en: Describes the extraordinary beauty of Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Elazar, such that a bullock could pass between them without touching them.
A matron accuses the two rabbis that their children are not theirs, implying their wives were unfaithful due to their beauty.
The rabbis respond that the matron's husband's desire is greater than theirs, so her children are even more likely not to be her husband's.

sub.text: Alternative answer of the rabbis (first version)
sub.text_en: Alternative answer of the rabbis (first version)
sub.desc_en: An alternative tradition records that the rabbis cited the verse 'כי כאיש גבורתו' (for his strength is as a man's) to explain their self-control.

sub.text: Alternative answer of the rabbis (second version)
sub.text_en: Alternative answer of the rabbis (second version)
sub.desc_en: Another alternative tradition records that the rabbis cited the verse 'אהבה דוחקת את הבשר' (love presses the flesh) to explain their self-control.
The Gemara asks why the rabbis bothered to respond to the matron at all, given the verse 'אל תען כסיל כאולתו' (answer not a fool according to his folly).
The Gemara answers that they responded in order not to bring a bad reputation upon their children.

items.text: The size of the rabbis' limbs
items.text_en: The size of the rabbis' limbs
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rav Papa describe the size of their own and others' limbs, comparing them to wine skins.
