sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that Rabbi Yishmael's limb was the size of a nine-kav wine skin.
Rav Papa reports that Rabbi Yochanan's limb was the size of a five-kav or three-kav wine skin.
Rav Papa describes his own limb as being like the beams of the Harpanaei.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's beauty and the comparison to Jacob
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's beauty and the comparison to Jacob
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan describes his own beauty as a remnant of the beautiful people of Jerusalem. The Gemara questions why he is not included in the chain of beauty from Adam to Rav Kahana, and answers that he lacked facial radiance.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan declares himself a remnant of the beautiful people of Jerusalem and describes his beauty with a vivid simile of a silver cup filled with pomegranate seeds.
The Gemara objects: why is Rabbi Yochanan not included in the chain of beauty from Adam to Rav Kahana?
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yochanan is excluded because he lacked facial radiance (הדרת פנים).

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan at the bathhouse and the evil eye
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan at the bathhouse and the evil eye
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan sits at the entrance to the bathhouse so that women will see him and bear beautiful, Torah-learned children. When the rabbis express concern about the evil eye, he explains that he is from the tribe of Joseph, which is immune to it.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan sits at the entrance to the bathhouse so that women who see him will bear beautiful, Torah-learned children.
The rabbis ask Rabbi Yochanan whether he is not afraid of the evil eye.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that he is from the tribe of Joseph, which is immune to the evil eye, citing the verse 'בן פורת יוסף בן פורת עלי עין' and Rabbi Abahu's homiletic reading.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's supporting proof
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's supporting proof
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina adds a supporting proof from the verse 'וידגו לרב בקרב הארץ', comparing Joseph's descendants to fish that are covered by water and immune to the evil eye.

items.text: The meeting of Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish
items.text_en: The meeting of Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish jumps into the Jordan after Rabbi Yochanan, who is impressed by his strength. Rabbi Yochanan offers his sister in marriage if Resh Lakish will return to Torah study. Resh Lakish agrees, becomes a great scholar, but later they argue about the point at which metal vessels become susceptible to impurity, leading to a bitter exchange.

sub.desc_en: The narrative opens with Rabbi Yochanan bathing in the Jordan; Resh Lakish jumps in after him, and Rabbi Yochanan offers his sister in marriage if Resh Lakish returns to Torah study; Resh Lakish accepts but cannot retrieve his clothes.
Rabbi Yochanan teaches Resh Lakish Torah and makes him a great man; they later argue in the study hall about when metal vessels become susceptible to impurity.
The Gemara asks when the manufacturing process is complete; Rabbi Yochanan answers 'when they are fired in the furnace,' and Resh Lakish answers 'when they are polished with water.'

Rabbi Yochanan insults Resh Lakish, saying 'a bandit knows his banditry'; Resh Lakish retorts that Rabbi Yochanan has not benefited him, and Rabbi Yochanan responds that he brought him under the wings of the Shechinah.

items.text: The death of Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan's grief
items.text_en: The death of Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan's grief
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan is upset, Resh Lakish falls ill and dies. Rabbi Yochanan grieves deeply, tearing his clothes. The rabbis send Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat to comfort him, but he fails to engage in the same dialectical style as Resh Lakish, causing Rabbi Yochanan to despair further until he too dies.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan becomes upset, Resh Lakish falls ill, and his sister pleads with Rabbi Yochanan to relent for the sake of her children.
Rabbi Yochanan refuses her pleas, citing verses that God will care for the orphans and widows.
Resh Lakish dies, Rabbi Yochanan grieves deeply, and the rabbis send Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat to comfort him.
Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat merely cites supporting baraitot, and Rabbi Yochanan objects that this lacks the dialectical challenge of Resh Lakish.
Rabbi Yochanan tears his clothes, weeps, and cries out for Resh Lakish until his mind departs, and the rabbis pray for him and he dies.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's suffering and his wife's care
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's suffering and his wife's care
items.desc_en: Despite his greatness, Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon accepted suffering upon himself. Each night, sixty mattresses were prepared for him, and in the morning, sixty basins of blood and pus were removed. His wife prepared sixty types of food for him, which he ate and recovered, and she prevented him from going to the study hall to avoid the rabbis troubling him.

sub.desc_en: Despite his greatness, Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon accepted suffering upon himself, and each night sixty mattresses were prepared for him with sixty basins of blood and pus removed in the morning.
His wife prepared sixty types of food for him daily, which he ate and recovered, and she prevented him from going to the study hall to avoid the rabbis troubling him.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's routine and his wife's departure
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's routine and his wife's departure
items.desc_en: At night, Rabbi Elazar would invite the rabbis, saying 'Come,' and in the morning he would send them away to avoid neglect of Torah. His wife, angered that he was wasting her father's wealth, left him and returned to her family. Later, sixty sailors brought him sixty servants with sixty purses, and he ate sixty types of food. His daughter visited him, and he sent a message to his wife that his provision was greater than theirs, quoting a verse.

sub.desc_en: The narrative describes Rabbi Elazar's routine: at night he invited the rabbis to study, and in the morning he sent them away to prevent neglect of Torah.
Rabbi Elazar's wife, hearing his invitation, rebukes him for wasting her father's wealth by hosting the rabbis.
The narrative reports that his wife became angry and left him to return to her family.
Sixty sailors arrive and bring Rabbi Elazar sixty servants with sixty purses, who prepare sixty types of food for him.

Rabbi Elazar's daughter visits him, and he sends a message to his wife that his provision is greater than theirs, quoting the verse 'הָיְתָה כָּאֳנִיּוֹת סוֹחֵר מִמֶּרְחָק תָּבִיא לַחְמָהּ' (She is like merchant ships, from afar she brings her bread).

items.text: Rabbi Elazar purifies blood and the rabbis' test
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar purifies blood and the rabbis' test
items.desc_en: Sixty types of blood were brought before Rabbi Elazar, and he declared them all pure. The rabbis murmured, doubting that none were doubtful. He responded with a test: if he was like them, all the children born from these women would be males; if not, one would be a female. All were males, and they were named 'Rabbi Elazar' after him.

sub.desc_en: Sixty types of blood were brought before Rabbi Elazar, and he declared them all pure.
The rabbis murmured, doubting that none of the blood samples were doubtful.
Rabbi Elazar proposed a test: if he was like them, all children born from these women would be males; if not, one would be a female.
All the children were males, and they were named 'Rabbi Elazar' after him.

items.text: Rabbi's comment on the proliferation
items.text_en: Rabbi's comment on the proliferation
items.desc_en: Rabbi (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi) remarked: How much fruitfulness and multiplication did this wicked woman (Rabbi Elazar's wife) cause to cease from Israel?

sub.desc_en: A baraita records Rabbi's lament that Rabbi Elazar's wife caused a great loss of fruitfulness and multiplication in Israel.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's death and burial instructions
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's death and burial instructions
items.desc_en: On his deathbed, Rabbi Elazar instructed his wife not to fear the rabbis and to place him in the upper chamber. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani reported that his mother heard from Rabbi Elazar's wife that he lay there for 18 to 22 years. When she would inspect his hair, a louse would cause blood to flow. Once she saw a worm coming from his ear and was distressed, but he appeared in a dream and said it was because he once heard a Torah scholar insulted and did not protest properly.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar on his deathbed instructs his wife not to fear the rabbis and to place him in the upper chamber.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani reports through Rabbi Yonatan's mother that Rabbi Elazar's wife said he lay in the upper chamber for 18 to 22 years.
When she would inspect his hair, a louse would cause blood to flow.
She saw a worm coming from his ear and was distressed, but he appeared in a dream explaining it was because he once heard a Torah scholar insulted and did not protest properly.

items.text: Posthumous judgment and the dispute over burial
items.text_en: Posthumous judgment and the dispute over burial
items.desc_en: When two litigants came to court, they would stand at the entrance, and a voice from the upper chamber would declare the verdict. Once his wife argued with a neighbor and said she should be like her husband who was not buried. The rabbis said this was improper. Some say Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai appeared in a dream, saying he had a precious pearl among them and they should bring it to him. The rabbis went to attend to him, but the people of Akhbarya prevented them because during Rabbi Elazar's lifetime no wild beast came to their town.

sub.desc_en: The gemara describes the posthumous judgment procedure: litigants stand at the entrance, and a voice from the upper chamber declares the verdict.
The gemara relates an incident where Rabbi Elazar's wife, in a quarrel with a neighbor, cursed her to be like her husband who was not buried.
The rabbis declare that such a statement is certainly improper behavior.

sub.text: Alternative tradition: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's dream
sub.text_en: Alternative tradition: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's dream
sub.desc_en: Some say Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai appeared in a dream, saying he had a precious pearl among them and they should bring it to him.
The people of Akhbarya prevented the rabbis from attending to Rabbi Elazar's burial, because during his lifetime no wild beast came to their town.

items.text: Burial in his father's cave and Rabbi's marriage proposal
items.text_en: Burial in his father's cave and Rabbi's marriage proposal
items.desc_en: On Yom Kippur eve, when the townspeople were busy, the rabbis sent people from Biri to bring his bier to his father's cave. A snake was guarding the entrance, but it opened when commanded. Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi) sent to his wife to propose marriage. She replied: Should a vessel used for holy purposes be used for profane? The local saying was: Where the master hung his weapons, the dog hangs his leash. He argued that he was greater in Torah, but she responded that he accepted suffering, implying his merit was greater.

sub.desc_en: On Yom Kippur eve, when the townspeople were busy, the rabbis sent men from Biri to bring Rabbi Elazar's bier to his father's cave.
A snake guarding the entrance was commanded to open and it opened, allowing the son to enter his father's cave.
Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi) sent messengers to Rabbi Elazar's widow to propose marriage, and she replied that a vessel used for holy purposes should not be used for profane.
A local saying is cited: Where the master hung his weapons, the dog hangs his leash.
Rabbi argued that although Rabbi Elazar was greater in Torah, perhaps he himself was greater in good deeds.
The widow replied that she did not know about Torah, but she knew that Rabbi Elazar accepted suffering, implying his merit was greater.

items.text: The dispute over seating and Rabbi Elazar's superiority
items.text_en: The dispute over seating and Rabbi Elazar's superiority
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Torah greatness: When Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha sat on benches, Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi sat on the ground. They would ask and answer, and the elders said they were drinking from them while they sat on the ground. Benches were made for them. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel said he had a precious pearl among them and they were trying to destroy it, so Rabbi was lowered. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha argued that one with a father should live and one without should die, so Rabbi Elazar was also lowered. Rabbi was upset, and from then on, Rabbi Elazar would contradict Rabbi's statements. Rabbi complained to his father, who consoled him that Rabbi Elazar was a lion son of a lion, while he was a lion son of a fox. This is why Rabbi said there were three humble ones: his father, etc.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Torah greatness Rabbi Elazar had, describing the seating arrangement where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha sat on benches while Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi sat on the ground.
The elders, who were learning from the two on the ground, protested that they were drinking from them while they sat on the ground, so benches were made and they were raised up.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel objected that Rabbi was a precious pearl among them and they were trying to destroy it, so Rabbi was lowered back to the ground.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha argued that one with a father should live and one without should die, so Rabbi Elazar was also lowered to the ground.
Rabbi was upset that Rabbi Elazar was considered his equal.
Until that day Rabbi Elazar supported Rabbi's statements, but afterward he contradicted Rabbi, saying his answers were bundles of empty responses.
Rabbi complained to his father, who consoled him that Rabbi Elazar was a lion son of a lion, while Rabbi was a lion son of a fox.
Rabbi concluded that this is why he said there were three humble ones, beginning with his father.

items.text: Opening discussion on humility and the examples of Bnei Beteira and Yonatan ben Shaul
items.text_en: Opening discussion on humility and the examples of Bnei Beteira and Yonatan ben Shaul
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the actions of Bnei Beteira (who appointed Hillel as Nasi) and Yonatan ben Shaul (who offered to be David's second-in-command) were motivated by humility or by recognition of superiority. It concludes that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel was certainly humble.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the examples of Bnei Beteira and Yonatan ben Shaul as potential cases of humility.
The Gemara questions whether these actions were truly humble or merely pragmatic recognition of superiority.
The Gemara concludes that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel was certainly humble, unlike the ambiguous cases.

items.text: The suffering of Rabbi and Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: The suffering of Rabbi and Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: Rabbi declares that afflictions are precious and accepts thirteen years of suffering. The Gemara contrasts his suffering with that of Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon, noting that Rabbi's suffering came and went due to specific events involving a calf and kittens, while Rabbi Elazar's suffering was purely out of love.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi declares that afflictions are precious and accepts thirteen years of suffering, alternating between two types of ailments.
The Gemara digresses to describe the extraordinary wealth of Rabbi's mule-driver and the loud noise of feeding animals, which was timed to Rabbi's bathroom visits.
The Gemara contrasts Rabbi's suffering with that of Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon, noting that Rabbi's came and went due to specific events, while Rabbi Elazar's was purely out of love.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi's suffering began because he showed no mercy to a calf seeking refuge, leading the heavenly court to decree afflictions upon him.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi's suffering ended because he showed mercy to kittens, leading the heavenly court to remove his afflictions.

items.text: The effects of their suffering on the world
items.text_en: The effects of their suffering on the world
items.desc_en: During Rabbi Elazar's years of suffering, no one died prematurely; during Rabbi's years, the world did not need rain. The Gemara explains the severity of rain and how the sages would pray to cancel it if not needed, yet even so, a well of water would appear when a radish was uprooted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that during Rabbi Elazar's years of suffering, no one died prematurely.
The Gemara adds that during Rabbi's years of suffering, the world did not need rain.
Rabbah bar Rav Sheila states that a day of rain is as severe as a day of judgment.
Ameimar adds that if the world does not need rain, the rabbis would pray and cancel it.
The Gemara concludes that despite the severity of rain, during Rabbi's years a well of water would appear when a radish was uprooted, showing the abundance of water.

items.text: Rabbi visits Rabbi Elazar's town and encounters his son
items.text_en: Rabbi visits Rabbi Elazar's town and encounters his son
items.desc_en: Rabbi asks about Rabbi Elazar's son, finds him, and ordains him. The son initially shows humility but later sits in Rabbi's study hall. After his death, a snake prevents his burial in his father's cave until a heavenly voice explains that the father suffered in a cave while the son did not.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi visits Rabbi Elazar's town and asks the townspeople whether the righteous man has a son.
The townspeople answer that he has a son, and add a proverb about the son's promiscuity.
Rabbi brings the son, ordains him, and entrusts him to his maternal uncle Rabbi Shimon ben Isi ben Lakonya.
The son initially feigns humility by saying he is going to his village, but later sits in Rabbi's study hall, and Rabbi recognizes his voice as similar to his father's.
A heavenly voice explains that the snake prevented burial not because one is greater, but because the father suffered in a cave while the son did not.

items.text: Rabbi visits Rabbi Tarfon's town and deals with his grandson
items.text_en: Rabbi visits Rabbi Tarfon's town and deals with his grandson
items.desc_en: Rabbi asks about Rabbi Tarfon's descendants, learns he has a granddaughter who is promiscuous, and convinces her to repent by offering her his daughter in marriage. There is a dispute about whether he married her or not, to avoid suspicion.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi visits Rabbi Tarfon's town and asks if he has a son, learning he has only a promiscuous granddaughter.
Rabbi brings the granddaughter, offers her his daughter in marriage if she repents, and she repents; there is a dispute whether he actually married her or not to avoid suspicion.

items.text: The reward for teaching Torah
items.text_en: The reward for teaching Torah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites teachings about the great reward for teaching Torah to a colleague's son and especially to an ignoramus's son, who can annul divine decrees. It further states that a chain of Torah scholars ensures Torah never ceases from their descendants, with God guaranteeing this promise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi went to such lengths to find a son for Rabbi Elazar ben Shimon, and introduces the teaching about the reward for teaching Torah.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda citing Rav / alternative attributions
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav / alternative attributions
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a teaching that one who teaches Torah to a colleague's son merits sitting in the heavenly academy, and one who teaches an ignoramus's son can annul divine decrees.
Rabbi Parnach teaches in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that a chain of three generations of Torah scholars ensures Torah never ceases from their descendants.
The Gemara explains that God guarantees the promise of Torah continuity, and Rabbi Yirmeya concludes that from that point Torah seeks its own lodging.

items.text: Rav Yosef and Rabbi Zeira's fasts for Torah continuity and protection
items.text_en: Rav Yosef and Rabbi Zeira's fasts for Torah continuity and protection
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef fasts forty days repeatedly until he is assured that Torah will not depart from his mouth, his son's mouth, and his grandson's mouth. Rabbi Zeira fasts three hundred fasts to forget Babylonian Talmud, avoid communal burdens, and be saved from Gehinnom, and tests himself with fire.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef fasts three sets of forty days, each time receiving a divine assurance that Torah will not depart from his mouth, his son's mouth, and his grandson's mouth, concluding that Torah now seeks its own lodging.

Rabbi Zeira fasts three hundred fasts: one hundred to forget the Babylonian Talmud so as not to be burdened by communal responsibilities, one hundred to avoid Rabbi Elazar's death overtaking him, and one hundred to be saved from the fire of Gehinnom.

Rabbi Zeira tests himself every thirty days by sitting in a heated oven without being burned, until once the rabbis cast an eye on him and his legs were singed, earning him the nickname 'short one with singed legs'.

items.text: Beginning of a new teaching on the destruction of the land
items.text_en: Beginning of a new teaching on the destruction of the land
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav begins a new discussion on the verse 'Who is the wise man who can understand this... why the land was destroyed,' but the daf cuts off before the explanation.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav opens a new discussion by citing the verse 'Who is the wise man who can understand this... why the land was destroyed,' but the daf cuts off before providing the explanation.

items.text: Opening statement on the sages and prophets who did not explain
items.text_en: Opening statement on the sages and prophets who did not explain
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a statement that sages and prophets did not explain a certain matter until God Himself explained it, quoting a verse. Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav interprets this as referring to the failure to recite a blessing over the Torah before study.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that sages and prophets did not explain a certain matter until God Himself explained it, citing a verse.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav interprets the verse as referring to the failure to recite a blessing over the Torah before study.

items.text: Rabbi Chama and Ulla on wisdom and lineage
items.text_en: Rabbi Chama and Ulla on wisdom and lineage
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chama interprets a verse about wisdom resting in the heart of a discerning person, applying it to a Torah scholar who is the son of a Torah scholar versus one who is the son of an ignoramus. Ulla adds a folk saying about a jar that makes noise.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chama interprets the verse 'בְּלֵב נָבוֹן תָּנוּחַ חָכְמָה וּבְקֶרֶב כְּסִילִים תִּוָּדֵעַ' (In the heart of the discerning wisdom rests, and among fools it becomes known), applying the first clause to a Torah scholar who is the son of a Torah scholar and the second to a Torah scholar who is the son of an ignoramus.
Ulla adds a folk saying: 'אִסְתֵּירָא בְּלָגִינָא קִישׁ קִישׁ קָרְיָא' (A jar that is empty makes noise), illustrating that a Torah scholar from humble origins is more vocal about his wisdom.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya and Rabbi Zeira on humility and Torah
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya and Rabbi Zeira on humility and Torah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira about a verse that seems redundant, and explains that it teaches: one who humbles himself over Torah in this world becomes great in the World to Come, and one who makes himself like a slave over Torah becomes free in the World to Come.

sub.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's question to Rabbi Zeira
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's question to Rabbi Zeira
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira about the apparent redundancy in the verse 'קָטֹן וְגָדוֹל שָׁם הוּא וְעֶבֶד חׇפְשִׁי מֵאֲדֹנָיו' (small and great are there, and the slave is free from his master).

Rabbi Yirmeya explains that the verse teaches: one who humbles himself over words of Torah in this world becomes great in the World to Come, and one who makes himself like a slave over Torah becomes free in the World to Come.

items.text: Reish Lakish's encounter with Rabbi Chiya's cave
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's encounter with Rabbi Chiya's cave
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish, while marking the caves of the rabbis, could not find Rabbi Chiya's cave and was distressed. A heavenly voice told him that while he had debated Torah like Rabbi Chiya, he had not disseminated Torah like him.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish was marking the caves of the rabbis, but when he reached Rabbi Chiya's cave it was hidden from him.
Reish Lakish was distressed and complained to God that he had debated Torah like Rabbi Chiya.
A heavenly voice responded that while he had debated Torah like Rabbi Chiya, he had not disseminated Torah like him.

items.text: Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Chiya's dispute over preserving Torah
items.text_en: Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Chiya's dispute over preserving Torah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Chiya argue about who is greater. Rabbi Chanina claims he could restore Torah through his pilpul if lost, while Rabbi Chiya describes his systematic method of teaching Torah to children to ensure it is never forgotten.

sub.desc_en: The narrator sets the scene: Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Chiya were arguing.
Rabbi Chanina asserts that if Torah were forgotten from Israel, he could restore it through his pilpul (dialectical reasoning).
Rabbi Chiya counters that his own systematic method of teaching Torah to children ensures it will never be forgotten from Israel.

items.text: Rabbi's praise of Rabbi Chiya's deeds
items.text_en: Rabbi's praise of Rabbi Chiya's deeds
items.desc_en: Rabbi declares how great Rabbi Chiya's deeds are. Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei asks if they are greater even than his own, and Rabbi affirms, but when asked if greater than his father's, Rabbi recoils.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi declares how great Rabbi Chiya's deeds are.
Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei asks Rabbi whether Rabbi Chiya's deeds are greater even than his own.
Rabbi affirms that Rabbi Chiya's deeds are greater than his own.
Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei asks whether Rabbi Chiya's deeds are greater even than Rabbi's father's deeds.
Rabbi recoils and rejects the comparison, saying such a thing should never be said in Israel.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's dream about the chain of tradition
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's dream about the chain of tradition
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira relates a dream in which he saw Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina, who told him the chain of tradition from Rabbi Yochanan back to Rabbi Chiya. When asked why Rabbi Yochanan did not study directly under Rabbi Chiya, he replied that in a place of fiery sparks, a blacksmith's son cannot enter.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira opens by relating a dream in which he saw Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's response
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's response
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina lists the chain of tradition from Rabbi Yochanan back to Rabbi Chiya.
Rabbi Zeira asks why Rabbi Yochanan did not study directly under Rabbi Chiya.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's answer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's answer
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina explains that in a place of fiery sparks and burning coals, a blacksmith's son (Rabbi Yochanan) cannot enter.

items.text: Story of the rabbi who saw the heavenly academy
items.text_en: Story of the rabbi who saw the heavenly academy
items.desc_en: Rav Chaviva bar Surmakei tells of a rabbi who was visited by Eliyahu and whose eyes were damaged from looking at Rabbi Chiya's aura in the heavenly academy. He was healed after prostrating at Rabbi Chiya's cave and reciting his teachings.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chaviva bar Surmakei reports that a certain rabbi who was visited by Eliyahu had damaged eyes from looking at Rabbi Chiya's aura in the heavenly academy, and Eliyahu warned him not to look at Rabbi Chiya's aura.
The rabbi could not restrain himself, looked at Rabbi Chiya's aura, was struck by fire and blinded, then was healed after prostrating at Rabbi Chiya's cave and reciting his teachings.

items.text: Eliyahu's delay from the heavenly academy
items.text_en: Eliyahu's delay from the heavenly academy
items.desc_en: Eliyahu was late to Rabbi's academy because he had to wake Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob for prayer, and they could not be woken together lest they bring the Messiah before his time.

sub.desc_en: The narrative sets the scene: Eliyahu was regularly present at Rabbi's academy, but one Rosh Chodesh he was late.
Rabbi asks Eliyahu why he was delayed.
Eliyahu explains that he was delayed because he had to wake Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob for prayer, and they cannot be woken together lest they bring the Messiah before his time.

items.text: Rabbi Chiya and his sons' power and Eliyahu's punishment
items.text_en: Rabbi Chiya and his sons' power and Eliyahu's punishment
items.desc_en: Rabbi asks if there is an earthly parallel to the patriarchs, and Eliyahu says Rabbi Chiya and his sons. Rabbi decrees a fast, and they demonstrate power over wind and rain, causing a stir in heaven. Eliyahu is punished for revealing this secret, and he appears as a fiery bear to scatter them.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi asks Eliyahu if there is an earthly parallel to the patriarchs.
Eliyahu answers that Rabbi Chiya and his sons are the earthly parallel.
Rabbi decrees a fast and brings Rabbi Chiya and his sons down to lead the prayers.
Rabbi Chiya demonstrates power over wind and rain, causing a stir in heaven when he reaches the blessing of reviving the dead.
The heavenly court identifies Eliyahu as the one who revealed the secret, punishes him with sixty fiery lashes, and he appears as a fiery bear to scatter the assembly.

items.text: Shmuel Yarchina'ah's treatment of Rabbi's eye
items.text_en: Shmuel Yarchina'ah's treatment of Rabbi's eye
items.desc_en: Shmuel Yarchina'ah, Rabbi's physician, offers to treat Rabbi's eye ailment but Rabbi refuses. Shmuel then places a sachet of herbs under Rabbi's pillow, and he is healed. Later, Rabbi struggles to ordain Shmuel, who reveals he saw Adam's book where it was written that Shmuel would be called 'Yarchina'ah'.

sub.desc_en: The narrative introduces Shmuel Yarchina'ah as Rabbi's physician; Rabbi's eye ailment is treated when Shmuel places a sachet of herbs under his pillow, and he is healed.
Rabbi struggles to ordain Shmuel, who reveals that he saw Adam's book where it was written that Shmuel would be called 'Yarchina'ah'.

items.text: Opening statement about the end of Mishnah and teaching
items.text_en: Opening statement about the end of Mishnah and teaching
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rabbi and Rabbi Natan mark the end of Mishnah, while Rav Ashi and Ravina mark the end of teaching (hora'ah), with a mnemonic from Psalms.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara declares that Rabbi and Rabbi Natan mark the end of Mishnah, while Rav Ashi and Ravina mark the end of teaching (הוראה), with a mnemonic from Psalms.

items.text: Rabbah bar Nachmani's flight from the king's agents
items.text_en: Rabbah bar Nachmani's flight from the king's agents
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana reports that Rabbah bar Nachmani died due to persecution. The king's agents pursued him because he exempted 12,000 Jews from the king's corvée. He fled through various locations, and the agent who found him was healed by Rabbah's instruction, but later betrayed him.

sub.text: Rav Kahana citing Rav Chama bar Barta deChasa
sub.text_en: Rav Kahana citing Rav Chama bar Barta deChasa
sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana reports that Rabbah bar Nachmani died due to persecution, because the king's agents accused him of exempting 12,000 Jews from the king's corvée.
The king's agent pursued Rabbah through various locations, found him in Pumbedita, and was hosted at Rabbah's inn, where he was given two cups of wine and his face turned backward.

sub.text: Rabbah bar Nachmani's instruction and the agent's response
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar Nachmani's instruction and the agent's response
sub.desc_en: Rabbah instructs them to give the agent one cup of wine to heal him, but the healed agent deduces Rabbah's presence and threatens to reveal him if tortured.

items.text: Heavenly dispute about a doubtful negaim case
items.text_en: Heavenly dispute about a doubtful negaim case
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Nachmani, while hiding in a swamp, studies and hears a dispute in the heavenly academy: if a bright spot precedes white hair, it is impure; if white hair precedes the bright spot, it is pure; in a case of doubt, the Holy One says pure, but the entire heavenly academy says impure. They decide that Rabbah bar Nachmani, an expert in negaim, should resolve it.

sub.desc_en: The narrative describes Rabbah bar Nachmani sitting on a palm branch studying, and introduces the heavenly dispute about the order of bright spot and white hair in negaim.
In a case of doubt, the Holy One rules pure, but the entire heavenly academy rules impure, creating a dispute.
The heavenly academy decides that Rabbah bar Nachmani, who claims expertise in negaim and ohalot, should resolve the doubt.

items.text: Rabbah's death and divine declaration of purity
items.text_en: Rabbah's death and divine declaration of purity
items.desc_en: The Angel of Death cannot approach Rabbah due to his constant study. A wind rustles reeds, and he mistakes it for a cavalry, praying for death rather than falling into the king's hands. As he dies, he declares 'pure, pure.' A bat kol proclaims him blessed, and a note falls in Pumbedita that he is summoned to the heavenly academy. Abaye and Rava find his body by observing birds shading a spot.

sub.desc_en: The heavenly academy sends a messenger for Rabbah, but the Angel of Death cannot approach him because he never stops studying.
A wind rustles reeds, Rabbah mistakes it for a cavalry, and he prays for death rather than being handed over to the king's authority.
As Rabbah dies, he declares 'pure, pure,' and a bat kol (heavenly voice) proclaims him blessed, saying his body and soul departed in purity.
A note falls from heaven in Pumbedita announcing that Rabbah bar Nachmani is summoned to the heavenly academy.
Abaye and Rava, unable to find Rabbah's body, observe birds shading a spot in the marsh and conclude that he is there.

items.text: Mourning for Rabbah and the calming of a storm
items.text_en: Mourning for Rabbah and the calming of a storm
items.desc_en: They eulogize Rabbah for three days and nights, then a note forbids departing. They eulogize for seven days, then a note says go home in peace. On the day of his death, a storm lifts an Arab traveler across the river; he questions why the world is being destroyed for Rabbah, and the storm subsides.

sub.desc_en: The gemara reports that they eulogized Rabbah for three days and nights, then a note forbade anyone from departing.
They eulogized for seven days, then a note told them to go home in peace.
On the day of Rabbah's death, a storm lifted an Arab traveler across the river; the traveler questioned why the world was being destroyed for Rabbah, and the storm subsided.

items.text: Anecdote about Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta's corpulence
items.text_en: Anecdote about Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta's corpulence
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta, being very fat, asks his daughter to fan him in exchange for spiced cakes. A wind blows, and he remarks on the worth of such cakes to the Master of the wind.

sub.desc_en: The narrator introduces Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta as a very fat man who, feeling hot, asks his daughter to fan him in exchange for spiced cakes.
A wind suddenly blows, and Rabbi Shimon remarks how many spiced cakes are owed to the Master of the wind, implying the wind's service is far greater than his daughter's.

items.text: Return to the Mishnah: 'All is according to regional custom' and the story of Rabban Yochanan ben Matya
items.text_en: Return to the Mishnah: 'All is according to regional custom' and the story of Rabban Yochanan ben Matya
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that 'all is according to regional custom' includes a place where it is customary to provide bread and dessert. If the employer says to provide it early, the workers can refuse. Then a story about Rabban Yochanan ben Matya telling his son to hire workers is introduced, but the Gemara notes a contradiction and explains the Mishnah is missing a clause: if the employer specified meals, the workers can demand them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what additional case is included by the Mishnah's phrase 'all is according to regional custom'.
The Gemara answers that it includes a place where it is customary to provide bread and dessert, and if the employer says to bring them early, the workers can refuse.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah cites a story of Rabban Yochanan ben Matya which seems to contradict the ruling just given.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah is missing a clause and should read: 'if the employer specified meals, the workers can demand them'.

items.text: Opening story: Rabbi Yochanan ben Matya and the workers' meals
items.text_en: Opening story: Rabbi Yochanan ben Matya and the workers' meals
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan ben Matya tells his son that even if he provides a feast like Solomon's, he cannot fulfill his obligation to the workers because they are descendants of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

items.text: Gemara's question: Is Abraham's feast greater than Solomon's?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Is Abraham's feast greater than Solomon's?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Abraham's feast is greater than Solomon's, citing the vast quantities of Solomon's provisions. It explains that Solomon's food was for his many wives, while Abraham's three oxen were for three guests, but Solomon's was for all of Israel and Judah.

items.text: Interpretation of 'barburim avusim'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'barburim avusim'
items.desc_en: Rav, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yochanan offer different interpretations of the phrase 'barburim avusim' (fattened fowl) in Solomon's feast.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan and Amemar on choice animals
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Amemar on choice animals
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that the choicest animal is an ox and the choicest bird is a chicken. Amemar adds a description of a specific type of chicken.

items.text: Derivation of three oxen from 'ben bakar rach v'tov'
items.text_en: Derivation of three oxen from 'ben bakar rach v'tov'
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the verse about Abraham taking a calf, deriving that 'ben bakar' is one, 'rach' is two, and 'v'tov' is three, and defends this derivation against alternative interpretations.

items.text: Objection and resolution: Why three calves?
items.text_en: Objection and resolution: Why three calves?
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Ulla objects that the verse says Abraham gave the calf to a single youth, implying one calf. Rav Chanan bar Rava answers that it was to serve three tongues with mustard. Rabbi Tanchum bar Chanilai adds a lesson about not changing custom, citing Moses and the angels.

items.text: Parallels between Abraham's actions and God's for Israel
items.text_en: Parallels between Abraham's actions and God's for Israel
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states that what Abraham did personally, God did for his children personally, and what Abraham did through a messenger, God did through a messenger. This is followed by a series of scriptural parallels and a statement by Rabbi Chama bar Chanina that for three acts of hospitality, Israel merited three gifts in the wilderness.

items.text: Abraham's request for water and the angels' response
items.text_en: Abraham's request for water and the angels' response
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yannai bar Rabbi Yishmael explains that when Abraham asked to wash the angels' feet, they responded that he should not suspect them of being Arabs who worship the dust of their feet, as Ishmael had already come from him.

items.text: The visit of the three angels and their identities
items.text_en: The visit of the three angels and their identities
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina explains that the day was the third after Abraham's circumcision, and God brought out the sun to prevent travelers. The Gemara then describes how Abraham sent Eliezer, then went himself, and identifies the three angels as Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael, with Michael also going to save Lot.

items.text: Comparison of Abraham and Lot's hospitality
items.text_en: Comparison of Abraham and Lot's hospitality
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to compare the language used regarding Abraham's hospitality and Lot's, but the segment is cut off.

items.text: Refusal to small vs. great
items.text_en: Refusal to small vs. great
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar derives from the verse that one may refuse a small person but not a great one.

sub.desc_en: The gemara questions the verse 'וַיִּפְצַר בָּם מְאֹד' (and he urged them greatly) regarding Abraham's hospitality.
Rabbi Elazar derives from the verse that one may refuse a small person but not a great one.

items.text: Righteous say little, do much
items.text_en: Righteous say little, do much
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar contrasts the righteous who say little and do much with the wicked who promise much but do even little, citing Abraham and Ephron as examples.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar contrasts the righteous who say little and do much with the wicked who promise much but do even little, citing Abraham and Ephron as examples.
The gemara proves the principle from Ephron, who initially offered the field for free but then charged a high price, taking only קינטרי (a type of coin).

items.text: Sarah's hospitality and purity
items.text_en: Sarah's hospitality and purity
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak notes that women are stingier with guests than men, and Ephraim Miksha'ah explains that Abraham ate unconsecrated food in purity while Sarah was a niddah, so she did not serve bread.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes the contradiction between the verses 'קמח' (flour) and 'סולת' (fine flour) in Abraham's hospitality, and Rabbi Yitzchak explains that women are stingier with guests than men.
The Gemara asks why Abraham served dairy and meat but no bread, despite Sarah having been told to prepare bread.

sub.text: Ephraim Miksha'ah in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.text_en: Ephraim Miksha'ah in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.desc_en: Ephraim Miksha'ah explains that Abraham ate unconsecrated food in purity (חולין בטהרה), while Sarah was a niddah (נידה) that day, so she could not serve bread.

items.text: Where is Sarah?
items.text_en: Where is Sarah?
items.desc_en: The angels' question about Sarah teaches her modesty; Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yitzchak explain it was to endear her to Abraham, while Rabbi Yosei says it was to send her the cup of blessing. A baraita notes the dot on 'eilev' teaches derech eretz, and Shmuel's ruling that one never asks about a woman's welfare is qualified when through her husband.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces the verse where the angels ask about Sarah, explaining it was to teach her modesty.
Rav Yehuda citing Rav (or alternatively Rabbi Yitzchak) explains that the angels knew Sarah was in the tent, but the question was to endear her to Abraham.
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina offers an alternative explanation: the question was to send her the cup of blessing (for kiddush).

sub.text: Baraita in the name of Rabbi Yosei
sub.text_en: Baraita in the name of Rabbi Yosei
sub.desc_en: A baraita in the name of Rabbi Yosei notes the dot on 'eilev' (אֵלָיו) teaches derech eretz (proper conduct) — that one should inquire about a guest's welfare.
The gemara objects: Shmuel ruled that one never asks about a woman's welfare at all.
The gemara resolves: asking about a woman through her husband is different and permitted.

items.text: Sarah's rejuvenation and God's alteration for peace
items.text_en: Sarah's rejuvenation and God's alteration for peace
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda describes Sarah's physical rejuvenation. The Gemara notes that God changed Sarah's words to Abraham for the sake of peace, as taught by the school of Rabbi Yishmael.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda explains that Sarah's words 'after I have withered' describe her physical rejuvenation: withered flesh became smooth and beauty returned.
The Gemara notes that the verse says 'my lord is old' (Sarah's words) but God later said 'I have grown old,' showing God altered her statement.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that peace is so great that even God altered Sarah's words, as the verse shows God said 'I have grown old' instead of 'my lord is old.'

items.text: Sarah nursing many children
items.text_en: Sarah nursing many children
items.desc_en: Rabbi Levi recounts the miracle at Isaac's weaning feast: Sarah's breasts opened like fountains and she nursed all the children, and Isaac's face was transformed to resemble Abraham's to silence skeptics.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how many children Sarah nursed, citing the verse 'מִי מִלֵּל לְאַבְרָהָם הֵנִיקָה בָנִים שָׂרָה' (Who would have said to Abraham that Sarah would nurse children).
Rabbi Levi recounts the miracle at Isaac's weaning feast: all nations slandered, claiming Isaac was a foundling, and Abraham made a great feast to prove his paternity.
Abraham invited all the great men of the generation, Sarah invited their wives, and a miracle occurred: Sarah's breasts opened like two fountains and she nursed all the children.
Despite the miracle, skeptics still doubted, so Isaac's face was transformed to resemble Abraham's, and all proclaimed 'אַבְרָהָם הוֹלִיד אֶת יִצְחָק' (Abraham fathered Isaac).

items.text: Institution of old age, illness, and recovery
items.text_en: Institution of old age, illness, and recovery
items.desc_en: Abraham prayed for old age, Jacob for illness, and Elisha for recovery from illness; a baraita lists three illnesses Elisha suffered.

sub.desc_en: The gemara states that until Abraham there was no old age, and Abraham prayed for it, as per the verse.
The gemara continues that until Jacob there was no illness, and Jacob prayed for it, as per the verse.
The gemara states that until Elisha there was no recovery from illness, and Elisha prayed for it, as per the verse.

items.text: Workers' entitlement to eat
items.text_en: Workers' entitlement to eat
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a dispute about whether a worker is entitled only to bread and legumes or bread and legumes separately, and introduces the Mishnah listing who may eat from the Torah.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists three illnesses Elisha suffered, including the one from which he died.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Yosef's question to Rav Chisda
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Yosef's question to Rav Chisda
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yosef asks Rav Chisda whether the Mishnah teaches 'bread of legumes' (פַּת קִטְנִית) or 'bread and legumes' (פַּת וְקִטְנִית) as separate items.
Rav Chisda swears that the text requires a vav (ו), meaning 'bread and legumes' are separate entitlements.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules that no explicit condition is needed; everything follows local custom.
The Gemara asks what the word 'all' (הַכֹּל) in Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statement comes to include.
The Gemara explains that 'all' includes the case of a worker hired as one of the townsmen, where Rabbi Yehoshua says he receives the minimum wage.
The Sages (Chachamim) disagree and rule that the wage is appraised between the two extremes.

The Mishnah lists those who may eat by Torah law: workers in attached produce at the time of completion, and in detached produce before the work is finished, and in anything that grows from the ground.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a worker may eat from produce that is not yet fully processed, detached from the ground after processing, or from something that does not grow from the ground.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a worker may eat from produce that is not yet fully processed, detached from the ground after processing, or from something that does not grow from the ground.

items.text: Gemara's initial derivation from vineyard
items.text_en: Gemara's initial derivation from vineyard
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of these laws, citing the verse about entering a vineyard. It derives that any item that grows from the ground and is at the time of completion of work allows a worker to eat, by analogy from a vineyard.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the laws of a worker eating from produce, citing the verse about entering a vineyard, and questions how to derive other items from the vineyard.

The Gemara answers by deriving from the vineyard: just as a vineyard is a unique case of something that grows from the ground and at the time of completion of work a worker may eat, so too any item that grows from the ground at the time of completion of work a worker may eat.

items.text: Challenge from gleanings and derivation from standing grain
items.text_en: Challenge from gleanings and derivation from standing grain
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the vineyard analogy because a vineyard is obligated in gleanings. It then derives from standing grain, using a verse, and clarifies that the grain must be obligated in challah through a verbal analogy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the vineyard analogy is flawed because a vineyard is obligated in gleanings (עוללות), which is a unique stringency.

sub.text: Gemara's answer — derivation from standing grain
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer — derivation from standing grain
sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the law is derived from standing grain (קמה), citing the verse 'כִּי תָבֹא בְּקָמַת רֵעֶךָ וְקָטַפְתָּ מְלִילוֹת בְּיָדֶךָ'.

sub.text: Gemara's objection — grain obligated in challah
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection — grain obligated in challah
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that standing grain is obligated in challah (חלה), which is also a unique stringency, and questions whether the verse refers to any grain or only grain obligated in challah.
The Gemara resolves the objection by invoking a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'קמה' in the verse 'מֵהָחֵל חֶרְמֵשׁ בַּקָּמָה', establishing that the grain must be obligated in challah.

items.text: Refutation and return of the argument
items.text_en: Refutation and return of the argument
items.desc_en: The Gemara refutes the derivation from standing grain because it is obligated in challah, and the vineyard refutes that. The argument returns, concluding that the common denominator is that both are items that grow from the ground and at the time of completion of work a worker may eat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the derivation from standing grain is flawed because grain is obligated in challah, and the vineyard refutes that; then the vineyard's derivation is flawed because it is obligated in gleanings, and the grain refutes that.
The argument returns, concluding that the common denominator is that both are items that grow from the ground and at the time of completion of work a worker may eat.

items.text: Challenge from the altar aspect and olive tree
items.text_en: Challenge from the altar aspect and olive tree
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the common denominator because both have an aspect of the altar, and olives also have that aspect. It then discusses whether an olive tree is called a vineyard, concluding it is not called a vineyard in general.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the common denominator of the vineyard and standing grain includes an aspect of the altar, and olives also have that aspect, so the derivation fails.
Rav Pappa answers that an olive tree is called 'כרם זית' (a vineyard of olives) in the verse, but it is not called 'כרם' (vineyard) by itself, so it is not included in the common denominator.

items.text: Shmuel's derivation from the sickle
items.text_en: Shmuel's derivation from the sickle
items.desc_en: Shmuel derives from the word 'sickle' to include all things harvested with a sickle. The Gemara questions this, but resolves that the exclusion of non-sickle items comes from another verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the previous derivation is still difficult, then introduces Shmuel's alternative derivation.
Shmuel states that the verse uses the word 'חרמש' (sickle) to include all things harvested with a sickle.
The Gemara objects that the word 'חרמש' is needed to teach that a worker may eat only during the time of sickle work, not otherwise.
The Gemara resolves that the time restriction is derived from the verse 'ואל כליך לא תתן', and then asks how we include items not harvested with a sickle.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak's derivation from standing grain
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak's derivation from standing grain
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak derives from 'standing grain' to include all things that stand tall. The Gemara resolves the earlier contradiction by explaining that before the sickle verse, the grain verse was limited, but now it includes all things harvested with a sickle, and the grain verse includes all standing things.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak resolves the difficulty by deriving from the word 'קָמָה' (standing grain) that the law applies to all things that stand tall.

items.text: Rava's explanation and additional halakhot from the verse
items.text_en: Rava's explanation and additional halakhot from the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the vineyard verse is needed, and Rava explains it is for its halakhot. The Gemara then expounds the verse to derive various laws: that it speaks of a worker, excludes a gentile's vineyard, excludes consecrated property, prohibits squeezing grapes, limits eating to grapes alone, equates the worker's appetite to the homeowner's, prohibits excessive eating, and conditions eating on not putting into the homeowner's vessel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: now that the laws of a worker eating are derived from 'חרמש' (sickle) and 'קמה' (standing grain), why is the verse 'כי תבוא בכרם רעך' (when you come into your neighbor's vineyard) needed?

Rava answers that the verse is needed for its specific halakhot (הלכותיו), and cites a baraita that uses a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) from the word 'ביאה' (coming) to establish that the verse speaks of a worker.
The baraita derives that the verse excludes a gentile's vineyard, and the Gemara questions this for the opinion that robbery of a gentile is permitted.

The Gemara resolves the difficulty by reinterpreting the exclusion as referring to consecrated property (הקדש), and derives additional laws: that the worker may not squeeze grapes (מוצץ) and may eat only grapes, not grapes with something else.
The baraita derives from 'כנפשך' (like your soul) that the worker's appetite is equated to the homeowner's, so the worker eats and is exempt from tithes just as the homeowner is.

The baraita derives from 'שבעך' (your fill) that excessive eating (אכילה גסה) is prohibited, and from 'ואל כליך לא תתן' (and do not put into your vessel) that the worker may eat only when not putting into the homeowner's vessel.

items.text: Rabbi Yannai's statement on tithes
items.text_en: Rabbi Yannai's statement on tithes
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yannai begins a statement about when produce becomes obligated in tithes, which is cut off at the end of the daf.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yannai begins a statement that untithed produce (טבל) is not obligated in tithes, but the statement is cut off at the end of the daf.

items.text: Opening statement: Rabbi Yannai's view
items.text_en: Opening statement: Rabbi Yannai's view
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yannai states that a courtyard does not determine liability for ma'aser; only seeing the face of the house (i.e., entering the house) matters, citing the verse 'I have removed the holy from the house'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yannai states that liability for ma'aser is determined only when the produce sees the face of the house, citing the verse 'I have removed the holy from the house'.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's opposing view
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's opposing view
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan argues that even a courtyard determines liability, citing the verse 'and they shall eat in your gates and be satisfied'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan asserts that even a courtyard (חצר) determines liability for maaser (tithe), citing the verse 'and they shall eat in your gates and be satisfied'.

items.text: Gemara's resolution of the contradiction
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution of the contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Yochanan can ignore the verse 'from the house', and answers that he requires a courtyard that is like a house—guarded. Similarly, it questions how Rabbi Yannai can ignore 'in your gates', and explains that verse teaches that entry must be through a gate, excluding roofs and enclosed areas.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Yochanan can ignore the verse 'from the house' (מן הבית), which requires a house for the obligation.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that a courtyard (חצר) must be like a house—guarded (משתמר)—to be valid for the obligation.
The Gemara asks how Rabbi Yannai can ignore the verse 'in your gates' (בשעריך), which seems to require a gate.
Rabbi Yannai explains that the verse 'in your gates' teaches that entry must be through a gate, excluding roofs (גגות) and enclosed areas (קרפפות).

items.text: Rav Chanina's challenge from a baraita
items.text_en: Rav Chanina's challenge from a baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Chanina the shoe-seller cites a baraita that a worker may eat and be exempt, implying a buyer is liable. He asks: does this refer to the field (i.e., before entering the courtyard)?

sub.desc_en: Rav Chanina the shoe-seller cites a baraita that a worker may eat and be exempt, implying a buyer is liable, and asks whether this refers to the field (i.e., before entering the courtyard).

items.text: Rav Pappa's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that the case involves a fig tree in a garden whose branches extend into a courtyard, and the liability depends on whether the courtyard is considered a house. He then addresses an objection: why isn't the homeowner liable? Because the homeowner's eyes are on his fig, while the buyer's eyes are on his purchase.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa resolves the objection by explaining that the case involves a fig tree standing in a garden with its branches extending into a courtyard, and the liability follows the opinion regarding whether a courtyard is like a house.
The Gemara objects: if so, why is the homeowner not liable? Rav Pappa answers that the homeowner's attention is on his fig tree, while the buyer's attention is on his purchase.

items.text: Question on buyer's liability from a baraita
items.text_en: Question on buyer's liability from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a buyer is liable at all from the Torah, citing a baraita that the shops of Beit Hino were destroyed because they upheld their own words over Torah law, implying they exempted buyers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a buyer is liable at all from the Torah, citing a baraita that the shops of Beit Hino were destroyed because they upheld their own words over Torah law, implying they exempted buyers.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Exemptions for seller and buyer
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Exemptions for seller and buyer
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the verse 'You shall surely tithe... and you shall eat' excludes a seller, and 'the produce of your seed' excludes a buyer. This is only rabbinic, with the verse as a mere support.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the verse 'עַשֵּׂר תְּעַשֵּׂר וְאָכַלְתָּ' (You shall surely tithe and eat) excludes a seller, and 'תְּבוּאַת זַרְעֶךָ' (the produce of your seed) excludes a buyer, but this is only rabbinic, with the verse as a mere support.

items.text: Gemara: Purpose of 'as your soul'
items.text_en: Gemara: Purpose of 'as your soul'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'as your soul' comes to teach. It cites a baraita: just as your own soul (i.e., your animal) is exempt if you muzzle it, so too a worker is exempt if you muzzle him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'as your soul' (כנפשך) comes to teach, given that the earlier derivation already established the law of muzzling.
The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from 'as your soul' (כנפשך) that just as your own animal is exempt if you muzzle it, so too a worker is exempt if you muzzle him.

items.text: Mar Zutra's challenge: 'when they become smooth'
items.text_en: Mar Zutra's challenge: 'when they become smooth'
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra challenges the idea that the Mishnah's 'granary' refers to the house. He cites a baraita about cucumbers and gourds becoming obligated in tithes when they become smooth (yefaksesu), and Rabbi Asi explains this means when their smoothness is removed. The Gemara clarifies that this refers to smoothing in the house, not the field, and explains the wording 'when they become smooth' rather than 'until they become smooth'.

sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra challenges the identification of 'granary' with the house by citing a baraita that cucumbers and gourds become obligated in tithes 'when they become smooth' (משיפקסו), and Rabbi Asi's explanation that this means when their smoothness is removed, implying this happens even in the field.
The Gemara answers that 'when they become smooth' refers to smoothing that occurs in the house, not the field.
The Gemara objects that if the baraita meant smoothing in the house, it should have used the phrase 'until they become smooth' (עד שיפקסו) rather than 'when they become smooth' (משיפקסו).

The Gemara resolves that if the baraita had said 'until they become smooth', one might think it means until their smoothing is completely finished, so the baraita uses 'when they become smooth' to teach that the obligation begins from the start of their smoothing process.

items.text: Mar Zutra's second challenge: completion of work
items.text_en: Mar Zutra's second challenge: completion of work
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra bar Rav Nachman challenges with a baraita that the granary for tithing is when their work is completed, i.e., the work of bringing them in. The Gemara explains that this refers to bringing into the house, not the field. Alternatively, Rabbi Yannai's statement applies only to olives and grapes, which are not subject to the granary, but for wheat and barley, the verse explicitly mentions 'granary'.

sub.text: Mar Zutra bar Rav Nachman's challenge
sub.text_en: Mar Zutra bar Rav Nachman's challenge
sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra bar Rav Nachman challenges with a baraita that the granary for tithing is when their work is completed, i.e., the work of bringing them in, implying even in the field.

The Gemara answers that the baraita refers to bringing into the house, not the field, and alternatively, Rabbi Yannai's statement applies only to olives and grapes, which are not subject to the granary, but for wheat and barley, the verse explicitly mentions 'granary'.

items.text: Deriving a worker eating from detached produce
items.text_en: Deriving a worker eating from detached produce
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the source for a worker eating from detached produce. It attempts a kal vachomer from an ox: if an ox, which does not eat attached produce, eats detached, then a person, who eats attached, should certainly eat detached. This is refuted because one is commanded against muzzling an ox but not a person. The Gemara then tries to derive that one should be commanded against muzzling a person via kal vachomer, but the verse 'as your soul' exempts it. Finally, it derives the law from the double mention of 'standing grain' (kamah).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have found that a person may eat attached produce and an ox may eat detached produce, but from where do we derive that a person may eat detached produce?

The Gemara proposes a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) from an ox: if an ox, which does not eat attached produce, eats detached produce, then a person, who eats attached produce, should certainly eat detached produce.
The Gemara refutes the kal vachomer: the case of an ox is stronger because one is commanded against muzzling it, whereas one is not commanded against muzzling a person.

The Gemara counters: let a person be commanded against muzzling via a kal vachomer from an ox — if an ox, which you are not commanded to sustain, you are commanded against muzzling it, then a person, whom you are commanded to sustain, should certainly be commanded against muzzling.

The Gemara rejects this: the verse 'כְּנַפְשְׁךָ' (as your soul) teaches that just as if you muzzle yourself you are exempt, so too if you muzzle a worker you are exempt — thus one is not commanded against muzzling a person.
The Gemara resolves: the verse 'קָמָה' (standing grain) is written twice — if it is not needed for a person eating attached produce, apply it to a person eating detached produce.

items.text: Rabbi Ami: No need for a verse for a worker eating detached
items.text_en: Rabbi Ami: No need for a verse for a worker eating detached
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami argues that a worker eating from detached produce does not require a verse, as the verse 'When you come into your neighbor's vineyard' deals with a worker hired to carry (detached produce), and the Merciful One says he may eat.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ami asserts that a worker eating detached produce requires no special verse, because the verse 'When you come into your neighbor's vineyard' already deals with a worker hired to carry (detached produce), and the Merciful One says he may eat.

items.text: Deriving an ox eating from attached produce
items.text_en: Deriving an ox eating from attached produce
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the source for an ox eating from attached produce. It attempts a kal vachomer from a person: if a person, who does not eat detached, eats attached, then an ox, which eats detached, should certainly eat attached. This is refuted because one is commanded to sustain a person but not an ox. The Gemara then tries to derive that one should be commanded to sustain an ox via kal vachomer, but the verse 'and your brother shall live with you' excludes an ox. Finally, it derives the law from the double mention of 'your neighbor' (rei'acha).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source permitting an ox to eat from attached produce.
The Gemara proposes a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) from a person to an ox, but refutes it because one is commanded to sustain a person but not an ox.
The Gemara attempts a reciprocal קל וחומר to obligate sustaining an ox, but it is rejected.
The Gemara refutes the second קל וחומר by citing the verse 'וְחֵי אָחִיךָ עִמָּךְ' (and your brother shall live with you), which excludes an ox.
The Gemara resolves the question by deriving the law from the double mention of 'רֵעֶךָ' (your neighbor), applying it to an ox eating from attached produce.

items.text: Ravina: No need for verses for either case
items.text_en: Ravina: No need for verses for either case
items.desc_en: Ravina concludes that neither a worker eating detached produce nor an ox eating attached produce requires a separate verse, as the verse 'You shall not muzzle an ox while it threshes' implies that the prohibition applies only to threshing (detached), but for attached produce, the ox may eat.

sub.desc_en: Ravina rules that neither a worker eating detached produce nor an ox eating attached produce requires a separate verse, because the verse 'You shall not muzzle an ox while it threshes' implies the prohibition applies only to threshing (detached), so for attached produce the ox may eat.

items.text: Deriving the law of muzzling from Shabbat and the reciprocal analogy
items.text_en: Deriving the law of muzzling from Shabbat and the reciprocal analogy
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah wrote 'ox' in the prohibition of muzzling, since all animals are included by the analogy to Shabbat. It answers that the word 'ox' serves to create a reciprocal analogy between the muzzler and the muzzled, teaching that both may eat from attached produce (the muzzler) and from detached produce (the muzzled).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah wrote 'ox' in the muzzling prohibition, since all animals are included by the analogy to Shabbat.

The Gemara answers that the word 'ox' creates a reciprocal analogy between the muzzler and the muzzled, teaching that both may eat from attached produce (the muzzler) and from detached produce (the muzzled).

items.text: First baraita: excluding milk, cheese, and butter
items.text_en: First baraita: excluding milk, cheese, and butter
items.desc_en: A baraita derives from the word 'dash' (threshing) that a worker may only eat from things that are grown from the ground, at the time of final processing. This excludes milking, curdling, and cheesemaking. The Gemara asks why this is needed, since it could be derived from the verse about entering a vineyard, and answers that it is necessary to exclude the possibility that 'standing grain' includes all things that stand.

sub.desc_en: A baraita derives from the word 'דיש' (threshing) that a worker may eat only from things grown from the ground at the time of final processing, excluding milking, curdling, and cheesemaking.
The Gemara asks why this baraita is needed, since the exclusion could be derived from the verse 'כי תבוא בכרם רעך' (when you enter your neighbor's vineyard).

The Gemara answers that the baraita is necessary because one might have thought that 'קמה' (standing grain) includes all things that stand, so the baraita teaches that only things grown from the ground are included.

items.text: Second baraita: excluding weeding at the wrong time
items.text_en: Second baraita: excluding weeding at the wrong time
items.desc_en: Another baraita derives from 'dash' that a worker may only eat at the time of final processing, excluding weeding garlic and onions which is not final processing. The Gemara asks why this is needed, since it could be derived from the verse 'and into your vessel you shall not give', and answers that it is necessary even when the worker is removing small weeds from among large ones.

sub.desc_en: A second baraita derives from 'dash' that a worker may eat only at the time of final processing, excluding weeding garlic and onions which is not final processing.
The Gemara asks why this baraita is needed, since the exclusion could be derived from the verse 'and into your vessel you shall not give'.
The Gemara answers that the baraita is necessary even when the worker is removing small weeds from among large ones, a case where the verse alone might not exclude.

items.text: Third baraita: excluding dates and figs after tithes
items.text_en: Third baraita: excluding dates and figs after tithes
items.desc_en: A baraita derives from 'dash' that a worker may eat only from produce not yet obligated in tithes, excluding one who separates dates and figs (which are already obligated). The Gemara cites a contradiction: another baraita says such a worker may eat. Rav Pappa resolves: that baraita refers to unripe dates (תוחלני).

sub.desc_en: A baraita derives from 'דיש' (threshing) that a worker may eat only from produce not yet obligated in tithes, excluding one who separates dates and figs (which are already obligated).
The Gemara objects: another baraita explicitly says that a worker who separates dates and figs may eat.
Rav Pappa resolves the contradiction: that baraita refers to unripe dates (תוחלני), which are not yet obligated in tithes.

items.text: Fourth baraita: excluding bread after challah, and resolution
items.text_en: Fourth baraita: excluding bread after challah, and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita derives from 'dash' that a worker may eat only from produce not yet obligated in challah, excluding kneading, cutting, and baking. The Gemara objects: such produce is already obligated in tithes! It answers that the baraita deals with outside the Land (where tithes don't apply) or with the first 14 years of conquest (when only challah applied). Ravina resolves by rephrasing the baraita to include both tithes and challah.

sub.desc_en: A baraita derives from 'דיש' (threshing) that a worker may eat only from produce whose work is not yet complete regarding חלה (challah), excluding kneading, cutting, and baking.
The Gemara objects: such produce is already obligated in מעשר (tithes), so why does the baraita only mention חלה?
The Gemara answers that the baraita deals with outside the Land (חוצה לארץ), where מעשר does not apply.
The Gemara objects: if outside the Land, even חלה does not apply, so the baraita's exclusion is meaningless.
The Gemara answers that the baraita refers to the first 14 years of the conquest of the Land, when only חלה applied and not מעשר.
The Gemara objects: the baraita's criterion is completion of work (גמר מלאכה), not the obligation of מעשר, so the historical exemption of מעשר is irrelevant.
Ravina resolves by rephrasing the baraita to include both מעשר and חלה as criteria for when a worker may eat.

items.text: Inquiry: may a worker roast produce before eating?
items.text_en: Inquiry: may a worker roast produce before eating?
items.desc_en: The Gemara inquires whether a worker may roast produce in fire before eating, comparing it to grapes and other items. It brings a baraita: the homeowner may give workers wine to prevent them from eating many grapes, and workers may dip their bread in brine to eat many grapes, implying that roasting is not permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara inquires whether a worker may roast produce in fire before eating, comparing it to grapes and other items.

The Gemara brings a baraita: the homeowner may give workers wine to prevent them from eating many grapes, and workers may dip their bread in brine to eat many grapes, implying that roasting is not permitted.

items.text: Initial question about enhancing fruit
items.text_en: Initial question about enhancing fruit
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a worker may process fruit (e.g., by heating) to improve it, having already established that enhancing the worker himself is permitted. A baraita is cited that workers eat grapes at the ends of clusters provided they do not heat them, implying a prohibition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a worker may enhance the fruit (e.g., by heating) to improve it, having already established that enhancing the worker himself is permitted.
A baraita is cited that workers eat grapes at the ends of clusters provided they do not heat them, implying a prohibition against enhancing fruit.

items.text: Rejection and new question about family
items.text_en: Rejection and new question about family
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof, explaining the baraita's restriction is due to idleness (bitul melakhah), not a prohibition on enhancing fruit. It then asks whether the rule differs when the worker has a wife and children to support.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the previous proof, explaining that the baraita's restriction on enhancing fruit is due to idleness (ביטול מלאכה), not a prohibition on enhancing the fruit itself.
The Gemara then asks whether the rule differs when the worker has a wife and children to support, implying a possible leniency.

items.text: Second baraita and its rejection
items.text_en: Second baraita and its rejection
items.desc_en: Another baraita is brought that prohibits heating, burying in earth, or crushing on a rock, but permits crushing by hand. The Gemara again rejects it as due to idleness, but notes that crushing on a rock does not sweeten the fruit, supporting the idleness interpretation.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that prohibits heating, burying in earth, or crushing on a rock, but permits crushing by hand.
The Gemara rejects the baraita, explaining that the prohibition there is due to idleness (ביטול מלאכה), not because of sweetening the fruit.
The Gemara provides supporting reasoning: if the concern were sweetening the fruit, crushing on a rock would not sweeten it at all, confirming the idleness interpretation.

items.text: Third baraita and the salting contradiction
items.text_en: Third baraita and the salting contradiction
items.desc_en: A baraita lists workers who may eat from their labor but forbids dipping in salt. The Gemara notes that salt is like grapes and another item, implying a prohibition on enhancing the fruit.

sub.desc_en: A baraita lists workers who may eat from their labor but forbids dipping in salt.
The Gemara notes that salt is like grapes and another item, implying a prohibition on enhancing the fruit.

items.text: Contradiction between baraitot on salting
items.text_en: Contradiction between baraitot on salting
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a second baraita that permits salting when cutting one fig at a time, but forbids it when cutting two. It asks whether this refers to the first clause (reisha) or the latter (seifa), concluding it must be the reisha, creating a contradiction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between the first baraita (which forbids salting) and a second baraita (which permits salting when cutting one fig at a time), and asks which clause of the second baraita the permission applies to.

The Gemara rejects the possibility that the permission applies to the latter clause (seifa), since once the worker has cut the figs he may eat them however he wants, concluding it must refer to the first clause (reisha), thereby creating a contradiction.

items.text: Abaye's resolution: Land of Israel vs. outside
items.text_en: Abaye's resolution: Land of Israel vs. outside
items.desc_en: Abaye resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the Land of Israel, where salting establishes a fixed meal for tithes, and outside the Land, where it does not. Rava objects that this would permit salting ab initio outside the Land, which is problematic.

sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the Land of Israel, where salting establishes a fixed meal for tithes, and outside the Land, where it does not.
Rava objects that Abaye's distinction would permit salting לכתחילה (the ideal standard) outside the Land, which is problematic because the Torah's law should apply uniformly.

items.text: Rava's resolution: one vs. two figs
items.text_en: Rava's resolution: one vs. two figs
items.desc_en: Rava explains that both in and outside the Land, salting one fig does not establish a fixed meal, but salting two does. He details the rules for cutting and salting, and cites a verse to prove that two figs constitute a fixed meal.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the contradiction by stating that both in and outside the Land, salting one fig does not establish a fixed meal, but salting two does, and details the rules for cutting and salting.

sub.text: Rav Mattana's proof from a verse
sub.text_en: Rav Mattana's proof from a verse
sub.desc_en: Rav Mattana cites the verse 'כי קבצם כעמר גרנה' (for He gathered them like sheaves to the threshing floor) to prove that two figs constitute a fixed meal.

items.text: Transition to new topic: cows treading grain
