items.text_en: Transition to new topic: cows treading grain
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new discussion about cows that tread grain, introducing a baraita on the topic.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita about cows that tread grain, beginning a new discussion.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Threshing with terumah and ma'aser
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Threshing with terumah and ma'aser
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who threshes with terumah and ma'aser does not violate 'bal tachsom' (muzzling), but due to appearance, one brings a clod from that species and hangs it on the animal's muzzle. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai says one brings carshinim (vetch) because it is better for the animal.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who threshes with terumah and ma'aser does not violate 'bal tachsom' (muzzling), but due to appearance, one brings a clod from that species and hangs it on the animal's muzzle.
Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai says one brings carshinim (vetch) because it is better for the animal.

items.text: Gemara's contradiction: Sources on threshing terumah and ma'aser
items.text_en: Gemara's contradiction: Sources on threshing terumah and ma'aser
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that contradicts the Mishnah: it states that cows threshing in produce do not violate 'bal tachsom', but those threshing terumah and ma'aser do violate it. This creates a contradiction between the two sources regarding terumah and ma'aser.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: a baraita states that cows threshing terumah and ma'aser do violate 'בל תחסם' (the prohibition of muzzling), contradicting the Mishnah which says they do not.

items.text: First resolution attempt: Terumah vs. its secondary growth
items.text_en: First resolution attempt: Terumah vs. its secondary growth
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially resolves the terumah contradiction by distinguishing between terumah itself and its secondary growth (gidulei terumah). However, the ma'aser contradiction remains, as secondary growth of ma'aser is chullin (non-sacred), not ma'aser, so the distinction fails for ma'aser.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the terumah contradiction by distinguishing between terumah itself and its secondary growth (gidulei terumah).
The Gemara objects that the same distinction fails for ma'aser, since secondary growth of ma'aser is chullin (non-sacred), not ma'aser.

items.text: Second resolution: First tithe vs. second tithe, and Rabbi Meir vs. Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Second resolution: First tithe vs. second tithe, and Rabbi Meir vs. Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the ma'aser contradiction by distinguishing between first tithe (ma'aser rishon) and second tithe (ma'aser sheni). Alternatively, both sources refer to second tithe, but one follows Rabbi Meir (who holds it is sacred property) and the other Rabbi Yehuda (who holds it is common property).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between first tithe (מעשר ראשון) and second tithe (מעשר שני).
Alternatively, both sources refer to second tithe, but one follows Rabbi Meir (who holds it is sacred property) and the other Rabbi Yehuda (who holds it is common property).

items.text: Clarification: Case of early separation and Rabbi Yehuda's view
items.text_en: Clarification: Case of early separation and Rabbi Yehuda's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the case where the animal threshes second tithe that was separated early (in the sheaves). For Rabbi Yehuda, since second tithe requires redemption within the wall, the case is where threshing occurs inside the wall of Beit Pagei (outside Jerusalem's wall but within the city's boundary).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the case of early separation of second tithe is possible, and answers that it occurs when one separated the tithe while it was still in the sheaves.
The Gemara addresses Rabbi Yehuda's requirement of a wall for second tithe, explaining that the threshing occurred inside the wall of Beit Pagei.

items.text: Third resolution: Definite vs. doubtful tithes (vadai vs. demai)
items.text_en: Third resolution: Definite vs. doubtful tithes (vadai vs. demai)
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers another resolution: the contradiction is between definite tithe (ma'aser vadai) and doubtful tithe (ma'aser demai). This also resolves the terumah contradiction by distinguishing between definite terumah (terumat vadai) and doubtful terumah (terumat demai). However, the Gemara questions whether terumat demai exists, citing that Rabban Gamliel only instituted terumah gedolah for demai, not terumat ma'aser. The Gemara then refines: the distinction is between definite terumat ma'aser and doubtful terumat ma'aser.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers a third resolution: the contradiction in the mishnayot is between definite tithe (מעשר ודאי) and doubtful tithe (מעשר דמאי), and similarly for terumah, between definite terumah (תרומת ודאי) and doubtful terumah (תרומת דמאי).

The Gemara objects that while doubtful tithe (מעשר דמאי) exists, doubtful terumah (תרומת דמאי) does not, citing a baraita that Rabban Gamliel only instituted the separation of תרומה גדולה (the great terumah) for demai produce, not תרומת מעשר (the terumah of the tithe).

The Gemara refines the resolution: the distinction is not between general terumah types but specifically between definite terumah of the tithe (תרומת מעשר ודאי) and doubtful terumah of the tithe (תרומת מעשר דמאי), which does exist for demai produce.

items.text: Question about a sick animal and proof from Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
items.text_en: Question about a sick animal and proof from Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if an animal is eating and defecating (i.e., sick), what is the law regarding muzzling? Is it permitted because the food does not benefit it, or prohibited because it sees and suffers? Rav Sheshet answers from the Mishnah: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai says one brings carshinim because they are best for it, implying the reason is benefit, not suffering from sight.

sub.desc_en: The questioners ask Rav Sheshet about a sick animal that eats and defecates: is muzzling permitted because the food does not benefit it, or prohibited because it sees and suffers?

Rav Sheshet answers by citing the Mishnah: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai says one brings carshinim because they are best for the animal, implying the reason is benefit, not suffering from sight, and concludes that this proves the point.

items.text: Question: May one tell a non-Jew to muzzle his animal?
items.text_en: Question: May one tell a non-Jew to muzzle his animal?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether one may tell a non-Jew to muzzle his animal and thresh with it. Is the prohibition of 'amirah l'nochri' (telling a non-Jew to do forbidden work) limited to Shabbat (a capital offense) but not to a negative commandment like muzzling? The Gemara attempts to prove from the baraita that a non-Jew threshing a Jew's animal does not violate 'bal tachsom', implying there is at least a prohibition (issura). However, the Gemara deflects, saying the baraita only states 'does not violate' but does not imply a prohibition. The Gemara then cites a second attempt from a source about oxen, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether one may tell a non-Jew to muzzle his animal and thresh with it, considering whether the prohibition of 'אמירה לנכרי' (telling a non-Jew to do forbidden work) applies only to Shabbat (a capital offense) or also to a negative commandment like muzzling.

The Gemara attempts to prove from the baraita that a non-Jew threshing a Jew's animal 'does not violate' the prohibition, implying there is at least an issura (prohibition), but deflects by saying the baraita only states 'does not violate' without implying a prohibition.
The Gemara cites a second source about oxen sent to Avuh d'Shmuel, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Question about stolen animals and the prohibition of causing them to be sold
items.text_en: Question about stolen animals and the prohibition of causing them to be sold
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about animals stolen by Arabs who then hide them; may one cause them to be sold? The response is that since deception was used against them, one may use deception to have them sold.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether one may cause animals stolen and hidden by Arabs to be sold, given the prohibition of causing them to be sold.
The response is sent: since deception was used against them (the Arabs), one may use deception to have the animals sold.

items.text: Rav Papa's explanation regarding the Westerners' ruling
items.text_en: Rav Papa's explanation regarding the Westerners' ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Papa explains that the Westerners (Jews in the West) follow Rabbi Chidka, who says Noahides are commanded about castration, and thus they violate 'before a blind person do not place a stumbling block'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Papa explains that the Westerners follow Rabbi Chidka, who holds that Noahides are commanded about castration, so they violate the prohibition of placing a stumbling block before the blind.

items.text: Rava's proposal and Abaye's objection
items.text_en: Rava's proposal and Abaye's objection
items.desc_en: Rava thought to say the animals should be sold for slaughter. Abaye objected: 'Is it a court that penalized them with a sale?'

sub.desc_en: Rava proposes that the stolen animals should be sold for slaughter.
Abaye objects: 'Is it a court that penalized them with a sale?' — questioning whether the sale is a proper penalty.

items.text: Case of selling to one's son: adult vs. minor
items.text_en: Case of selling to one's son: adult vs. minor
items.desc_en: It is obvious that selling to one's adult son is like selling to another. For a minor son, Rav Achai forbids and Rav Ashi permits. Marimar and Mar Zutra (or the two pious ones) would exchange with each other.

sub.desc_en: The gemara states that it is obvious that selling to one's adult son is like selling to another person.
The gemara raises a question about the case of selling to a minor son.
Rav Achai forbids selling to a minor son.
Rav Ashi permits selling to a minor son.
Marimar and Mar Zutra (or the two pious ones) would exchange with each other, illustrating a practical approach to the issue.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's inquiries about indirect muzzling
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's inquiries about indirect muzzling
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks: if a thorn lodged in the animal's mouth, what is the law? The Gemara corrects the phrasing: if a thorn sat in its mouth (naturally). Then he asks about a lion lying outside, placing its young outside, the animal being thirsty, or spreading a cloth over the grain. All these are cases where the animal is prevented from eating indirectly.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks about a thorn lodged in the animal's mouth, but the Gemara corrects the phrasing to a naturally sitting thorn.
Rami bar Chama asks about a series of indirect muzzling scenarios: a lion lying outside, placing its young outside, the animal being thirsty, or spreading a cloth over the grain.

items.text: Resolution from a baraita and distinction
items.text_en: Resolution from a baraita and distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves one case from a baraita: the owner may starve his cow so it eats much from the grain, and the householder may untie a bundle of sheaves before the animal so it does not eat much. The Gemara distinguishes: there the animal eats (so it is not muzzled). Alternatively, the householder may untie the bundle from the outset so it does not eat much.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves one of the earlier questions by citing a baraita that permits the owner to starve his cow so it eats much from the grain, and permits the householder to untie a bundle of sheaves before the animal so it does not eat much.

The Gemara distinguishes that in the baraita the animal actually eats (so it is not muzzled), and alternatively explains that the householder may untie the bundle from the outset to prevent it from eating much.

items.text: Rabbi Yonatan's inquiry to Rabbi Simai about muzzling from outside
items.text_en: Rabbi Yonatan's inquiry to Rabbi Simai about muzzling from outside
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yonatan asks Rabbi Simai: if one muzzles the animal from outside (not in the grain), what is the law? Is the prohibition only when the animal is in its threshing, or is it a general prohibition against muzzling? Rabbi Simai answers by analogy: from your father's house you learn that just as the verse about wine for priests prohibits drinking only at the time of entering the Tent of Meeting, so too muzzling is prohibited only at the time of threshing.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yonatan asks Rabbi Simai: if one muzzles the animal from outside (not in the grain), is the prohibition limited to when the animal is in its threshing, or is it a general prohibition against muzzling?

Rabbi Simai answers by analogy: from your father's house you learn that just as the verse about wine for priests prohibits drinking only at the time of entering the Tent of Meeting, so too muzzling is prohibited only at the time of threshing.

Rabbi Simai concludes the analogy: just as the prohibition of drunkenness applies only at the time of entering the Tent of Meeting, so too the prohibition of muzzling applies only at the time of threshing.

items.text: Baraita: one who muzzles or yokes kilayim is exempt from lashes
items.text_en: Baraita: one who muzzles or yokes kilayim is exempt from lashes
items.desc_en: The Sages taught: one who muzzles a cow or yokes diverse kinds is exempt from lashes; he is only liable when he actually threshes or leads them.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that one who muzzles a cow or yokes diverse kinds is exempt from lashes, and is only liable when he actually threshes or leads them.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish about muzzling by voice
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish about muzzling by voice
items.desc_en: It was stated: if one muzzled the animal by voice and led it by voice, Rabbi Yochanan says liable, Reish Lakish says exempt. Rabbi Yochanan: the twisting of its mouth is an act. Reish Lakish: voice is not an act. Rabbi Yochanan then challenged Reish Lakish from a baraita.

sub.desc_en: The gemara states a dispute: if one muzzled the animal by voice and led it by voice, Rabbi Yochanan says liable, Reish Lakish says exempt.
Rabbi Yochanan explains his ruling: the twisting of the animal's mouth (in response to the voice) constitutes an act.
Reish Lakish explains his ruling: voice is not considered an act.
Rabbi Yochanan challenges Reish Lakish by citing a supporting baraita.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's ruling on substitution (temurah)
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's ruling on substitution (temurah)
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's statement that one who substitutes an animal is flogged aligns with Rabbi Yehuda's view that a prohibition without a physical act is punishable. It then challenges this by noting that the Mishnah's inclusion of an heir as one who can substitute contradicts Rabbi Yehuda's position that an heir cannot substitute or lay hands. The resolution is that this Tanna agrees with Rabbi Yehuda on one point but disagrees on another.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's ruling that one who substitutes an animal is flogged aligns with Rabbi Yehuda's view that a prohibition without a physical act is punishable.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah cannot be Rabbi Yehuda because it includes an heir as one who can substitute, while Rabbi Yehuda holds that an heir cannot substitute or lay hands.
The Gemara resolves that this Tanna agrees with Rabbi Yehuda on one point (flogging for a verbal prohibition) but disagrees on another (the heir's ability to substitute).

items.text: Baraita on muzzling and threshing: liability for lashes and payment
items.text_en: Baraita on muzzling and threshing: liability for lashes and payment
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one who muzzles a cow and threshes with it is flogged and pays compensation. The Gemara notes that generally one is not flogged and also pays, but Abaye explains that this follows Rabbi Meir's view that one can be both flogged and pay.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one who muzzles a cow and threshes with it is flogged and pays compensation of four kav for a cow and three for a donkey.
The Gemara objects that generally one is not both flogged and required to pay compensation.
Abaye resolves the difficulty by identifying the baraita as following Rabbi Meir's view that one can be both flogged and pay.

items.text: Rava and Rav Pappa's explanations for the baraita
items.text_en: Rava and Rav Pappa's explanations for the baraita
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the Torah forbids the hire of a prostitute (etnan) even if one had relations with his mother. Rav Pappa explains that liability for feeding the animal begins at the time of acquisition (meshikhah), but lashes are not incurred until the act of muzzling.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that the Torah forbids the hire of a prostitute (אתנן) even if one had relations with his mother.
Rav Pappa explains that liability for feeding the animal begins at the time of acquisition (משיכה), but lashes are not incurred until the act of muzzling.

items.text: Two questions from the house of Rav Pappa bar Abba: one answered correctly, one not
items.text_en: Two questions from the house of Rav Pappa bar Abba: one answered correctly, one not
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa reports that the house of Rav Pappa bar Abba asked him two questions, and he answered both as forbidden – one in accordance with halakha, the other not. The first question was about kneading dough with milk; the baraita forbids it because it leads to habitual transgression. The second question was about inserting a species with a non-species into a corral (for crossbreeding); he answered forbidden, but this is not halakha, as Shmuel taught that for adulterers the prohibition is only when they act like adulterers (seeing each other), and for kilayim only when one inserts as much as a stylus into a tube.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa reports that the house of Rav Pappa bar Abba asked him two questions, and he answered both as forbidden – one in accordance with halakha, the other not.

sub.text: House of Rav Pappa bar Abba's first question
sub.text_en: House of Rav Pappa bar Abba's first question
sub.desc_en: The first question asks whether it is permitted to knead dough with milk.
Rav Pappa answered that it is forbidden, citing a baraita that forbids kneading dough with milk because it leads to habitual transgression, and similarly forbids greasing an oven with fat.

sub.text: House of Rav Pappa bar Abba's second question
sub.text_en: House of Rav Pappa bar Abba's second question
sub.desc_en: The second question asks whether it is permitted to insert a species with a non-species into a corral (for crossbreeding).
Rav Pappa answered that it is forbidden, but this ruling is not in accordance with the halakha.
Shmuel teaches that for adulterers the prohibition is only when they act like adulterers (seeing each other), and for kilayim only when one inserts as much as a stylus into a tube.

items.text: Rav Achadvoi bar Ami's objection: the verse 'kilayim' implies even holding is forbidden
items.text_en: Rav Achadvoi bar Ami's objection: the verse 'kilayim' implies even holding is forbidden
items.desc_en: Rav Achadvoi bar Ami objects: if the verse only said 'your animal you shall not crossbreed', one might think one may not even hold the animal when a male mounts it. Therefore the verse adds 'kilayim' to teach that only actual crossbreeding is forbidden. This implies that for kilayim, even holding is not forbidden? The Gemara answers that 'holding' here means 'insertion', and it is called 'holding' as a euphemism.

sub.desc_en: Rav Achadvoi bar Ami objects: if the verse only said 'your animal you shall not crossbreed', one might think holding is forbidden; the verse adds 'kilayim' to teach that only actual crossbreeding is forbidden.
The Gemara asks: does this not imply that for kilayim, even holding is not forbidden?
The Gemara answers: 'holding' here means 'insertion', and it is called 'holding' as a euphemism.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's ruling: same species may be inserted like a stylus into a tube
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's ruling: same species may be inserted like a stylus into a tube
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states that for animals of the same species, it is permitted to insert as much as a stylus into a tube, and there is no concern for licentiousness because the animal is preoccupied with its own work. Rav Achadvoi bar Ami then raises an objection (which continues on the next amud).

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that for animals of the same species, it is permitted to insert as much as a stylus into a tube, and there is no concern for licentiousness because the animal is preoccupied with its own work.
Rav Achadvoi bar Ami raises an objection against Rav Yehuda's ruling, which continues on the next amud.

items.text: Interpretation of the prohibition of kilayim in animals
items.text_en: Interpretation of the prohibition of kilayim in animals
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse 'You shall not crossbreed your animal' to forbid only kilayim (crossbreeding), but allowing holding an animal to mate with its own kind. It clarifies that 'holding' actually means 'inserting' (the male into the female), and the term 'holding' is a euphemism.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse 'You shall not crossbreed your animal' to forbid only kilayim (crossbreeding), but permitting holding an animal for mating with its own kind.
The Gemara questions whether the permission for holding extends only to holding (אחיזה) but not to inserting (הכנסה) the male into the female.
The Gemara explains that 'holding' is a euphemism for 'inserting', so the permission includes insertion.

items.text: Question about inserting mixed species into a pen
items.text_en: Question about inserting mixed species into a pen
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi reports that the house of Rav Nechemya the Exilarch asked whether one may insert an animal of the same species together with one of a different species into a pen. The answer was that it is forbidden, not because of the Torah prohibition, but due to licentiousness.

sub.text: Rav Ashi's report of the question from the house of Rav Nechemya the Exilarch
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's report of the question from the house of Rav Nechemya the Exilarch
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi reports that the house of Rav Nechemya the Exilarch asked whether one may insert an animal of the same species together with one of a different species into a pen, questioning whether the animal follows its own species or not.

sub.text: The house of Rav Nechemya's resolution
sub.text_en: The house of Rav Nechemya's resolution
sub.desc_en: They resolved that it is forbidden, not because of the Torah prohibition of kilayim, but due to licentiousness (פריצותא).

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on the manner of work for a worker to eat
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on the manner of work for a worker to eat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a worker may eat from the produce even if he works only with his hands, feet, or shoulder. Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda requires both hands and feet. The Gemara explains the reasoning: the verse 'When you come into your neighbor's vineyard' implies any manner of work, while Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda derives from the ox that it must work with hands and feet.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a worker may eat from the produce even if he works only with his hands, feet, or shoulder, while Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda requires both hands and feet.
The Gemara asks for the reasoning behind the Tanna Kamma's lenient position.
The Gemara explains that the verse 'כִּי תָבֹא בְּכֶרֶם רֵעֶךָ' (When you come into your neighbor's vineyard) implies any manner of work.
The Gemara asks for the reasoning behind Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's stricter position.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda derives from the ox that just as the ox works with both hands (forelegs) and feet (hind legs), so too a worker must work with both hands and feet.

items.text: Question about threshing with geese and chickens
items.text_en: Question about threshing with geese and chickens
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna asks: According to Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, if one threshes with geese and chickens (using their feet), is that considered working with hands and feet? The question remains unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna asks whether threshing with geese and chickens counts as working with hands and feet according to Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, and the question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Rav Nachman's ruling on workers eating grapes and drinking wine
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling on workers eating grapes and drinking wine
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman says in the name of Rabbah bar Avuh: Workers may eat grapes but not drink wine until they have trodden the winepress; after that, they may eat grapes and drink wine.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuh
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuh
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules in the name of Rabbah bar Avuh that workers may eat grapes but not drink wine before treading the winepress, but after treading they may eat grapes and drink wine.

items.text: Mishnah on eating from different types and during travel
items.text_en: Mishnah on eating from different types and during travel
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a worker working on figs may not eat grapes, and vice versa, but may refrain until reaching better produce. Additionally, workers may eat during their walk from one press to another and when unloading a donkey, due to returning lost property to the owner.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a worker working on figs may not eat grapes, and vice versa.
The Mishnah adds that a worker may refrain from eating until reaching better produce.
The Mishnah restricts the eating right to the time of work, but permits eating during travel from one press to another and when unloading a donkey, due to returning lost property to the owner.

items.text: Gemara's discussion on eating from a different vine
items.text_en: Gemara's discussion on eating from a different vine
items.desc_en: The Gemara debates whether a worker working on one vine may eat from another vine. It brings several proofs and counter-proofs, including a case of a vine trellis (שרכא) and a vine trained on a frame (מודלית). The discussion concludes with two versions: one that a worker may not eat from another vine, and another that he may, but the matter remains unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara poses an unresolved question: whether a worker laboring on one vine may eat from another vine, comparing the rule of 'eating from what you give to the owner's vessels' to the specific case.
The Gemara raises an objection: if a worker cannot eat from another vine, how can an ox eat from growing produce (מחובר) while working, citing the principle that an ox may eat while threshing.

sub.text: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi answers that the ox's eating is possible in the case of a שרכא (a trellised vine where the produce is accessible from the work area).
The Gemara cites a baraita: if one works on figs, he may not eat grapes, implying that for the same species (figs to figs, grapes to grapes) he may eat across vines.
The Gemara objects: if a worker cannot eat from another vine, how can the Mishnah's case of figs and grapes as parallel species be explained?

sub.text: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi resolves the objection by explaining that the case involves a מודלית (vine trained on a frame), where different vines are considered connected.

sub.text: First version of the Gemara's reasoning
sub.text_en: First version of the Gemara's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The first version brings another proof from the Mishnah that a worker may delay eating until reaching better fruit, implying that across separate vines he may not eat, otherwise he could simply walk and eat.

The Gemara responds that the Mishnah's case involves interruption of work (ביטול מלאכה), but the real question is about a scenario where the worker's wife and children are also working in the vineyard, raising a distinct issue.

The first version infers from the Mishnah's ruling about workers' eating during walking (בהליכתן) that only due to השבת אבידה (returning lost property) do they eat, implying that in Torah law they do not eat from a different vine.

sub.text: Second version of the Gemara's reasoning
sub.text_en: Second version of the Gemara's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The second version states that a worker may eat from another vine, and that walking (מהלך) is not considered equivalent to performing labor (עושה מעשה) for the purpose of the Torah allowance.
The alternative version holds that walking is not considered 'performing labor,' so the Torah allowance applies to actual work, implying that a worker on one vine may eat from another vine.
The Gemara concludes with the second version's final position: a worker laboring on one vine may not eat from another vine, rejecting the alternative view.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's law regarding a donkey eating while unloading
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's law regarding a donkey eating while unloading
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the Mishnah's statement about a donkey eating while unloading, explaining that it means until it unloads, and cites a baraita that a donkey and camel may eat from their load as long as the worker does not hand-feed them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's phrase 'when it is unloading' (כְּשֶׁהִיא פּוֹרֶקֶת), noting that a donkey cannot eat while actually unloading, and reinterprets it as 'until it unloads' (עַד שֶׁתְּהֵא פּוֹרֶקֶת).
The Gemara cites a baraita (תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן) that a donkey and camel may eat from their load as long as the worker does not hand-feed them, supporting the reinterpretation.

items.text: Mishnah: Worker's right to eat and the dispute with Rabbi Elazar Chasma
items.text_en: Mishnah: Worker's right to eat and the dispute with Rabbi Elazar Chasma
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a worker may eat cucumbers or dates even if they are worth a dinar, but Rabbi Elazar Chasma prohibits eating more than his wages, while the Sages permit it. However, they teach that one should not be gluttonous.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule that a worker may eat cucumbers or dates even if worth a dinar, and records the dispute between Rabbi Elazar Chasma (who prohibits eating more than his wages) and the Sages (who permit it).
The Mishnah adds that one should teach a person not to be gluttonous and thus close the door in his own face.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the dispute: two possible differences
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the dispute: two possible differences
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the difference between the Tanna Kamma and the Sages, suggesting first that it is the teaching about not being gluttonous, then offering two alternative distinctions: the ruling of Rav Asi that a worker may eat even from a single cluster, and the necessity of both rulings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: the Sages in the Mishnah are identical to the Tanna Kamma, so what is the difference between them?
The Gemara answers: the difference is the teaching that one should not be gluttonous — the Tanna Kamma does not have this teaching, while the Sages do.
Alternatively, the difference is the ruling of Rav Asi that a worker may eat even if hired only to pick a single cluster.

The Gemara explains that both rulings are necessary: the first ruling teaches that a worker may eat even when there is no vessel for the owner, and the second ruling teaches that even when the produce cannot be preserved until the end, the worker may still eat.

items.text: Alternative distinction: Rav's tradition about Isi ben Yehudah
items.text_en: Alternative distinction: Rav's tradition about Isi ben Yehudah
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers another distinction based on Rav's finding in a scroll of Rabbi Chiyya, where Isi ben Yehudah interprets the verse 'When you come into your neighbor's vineyard' as referring to any person, not just a worker. Rav Ashi explains that even if workers eat during their meal, the owner prefers to hire workers rather than have everyone eat his produce.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an alternative distinction based on Rav's finding in a hidden scroll of Rabbi Chiyya, where Isi ben Yehudah interprets the verse 'כי תבוא בכרם רעך' (When you come into your neighbor's vineyard) as referring to any person, not just a worker.
Rav comments that Isi ben Yehudah's interpretation leaves no living person exempt from the right to eat from another's vineyard.

sub.text: Rav Ashi's question to Rav Kahana
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's question to Rav Kahana
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi questions whether the verse applies only to workers who eat during their meal, not to any passerby.
Rav Kahana answers that even so, the owner prefers to hire workers rather than have everyone eat his produce.

items.text: Inquiry: Does the worker eat from his own or from Heaven?
items.text_en: Inquiry: Does the worker eat from his own or from Heaven?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a worker eats from his own wages or from a gift from Heaven, and explores the practical difference: if he says 'give to my wife and children.' It attempts to prove from the Mishnah that it is from Heaven, since a worker hired for a small wage can eat expensive produce.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an inquiry: does a worker eat from his own wages or from a gift from Heaven?
The Gemara asks the practical difference: if the worker says 'give to my wife and children,' the ruling depends on whether the right is his own or a gift from Heaven.
The Gemara attempts to prove from the Mishnah that a worker hired for a small wage can eat expensive produce, concluding that this must be a gift from Heaven.

items.text: Rejection of proof from Rabbi Elazar Chasma's dispute
items.text_en: Rejection of proof from Rabbi Elazar Chasma's dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof from the dispute between Rabbi Elazar Chasma and the Sages, explaining that both agree the worker eats from his own, but they disagree about the interpretation of 'with your soul' (כְּנַפְשְׁךָ): one says it refers to something one risks his life for, the other that it teaches that if you muzzle the worker you are exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove the dispute about whether the worker eats from his own or from Heaven by citing the Mishnah where Rabbi Elazar Chasma and the Sages disagree about the worker eating more than his wages.

The Gemara rejects the proof, explaining that both sides agree the worker eats from his own, but they disagree about the interpretation of 'כְּנַפְשְׁךָ' (like your soul): one says it refers to something one risks his life for.
The Gemara concludes that the other opinion interprets 'כְּנַפְשְׁךָ' to teach that just as muzzling yourself exempts you, so muzzling a worker exempts the employer.

items.text: Proof from a Nazirite and a worker's request to give to family
items.text_en: Proof from a Nazirite and a worker's request to give to family
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove from a Nazirite who says 'give to my wife and children' that we do not listen, and similarly a worker who says so, concluding that the worker eats from Heaven. It resolves that the worker case is actually about a Nazirite, but the verse 'do not put into your vessel' is cited for the worker.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove from a Nazirite who says 'give to my wife and children' that we do not listen, implying the worker eats from his own.
The Gemara objects that the worker case is actually about a Nazirite, but questions why it is taught separately.
A baraita cites the verse 'וְאֶל כֶּלְיְךָ לֹא תִתֵּן' (do not put into your vessel) for the worker, but the Gemara objects that this is the Nazirite's reason.
The Gemara resolves that indeed it is about a Nazirite, but because the baraita was taught in the language of a worker, it cites the worker's verse.

items.text: Beginning of a new proof from a baraita about a worker cutting figs
items.text_en: Beginning of a new proof from a baraita about a worker cutting figs
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to cite a baraita about a worker hired to cut figs, which will be used to further clarify the issue.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita about a worker hired to cut figs, as a potential proof for the ongoing discussion.

items.text: Challenge from the Mishnah's case of a worker eating with his son
items.text_en: Challenge from the Mishnah's case of a worker eating with his son
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the view that the worker eats from the owner's portion by citing the Mishnah where a worker stipulates that his son may eat in his stead. The son is liable for tithes, which would be problematic if the worker eats from the owner's portion, as the son would then be eating from the owner's produce. Ravina answers that it appears like a transaction (מקח), so the son is liable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's case where a worker stipulates that his son may eat in his stead; the worker is exempt from tithes but the son is liable.
The Gemara challenges: if the worker eats from the owner's portion, why is the son liable for tithes?
Ravina answers that the son is liable because the arrangement appears like a transaction (מקח), not a gift from Heaven.

items.text: Challenge from the case of neta revai
items.text_en: Challenge from the case of neta revai
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a worker hired to work in a neta revai (fourth-year vineyard) of the owner. If the owner did not inform the worker, he redeems the fruit and feeds them. This challenges the view that the worker eats from Heaven's portion, because if so, why would the owner need to redeem? The Gemara answers that it appears like a mistaken transaction (מקח טעות).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a worker hired for a neta revai (fourth-year vineyard) who may not eat unless the owner redeems the fruit, challenging the view that the worker eats from Heaven's portion.
The Gemara asks: if the worker eats from Heaven's portion, why would the owner need to redeem the fruit, since Heaven does not grant forbidden items?
The Gemara answers that the redemption is necessary because it appears like a mistaken transaction (מקח טעות), not because the worker eats from Heaven's portion.

items.text: Challenge from the case of opened wine barrels
items.text_en: Challenge from the case of opened wine barrels
items.desc_en: The Gemara continues with the baraita's second case: if the owner's fig cakes were broken or wine barrels opened, the workers do not eat, but if not informed, the owner tithes and feeds them. This again challenges the view that the worker eats from Heaven's portion. The Gemara questions whether the appearance of a mistaken transaction applies to opened barrels, since the workers know the wine is already liable for tithes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the view that the worker eats from Heaven's portion by citing the baraita's second case: if the owner's fig cakes were broken or wine barrels opened, the workers do not eat, and if not informed, the owner tithes and feeds them — asking why tithing is needed if the worker's portion is exempt.

The Gemara objects that while the case of broken fig cakes might appear as a mistaken transaction, opened wine barrels cannot be explained that way because the workers know the wine is already liable for tithes.

items.text: Resolution of the barrel case via Rabbi Akiva's opinion
items.text_en: Resolution of the barrel case via Rabbi Akiva's opinion
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet answers that the barrels were opened into the pit, and the Gemara notes that wine becomes liable for tithes only when it goes into the pit. The Gemara then invokes Rabbi Akiva's opinion that liability begins when the wine forms a crust (מקפה). The workers could claim they did not know the wine had formed a crust, and in that locale, the owner was the one who would skim it. The Gemara then cites Rav Zevid's tradition that wine is liable when it goes into the pit and forms a crust, and Rabbi Akiva says when it is drawn into barrels. The workers could claim they did not know the wine had been drawn, and in that locale, the one who seals the barrels is the one who draws.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet answers that the barrels were opened into the pit, explaining why the workers could not have known the wine became liable for tithes.
The Gemara objects that a baraita states wine becomes liable for tithes only when it goes into the pit, so the workers would have known.
The Gemara resolves that the case follows Rabbi Akiva's opinion that liability begins when the wine forms a crust (מקפה), so the workers could claim ignorance.
The Gemara objects that the workers could still be expected to anticipate the crust formation.

The Gemara suggests that the owner could have told the workers to be aware of the crust, but then notes that in that locale, the owner himself would skim the crust, so the workers had no reason to suspect it.
Rav Zevid cites a tradition from the school of Rabbi Hoshaya that wine is liable when it goes into the pit and forms a crust, while Rabbi Akiva says when it is drawn into barrels.
The Gemara now resolves even if the barrels were not opened into the pit, the workers could claim they did not know the wine had been drawn into barrels.
The Gemara objects that the owner could have told the workers to anticipate the drawing.
The Gemara answers that in that locale, the one who seals the barrels is the one who draws the wine, so the workers had no reason to suspect the drawing occurred.

items.text: Challenge from the Mishnah of cutting produce for dependents
items.text_en: Challenge from the Mishnah of cutting produce for dependents
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where a worker may cut produce for himself, his adult children, his adult slaves, and his wife, but not for minors or animals. The Gemara initially assumes the worker is providing their meals, and challenges: if the worker eats from the owner's portion, why can't he cut for minors? The Gemara answers that the case is where the worker does not provide their meals, and adults can waive their rights.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah (baraita) listing whom a worker may cut produce for: himself, adult children, adult slaves, and his wife, but not minors or animals.
The Gemara assumes the worker provides their meals and challenges: if the worker eats from the owner's portion (משלו), why can't he cut for minors?
The Gemara answers that the case is where the worker does not provide their meals, and adults can waive their rights.

items.text: Reconciliation of the baraita with the Mishnah
items.text_en: Reconciliation of the baraita with the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita from Rabbi Hoshaya that allows cutting for adult children and Canaanite slaves (both adult and minor) but not for minor children. The Gemara initially suggests the dispute is about whether the worker eats from his own portion or Heaven's, but concludes that both agree it is from his own portion. The difference is whether the worker provides meals: the Mishnah is where he does not, the baraita is where he does. The Gemara then questions why minors cannot cut in the baraita, and answers that the Torah did not grant the worker the pain of his minor children. Finally, the Gemara confirms that the Mishnah is where the worker does not provide meals.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita from Rabbi Hoshaya that permits cutting (קוֹצֵץ) for oneself, one's wife, adult children, and Canaanite slaves (both adult and minor), but not for minor children or animals.

The Gemara initially assumes both the Mishnah and the baraita deal with a case where the worker provides meals (מַעֲלֶה לָהֶן מְזוֹנוֹת), and the dispute is whether the worker eats from his own portion (מִשֶּׁלּוֹ) or from Heaven's (מִשֶּׁל שָׁמַיִם).

The Gemara rejects this, stating that all agree the worker eats from his own portion; the difference is that the Mishnah deals with a case where the worker does not provide meals (בְּשֶׁאֵין מַעֲלֶה לָהֶן מְזוֹנוֹת), while the baraita deals with one where he does.
The Gemara questions: if the baraita is where the worker provides meals, why can't he cut for minor children as well?
The Gemara answers that the Torah did not grant the worker the right to the pain (צַעֲרַיְיהוּ) of his minor children, so he cannot cut for them.
The Gemara confirms that the Mishnah is established as a case where the worker does not provide meals (בְּשֶׁאֵין מַעֲלֶה לָהֶן מְזוֹנוֹת).

items.text: Resolving the dispute about the master's right to withhold food
items.text_en: Resolving the dispute about the master's right to withhold food
items.desc_en: The Gemara first questions how the Mishnah's ruling fits with the view that a master can say 'work with me and I will not feed you'. It then reinterprets the dispute as being about whether the worker eats from heaven's portion or the owner's, and concludes that the disagreement is about whether the worker eats from his own (heaven's) or the owner's.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Mishnah's ruling fits with the view that a master can say 'work with me and I will not feed you'.
The Gemara proposes that both views agree the worker eats from heaven's portion, but then objects that Rabbi Yochanan would be abandoning the Mishnah for a baraita.
The Gemara resolves that everyone agrees the worker eats from heaven's portion, and the dispute is about whether the master can withhold food (מזונות).
The Gemara concludes that the dispute is actually about whether the worker eats from the owner's portion or from heaven's portion.

items.text: Mishnah: Who may stipulate to eat from produce
items.text_en: Mishnah: Who may stipulate to eat from produce
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that a person may stipulate to eat from produce on behalf of himself, his adult children, his adult slaves, and his wife, because they have understanding. But he may not stipulate for minors or for his animal, because they lack understanding.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that a person may stipulate to eat from produce on behalf of himself, his adult children, his adult slaves, and his wife, because they have understanding, but not for minors or his animal.

items.text: Mishnah: Workers in a fourth-year vineyard and other cases
items.text_en: Mishnah: Workers in a fourth-year vineyard and other cases
items.desc_en: The Mishnah continues: If one hires workers to work in his fourth-year vineyard (netta revai), they may not eat. If he did not inform them, he redeems the fruit and feeds them. Similarly, if his fig cakes crumbled or his wine jars burst, workers may not eat; if not informed, he tithes and feeds them.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that if one hires workers for his neta revai (fourth-year vineyard), they may not eat; if he did not inform them, he redeems and feeds them; similarly for broken wine barrels.

items.text: Mishnah: Fruit watchmen eat by regional custom, not Torah law
items.text_en: Mishnah: Fruit watchmen eat by regional custom, not Torah law
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that fruit watchmen may eat from the produce by regional custom (hilchot medina), but not by Torah law.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that fruit guards eat by regional custom (הלכות מדינה), but not by Torah law.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel about watchmen, with objections and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel about watchmen, with objections and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav limits the Mishnah to watchmen of gardens and orchards, but watchmen of winepresses and stacks eat by Torah law, since guarding is like working. Shmuel reverses this: watchmen of winepresses and stacks eat by custom, but garden watchmen eat neither by Torah nor custom. The Gemara brings objections from a baraita about a cow and from a mishna about melons, and resolves them. Finally, Rav Ashi supports Shmuel from a tannaitic source.

sub.desc_en: Rav limits the Mishnah's rule to watchmen of gardens and orchards, but watchmen of winepresses and stacks eat by Torah law, since guarding is like working.
Shmuel reverses Rav's position: watchmen of winepresses and stacks eat by custom, but garden watchmen eat neither by Torah nor custom, since guarding is not like working.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Huna's objection
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Huna's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Huna objects from a baraita about a watchman of a cow who becomes impure, arguing that if guarding is not like working, why would the watchman become impure?
Rabbah bar Ulla rejects the objection by explaining that the impurity is a decree (גזירה) lest the watchman move a limb of the cow, not because guarding is considered working.
Rav Kahana objects from a mishna about a watchman of melon patches who may eat from each patch proportionally, arguing that if guarding is not like working, why may he eat?

Rav Shimi bar Ashi rejects the objection by explaining that the mishna refers to uprooted melons (עקורין) whose work is not yet complete for tithes, so the watchman eats by Torah law as a worker, not as a guard.
Rav Ashi supports Shmuel by citing a tannaitic source that distinguishes between those who eat by Torah law and those who eat only by custom, implying that some watchmen eat only by custom.
The Gemara resolves the support by analyzing the tannaitic source's second clause, which lists those who eat neither by Torah nor by custom, including garden watchmen, confirming Shmuel's position.

items.text: Mishnah: The four watchmen and their liability rules
items.text_en: Mishnah: The four watchmen and their liability rules
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the four types of watchmen: unpaid watchman, borrower, paid watchman, and renter. The unpaid watchman swears to all cases, the borrower pays for all. The paid watchman and renter swear for breakage, captivity, and death, but pay for loss and theft.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the four types of watchmen and their respective liability rules: the unpaid watchman swears in all cases, the borrower pays for all, and the paid watchman and renter swear for breakage, captivity, and death but pay for loss and theft.

items.text: Gemara: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah and the dispute about the renter
items.text_en: Gemara: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah and the dispute about the renter
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak identifies the Tanna as Rabbi Meir, who holds that a renter is like a paid watchman. Rava questions this, noting that Rabbi Meir elsewhere says a renter is like an unpaid watchman. Rabbah bar Avuh reverses the tradition. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak concludes: there are four watchmen but only three distinct laws.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna of the Mishnah that lists four watchmen.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak identifies the Tanna as Rabbi Meir, who holds that a renter is like a paid watchman.
Rava objects that everyone agrees there are four watchmen, so the identification is trivial.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak clarifies that the question is specifically who teaches that a renter is like a paid watchman, and that is Rabbi Meir.
The Gemara objects that elsewhere Rabbi Meir says a renter is like an unpaid watchman, contradicting the Mishnah's position.
Rabbah bar Avuh reverses the tradition, so that Rabbi Meir holds the renter is like a paid watchman and Rabbi Yehuda like an unpaid one.
The Gemara asks: if the renter and paid watchman are identical, there are only three distinct laws, not four.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves: there are four watchmen but only three distinct laws, since the renter and paid watchman share the same law.

items.text: Anecdote: Shepherd whose animal fell into the river
items.text_en: Anecdote: Shepherd whose animal fell into the river
items.desc_en: A shepherd was grazing animals on the bank of the Papa River. One animal slipped and fell into the water. The shepherd came before Rabbah, who exempted him, saying: What could he have done?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara tells a story of a shepherd whose animal fell into the river, and Rabbah exempted him, saying: what could he have done?
Rabbah exempts the shepherd from liability, reasoning that the shepherd could not have prevented the accident.

items.text: Abaye's challenge to Rava's definition of proper guarding
items.text_en: Abaye's challenge to Rava's definition of proper guarding
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rava's earlier statement that a watchman who guards like people normally do is exempt. He asks: if a watchman enters the city when people normally enter, or sleeps when people normally sleep, is he also exempt? Rava answers yes, implying that normal behavior is sufficient.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents Abaye's challenge to Rava: if a watchman guards like people normally do, is he exempt even when entering the city or sleeping at normal times? Rava answers yes.

items.text: Objections from the story of David and Jacob
items.text_en: Objections from the story of David and Jacob
items.desc_en: Abaye brings a baraita listing unavoidable accidents for a paid watchman, citing the verse about David's shepherds being taken by raiders. Rava deflects, saying those were city guards. Abaye then cites Jacob's statement about his guarding, and Rava explains that Jacob guarded like city guards, implying a higher standard.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects by citing a baraita that lists unavoidable accidents (אונסין) for a paid watchman, including the verse about David's shepherds being taken by raiders.
Rava deflects by explaining that those shepherds were city guards (חזני מתא), who are held to a higher standard.
Abaye objects again by citing a baraita about a paid watchman's duty, quoting Jacob's statement about his guarding.
Rava explains that Jacob also guarded like city guards (חזני מתא), implying a higher standard, and Abaye accepts this.

items.text: The case of the shepherd who left his flock
items.text_en: The case of the shepherd who left his flock
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses a shepherd who left his flock and went to town; if a wolf or lion attacks, we assess whether he could have saved them. Abaye initially thinks this refers to entering during normal entry times, but Rava explains it's when he entered at an unusual time. The Gemara then questions why he is exempt if his initial negligence led to the unavoidable accident, and answers that he heard the lion's roar and fled, but he should have gathered other shepherds and sticks.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: a shepherd who left his flock and went to town, and a wolf or lion attacked, is assessed based on whether he could have saved them.
The Gemara asks whether the baraita refers to the shepherd entering the town at a normal time when people usually enter.
Rava answers that the baraita refers to the shepherd entering at an unusual time when people do not normally enter.
The Gemara objects: if the shepherd entered at an unusual time, his initial act was negligent, so even if the final event was an unavoidable accident (אונס), he should be liable.
The Gemara answers that the shepherd heard the lion's roar and fled, so his entry was not negligent but a response to danger.
The Gemara objects: if he fled because of the lion's roar, why assess him at all? He could not have done anything.
The Gemara resolves that the shepherd should have gathered other shepherds and sticks to confront the lion, so his failure to do so makes him liable.

items.text: Distinction between paid and unpaid watchmen
items.text_en: Distinction between paid and unpaid watchmen
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the baraita specifically mentions a paid watchman, since even an unpaid watchman would be liable if he failed to gather help. The answer is that an unpaid watchman is liable without payment, while a paid watchman is liable with payment. The Gemara then explains that a paid watchman who is liable for an unavoidable accident pays the owner and then recovers from the thief.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the baraita specifically mentions a paid watchman, since an unpaid watchman would also be liable if he failed to gather help, and answers that the unpaid watchman is liable without payment while the paid watchman is liable with payment.
The Gemara asks up to what amount the paid watchman pays, and answers that he pays up to the value of the animals, recovering from the thief.

items.text: Rav Pappa's question and the opinion of Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's question and the opinion of Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye what practical difference the higher standard of guarding makes. Abaye answers that it affects the animal's fitness or the extra effort required. Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna disagree with Rabbah's earlier ruling, holding that the extra wage is for extra guarding.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye what practical difference the higher standard of guarding makes, and Abaye answers that it affects the animal's fitness (כושרה דחיותא).
Abaye adds that the higher wage also compensates for the extra effort (טרחא יתירתא) required.

sub.text: Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna's disagreement
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna's disagreement
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna reject Rabbah's earlier ruling, holding that the extra wage is explicitly for extra guarding (נטירותא יתירתא).

items.text: The case of Bar Adda the porter
items.text_en: The case of Bar Adda the porter
items.desc_en: Bar Adda the porter was transporting animals across a bridge; one animal pushed another into the water. Rav Pappa held him liable, saying he should have crossed them one by one. Bar Adda protested that he was unable to do so, and Rav Pappa responded that earlier authorities had already complained about him.

sub.desc_en: Introduces the case of Bar Adda the porter, who was transporting animals across a bridge and one animal pushed another into the water.
Rav Pappa holds Bar Adda liable, ruling that he should have crossed the animals one by one.
Bar Adda protests that he was unable to cross them one by one, implying the animals were too unruly.
Rav Pappa dismisses the protest, stating that earlier authorities had already complained about Bar Adda's negligence.

items.text: The case of Ayvu's flax and the ruling of Rav Nachman
items.text_en: The case of Ayvu's flax and the ruling of Rav Nachman
items.desc_en: Ayvu deposited flax with a storekeeper; it was stolen, and later the thief was caught. Rav Nachman held the storekeeper liable. The Gemara questions whether this conflicts with Rav Huna bar Avin's ruling that a paid watchman may choose to make a claim against the thief rather than swear. Rava explains that in Ayvu's case, there were guards nearby who could have been summoned, so the storekeeper was negligent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the case: Ayvu deposited flax with a storekeeper, it was stolen, the thief was caught, and Rav Nachman held the storekeeper liable.
The Gemara questions whether Rav Nachman's ruling conflicts with Rav Huna bar Avin's ruling that a paid watchman may choose to make a claim against the thief rather than swear.
Rava explains that in Ayvu's case, there were guards nearby who could have been summoned, so the storekeeper was negligent and liable.

items.text: Mishnah: Definitions of unavoidable accidents
items.text_en: Mishnah: Definitions of unavoidable accidents
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists what constitutes an unavoidable accident for a shepherd: one wolf is not an unavoidable accident, but two are; Rabbi Yehuda says in a time of wolf attacks even one is. Two dogs are not an unavoidable accident; Yadua the Babylonian says from one direction it is not, from two directions it is. Bandits are an unavoidable accident; lion, bear, leopard, lynx, and snake are unavoidable accidents. This applies when they come on their own, but if the shepherd led them to a place of wild animals or bandits, it is not an unavoidable accident. If an animal dies naturally it is an unavoidable accident; if he starved it, it is not; if it climbed to high places and fell, it is an unavoidable accident; if he led it to high places and it fell, it is not.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one wolf is not an unavoidable accident, but two are.
Rabbi Yehuda says that in a time of wolf attacks, even one wolf is an unavoidable accident.
The Mishnah states that two dogs are not an unavoidable accident, but Yadua the Babylonian says in the name of Rabbi Meir that from one direction it is not, from two directions it is.

sub.text: Yadua the Babylonian in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.text_en: Yadua the Babylonian in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.desc_en: Yadua the Babylonian reports in the name of Rabbi Meir that dogs from one direction are not an unavoidable accident, but from two directions they are.
The Mishnah lists bandits, lion, bear, leopard, lynx, and snake as unavoidable accidents.

The Mishnah qualifies that these are unavoidable accidents only when the animals come on their own, but if the shepherd led the flock to a place of wild animals or bandits, it is not an unavoidable accident.
The Mishnah concludes that natural death is an unavoidable accident, but if the shepherd starved the animal or led it to high places where it fell, it is not an unavoidable accident.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying the dispute about one wolf
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying the dispute about one wolf
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: a baraita states that one wolf is an unavoidable accident. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves this by saying that baraita refers to a time of wolf attacks, and it follows Rabbi Yehuda's opinion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: a baraita states that one wolf is an unavoidable accident (אונס), contradicting the Mishnah's ruling.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the contradiction by explaining that the baraita refers to a time of wolf attacks (שעת משלחת זאבים) and follows Rabbi Yehuda's opinion.

items.text: Gemara: Bandits and the question of armed confrontation
items.text_en: Gemara: Bandits and the question of armed confrontation
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why bandits are an unavoidable accident; shouldn't the shepherd confront them? Rav answers that these are armed bandits. The Gemara then raises a question: if both the bandits and the shepherd are armed, what is the law? Is the shepherd expected to confront them, or does he not risk his life? The conclusion is that the bandit risks his life, but the shepherd does not. Abaye then tells Rava about a shepherd who confronted a thief and was killed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why bandits are classified as an unavoidable accident (אונס), arguing that a shepherd should be able to confront them man-to-man.
Rav answers that the case involves armed bandits (ליסטים מזויין), so the shepherd is not expected to risk confrontation.
The Gemara raises a further inquiry: if both the bandits and the shepherd are armed, what is the law — is the shepherd expected to confront them?
The Gemara resolves that the bandit risks his life (מסר נפשיה) but the shepherd does not, so the shepherd is not obligated to confront him.
Abaye tells Rava about a shepherd who confronted a thief and was killed, illustrating the danger of armed confrontation.

items.text: Opening narrative from the previous Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening narrative from the previous Mishnah
items.desc_en: A story is cited about a shepherd who claimed various dangers and took the animal, raising a question about liability. The Gemara will later address this.

sub.desc_en: A story is cited about a shepherd who claimed various dangers and took the animal, raising a question about liability.

items.text: Mishnah: Stipulations for exemption
items.text_en: Mishnah: Stipulations for exemption
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a bailee can stipulate to be exempt from the usual Torah obligations, but any stipulation that contradicts Torah law is void. It also introduces the rule that a condition must precede the action to be valid, and that a condition must be possible to fulfill at the end.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a bailee can stipulate exemption from Torah obligations, but any stipulation contradicting Torah law is void, and a condition must precede the action and be possible to fulfill.

items.text: Gemara's question and answer: Rabbi Judah's view
items.text_en: Gemara's question and answer: Rabbi Judah's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah allows stipulations to exempt from Torah obligations, since any condition contradicting Torah law is void. It answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Judah, who holds that in monetary matters such a condition is valid, citing a baraita about betrothal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah allows stipulations that contradict Torah law, since any such condition is normally void.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Judah, who holds that in monetary matters a condition contradicting Torah law is valid, citing a baraita about betrothal.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding the Mishnah's first clause
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding the Mishnah's first clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's first clause (all conditions contradicting Torah are void) seems to follow Rabbi Meir, not Rabbi Judah. It resolves that the entire Mishnah is Rabbi Judah, and the first clause refers to a non-monetary matter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's later clause (all conditions contradicting Torah are void) seems to follow Rabbi Meir, not Rabbi Yehuda.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah is entirely Rabbi Yehuda, and the later clause refers to a non-monetary matter.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding the second clause
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding the second clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the second clause (condition must precede action) follows Rabbi Meir, not Rabbi Judah. It resolves that the entire Mishnah is Rabbi Meir, and the first clause is different because the bailee never obligated himself from the start.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the second clause (a condition preceded by an action is void) follows Rabbi Meir, not Rabbi Judah, citing a baraita where Abba Chalaphta states this rule in Rabbi Meir's name.
The Gemara resolves that the entire Mishnah follows Rabbi Meir, and the first clause is different because the bailee never obligated himself from the start.

items.text: Stipulation for a paid bailee to be like a borrower
items.text_en: Stipulation for a paid bailee to be like a borrower
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that a paid bailee can stipulate to be liable as a borrower. The Gemara asks how this is effective, and Shmuel says it requires a kinyan, while Rabbi Yochanan says even without a kinyan, the benefit of being trusted obligates him.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that a paid bailee can stipulate to be liable as a borrower.
The Gemara asks how this stipulation is effective — merely by words?
Shmuel answers that it requires a formal kinyan (acquisition) from him.
Rabbi Yochanan says that even without a kinyan, the benefit of being trusted (reputation as a reliable person) obligates him.

items.text: Dispute about conditions impossible to fulfill at the end
items.text_en: Dispute about conditions impossible to fulfill at the end
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the Mishnah's rule that a condition must be possible to fulfill at the end. Rav Tabla cites Rabbi Judah ben Teima who says such a condition is void, while the Sages say it is valid. A baraita illustrates with impossible conditions in a get.

sub.desc_en: Rav Tabla cites Rav that the Mishnah's rule that a condition possible to fulfill at the end is valid reflects only Rabbi Judah ben Teima's position, but the Sages hold that even an impossible condition is valid if stipulated from the start.
A baraita is cited illustrating that a condition impossible to fulfill (e.g., ascending to heaven) is valid if fulfilled, and the get is valid.
Rabbi Judah ben Teima rules that such an impossible condition is merely a playful expression (מפליגה) and the get is valid, contradicting the Sages' view that the condition itself is valid.

items.text: Ruling and proof from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Ruling and proof from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Judah ben Teima. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak proves this from the Mishnah's wording, which implies that only a possible condition is valid, but an impossible one is void.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rav rules that the halacha follows Rabbi Yehuda ben Teima, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak supports this from the Mishnah's wording.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak proves this from the Mishnah's precise wording, which implies that only a possible condition is valid, but an impossible one is void.

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter and next Mishnah
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter and next Mishnah
items.desc_en: The chapter concludes with 'Hadran alach', and the next Mishnah begins discussing the case of a borrower who also borrows the owner, exempting from payment.

sub.desc_en: The chapter concludes with the standard 'Hadran alach' formula, marking the end of the tractate chapter.
The Mishnah introduces the case of a borrower who also borrows the owner, exempting from payment, citing the verse 'If its owner is with him, he shall not pay'.

items.text: Analysis of the Mishnah's case: borrowing the animal after the owner
items.text_en: Analysis of the Mishnah's case: borrowing the animal after the owner
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's phrasing that the first clause ('with it') means the owner is literally with the animal at the time of borrowing. It then questions how this is possible if the animal requires meshikhah (acquisition by pulling) while the owner is acquired by verbal agreement. Two answers are offered: either the animal is already in the borrower's courtyard (no meshikhah needed), or the owner says 'you yourself are not borrowed until the moment of the animal's meshikhah'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's phrasing that 'with it' means the owner is literally with the animal, and questions how this is possible given that the animal requires meshikhah (acquisition by pulling) while the owner is acquired by verbal agreement.
The first answer proposes that the animal is already in the borrower's courtyard, so no meshikhah (pulling) is needed.
The second answer proposes that the owner says 'you yourself are not borrowed until the moment of the animal's meshikhah (pulling)', so both are acquired simultaneously.

items.text: Mishnah: The four guardians
items.text_en: Mishnah: The four guardians
items.desc_en: The Mishnah enumerates the four types of guardians: unpaid guardian, borrower, paid guardian, and renter. It states their respective liabilities: the unpaid guardian swears to all cases, the borrower pays for all, and the paid guardian and renter swear for breakage, captivity, and death but pay for loss and theft.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing the four types of guardians: unpaid guardian, borrower, paid guardian, and renter.
The Mishnah states the liability of the unpaid guardian (swears in all cases) and the borrower (pays for all).
The Mishnah states the liability of the paid guardian and renter: they swear for breakage, captivity, and death, but pay for loss and theft.

items.text: Derivation of the guardians from the Torah
items.text_en: Derivation of the guardians from the Torah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that identifies the three Torah portions: the first (Exodus 22:6-8) for the unpaid guardian, the second (Exodus 22:9-12) for the paid guardian, and the third (Exodus 22:13-14) for the borrower. It questions why the second is assigned to the paid guardian rather than the first, and resolves this by arguing that liability for principal without an oath is more stringent than double payment with an oath, as demonstrated by the borrower who pays only principal but has all benefit.

sub.desc_en: The baraita identifies the three Torah portions: first for the unpaid guardian, second for the paid guardian, third for the borrower.
The Gemara questions why the second portion is assigned to the paid guardian rather than the first, since the first could also apply.
The Gemara first argues that the second portion fits the paid guardian because he is liable for theft and loss, but an objection is raised that the first portion involves double payment.
The Gemara resolves that liability for principal without an oath is more stringent than double payment with an oath, as demonstrated by the borrower who pays only principal but has all benefit.
An objection is raised that the borrower does not have all benefit because he must feed and guard the animal.
The Gemara offers alternative answers: either say 'most benefit' instead of 'all benefit', or apply the case to borrowing vessels which require no upkeep.

items.text: Source for the paid guardian's liability for loss
items.text_en: Source for the paid guardian's liability for loss
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the source for the paid guardian's liability for loss (avaidah). It cites a baraita that derives it from the verse 'if it is stolen' (Exodus 22:11), interpreting the doubled language to include loss. It then addresses the objection that this derivation works only for those who hold that the Torah does not speak in human language; for those who do, an a fortiori argument is offered: if theft (close to an unavoidable accident) is paid, then loss (close to negligence) certainly should be.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the source for theft (גניבה) is explicit in the verse, and asks: from where do we derive the paid guardian's liability for loss (אבידה)?
A baraita is cited, deriving loss from the doubled language 'אם גנוב יגנב' (if it is stolen) — implying any loss, not just theft.
The Gemara objects that this derivation works only for those who hold that the Torah does not speak in human language; for those who hold that it does, what can be said?

The sages in the West (אָמְרִי בְּמַעְרְבָא) offer an a fortiori argument: if theft, which is close to an unavoidable accident (אונס), is paid, then loss, which is close to negligence (פשיעה), certainly should be paid.
The Gemara resolves that even for those who hold the Torah speaks in human language, the verse nonetheless wrote the matter explicitly despite its being derivable by a fortiori reasoning.

items.text: Source for the borrower's liability for captivity
items.text_en: Source for the borrower's liability for captivity
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the borrower's liability for captivity (shevuyah). It rejects a logical derivation from breakage and death because captivity is a less foreseeable accident. It then proposes a gezerah shavah from the paid guardian, but that is refuted. Finally, it adopts Rabbi Natan's view that the word 'or' in the verse (Exodus 22:13) includes captivity. The Gemara then addresses an objection that 'or' is needed to divide liability, and discusses the dispute between Rabbi Yoshiya and Rabbi Yonatan regarding the interpretation of such inclusive language.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: for the borrower, breakage and death are explicit in the verse, but whence do we derive liability for captivity (שבויה)?
The Gemara rejects a logical derivation from breakage and death, because captivity is a less foreseeable accident (אונסא דלא סליק אדעתא).
The Gemara proposes a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the paid guardian, where captivity is included alongside breakage and death.
The Gemara refutes the verbal analogy: the paid guardian is a lenient case (liable only for negligence), while the borrower is a strict case (liable for all accidents), so the analogy is invalid.
The Gemara adopts Rabbi Natan's view that the word 'אוֹ' (or) in the verse (Exodus 22:13) includes captivity.
An objection is raised: the word 'אוֹ' is needed to divide liability (to teach that the borrower is liable for each accident separately, not only when both occur together).
The Gemara notes that this objection applies only according to Rabbi Yonatan, but asks what can be said according to Rabbi Yoshiya.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yoshiya interprets the word 'וְאֶת' (and) in the verse about cursing parents to include each parent individually, showing that inclusive language can add cases.
The Gemara cites Rabbi Yonatan's opposing view that the same verse implies both together and each individually, explaining the dispute over how inclusive language works.

items.text: Rejecting the need for a verse to divide
items.text_en: Rejecting the need for a verse to divide
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the possibility that Rabbi Yoshiyah would require a verse to divide the case of a borrower who kills part of an animal, arguing that it is logical: killing half is like killing the whole.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that a verse must specify 'together' to divide liability.
The Gemara rejects the need for a verse to divide in this case, arguing that even Rabbi Yoshiyah would agree because killing half the animal is logically equivalent to killing the whole.

items.text: Deriving theft and loss for a borrower via a fortiori
items.text_en: Deriving theft and loss for a borrower via a fortiori
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of a borrower's liability for theft and loss. It rejects learning from breakage and death because those are unavoidable, and instead cites a baraita that uses a kal vachomer from a paid bailee, concluding it is a kal vachomer with no refutation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of a borrower's liability for theft and loss, and rejects learning from breakage and death because those are unavoidable.
A baraita is cited that derives the borrower's liability for theft and loss via a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) from a paid bailee, concluding it is an irrefutable kal vachomer.

items.text: Explaining the kal vachomer's irrefutability
items.text_en: Explaining the kal vachomer's irrefutability
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the kal vachomer cannot be refuted: even though one could argue that a paid bailee pays double payment when claiming armed thieves, the borrower's principal is superior. Alternatively, the Gemara suggests that armed thieves are considered robbers, not thieves.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the baraita means by saying the kal vachomer has 'no refutation'.
