The Gemara explains that even though one could object that a paid bailee pays double payment when claiming armed thieves, the borrower's principal is superior, so the kal vachomer stands.
The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: the kal vachomer is irrefutable because armed thieves are considered robbers (גזלן), not thieves, so the paid bailee's liability for them is irrelevant.

items.text: Deriving the exemption for theft and loss when the owner is present
items.text_en: Deriving the exemption for theft and loss when the owner is present
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the source for exemption from theft and loss when the owner is present. It rejects learning from breakage and death (which are unavoidable) and instead derives it from a paid bailee via the principle of 'dayo' (it is sufficient for the derived case to be like the source).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have found the source for liability (of theft and loss for a borrower), from where do we derive the exemption (when the owner is present)?

The Gemara objects: if you say we derive the exemption from breakage and death (where the borrower is exempt when the owner is present), that is rejected because breakage and death are unavoidable (אונס), unlike theft and loss.

The Gemara answers: rather, the exemption for theft and loss when the owner is present is derived from a paid bailee (שומר שכר), and the paid bailee's exemption itself is derived from the borrower via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy).

The Gemara objects: with what method is the derivation made? If by a בנין אב (pattern), it can be refuted because the paid bailee is exempt from breakage and death (which are unavoidable), unlike the borrower.

The Gemara answers: rather, the verse 'וכי ישאל' (when a man borrows) uses a vav (ו) that adds to the preceding subject, teaching that the upper case (borrower) learns from the lower case (paid bailee).
The Gemara objects: still, the borrower cannot learn from the paid bailee because the paid bailee is exempt from breakage and death, while the borrower is liable for them.

The Gemara resolves: the liability for theft and loss in a borrower is derived from a paid bailee via a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument), but the principle of דיו (it is sufficient for the derived case to be like the source) limits the liability so that the exemption when the owner is present applies equally to the borrower.

items.text: Alternative derivation without 'dayo'
items.text_en: Alternative derivation without 'dayo'
items.desc_en: The Gemara addresses the view that does not accept the principle of 'dayo', and instead derives both liability and exemption from the extra 'vav' in the verse, teaching that the upper (borrower) learns from the lower (paid bailee) and vice versa.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: this works for the view that accepts the principle of 'dayo' (the derived law is limited to the original), but what can be said for the view that does not accept 'dayo'?

The Gemara answers: instead, the verse 'וכי ישאל' (and if a man borrows) teaches through the extra 'vav' that the upper category (borrower) learns from the lower (paid bailee) and the lower learns from the upper, without needing the 'dayo' principle.

items.text: Dispute over negligence when the owner is present
items.text_en: Dispute over negligence when the owner is present
items.desc_en: Rav Acha and Ravina dispute whether a borrower is exempt for negligence when the owner is present. One holds that the verse 'if its owner is with him' applies only to the explicit liabilities of a paid bailee and borrower, not to negligence derived via kal vachomer. The other holds that the verse applies even to a paid bailee and thus exempts negligence.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a dispute between Rav Acha and Ravina regarding whether a borrower is liable for negligence when the owner is present.
Rav Acha holds that the verse 'if its owner is with him' applies only to the explicit liabilities of a paid bailee and borrower, not to negligence derived via kal vachomer.
Ravina holds that the verse applies even to a paid bailee and thus exempts negligence.

items.text: Challenging the Mishnah's omission of an unpaid bailee
items.text_en: Challenging the Mishnah's omission of an unpaid bailee
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah lists cases of a borrower and a paid bailee being exempt when the owner is present, but does not mention an unpaid bailee. It responds that the Tanna is teaching a case in point, and the omission is not problematic.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Mishnah: it lists cases of a borrower and a paid bailee being exempt when the owner is present, but does not mention an unpaid bailee.
The Gemara retorts: by your reasoning, does the Mishnah even mention a paid bailee explicitly? (It does not, so the omission is not unique.)
The Gemara resolves: the Tanna is merely teaching a case in point (מִילְּתָא), and the omission of the unpaid bailee is not problematic.

items.text: Gemara's initial question about the Mishnah's omission
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question about the Mishnah's omission
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah includes cases derived from explicit verses but omits those derived from exposition, questioning why certain cases are included or excluded.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah includes cases derived from explicit verses but omits those derived from exposition.

items.text: Attempts to identify the Mishnah's author
items.text_en: Attempts to identify the Mishnah's author
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a Mishnah listing cases where the owner is with the animal and the borrower is exempt. It first suggests the author is Rabbi Yehuda, who equates a renter with a paid bailee, but notes the Mishnah omits the unpaid bailee. It then suggests Rabbi Meir, who equates a renter with an unpaid bailee, and the Mishnah includes the unpaid bailee by implication. Alternatively, it cites a version where Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda's views are reversed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah listing cases where the owner is with the animal and the borrower is exempt.
The Gemara suggests the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda, who equates a renter with a paid bailee, but notes the Mishnah omits the unpaid bailee.
The Gemara alternatively suggests the Mishnah follows Rabbi Meir, who equates a renter with an unpaid bailee, and the Mishnah includes the unpaid bailee by implication.
An alternative version is cited where Rabba bar Avuh reverses the views: Rabbi Meir equates a renter with a paid bailee, and Rabbi Yehuda with an unpaid bailee.

items.text: Rav Hamnuna's statement on 'בעליו עמו'
items.text_en: Rav Hamnuna's statement on 'בעליו עמו'
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna asserts that the exemption applies only if the owner is with the animal from the time of borrowing until the accident, implying that 'בעליו עמו' covers the entire period.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna states that the borrower is always liable unless the owner is with the animal from the time of borrowing until the accident, interpreting 'בעליו עמו' to apply to the entire period.

items.text: Rava's objection and resolution of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rava's objection and resolution of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rava objects by citing the Mishnah that exempts even when the owner is doing other work elsewhere. The Gemara initially interprets this as a different type of work, but then suggests it is the same type of work, and the Mishnah teaches a novelty in both the first and last clauses. The Gemara rejects this explanation, arguing that if both clauses refer to the same work, there is no novelty.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects by citing the Mishnah that exempts even when the owner is doing other work elsewhere, and asks whether this implies the owner was engaged in a different type of work.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah refers to the same type of work, and explains that 'another place' means the owner is walking ahead of the animal, not working elsewhere.
The Gemara objects that the latter clause of the Mishnah explicitly says 'on its back', implying the first clause refers to a different type of work.

The Gemara answers that both clauses refer to the same work, and each teaches a novelty: the first exempts even when the owner is not on the animal, and the second holds liable even when the owner is on the animal.
The Gemara rejects this, arguing that the novelty only makes sense if the first clause is a different type of work and the latter clause is the same type.
The Gemara concludes that if both clauses refer to the same work, there is no novelty, as both cases are identical.

items.text: Two baraitot contradicting Rav Hamnuna
items.text_en: Two baraitot contradicting Rav Hamnuna
items.desc_en: Two baraitot are cited: one requires the owner to be present at the time of borrowing but not at the accident, and the other requires the owner to be present at the time of the accident but not at the borrowing. Both contradict Rav Hamnuna's view that the owner must be present throughout, leading to his refutation.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited, deriving from the verse 'אִם בְּעָלָיו עִמּוֹ לֹא יְשַׁלֵּם' that if the owner was present at the time of borrowing, he need not be present at the accident, but if present at the accident, he must have been present at the borrowing.

A second baraita is cited, deriving from the verse 'בְּעָלָיו אֵין עִמּוֹ שַׁלֵּם יְשַׁלֵּם' that once the animal left the owner's domain for even one hour with the owner present and then died, the borrower is exempt, which contradicts Rav Hamnuna's position and constitutes his refutation.

items.text: Abaye and Rava's resolution of the baraitot
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava's resolution of the baraitot
items.desc_en: Abaye follows Rabbi Yoshiya and explains the verses to mean that if the owner is present at either the borrowing or the accident, the borrower is exempt. Rava follows Rabbi Yonatan and explains that the verses require the owner to be present at both times for exemption. The Gemara elaborates on Abaye's interpretation, showing how each verse implies a different condition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that Abaye follows Rabbi Yoshiya and Rava follows Rabbi Yonatan in interpreting the verses.

Abaye, following Rabbi Yoshiya, explains that the verse 'בְּעָלָיו אֵין עִמּוֹ' implies that only if the owner is absent at both times is the borrower liable, but if present at either time, he is exempt.
Abaye further explains that the verse 'אִם בְּעָלָיו עִמּוֹ' teaches that only if the owner is present at both times is the borrower exempt, but if present at only one time, he is liable.

The Gemara concludes Abaye's position: if the owner was present at the time of borrowing, he need not be present at the time of breakage or death; but if present at the time of breakage or death, he must also have been present at the time of borrowing.

items.text: Rava's interpretation of the verses and the debate over which time is primary
items.text_en: Rava's interpretation of the verses and the debate over which time is primary
items.desc_en: Rava holds like Rabbi Yonatan and reconciles the verses: 'If its owners are with it' implies both are present, and 'its owners are not with it' implies both are absent, teaching that presence at the time of borrowing suffices without presence at the time of breakage, but presence at the time of breakage requires presence at the time of borrowing. The Gemara debates whether the time of borrowing or the time of breakage is more significant, concluding that borrowing is primary because it brings the animal into the borrower's domain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rava holds like Rabbi Yonatan and reconciles the verses: 'If its owners are with it' implies both are present, and 'its owners are not with it' implies both are absent, teaching that presence at the time of borrowing suffices without presence at the time of breakage, but presence at the time of breakage requires presence at the time of borrowing.
The Gemara asks: Why not reverse the logic, making the time of breakage primary? It suggests that the time of borrowing is more significant because it brings the animal into the borrower's domain.
The Gemara objects: On the contrary, the time of breakage is more significant because the borrower is liable for unavoidable accidents (אונסין).

The Gemara resolves that the time of borrowing is primary because without borrowing there is no breakage, and the borrower is also liable for the animal's sustenance (מזונות), which is a continuous obligation.

items.text: Rav Ashi's alternative derivation from the verse
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's alternative derivation from the verse
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi derives the law directly from the verse 'When a man borrows from his fellow' – if the fellow is not with him, he pays; if the fellow is with him, he is exempt. The Gemara questions why the other verses are needed, and answers that without them one might think the phrasing is just the normal style of the verse.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi derives the law directly from the verse: if the fellow is not with him, he pays; if the fellow is with him, he is exempt.
The Gemara asks why the other verses ("if its owner is with him" and "if its owner is not with him") are needed if Rav Ashi's derivation suffices.
The Gemara answers that without those verses, one might think the phrasing is just the normal style of the verse, so they are needed to clarify the law.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's series of unresolved questions (בעיות)
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's series of unresolved questions (בעיות)
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama raises seven questions about various borderline cases of borrowing: borrowing a cow for plowing (where the owner is present but not for the main purpose), borrowing to show off, borrowing for less than a perutah's worth of work, borrowing two cows for a perutah's worth of work, borrowing from partners when only one is present, partners borrowing when only one is present, and a husband or wife borrowing when the other is present. Each question is left unresolved (תיקו).

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks whether borrowing a cow for breeding (plowing) is considered a valid borrowing, given that people usually borrow for work, not for this purpose.
Rami bar Chama asks whether borrowing a cow just to show it off is a valid borrowing, questioning if the required monetary value must provide benefit to the borrower.
Rami bar Chama asks whether borrowing a cow for work worth less than a perutah is valid, since less than a perutah is legally insignificant.
Rami bar Chama asks whether borrowing two cows for a perutah's worth of work is valid, considering whether we follow the borrower/lender or each cow individually.
Rami bar Chama asks whether borrowing from partners when only one is present exempts the borrower from liability for the absent partner's share.
Rami bar Chama asks whether partners who borrow together are exempt if only one of them is present with the owner at the time of borrowing.

Rami bar Chama asks whether a husband or wife borrowing from the other is considered 'with the owner,' depending on whether ownership of produce (קניין פירות) is like ownership of the body (קניין הגוף).

items.text: Ravina's question about an agent
items.text_en: Ravina's question about an agent
items.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi about one who says to his agent 'Go and borrow for me with my cow' – do we require the actual owner to be present, or is an agent considered like the owner? This question is left unresolved.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi whether an agent who borrows an animal is considered like the owner for the exemption of 'בעליו עמו' (the owner being with it), or if the actual owner must be present.

items.text: Rav Acha's clarification: the disputes behind the husband and agent questions
items.text_en: Rav Acha's clarification: the disputes behind the husband and agent questions
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Avya tells Rav Ashi that the question about a husband is a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish (whether קניין פירות is like קניין הגוף), and the question about an agent is a dispute between Rabbi Yonatan and Rabbi Yoshiya (whether a person's agent is like himself). The Gemara cites the relevant sources for each dispute.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Avya to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Avya to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Avya informs Rav Ashi that the question about a husband is a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish, and the question about an agent is a dispute between Rabbi Yonatan and Rabbi Yoshiya.

sub.text: Gemara citing the dispute of Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish
sub.text_en: Gemara citing the dispute of Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the dispute: one who sells a field for its produce — Rabbi Yochanan says he brings first fruits and recites the declaration, Reish Lakish says he brings but does not recite, reflecting their disagreement on whether קניין פירות (acquisition of produce) is like קניין הגוף (acquisition of the body).

sub.text: Gemara citing the dispute of Rabbi Yonatan and Rabbi Yoshiya
sub.text_en: Gemara citing the dispute of Rabbi Yonatan and Rabbi Yoshiya
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: one who tells an agent to annul his wife's vows — Rabbi Yoshiya says the annulment is invalid, Rabbi Yonatan says a person's agent is like himself, establishing the dispute underlying the agent question.

items.text: Rav Ilish's question about a slave and Rava's answer
items.text_en: Rav Ilish's question about a slave and Rava's answer
items.desc_en: Rav Ilish asks Rava about one who says to his slave 'Go and borrow with my cow' – the question is considered from both sides: for one who says an agent is like himself, perhaps a slave (who is not obligated in mitzvot) is different; for one who says an agent is not like himself, perhaps a slave's hand is like his master's hand. Rava rules that a slave's hand is like his master's hand.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ilish asks Rava about one who says to his slave 'Go and borrow with my cow', raising the question from both sides of the dispute about whether a slave is like an agent.

Rav Ilish elaborates the two possible considerations: for one who says an agent is like himself, perhaps a slave (not obligated in מצוות) is different; for one who says an agent is not like himself, perhaps a slave's hand is like his master's hand.
Rava rules that a slave's hand is like his master's hand, resolving the question.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's question about a husband in his wife's property
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's question about a husband in his wife's property
items.desc_en: The daf ends with Rami bar Chama beginning a new question about the status of a husband with regard to his wife's property, which is cut off.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama raises a question about the legal status of a husband with regard to his wife's property, which is cut off at the end of the daf.

items.text: Initial question: borrower or renter?
items.text_en: Initial question: borrower or renter?
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a question: if a husband borrows a cow from his wife, is he considered a borrower (שואל) or a renter (שוכר)? This distinction affects liability and the applicability of the exemption of 'borrowing with the owner' (שאלה בבעלים).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a question: if a husband borrows a cow from his wife, is he considered a borrower (שואל) or a renter (שוכר)?

items.text: Rava's initial answer and Rami bar Chama's refinement
items.text_en: Rava's initial answer and Rami bar Chama's refinement
items.desc_en: Rava initially dismisses the question, arguing that whether the husband is a borrower or renter, he is exempt because the wife is considered 'with him' (בבעלים). Rami bar Chama then refines the case: the husband first rented the cow and then married the owner. The question is whether the later marriage retroactively cancels the rental (making him a borrower with exemption) or the rental remains independent.

sub.desc_en: Rava dismisses the question, arguing that whether the husband is a borrower or renter, the wife's involvement makes it a case of 'with the owners' (בבעלים), exempting him.
Rami bar Chama refines the case: the husband first rented the cow from the woman and then married her, raising the question of his status.

sub.text: Gemara's analysis of the two possibilities
sub.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the two possibilities
sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the two possibilities: if he is a borrower, the later borrowing 'with the owners' cancels the earlier rental; if he is a renter, the rental stands as is.
The Gemara objects: why distinguish between borrower and renter? In either case, the later 'with the owners' status should cancel the earlier arrangement.

items.text: Refined case: husband rented from a third party
items.text_en: Refined case: husband rented from a third party
items.desc_en: The Gemara refines the case further: the husband rented a cow from a third party, then married the owner. The question is now only relevant according to Rabbi Yosei, who holds that the cow returns to the original owner (the wife). According to the Rabbis, the husband is clearly a borrower with exemption.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara refines Rami bar Chama's question to a case where the wife herself rented the cow from a third party, then the husband married her.

sub.text: Gemara's clarification according to the Rabbis
sub.text_en: Gemara's clarification according to the Rabbis
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to the Rabbis, who hold that a borrower pays the renter, the question is unnecessary because the husband is clearly a borrower with exemption.

sub.text: Gemara's question according to Rabbi Yosei
sub.text_en: Gemara's question according to Rabbi Yosei
sub.desc_en: The Gemara poses the question according to Rabbi Yosei, who holds that the cow returns to the original owners, asking whether the husband is a borrower or a renter.

items.text: Rava: The husband is a purchaser, not a borrower or renter
items.text_en: Rava: The husband is a purchaser, not a borrower or renter
items.desc_en: Rava resolves the question by stating that the husband is neither a borrower nor a renter, but a purchaser (לוקח), based on a ruling of Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina. This status affects the husband's rights to the cow and his liability.

sub.desc_en: Rava answers: the husband is neither borrower nor renter but a purchaser (לוקח), based on the enactment of Usha cited by Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina.

items.text: Question: Does a husband commit me'ilah with his wife's property?
items.text_en: Question: Does a husband commit me'ilah with his wife's property?
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks whether a husband who uses his wife's consecrated property commits me'ilah (misuse of sacred property). Rava responds that the husband does not commit me'ilah because he is considered a purchaser only for permitted use, not for prohibited use. Ultimately, Rava concludes that the husband commits me'ilah only when he removes the property from sacred to secular use.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks whether a husband who uses his wife's consecrated property commits me'ilah (misuse of sacred property).
Rava answers that the husband does not commit me'ilah because he only acquires the property for permitted use, not for prohibited use.
The Gemara objects that the wife herself should also not commit me'ilah, as she too does not intend to acquire the property for permitted use.
Rava answers that the court (בית דין) enacted the husband's acquisition only for permitted use, not for prohibited use, so the husband does not commit me'ilah.
Rava concludes that the husband commits me'ilah only when he removes the property from sacred to secular use, i.e., when he takes it out of the sacred domain.

items.text: Liability for weight loss or death from work
items.text_en: Liability for weight loss or death from work
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a borrower is liable if the animal loses weight or dies due to the work for which it was borrowed. Rava rules that the borrower is exempt, even if the animal dies, because the owner implicitly allows the animal to be used for that work, and the borrower can argue that he borrowed it for work, not for idleness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: if the animal lost flesh due to the work, what is the law — is the borrower liable?

sub.text: A certain rabbi named Rav Chilkiyah bar Rav Avya
sub.text_en: A certain rabbi named Rav Chilkiyah bar Rav Avya
sub.desc_en: A certain rabbi, Rav Chilkiyah bar Rav Avya, objects: does this imply that if the animal died from the work, the borrower would be liable?

sub.text: Rav Chilkiyah bar Rav Avya's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Chilkiyah bar Rav Avya's answer
sub.desc_en: He answers: one can say to the borrower, 'Did I not borrow it to stand idle?' — implying the borrower is exempt even for death from work.

items.text: Case of a broken borrowed axe
items.text_en: Case of a broken borrowed axe
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case where a borrowed axe broke. Rava rules that if the borrower can bring witnesses that he did not alter the axe, he is exempt. If not, Rav rules that he must pay for a good axe. Rav Kahana and Rav Asi question Rav's ruling, but the Gemara does not record their objection's resolution.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case where a man borrowed an axe from his friend and it broke, and he came before Rava.
Rava rules that if the borrower brings witnesses that he did not alter the axe, he is exempt from payment.
The Gemara asks what happens if there are no witnesses.
The Gemara cites a parallel case where Rav ruled that the borrower must pay for a good axe if no witnesses exist.

sub.text: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi's objection
sub.text_en: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi object to Rav's ruling, though their objection is not recorded in full.

items.text: Ruling on returning broken vessel and paying its value
items.text_en: Ruling on returning broken vessel and paying its value
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the law follows Rav Kahana and Rav Asi, who require the borrower to return the broken pieces and pay the value of the vessel. This is presented as the final ruling after Rav's silence.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rules that the law follows Rav Kahana and Rav Asi, requiring the borrower to return the broken pieces and pay the value of the vessel, citing Rav's silence as confirmation.

items.text: Cases of unusual damage: bucket and cat
items.text_en: Cases of unusual damage: bucket and cat
items.desc_en: Two cases are brought: a borrowed bucket that broke, where Rav Pappa required witnesses that the borrower did not alter it; and a borrowed cat killed by mice, where Rava's ruling is cited that such a case is not subject to legal liability.

sub.desc_en: A case is introduced: a man borrowed a bucket from his friend and it broke.
Rav Pappa rules that the borrower must bring witnesses that he did not alter the bucket, and then he is exempt.
A second case is introduced: a man borrowed a cat from his friend, and mice gathered and killed it.
Rav Ashi deliberates whether this case is like death due to the work (exempting the borrower) or not.

sub.text: Rav Mordechai citing Avimi from Hagronya in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Mordechai citing Avimi from Hagronya in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Mordechai reports in the name of Avimi from Hagronya citing Rava: a cat killed by mice is not subject to legal liability.

items.text: Strategy to be exempt as a borrower with owner present
items.text_en: Strategy to be exempt as a borrower with owner present
items.desc_en: Rava advises that one who wants to borrow something and be exempt should first ask the owner for water, making the borrowing a 'שאלה בבעלים'. A clever owner can counter by asking for the item first.

sub.desc_en: Rava advises that one who wants to borrow an item and be exempt from liability should first ask the owner for water, making the borrowing a 'שאלה בבעלים' (borrowing with the owner present).
Rava adds that if the owner is clever, he can counter by asking to borrow the item first, and only then give water, thus avoiding the 'שאלה בבעלים' exemption.

items.text: Workers during their work are like borrowers with owner present
items.text_en: Workers during their work are like borrowers with owner present
items.desc_en: Rava states that teachers, planters, butchers, and craftsmen during their work are considered like 'שאלה בבעלים'. The Gemara then discusses a case where the Rabbis asked Rava a question, and he was upset, leading to a clarification about the timing of questions.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that teachers, planters, butchers, and craftsmen during their work are considered like borrowers with the owner present (שאלה בבעלים).
The Rabbis ask Rava to borrow something from them, seeking to invoke the exemption of שאלה בבעלים.
Rava becomes upset and rebukes them, arguing that they are trying to extract his money, and that he could evade them by switching tractates but they cannot evade him.
The Gemara resolves the confusion: Rava actually borrowed from them on the day of the assembly (יוֹמָא דְכַלָּה), while they borrowed from him on other days.

items.text: Case of hired mule and the embarrassment of Rava
items.text_en: Case of hired mule and the embarrassment of Rava
items.desc_en: Marimar bar Chanina hired a mule, and the hirers were negligent, causing its death. Rava held them liable, but the Rabbis said it was negligence with the owner present, causing Rava embarrassment. Later it was revealed the owner went to tie the load, not to work. The Gemara discusses two versions of the case.

sub.desc_en: Marimar bar Chanina hired a mule from the people of Chozai, went out to help load it, but the hirers were negligent and the mule died; Rava held them liable.
The Rabbis objected to Rava that this was negligence with the owner present (פשיעה בבעלים), which should exempt the hirers, causing Rava embarrassment.
It was later revealed that the owner had only gone to tie the load, not to work alongside them, so the owner was not present for the work and the hirers were liable.

items.text: Mishnah: Partial borrowing and hiring
items.text_en: Mishnah: Partial borrowing and hiring
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where one borrows a cow for half a day and hires it for half a day, or borrows one day and hires the next, or hires one and borrows another. If the cow dies, the lender claims the borrowed one died, and the borrower claims the hired one died.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of partial borrowing and hiring of a cow.
The Mishnah lists additional scenarios: borrowing one day and hiring the next, or hiring one cow and borrowing another.
The Mishnah presents the dispute: the lender claims the borrowed cow died, and the borrower claims the hired one died.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Conflicting claims about a dead animal
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Conflicting claims about a dead animal
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases where the borrower or renter claims the animal died under their respective status, and the other party admits ignorance or disputes. It rules on liability and oath requirements, and when both are ignorant, they divide the loss.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case where the borrower claims the animal died while borrowed, and the other party (the lender) says 'I don't know' — the borrower is liable.
The Mishnah presents the opposite case: the renter claims the animal died while rented, and the other party says 'I don't know' — the renter is exempt.
The Mishnah rules that when one claims 'borrowed' and the other claims 'rented', the renter takes an oath that it died while rented.
The Mishnah concludes that when both parties say 'I don't know', they divide the loss.

items.text: Gemara's inference: 'I don't know' implies liability
items.text_en: Gemara's inference: 'I don't know' implies liability
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's first case that if someone claims 'You owe me a maneh' and the other says 'I don't know', the defendant is liable, challenging Rav Nachman's ruling that he is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's first case that if someone claims 'You owe me a maneh' and the other says 'I don't know', the defendant is liable, challenging Rav Nachman's ruling that he is exempt.

items.text: Challenge to Rav Nachman's position
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav Nachman's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents the dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda (liable) versus Rav Nachman and Rabbi Yochanan (exempt) regarding 'Maneh li b'yadcha' where the defendant says 'I don't know', and suggests this is a refutation of Rav Nachman.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Nachman by citing the dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda (liable) versus Rav Nachman and Rabbi Yochanan (exempt) regarding 'Maneh li b'yadcha' where the defendant says 'I don't know', suggesting this refutes Rav Nachman's position.

items.text: First answer: There is an עסק שבועה
items.text_en: First answer: There is an עסק שבועה
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that Rav Nachman's ruling applies only when there is an 'עסק שבועה' (a context involving an oath) between them, and here too there is such a context, so the Mishnah does not refute him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that Rav Nachman's ruling applies only when there is an 'עסק שבועה' (a context involving an oath) between them, and here too there is such a context, so the Mishnah does not refute him.

items.text: Question: What is an עסק שבועה?
items.text_en: Question: What is an עסק שבועה?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks to clarify the definition of 'עסק שבועה', introducing Rava's explanation that follows.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what constitutes an 'עסק שבועה' (a case involving an oath), and introduces Rava's explanation that follows.

items.text: Rava's principle stated
items.text_en: Rava's principle stated
items.desc_en: Rava's general rule is introduced: if someone claims 'I have a maneh of yours' and the other admits to only fifty and is uncertain about the rest, since he cannot swear (to deny the rest), he must pay.

sub.desc_en: Rava states the general rule: if one claims a maneh and the other admits to fifty and is uncertain about the rest, since he cannot swear, he must pay.

items.text: Rava's application: opening clause with two cows, closing clause with three
items.text_en: Rava's application: opening clause with two cows, closing clause with three
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to Rava, the opening clause (reisha) involves two cows, and the closing clause (seifa) involves three. In the opening clause, the borrower admits one cow died during the borrowing period but is uncertain about the other, so he pays. In the closing clause, with three cows (two borrowed, one rented), the borrower admits one borrowed cow died but is uncertain about the identity of the surviving cow, so he pays.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that according to Rava, the opening clause (reisha) involves two cows and the closing clause (seifa) involves three.
The Gemara elaborates the opening clause scenario: the lender gave two cows, part of the day as a borrowing and part as a rental, and both died during the borrowing period.
The borrower admits one cow died during the borrowing period but is uncertain about the other, so due to the principle of 'since he cannot swear, he pays' (מתוך שאינו יכול לישבע משלם), he pays.

The Gemara elaborates the closing clause scenario: the lender gave three cows (two borrowed, one rented), two borrowed cows died, and the borrower admits one borrowed cow died but is uncertain about the identity of the surviving cow, so he pays.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's alternative: opening clause with three, closing clause with four
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's alternative: opening clause with three, closing clause with four
items.desc_en: According to Rami bar Chama, who requires partial denial and partial admission for the four guardians, the opening clause involves three cows and the closing clause four. In the opening clause, the borrower denies one cow entirely, admits one died during borrowing, and is uncertain about the third, so he pays. The closing clause with four cows (three borrowed, one rented) is introduced but cut off.

sub.text: Gemara's introduction of Rami bar Chama's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's introduction of Rami bar Chama's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that according to Rami bar Chama, who requires partial denial and partial admission for the four guardians, the opening clause involves three cows and the closing clause four.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the opening clause
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the opening clause
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the opening clause with three cows: the owner gave three cows, two borrowed and one rented, and all three died during the borrowing period.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the borrower's response
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the borrower's response
sub.desc_en: The borrower denies one cow entirely, admits one died during borrowing, and is uncertain about the third, so he pays due to the principle that one who cannot take an oath must pay.

sub.text: Gemara's introduction of the closing clause
sub.text_en: Gemara's introduction of the closing clause
sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins to explain the closing clause with four cows (three borrowed, one rented), but the explanation is cut off.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Conflicting claims of borrower and renter
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Conflicting claims of borrower and renter
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where one claims the animal was borrowed and the other claims it was rented, and the renter must swear that it died while rented. The Gemara questions why the renter swears when the claim is not directly admitted.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where one claims the animal was borrowed and the other claims it was rented, and the renter must swear that it died while rented.

items.text: Gemara's question and Ulla's answer via גלגול
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Ulla's answer via גלגול
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the renter swears when the borrower's claim is not admitted. Ulla answers that it is through גלגול (extension of an oath), as the borrower demands an oath that the animal died naturally, and through that, the renter also swears it was rented.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that when one claims the animal was borrowed and the other claims it was rented, the renter swears that it died while rented.
The Gemara objects: why should the renter swear at all, since the borrower neither admitted to the renter's claim nor claimed what the renter admitted?
Ulla answers that the renter's oath comes through גלגול (extension of an oath).
Ulla explains that the borrower first demands an oath that the animal died naturally, and through that oath the renter also swears it died while rented.

items.text: Attribution to Sumchos: divided in doubt
items.text_en: Attribution to Sumchos: divided in doubt
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the Mishnah's ruling that one who says 'I don't know' is liable to pay as following Sumchos, who holds that money in doubt is divided.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna of the Mishnah's ruling that when one says 'I don't know' and the other says 'I know', the money is split.
The Gemara answers that it is the opinion of Sumchos, who holds that money in doubt is divided.

items.text: Rabbi Abba bar Memel's series of questions on borrowing and renting with or without owners
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba bar Memel's series of questions on borrowing and renting with or without owners
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Memel raises a series of unresolved questions (תיקו) about the legal status when an animal is borrowed with the owner present and rented without, or vice versa, and whether subsequent changes revert the status.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Memel raises the first question: if one borrowed the animal with the owner present (פטור from theft/loss) and then rented it without the owner present, what is the law — are borrowing and renting independent, or does renting connect to borrowing such that the borrower's liability for theft/loss applies?

sub.text: Rabbi Abba bar Memel's second question
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba bar Memel's second question
sub.desc_en: Assuming renting connects to borrowing, Rabbi Abba bar Memel raises a second question: if one rented with the owner present and then borrowed without the owner present, does borrowing not connect to renting at all, or since it connects in part, is it considered as if it connects entirely?

sub.text: Rabbi Abba bar Memel's third question
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba bar Memel's third question
sub.desc_en: Assuming borrowing does not connect to renting even in part, Rabbi Abba bar Memel raises a third question: if one borrowed with the owner present, then rented without the owner present, and then borrowed again, does the borrowing revert to its original status (with owner present), or does the intervening rental interrupt the connection?

sub.text: Rabbi Abba bar Memel's fourth question
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba bar Memel's fourth question
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Memel raises a fourth question: if one rented with the owner present, then borrowed, and then rented again, does the renting revert to its original status (with owner present), or does the intervening borrowing interrupt the connection?
All four questions remain unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Mishnah: Delivery and return of a borrowed animal
items.text_en: Mishnah: Delivery and return of a borrowed animal
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if the borrower sends the animal via the lender's agent and it dies, the borrower is exempt. But if the borrower instructs the lender to send via a specific agent, or the lender offers and the borrower agrees, the borrower is liable. The same applies when returning the animal.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that if a borrower sends a borrowed cow via the lender's agent and it dies, the borrower is exempt.
The Mishnah shifts to the case where the borrower instructs the lender to send via a specific agent, or the lender offers and the borrower agrees, making the borrower liable if the animal dies.
The Mishnah concludes by stating that the same rule applies when the borrower returns the animal.

items.text: Gemara's initial question and two answers
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question and two answers
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that sending via a slave makes the borrower liable, citing the principle that a slave's hand is like his master's. Shmuel explains it refers to a Hebrew slave (who does not own himself), while Rav says even a Canaanite slave is considered as if the owner said 'hit it with a stick and it will come.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that sending via a slave makes the borrower liable, citing the principle that a slave's hand is like his master's.
Shmuel explains the Mishnah refers to a Hebrew slave (עבד עברי) who does not own himself.
Rav says even a Canaanite slave is considered as if the owner said 'hit it with a stick and it will come.'

items.text: Objection from a baraita and Rav's resolution
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita and Rav's resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita states that if a borrower sends a cow via his slave, the borrower is exempt. This challenges Rav, who holds a Canaanite slave is like the owner's agent. Rav responds by clarifying that his case is specifically when the owner said 'hit it with a stick and it will come,' not a general agency.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita: if a borrower sends a cow via his son, agent, or slave, the borrower is liable only via son or agent, but exempt via his own slave.
The Gemara notes that the baraita is consistent with Shmuel's view (who limits the mishnah to an עבד עברי (Hebrew slave)), but poses a difficulty for Rav.
Rav responds by clarifying that his earlier statement was not a general rule but specifically refers to a case where the owner said 'hit it with a stick and it will come,' not a standard agency.

items.text: Rav's ruling on a specific case and Rav Ashi's qualification
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on a specific case and Rav Ashi's qualification
items.desc_en: Rav rules that if the owner says 'hit it with a stick and it will come,' the borrower is liable once the animal leaves the owner's domain. Rav Ashi qualifies this to a case where the borrower's courtyard is inside the owner's, so the animal definitely goes there, and even if there are thorns, the borrower relies on it coming.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a case where the owner says 'hit it with a stick and it will come,' and Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha in the name of Rav rules that once the animal leaves the owner's domain and dies, the borrower is liable.
The gemara asks whether a supporting baraita (cited in the same language) supports Rav's ruling.
Rav Ashi qualifies the case: the borrower's courtyard is inside the owner's, so the animal definitely goes there.
The gemara objects: if so, what is the novelty? The gemara then explains that the case involves thorns (גזייתא) that might deter the animal.
The gemara resolves that despite the thorns, the borrower relies on the animal coming, so Rav's ruling stands.

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling on borrowing an axe
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling on borrowing an axe
items.desc_en: Rav Huna states that if one borrows an axe and splits with it, he acquires it (for liability purposes); if not, he does not. The Gemara clarifies this applies to the right to retract: if he used it, the lender cannot retract; if not, he can.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that if one borrows an axe and splits with it, he acquires it (for liability purposes); if he does not split with it, he does not acquire it.
The Gemara asks what Rav Huna's ruling applies to, and clarifies it is not about liability for accidents (אונסין) but about the right to retract.
The Gemara resolves that if the borrower used the axe, the lender cannot retract; if not, the lender can retract.

items.text: Dispute with Rabbi Ami regarding hekdesh
items.text_en: Dispute with Rabbi Ami regarding hekdesh
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami rules that if one borrows a consecrated axe, he commits me'ilah (misuse) based on the benefit of use, and the borrower may split with it initially. The Gemara objects: if the borrower does not acquire it (per Rav Huna), why would he commit me'ilah? This shows a dispute between Rav Huna and Rabbi Ami.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ami rules that one who lends a consecrated axe commits me'ilah (misuse) based on the benefit of use, and the borrower may split with it לכתחילה (the ideal standard).

The Gemara objects: if the borrower does not acquire the axe (per Rav Huna), why would he commit me'ilah, and why would the borrower be permitted to use it לכתחילה (the ideal standard)? Rather, let the lender take it back so the borrower does not acquire it and does not commit me'ilah.

items.text: Dispute with Rabbi Elazar and a supporting baraita
items.text_en: Dispute with Rabbi Elazar and a supporting baraita
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that just as meshichah (pulling) was instituted for buyers, so too for bailees (borrowers). A baraita supports this, indicating that acquisition for liability occurs through meshichah, not just use.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that just as the Sages instituted meshichah (pulling) for buyers, so too they instituted meshichah for bailees (borrowers).
A baraita supports Rabbi Elazar, stating that meshichah was instituted for bailees just as for buyers.

items.text: Opening analogy: rental acquired like land
items.text_en: Opening analogy: rental acquired like land
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that just as land is acquired through money, deed, or possession, so too is rental. Rav Chisda clarifies that this refers to rental of land.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that just as land is acquired through money, deed, or possession, so too is rental.
The Gemara asks what rental could possibly mean in this context.
Rav Chisda answers that the statement refers to rental of land.

items.text: Samuel's ruling on stolen date cakes
items.text_en: Samuel's ruling on stolen date cakes
items.desc_en: Samuel rules that if one steals a cake of dates containing fifty dates, the compensation differs: if sold together, they are worth fifty minus one; if sold individually, fifty. For a commoner, he pays fifty minus one; for the Temple treasury, he pays fifty plus a fifth, unlike a damager who pays no fifth.

sub.desc_en: Samuel rules that if one steals a cake of dates containing fifty dates, the compensation depends on the market value: if sold together, they are worth fifty minus one; if sold individually, fifty.

The Gemara explains that for a commoner, the thief pays fifty minus one; for the Temple treasury, he pays fifty plus a fifth, unlike a damager who pays no fifth, citing the verse 'וְאִישׁ כִּי יֹאכַל קֹדֶשׁ' (and if a man eats sacred property) which excludes a damager.

items.text: Rav Bibi's objection
items.text_en: Rav Bibi's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Bibi bar Abaye objects: why should the thief pay fifty minus one to a commoner? The thief could argue he would have sold them individually for fifty.

sub.desc_en: Rav Bibi bar Abaye objects: why should the thief pay fifty minus one to a commoner? The thief could argue he would have sold them individually for fifty.

items.text: Rav Huna's answer from a Mishnah
items.text_en: Rav Huna's answer from a Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua answers by citing a Mishnah: 'One assesses a beit se'ah in that field,' implying that valuation is based on the whole, not individual parts.

sub.text: Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua
sub.text_en: Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua answers by citing a Mishnah: 'One assesses a beit se'ah in that field,' implying that valuation is based on the whole, not individual parts.

items.text: Inquiry into Samuel's view and resolution
items.text_en: Inquiry into Samuel's view and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Samuel holds that the law for a commoner is not like that for the Temple treasury, citing a Mishnah about misuse of Temple property. Rabbi Avahu reports Samuel's statement that one who lives in another's courtyard without permission must pay rent, but Rabbi Yochanan says Samuel retracted. The Gemara concludes Samuel retracted from that statement, as per Rava's principle: Temple property without knowledge is like commoner property with knowledge.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Samuel holds that the law for a commoner is not like that for the Temple treasury, citing a Mishnah about misuse of Temple property.
Rabbi Avahu reports in Samuel's name that one who lives in another's courtyard without permission must pay rent.
Rabbi Yochanan objects that Samuel retracted from that statement.
The Gemara concludes Samuel retracted from that statement, as per Rava's principle: Temple property without knowledge is like commoner property with knowledge.

items.text: Rava's ruling on broken wine barrels
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on broken wine barrels
items.desc_en: Rava rules: if porters broke a wine barrel for a shopkeeper, on market day it sells for five, on other days for four. If they return it on market day, they return a barrel of wine; on other days, they return five. This applies only if the shopkeeper had no wine to sell; otherwise, he should have sold it. They deduct for their labor and the cost of the stopper.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that porters who broke a wine barrel for a shopkeeper must compensate based on market-day price (five) or other-day price (four), and return a barrel on market day or five on other days.
The Gemara clarifies that Rava's ruling applies only if the shopkeeper had no wine to sell; otherwise, he should have sold it and the porters are not liable for the higher price.
The Gemara concludes that the porters deduct from the payment their labor costs and the cost of the stopper (ברזניתא).

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases of dispute over ownership of a calf born after an exchange, or a child born to a sold maidservant, where both parties claim it belongs to their period of ownership. It also addresses disputes over the size of purchased slaves or fields, with rules for when one party is uncertain or both are certain.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of exchanging a cow for a donkey and the cow giving birth, or selling a maidservant who gives birth, where each party claims the offspring belongs to their period of ownership, and the ruling is that they divide it.
The Mishnah introduces a second case: one who had two slaves (one large, one small) or two fields (one large, one small) and sold one.
The Mishnah rules: if the buyer claims he bought the large one and the seller says 'I don't know', the buyer acquires the large one.
The Mishnah rules: if the seller claims he sold the small one and the buyer says 'I don't know', the buyer gets only the small one.
The Mishnah rules: if one says 'large' and the other says 'small', the seller takes an oath that he sold the small one.
The Mishnah concludes: if both say 'I don't know', they divide the disputed item.

items.text: Gemara's first question and answer
items.text_en: Gemara's first question and answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the parties divide the disputed property; it should be determined by who possesses it, and the other party would bear the burden of proof. Rav Chiya bar Avin answers in the name of Shmuel that the case involves a cow standing in a marsh (not in anyone's domain) and a maidservant standing in a public area.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the parties divide the disputed property; it should be determined by who possesses it, and the other party would bear the burden of proof.

sub.text: Rav Chiya bar Avin in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Chiya bar Avin in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiya bar Avin answers in the name of Shmuel that the case involves a cow standing in a marsh (not in anyone's domain) and a maidservant standing in a public area.

items.text: Challenge and attribution to Sumchos
items.text_en: Challenge and attribution to Sumchos
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that even if the property is in a neutral area, it should be presumed to belong to the original owner, and the other party would bear the burden of proof. It answers that the Mishnah follows Sumchos, who holds that uncertain money is divided without an oath.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that even when the animal stands in a neutral area, the property should be presumed to belong to the original owner, so the other party would bear the burden of proof.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah follows Sumchos, who holds that uncertain money (ממון המוטל בספק) is divided without an oath.

items.text: Debate over Sumchos's opinion: certain vs. uncertain claims
items.text_en: Debate over Sumchos's opinion: certain vs. uncertain claims
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Sumchos applies only when both claims are uncertain (שמא ושמא) or also when both are certain (ברי וברי). Rabba bar Rav Huna says Sumchos applies even to certain claims, while Rava limits it to uncertain claims. The Gemara analyzes the Mishnah's structure to support Rava's view, and explains that the latter clause (uncertain claims) was taught to clarify that the first clause involves certain claims.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Sumchos's principle of dividing uncertain property applies only when both claims are uncertain (שמא ושמא) or also when both are certain (ברי וברי).
Rabba bar Rav Huna asserts that Sumchos applies even to certain claims (ברי וברי).
Rava counters that Sumchos only applies to uncertain claims (שמא ושמא), citing the Mishnah's wording that both parties say 'perhaps' (שמא).

The Gemara analyzes the Mishnah's structure: for Rava, the latter clause (uncertain claims) implies the first clause is also uncertain; for Rabba bar Rav Huna, if certain claims already yield division, uncertain claims would be redundant.
The Gemara resolves that the latter clause was taught to clarify that the first clause involves certain claims (ברי וברי), and even so they divide — supporting Rabba bar Rav Huna's view.

items.text: Challenge from the Mishnah's oath requirement
items.text_en: Challenge from the Mishnah's oath requirement
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah requires the seller to swear when one claims large and the other small. This supports Rava's view that Sumchos does not apply to certain claims, as an oath is needed. For Rabba bar Rav Huna, the Mishnah should have ruled that they divide without an oath. The Gemara answers that Sumchos concedes where a Torah oath is applicable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's ruling that when one claims large and the other small, the seller must swear that he sold the small one.

The Gemara explains that for Rava, who limits Sumchos to doubtful claims, the oath is necessary, but for Rabba bar Rav Huna, who extends Sumchos even to certain claims, the Mishnah should have ruled that they divide without an oath.
The Gemara answers that Sumchos concedes where a Torah oath is applicable, resolving the challenge to Rabba bar Rav Huna.

items.text: Analysis of the oath in the slave and field dispute
items.text_en: Analysis of the oath in the slave and field dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why an oath is administered in the case of two slaves or fields, since the claim is not a standard admission (מודה במקצת) and slaves are not subject to oaths. Rav explains that the dispute is over the value (money), while Shmuel says it is over the clothing or produce. Both interpretations allow for a valid oath.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why an oath is administered in the case of two slaves or fields, since the claim is not a standard admission (מודה במקצת).
The Gemara adds that the disputed item is already in the buyer's possession, so the seller should be the one bringing proof.
The Gemara further objects that oaths are not administered regarding slaves (since they are considered movable property with a different legal status).
Rav explains that the dispute is actually over the monetary value (דמים) of the slave or field, not the slave or field itself, which allows for a valid oath.
Shmuel explains that the dispute is over the clothing or produce (כְּסוּת / עוֹמְרֵי) of the slave or field, which are movable items subject to oaths.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and initial Gemara question
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and initial Gemara question
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one claims a garment and the defendant admits to part, the oath applies. The Gemara questions how this applies to a slave or field, since they are not movable property. Rav Pappa explains the case involves a 'delyafei' (a specific type of garment).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule for a garment claim where the defendant admits to part.
Rav Pappa explains that the case involves a 'delyafei' (a specific type of garment), resolving the Gemara's question about applicability to slaves and fields.

items.text: Rabbi Hoshaya's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Rabbi Hoshaya's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Hoshaya objects that the Mishnah says 'garment' not 'slave'. He explains the case is about a slave with his garment or a field with its sheaves. Rav Pappa again invokes 'delyafei' to explain the partial admission.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Hoshaya objects that the Mishnah says 'garment' (כְּסוּת) not 'slave' (עֶבֶד), questioning the relevance of the Mishnah's wording.
Rabbi Hoshaya resolves that the case involves a slave with his garment or a field with its sheaves, explaining the Mishnah's wording.
The Gemara objects that even with this explanation, the Mishnah's rule still does not fit the partial admission pattern.
Rav Pappa answers that the case involves a partial admission through the principle of 'דליפי' (the claim and admission are on different items).

items.text: Rav Sheshet's objection and attribution to Rabbi Meir
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's objection and attribution to Rabbi Meir
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet objects that the Mishnah's ruling about 'joining' properties for oaths is already known. He attributes the Mishnah to Rabbi Meir, who considers a slave like movable property. The Gemara then notes that even Rabbi Meir would require the admission to match the claim, but resolves this by invoking Rabban Gamliel's opinion that partial admission of a different type obligates an oath.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet objects that the Mishnah's ruling about 'joining' properties for oaths is already known from a baraita.
Rav Sheshet answers that the Mishnah is attributed to Rabbi Meir, who considers a slave like movable property (מטלטלין).
The Gemara notes the remaining problem of mismatched admission and claim, and resolves it by invoking Rabban Gamliel's opinion that partial admission of a different type obligates an oath.

items.text: Rava's resolution: damaged slave and field
items.text_en: Rava's resolution: damaged slave and field
items.desc_en: Rava explains the Mishnah's case is where the slave's hand was cut off or the field was dug with pits, so the admission matches the claim in kind.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the difficulty by specifying that the Mishnah's case involves a slave whose hand was cut off or a field dug with pits, so the admission matches the claim in kind.

items.text: Contradiction in Rabbi Meir's view resolved
items.text_en: Contradiction in Rabbi Meir's view resolved
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: elsewhere Rabbi Meir says a stolen slave that aged is returned as is, but here he treats slaves as movable. Rabba bar Avuh reverses the tradition, attributing the lenient view to the Sages.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: elsewhere Rabbi Meir rules that a stolen slave that aged is returned as-is, implying slaves are like land, but here he treats slaves as movable property.
Rabba bar Avuh resolves the contradiction by reversing the tradition: the lenient view (slave returned as-is) is actually the Sages, and Rabbi Meir holds the strict view (pay at time of theft).

items.text: Proof that Rabbi Meir equates land and slaves for oaths
items.text_en: Proof that Rabbi Meir equates land and slaves for oaths
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks to prove that Rabbi Meir allows oaths on land by analogy to slaves. It cites a baraita about a cow and donkey, where Rabbi Meir requires an oath on slaves and land. The Gemara considers alternative interpretations and concludes with Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's distinction about grapes ready for harvest.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how we know Rabbi Meir equates land with slaves for oaths, suggesting perhaps he only allows oaths on slaves but not on land.
The Gemara cites a baraita about exchanging a cow for a donkey and a maidservant who gave birth, where Rabbi Meir requires an oath on both slaves and land, while the Sages exempt both.
The Gemara infers from the baraita that Rabbi Meir must hold that oaths are taken on both slaves and land.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the Sages were saying to Rabbi Meir: just as you concede to us regarding land, concede also regarding slaves, not that he actually holds oaths on land.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Meir distinguishes between items that are like land and not like land, regarding ten vines, while the Sages consider anything attached to land as land.

Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina resolves the dispute: the disagreement between Rabbi Meir and the Sages concerns grapes ready for harvest, where one view treats them as already detached and the other as still attached.

items.text: Final resolution: necessity of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Final resolution: necessity of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Hoshaya's explanation, and it was necessary to teach that the slave's garment is not like the slave, and the field's sheaves are not like the field, thus requiring the oath.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Hoshaya's explanation, and it was necessary to teach that the slave's garment is not like the slave and the field's sheaves are not like the field, thus requiring the oath.

items.text: Analysis of the baraita: attribution to Sumchos
items.text_en: Analysis of the baraita: attribution to Sumchos
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the anonymous 'they divide' ruling as Sumchos. It questions why the seller takes an oath in the case of conflicting claims, and resolves that Sumchos agrees when a Torah oath applies, as in Rava's case of a damaged slave.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the anonymous ruling 'they divide' in the baraita as the opinion of Sumchos, who holds that disputed money is divided.
The Gemara questions why the seller takes an oath in the case of conflicting claims, since according to Rabba bar Rav Huna, Sumchos applies division even when both parties are certain.
The Gemara resolves that Sumchos concedes when a Torah oath applies, as in Rava's case of a damaged slave.

items.text: Mishnah on olive trees sold for wood and its Gemara
items.text_en: Mishnah on olive trees sold for wood and its Gemara
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses olives sold for wood that produce less than a quarter-log per se'ah, and the Gemara clarifies the conditions: if the buyer said 'cut immediately' or 'whenever you want', and the general rule that people do not care about less than a quarter-log.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one sells olive trees for wood and they produce less than a quarter-log per se'ah, the olives belong to the seller.
The Mishnah adds that if they produced a quarter-log per se'ah, the buyer and seller each claim the olives grew from their own property, so they divide the produce.
The Mishnah presents a parallel case: if a river swept olives into another's field, the same dispute and division apply.

The Gemara questions the Mishnah's distinction: if the buyer said 'cut immediately,' even less than a quarter-log should go to the landowner; if 'cut whenever you want,' even a quarter-log should go to the olive owner.

The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah speaks of an unspecified sale: people do not care about less than a quarter-log, so it stays with the seller, but they do care about a quarter-log, so it is disputed.
Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi begins to cite a tradition about the quarter-log measure mentioned in the Mishnah.

items.text: Opening Mishnah excerpt
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah excerpt
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the tenant is entitled to the produce except for the cost of harvesting.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the tenant is entitled to the produce except for the cost of harvesting.

items.text: Gemara's discussion on olive trees swept by a river
items.text_en: Gemara's discussion on olive trees swept by a river
items.desc_en: Ulla and Ravin report Resh Lakish's rulings on when the owner of the trees retains rights. The Gemara questions the logic and resolves it with a distinction between within three years and after three years, considering the planter's potential use of the land.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a case where a river swept away olive trees, and cites Ulla quoting Resh Lakish: the Mishnah's rule applies only if the trees were uprooted with their clods of earth and after three years.
Resh Lakish rules that within three years, all the produce belongs to the olive owner, because the tenant could not have eaten it had he planted.
The Gemara objects: the tenant could argue that had he planted, he would have eaten all the produce after three years, but now the owner eats half with him.

Ravin reports Resh Lakish's reversed ruling: the Mishnah applies only when uprooted with clods within three years; after three years, all produce goes to the landowner, who could have eaten it all had he planted.
The Gemara objects that the tenant could still argue he eats only half now, but the landowner counters that had he planted, he would have planted vegetables under the trees.

items.text: Baraita on the tenant's claim 'I take my olives'
items.text_en: Baraita on the tenant's claim 'I take my olives'
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if the tenant says 'I take my olives,' we do not listen to him. Rabbi Yochanan explains the reason is for the settlement of Eretz Yisrael, and Rabbi Yirmeya notes the importance of this ruling.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if a tenant says 'I am taking my olives,' we do not listen to him, and Rabbi Yochanan explains the reason is for the settlement of Eretz Yisrael.
Rabbi Yirmeya remarks that such a ruling requires a great scholar.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that the reason is for the settlement of Eretz Yisrael (יישוב ארץ ישראל).
Rabbi Yirmeya notes that this ruling is a significant and necessary teaching.

items.text: Discussion on Rabbi Yehuda's ruling about a tenant on ancestral land from a non-Jew
items.text_en: Discussion on Rabbi Yehuda's ruling about a tenant on ancestral land from a non-Jew
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes Rabbi Yehuda's statement that one who rents a field of his ancestors from a non-Jew must tithe and give it to him. Two interpretations are explored: one assuming no non-Jewish acquisition in Eretz Yisrael, the other assuming acquisition and a special rabbinic penalty for the heir. Rabbi Yochanan explains the penalty is to keep the land in his possession.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda rules that one who rents his ancestral field from a non-Jew must tithe and give it to him.
The Gemara explains that 'ancestral field' refers to Eretz Yisrael, the land of the patriarchs.
The Gemara assumes that Rabbi Yehuda holds that a non-Jew has no power of acquisition in Eretz Yisrael to exempt the produce from tithes.
The Gemara compares the tenant to a חוֹכֵר (sharecropper) who must tithe regardless of yield, as he is repaying a debt.
Rav Kahana objects to Rav Papi (or Rav Zevid) that the baraita's mention of a 'מֵצִיק' (oppressive non-Jew) is superfluous, since the rule should apply even without such a context.
The Gemara answers that in truth a non-Jew does have acquisition power to exempt from tithes, and the tenant is not like a sharecropper.
The Gemara explains that 'ancestral field' means the actual ancestral inheritance, and the Sages penalized only the heir because the land is especially dear to him, but not an ordinary person.
The Gemara asks why the Sages penalized the heir specifically.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that the penalty ensures the land remains in the heir's possession (so he does not lose it to the non-Jew).
Rabbi Yirmeya comments that this ruling is a great necessity (i.e., a profound halachic insight).

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on an unauthorized planter
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on an unauthorized planter
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel argue about how to compensate an unauthorized planter. Rav says we assess the value and he gets the lower hand, while Shmuel says we estimate what a person would pay to plant. Rav Pappa reconciles them based on whether the field is typically planted. A story illustrates Rav's ruling in practice.

sub.desc_en: The gemara states the dispute: Rav says we assess the value and the planter gets the lower hand, while Shmuel says we estimate what a person would pay to plant the field.
Rav Pappa reconciles Rav and Shmuel by distinguishing between a field typically planted (Shmuel's rule) and one not typically planted (Rav's rule).
The gemara notes that Rav's ruling was not stated explicitly but derived from a case where Rav told a litigant to assess and give the planter the lower hand.
When the litigant later fenced and guarded the field, Rav reversed his ruling, giving the planter the upper hand because the owner's actions showed he wanted the planting.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet on an unauthorized builder
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet on an unauthorized builder
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet argue whether an unauthorized builder can take his materials. The Gemara challenges Rav Nachman with a Tannaitic dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, and suggests he follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar. The discussion ends with Rabbi Yochanan's unresolved opinion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the dispute: Rav Nachman says the unauthorized builder may take his materials, Rav Sheshet says he may not.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita where Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel dispute the same issue, suggesting Rav Nachman follows Beit Shammai.

The Gemara rejects the objection, explaining that Rav Nachman follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, who holds that the builder is heard, while the dispute of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel is cited by Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
The Gemara asks what the final ruling is, and cites Rabbi Yaakov in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, but the opinion is left unresolved.

items.text: Opening dispute about eviction in a house vs. field
items.text_en: Opening dispute about eviction in a house vs. field
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that in a house the landlord is listened to (can evict), but in a field he is not. The Gemara explains the reason: either because of settling the Land of Israel or because of weakening the land. The difference between these reasons is for outside the Land.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: in a house the landlord is listened to (can evict), but in a field he is not.
The Gemara asks: what is the reason for the distinction between a house and a field?
One answer: because of settling the Land of Israel (יישוב ארץ ישראל).
Another answer: because of weakening the land (כחש דארעא).
The Gemara notes the practical difference between the two reasons: the case of outside the Land of Israel (חוצה לארץ).

items.text: Mishnah: Periods of notice for renting a house
items.text_en: Mishnah: Periods of notice for renting a house
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one rents a house during the rainy season, the tenant cannot be evicted from Sukkot until Passover; during the dry season, thirty days; in cities, twelve months; for shops, twelve months; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says a baker's or dyer's shop is three years.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists periods of notice for evicting a tenant: from Sukkot to Passover in the rainy season, thirty days in the dry season, twelve months in cities and for shops, and three years for a baker's or dyer's shop according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

items.text: Gemara's question and resolution about the Mishnah's periods
items.text_en: Gemara's question and resolution about the Mishnah's periods
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the rainy season has a longer period, and answers that it is because houses are not readily available for rent. It then addresses a contradiction from the case of cities, and Rav Yehuda explains that the Mishnah is teaching about giving notice. A baraita supports this, adding that the tenant also needs to give notice.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah distinguishes between the rainy season and the dry season, since in both cases a tenant presumably rents for the entire season.
The Gemara answers that during the rainy season houses are not readily available for rent, so the tenant needs more protection.
The Gemara objects from the case of cities where the period is twelve months even during the rainy season, contradicting the earlier reasoning.
Rav Yehuda resolves that the Mishnah is teaching about the requirement to give notice, not about the rental period itself.
A baraita supports Rav Yehuda's interpretation, adding that the tenant also needs to give notice because he could have found a better tenant.

items.text: Rav Asi's clarification on entering the rainy season
items.text_en: Rav Asi's clarification on entering the rainy season
items.desc_en: Rav Asi states that if the tenant entered even one day of the rainy season, he cannot be evicted from Sukkot until Passover. The Gemara questions this against the Mishnah's thirty days, and Rav Asi clarifies that it means one day within those thirty days.

sub.desc_en: Rav Asi states that if the tenant entered even one day of the rainy season, he cannot be evicted from Sukkot until Passover.
The Gemara objects: the Mishnah explicitly says thirty days, not one day.
Rav Asi clarifies: he meant one day within those thirty days, so the tenant cannot be evicted from Sukkot until Passover.

items.text: Rav Huna and Rav Nachman on increasing rent and cases of sale or inheritance
items.text_en: Rav Huna and Rav Nachman on increasing rent and cases of sale or inheritance
items.desc_en: Rav Huna says that if the landlord wants to increase the rent, he may. Rav Nachman objects, but Rav Huna explains it is when houses become expensive. The Gemara then discusses cases where the landlord sells, inherits, or gives the house as a gift, and the tenant says 'you are no better than the one from whom you came.' For a son-in-law, if possible, notice must be given.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that if the landlord wants to increase the rent, he may do so.
Rav Nachman objects, asking rhetorically whether the landlord may simply seize the tenant by his garment to force him out.
The Gemara explains that Rav Huna's ruling applies only when houses have become more expensive, so the increase is justified.
The Gemara asks about a case where the landlord inherited a house, and the tenant says 'you are no better than the one from whom you came.'
The Gemara adds that if the landlord sold, inherited, or received the house as a gift, the tenant says 'you are no better than the person from whom you came.'
The Gemara rules that if the landlord gave the house to his son-in-law, we examine whether it was possible to give notice; if so, he must, otherwise the tenant says 'you are no better than me.'

items.text: Story of the woman who rented space and then evicted the tenant
items.text_en: Story of the woman who rented space and then evicted the tenant
items.desc_en: A story is told of a man who bought wine and asked a woman for space. She initially refused, but after he betrothed her, she gave him space. He then sent her a get, and she hired porters to remove his wine. Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua says 'as he did, so shall be done to him.' The Gemara adds that even a courtyard meant for rent, she can refuse him because he is like a lion in ambush.

sub.desc_en: A story is told of a man who bought wine, could not find space, asked a woman who refused, then betrothed her, she gave space, he sent a get, and she hired porters to remove his wine.
Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua rules that as he did, so shall be done to him, citing the verse 'his retribution shall return upon his head'.
The Gemara adds that even a courtyard meant for rent, she can refuse him because he is like a lion in ambush.

items.text: Explanation of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statement
