items.text_en: Explanation of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statement
items.desc_en: A baraita explains that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling that a baker's or dyer's shop is three years is because their clientele is extensive.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling that a baker's or dyer's shop has a three-year lease period.
The Tanna explains that the reason for the three-year period is because their clientele is extensive (הקפן מרובה).

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on landlord and tenant responsibilities for repairs
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on landlord and tenant responsibilities for repairs
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the landlord is responsible for items requiring a craftsman (door, bolt, lock), while the tenant is responsible for items not requiring a craftsman. The Gemara brings a baraita detailing specific responsibilities. A question is raised about the mezuzah, and Rav Sheshet answers that its placement is not a craftsman's work, so the tenant does it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the landlord is responsible for items requiring a craftsman (door, bolt, lock), while the tenant is responsible for items not requiring a craftsman.
The Mishnah adds that the manure belongs to the landlord, except for that from the oven and stove, which belongs to the tenant.
A baraita details specific responsibilities: the landlord provides doors, windows, roof, and beams; the tenant provides a ladder, railing, gutter, and plastering the roof.

The Gemara asks Rav Sheshet who is responsible for the mezuzah, then clarifies that the question is about the place for the mezuzah (the doorpost preparation), not the mezuzah itself, since Rav Mesharshiya already stated that the mezuzah is the dweller's obligation.

Rav Sheshet answers that the tenant is responsible, citing the Mishnah's rule that a non-craftsman item is the tenant's duty, and the doorpost preparation is not a craftsman's work since it is possible for a layperson.

items.text: Opening phrase
items.text_en: Opening phrase
items.desc_en: The daf begins with a brief Aramaic phrase: 'In a reed hut.' This serves as a transition from the previous page.

sub.desc_en: The gemara opens with the phrase 'In a reed hut,' serving as a transition from the previous discussion.

items.text: Baraita on mezuzah and the story of a tenant
items.text_en: Baraita on mezuzah and the story of a tenant
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a tenant's obligation to affix a mezuzah and not take it when leaving, except for a gentile. A story is told of a man who took it and suffered tragedy. The Gemara questions the story's purpose and Rav Sheshet explains it was a case of a gentile tenant.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that a tenant must affix a mezuzah and not remove it when leaving, except for a gentile tenant, and relates a story of a man who removed it and buried his wife and two sons.
The Gemara objects that the story seems to contradict the baraita's ruling.
Rav Sheshet resolves that the story involved a gentile tenant, who is permitted to take the mezuzah.

items.text: The manure of the landlord and the principle of Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina
items.text_en: The manure of the landlord and the principle of Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that manure belongs to the landlord, except for what comes from the oven and stove. The Gemara clarifies that this refers to a courtyard not rented to the tenant, where the manure comes from animals that entered from outside. This supports Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's principle that a person's courtyard acquires for him without his knowledge.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that manure belongs to the landlord, except for what comes from the oven and stove.
The Gemara asks what case the Mishnah refers to, rejecting the possibility that the courtyard is rented to the tenant with the tenant's oxen, as that would obviously give the manure to the tenant.
The Gemara clarifies that the case is where the courtyard belongs to the landlord and the oxen that entered from outside deposited manure there.

sub.text: Supporting citation of Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina
sub.text_en: Supporting citation of Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that this supports Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's principle that a person's courtyard acquires for him without his knowledge.

items.text: Objection from a mishnah about a courtyard that does not acquire
items.text_en: Objection from a mishnah about a courtyard that does not acquire
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a mishnah where a person says 'all findings that come into my courtyard today shall be acquired by my courtyard' and it is ineffective. The Gemara answers that this refers to an unguarded courtyard. The Gemara then questions the continuation of that mishnah, and explains that when a lost item is publicized, people avoid it, making the courtyard guarded.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a mishnah where a person declares that all findings entering his courtyard today should be acquired for him, yet the mishnah rules it ineffective, contradicting Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's principle that a courtyard acquires without knowledge.
The Gemara answers that the mishnah deals with an unguarded courtyard, which does not acquire for its owner.
The Gemara questions the continuation of the mishnah, which says that if the lost item was publicized in the city, his words stand, asking why this would help in an unguarded courtyard.
The Gemara explains that once the lost item is publicized, people avoid it, effectively making the courtyard guarded and thus capable of acquisition.

items.text: Objection from a baraita about manure and the principle of courtyard acquisition
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita about manure and the principle of courtyard acquisition
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises another objection from a baraita that states manure collected from the air is the tenant's, contradicting Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's principle. Abaye answers that it refers to a case where one attaches a vessel to the cow's udder. Rava answers that air that does not come to rest is not considered placed. The Gemara then questions Rava's certainty, citing his own dilemma about a purse thrown through one opening and exiting another, and distinguishes the cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita stating that manure collected from the air belongs to the tenant, contradicting Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's principle that a person's courtyard acquires for him without his knowledge.
Abaye answers that the baraita refers to a case where one attaches a vessel to the cow's udder, so the manure falls directly into the tenant's vessel, not into the courtyard's airspace.
Rava answers that airspace that does not ultimately come to rest is not considered as if the object were placed there, so the courtyard does not acquire the manure.

The Gemara questions Rava's certainty, citing his own unresolved dilemma about a purse thrown through one opening and exiting another, asking whether airspace that does not come to rest is considered as placed or not.

The Gemara resolves the difficulty by distinguishing the cases: there, no vessel interrupts the airspace, but here, a vessel (attached to the cow) interrupts, so the manure is not acquired by the courtyard.

items.text: Clarification of the baraita about manure in the stable and courtyard
items.text_en: Clarification of the baraita about manure in the stable and courtyard
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a redundancy in the baraita: 'in the stable and in the courtyard.' Abaye explains it means 'in the stable that is in the courtyard.' Rav Ashi derives from this that when one rents a courtyard, the stable is not included.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the redundancy in the baraita, which lists both 'in the stable' and 'in the courtyard' as belonging to the homeowner, asking why both are needed.
Abaye resolves the redundancy by explaining that the baraita means 'the manure in the stable that is in the courtyard' — a single location described with two terms.
Rav Ashi derives from the baraita's phrasing that when one rents out a courtyard without specification, the stable within it is not included in the rental.

items.text: Objection from the law of sending away the mother bird
items.text_en: Objection from the law of sending away the mother bird
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a mishnah about doves in a dovecote that are subject to the mitzvah of sending away the mother bird and are forbidden for theft due to darkhei shalom. This contradicts Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's principle. Rava answers that the obligation applies when the egg has mostly emerged, but acquisition does not occur until it falls into the courtyard. The Gemara then discusses the prohibition of theft and the principle that if one cannot acquire, his courtyard cannot acquire. The Gemara concludes with a discussion about a minor who cannot perform the mitzvah, and the father's obligation to return the eggs due to darkhei shalom.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a mishnah about doves in a dovecote that are subject to the mitzvah of sending away the mother bird and are forbidden for theft due to darkhei shalom, which contradicts Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's principle that a courtyard acquires for a person without his knowledge.

The Gemara questions how the mishnah can be reconciled with Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's principle, since the dovecote is a courtyard that should acquire the eggs for the owner, making them 'ready' (מזומן) and exempt from the mitzvah of sending away the mother bird.

Rava answers that the obligation of sending away the mother bird applies when the egg has mostly emerged, but acquisition does not occur until it falls into the courtyard, so the mishnah speaks before the egg falls.
The Gemara questions why the doves themselves are forbidden for theft, since if the eggs are not yet acquired, the doves should be ownerless.
An alternative answer is offered: the mishnah refers to eggs, and once the majority of the egg has emerged, the mother's mind is on it, making it considered acquired by her presence.

The Gemara cites Rav Yehuda quoting Rav that it is forbidden to acquire the eggs while the mother is roosting, because the verse requires sending the mother first, and the principle that a courtyard cannot acquire for a person what he himself cannot acquire.
The Gemara questions why the mishnah says the doves are forbidden only due to darkhei shalom, since if one sent the mother, it would be outright theft, and if not, one must send her.
The Gemara answers that the mishnah deals with a minor who is not obligated in the mitzvah of sending away the mother bird, and the father must return the eggs due to darkhei shalom.

items.text: Mishnah: Leap year in a rental contract
items.text_en: Mishnah: Leap year in a rental contract
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one rents a house for a year and the year becomes a leap year, the extra month belongs to the tenant. If rented by the month, the extra month belongs to the landlord. A story from Tzippori is cited about a bathhouse rented for twelve gold coins per year, at one gold coin per month.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule: if one rents a house for a year and the year becomes a leap year, the extra month belongs to the tenant.
The Mishnah shifts to the second case: if rented by the month, the extra month belongs to the landlord.
The Mishnah cites a story from Tzippori about a bathhouse rented for twelve gold coins per year, at one gold coin per month, illustrating the practical application of the rule.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's correction
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's correction
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where a bathhouse was rented for twelve gold coins per year, one gold dinar per month, and the tenant left mid-month; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yosei ruled they divide the intercalated month. The Gemara notes the Mishnah is missing a clause and reconstructs it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where a bathhouse was rented for twelve gold coins per year, one gold dinar per month, and the tenant left mid-month; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yosei ruled they divide the intercalated month.

The Gemara notes the Mishnah is missing a clause and reconstructs it, explaining that the case was about a rental at twelve gold coins per year from a gold dinar per month, and the ruling to divide the intercalated month applies.

items.text: Rav's ruling and the principle of 'grasp the latter language'
items.text_en: Rav's ruling and the principle of 'grasp the latter language'
items.desc_en: Rav says he would have given the entire month's rent to the landlord, applying the principle of 'grasp the latter language' (תפוס לשון אחרון). The Gemara questions why Rav repeats this principle, and explains that without this case one might have thought the latter language merely clarifies rather than overrides.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that if he had been present, he would have given the entire month's rent to the landlord.
The Gemara asks what Rav is teaching us, answering that it is the principle of 'grasp the latter language' (תפוס לשון אחרון).
The Gemara objects that Rav already taught this principle elsewhere, citing the case of 'an istera (a coin) equals one hundred ma'ahs' or 'one hundred ma'ahs equals an istera'.
The Gemara resolves that without this case one might have thought the latter language merely clarifies rather than overrides, so Rav teaches us otherwise.

items.text: Shmuel's distinction and the objection from a sale case
items.text_en: Shmuel's distinction and the objection from a sale case
items.desc_en: Shmuel distinguishes based on when the tenant arrived: if at month's start, all to landlord; if at month's end, all to tenant; only mid-month do they divide. The Gemara objects that Shmuel elsewhere agrees with 'grasp the latter language' in a sale case, but resolves that here the landlord is in possession (תפיס).

sub.desc_en: Shmuel distinguishes the case: if the tenant arrived at month's start, all goes to the landlord; if at month's end, all to the tenant; only mid-month do they divide.
The Gemara objects that Shmuel elsewhere agrees with the principle of 'grasp the latter language' in a sale case, contradicting his ruling here.
The Gemara resolves that in the sale case the buyer is in possession (תפיס), and here too the landlord is in possession, so the principle does not apply.

items.text: Rav Nachman's ruling: land remains in owner's possession
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling: land remains in owner's possession
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that the land remains in the owner's possession (קרקע בחזקת בעליה קיימת), applying 'grasp the latter language' even when the order of terms is reversed, unlike Rav's case.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman states that the land remains in the owner's possession (קרקע בחזקת בעליה קיימת).
The Gemara asks what Rav Nachman is teaching us, suggesting it is the principle of 'grasp the latter language' (תפוס לשון אחרון).
The Gemara answers that Rav Nachman's ruling applies the principle even when the order of terms is reversed, unlike Rav's case.

items.text: Burden of proof on the final day of the rental period
items.text_en: Burden of proof on the final day of the rental period
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yannai is asked: if the tenant claims he paid and the landlord denies receipt, who must bring proof? The Gemara notes that within the term or after it, the answer is known from a mishna about redemption of a firstborn. The question is specifically about the final day: do people pay on that day? Rabbi Yochanan answers that they have already learned this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks Rabbi Yannai: if a tenant claims he paid rent and the landlord denies receipt, who must bring proof?
The Gemara clarifies: if the claim is within the rental term or after it, the answer is already known from a mishna about redemption of a firstborn (בכור).
The Gemara specifies: the question is about the final day of the rental term — do people pay on that day or not?
Rabbi Yochanan answers that they have already learned this from a mishna.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's initial question
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's initial question
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a hired worker who demands his wages on time takes an oath and receives payment. The Gemara explains that the rabbis imposed an oath on the worker because the employer is busy with his workers, but here the employer is deemed credible with an oath.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a hired worker who demands his wages on time takes an oath and receives payment.
The Gemara explains that the rabbis imposed an oath on the worker because the employer is busy with his workers, but here the employer is deemed credible with an oath.

items.text: Rava's ruling on a rental contract and Rav Acha's challenge
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on a rental contract and Rav Acha's challenge
items.desc_en: Rava quotes Rav Nachman: If someone rents a house for ten years and the landlord claims only five have passed, the landlord is believed. Rav Acha challenges: If someone lent money with a document and claims half was repaid, is he also believed? Rava distinguishes: a loan document is for collection, so repayment should be recorded, but a rental contract is only to prevent the tenant from claiming ownership.

sub.desc_en: Rava states in the name of Rav Nachman that if someone rents a house for ten years and the landlord claims only five have passed, the landlord is believed.

sub.text: Rav Acha from Difti to Ravina
sub.text_en: Rav Acha from Difti to Ravina
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha challenges: if someone lent money with a document and claims half was repaid, would he also be believed?

Ravina distinguishes: a loan document is for collection, so repayment should be recorded on it, but a rental contract is only to prevent the tenant from claiming ownership through hazakah (presumption of ownership).

items.text: Rav Nachman's ruling on borrowing a tool
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling on borrowing a tool
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that a person may borrow a tool indefinitely. Rav Mari bar Bat Shmuel adds that this applies only if the borrower acquired ownership of the tool. Rav Mari bar Rav Ashi adds that the borrower must return the handle.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that a person may borrow a tool indefinitely, based on the principle of borrowing with goodwill.

sub.text: Rav Mari bar Bat Shmuel's addition
sub.text_en: Rav Mari bar Bat Shmuel's addition
sub.desc_en: Rav Mari bar Bat Shmuel adds that this ruling applies only if the borrower acquired ownership of the tool from the lender.

sub.text: Rav Mari bar Rav Ashi's addition
sub.text_en: Rav Mari bar Rav Ashi's addition
sub.desc_en: Rav Mari bar Rav Ashi adds that the borrower must return the handle of the tool when finished.

items.text: Rava's ruling on borrowing a hoe for a specific orchard
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on borrowing a hoe for a specific orchard
items.desc_en: Rava rules: If one says 'Lend me a hoe to dig this orchard,' he may dig only that orchard. If he says 'an orchard,' he may dig any orchard he wishes, but must return the handle.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that if one borrows a hoe for a specific orchard, he may dig only that orchard; if he says 'an orchard,' he may dig any orchard; if he says 'orchards,' he may dig all of them, but must return the handle.

items.text: Rav Pappa's ruling on borrowing a beam
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's ruling on borrowing a beam
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa rules: If one says 'Lend me this beam' and it breaks, he does not rebuild it. If he says 'a beam' and it breaks, he rebuilds it. If he says 'a house of beams,' he may dig in his land until he finds one, but must acquire ownership from him.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa rules that if one says 'Lend me this beam' and it breaks, he does not rebuild it.
Rav Pappa rules that if one says 'a beam' and it breaks, he rebuilds it.
Rav Pappa rules that if one says 'a house of beams,' he may dig in his land until he finds one, but must acquire ownership from him.

items.text: Mishnah on a collapsed rented house and Gemara's analysis
items.text_en: Mishnah on a collapsed rented house and Gemara's analysis
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a rented house collapses, the landlord must provide another. It cannot be made larger or smaller, nor can rooms be changed without consent. The Gemara questions the case: if 'this house' was specified, it's gone; if 'a house' was unspecified, why can't it be changed? Resh Lakish explains that the landlord specified dimensions. Ravin's version says the landlord said 'a house like this,' and the Gemara clarifies that the house was on a riverbank, so the specification refers to that location.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rules for a landlord when a rented house collapses: he must provide another, cannot change its size or number of rooms, and cannot alter windows without both parties' consent.
The Gemara asks: what are the circumstances? If the landlord specified 'this house,' it's gone; if he said 'a house' without specification, why can't he change its size or divide it?
Resh Lakish answers that the landlord specified the house's dimensions, so the tenant is entitled to a house of those exact measurements.
The Gemara objects: if so, what is the novelty of the Mishnah's ruling?

Ravin reports that Resh Lakish revised the explanation: the landlord said 'a house like this,' and the Gemara clarifies that the house was on a riverbank, so the specification refers to that location, teaching that the tenant is entitled to a house in that same location.

items.text: Conclusion of chapter and beginning of next Mishnah
items.text_en: Conclusion of chapter and beginning of next Mishnah
items.desc_en: The chapter concludes with 'Hadran alach HaSho'el' and the next Mishnah begins, discussing the laws of a sharecropper who receives a field, stating that all practices follow local custom, and that produce and byproducts are divided accordingly.

sub.desc_en: The chapter concludes with the formula 'Hadran alach HaSho'el' and the next Mishnah begins, introducing the laws of a sharecropper who receives a field, stating that all practices follow local custom and that produce and byproducts are divided accordingly.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that in a sharecropping arrangement, both parties share in the vines and reeds, and both supply the reeds.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that in a sharecropping arrangement, both parties share in the vines and reeds, and both supply the reeds.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's first clause
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's first clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Tanna's ruling that where custom is to reap, one may not uproot, and vice versa, because each party has different interests. It clarifies that the phrase 'both prevent each other' explains the rationale.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna states the rule that where custom is to reap, one may not uproot, and vice versa, and each party prevents the other.
The Gemara explains the rationale: the reaper wants the land to be strengthened, the uprooter wants straw, and each party's interest prevents the other's method.
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah adds 'both prevent each other' and answers that it explains the reason for the previous rulings.

items.text: Clarification regarding plowing after harvesting
items.text_en: Clarification regarding plowing after harvesting
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a case where the sharecropper plows after harvesting in a place where weeding is not customary, teaching that he must explicitly inform the landowner of his intention.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the sharecropper plows after harvesting, he may plow.
The Gemara asks: This is obvious — why is it stated?
The Gemara explains: The case is necessary where weeding is not customary, but the sharecropper went and weeded.
The Gemara raises a concern: One might think the sharecropper could claim he weeded only to avoid plowing, not to improve the field.
The Gemara resolves: The Mishnah teaches that the sharecropper must explicitly inform the landowner of his intention to plow.

items.text: Expansion of 'everything follows local custom'
items.text_en: Expansion of 'everything follows local custom'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that 'everything' includes the custom of renting trees with the land. It discusses cases where one deviates from the standard rental rate, teaching that he must explicitly state his intention.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what additional case the word 'הכל' (everything) in the Mishnah comes to include.
The Gemara answers that 'הכל' includes the baraita's rule: in a place where it is customary to rent trees together with the land, one may do so; where not, one may not.
The Gemara objects that the first clause of the baraita is obvious and needs no inclusion.

The Gemara resolves that the baraita is needed for a case where everyone pays a third of the crop as rent, but this tenant pays only a quarter; without explicit stipulation, he cannot later claim the reduction was because he did not rent the trees.

items.text: Division of straw and other items
items.text_en: Division of straw and other items
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that straw and stubble are divided like produce. Rav Yosef notes that in Babylonia, straw is not given to the sharecropper, and he lists items that belong to the landowner versus the sharecropper based on their nature.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that straw and stubble are divided like produce.
Rav Yosef notes that in Babylonia, straw is not given to the sharecropper, and if someone does give it, it is considered generous and not a precedent.

Rav Yosef lists items that belong to the landowner versus the sharecropper based on their nature, with a general rule that permanent items belong to the landowner and temporary care belongs to the sharecropper.

items.text: Division of vines and reeds
items.text_en: Division of vines and reeds
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that vines and reeds are divided like wine. The Gemara explains that these are reeds used to support vines, and both parties share them because both supply them.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that just as they divide wine, so too they divide vines and reeds.
The Gemara asks: what function do reeds serve in this context?
The school of Rabbi Yannai explains that these are designated reeds used to support the vines.
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah adds that both supply the reeds.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah is explaining the reason: both divide the reeds because both supply them.

items.text: Mishnah on irrigation and tree damage
items.text_en: Mishnah on irrigation and tree damage
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses a case where a sharecropper receives a field with an irrigation canal or trees; if the canal dries up or trees are cut, he does not deduct from his rent unless he specified that particular field. The Gemara clarifies that this applies to a small canal, not a major river.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a sharecropper receives a field that is irrigated or planted with trees, and the water source dries up or the trees are cut, he does not deduct from his rent unless he specified that particular field.
The Gemara asks what case the Mishnah describes, objecting that if a major river dried up, the sharecropper should deduct because it is a regional calamity.
Rav Pappa answers that the Mishnah refers to a small canal that dried up, not a major river, so the sharecropper cannot claim a regional calamity.

items.text: Opening inquiry about bringing produce in a basket
items.text_en: Opening inquiry about bringing produce in a basket
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question about bringing produce in a basket (דוולא), likely related to the Mishnah's discussion of sharecropping.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an inquiry about bringing produce in a basket (דוולא), likely related to the sharecropping arrangement.

items.text: Rav Pappa's distinction between the first two Mishnayot and later ones
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's distinction between the first two Mishnayot and later ones
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that the first two Mishnayot of the chapter apply to both sharecropping (קבלנותא) and fixed-rent leasing (חכרנותא), but from that point onward, each Mishnah applies exclusively to one type of arrangement.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that the first two Mishnayot apply to both sharecropping (חכרנותא) and contracting (קבלנותא), but from there onward each applies to only one arrangement.

items.text: Gemara's challenge from the Mishnah's phrase 'this irrigated field'
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge from the Mishnah's phrase 'this irrigated field'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah specifies 'this irrigated field' (שדה בית השלחין זה), arguing that the lessor could claim he only sold a name, citing a baraita about selling a 'beis kor' or 'vineyard' even if the land is smaller or lacks vines. The Gemara concludes that the same logic should apply here.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah's phrase 'this irrigated field' matters, arguing the lessor could claim he only sold a name.
The Gemara cites a baraita that when one sells a 'beis kor' or 'vineyard' or 'orchard', even if the land is smaller or lacks vines/trees, the sale stands because only the name was sold.
The Gemara concludes that the same logic should apply here: the lessor could claim he only sold a name.

items.text: Shmuel's resolution: who speaks determines the meaning
items.text_en: Shmuel's resolution: who speaks determines the meaning
items.desc_en: Shmuel resolves the contradiction: when the lessor (מחכיר) says to the lessee (חוכר), it is merely a name; when the lessee says to the lessor, it is a specific condition (קפידא).

sub.desc_en: Shmuel resolves the contradiction: when the owner (מחכיר) specifies to the sharecropper (חוכר), it is merely a name; when the sharecropper specifies to the owner, it is a strict condition (קפידא).

items.text: Ravina's alternative resolution: the word 'this' indicates specificity
items.text_en: Ravina's alternative resolution: the word 'this' indicates specificity
items.desc_en: Ravina argues that in both cases the lessor speaks, but the word 'this' (זה) shows they are standing in the field, and 'irrigated field' (בית השלחין) means the field as it currently is, so it is a specific condition.

sub.desc_en: Ravina offers a different resolution: in both cases the owner speaks, but the word 'זה' (this) indicates the field is before them, and 'בית השלחין' specifies the current condition.

items.text: Mishnah: one who leaves a field fallow must pay
items.text_en: Mishnah: one who leaves a field fallow must pay
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a sharecropper (מקבל) leaves the field fallow (הובירה), the court assesses its potential yield and he must pay, as the contract includes a clause: 'If I leave fallow and do not work, I will pay with the best.'

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states: one who receives a field from another and leaves it fallow is assessed for its potential yield and must pay, as the contract stipulates 'if I leave it fallow and do not work it, I will pay from the best.'

items.text: Gemara: Sages who interpret standard contractual language (לשון הדיוט)
items.text_en: Gemara: Sages who interpret standard contractual language (לשון הדיוט)
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites baraitot showing that Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, Hillel the Elder, and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa all derive halakhot from standard contractual language (לשון הדיוט). Rabbi Meir cites the fallow clause; Rabbi Yehuda cites a ketubah clause; Hillel cites Alexandrian ketubot; Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa cites a loan document clause. The Gemara then questions Rabbi Yehoshua's ruling based on Rabbi Yoḥanan's principle about returning a pledge.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that Rabbi Meir interpreted standard contractual language (לשון הדיוט).
A baraita cites Rabbi Meir's ruling that the tenant's clause 'If I leave it fallow and do not work it, I will pay from the best' is binding.
The Gemara introduces that Rabbi Yehuda also interpreted standard contractual language.
A baraita cites Rabbi Yehuda's ruling that a husband brings a rich person's offering for his wife based on the ketubah clause 'that you have upon me from before this.'
The Gemara introduces that Hillel the Elder interpreted standard contractual language.
A baraita describes the Alexandrian problem where men would kidnap brides, and the sages sought to declare the children mamzerim.
Hillel examined the ketubot and found the clause 'When you enter the wedding canopy, be my wife,' which prevented the children from being mamzerim.
The Gemara introduces that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa interpreted standard contractual language.

sub.text: Supporting baraita for Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita for Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa
sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa's ruling that a creditor may not take a pledge worth more than the debt, based on the loan document clause 'your payment that you have against me, corresponding to this.'
The Gemara infers that without the clause, the creditor would not acquire the pledge, and questions this based on Rabbi Yoḥanan's principle.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yoḥanan ruled that if one took a pledge and returned it, and the debtor died, the creditor may collect it from the heirs, implying acquisition without a special clause.

items.text: Opening statement: Writing is for reduction
items.text_en: Opening statement: Writing is for reduction
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the principle that a written document is interpreted strictly, meaning that any written amount is taken as the final obligation, not subject to inflation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the principle that a written document is interpreted strictly for reduction, meaning the written amount is the final obligation.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei's interpretation of local custom and the practice of Nehardeans
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei's interpretation of local custom and the practice of Nehardeans
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei rules that the local custom determines whether a ketubah is collected as a loan or as half. The Nehardeans collect a third, and Marimar also collects the appreciation.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei rules that local custom determines whether a ketubah is collected as a loan or as half.
The Nehardeans collect a third of the appreciation, and Marimar also collects the appreciation.

items.text: Ravina's question to Marimar and resolution
items.text_en: Ravina's question to Marimar and resolution
items.desc_en: Ravina challenges Marimar's practice based on the baraita that says one collects half when the custom is to double. Marimar resolves that the baraita refers to a case where they acquired from him, while his case is where they did not acquire from him.

sub.desc_en: Ravina questions Mareimar, citing the baraita that for a doubled amount one collects only half, implying a contradiction.
Mareimar resolves the contradiction: the baraita applies when they acquired the property from him, while the practice applies when they did not acquire it.

items.text: Ravina's practice with his daughter's ketubah
items.text_en: Ravina's practice with his daughter's ketubah
items.desc_en: Ravina praises and writes for his daughter. When asked to acquire from him, he explains that if they acquire, there is no doubling; if they double, there is no acquisition.

sub.desc_en: Ravina praises and writes for his daughter, explaining that if they acquire from him, there is no doubling; if they double, there is no acquisition.
People ask Ravina to let them acquire the property from him for the daughter.
Ravina explains that if they acquire the property, there is no doubling of the ketubah value; if they double, there is no acquisition.

items.text: Case of a man promising 400 zuz for his daughter's ketubah
items.text_en: Case of a man promising 400 zuz for his daughter's ketubah
items.desc_en: A man says 'give her 400 zuz for her ketubah.' Rav Ashi rules that if he said 'give her,' it means 400 that are 800; if 'write for her,' it means 400 that are 200. An alternative version distinguishes between 'for her ketubah' and 'in her ketubah.' The Gemara concludes that unless he said 'give her' explicitly, it means 400 that are 200.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case where a man instructs to give 400 zuz to his daughter for her ketubah, and Rav Acha asks Rav Ashi whether this means 400 that are 800 or 400 that are 200.
Rav Ashi rules that if he said 'give her' (הבו לה), it means 400 that are 800; if he said 'write for her' (כתבו לה), it means 400 that are 200.

sub.text: Alternative version of Rav Ashi's ruling
sub.text_en: Alternative version of Rav Ashi's ruling
sub.desc_en: An alternative version distinguishes between 'for her ketubah' (לכתובתה) meaning 400 that are 800, and 'in her ketubah' (בכתובתה) meaning 400 that are 200.
The Gemara concludes that both 'for her ketubah' and 'in her ketubah' mean 400 that are 200, unless he explicitly said 'give her' (הבו לה) without qualification.

items.text: Case of a tenant who promised 1000 zuz if he improves the land
items.text_en: Case of a tenant who promised 1000 zuz if he improves the land
items.desc_en: A tenant says if he improves the land he will pay 1000 zuz. He improves a third. The Nehardeans say he pays 333 1/3. Rava says it is an asmachta and not binding. The Gemara distinguishes from a case where one says 'if I do not do, I will pay,' because there he does not exaggerate, but here he exaggerates.

sub.desc_en: Presents the case of a tenant who accepted a field and promised 1000 zuz if he improves it, and he improved one-third.
The Nehardeans rule that the tenant pays 333 1/3 zuz, proportional to the improvement.
Rava objects that the promise is an אסמכתא (exaggerated commitment) and therefore not legally binding.
The Gemara asks Rava: what distinguishes this case from the Mishnah where one says 'if I do not improve, I will pay' and it is binding?
The Gemara answers: there the tenant does not exaggerate, but here he promises an excessive amount, so it is mere exaggeration (גוזמא).

items.text: Case of a tenant who planted wheat in a field designated for sesame
items.text_en: Case of a tenant who planted wheat in a field designated for sesame
items.desc_en: A tenant accepts a field for sesame, plants wheat, and the wheat yields like sesame. Rav Kahana thought to deduct the land's depletion. Rav Ashi told him that people say: let the land be depleted, but not its owner.

sub.desc_en: A tenant accepts a field for sesame, plants wheat, and the wheat yields like sesame.
Rav Kahana thought to deduct from the tenant the land's depletion (the loss of value from planting wheat instead of sesame).
Rav Ashi tells Rav Kahana that people say: let the land be depleted, but not its owner (the tenant should not suffer a deduction).

items.text: Case of a tenant who planted wheat and got more than sesame
items.text_en: Case of a tenant who planted wheat and got more than sesame
items.desc_en: A tenant accepts a field for sesame, plants wheat, and gets more than sesame. Ravina thought to give him the intermediate appreciation. Rav Acha from Difti said: Did he improve? Did the land not improve?

sub.desc_en: Ravina thought to say that the tenant gives the intermediate appreciation.
Rav Acha objects to Ravina: did he alone improve? Did the land not also improve?
Rav Acha from Difti objects: Did the tenant improve the land? Did the land not improve itself? — implying the tenant deserves no special compensation.

items.text: Discussion of the 'isqa' arrangement
items.text_en: Discussion of the 'isqa' arrangement
items.desc_en: The Nehardeans say an isqa is half loan and half deposit, a convenience for both parties. Rava says it is called isqa because it is for business, not for drinking. Rav Idi bar Avin says if the borrower dies, it becomes movable property for his sons; Rava disagrees. Rava concludes: one isqa and two documents is a loss for the lender.

sub.desc_en: The Nehardeans state that an isqa arrangement is half loan and half deposit, instituted as a convenience for both borrower and lender.
The Gemara notes that since half is a loan, the borrower may use it to drink beer, which is permitted.
Rava explains that the arrangement is called isqa because it is given for business dealings, not for drinking beer.
Rav Idi bar Avin adds that if the borrower dies, the isqa becomes movable property (מטלטלין) for his sons.
Rava disagrees, stating that the isqa is called such precisely so that if the borrower dies, it does not become movable property for his sons.
Rava concludes that one isqa with two documents results in a loss for the lender.

items.text: Opening statement on two businesses with one document
items.text_en: Opening statement on two businesses with one document
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that when two business ventures are recorded in a single document, the loss falls on the borrower. This sets the stage for the subsequent rulings of Rava.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states a general rule: when two business ventures are recorded in a single document, the loss falls on the borrower.

items.text: Rava's first ruling: covering a loss without informing the partner
items.text_en: Rava's first ruling: covering a loss without informing the partner
items.desc_en: Rava rules that if a business manager (מקבל עיסקא) covers a loss from his own pocket without informing the investor, he cannot later demand the investor share the loss, because the investor can say he did so to avoid being called a 'business loser'.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that if a business manager suffered a loss and then worked to cover it without informing the investor, the investor cannot later demand that the manager share the loss, because the manager can say he worked to avoid being called a 'business loser'.

items.text: Rava's second ruling: partners and profit distribution
items.text_en: Rava's second ruling: partners and profit distribution
items.desc_en: Rava discusses a case where two partners in a business (עיסקא) made a profit. If one wants to divide the profit immediately, the other can delay by saying they should earn more. If one demands his share of profit, the other can say profit is subordinate to the capital. If one demands both profit and capital, the other can say the business is jointly liable. If one proposes dividing both profit and capital and sharing future losses, the other can refuse because the luck of two partners is better.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that if one partner wants to divide profit immediately, the other can delay by saying they should earn more.
Rava rules that if one demands his share of profit, the other can say profit is subordinate to the capital.
Rava rules that if one demands both profit and capital, the other can say the business is jointly liable.
Rava rules that if one proposes dividing both profit and capital and sharing future losses, the other can refuse because the luck of two partners is better.

items.text: Mishnah: tenant who refuses to weed
items.text_en: Mishnah: tenant who refuses to weed
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that if a tenant (מקבל שדה) refuses to weed the field, and the landowner says 'what do I care, since I give you your rent?', we do not listen to the tenant. The reason is that the landowner can say: 'Tomorrow you will leave the field and leave weeds before me.'

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if a tenant farmer refuses to weed the field, the landowner can compel him because the weeds will remain when the tenant leaves.

items.text: Gemara: tenant's alternative proposals and their rejection
items.text_en: Gemara: tenant's alternative proposals and their rejection
items.desc_en: The Gemara explores possible responses from the tenant: if he offers to plow later, the landowner wants good wheat; if he offers to buy wheat from the market, the landowner wants wheat from his own field; if he offers to weed only his portion, the landowner says he is giving the field a bad name. The Gemara then questions the Mishnah's reason (weeds) and explains that the real reason is that the landowner can say 'the seed that falls, falls' (i.e., the tenant's negligence causes permanent damage).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explores three hypothetical tenant proposals (plowing later, buying wheat from market, weeding only his portion) and the landowner's rejection of each.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's stated reason is that weeds grow, not the landowner's concerns about reputation or seed quality.
The Gemara resolves that the real reason is the landowner can say 'the seed that falls, falls' (i.e., the tenant's negligence causes permanent damage to the field).

items.text: Mishnah: field that did not produce
items.text_en: Mishnah: field that did not produce
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a tenant received a field and it did not produce, if there is enough to form a pile (כרי), he is obligated to tend it. Rabbi Yehuda asks: what is the measure of a pile? Rather, if there is enough for a 'fall' (נפילה).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a field does not produce, the tenant must tend it if there is enough to form a stack; Rabbi Yehuda defines the measure as 'enough for a fall'.
Rabbi Yehuda asks: what is the measure of a pile (כרי)?
Rabbi Yehuda proposes an alternative measure: if there is enough for a 'fall' (נפילה), the tenant is obligated.

items.text: Gemara: baraita on the tenant's obligation and the measure of a pile
items.text_en: Gemara: baraita on the tenant's obligation and the measure of a pile
items.desc_en: A baraita elaborates that the tenant is obligated to tend the field if it can produce a pile, because the contract stipulates he will do all agricultural work and the landowner will take half. The Gemara then discusses the measure of a pile: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina says enough to support a winnowing shovel (רחת). A question arises about the shovel's span. Rabbi Avahu clarifies from Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina that it means the shovel's handle sees the sun. Levi says three se'ah, the school of Rabbi Yannai says two se'ah. Reish Lakish says the two se'ah are exclusive of expenses.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that a tenant who receives a field that did not produce is obligated to tend it if it can yield a pile, because the contract stipulates he will do all work and the landowner will take half.
The Gemara asks what measure constitutes a pile, and Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina answers: enough to support a winnowing shovel (רחת).
A question is raised: does the shovel's span refer to its full width from one side to the other?
Rabbi Avahu clarifies from Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina that the measure is when the shovel's handle (the part that gathers) sees the sun, i.e., the pile is large enough that the handle is exposed.
Levi says the pile is three se'ah, while the school of Rabbi Yannai says two se'ah.
Reish Lakish resolves that the two se'ah measure is exclusive of expenses (the tenant's costs).

items.text: Digression: Perutzey zeitim (broken olives) and their measure
items.text_en: Digression: Perutzey zeitim (broken olives) and their measure
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about broken olives and grapes (פריצי זיתים וענבים) where Beit Shammai deem them susceptible to impurity and Beit Hillel deem them pure. Rav Huna explains 'perutzey zeitim' as 'wicked olives'. Rav Yosef cites a verse. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites another. The measure of these olives is debated: Rabbi Elazar says four kav per beam, the school of Rabbi Yannai says two se'ah per beam. They are not in dispute, as it depends on local practice of loading one or three kor per beam.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about broken olives and grapes (פריצי זיתים וענבים) where Beit Shammai deem them susceptible to impurity and Beit Hillel deem them pure.
The Gemara asks what 'perutzey zeitim' means.
Rav Huna explains 'perutzey zeitim' as 'wicked olives'.
Rav Yosef cites a verse (Daniel 11:14) using the word 'paritzey' to support the interpretation.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's alternative scriptural support
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's alternative scriptural support
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites a different verse (Ezekiel 18:10) using 'paritz' to support the same interpretation.
The Gemara asks what the measure of these broken olives is.
Rabbi Elazar says the measure is four kav per beam.
The school of Rabbi Yannai says the measure is two se'ah per beam.
The Gemara resolves that the two opinions are not in dispute, as they refer to different local practices of loading one or three kor per beam.

items.text: Introduction to a new baraita
items.text_en: Introduction to a new baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new baraita with the phrase 'תנו רבנן', indicating a forthcoming teaching that will be discussed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita with the standard formula 'תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן' (the Sages taught).

items.text: Definition of weak force for tree and hut
items.text_en: Definition of weak force for tree and hut
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that ascending a tree or hut with weak force renders one impure. The Gemara defines weak force for a tree as one whose trunk lacks a quarter-log of wood, and for a hut as one whose interior is hidden from view.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that ascending a tree or hut with weak force renders one impure.
The Gemara asks: what constitutes a tree with weak force?
Devei Rabbi Yannai defines a weak tree as one whose trunk lacks a quarter-log of wood.
The Gemara asks: what constitutes a hut with weak force?
Reish Lakish defines a weak hut as one whose interior is hidden from view.

items.text: Definition of weak force for person and animal
items.text_en: Definition of weak force for person and animal
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that walking in a beit hapras over stones that can be moved, or over a person or animal with weak force, renders one impure. The Gemara defines weak force for a person as one whose knees knock when riding, and for an animal as one that defecates while being ridden.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who walks in a beit hapras over movable stones, or over a person or animal with weak force, becomes impure.
The Gemara asks for the definition of a person with weak force.
Reish Lakish defines a person with weak force as one whose knees knock when riding.
The Gemara asks for the definition of an animal with weak force.
Devei Rabbi Yannai defines an animal with weak force as one that defecates while being ridden.

items.text: Measure of four kav for prayer and tefillin
items.text_en: Measure of four kav for prayer and tefillin
items.desc_en: Devei Rabbi Yannai states that four kav is the measure for prayer and tefillin. For prayer, if one carries a load of less than four kav, he may shift it behind him and pray; if four kav, he must place it on the ground. For tefillin, if one carries a load on his head and the tefillin are pressed, it is forbidden; the measure is a load of four kav.

sub.desc_en: Devei Rabbi Yannai states that the measure of four kav applies to prayer and tefillin.
The Gemara asks what the measure of four kav means for prayer.
A baraita explains that one carrying less than four kav may shift the load behind him and pray, but with four kav he must place it on the ground.
The Gemara asks what the measure of four kav means for tefillin.
A baraita states that if one carries a load on his head and the tefillin are pressed, it is forbidden; the measure is a load of four kav.

items.text: Proper conduct with tefillin while carrying dung
items.text_en: Proper conduct with tefillin while carrying dung
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya teaches that one carrying dung on his head while wearing tefillin should not remove them to his side or tie them around his waist, as that would be disrespectful, but may tie them on his arm in the proper place. In the name of Rabbi Sheila, it is added that even a cloth is forbidden to place on a head that has tefillin; Abaye says even a small cloth of Pumbedita.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya teaches that one carrying dung on his head while wearing tefillin should not remove them to his side or tie them around his waist, as that would be disrespectful, but may tie them on his arm in the proper place.

sub.text: Addition in the name of Rabbi Sheila
sub.text_en: Addition in the name of Rabbi Sheila
sub.desc_en: In the name of Rabbi Sheila, it is added that even a cloth is forbidden to place on a head that has tefillin; Abaye specifies the measure as even a small cloth of Pumbedita.

items.text: Measure of kedei nefilah for a kor
items.text_en: Measure of kedei nefilah for a kor
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda asks what is the measure of kedei nefilah (enough to cause a fall) in a kor. Rabbi Ami quoting Rabbi Yochanan says four se'ah per kor; Rabbi Ami himself says eight se'ah per kor. An elder explains to Rav Chama that in Rabbi Yochanan's years the land was fertile, in Rabbi Ami's years it was lean.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda asks what is the measure of kedei nefilah (enough to cause a fall) in a kor.
Rabbi Ami, quoting Rabbi Yochanan, answers that the measure is four se'ah per kor.
Rabbi Ami himself gives a different answer: eight se'ah per kor.
An elder explains to Rav Chama that the discrepancy is due to differing land fertility: in Rabbi Yochanan's years the land was fertile, in Rabbi Ami's years it was lean.

items.text: Measure of kedei nefilah for leket
items.text_en: Measure of kedei nefilah for leket
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if wind scattered sheaves, one estimates how much leket they would have produced and gives to the poor; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says give kedei nefilah. The Gemara debates the measure: Rabbi Elazar or Rabbi Yochanan say four kav per kor. Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether it is per kor of seed or produce, and whether the fall is by hand or by oxen. Ravin brings a resolution: four kav per kor of seed, but the other question remains unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if wind scattered sheaves, one estimates the leket and gives to the poor; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says give kedei nefilah.
The Gemara asks the measure of kedei nefilah, and Rav Dimi cites Rabbi Elazar or Rabbi Yochanan: four kav per kor.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether the measure is per kor of seed or produce, and whether the fall is by hand or by oxen.
Ravin brings a resolution: four kav per kor of seed, but the other question remains unresolved (teiku).

items.text: Field rental: deduction for national blight
items.text_en: Field rental: deduction for national blight
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a tenant farmer's field is eaten by locusts or blighted, if it is a national blight he deducts from his rent, otherwise not. Rabbi Yehuda says if he paid in cash, he never deducts. The Gemara defines national blight: Rav Yehuda says if most of the valley is blighted; Ulla says if four fields around it are blighted. Ulla reports that in the West they asked about partial blight or remaining strips, and about a canal breaking, but the text cuts off.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: if a tenant farmer's field is eaten by locusts or blighted, if it is a national blight he deducts from his rent, otherwise not; Rabbi Yehuda says if he paid in cash, he never deducts.
The Gemara asks: what constitutes a national blight?
Rav Yehuda answers: if most of the valley is blighted.
Ulla answers: if four fields around it are blighted.
Ulla reports that in the West they asked about partial blight (a single strip across the entire field), remaining strips, and a canal breaking, but the text cuts off.

items.text: Opening questions on mixed seeds and blight
items.text_en: Opening questions on mixed seeds and blight
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises unresolved questions about whether different grains are considered 'other seed' for tenancy disputes, and whether a tenant can claim exemption if his crop fails while others succeed, or vice versa, concluding with 'teiku' (let it stand).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises unresolved questions about whether wheat relative to barley is considered 'other seed' for tenancy disputes, and whether a tenant can claim exemption if his crop fails while others succeed or vice versa, concluding with 'teiku' (let it stand).

items.text: Tenant planted barley instead of wheat and blight struck
items.text_en: Tenant planted barley instead of wheat and blight struck
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers a case where the tenant was told to plant wheat but planted barley, and most of the field was blighted including his barley. It suggests the tenant can argue that had he planted wheat, the verse 'You shall decree a thing and it shall be established' would have protected him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: if a tenant was told to plant wheat but planted barley, and a blight struck most of the field including his barley, can the tenant argue that had he planted wheat, the verse 'You shall decree a thing and it shall be established' would have protected him?
The Gemara concludes that the tenant can indeed argue that had he planted wheat, the verse would have been fulfilled for him, so he is exempt from liability.

items.text: All of the lessor's fields were blighted
items.text_en: All of the lessor's fields were blighted
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the tenant can deduct rent if all of the lessor's fields were blighted, even though most of the region was not. It concludes that the lessor can argue that the blight was due to the tenant's bad luck, as the verse 'For we are left but a few of many' suggests some should have survived.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the tenant can deduct rent when all of the lessor's fields were blighted but most of the region was not, considering the lessor might blame the tenant's bad luck.
The Gemara concludes that the lessor can argue that if the blight were due to the tenant's bad luck, some of his fields would have survived, citing the verse 'For we are left but a few of many'.

items.text: All of the tenant's fields were blighted
items.text_en: All of the tenant's fields were blighted
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the tenant can deduct rent if all of his own fields were blighted and most of the region was also blighted. It concludes that the lessor can argue the blight was due to the tenant's bad luck, because if any survival were possible, some would have remained from the tenant's own fields.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the tenant can deduct rent when all his own fields were blighted and most of the region was also blighted, presenting two possibilities.
The Gemara concludes that the lessor can argue the blight was due to the tenant's bad luck (לַתָּא), so no deduction is made.
The Gemara objects: why not say here too that if the blight were due to the lessor's bad luck, some survival would have remained, as per the verse?
The Gemara answers: the lessor can respond that if any survival were possible for the tenant, some would have remained from the tenant's own fields, proving the blight was the tenant's bad luck.

items.text: Challenge from the Mishnah on blight and famine years
items.text_en: Challenge from the Mishnah on blight and famine years
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a year of blight or famine does not count toward the lease term, implying that only total crop failure exempts, not partial. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the verse 'According to the number of years of crops' refers only to years with some produce, so partial failure still counts.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that a year of blight, mildew, the Sabbatical year, or famine years like Elijah's does not count toward the lease term.
The gemara infers from the baraita that only total crop failure exempts, not partial failure, implying that a year with some produce counts toward the lease.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the challenge by citing the verse 'According to the number of years of crops,' which refers only to years with some produce, so partial failure still counts.

items.text: Discussion on the Sabbatical year
items.text_en: Discussion on the Sabbatical year
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks why the Sabbatical year does not count toward the lease, since produce exists outside Israel. Rav Kahana answers that the Sabbatical is a royal decree. Mar Zutra then questions why the tenant still pays a reduced rent during Sabbatical, and Ravina explains that the land can still be used for drying fruit.

sub.text: Rav Ashi's question to Rav Kahana
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's question to Rav Kahana
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks Rav Kahana: if the Sabbatical year (שביעית) should count toward the lease because produce exists outside Israel, why does the Mishnah exclude it?
Rav Kahana answers that the Sabbatical year is a royal decree (אפקועתא דמלכא), meaning the land is legally ownerless and cannot be counted.
Mar Zutra asks Ravina: if the Sabbatical year does not count toward the lease, why does the Mishnah say the tenant pays a reduced rent (סלע ופונדיון) for that year?
Ravina explains that the Sabbatical year is different because the land can still be used for drying fruit (למישטחא בה פירי), so the tenant pays a reduced rent for that benefit.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on locusts and the principle of miraculous intervention
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on locusts and the principle of miraculous intervention
items.desc_en: Shmuel rules that the tenant can deduct only if he sowed and locusts ate the crop, but not if he never sowed, as he could have relied on the verse 'They shall not be ashamed in the evil time.' Rav Sheishet challenges with a case of a shepherd who left his flock, where we do not assume miraculous intervention. The Gemara answers that one cannot rely on a great miracle like David's, but a small miracle might be expected.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that the tenant can deduct only if he sowed and locusts ate the crop, but not if he never sowed, as he could have relied on the verse that the righteous will not be ashamed in evil times.

Rav Sheishet challenges Shmuel with a baraita about a shepherd who left his flock and a predator attacked, where we do not assume miraculous intervention, asking why we don't apply the same logic of relying on a miracle.
The Gemara answers that one cannot rely on a great miracle like David's, but a small miracle like Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa's might be expected, so the tenant can rely on a small miracle.

items.text: Resolving the contradiction between two baraitot on chazakah
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction between two baraitot on chazakah
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: one baraita states that after the first and second sowing the field is sown, but not the third; another states that the third is sown but not the fourth. The Gemara resolves this by attributing the first to Rabbi (who holds that chazakah is established after two times) and the second to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel (who holds it is after three times).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between two baraitot regarding the number of sowings required for chazakah (presumption of ownership).
Two baraitot are cited: one states that after the first and second sowing the field is sown but not the third; the other states that the third is sown but not the fourth.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by attributing the first baraita to Rabbi, who holds that chazakah is established after two times, and the second to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who holds it is after three times.

items.text: Reish Lakish's distinction and Rav Pappa's limit
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's distinction and Rav Pappa's limit
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish says the ruling only applies when the crop grew and was eaten by locusts, but if it did not grow, the landowner can say 'sow it all your days.' Rav Pappa adds that this continues until sharecroppers from the desert come and stand on their land.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish distinguishes that the ruling of a three-year presumption only applies when the crop grew and was eaten by locusts, but if it did not grow, the landowner can say 'sow it all your days.'
Rav Pappa limits the duration of this claim: until sharecroppers from the desert come and stand on their land.

items.text: Challenge from the seasons and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from the seasons and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita from Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel in the name of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya divides the year into seasons, with Rabbi Yehuda counting from Tishrei and Rabbi Shimon from Marcheshvan. The Gemara asks: who is lenient in all these? It is Rabbi Shimon, yet he did not say all this! The Gemara resolves: the case where he accepted the field in the cold season is different from where he accepted it in the warm season.

sub.desc_en: A baraita from Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel in the name of Rabbi Meir, and Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya, divides the year into six seasons of two months each.
The baraita records that Rabbi Yehuda counts the seasons from Tishrei and Rabbi Shimon counts from Marcheshvan.
The Gemara asks: who is lenient in all these seasons? It is Rabbi Shimon, yet he did not say all this (the entire baraita's detailed division)!
The Gemara resolves: the case where he accepted the field in the cold season is different from where he accepted it in the warm season.

items.text: Case of the flooded field and Rabbi Yehuda's ruling
items.text_en: Case of the flooded field and Rabbi Yehuda's ruling
items.desc_en: A man accepted a field for garlic near the King's Canal for zuzim, and the canal was blocked. Rava ruled it is a regional calamity and he may deduct. The rabbis challenged Rava from the Mishnah that Rabbi Yehuda says if he accepted it for money, he may not deduct. Rava dismissed Rabbi Yehuda's opinion.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Rabbi Yehuda's ruling that if one accepted a field for money, he may not deduct from the rental payment regardless of circumstances.
A man accepted a field for garlic near the King's Canal for zuzim, the canal was blocked, and Rava ruled it is a regional calamity (מכת מדינה) and he may deduct.
The rabbis challenged Rava from the Mishnah that Rabbi Yehuda says if he accepted it for money, he may not deduct in any case.
Rava dismissed Rabbi Yehuda's opinion, stating that no one pays heed to it.

items.text: Mishnah: Lessee pays from the crop if it fails
items.text_en: Mishnah: Lessee pays from the crop if it fails
items.desc_en: If one accepts a field for ten kor of wheat per year and it fails, he pays from within it. If the wheat is good, he cannot buy from the market but must give from within it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one accepts a field for ten kor of wheat per year and it fails, he pays from within it; if the wheat is good, he cannot buy from the market but must give from within it.

items.text: Case of alfalfa and the principle of the land's agency
items.text_en: Case of alfalfa and the principle of the land's agency
items.desc_en: A man accepted a field for alfalfa, plowed it, and sowed barley which failed. Rav Aviva asked Ravina whether this is like 'it failed, he pays from within it.' Ravina distinguished: there the land did not fulfill its master's agency, but here it did (since alfalfa was not sown).

sub.desc_en: Rav Aviva asks Ravina whether the case of a man who accepted a field for alfalfa, plowed it, and sowed barley which failed, is comparable to the mishnah's rule that if the crop fails, the tenant pays from within the field.

Ravina distinguishes the cases: in the mishnah the land did not fulfill its master's agency (the crop failed due to the land's fault), but here the land did fulfill its agency (since alfalfa was not sown, the failure is the tenant's fault).

items.text: Case of the vineyard and Rav Ashi's distinction
items.text_en: Case of the vineyard and Rav Ashi's distinction
items.desc_en: A man accepted a vineyard for ten barrels of wine, and the wine turned sour. Rav Kahana thought it is like the Mishnah, but Rav Ashi said no: there the land did not fulfill its agency, but here it did (the grapes grew). Rav Ashi concedes regarding red raisins and a field that failed in its stalks.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a case: a man accepted a vineyard from his fellow for ten barrels of wine, and the wine turned sour.
Rav Kahana thought this case is identical to the Mishnah's rule: if the produce failed, the tenant gives from the same produce.
Rav Ashi objects: the cases are not comparable — there the land did not fulfill its agency (the crop failed), but here the land did fulfill its agency (the grapes grew, but the wine soured).
Rav Ashi concedes that in two specific cases — red raisins and a field that failed in its stalks — the tenant may deduct from the agreed rent.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on changing crops and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's reason
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on changing crops and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's reason
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one accepts a field for barley, he may not sow wheat, but if for wheat, he may sow barley; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel prohibits. Rav Chisda explains his reason from the verse about not speaking deceit. A challenge is brought from the laws of Purim collection, but the text cuts off.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: one who accepts a field for barley may not sow wheat, but if for wheat may sow barley; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel prohibits any change.
Rav Chisda explains Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's reason from the verse 'שארית ישראל לא יעשו עולה ולא ידברו כזב' (the remnant of Israel shall not do iniquity nor speak lies).
A challenge is brought from the laws of Purim collection, where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's position seems contradicted, but the text cuts off.

items.text: Abaye explains Rabban Shimon's view on crop rotation
items.text_en: Abaye explains Rabban Shimon's view on crop rotation
items.desc_en: Abaye explains the reasoning behind Rabban Shimon's position: one who wants his field to be ruined should alternate planting wheat and barley, and alternate between sowing and fallowing. This applies only if he does not plow and repeat, but if he plows and repeats, we do not hold that view.

sub.desc_en: Abaye introduces the reasoning behind Rabban Shimon's position: one who wants his field ruined should alternate planting wheat and barley, and alternate between sowing and fallowing.
Abaye qualifies that this applies only if he does not plow and repeat, but if he plows and repeats, we do not hold that view.

items.text: Dispute about planting legumes in a harvested field
items.text_en: Dispute about planting legumes in a harvested field
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda taught Ravin that one may plant legumes in a field that produced grain, contradicting the Mishnah which forbids it. Rav Yehuda resolves the contradiction by explaining that the Mishnah applies to Babylonia (where the soil is poor) while his ruling applies to Eretz Yisrael (where the soil is rich).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited: one may not plant legumes in a field that produced grain.
Rav Yehuda taught Ravin that one may plant legumes in a grain field, and Ravin objects citing the Mishnah's prohibition.
Rav Yehuda resolves the contradiction: the Mishnah applies to Babylonia (poor soil), while his ruling applies to Eretz Yisrael (rich soil).

items.text: Laws of flax stalks and theft
items.text_en: Laws of flax stalks and theft
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda tells Ravin that flax stalks from a flax field are not subject to theft laws unless they are standing on the boundary (where they are noticeable). However, if they have taken root and grown, even those in the field are subject to theft because the owner has suffered a loss.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda tells Ravin that flax stalks from a flax field are not subject to theft laws unless they are standing on the boundary (where they are noticeable).
Rav Yehuda adds that if the stalks have taken root and grown, even those in the field are subject to theft because the owner has suffered a loss.

items.text: Tree on a boundary line: dispute between Rav and Shmuel
items.text_en: Tree on a boundary line: dispute between Rav and Shmuel
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda tells Ravin about the custom in Egypt regarding a tree that leans over a boundary. The Gemara cites a dispute: Rav says each side takes the branches that lean toward it, while Shmuel says they divide. A challenge is raised from a baraita that says they divide, which is resolved by interpreting Rav's statement as referring to a tree that fills the entire boundary, and further refined to a case where the branches lean to one side.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda tells Ravin about the Egyptian custom regarding a tree that leans over a boundary: each side takes the branches that lean toward it.
The Gemara cites the dispute: Rav says each side takes the branches that lean toward it, while Shmuel says they divide the tree and its produce equally.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that says they divide, which contradicts Rav, and Shmuel explains Rav's position as referring to a tree that fills the entire boundary.

The Gemara refines the case: even if the tree fills the boundary, the dispute applies only when the branches lean to one side, and Rav's ruling teaches that the owner of that side can demand division according to the lean.

items.text: Aggadic interpretations of blessings in Deuteronomy
items.text_en: Aggadic interpretations of blessings in Deuteronomy
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda advises Ravin not to buy land near a town, citing Rav's teaching that one should not stand in a friend's field when it is full of standing grain. The Gemara then recounts a discussion between Rabbi Abba and Rav's students about the meaning of the blessings in Deuteronomy 28:3-6, with Rav and Rabbi Yochanan offering different interpretations, including that one's house should be near a synagogue (Rav) or near a toilet (Rabbi Yochanan), and that one's property should be diversified or near the city.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda advises Ravin not to buy land near a town, citing Rav's teaching that one should not stand in a friend's field when it is full of standing grain.
The Gemara objects: Did not Rabbi Abba find Rav's students and ask them what Rav said about the blessings in Deuteronomy 28:3-6?

Rav's students report Rav's interpretation: 'Blessed in the city' means your house should be near the synagogue; 'blessed in the field' means your property should be near the city; 'blessed in your coming' means your wife should not be a ספק נדה (doubtfully menstruating) when you return from a journey; 'blessed in your going out' means your offspring should be like you.

Rabbi Abba objects that Rabbi Yochanan disagrees: 'Blessed in the city' means the toilet should be near your table, not the synagogue, because Rabbi Yochanan holds that walking to the synagogue earns reward for each step.

Rabbi Yochanan interprets 'Blessed in the field' as having diversified property (a third in grain, olives, and vines), and interprets 'blessed in your coming and going' as dying without sin, just as one was born without sin.

items.text: Distinction regarding returning a wall and its lock
items.text_en: Distinction regarding returning a wall and its lock
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a contradiction by distinguishing between cases where one returns a wall and its lock and where one does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a contradiction by distinguishing between a case where one returns the wall and its lock and a case where one does not.

items.text: Interpretations of 'כׇּל חֹלִי' by various rabbis
items.text_en: Interpretations of 'כׇּל חֹלִי' by various rabbis
items.desc_en: Rav, Shmuel, Rabbi Chanina, Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina, and Rabbi Elazar each identify the 'illness' mentioned in the verse with different things: the evil eye, wind, cold, nasal/ear wax, and the gallbladder, respectively. Each supports their view with a proof or a general principle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the verse and presents Rav's identification of the 'illness' as the evil eye.
The Gemara supports Rav's view by citing his practice at a cemetery, where he said that 99 out of 100 die from the evil eye and only one from natural causes.

Shmuel identifies the illness as wind (a harmful draft), consistent with his general principle that everything depends on wind, and he addresses an objection about those killed by the government by saying that with a remedy they would have survived.
Rabbi Chanina identifies the illness as cold (צִנָּה), citing his principle that everything is in Heaven's hands except cold and drafts, supported by a verse.
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina identifies the illness as nasal or ear wax (צוֹאָה), citing a teaching that most of it is harmful and a minority is beneficial.

Rabbi Elazar identifies the illness as the gallbladder (מָרָה), supported by a baraita that calls it 'מחלה' because it sickens the whole body, and notes that all these ailments are nullified by morning bread with salt and a jug of water.

items.text: Thirteen benefits of morning bread
items.text_en: Thirteen benefits of morning bread
items.desc_en: A baraisa lists thirteen benefits of eating bread with salt and a jug of water in the morning, including protection from heat, cold, demons, and various physical and spiritual benefits.

sub.desc_en: The baraisa opens by listing the first eleven of thirteen benefits of eating morning bread with salt and water.
The baraisa concludes with the remaining two benefits and an alternative tradition that morning bread also removes jealousy and brings love.

items.text: Proof for the folk saying about morning bread
items.text_en: Proof for the folk saying about morning bread
items.desc_en: Rabbah asks Rava bar Mari for the source of the folk saying that sixty runners cannot catch a man who eats in the morning. Rava bar Mari first cites a verse from Isaiah, then Rabbah himself cites a verse from Exodus to show that eating bread in the morning removes illness.

sub.text: Rabbah's question to Rava bar Mari
sub.text_en: Rabbah's question to Rava bar Mari
sub.desc_en: Rabbah asks Rava bar Mari for the scriptural source of the folk saying that sixty runners cannot catch a man who eats bread in the morning, and cites the rabbinic dictum to eat early.
Rava bar Mari cites the verse 'לֹא יִרְעָבוּ וְלֹא יִצְמָאוּ' (they shall not hunger nor thirst) to prove that eating in the morning protects from heat and sun.

Rabbah adds a second proof from the verse 'וַעֲבַדְתֶּם אֵת ה׳... וַהֲסִרֹתִי מַחֲלָה מִקִּרְבֶּךָ' (you shall serve the Lord... and I will remove sickness from your midst), interpreting the bread and water as morning bread with salt and a pitcher of water.

items.text: Laws of measuring riverbanks for planting
items.text_en: Laws of measuring riverbanks for planting
