items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda instructs Rav Adda Mashocha'ah not to be negligent in measuring, as every bit is significant for saffron. He distinguishes between measuring four cubits on a river for the residents and on a river for the whole world.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda's instruction to Rav Adda Mashocha'ah
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda's instruction to Rav Adda Mashocha'ah
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda tells Rav Adda Mashocha'ah not to be negligent in measuring, because every bit is significant for saffron.
Rav Yehuda distinguishes between measuring four cubits on a river for the residents and on a river for the whole world, instructing to be lenient with the former and not to measure the latter at all.

items.text: Dispute about cutting trees on a riverbank
items.text_en: Dispute about cutting trees on a riverbank
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami declares that a full shoulder-width of porters on both sides of the river is sufficient for cutting. Rav Natan bar Hoshaya cut sixteen cubits, but the residents of Mashronya covered it, as they thought it was a public domain, but the Gemara explains that here only enough for the porters to pass is needed.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ami declares that a full shoulder-width of porters on both sides of the river is sufficient for cutting trees.
Rav Natan bar Hoshaya cut sixteen cubits, exceeding the minimum.
The residents of Mashronya covered the cut area, objecting to the excessive width.
The Gemara explains that Rav Natan bar Hoshaya mistakenly thought it was a public domain, but in fact only a shoulder-width of porters is needed.

items.text: Rabbah bar Rav Huna's refusal to cut first
items.text_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna's refusal to cut first
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna had a tree on a riverbank. When asked to cut it, he told others to cut first, then he would cut. The Gemara questions this, citing the principle of 'first straighten yourself, then straighten others.' It explains that the tree was on the property of the Parzak Rufila, and he reasoned that if they cut, he would cut, but if not, why should he cut?

sub.desc_en: The narrative introduces that Rabbah bar Rav Huna had a tree on a riverbank, and when asked to cut it, he told others to cut first and then he would cut.
The Gemara objects, citing the verse 'התקוששו וקושו' and Resh Lakish's principle that one should straighten oneself before straightening others.

The Gemara answers that the tree was on the property of the Parzak Rufila, and Rabbah bar Rav Huna reasoned that if others cut, he would cut, but if not, why should he cut, since if they start, the branches will suffice for them.

items.text: Opening statement on preemptive rights
items.text_en: Opening statement on preemptive rights
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that if a neighbor does not protest the sale, the sale stands; otherwise, the neighbor can force the buyer to sell to him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the basic rule of preemptive rights: if the neighbor does not protest, the sale stands; otherwise, the neighbor can force the buyer to sell.

items.text: Story of Rabbah bar Rav Nachman and the tree
items.text_en: Story of Rabbah bar Rav Nachman and the tree
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Nachman cuts down a tree belonging to Rabbah bar Rav Huna without permission, leading to a curse that Rabbah bar Rav Nachman would have no surviving children.

sub.text: Story about Rabbah bar Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Story about Rabbah bar Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: A story is told about Rabbah bar Rav Nachman who cut down a tree belonging to Rabbah bar Rav Huna, citing a verse about the leaders' involvement in the trespass, and as a result, Rabbah bar Rav Nachman never had children.
Rabbah bar Rav Nachman cites a verse about leaders being first in transgression and orders the tree cut down.
Rabbah bar Rav Huna finds the cut tree and curses that the cutter's branches be cut, resulting in Rabbah bar Rav Nachman having no surviving children.

items.text: Exemptions from preemptive rights
items.text_en: Exemptions from preemptive rights
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that preemptive rights apply to all neighbors, even orphans, but not to Torah scholars, who do not need protection. However, for a wide field, even a scholar must be notified. The Gemara adds that this only applies if the neighbor does not go out in a procession; if he does, even a scholar must be informed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the reason: Torah scholars do not need protection from neighbors.
Rav Yehuda adds that for a wide field, even a Torah scholar must be notified.

items.text: Obligation to assist in irrigation
items.text_en: Obligation to assist in irrigation
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that for a river channel, lower neighbors must assist upper neighbors, but not vice versa; the opposite applies for rainwater.

sub.text: Rav Yehudah's rule on water rights
sub.text_en: Rav Yehudah's rule on water rights
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehudah rules that for a river channel, lower fields assist upper fields, but not vice versa; the opposite applies for rainwater.

items.text: Supporting baraita for irrigation rules
items.text_en: Supporting baraita for irrigation rules
items.desc_en: A baraita supports Rav Yehuda's ruling: five gardens drawing from one spring must all repair with the uppermost; the lowermost repairs with all and for itself. The opposite applies for five courtyards sharing a drain.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Rav Yehudah's rule with examples of five gardens sharing a spring and five courtyards sharing a drain, detailing how the upper and lower parties cooperate in repairs.

items.text: Acquisition of riverbank land
items.text_en: Acquisition of riverbank land
items.desc_en: Shmuel rules that one who takes possession of a riverbank is considered presumptuous but is not removed. However, nowadays, since Persians write in their deeds 'acquire up to the horse's neck in water,' he is removed.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that one who takes possession of a riverbank is considered presumptuous but is not evicted; however, nowadays, since Persians write 'acquire up to the horse's neck in water,' he is evicted.
The Gemara notes that nowadays, since Persians write in their deeds 'acquire up to the horse's neck in water,' the encroacher is removed.

items.text: Dispute on removing a presumptuous buyer among partners
items.text_en: Dispute on removing a presumptuous buyer among partners
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav rules that one who takes possession among brothers or partners is presumptuous but not removed. Rav Nachman says he is removed. Nehardeans say he is even removed due to the law of the neighbor (dina de'bar metzra), based on the verse 'do what is right and good.'

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav rules that one who takes possession among brothers or partners is presumptuous (חציפא) but is not removed.
Rav Nachman disagrees and says that such a buyer is indeed removed, except when the removal is based on the law of the neighbor (דינא דבַר מִצְרָא).
The Nehardeans assert that even on grounds of the neighbor's right (דינא דבַר מִצְרָא) the buyer is removed, citing the verse 'do what is right and good in the eyes of the Lord'.

items.text: Requirement of formal acquisition when neighbor consults
items.text_en: Requirement of formal acquisition when neighbor consults
items.desc_en: If a seller consults the neighbor and the neighbor agrees, a formal acquisition (kinyan) is required. Ravina says no, Nehardeans say yes, and the halakha follows the Nehardeans. If no acquisition was made, the property remains in the seller's hands for profit or loss.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a formal acquisition (קִנְיָן) is required when the seller consults the neighbor and the neighbor agrees.
Ravina rules that no formal acquisition is required.
The Nehardeans rule that a formal acquisition is required.
The Gemara rules that the halakha follows the Nehardeans, requiring a formal acquisition.
The Gemara clarifies that if no acquisition was made, the property remains in the seller's hands for any profit or loss.

items.text: Cases of overpricing and underpricing
items.text_en: Cases of overpricing and underpricing
items.desc_en: If the buyer paid 100 for land worth 200, and he sells to all, the neighbor pays 100 and takes it; otherwise, he pays 200. If he paid 200 for land worth 100, the buyer can say 'I sent you to fix, not to ruin.' Mar Kashisha cites Nehardeans citing Rav Nachman that there is no overcharge (ona'ah) for land.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case: if one bought land worth 200 for 100, the neighbor pays 100 if the seller generally discounts, otherwise pays 200.
The Gemara raises a second case: if one paid 200 for land worth 100, the buyer can say 'I sent you to fix, not to ruin.'

sub.text: Mar Kashisha citing Nehardeans citing Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Mar Kashisha citing Nehardeans citing Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Mar Kashisha tells Rav Ashi that the Nehardeans said in the name of Rav Nachman that there is no overcharge (אונאה) for land.

items.text: Sale of a specific plot within larger property
items.text_en: Sale of a specific plot within larger property
items.desc_en: If one sold a specific measure of land within his property, we examine whether it is superior or inferior land; the sale is valid accordingly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rules: if one sold a griva of land in the middle of his property, we see if it is superior or inferior land; the sale stands accordingly.

items.text: Gemara's question about evasion
items.text_en: Gemara's question about evasion
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises the concern that a seller might evade the neighbor's right by pretending to give a gift. It states that a gift is not subject to the law of the neighbor.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises the concern that a seller might evade the neighbor's right by pretending to give a gift.

items.text: Gift with guarantee
items.text_en: Gift with guarantee
items.desc_en: Amemar rules that if the seller writes a guarantee (אחריות) for the gift, it is considered a sale and is subject to the neighbor's right.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that a gift is not subject to the law of the neighbor (דִּינָא דְּבַר מִצְרָא).
Amemar rules that if the seller writes a guarantee of liability (אחריות) for the gift, it is subject to the neighbor's right.

items.text: Exemptions: all property, original owners, buying from or selling to a gentile
items.text_en: Exemptions: all property, original owners, buying from or selling to a gentile
items.desc_en: The Gemara lists three cases where the neighbor's right does not apply: selling all property to one person, selling to the original owners, and buying from or selling to a gentile.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that selling all one's property to a single buyer is not subject to the neighbor's right.
The Gemara states that selling back to the original owners is not subject to the neighbor's right.
The Gemara states that buying from or selling to a gentile is not subject to the neighbor's right.

items.text: Reason for gentile exemption and penalty
items.text_en: Reason for gentile exemption and penalty
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the reason for the exemption when buying from a gentile (the seller is not obligated to the neighbor) and when selling to a gentile (the gentile is not bound by the law). It adds that the seller is excommunicated until he accepts responsibility for any damages.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that buying from a gentile is exempt because the seller can say 'I saved you from your neighbor's claim.'
The Gemara explains that selling to a gentile is exempt because a gentile is not obligated in the commandment 'do what is right and good' (וְעָשִׂיתָ הַיָּשָׁר וְהַטּוֹב).
The Gemara rules that the seller is placed under a ban (שמתא) until he accepts responsibility for any damages that arise from the sale.

items.text: Mortgage (משכנתא) exemption
items.text_en: Mortgage (משכנתא) exemption
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi reports that the elders of the city of Machseya explained that a mortgage is not subject to the neighbor's right because the word 'משכנתא' implies that the property is 'dwelling' (שכונה) with the creditor, not sold.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that a mortgage (משכנתא) is not subject to the neighbor's right.

Rav Ashi cites the elders of the city of Machseya who explain that the term 'משכנתא' (mortgage) implies that the property is 'neighboring' (שכונה) with the creditor, so the neighbor's right does not apply.
The Gemara notes that the practical difference of this etymology is for the law of the neighbor (דִּינָא דְּבַר מִצְרָא).

items.text: Selling distant or poor quality land
items.text_en: Selling distant or poor quality land
items.desc_en: The Gemara rules that if one sells a distant field to redeem a nearby one, or a poor quality field to redeem a good one, the neighbor's right does not apply.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that selling a distant field to redeem a nearby one, or selling a poor field to redeem a better one, is not subject to the neighbor's right.

items.text: Sales for tax, sustenance, burial, and to special parties
items.text_en: Sales for tax, sustenance, burial, and to special parties
items.desc_en: The Gemara rules that sales for tax, sustenance, and burial are not subject to the neighbor's right, citing the Nehardeans that these are sold without proclamation. Similarly, sales to a woman, orphans, or partners are exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that selling for taxes (כרגא), for sustenance (מזוני), or for burial (קבורה) is not subject to the neighbor's right.
The Nehardeans state that for taxes, sustenance, and burial, property is sold without public announcement (אכרזתא).
The Gemara states that selling to a woman, to orphans, or to partners is not subject to the neighbor's right.

items.text: Priority among claimants
items.text_en: Priority among claimants
items.desc_en: The Gemara establishes a hierarchy: neighbors of the city precede neighbors of the field; a Torah scholar precedes a neighbor; a relative precedes a neighbor? The Gemara cites a verse to resolve the question of neighbor vs. relative.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states a hierarchy: neighbors of the city (שְׁכֵינֵי הָעִיר) precede neighbors of the field (שְׁכֵינֵי שָׂדֶה) in the right of pre-emption.
The Gemara states that a Torah scholar (תַּלְמִיד חָכָם) precedes a neighbor (שָׁכֵן) in the right of pre-emption.
The Gemara states that a Torah scholar (תַּלְמִיד חָכָם) precedes a relative (קָרוֹב) in the right of pre-emption.
The Gemara raises a question: between a neighbor (שָׁכֵן) and a relative (קָרוֹב), which one takes precedence?
The Gemara resolves the question by citing the verse 'טוֹב שָׁכֵן קָרוֹב מֵאָח רָחוֹק' (a close neighbor is better than a distant brother), indicating that a neighbor precedes a relative.

items.text: Different payment methods
items.text_en: Different payment methods
items.desc_en: The Gemara rules that if the buyer pays with good coins and the neighbor offers heavy (poor) coins, or if the buyer's coins are bound and the neighbor's are loose, the neighbor's right does not apply.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that if one offers good coins and another offers heavy coins (of lower value), the neighbor's right does not apply.
The Gemara states that if one offers tied coins and another offers loose coins, the neighbor's right does not apply.

items.text: Waiting for the neighbor to bring money
items.text_en: Waiting for the neighbor to bring money
items.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes: if the neighbor says he will go and bring money, we do not wait; but if he is a reliable person who can bring money, we wait.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that if a neighbor says 'I will go and work to bring money,' we do not wait for him.
The Gemara rules that if the neighbor says 'I will go and bring money,' we assess: if he is a reliable person who can go and bring money, we wait for him; otherwise, we do not.

items.text: Land and houses owned by different people
items.text_en: Land and houses owned by different people
items.desc_en: The Gemara rules that the owner of the land can prevent the owner of the houses from selling to a stranger, but not vice versa. Similarly, the owner of the land can prevent the owner of the palm trees from selling, but not vice versa.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that if the land belongs to one person and the houses to another, the owner of the land can prevent the owner of the houses from selling, but not vice versa.
The Gemara states that if the land belongs to one person and the palm trees to another, the owner of the land can prevent the owner of the trees from selling, but not vice versa.

items.text: Land for building vs. land for planting
items.text_en: Land for building vs. land for planting
items.desc_en: The Gemara rules that if one sells land for building and another wants it for planting, settlement (building) takes precedence, and the neighbor's right does not apply.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that land for building takes precedence over land for planting, and the neighbor's right does not apply.

items.text: Interruption by a ditch or palm row
items.text_en: Interruption by a ditch or palm row
items.desc_en: The Gemara rules that if a ditch or a row of palm trees separates the fields, we see if the neighbor can still enter even one furrow; if so, the neighbor's right applies, otherwise not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rules that if a ditch or a row of palm trees separates the fields, we assess: if one can insert even one furrow into the gap, the neighbor's right applies; otherwise, it does not.

items.text: Multiple neighbors and division
items.text_en: Multiple neighbors and division
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that if one of four neighbors buys the field first, his purchase is valid. If they all come together, they divide the field equally (by lot or auction).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that if there are four neighbors and one of them precedes and buys, his purchase is valid.
The Gemara rules that if all the neighbors come together, they divide the property by lottery (קרנזיל).

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah distinguishes between a short-term lease (where the tenant may not plant flax and has no rights to sycamore trunks) and a seven-year lease (where he may plant flax and has rights to sycamore trunks).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: a short-term lessee may not plant flax and has no rights to sycamore trunks, while a seven-year lessee may plant flax and has rights to sycamore trunks.

items.text: Abaye and Rava dispute the scope of compensation
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava dispute the scope of compensation
items.desc_en: Abaye holds that the tenant has no rights to the trunks of sycamore trees but does have rights to the improvement (שבח) of the trees. Rava argues that even the improvement is not compensated.

sub.desc_en: Abaye states that the tenant has no rights to the trunks of sycamore trees but does have rights to the improvement (שבח) of the trees.
Rava argues that even the improvement (שבח) of the sycamore trees is not compensated to the tenant.

items.text: First challenge to Rava from a baraita
items.text_en: First challenge to Rava from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that says when a tenant leaves, we assess compensation for him. The Gemara initially assumes this refers to the improvement of sycamore trees, but deflects by explaining it refers to vegetables and beets that were not yet marketable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that assesses compensation for a tenant when his time ends, and challenges Rava by assuming this refers to the improvement of sycamore trees.
The Gemara deflects the challenge by explaining that the baraita refers to vegetables and beets, not sycamore improvement.
The Gemara objects that vegetables and beets are normally uprooted and taken, so why would compensation be assessed?
The Gemara resolves that the case involves vegetables that have not yet reached market day, so they cannot be sold and compensation is assessed.

items.text: Second challenge from a baraita about the Jubilee year
items.text_en: Second challenge from a baraita about the Jubilee year
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a tenant who leaves at the Jubilee, and after textual emendations, concludes that the compensation must be for the improvement of sycamore trees, supporting Rava's position that such improvement is not compensated in ordinary cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a tenant who leaves at the Sabbatical year, where the court assesses compensation, as a challenge to Rava.
The Gemara objects that the Sabbatical year does not terminate a tenancy, so it emends the baraita to refer to the Jubilee year.

items.text: Abaye explains the baraita according to Rava
items.text_en: Abaye explains the baraita according to Rava
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that the baraita about the Jubilee is different because the verse says 'the sale shall go out,' meaning the sale itself reverts but not the improvement, and this is a special case of a proper sale, not a tenancy.

sub.desc_en: Abaye explains that the case of the Jubilee is different because the verse 'וְיָצָא מִמְכַּר בַּיִת' indicates that the sale itself reverts but not the improvement.
The Gemara asks whether one could derive from this case that improvement is never returned in a tenancy.
The Gemara answers that the Jubilee case involves a proper sale (זְבִינֵי מְעַלְּיָא) and the Jubilee is a royal decree (אַפְקַעְתָּא דְּמַלְכָּא), so it cannot be compared to a tenancy.

items.text: Rav Pappa's case of planting saffron
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's case of planting saffron
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa leased land for saffron, and palm trees grew there. When he left, he demanded compensation for the improvement. Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi challenged him, and Rav Pappa argued that he had entered with the specific intention of planting saffron, so the trees were an unexpected improvement. The Gemara concludes that he receives only the value of the wood.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa leased land for saffron, palm trees grew there, and when he left he demanded compensation for the improvement.

sub.text: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's objection
sub.text_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi objected: if a date palm grew and became strong, would the master also demand its improvement?
Rav Pappa answered that there he did not enter with that intention, but here he entered specifically for saffron, so the trees were an unexpected improvement.
The Gemara analyzes that Rav Pappa's position aligns with Abaye who grants improvement of sycamores, or even with Rava who denies it, because here there is a loss.

sub.text: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's counter-objection
sub.text_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's counter-objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi countered: what is your loss? Take the saffron hand and go.
Rav Pappa claimed he had planted expensive saffron, but Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi concluded that since he revealed his intent to take and leave, he receives only the value of the wood.

items.text: Rav Beivai bar Abaye's case of thorn bushes
items.text_en: Rav Beivai bar Abaye's case of thorn bushes
items.desc_en: Rav Beivai bar Abaye leased land and returned it with a ditch, and thorn bushes grew. When he sought compensation, Rav Pappi rebuked him, noting that unlike Rav Pappa's case, there was no loss to the tenant here.

sub.desc_en: Rav Beivai bar Abaye leased a field and returned it with a ditch, and thorn bushes grew in it.
When he was leaving, Rav Beivai bar Abaye asked the landowners to give him compensation for the improvement.
Rav Pappi rebuked Rav Beivai bar Abaye, noting that unlike Rav Pappa's case where there was a loss, here there was no loss to the tenant.

items.text: Rav Yosef's case of a sharecropper's heirs
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's case of a sharecropper's heirs
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef had a sharecropper who died leaving five sons. He feared they would cause him loss, so he offered them compensation to leave, citing a ruling that heirs of a deceased sharecropper can be removed without compensation, though the Gemara dismisses that ruling.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef had a sharecropper who died leaving five sons, and he feared they would cause him loss.

sub.text: Rav Yosef's offer to the heirs
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef's offer to the heirs
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef offered the heirs compensation to leave voluntarily, threatening to remove them without compensation if they refused.

sub.text: Citation of a ruling by Rav Yehuda (or Rav Huna or Rav Nachman)
sub.text_en: Citation of a ruling by Rav Yehuda (or Rav Huna or Rav Nachman)
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef cited a ruling that the heirs of a deceased sharecropper can be removed without compensation.
The Gemara dismisses that ruling as not authoritative.

items.text: Dispute about a sharecropper who stipulated to leave if he causes loss
items.text_en: Dispute about a sharecropper who stipulated to leave if he causes loss
items.desc_en: A sharecropper stipulated that if he causes loss, he will leave. Rav Yehuda says he leaves without compensation, Rav Kahana says he leaves with compensation (unless he stipulated otherwise), and Rava says the stipulation is merely an asmachta and not binding. The Gemara distinguishes this from a case where one must pay for damage.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a case of a sharecropper who stipulated that if he causes loss he will leave, and he indeed caused loss.
Rav Yehuda rules that the sharecropper leaves without compensation for his improvements.
Rav Kahana rules that the sharecropper leaves with compensation, unless he explicitly stipulated to leave without it.
Rava rules that the stipulation is an אסמכתא (a conditional commitment made without full intent) and is not legally binding.
The Gemara asks Rava: what distinguishes this from the Mishnah where one who stipulates 'if I let the field lie fallow I will pay with the best' is bound?

The Gemara resolves: there the stipulation is to pay for the loss, which is enforceable; here the stipulation is to forfeit compensation for improvements, which is an אסמכתא (a conditional commitment made without full intent) and not binding.

items.text: Ravina's sharecropper Runya and Rava's ruling
items.text_en: Ravina's sharecropper Runya and Rava's ruling
items.desc_en: Runya, Ravina's sharecropper, caused loss and was dismissed. He complained to Rava, who upheld the dismissal even without prior warning, consistent with Rava's view that a teacher of children, a sharecropper, a butcher, and a craftsman can be dismissed without warning if they cause loss.

sub.desc_en: The gemara recounts that Runya, Ravina's sharecropper, caused loss and was dismissed; he complained to Rava, who upheld the dismissal even without prior warning.
The gemara notes that Rava's ruling aligns with his own stated principle that a teacher of children, a sharecropper, a butcher, and a craftsman can be dismissed without warning if they cause loss.

items.text: General principle regarding loss that cannot be restored
items.text_en: General principle regarding loss that cannot be restored
items.desc_en: The Gemara states a general rule: any loss that cannot be restored is considered as if the parties are already permitted to act. This sets the stage for the following cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states a general rule: any loss that cannot be restored is considered as if the parties are already permitted to act.

items.text: Case of the planter who wants to go to Eretz Yisrael
items.text_en: Case of the planter who wants to go to Eretz Yisrael
items.desc_en: A planter asks for his share of the improvement to go to Eretz Yisrael. Rava and Rav Pappa bar Shmuel debate how much he should receive, eventually settling on a quarter of the improvement.

sub.desc_en: A planter requests his share of the improvement to go to Eretz Yisrael, and the case is brought before Rav Pappa bar Shmuel.
Rav Pappa bar Shmuel rules to give the planter his improvement, but Rava objects that only the planter improved the land, not the land itself.
Rav Pappa bar Shmuel clarifies he meant half the improvement, but Rava objects that the owner must now give a share to a new tenant, so they settle on a quarter of the improvement.

items.text: Rav Ashi's interpretation of 'quarter' and the objection
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's interpretation of 'quarter' and the objection
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi initially thought 'quarter' means a quarter of a sixth (i.e., one twenty-fourth), citing Rav Minyomi's ruling. The Gemara objects that if it were a literal quarter, the owner would suffer a loss.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi initially thought that 'quarter' means a quarter of a sixth (one twenty-fourth), citing Rav Minyomi's ruling that the planter receives his share and is dismissed to prevent loss to the owner.
The Gemara objects that if 'quarter' were literal (a quarter of the total), the owner would suffer a loss of half a sixth, which contradicts the principle of preventing loss.

items.text: Rav Acha's suggestion and Rav Ashi's response
items.text_en: Rav Acha's suggestion and Rav Ashi's response
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Yosef suggests that the planter should give his share to the sharecropper, but Rav Ashi deflects the question, saying to ask him when they reach the topic of slaughter of consecrated animals.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Yosef suggests to Rav Ashi that the planter should give his own share to the sharecropper, since the planter can do what he wants with his own portion.
Rav Ashi deflects the question, telling Rav Acha to raise it when they reach the topic of slaughter of consecrated animals.

items.text: Rav Minyomi's ruling and additional case
items.text_en: Rav Minyomi's ruling and additional case
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Minyomi's ruling about a planter who leaves early, and adds a case: if an old palm tree is worth half, but if a river washed it away, it is worth a quarter.

sub.desc_en: Rav Minyomi bar Rav Nechumi states the ruling that a planter who leaves early is given his improvement and removed, so the owner does not lose.
Rav Minyomi bar Rav Nechumi adds a case: an old palm tree is worth half, but if a river washed it away, it is worth a quarter.

items.text: Dispute between Abaye and Rava about a pledged orchard
items.text_en: Dispute between Abaye and Rava about a pledged orchard
items.desc_en: A man pledged his orchard for ten years, but it produced fruit after five years. Abaye says the fruit is produce (belonging to the creditor), while Rava says it is principal, to be used to buy land whose produce the creditor may eat.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a case: a man pledged his orchard for ten years, but it produced fruit after five years.
Abaye rules that the fruit is produce (פֵּירָא), belonging to the creditor as his profit.
Rava rules that the fruit is principal (קַרְנָא), to be used to buy land whose produce the creditor may eat.

items.text: Attempted proof from a baraita and its rejection
items.text_en: Attempted proof from a baraita and its rejection
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to prove Rava's view from a baraita about a dried or cut tree, but rejects the proof by comparing the cases differently: the cut tree is like a dried tree out of season.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a dried or cut tree, arguing that since both cases are parallel and the baraita rules that the wood is sold and the proceeds used to buy land from which the creditor eats the produce, this supports Rava's view that the produce is considered principal (קרנא).

The Gemara rejects the proof by reversing the comparison: the cut tree is analogous to the dried tree, which is out of season, so the baraita only applies to an untimely cut, not to the timely case at hand.

items.text: Beginning of another baraita
items.text_en: Beginning of another baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to cite another baraita about old vines and olive trees, continuing the discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita about old vines and olive trees that fell to a woman, continuing the discussion.

items.text: Resolution of the earlier Mishnah's case
items.text_en: Resolution of the earlier Mishnah's case
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers two alternative resolutions for the earlier Mishnah's case where a woman sold her usufruct property: either the trees were sold for firewood and the proceeds used to buy land (which the husband eats the produce of), or the case is where the property was in another field and the principal was being consumed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the trees were sold for firewood and the proceeds used to buy land, whose produce the husband eats, and suggests the Mishnah's phrase 'and they aged' refers to the trees.
The Gemara offers an alternative resolution: the case is where the property was in another field and the principal was being consumed.

items.text: Dispute over loan term: three vs. two years
items.text_en: Dispute over loan term: three vs. two years
items.desc_en: A lender claims a three-year loan term, the borrower says two; the lender already consumed the produce. Rav Yehuda and Rav Kahana dispute who is believed. The Gemara rules like Rav Kahana that produce is in the possessor's presumption, but notes a contradiction with Rav Nachman's ruling that land is in the owner's presumption; the resolution is that here the matter will become known (by the document) so the court does not trouble itself twice.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case: a loan document with an unspecified term; the lender claims three years, the borrower says two, and the lender already consumed the produce; the question is who is believed.
Rav Yehuda rules that the land remains in the presumption (חזקה) of its owner, so the lender is not believed.
Rav Kahana rules that the produce is in the presumption (חזקה) of its consumer, so the lender is believed.
The Gemara rules in accordance with Rav Kahana that produce is in the presumption of its consumer.
The Gemara objects: we already have a ruling that the land is in the owner's presumption (like Rav Nachman), which contradicts Rav Kahana's position.
The Gemara resolves: there the matter is not destined to become known, but here it will become known (by the document), so the court does not trouble itself twice.

items.text: Lender claims five years, borrower says three; document lost
items.text_en: Lender claims five years, borrower says three; document lost
items.desc_en: The lender claims a five-year term, the borrower says three; the lender says his document was lost. Rav Yehuda rules the lender is believed due to מיגו (he could have claimed the land was purchased). Rav Pappa reports that Rav Zevid and Rav Avira disagree, arguing that since the document was for collection, the lender would guard it carefully, and his claim of loss is a cover for having suppressed it to eat produce extra years.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a case: the lender claims a five-year term, the borrower says three, and the lender says his document was lost.
Rav Yehuda rules that the lender is believed, invoking the principle of מיגו (since he could have claimed the land was purchased from the borrower).

sub.text: Rav Pappa reporting Rav Zevid and Rav Avira
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa reporting Rav Zevid and Rav Avira
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa reports to Rav Ashi that Rav Zevid and Rav Avira disagree with Rav Yehuda, arguing that since the document was for collection, the lender would guard it carefully, and his claim of loss is a cover for having suppressed it to eat produce extra years.

items.text: Challenge from the Surai mortgage document
items.text_en: Challenge from the Surai mortgage document
items.desc_en: Ravina challenges Rav Ashi: in a Surai mortgage where the document states the land will be released without payment after a set term, if the lender suppresses the document and claims the land was purchased, would he be believed? Rav Ashi distinguishes: there the Sages instituted that the landowner pays tax and performs labor, so the lender cannot claim purchase; if the land has no such obligations, the lender should have protested, and if he did not, he caused his own loss.

sub.desc_en: Ravina challenges Rav Ashi: in a Surai mortgage document that states the land will be released without payment after a set term, if the lender suppresses the document and claims the land was purchased, would he be believed?
Ravina objects: would the Sages institute a practice that leads to loss?
Rav Ashi answers: there the Sages instituted that the landowner pays tax and performs labor, so the lender cannot claim purchase.
Ravina asks: what about land that has no such obligations?
Rav Ashi answers: the lender should have protested publicly.
Rav Ashi concludes: if he did not protest, he caused his own loss.

items.text: Dispute between tenant and landlord over sharecropping terms
items.text_en: Dispute between tenant and landlord over sharecropping terms
items.desc_en: A tenant claims he descended for half, the landlord says for a third. Rav Yehuda believes the landlord; Rav Nachman says everything follows local custom. Initially thought they do not dispute (each refers to a different locale), but Rav Mari bar Bat Shmuel reports Abaye says they dispute even where the custom is half: Rav Yehuda believes the landlord because he could claim the tenant was a hired laborer.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a dispute: a tenant claims he descended for half the produce, the landlord claims he descended for a third, and asks who is believed.
Rav Yehuda rules that the landlord is believed.
Rav Nachman rules that everything follows local custom.
The gemara initially thought the two rabbis do not dispute, each referring to a different locale (one where the custom is half, the other where it is a third).

sub.text: Rav Mari bar Bat Shmuel citing Abaye
sub.text_en: Rav Mari bar Bat Shmuel citing Abaye
sub.desc_en: Rav Mari bar Bat Shmuel reports that Abaye says they dispute even where the custom is half, because Rav Yehuda believes the landlord could claim the tenant was a hired laborer.

items.text: Dispute between orphans and creditor over improvement
items.text_en: Dispute between orphans and creditor over improvement
items.desc_en: Orphans claim they improved the land, the creditor says their father did; the Gemara asks who bears the burden of proof.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute between orphans and a creditor over who improved the land, and asks who bears the burden of proof.

items.text: Burden of proof on orphans regarding field improvement
items.text_en: Burden of proof on orphans regarding field improvement
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina initially holds that the field is presumed to belong to the orphans, so the creditor must bring proof. A certain elder cites Rabbi Yochanan that the orphans must bring proof because the field is already designated for collection. Abaye supports this with a parallel from a mishna about cutting a tree.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina initially holds that the field is presumed to belong to the orphans, so the creditor must bring proof of improvement.

sub.text: A certain elder citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: A certain elder citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: A certain elder objects, citing Rabbi Yochanan that the orphans must bring proof because the field is already designated for collection.
Abaye supports Rabbi Yochanan's position with a parallel from a mishna about cutting a tree, where the burden of proof falls on the one seeking payment.

items.text: Compensation for orphans' improvement
items.text_en: Compensation for orphans' improvement
items.desc_en: When the orphans bring proof that they improved the field, Rabbi Chanina initially thinks they should be compensated with land. The Gemara rejects this, ruling that they are compensated with money, based on Rav Nachman's statement about three cases where the court appraises the improvement and pays in cash.

sub.desc_en: After the orphans bring proof of improvement, Rabbi Chanina holds that they are compensated with land.

sub.text: Stam's rejection and citation of Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Stam's rejection and citation of Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: The gemara rejects Rabbi Chanina's position and rules that compensation is in money, citing Rav Nachman's list of three cases where the court appraises the improvement and pays in cash.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on creditor collecting improvement from a purchaser
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on creditor collecting improvement from a purchaser
items.desc_en: Ravina questions Shmuel's inclusion of a creditor collecting from a purchaser, since Shmuel elsewhere says the creditor collects the improvement. The Gemara distinguishes between improvement that can be carried away and that which cannot, and between cases where the debt equals the land's value plus improvement or not. It concludes with a case where the field was mortgaged.

sub.desc_en: Ravina questions Rav Ashi about Shmuel's inclusion of a creditor against purchasers, noting that Shmuel elsewhere rules that a creditor collects even improvement that is already portable, which seems contradictory.
Rav Ashi resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between cases where the debt covers both land and improvement versus where it does not.
The gemara objects that according to the view that a purchaser can redeem with money, the purchaser could demand a portion of land equal to the improvement value, undermining the distinction.
The gemara resolves the objection by explaining that the case involves a specific pledge (אפותיקי), where the creditor's recourse is limited to that particular property.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of hired worker's wage collection times
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of hired worker's wage collection times
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents rules for when a hired worker can collect his wages: a day worker collects all night, a night worker collects all day, an hourly worker collects all night and day, and workers hired for longer periods collect based on when they finish.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents rules for when a hired worker can collect his wages: a day worker collects all night, a night worker collects all day, an hourly worker collects all night and day, and workers hired for longer periods collect based on when they finish.

items.text: Gemara: Biblical sources for wage collection times
items.text_en: Gemara: Biblical sources for wage collection times
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives the day worker's collection time from 'until morning' and the night worker's from 'on his day you shall give his hire'. It then questions whether the verses might be reversed, but notes that hired labor is only paid at the end.

sub.text: Baraita: scriptural sources for wage collection times
sub.text_en: Baraita: scriptural sources for wage collection times
sub.desc_en: A baraita derives the day-worker's collection time from 'לֹא תָלִין... עַד בֹּקֶר' and the night-worker's from 'בְּיוֹמוֹ תִתֵּן שְׂכָרוֹ'.
The gemara objects that the verses could be interpreted in reverse, since wages are typically paid only at the end of the work period.

items.text: The scope of the prohibition and additional violation
items.text_en: The scope of the prohibition and additional violation
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the prohibition of delaying wages only applies until the first morning. After that, Rav says one violates 'do not delay', and Rav Yosef cites a verse from Proverbs.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the phrase 'עד בוקר' (until morning) in the verse 'לֹא תָלִין' (do not delay) indicates the prohibition only applies until the first morning.
The Gemara asks what violation applies after the first morning has passed.
Rav states that after the first morning, one violates the prohibition of 'בל תשהא' (do not delay).
Rav Yosef cites a verse from Proverbs (3:28) as the scriptural source for the prohibition of 'בל תשהא'.

items.text: Agent who hires workers is exempt from wage delay prohibition
items.text_en: Agent who hires workers is exempt from wage delay prohibition
items.desc_en: A baraita states that if one tells another to hire workers for him, neither the employer nor the agent violates the prohibition of delaying wages, since the agent did not hire them and the employer did not hire them directly.

sub.text: Baraita: employer and agent exempt from 'בל תלין'
sub.text_en: Baraita: employer and agent exempt from 'בל תלין'
sub.desc_en: A baraita states that when one tells another to hire workers for him, neither the employer nor the agent violates 'בל תלין'.

items.text: Clarifying the case of a worker hired for another's field
items.text_en: Clarifying the case of a worker hired for another's field
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies a previous statement about a worker who is hired to work in his employer's field but is shown another's field. It distinguishes between the employer saying 'your wages are upon me' versus 'upon the homeowner,' and cites a practice of Yehuda bar Merimar and others.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: In what case does the rule that the worker's wages are not with the employer apply?

The Gemara answers: If the employer said 'your wages are upon me,' then the wages are on him, citing a baraita that the worker is paid by the employer and then the employer recoups from the homeowner.
The Gemara resolves: The case is where the employer said 'your wages are upon the homeowner,' so the worker has no claim against the employer.
The Gemara cites the practice of Yehuda bar Merimar and others who hired workers and told them 'your wages are upon the homeowner,' and Marimar and Mar Zutra hired each other.

items.text: Rabbah bar Rav Huna on market-day workers
items.text_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna on market-day workers
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna states that market-day workers in Sura do not violate 'bal talin' because they rely on market day, but they do violate 'bal teshah' if payment is delayed.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna states that the market porters of Sura do not violate 'בל תלין' (do not delay wages overnight) because they rely on market day, but they do violate 'בל תשהא' (do not withhold).

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on hourly worker's collection time
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on hourly worker's collection time
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that an hourly worker collects all night and all day. Rav limits this: a daytime hourly worker collects all day, a nighttime hourly worker collects all night. Shmuel argues that a nighttime hourly worker collects all night and all day. The Gemara challenges Rav from the Mishnah and a baraita, and Rav deflects by interpreting the Mishnah as referring to different cases or as a dispute between Tanna'im.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that an hourly worker collects his wages all night and all day.
Rav says: An hourly worker of the day collects all day; an hourly worker of the night collects all night.
Shmuel says: An hourly worker of the day collects all day; an hourly worker of the night collects all night and all day.

items.text: Five transgressions for withholding wages and Rav Chisda's resolution
items.text_en: Five transgressions for withholding wages and Rav Chisda's resolution
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists five prohibitions violated by one who withholds wages. The Gemara questions how all five can apply simultaneously since some apply only by day and others only by night. Rav Chisda answers that the prohibition is due to the general concept of hired labor.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who withholds wages violates five prohibitions and a positive commandment.
The Gemara questions how all five prohibitions can apply simultaneously, since some apply only by day and others only by night.
Rav Chisda answers that the prohibition is due to the general concept of hired labor (שם שכירות בעלמא), which applies regardless of time.

items.text: Defining theft and oppression in wage context
items.text_en: Defining theft and oppression in wage context
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda defines oppression as saying 'go and come back' repeatedly, and theft as denying having the worker's money. Rav Sheshet objects, requiring a parallel to a deposit where one denies the money, and redefines oppression as claiming 'I gave it to you.' Abaye further objects regarding theft, redefining oppression as 'I never hired you' and theft as 'I gave it to you.' The Gemara explains Rav Sheshet's distinction and concludes with Rava's view that both are the same, and the Torah separated them to impose two prohibitions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: What constitutes oppression (עושק) and what constitutes theft (גזל) in the context of wage withholding?
Rav Chisda defines oppression as repeatedly telling the worker 'go and come back' without paying, and theft as denying having the worker's money.
Rav Sheshet objects that the definition of oppression must parallel the case of a deposit (פקדון), where the defendant denies the money, to be subject to a guilt-offering.
Rav Sheshet redefines oppression as claiming 'I gave it to you' (but not actually paying), and theft as denying having the money.
Abaye objects that the definition of theft must also parallel the deposit case, requiring a denial of money.
Abaye redefines oppression as claiming 'I never hired you' and theft as claiming 'I gave it to you' (but not actually paying).
The Gemara asks: Why did Rav Sheshet object only to the definition of oppression but not to theft?

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rav Sheshet's view
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rav Sheshet's view
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that in theft, the employer first takes the money and then denies it, so the denial is secondary; but in oppression, the denial is the primary act.
The Gemara objects: Even in oppression, the employer could later deny the debt, so why is it different?

The Gemara resolves: In theft, the verse says 'or in theft' (או בגזל), implying an initial admission, but in oppression, the verse says 'or he oppressed' (או עשק), implying the oppression already occurred without a prior admission.
Rava concludes that oppression and theft are essentially the same act, and the Torah separated them only to impose two separate prohibitions (לאוין).

items.text: Mishnah: Scope of wage laws and exceptions
items.text_en: Mishnah: Scope of wage laws and exceptions
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the laws of timely payment apply to hiring people, animals, and vessels, but only if the worker demanded payment. If the employer directed the worker to a storekeeper or money-changer, he does not violate the prohibition. A hired worker within his time swears and takes; after the time, he does not. A ger toshav is subject to 'be-yomo titen sekharo' but not 'bal talin.'

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that the laws of timely payment apply to hiring people, animals, and vessels, and specifies the condition of the worker's demand.
The Mishnah adds that if the employer directed the worker to a storekeeper or money-changer, he does not violate the prohibition.
The Mishnah rules that a hired worker within his time swears and takes, but after the time he does not, unless there are witnesses that he demanded payment in time.
The Mishnah concludes that a ger toshav is subject to 'be-yomo titen sekharo' but not 'bal talin'.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's authorship
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's authorship
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who authored the Mishnah, suggesting it is neither the first Tanna who derives from 'meiachecha' nor Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda, and begins to cite a baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Who is the Tanna of this Mishnah?
The Gemara answers: It is neither the first Tanna of 'from your brothers' nor Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda, as will be explained in a baraita.

items.text: Opening baraita on the scope of wage payment laws
items.text_en: Opening baraita on the scope of wage payment laws
items.desc_en: The baraita derives from verses that the laws of timely payment apply to a Jewish worker, a righteous convert, and even one who eats carrion. It extends to animals and utensils via 'in your land'. Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda limits the application for a resident alien and for animals and utensils.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by deriving from the verse that the laws of timely payment exclude non-Jews, include a righteous convert (גר צדק), and include one who eats carrion.
The baraita extends the law to animals and utensils by the verse 'in your land' (בארצך), and states that all these violate the same prohibitions.

sub.text: Baraita's conclusion with Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's position
sub.text_en: Baraita's conclusion with Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's position
sub.desc_en: The baraita concludes that all types of hire are subject to the law of 'in its day you shall give his hire' and 'do not let the wage of a hired worker remain overnight', but Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda limits the resident alien (גר תושב) to only the former, and animals and utensils only to the prohibition of oppression (בל תעשוק).

items.text: Gemara's question on the identity of the baraita's author
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the identity of the baraita's author
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions who authored the baraita, noting that neither the first tanna nor Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda can be the sole author without contradiction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who authored the baraita, noting that neither the first tanna nor Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda can be the sole author without contradiction.

items.text: Rava's resolution: the baraita is from the school of Rabbi Yishmael
items.text_en: Rava's resolution: the baraita is from the school of Rabbi Yishmael
items.desc_en: Rava identifies the baraita as from the school of Rabbi Yishmael, which holds that animals and utensils are subject to both laws, while a resident alien is only subject to the positive command.

sub.desc_en: Rava answers that the baraita is from the school of Rabbi Yishmael, which holds that a ger toshav (resident alien) is subject to the law of 'בְּיוֹמוֹ תִתֵּן שְׂכָרוֹ' (pay on the day) but not to 'בַּל תָּלִין' (do not delay).

items.text: Debate on the derivation of the laws for a resident alien
items.text_en: Debate on the derivation of the laws for a resident alien
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute: the first tanna learns a verbal analogy from 'שָׂכִיר' to include a resident alien, while Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda does not. It then questions why animals and utensils are excluded from the positive command, and resolves with a verse limiting it to those who can become poor or rich. Further discussion clarifies the use of the verse for prioritizing the poor.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the reasoning of the first tanna and Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, explaining that the first tanna learns a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) from 'שָׂכִיר' to include a resident alien, while Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda does not.
The Gemara objects: even if Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda does not learn the verbal analogy, why should animals and utensils not be liable under the positive command of 'בְּיוֹמוֹ תִתֵּן שְׂכָרוֹ'?
Rabbi Chananya teaches a baraita that the verse 'כִּי עָנִי הוּא' (for he is poor) limits the positive command to those who can become poor or rich, excluding animals and utensils.
The Gemara asks what the first tanna does with the verse 'כִּי עָנִי הוּא', and answers that it is used to prioritize the poor over the rich.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's alternative derivation
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's alternative derivation
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda derives the priority of the poor over the rich from the verse 'לֹא תַעֲשֹׁק שָׂכִיר עָנִי וְאֶבְיוֹן' (do not oppress a poor and needy hired worker).

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the first tanna's two verses
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the first tanna's two verses
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the first tanna uses one verse to prioritize the poor over the rich and another to prioritize the poor over the needy.

The Gemara explains that both verses are necessary: one for the needy (who is embarrassed to ask) and one for the rich (who does not need the money), to teach that the poor worker is prioritized in both cases.

items.text: Analysis of our baraita's position on the verbal analogy
items.text_en: Analysis of our baraita's position on the verbal analogy
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the baraita's consistency: if it learns the verbal analogy, it should include a resident alien; if not, how does it include animals and utensils? It answers that the baraita does not learn the analogy but derives animals and utensils from 'אִתְּךָ', and excludes a resident alien via 'רֵעֲךָ'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the baraita's consistency: if it learns the verbal analogy, it should include a resident alien; if not, how does it include animals and utensils?
The Gemara answers that the baraita does not learn the verbal analogy but derives animals and utensils from the word 'אִתְּךָ' (with you).
The Gemara objects that if so, the resident alien should also be included, and the baraita answers that the word 'רֵעֲךָ' (your fellow) excludes the resident alien.
The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction by explaining that animals and utensils are included because they are in the category of 'your fellow's property', while a resident alien is not.

items.text: Use of 'רֵעֲךָ' to exclude a gentile and permit oppression and theft
items.text_en: Use of 'רֵעֲךָ' to exclude a gentile and permit oppression and theft
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the first tanna and Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda use 'רֵעֲךָ' to exclude a gentile from the prohibition of delaying wages, and also to permit oppressing and stealing from a gentile, with a need for both derivations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the first tanna and Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda do with the word 'רֵעֲךָ' (your fellow), since they already derive the exclusion of a gentile from 'מֵאַחֶיךָ' (from your brothers).

The Gemara answers that 'רֵעֲךָ' is needed to exclude a gentile from the prohibition of delaying wages, as taught in a baraita, while the exclusion of a gentile from the prohibition of oppression already comes from 'מֵאַחֶיךָ'.

The Gemara explains that one derivation permits oppressing a gentile and the other permits stealing from him, and both are necessary because each case has a unique leniency that might otherwise lead one to think it is forbidden.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's use of 'בַּל תָּלִין' and the alternative derivation
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's use of 'בַּל תָּלִין' and the alternative derivation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda uses the verse 'בַּל תָּלִין' to teach that even hiring for a single cluster of grapes incurs the prohibition, as per Rav Asi. The other opinion derives this from 'וְאֵלָיו הוּא נֹשֵׂא אֶת נַפְשׁוֹ'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda interprets the verse 'לֹא תָלִין פְּעֻלַּת שָׂכִיר אִתְּךָ עַד בֹּקֶר' (the wage of a hired worker shall not remain with you until morning).

The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda uses the verse for Rav Asi's teaching: even if one hired a worker only to pick a single cluster of grapes, the employer violates the prohibition of 'בַּל תָּלִין' (withholding wages overnight).

The other opinion (the first Tanna) derives the same halacha (that even minimal hiring triggers the prohibition) from the verse 'וְאֵלָיו הוּא נֹשֵׂא אֶת נַפְשׁוֹ' (and to it he lifts his soul), referring to something for which the worker risks his livelihood.

items.text: Exposition of the verse "וְאֵלָיו הוּא נֹשֵׂא אֶת נַפְשׁוֹ" and dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Chisda
items.text_en: Exposition of the verse "וְאֵלָיו הוּא נֹשֵׂא אֶת נַפְשׁוֹ" and dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Chisda
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the additional verse as teaching that the worker risks his life for his wages, and that withholding wages is like taking his life. Rav Huna and Rav Chisda dispute whether the verse refers to the life of the robber or the robbed, each citing a prooftext.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the verse 'וְאֵלָיו הוּא נֹשֵׂא אֶת נַפְשׁוֹ' as teaching that a worker risks his life for his wages.
The Gemara offers an alternative interpretation: withholding wages is like taking the worker's life.

sub.text: Rav Huna and Rav Chisda's dispute
sub.text_en: Rav Huna and Rav Chisda's dispute
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna and Rav Chisda dispute whether the verse refers to the life of the robber or the robbed.
The one who says the life of the robber cites verses about God taking the life of the oppressor.
The one who says the life of the robbed cites a verse about the robber taking the life of the owner.
The Gemara objects that the verse says 'the life of its owner', which refers to the current owner (the robber).
The Gemara objects that the verse says God takes the life of the oppressors because they took the life of the oppressed.

items.text: Conditions for violating the prohibition of delaying wages
items.text_en: Conditions for violating the prohibition of delaying wages
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the word "אִתְּךָ" that the prohibition only applies when the worker demands payment, when the employer has the means to pay, and when the employer did not direct the worker to a storekeeper or money changer.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that the prohibition of delaying wages only applies when the worker demands payment.
The baraita derives from the word 'אִתְּךָ' (with you) that the prohibition applies only when the employer has the means to pay and did not direct the worker to a storekeeper or money changer.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Sheshet and Rabbah: Does the worker have a right to reclaim payment from the employer after being directed to a storekeeper?
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Sheshet and Rabbah: Does the worker have a right to reclaim payment from the employer after being directed to a storekeeper?
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: if the employer directed the worker to a storekeeper, can the worker later demand payment from the employer? Rav Sheshet says he cannot, while Rabbah says he can. Rabbah argues from the baraita's wording that only the prohibition is lifted, but the debt remains.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises the question: after the employer directed the worker to a storekeeper, can the worker later reclaim payment from the employer, or not?
Rav Sheshet rules that the worker cannot reclaim payment from the employer.
Rabbah rules that the worker can reclaim payment from the employer.
Rabbah argues from the baraita's wording that only the prohibition is lifted, but the debt remains, so the worker can reclaim.
Rav Sheshet rejects Rabbah's argument, explaining that the baraita means the employer is not even subject to the prohibition at all.

items.text: Question about a craftsman's payment: Is it a loan or wages?
items.text_en: Question about a craftsman's payment: Is it a loan or wages?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a craftsman who improves a vessel acquires the improvement, making the payment a loan (and thus subject to the prohibition of delaying a loan) or not (making it wages). Rav Sheshet rules that the prohibition applies, and clarifies that the earlier baraita about no violation refers to a case where the worker was directed to a storekeeper.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks Rav Sheshet whether a craftsman who improves a vessel acquires the improvement, making the payment a loan (subject to the prohibition of delaying a loan) or not, making it wages.
Rav Sheshet rules that the prohibition of delaying payment does apply to a craftsman's payment.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that states the prohibition does not apply in certain cases.
Rav Sheshet resolves the contradiction by explaining that the baraita refers to a case where the employer directed the worker to a storekeeper or money changer for payment.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita about a craftsman and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita about a craftsman and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita states that if a craftsman finishes a garment and informs the owner, the owner does not violate the prohibition until nightfall. This challenges the view that a craftsman acquires the improvement (making it a loan). Rav Mari bar Rav Kahana resolves that the case involves scraping a cloak, where the improvement is minimal, or that the craftsman was hired for a specific task like beating, which is pure labor.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a craftsman who finishes a garment and informs the owner, stating that the owner does not violate the prohibition until nightfall, to challenge the view that a craftsman acquires the improvement (making it a loan).
The Gemara objects: if the craftsman acquires the improvement (making it a loan), why would the owner violate the prohibition at all?

sub.text: Rav Mari bar Rav Kahana's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Mari bar Rav Kahana's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Mari bar Rav Kahana answers that the baraita deals with scraping a cloak, where the improvement is minimal and the craftsman does not acquire it.

sub.text: Rav Mari bar Rav Kahana's alternative resolution
sub.text_en: Rav Mari bar Rav Kahana's alternative resolution
sub.desc_en: Rav Mari bar Rav Kahana alternatively resolves that the craftsman was hired for a specific task like beating, which is pure labor with no improvement, so the owner remains liable.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's question
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's question
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's rule that a hired worker who claims his wages on time swears and takes payment. It then asks why the Sages instituted this special oath for the worker.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's rule that a hired worker who claims his wages on time swears and takes payment, and asks why the Sages instituted this special oath for the worker.

items.text: First answer: Great laws or enactments
items.text_en: First answer: Great laws or enactments
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quoting Shmuel says these are 'great laws,' but the Gemara objects that they are enactments, not laws. Rav Yehuda then corrects to 'great enactments,' prompting a question about whether there are also 'small' ones.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel that the mishna teaches 'great laws' (הלכות גדולות) regarding the hired worker's oath.
The Gemara objects that these are enactments (תקנות), not laws (הלכות), because the rabbis instituted the oath for the worker's benefit.
Rav Yehuda corrects Shmuel's statement to 'great enactments' (תקנות גדולות) instead of 'great laws.'
The Gemara questions the term 'great' (גדולות), implying there must also be 'small' enactments (קטנות).

items.text: Second answer: Fixed enactments and the rationale
items.text_en: Second answer: Fixed enactments and the rationale
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman quoting Shmuel says these are 'fixed enactments.' The Gemara explains that the oath originally belonged to the homeowner, but the Sages transferred it to the worker for the worker's livelihood. This raises the objection that doing so would harm the homeowner.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel provides a second answer: the mishnah teaches fixed enactments (תקנות קבועות).
The Gemara explains the rationale: the oath originally belonged to the homeowner, but the Sages transferred it to the worker for the worker's livelihood (משום כדי חייו דשכיר).
The Gemara objects: for the sake of the worker's livelihood, do we cause a loss to the homeowner?

items.text: Rejected rationale: Mutual benefit
items.text_en: Rejected rationale: Mutual benefit
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the homeowner prefers the worker to swear and collect so workers will hire themselves out, but counters that the worker would prefer the homeowner to swear and be exempt so he would be hired. The Gemara concludes that the worker is hired under compulsion, so this reasoning fails.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the homeowner himself prefers the worker to swear and collect, so that workers will hire themselves out to him.
The Gemara counters that the worker himself would prefer the homeowner to swear and be exempt, so that the homeowner would hire him.
The Gemara rejects the mutual-benefit reasoning, noting that the worker is hired under compulsion (על כרחו), so the homeowner's preference is irrelevant.

items.text: Accepted rationale: Homeowner's distraction
items.text_en: Accepted rationale: Homeowner's distraction
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the homeowner is busy with his workers, so the Sages instituted the worker's oath to appease the homeowner. The Gemara questions why the worker cannot simply be paid without an oath, and answers that the oath is to satisfy the homeowner.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the homeowner is busy with his workers, so the Sages instituted the worker's oath to appease the homeowner.
The Gemara questions why the worker cannot simply be paid without an oath.
The Gemara answers that the oath is to satisfy the homeowner.

items.text: Rejected alternatives: Witnesses or immediate payment
items.text_en: Rejected alternatives: Witnesses or immediate payment
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the worker cannot bring witnesses, and answers that it is too burdensome. It then asks why the worker cannot be paid upfront, and answers that both parties prefer credit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the worker cannot simply bring witnesses to prove his claim.
The Gemara answers that bringing witnesses is too burdensome for the worker.
The Gemara asks why the employer cannot pay the worker immediately at the start of the day.
The Gemara answers that both the employer and the worker prefer credit (הקפה) rather than immediate payment.

items.text: Challenge from a fixed-price contract
items.text_en: Challenge from a fixed-price contract
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the rationale by asking why the same rule does not apply to a fixed-price contract, citing a baraita where the craftsman must bring proof. It answers that people remember fixed prices well.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: if the reason for the special oath is that the employer is busy, then the same should apply even to a fixed-price contract (קָצַץ).
The Gemara cites a baraita that in a fixed-price contract, the craftsman who claims two payments must bring proof, showing that the rule does not apply there.
The Gemara answers: people remember fixed-price agreements (קְצִיצָה) well, so the employer is not presumed to forget, and the craftsman must bring proof.

items.text: Challenge from after the time and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from after the time and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the same rule does not apply after the time has passed, citing the Mishnah that after the time the worker does not swear and collect. It answers with a presumption that the homeowner does not violate the prohibition of delaying wages. The Gemara then resolves an apparent contradiction with the earlier statement about the homeowner being busy, explaining that the busyness applies before the time of obligation arrives.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: if the reason for the worker's oath is the homeowner's busyness, then the same rule should apply even after the time for payment has passed, yet the Mishnah rules that after the time the worker does not swear and collect.

The Gemara answers that there is a presumption (חזקה) that the homeowner does not violate the prohibition of delaying wages (בל תלין), so after the time has passed the worker cannot claim non-payment.
The Gemara objects: but you previously said that the homeowner is busy with his workers, which would explain why he might not pay on time even after the time has passed.
The Gemara resolves: that statement about the homeowner being busy applies only before the time of obligation arrives, not after it has passed.

items.text: Gemara's question on the hired worker's oath
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the hired worker's oath
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a hired worker who claims his wages is believed with an oath, given the principle of 'bal tigzol' (do not steal). It distinguishes between two strong presumptions in the case of the employer (that he does not violate 'bal talin' and that the worker does not delay his wages) versus one presumption here.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a hired worker is believed with an oath, given the principle of 'בל תגזול' (do not steal), and distinguishes between two presumptions in the employer's case versus one presumption here.

items.text: Discussion of the condition 'if there are witnesses that he claimed'
items.text_en: Discussion of the condition 'if there are witnesses that he claimed'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if there are witnesses that the worker claimed his wages, he swears and takes. The Gemara questions why he needs witnesses if he is claiming before us. Rabbi Asi explains that the claim was made at the proper time. Abaye adds that he claimed throughout the entire period. Rav Hama bar Ukva clarifies that the oath is only regarding that day of the claim.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if there are witnesses that the worker claimed his wages, he swears and takes.
The Gemara asks why witnesses are needed if the worker is already claiming before us.
Rabbi Asi explains that the claim was made at the proper time.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the employer paid after the proper time.
Abaye adds that the worker claimed throughout the entire period.
The Gemara asks whether the employer never paid at all.
Rav Hama bar Ukva clarifies that the oath is only regarding that day of the claim.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: laws of taking collateral
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: laws of taking collateral
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that a lender may not take collateral except through court. He may not enter the debtor's home to take it, as it says 'stand outside'. If the debtor has two vessels, the lender takes one and leaves one. He must return a pillow at night and a plow by day. If the debtor dies, he does not return to heirs. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says he only returns for thirty days, then sells them in court.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states: one who lends to another may not take a pledge except through a court, and may not enter his house to take it; if he has two vessels, he takes one and leaves one.
The Mishnah continues: he returns the pillow at night and the plow by day; if the borrower dies, he does not return it to his heirs.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: even to the borrower himself he only returns the pledge for up to thirty days, and after thirty days the court sells them.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on the court agent and the Gemara's challenge
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on the court agent and the Gemara's challenge
items.desc_en: Shmuel rules that a court agent may appraise property but not take collateral. The Gemara challenges from the Mishnah which implies that through court one may take collateral. Shmuel reinterprets the Mishnah to mean 'not appraise except through court'. The Gemara supports this from the latter clause about not entering the home, which must refer to the court agent, not the creditor.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that a court agent may appraise property but not take collateral.
The Gemara challenges Shmuel from the Mishnah, which implies that through court one may take collateral.
Shmuel reinterprets the Mishnah to mean 'not appraise except through court'.
The Gemara supports Shmuel's interpretation from the latter clause about not entering the home, which must refer to the court agent, not the creditor.
The Gemara resolves the challenge by clarifying that the Mishnah permits the court agent to take collateral, while the creditor may not even appraise, to prevent entering the home.

items.text: Rav Yosef's objection and Rav Pappa's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's objection and Rav Pappa's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects from verses: 'Do not take a millstone' implies other items may be taken; 'Do not take a widow's garment' implies others' garments may be taken. If this refers to the creditor, it contradicts 'do not enter his home'. So it must refer to the court agent. Rav Pappa resolves that it always refers to the creditor, and the verses are to transgress two negative commandments.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects from verses that imply other items may be taken and other garments may be taken, arguing that if this refers to the creditor it contradicts 'do not enter his home', so it must refer to the court agent.
Rav Pappa resolves that the verses always refer to the creditor, and they are meant to transgress two negative commandments.

items.text: Final proof from the verse 'stand outside'
items.text_en: Final proof from the verse 'stand outside'
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a final proof: from the verse 'stand outside' one already knows that the debtor brings out the collateral. Why then say 'the man'? To include the court agent. The Gemara asks: does this mean the court agent is like the creditor?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a supporting baraita: from the verse 'Stand outside' it is obvious that 'the man to whom you are a creditor shall bring out' — so why the extra word 'the man'?
The baraita answers: the extra word 'the man' comes to include a court agent.
The Gemara asks: does this not imply that a court agent is like a creditor (and may take a pledge)?

items.text: Rejection of the comparison to a creditor
items.text_en: Rejection of the comparison to a creditor
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the idea that a court agent is like a creditor, implying a distinction between them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the comparison of a court agent to a creditor, stating they are not equivalent.

items.text: Proof from a verse that the law applies to a court agent
items.text_en: Proof from a verse that the law applies to a court agent
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita that interprets the verse 'If you take a garment as a pledge' as referring to a court agent, not a creditor, since the creditor is already addressed elsewhere.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a supporting baraita that interprets the verse 'אִם חָבֹל תַּחְבֹּל' as referring specifically to a court agent, not a creditor.

items.text: Dispute among Tannaim about the court agent's entry
items.text_en: Dispute among Tannaim about the court agent's entry
items.desc_en: Two baraitot are presented: one says the court agent must stand outside and the debtor brings out the pledge, while the other says the court agent may enter the house to take the pledge. The Gemara also lists items that cannot be taken and what must be left for the debtor.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute among Tannaim by citing a baraita that states the court agent must stand outside while the debtor brings out the pledge.
A second baraita is cited, which rules that the court agent may enter the debtor's house to take the pledge, while the creditor himself must remain outside.
The baraita lists items that cannot be taken as a pledge and specifies what must be left for the debtor, distinguishing between rich and poor.
